This is a <term>digital copy<note>An electronic reproduction of a physical text, created by scanning the original pages.</note></term> of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the <term>copyright<note>The legal right that grants the creator of an original work exclusive rights to its use and distribution for a limited time.</note></term> to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain<note>The state of belonging or being available to the public as a whole, and therefore not subject to copyright.</note></term>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia<note>Notes, scribbles, or comments written in the margins of a book by previous readers or owners.</note></term> present in the original volume will appear in this file - a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. <term>Copyright infringement<note>The use of works protected by copyright law without permission, infringing certain exclusive rights granted to the copyright holder.</note></term> liability can be quite severe.

### TO THE MOST EMINENT
### AND MOST SERENE
## PRINCES OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE
# ELECTORS
->MY MOST MERCIFUL LORDS.<-

It is only right that the erection of the Obelisks, which we are presently about to carry out, should be dedicated to those through whom the inviolate Majesty of the Holy Roman Empire has stood firm until this very time. For to you, Most Serene Lords, all Germany owes the fact that—wearied by long-lasting war <note>A reference to the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), which devastated Central Europe shortly before this text was written</note>, having struggled through so many crises, successions of slaughter, and the uncertain outcomes of battles—she has at last finally raised her joyful brow toward the Olive branch of peace, and, not unmindful of ancient triumphs, has confirmed herself in an illustrious and unchangeable state. Indeed, whether in peace or in war, you have looked to this one thing: that the ancient dignity of the Most Glorious Empire should not be diminished by any calamity of fortune. If the Danube beheld the sword drawn from its sheath, if the Elbe and the Main flowed discolored with blood for a long time, and the Rhine wept over the dead; all these things came to pass with this purpose: that through such a violent shaking, this most brave Nation might happily discharge into the surrounding seas the flood of filth collected over a long series of years. Therefore, let these same rivers, witnesses to your virtue, look upon the trophies fixed on both banks, the Pyramids raised, the Obelisks erected, and let them comfort their old grief with the new memory of the happiness procured by You. Likewise, among other things, it shall be most noble for Caesar Ferdinand III <note>Ferdinand III (1608–1657), Holy Roman Emperor and the author's patron</note>—under whose auspices we have labored upon this Work, however great it may be—to be seen in this same Theater of perennial glory, alongside the monuments of your virtue, which are just as many bases and most solid pillars for that Majesty which he himself holds.

<header>OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS</header>

# Several Authorities on Hieroglyphic Doctrine to be explained in the course of this Work.

->I.<-

### Aristotle, in his mystical Theology according to the mind of the Egyptians, received by word of mouth from Plato. Book 14, Chapter 14.
<note>original: "Theologia... iuxta mentem Aegyptiorum". This refers to the "Theology of Aristotle," a text actually based on Plotinus that was highly influential in the Renaissance and attributed to Aristotle.</note>

*The wise men of Babylon and Egypt, with sharpness of mind, looked into the species of the intellectual World, having embraced a knowledge either handed down from elsewhere or discovered by themselves, a profession which they claimed for themselves. Indeed, when they were about to relate something, they used intellectual doctrine, and not merely human methods like some others. Those who consulted them did not yet seem to themselves to learn firmly enough from opinions rendered in speech; therefore, they wrote down the concepts received in their minds—as we read with the evidence of our own eyes—upon stones through figures. They did the same in all sciences and arts, placing them in temples like pages to be read through; such were their useful books. They did this to indicate also that the immaterial acting intellect created all things according to the proper reason and likeness of each essence, which was a most excellent and beautiful teaching. Through this, I wish they would also indicate by what means they reached those wonderful and hidden forms, for thus their sacrament would be more worthy of praise—a condition which happens to few men.*

---

->II.<-

### Iamblichus, in his book on the Mysteries of the Egyptians.
<note>Iamblichus was a 4th-century Neoplatonist who defended theurgy (divine ritual) and Egyptian symbolism as a path to the divine.</note>

*The Egyptians, imitating the very nature of the universe and the fabric of the Gods, also display certain images of mystical and recondite notions in the making of symbols, just as nature expresses hidden reasons in apparent forms through symbols, and the Gods express the truth of ideas through manifest images.*

*Since they perceive, therefore, that all higher things delight in the likeness of lower things, and moreover desire to be filled with goodness from the higher powers so far as they may imitate them, they rightly offer a mode of acting suitable to the Higher Beings. They do this when they introduce the hidden mysteries of secret things into manifest symbols, in the interpretation of which: leave behind the words, and take the meanings. And on page 354: Now truly, they are not accustomed to contemplate these things with naked speech and reason; but they further admonish and teach that our nature progresses toward God himself, the Maker of the World, reaching toward things more excellent, more universal, and superior to fate; provided that it carries neither matter with it, nor anything else except the observation of the opportune time. They teach that we attain this through sacred works, and at the same time they bring it to pass. Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> himself handed down this way to us, but the Prophet Bitis interpreted it for King Ammon, having found it in the inner sanctuaries of the temple in the city of Sais in Egypt. Inscribed in sacred letters—that is, hieroglyphics—it also provided us with the name of GOD which runs through the universe.*

---

->III.<-

### Plotinus, Book 8 of the 5th Ennead, Chapter 6.

The wise men of the Egyptians also seem to me—whether they grasped it by accurate science or by an innate knowledge—to show forth through wisdom those things they wished to reveal. They did not use the forms of letters which travel through words and propositions, nor did they use the imitation of voices and the delivery of axioms; but by drawing images, and representing each individual thing...
<note>original Greek: "Δοκοῦσι δέ μοι καὶ οἱ Αἰγυπτίων σόφοι..." Kircher provides the Greek text of Plotinus to argue that hieroglyphs represent direct "intellectual intuition" rather than phonetic language.</note>

<summary>This page presents testimonies from ancient philosophers like Aristotle (Pseudo-Aristotle), Iamblichus, and Plotinus to justify the study of hieroglyphs as a divine, symbolic language. These authorities argue that Egyptian symbols were designed to bypass ordinary speech and communicate profound, hidden truths about the nature of the universe and the divine.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotle, Iamblichus, Plotinus, Hieroglyphics, Egyptian Mysteries, Hermes Trismegistus, Sais, Symbolism, Neoplatonism, Sacred Letters</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the nature of Egyptian hieroglyphs, moving from philosophical definitions to mystical and kabbalistic interpretations of their symbolic power.</meta>

# THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHICS

->[The Greek text above is a passage from Plotinus, *Enneads* 5.8.6, which the author subsequently translates into Latin below.]<-

...of the matter; by sculpting an image in the sacred places, he made the discourse of that thing visible. For each image is a kind of knowledge and wisdom, a subject and a whole, and not a process of reasoning or deliberation. But later, from this image, an unfolded likeness is produced in another medium, speaking in a discursive way and finding the causes why things are so rightly and beautifully arranged; and you marvel at this creation. <note>original: "πράγματος· ἄγαλμα ἐκτυπώσας..." This passage from the Neoplatonist Plotinus argues that hieroglyphs represent direct, divine intuition rather than step-by-step logic.</note>

It truly seems to me that the Sages of Egypt—whether through a certain perfected wisdom or a natural instinct of the mind—when they decided to signify the mysteries of wisdom to us, did not use the forms of letters which signify the discourses of speech and certain propositions, nor did they imitate the sounds and pronunciations of rules. Instead, by describing the individual images of individual things and painting them, they signified the discourse of the thing itself secretly in their sacred rites. This was because each image or exemplar is a certain knowledge and wisdom, a whole spectacle collected together, and not a mere thought or plan. But afterwards, from that exemplary image (or total wisdom), a likeness is formed in another medium, now unfolded and speaking in a discursive manner, finding the reasons why things were so established; while the very arrangement of things, because it is so well-ordered, moves one to admiration.

### IV.
### Simeon Ben Jochai in the book Zohar:

<note>The following is a translation of the Hebrew/Aramaic text provided in the manuscript, which discusses the four worlds of Kabbalah in relation to Egypt.</note>

The priests of Egypt explained their wisdom through signs, the likenesses of which are the likenesses of animals, and herbs, and all kinds of instruments. These were the signs of the 4 Worlds, of which the 1st is the World of Emanation <term>Atziluth; the highest realm of divine light</term>, the 2nd is the World of Angels <term>Beriyah/Yetzirah</term>, the 3rd is the World of the Spheres <term>Asiyah; the celestial bodies</term>, and the 4th is the World of the 4 Elements <note>original: "ד' טבעות" (four natures/elements)</note>. And all these 4 Worlds the Egyptians explained in parables of animals, and spoke of them in riddles, indicating how one is within the other, and how all testify that "the High One over the high is the guardian" <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 5:8</note>, and He is the Lord and Master, and the fashioner of all Worlds, and of all things that are in them.

---

### V.
### Mar Isaac, Chapter 6 of Philosophy:

<note>The following is a translation of the Syriac text provided, attributed to "Mar Isaac" (likely Isaac of Nineveh or a similar Eastern Christian authority).</note>

The method of Magic Science is perfected by the supreme powers together with the earthly powers, having a familiarity and agreement of the higher things with the lower things which are beneath the Moon; and this was the wisdom of the Philosophers of Egypt, carved into massive stones.

<meta>catchword: Aben- (referring to the next author, likely Abenephius or Ibn Wahshiyya)</meta>

OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS
<page-num>4</page-num>

# V. I.
## Ibn Wahshiyya, *Book on the Service of Egypt*.

Truly, many of the people of this land do not know what this riddle indicates, for the teaching was not of the people of Egypt, nor did they raise them; but a man came to us long ago from the land of Canaan, and he was excellent in wisdom, in grammar, in surveying, in calculation, in geometry, and in music, and in philosophy and the other common sciences which the ancients called the "teachings" [the Quadrivium]; and he offered this image as a gift to God. <note>original Arabic: "وإن كثيرين أهل هذا بلد..." This quote is from the work of Ibn Wahshiyya, a 9th-century scholar whose "Ancient Alphabets" Kircher believed provided a link to Egyptian wisdom. The "man from Canaan" is often interpreted as Abraham or Joseph.</note>

> Indeed, many among the people of this region are ignorant of what such enigmas signify, and this is because the natives did not consecrate them; but a certain man once withdrew to us from the land of Canaan, who was eminent in Wisdom, and in Grammar, Geometry, Music, Arithmetic, Philosophy, and the rest of the signified sciences, which the Ancients mark as "the disciplines"; and he offered these figures as a gift, that they might be sacred to God.

# Suppositions of the Hermeneutic or Interpretive Art of Hieroglyphics.

1. The Hieroglyphic doctrine of the Egyptians is nothing other than the science of the secrets of God, divine Ideas, Angels, Demons, and the other classes and orders of World Powers, primarily inscribed upon stones.

2. Hieroglyphic symbols, established after the model of nature, do not form the senses of hidden mysteries through letters, syllables, words, or sentences, but through the *Ideal concepts* of those mysteries.

3. Hieroglyphic symbols on Obelisks and other Egyptian monuments are not heaped together randomly or <note>original Greek: ἀλόγως καὶ ἀτάκτως—without reason and without order</note>, but exhibit the sacraments of formed concepts with the highest degree of connection.

4. Hieroglyphs involve various meanings according to the variety and analogy of the "Worlds" which they have toward each other. That is, one and the same symbol—for example, a <term>Hawk</term> [denoting the Sun]—indicates the Sun not only of the Starry world, but also of the Archetypal, Intellectual, Ethical, Political, and Chemical Worlds, depending on the condition of the accompanying marks. Thus, the said symbol can equally express the supramundane <term>Osiris</term>, as well as the Starry and Material versions of him, according to the intended analogy. The same is to be understood regarding <term>Isis</term>, <term>Mophta</term>, <term>Anubis</term>, and the other monstrous forms of the Gods; likewise for the bowls, waters, vessels, and the rest.

5. Hieroglyphic symbols were not only significative of sublime sacraments; they were also believed to have a certain natural efficacy. They were thought to attract good <term>Genii</term> [spirits] with whom they possessed an occult sympathy hiding in the deep abyss of nature; and they were thought to restrain and drive away contrary and "anti-craft" Spirits due to their natural antipathy toward them.

6. Hieroglyphic symbols were considered to be nothing other than certain prophylactic [protective] signs, capable of averting all evils, because of the wonderful agreement and connection of the "world-chains." <note>This refers to the "Great Chain of Being," the Hermetic belief that all parts of the universe are linked by spiritual resonances.</note>

With these things having been set forth, let us now at last, under the auspices of the divine Power, begin the work we have undertaken—a work truly difficult, and to be dreaded even by the shoulders of Hercules.

<summary>Kircher establishes six foundational rules for interpreting hieroglyphs, arguing they are not phonetic letters but symbols of divine "Ideas" that possess magical efficacy to attract spirits and protect the wearer.</summary>
<keywords>Ibn Wahshiyya, Canaan, Hermeneutics, Hieroglyphics, Hawk, Osiris, Isis, Anubis, Genii, Prophylactic, Sympathy and Antipathy, Great Chain of Being</keywords>

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS
## OR THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER Volume III.
### PREFACE TO THE MOST WISE FERDINAND III, ROMAN EMPEROR, JUST, PIOUS, AND BLESSED.

We finally reveal, Most Sacred Caesar, the polymorphous <note>meaning many-shaped</note> kingdom of Hieroglyphic *Morpheus* <note>The god of dreams and shapes, here used to represent the shifting forms of symbols</note>; a Theater, I say, filled with an immense variety of monsters; I do not mean bare monsters of nature, but those adorned with the enigmatic *Chimeras* of ancient wisdom, such that I trust sagacious minds may dig out from them immense treasures of the sciences, not without benefit to literature. Here the *Dog of Bubastis* <note>original: "Bubasticus Canis"; a reference to the jackal-headed god Anubis</note>, the *Lion of Sais*, the *Goat of the Mendesians*, and the *Crocodile*, formidable with the foul gaping of its jaws, reveal the hidden senses of divinity, nature, and souls, which the ancient Sages tucked away under the shadowy mockery of images. Here thirsty *Dipsades* <note>serpents whose bite was thought to cause intense thirst</note>, virulent *Aspics*, clever *Ichneumons* <note>a type of mongoose believed by ancients to be the enemy of the crocodile</note>, cruel *Hippopotami*, monstrous *Dragons*, the pot-bellied toad, the coiled snail shell, and the hairy caterpillar—countless ghosts—exhibit a wondrous series and order in the sanctuaries of nature. 

Here occur a thousand species of things transformed by a certain exotic metamorphosis, where human figures are converted into various other images and joined back to themselves in a mutual bond; where wildness meets humanity, and humanity meets an affected divinity; and where divinity itself, to speak with *Porphyry* <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>, passing through the species of all things, seems to have meditated a monstrous marriage with all. Where now, sublime with a variegated face, one here bears a *Cynocephalus* <note>original: "Cynocephalum"; a dog-headed baboon</note> raising its canine neck; another, dressed in the beaked mask of the foul *Ibis* or the *Hawk*, acts out the bird of Great Jove; yet another, charming with a maiden's face in the cloak of a *Beetle*, counterfeits with the sting <note>original: "acu-", likely "aculeum" or sting, completed on the next page</note>—

<meta>The catchword "acu-" at the bottom of the page indicates the continuation of the word "aculeum" (sting or point) on the following page.</meta>

<summary>This page serves as a rhetorical and metaphorical introduction to the third volume, dedicated to Emperor Ferdinand III. Kircher describes his work as a "theater" of Egyptian symbols—ranging from animals like the crocodile and ibis to monstrous hybrids—which he believes encode the deep scientific and divine secrets of the ancient world.</summary>
<keywords>Ferdinand III, Hieroglyphic Theater, Anubis, Porphyry, Cynocephalus, Egyptian mythology, natural philosophy, symbolism</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface to Emperor Ferdinand III. Kircher moves from listing specific Egyptian creatures and symbols to describing the "Theater of Nature" as a whole—a place of monsters and confusion that has defeated previous scholars like Pliny. He frames his own attempt as a divine mission supported by the Emperor's patronage, leading into the "practical interpretation" of hieroglyphs.</meta>

...sting. Others, with various species of things joined together into one truly ridiculous fiction, appear now as three-formed Sphinges, now—to summarize much in a few words—as Chimeras or *wolf-fly-lions* <note>original: "λυκό-μυιο-λέοντες"; a hybrid monster combining a wolf, fly, and lion</note>; others seem to represent Cerberuses <note>the multi-headed hound of the underworld</note> emerging, as it were, from Pluto’s workshop. Nor are the shapeless Canopic jars <note>Egyptian vessels used for organs, often topped with animal or human heads</note> of the Isiacs missing, protruding with such excessive swelling of the body that you might call them nothing but bellies. What more? You might see here that shameful long-tailed monkey gesturing in various ways, wearing a woven cap, and standing in the guise of the shepherds' *Catamite* <note>another name for Ganymede, the cup-bearer to the gods; here Kircher is mocking the perceived absurdity of the symbols</note> dressed in saffron and Phrygian robes. You would also see an ox of enormous thickness, the fertile deity of the omnipotent Goddess <note>likely Isis or Hathor</note>, conspicuous with a rhythmic gait and wings stuck on, as if attempting flight; both are so adorned with these symbols that you might call the former Bellerophon and the latter Pegasus, yet you would laugh at both. In a word, whatever Egypt—that fertile mother of portents—ever devised, or whatever the playful genius of poetry invented, we contemplate here in this all-shaping theater of nature, placed before our eyes under the allegorical veil of hidden meaning. Furthermore, who, gazing upon this bristling face of things, would not immediately lose heart? Who would safely commit himself to this monster-filled desert through inhospitable wastes, rough paths, and countless cliffs of precipices without a guide skilled in the ways? Who, having entered these theaters, would dare to encounter so many monsters and portents with impunity, and—unless equipped with only leaden and blunt daggers—rashly, so to speak, *act as an amateur* <note>original: "ἰδιωτεύειν"; to play the layman or unskilled person</note>? I see Pliny <note>the Roman author of the 'Natural History'</note>, the expert on all of nature, fall in this battle; I also see Aelian, the clever investigator of nature, as well as Marcellinus and Hermapion—the "Cymbals of the World" <note>Hermapion was an ancient translator of obelisks mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus; "Cymbals of the World" was a nickname for the empty noise of certain scholars</note>—and other heroes who, desponding of victory at the first conflict, spun fables for themselves as an ingenious, or if you prefer, a cunning escape. Will I not, therefore, in this contest be deservedly called rash by everyone, as if attempting Icarus-like daring? But take heart!

<margin>Quintus of Smyrna, Book 12.</margin>
> For the Gods placed troubles before the feet of men,
> But blessings very far away, and in the middle they established toil.

Where human strength fails, divine goodness will be present, which has spurred me toward this from my early years, and will grant me the grace to complete what I have asked to be possible through its help. But to explain my mind a little more clearly, by the divine auspice of the Godhead, we proceed to the ultimate and sole goal of our intention, toward which we have aimed thus far with such laborious preparation in these two volumes: that is, to the practical <term>hieroglyphic</term> <note>Kircher believed hieroglyphs were purely symbolic and mystical rather than phonetic</note> interpretation, to be completed with the best possible manner and method. A truly arduous work, entangled in countless difficulties, promised to the Republic of Letters twenty years ago, and now finally to be presented as a debt paid. That which you commanded, Most Sacred Caesar <note>Emperor Ferdinand III</note>, I have executed according to the modesty of my talent; so that henceforth, whatever is found excellent in this work should be called yours rather than mine, born from your will, from the sign of your favorable disposition toward the learned, and from your singular generosity of support. Let grateful posterity know that you were divinely chosen by God in this propagation of a harder time, so that what no one [could]...

# THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHS.

*...which no Caesar before you, by any force or power, could obtain, you might obtain, you might complete, and you might fulfill and perfect in every respect.*

*But the same thing seems to have happened to me here as happened to Isis, who, though she had steadfastly overcome all her struggles, could not escape the cruelty of the Titans. Having thoroughly tamed the aforementioned monsters and subjugated the bloody beasts through constant labor, while I am restoring Osiris <note>In Egyptian myth, Isis gathered the scattered pieces of her husband Osiris to restore him; Kircher uses this as a metaphor for his attempt to reassemble the "scattered" knowledge of hieroglyphs</note>, Horus—the offspring conceived with such great effort—is attacked by the cruelty of the Titans. While, I say, I labor to recall that sublime and hitherto unattempted science of hieroglyphs, which had been scattered and destroyed by the cruelty of Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos who murdered Osiris</note>—that is, by the injustice of the ages—and having now tamed all the monsters of difficulty and restored the lost Osiris to wholeness; I lose Horus through the injustice of the Titans. That is to say, unjust censors of things will perhaps attempt in every way to snatch away this offspring, born of my own industry, supreme labor, stubborn effort, and finally, concentrated study. For in this material—at once new, rare, curious, and full of an abundance and plenty of extraordinary things—it is also highly exposed to envy (which is like a shadow accompanying shining glory). I foresee that the perverse judgments of certain Aristarchuses <note>original: "Aristarcharum"; a reference to Aristarchus of Samothrace, a famously severe literary critic</note> and Momian <note>original: "Momicas"; relating to Momus, the Greek god of mockery and unfair criticism</note> rebukes will by no means be lacking; no learned man sweating in such an arduous and glorious struggle has ever been able to escape them. Yet their attacks are not to be feared. For although I may not have perhaps reached total perfection in this work, I am nonetheless not unaware that the boundaries of human strength are limited, and that "it is something to have advanced this far, even if it is not granted to go further" <note>A quote from the Roman poet Horace, expressing that partial progress in a difficult task is still honorable</note>. For if I wished to discourse worthily on the excellence or utility of the present subject, or the knowledge and explanation it brings, no end would ever be found. So be it, then, that I cannot—nor can anyone else—exhaust this whole sea of mysteries, or completely survey its widely extended circuit; should one therefore abandon a noble and laborious undertaking because it is denied to one man to excel? Not at all. Those are greatly deluded who consider nothing worthy or precious unless it is perfect in every respect; let them persuade themselves that such perfection is by no means reserved for man situated in this fleeting world, but for one drawn away into the other life. Let the attackers of things they do not understand cease, therefore, to reproach me for a subject of such great weight. I labor for God, who, through His infinite mercy, will grant that I may bring what I have undertaken to a conclusion. You, Caesar, commanded me, and I thought it a sin not to obey. Almost the entire world of letters has urged me to proceed; why do I delay? Let the Work come forth, then, in which whatever is erroneous, crippled, mutilated, and imperfect, you should ascribe entirely to my insufficiency; but whatever is*

->*perfect, and worthy of admiration, I wish you to ascribe to God,*<-
->*the Best and Greatest.*<-

# PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE.
## On Hieroglyphs in General.
### CHAPTER I.
#### On the Etymology, Origin, and Spread of Hieroglyphic Teaching.

<margin>What a hieroglyph is.</margin>
The word HIEROGLYPHIC—derived from the Greek *hieron* [sacred] and *glyphein* [to carve] <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ ἱεροῦ καὶ γλύφειν"</note>—is nothing other than a "symbol of a sacred thing" carved into stone. It is called a "Symbol" to indicate that it contains a mysterious meaning. It is called a "sacred thing" to distinguish it from common or profane symbols. <margin>Two types of parables among the Egyptians.</margin> For there were two types of parables <note>Kircher uses "parable" here to mean a figurative representation or story</note> used by the Egyptians: one was "popular" <note>original: "δημώδες" (demodes), referring to common or demotic script/speech</note>, which embraced common and everyday comparisons; the other was "sacred" <note>original: "ἱερον" (hieron)</note>, which was drawn from a more holy and secret doctrine. <margin>What the Egyptians carved hieroglyphically.</margin> It will soon become clear that the Egyptians did not carve hieroglyphs to record histories, the praises of Kings and Princes, the liberal arts, or any other such human inventions—as many have falsely convinced themselves until now. Rather, they carved them to represent sacred matters, pertaining either to the properties of the divine nature, the distribution of the orders and protections of Angels and Spirits, or the methods of theurgy <note>The practice of rituals intended to invoke the presence of or communicate with gods or spirits</note> and sacred purifications. <margin>Hieroglyphs were carved not only on stone but also on other materials.</margin> We say "carved in stone" not because they did not also write them on other materials (for I find them carved on wood, papyrus, pottery, and the wrappings and fringes of burial shrouds), but because they primarily carved the entire substance of hieroglyphic teaching on the walls and gates of temples, on Obelisks, on statues of the Gods, and on stone tablets, so that these things might be preserved faithfully for all posterity against the ravages of time. Those items intended for the private use of the Egyptians, such as the amulets common to all, were carved on whatever material a person could afford. <margin>Saint Cyril.</margin> Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria, a 5th-century Church Father</note> says in Book 9 of *Against Julian*: *“Among the Egyptians, there were certain men endowed with great industry and gravity regarding enigmas, whom they usually called 'hieroglyphs' [sacred carvers]. These men carved signs onto temples and Obelisks; they did not use common letters, but rather depicted the natures of things through various figures, thereby increasing the knowledge of the wise.”*

<margin>The study of wisdom flourished in every age among some people.</margin>
Furthermore, as to who was the original Author of Hieroglyphs: although I have discussed this very extensively in my work *The Pamphili Obelisk* <note>Kircher refers to his 1650 book *Obeliscus Pamphilius*, which analyzed the obelisk in Rome’s Piazza Navona</note>, I have thought it appropriate to insert certain things here that I omitted there. It should be noted that no age has ever existed so shrouded in the darkness of ignorance that it did not emit at least some ray of wisdom, as if through the clouds, or at least shimmer with a refracted and dim light. For Wisdom is a charming conciliator, and like a seductive cloak of knowledge, she does not allow a human being to be cast down forever like a useless beast of a fattened body to mere feeding and trivial cares. Instead, she has fixed a certain image of honor in the human heart; and if this image is frequently stirred up...

...earlier, he will clearly fan those little sparks of knowledge that we perceive in human minds. From this source, all the arts and sciences have flourished, by which the mind—struggling bravely against the burden of the body and that treacherous scarcity of material things—has ensured that the light of genius grows in the most noble studies. Eventually, it strives toward the form of a more transformed knowledge, reaching it not by gentle slopes, but through the various windings of difficulties. Among all mortals, however, it has been proved throughout my work *The Pamphilian Obelisk* that no one was stronger in this competitive goal of letters than **Hermes Trismegistus**. Indeed, nothing was so important to him as to restore **Wisdom**—passed down by the world's earliest Patriarchs and by far the most excellent of all things that could be desired in human affairs. To prevent it from being contaminated by common minds, he wrapped it in the coverings of hieroglyphic figures in such a way that he might open the "marrow" of his wisdom only to those whom he himself judged worthy and fit. To the rest, placed outside the barriers of the Priestly order he established, only the "bark" <note>Kircher uses the metaphor of the "bark" or "rind" of a fruit to describe the superficial, literal meaning that the uninitiated see, while the "marrow" represents the hidden, spiritual truth.</note> was left.

<margin>Hieroglyphic doctrine was communicated by Trismegistus to the Priests alone.</margin>
For when he contemplated this world, joined together from such a great variety of things like a stage decorated with the most refined images, he rightly thought that the likenesses of created things of this sort should be pronounced <term>the symbols of God</term> <note>original Greek: "τὰ Θεοῦ σύμβολα"</note>. These are the very things God impressed upon us through so many visible forms of Himself—so many letters illuminated by the great radiance of divinity, with which that Power of the Eternal Mind might sign His own name.

<margin>The origin of Hieroglyphic doctrine.</margin>
And from here, the first <term>elementary principles</term> <note>original Greek: "στοιχειώσεις" (stoicheioseis), referring to the basic components or "alphabet" of a system.</note> of hieroglyphics emerged. Sketched out by the first Patriarchs—*Adam, Enoch, Noah, and Ham*—and perfected in every detail by Hermes, they rose into a more noble form through the stupendous architecture of the Hieroglyphs. This system was thereafter held in such high renown among the Egyptians that even the sacred text itself affirms that *Moses* did not disdain this teaching; it says that *Moses* was endowed with all the wisdom of the Egyptians. *Philo*, in his book on the life of Moses (whose words I have cited elsewhere), says this was nothing other than the occult Philosophy, written in what they call hieroglyphic letters:

<margin>Moses was instructed in hieroglyphic doctrine. Philo.</margin>
> "The philosophy expressed through symbols, which he displays in the so-called letters, and through the use of animals, which they even honor with the dignity of Gods;" <note>original Greek: "Τὴν διὰ συμβόλων φιλοσοφίαν ἥν ἐν τοῖς λεγομένοις γράμμασιν ἐπιδείκνυται, καὶ διὰ τῆς ζώων ἀποδοχῆς, ἃ καὶ Θεῶν τιμῆς γεράρουσι;"</note>

that is, *by the marks of animals which they themselves worship as Divinities.* So it is clear from this chapter alone how ancient that wisdom is, which had *Moses* himself as a student.

<margin>Hermes Trismegistus is the Author of hieroglyphic doctrine. Plato. Philo of Byblos.</margin>
That *Hermes* was truly the Author of this literature is taught by *Plato* himself in the *Phaedrus*, where he calls him *Thautus* or *Thoth*. Also, *Philo of Byblos*—who translated the history of *Sanchuniathon* (a very ancient author contemporary with *Moses*) into Greek—openly teaches that *Tautus*, or *Hermes Trismegistus*, was the first Teacher of symbolic literature. All these things have been proven at great length in the second book of *The Pamphilian Obelisk*, to which I refer the reader so that I am not forced to repeat the same things so many times. Therefore, since the hieroglyphic doctrine and its Author flourished long before the time of *Moses*, that author could certainly be no other than **Mercury Trismegistus** (whom the Arabs call <term>Idris</term> <note>original Arabic: "إدريس"</note>), the Priest, Philosopher, and greatest King of Egypt. It has been more than sufficiently demonstrated in this entire Work that he flourished in the time of Abraham, while *Misraim*, the first Pharaoh, held power in Egypt. This is confirmed by *Iamblichus* in the first chapter of *On the Mysteries*, where he mentions that *Pythagoras*, *Plato*, *Eudoxus*, and the other [scholars] of Greece...

# CHAPTER II.

->*How Hieroglyphs are distinguished from the letters of other diverse Nations, and especially in what way the Characters of the Chinese differ from Hieroglyphs.*<-

<margin>Almost all nations have characters that signify concepts.</margin>
<margin>The Chinese, Brahmins, and Mexicans especially.</margin>
The experience of time has made it known to us that there is almost no nation so barbarian, no nation so unrefined, that it does not use its own characters to manifest concepts to one another. However, we are not speaking here of letters and characters established and defined by a certain alphabet, but of significative characters involving the entire concept of a certain thing. And it is established that three nations, above all other peoples of the world, have used these: namely, the Chinese, the Brahmins, and the Mexicans; we shall discuss their letters and characters in this place, beginning our start with the Chinese.

### *The Hieroglyphic Characters of the Chinese.*

<margin>When the characters of the Chinese were instituted.</margin>
The Chinese, from the connection of their own Annals and times, place the first invention of letters almost three hundred years after the Flood; their first founder and King was a man named Fohi <note>Kircher refers to Fu Xi, the legendary first emperor of China, to whom the invention of writing and the I Ching hexagrams are traditionally attributed.</note>. This is held in the *Book of the Succession of Kings*. And the first form of the characters is found in the *Book on the Method of Forming Chinese Letters*, which, while I was writing this, was shared with me by the Reverend Father Michael Boym, a Pole of the Society of JESUS. He had traveled to Rome from the region of the Chinese for the sake of business and is most skilled both in the Chinese language and in all matters pertaining to the customs and habits of the said Kingdom. From him, I received by word of mouth many things regarding the Chinese method of reading and writing; from these, I shall describe only those things which are proper to my purpose. The curious reader will find the remaining things concerning the Kingdom of the Chinese, its government, and the nature of the language described most copiously in the *Summary Explanation of Chinese Affairs* <note>original: "dilucidatio ſummaria rerum Sinicarum"</note>, which was most richly and carefully prepared by the aforementioned Father.

<margin>The descendants of Ham seem to have sent colonies into China.</margin>
I said that almost three hundred years after the Flood, at nearly the same time when the sons of Noah <note>original: "Noëmi"</note> were ruling the world, they [extended] their empire to the ends of the entire world...

### THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER. CHAPTER II.

...propagating [the idea] that the first invention of letters was discovered by the Emperor Fohi <note>Fuxi, the legendary first emperor of China, whom Kircher identifies with the biblical line of Noah</note>, who was taught this only by the descendants of Noah. For as was related in the first Volume, Ham <note>original: "Cham"</note> first transferred his colonies from Egypt into Persia, and from there into Bactria; we have established that he is the same person as Zoroaster, the King of the Bactrians. Now Bactria, the most remote region of Persia, bordering the Kingdom of the Mughals, is situated in such a convenient location that from there, colonies could easily be transferred into China—the furthest nation of the inhabited world. Along with these colonies, they were able to transfer the first elements of letters, which they had learned (though imperfectly) from their father Ham and from Mercury Trismegistus, the advisor to Ham's son Mizraim <note>original: "Mefraimi," the biblical progenitor of the Egyptians</note> and the first teacher of hieroglyphs. Certainly, an argument of great weight that leads me to believe this is

<margin>Chinese characters are similar to hieroglyphs.</margin>
those ancient characters of the Chinese, which in every way rival the hieroglyphs. First, it is clear from their own chronicles that the first Chinese constructed their characters from all things of the world, and the very form of the characters demonstrates this more than enough. Just like the Egyptians, they formed their characters from animals, birds, reptiles, fish, herbs, tree branches, ropes, threads, points, circles, and similar things, though arranged in one way or another. Later, however, the Chinese became more learned through experience; when they saw the great confusion in such a vast heap of animals and plants, they imitated these variously shaped characters with certain strokes of points and lines, refining them into a shorter method which they use to this very day. Indeed, the number of these is so great that

<margin>The huge multitude of Chinese characters.</margin>
today, no one is counted among the highest literati who does not possess a knowledge of at least eighty thousand characters; and thus, the more letters a person knows, the more learned he is considered compared to others. Nevertheless, ten thousand of these are sufficient for learning the language so that one can converse passably. Furthermore, the Chinese have their letters arranged in no way like an Alphabet, as is the custom with other nations, nor do they have words composed of letters and syllables.

<margin>Individual Chinese characters correspond to individual words.</margin>
Instead, individual characters correspond to individual words and names; and thus they need as many characters as there are things they wish to express through the concepts of the mind. For instance, if someone attempted to translate an entire <term>Calepinus</term> <note>A reference to the "Dictionarium" by Ambrogio Calepino, which was the standard comprehensive dictionary of the time; Kircher uses it to mean "an entire vocabulary."</note> into their language, it would be necessary to have as many diverse and different characters as there are different words in it. They use neither declensions nor conjugations, since all these things (as will be seen shortly) are implied in the characters themselves. Therefore, one must be endowed with a great memory if they intend to reach even a moderate level of learning proper to the Chinese. It is for this reason, not without merit, that those who have reached the highest level of erudition—spending their entire lives and undergoing the greatest labors to learn the characters—are assigned the first ranks and titles in the administration of the Kingdom.

CHAPTER II. 12 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

### Anatomy of the Ancient Chinese Characters.

<margin>Examples of ancient Chinese characters.</margin>
<margin>The Ancient Chinese formed characters from all things.</margin>
We have said in the preceding pages that the first Chinese <note>original: "Sinas"</note> took their original characters from all things presented to the sight, and manifested the concepts of their minds only through the various order and arrangement of these assembled things. Hence, when they intended to treat a subject of a fiery nature, they used serpents, asps, and dragons, which—arranged in such and such an order—signified such and such a thing. In describing things of the air, they used the various arrangement of birds; in a subject concerning water, fish; in describing the nature of plants, they used flowers, leaves, and branches; in the stars, they used points or circles, each of which expressed individual stars. In other neutral subjects, they employed wood, spheres, and threads arranged according to a certain law.

But so that these things may appear more clearly, I have thought it necessary to set down here the original characters of the ancient Chinese, so that the curious reader may more clearly see the difference between them and the modern <note>By "modern," Kircher refers to the 17th-century Chinese scripts, such as Clerical or Standard script, provided to him by Jesuit missionaries like Michael Boym.</note> characters, and the hieroglyphs of the Egyptians. For the moderns no longer seem to use figurative characters of that kind, but rather certain strokes of lines; nevertheless, these strokes closely resemble the figurative letters used by the Ancients, as appears in the following figures. In these, letter **A** imitates the same strokes as the figurative letter **B** of the ancients. The same will appear in the moderns' letter **C** compared to the ancients' letter **D**, as also **E** to **F**, and **G** to **H**, and **I** to **K**. Both of these last two signify a "river" <note>original: "flumen"</note> based on a certain arrangement of fish, which the moderns imitate through letter **I**, formed from similar strokes.

1. Label A shows a modern script character (resembling 'Seal' script), and label B shows three stylized trees/branches, further marked with the Greek letter β. 
2. Label C shows a modern script character, and label D shows four undulating, serpent-like lines, further marked with the Greek letter α. 
3. Label E shows a modern script character, and label F shows a celestial star/sun symbol resting on a pedestal, further marked with the Greek letter ζ.

5. Label I shows a modern script character (representing 'river'), and label K shows several fish swimming vertically, further marked with the letter X.</image-desc>

Therefore, in the same way that the earliest people arranged such figurative characters from the shapes of different animals to manifest their concepts, their descendants exhibited them not with animals, but with certain strokes of lines and points. As has been said, this custom has remained until this very day, as can be seen in the figures proposed just above, **A B C D E F G H I K**. Where the ancients used branches, leaves, and fish arranged in a certain order, the moderns use certain strokes that are nevertheless similar and, in a way, parallel. But let us return to our purpose.

THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER II.

## The difference between Chinese characters and the Hieroglyphics of the Egyptians.

<margin>The handled cross and the statue of Serapis among the Chinese characters.</margin>
**W**e have said in the preceding pages that it is likely that the descendants of Ham, having propagated colonies as far as the most remote region of the Chinese, also propagated letters at the same time; however, these were not adorned with as much apparatus of mysteries as the Egyptian hieroglyphs, but were prepared with a simple wit <note>original: "rudi Minerva," a Latin idiom meaning simply or without much artifice</note> as much as was sufficient for explaining the concepts of the mind. Certainly, among the Chinese characters, the Cross—which is held in such great honor among the Egyptians—is very frequently seen, as figure O shows; just as among the Egyptians, it signifies the number ten, a symbol of perfection. If they place another line beneath this, as appears in N, a character is formed that signifies the earth. If they add another line at the top, parallel to the lower one, as appears in M, a character is formed that signifies a King. If they add a small stroke to this figure, as appears in L, a character is formed that signifies a gem. Just as these last three characters indicate a certain perfection in their own kind, so they are not incongruously formed by means of the cross.

<margin>10 ten</margin>
<margin>Earth</margin>
<margin>King</margin>
<margin>Stone, gem, *yú* <note>Kircher correctly identifies "yu" as the Chinese word for jade.</note></margin>
<image-desc>A vertical column of four large Chinese characters, each identified by a letter and a Latin gloss.
- O: 十 (the character for ten, which Kircher interprets as a cross).
- N: 土 (the character for earth).

<margin>The difference between the characters of the Chinese and the hieroglyphs of the Egyptians.</margin>
And although the Chinese, no differently than the Egyptians, expressed the meanings of their minds from a variety of animals, plants, and tools, there nevertheless existed a great difference between both methods of writing. For the Egyptians by no means employed hieroglyphics in common conversation, nor was it permitted for just anyone to learn them, but only those who were deputed to it by law and political institution. For they did not use the figures of animals randomly or <term>without reason</term> <note>original: "ἀλόγως" (alogōs)</note>, but signified the highest mysteries in the nature of things through their hidden virtues and operations, as is evident from this entire Work. Furthermore, hieroglyphic letters did not involve simple utterances or names, but entire ideal concepts; thus, looking upon the Scarab, they did not understand the animal, or the Sun precisely, but the hidden operations which not only the material Sun effects in this sensible World, but also the archetype effects in the intelligible World. All of these things are lacking in the structure of Chinese characters, since these were instituted precisely only to indicate the simple concepts of words and names, with no other mystery lying hidden beneath them. I do not deny, however, that the Chinese occasionally adapt the meanings of different characters in such a way that a meaning of ingenious allusion emerges from them; these, however, by no means approach the subtlety and the clever allusions of the hieroglyphs, as is evident from the following compositions of letters; where the character C signifies the same thing as "to be afflicted," and is composed of two characters, B and A, of which the former signifies the heart, and the latter a gate; as if...

The Chinese have countless other characters of this kind, composed from the joining together of diverse characters, with which they allude—not without ingenuity—to the secret meanings of things; these we deliberately omit.

### THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHS: CHAPTER II.

...driven by the pressing prayers of several people, I am compelled to fulfill this task.

<margin>The Chinese language is most difficult.</margin>
Since, therefore, the Chinese language is equivocal <note>Meaning many words sound the same but have different meanings.</note> in a surprising manner, and a single word often signifies ten, or even twenty different things, distinguished only by the delivery of a different accent, it is rendered difficult beyond what can be expressed; it cannot be learned by foreigners except with the greatest labor, intense study, and with a thousand deliberations.

<margin>The language of the Chinese Mandarins.</margin>
The Mandarin language is common to the whole Kingdom, and its principal use is in the Courts and the Royal Palace, which are located in Peking <note original: "Paquini">Beijing</note> and Nanjing <note original: "Nanchini">Nanjing</note>; it is the same throughout the whole Kingdom, just as Castilian is in Spain and Tuscan is in Italy.

<margin>The Chinese character is the same as that of the Japanese and other adjacent Nations.</margin>
The characters are common to the entire Kingdom of China, as well as to Japan, Korea, Cochinchina <note>The southern region of modern-day Vietnam.</note>, and Tonkin <note>The northern region of modern-day Vietnam.</note>; yet the spoken language is very different. Hence the peoples of Japan, Cochinchina, Korea, and Tonkin certainly understand books and letters written in this kind of character, yet they cannot speak to one another, nor understand one another when speaking; this is no different than how the figures of numbers used everywhere across Europe are understood by everyone, even though the words by which they are pronounced are very different. For the characters are signs of concepts of things common to all.

<margin>The Chinese character signifies different things according to the various changes of accent.</margin>
From this it follows that it is one thing to know the Chinese characters, and another to speak the Chinese language; for a foreigner endowed with a good memory and diligent study could arrive at the highest erudition through the reading of Chinese books, even if he could neither speak nor understand the spoken language.

<margin>Accents discovered by Europeans for pronouncing Chinese characters.</margin>
However, because the spoken language is entirely necessary for the Apostolic Men <note>Missionaries, specifically Jesuits like Kircher's sources.</note> laboring in the cause of God, they have discovered marks—similar to musical notes such as *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la* <note>The traditional "solfège" syllables used in music; "ut" was later changed to "do."</note>—to track the rise and fall of Chinese accents observed in pronunciation, by which they might be helped in overcoming the difficulty of the language. These marks, written above the Chinese words transcribed in the European manner, are expressed in the following way: ^, -, `, ', ˇ. 

The first mark of the five Chinese accents, ^, corresponds to the musical *ut*, and the sound or pronunciation is called *chŏ pîm* <note>Level tone (Píng).</note> in Chinese, as if you were to say: the first voice coming forth evenly. The second mark, -, corresponds to the musical *re*, and the sound is called *pîm xīm* in Chinese, as if you were to say: a clear, even voice. The third mark, `, corresponds to the musical *mi*, and the sound is called *xăm xǐm* in Chinese, that is: a high voice. The fourth mark, ', corresponds to the musical *fa*, called *kiú xǐm* in Chinese, that is: the high voice of one departing. The fifth mark, ˇ, corresponds to the musical *sol*, called *gè xǐm* in Chinese, that is: the hurried voice of one entering. 

Thus, for example, a single word, *ya*, written with European letters and marked with the five accents above, must be pronounced with different voices and tones, just as it is written by the Chinese with different characters. So that the same spoken word might convey different meanings to the ears of the listeners, the speech, delivered bit by bit, resembles the timing of music—an ordered harmony arising from monosyllabic words (for there are no polysyllables among the Chinese). We have expressed the forms of the five vowels or accents placed above here as you see:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| Tooth | yâ | 牙 |
| Mute | yā | 啞 |
| Excellent | yà | 雅 |
| Amazement | yá | 訝 |
| Goose | yǎ | 鴉 |

With the help of these marks, foreigners learn the language; yet with how much labor and with how many deliberations, it is easier to imagine than to depict with a pen. However, the Chinese...

# CHAPTER II. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

however, they do not use accent marks of this kind, but grow accustomed to these pronunciations from childhood, as nearly all nations do; nevertheless, their scholars know and teach how any character should be pronounced with its due accent, not only in practice but also in theory <note>Kircher uses the Scholastic terms 'in actu exercito' (in the act itself) and 'in actu signato' (as a formal concept or sign).</note>. They marvel, moreover, that Europeans are able to write their spoken words using Latin letters and represent them so authentically. Since, as we have said, they lack both their own and our alphabet, any of their characters can serve as a first, middle, or last "letter," as each one signifies a specific sound and an entire word. These words indeed have a great variety of meanings; for example, this word *y* has at least thirty different meanings depending on the diversity of characters and pronunciation. Furthermore, a primary character such as *Chùn* is pronounced one way in the Mandarin language, another in Japan, and another in different kingdoms, although it always signifies the same thing. Thus, whoever sees this character <note>Archaic Chinese character for "respect" (zun 尊)</note> forms the concept *çún*, which is the same as "to revere"; and so it is with others. It is for this reason that I said that he who knows one of their languages along with the characters will be able to travel not only through the whole Kingdom of China, but through many others by means of writing. But having proposed these things, it is now time for us to examine the characters of the ancient Chinese.

### An explanation of the most ancient Chinese characters.

<margin>An explanation of the most ancient Chinese characters.</margin>
<margin>The ancient Chinese, in the manner of the Egyptians, used various figures of natural things for writing.</margin>
<margin>The first Emperor of the Chinese invented characters from the figures of serpents.</margin>
The primitive Chinese, as I have said, followed the Egyptians from whom they were descended, and conducted their writing not by the composition of letters, but by figures composed of various natural things; to these, as many different signs corresponded as there were concepts of things. The first Emperor of the Chinese, Fohì <note>Fu Xi, a legendary culture hero in Chinese mythology</note>, invented a certain type of character made from serpents and dragons, the use of which is recorded in the Chinese Annals. From this, the book he wrote on Mathematical and Astrological matters is called the "Book of Dragons." We place the form of the characters here, and they are marked with the letters A, B, C, D, and E. These are explained by the modern Chinese characters marked with the number 3: *Fohì xìlùm xù*, <note original: "Fohì xìlùm xù">伏羲氏龍書 (Fu Xi Shi Long Shu)</note> that is, "The Dragon Book of Fu Xi." You see here serpents wonderfully intertwined and transformed into various shapes according to the diversity of things they signified; although there are few among the Chinese today who have knowledge of them, as they have been lost through extreme antiquity.

And these are the forms of letters used by the ancient Chinese; I have chosen to explain them here more fully so that their correspondence with hieroglyphics might be more clearly evident. As for the hand you see depicted with a brush, you should know that the Chinese do not use pens like ours, nor liquid ink; instead, they rub a small amount of black pigment on a marble stone to soak the brush, which they hold with their fingers in such a way—while writing, or rather, while painting—as appears in the preceding figure. # CHAPTER III.

->Concerning the letters of the Brahmins, or Gymnosophists.<-

<margin>Gymnosophists or Brahmins.</margin>
Among the most ancient masters of sacred mysteries <term>Hieromantas: from the Greek for "sacred diviners," referring here to those who interpret divine wisdom</term>, the Gymnosophists <term>Gymnosophists: meaning "naked philosophers," a name given by the Greeks to Indian ascetics who wore little clothing and practiced extreme self-discipline</term> were particularly illustrious for their reputation for wisdom; later generations called them Brahmins. And what the Magi were to the Chaldeans, the Cabalists to the Hebrews, the Philosophers to the Greeks, and the Priests and Prophets to the Egyptians, the Gymnosophists were to the Indians.
<margin>Xenophon.</margin>
For these men, as recorded by Philostratus and Xenophon, left behind the deceptive company of foolish people. Casting aside all luxuries, wealth, and the pleasures of convenience, they devoted themselves solely to the study of Wisdom, living their lives in the deserts of East India.
<margin>Their way of living.</margin>
Their food consisted of the roots of herbs, fruits, and similar life-sustaining provisions which kind Mother Earth supplied to them; they quenched their thirst with the healthiest water; for a home they had a cave, and for a bed the ground spread with grasses and leaves. Through these institutions of life, they arrived at a great knowledge of things;
<margin>The character of the Brahmins or Gymnosophists.</margin>
and so that they would not seem to have lived for themselves alone, they recorded the remarkable secrets of nature in a certain type of writing—

<meta>catchword: type— (gene-)</meta>

He compares these Indian sages to the intellectual elites of other ancient civilizations and describes their ascetic lifestyle in the desert.</summary>

### CHAPTER III. 225 OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
Mount Pagoda in India
</margin>
...they consigned these things to posterity, yet enveloped in such veils of obscurity that access to penetrate them was granted only to the Wise. However, because signs of this kind can cause no small amount of trouble even for the Wise themselves, I thought it my duty as an Oedipus <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus was the hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx. Kircher frequently uses this name to describe his role as a decoder of ancient mysteries.</note> to explain some of them in this place. My goal is to reveal to the curious reader what they indicated through these signs and how they are distinguished from the hieroglyphic literature of the Egyptians. These marks were first communicated to me by Master Franciscus Stellatus; he had originally arranged for them to be excerpted from a very ancient codex out of his own intellectual curiosity and his affection for more recondite <note>Hidden or obscure</note> letters, on behalf of the most excellent Cesi, Duke of Acquasparta <note>Federico Cesi (1585–1633), the founder of the Lincean Academy.</note>. A great abundance of these was also sent to me about six years ago from the East Indies to be deciphered by Father Antonio Ceschi—a man of exceptional piety, highly instructed in every kind of virtue and science, and a priest of our Society <note>The Jesuits.</note>. He had extracted them from a certain mountain in India called Mount Pagoda, located in the territory of Chaul <note>A historic port city near modern-day Mumbai.</note>. This mountain is the most famous in all of India and is very frequently crowded with people flocking there for the sake of pilgrimage. It is so full on every side that entry to the interior is open from only one side; the whole mountain is inscribed with characters of this kind, which are held in great veneration and worship by everyone. Therefore, out of his own desire to promote the common good, the aforementioned Father Ceschi sent copies of these to me so that he might test my industry in explaining them.

<margin>
Whether the characters of the Brahmins or Gymnosophists are hieroglyphic
</margin>
The question is asked, therefore: are characters of this kind truly hieroglyphic? I respond that hieroglyphs can be considered in two ways: either simply as sacred signs of secret things, or as signs of great mysteries composed from the hidden structure of animals, plants, tools, and similar things. These latter ones can properly be called "hieroglyphic," for such characters are not only indicators of mysterious things, but in their own mystical structure, they contain the properties of the very things they indicate; such were the hieroglyphic characters unique to the Egyptians. The characters of the Brahmins <term>Brachmanum: Kircher uses this term for the Hindu priestly caste, the Brahmins.</term>, although they indicate secret matters, cannot properly be called hieroglyphs; they are merely naked and simple marks of the said things, imposed upon them by the arbitrary institution of the aforementioned Sages—as will be seen shortly—just like the characters they call "magical seals." But so that these matters may be deduced more clearly, it seemed appropriate to begin from a slightly higher point of origin.

<margin>
The Wise prove a triple world.
</margin>
<margin>
Characters appropriated to Celestial things by the Brahmin Sages.
</margin>
Those Sages—whether through tradition received from the Egyptians or through science acquired by their own invention and study—posited a triple World: the Intelligible, the Celestial, and the Elemental. Indeed, they believed these three Worlds were so subordinated to one another that the lower World is influenced by the Celestial, and this in turn by the Intelligible. Thus, nothing lies hidden in the lap of the Sublunary World <note>The Earthly realm below the moon.</note> that does not have its own star in the Sidereal <note>Starry</note> World by which it is influenced; nor is there a star to which an Intelligence <note>An angelic or spiritual being.</note> in the Intellectual World does not correspond as the ruler of both the Celestial and Elemental star. This opinion, as we have said in the preceding sections, is entirely Egyptian. Hence, for the twelve signs of the Zodiac, the seven Planets, and the things of the Elemental World, they assigned certain letters...

<meta>The catchword "ras" indicates the beginning of the word "rursus" or a similar continuation on the following page regarding the assignment of these letters.</meta>

<summary>Kircher discusses the origins and nature of Brahmin characters found on "Mount Pagoda" in India, distinguishing them from Egyptian hieroglyphs by defining them as symbolic marks rather than pictorial representations. He introduces the concept of the "Triple World" (Intelligible, Celestial, and Elemental) as the philosophical framework for these scripts.</summary>

### THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER III.

...they assigned specific qualities, by which one could distinguish which thing was subject to which zodiac sign or planet. For example, they determined what effects Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon would produce in each of the twelve signs of the Zodiac. They did not only attribute much to the stars, but also to the Heavens themselves, even without respect to the stars. But now, let us subjoin the characters of each of the aforementioned things.

<margin>Characters of the Brahmans <note>original: "Brachmanum"</note> regarding the heavens and stars.</margin>

<margin>The effects of the Moon’s heaven according to the Brahmans.</margin>

There follow now other characters which they attributed to the Heavens and the orbs themselves, rather than the stars. First, they presented seven Heavens filled with influences, in which their Kabbalistic effects and properties were stored, arranged through various combinations of letters. In the first Heaven of the Moon, which they called *Samayn* <note>original: "Samayn," from the Hebrew *Shamayim*, meaning "the Heavens"</note>, seven general influences expressed by their own signs were contained. The first influence was called *Lorpeny* by the Gymnosophists <note>A Greek term for ancient Indian philosophers who practiced asceticism and went naked</note>, and it displayed matters pertaining to medicine. The second, *Tygara*, contained edible things. The third, named *Dana*, concerned matters of the sciences. The fourth, called *Kalamia*, indicated things pertaining to loves. The fifth, *Astimor*, was concerned with speech. The sixth, *Bartaz*, treated of travels. The seventh, *Broel*, assigned the business of interpretation.

<margin>Effects of the heaven of Mercury.</margin>

<margin>Influences of the heaven of Mercury.</margin>

The second Heaven of Mercury, which they call *Raquia* <note>original: "Raquia," from the Hebrew *Rakia*, usually translated as "Firmament"</note>, contains twelve general influences, each of which has its own assigned signs, which possess—as they believe—great virtues. The first influence is called *Armad* by the Gymnosophists, and it signifies peace. The second, *Iboy*, denotes proportions. The third, *Lycy*, treats of matters pertaining to separations. The fourth, *Hary*, displays things pertaining to a miserable state. The fifth is for labors, and is called *Quym*. The sixth, *Abythaur*, for security. The seventh, *Batbaya*, for flight. The eighth, *Abracy*, for custody. The ninth, *Igushy*, for defense. The tenth, *Lachry*, for vengeance. The eleventh, *Rubdy*, for restoration. The twelfth, *Artimony*, contains matters pertaining to healing.

### THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER. 27 CHAPTER III.

<margin>
The effects and influence of the heaven of Venus.
</margin>

The third Heaven is called <gloss>Suaquyn</gloss> *Suaquyn*, and it is the sphere of Venus; it contains three general influences <note>original: "influentias," referring to the astrological belief that celestial powers "flow" down from the stars to the earth</note> with their respective signs. The first, called <gloss>Itasuny</gloss> *Itasuny*, manifests the work of cooling. The second, <gloss>Lyachy</gloss> *Lyachy*, denotes motion; the third, <gloss>Idalquy</gloss> *Idalquy*, claims for itself matters pertaining to sight.

<margin>
The effects and influence of the heaven of the Sun.
</margin>

The fourth Heaven, that of the Sun, called *Laon*, possesses two influences. The first, *Abrastas*, concerns matters of divination. The second, *Paratpyel*, presents matters regarding the conducting of counsels.

<margin>
The effects of the heaven of Mars.
</margin>

The fifth Heaven, that of Mars, called *Mahum*, has twelve signs, by which the celestial influx upon the twelve months is indicated.

<margin>
The characters of the heavens of Jupiter and Saturn.
</margin>

The influences of the sixth and seventh Heavens were missing in the original copy; however, in another copy, the sixth—the Heaven of Jupiter, called *Telut*—possesses these figures for itself: <note>four magical hieroglyphs: a vertical line with a hook at the bottom pointing left; a vertical line with a loop at the top right and a small horizontal crossbar; a wide U-shape containing three dots; and a circle bisected by a horizontal line with a short vertical stroke on top.</note> The seventh Heaven, that of Saturn, called *Araboh*, contains other figures: <note>repetition of the previous four magical hieroglyphs</note>. It possesses, moreover, many other characters by which the influences of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, the twelve months, the weeks, and the hours—both of day and night—are indicated. But since those require a specialized treatise and do not contribute so much to our current purpose, sparing both time and expense, we have deliberately omitted them. And from this school of the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by ancient Greeks and later by Kircher to refer to Indian Brahmans and yogis</note>, the Arabs extracted most of their magical signs—which they also call "Indian" and which are inscribed on all sorts of amulets <term>periaptis: charms or amulets worn on the person for protection</term>; see a more extensive treatise on these in the *Saracen Kabbalah*, where you will also find it indicated from where they were extracted and from where they had their primary origin.

<margin>
A mountain of Pagodas full of the characters of the Gymnosophists.
</margin>

An entire mountain in India—which the Portuguese call *Pagoda Canarim* <note>likely referring to the Kanheri Caves in modern-day Mumbai, known for their rock-cut Buddhist sculptures and inscriptions</note> because it was dedicated to the Gods by the Eastern peoples—is seen engraved with characters of this kind; I learned this by word of mouth from an eyewitness, Father Giovanni Maracci, who, while I am writing this, acts as the procurator of India in Rome. Although the said signs could not be understood by any of the natives until now, it is no wonder; for they are of that class of letters which, instead of a [phonetic] letter, present the complete meaning of a certain thing, as was clear from the interpretation of the preceding ones. The ancient Sages of India used to mark the rocky surface of the mountain with characters of this kind for the reason that they thought these signs possessed remarkable virtue and power for preserving the mountain under the protection and inviolable guardianship of the Gods to whom it was dedicated. Such characters are those which are seen engraved around the Cross of Saint Thomas the Apostle, fashioned in blood, at Mylapore in Narsinga <note>Meliapor is a neighborhood in modern Chennai; Narsinga refers to the Vijayanagara Empire</note>; see the interpretation of these provided in the *Coptic Prodromus*, page 108. And these are the things I thought should be said concerning the signs of the Gymnosophists or the ancient Brahmans.

CHAPTER IV. 28 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS

<note>Significant bleed-through from the reverse side of the page makes some lines in the upper half difficult to read.</note>

# CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning the Literature of the Mexicans, and whether it can properly be called hieroglyphic.*<-

<margin>The Mexican language and its letters</margin>
The indigenous people of New Spain <note>Modern-day Mexico</note> differ among themselves with an almost infinite variety of languages; these vary not only by dialect but are entirely distinct. Among these, the Mexican language <note>Nahuatl</note> excels; it became so common among both neighboring and distant nations—after the Mexicans expanded the borders of their empire far and wide—that it became as universal as Latin is in Europe or Arabic in the East. As a result, interpreters of this language are found in almost every province, whom they call *Naquatlatos* <note>original: "Naquatlatos," a corruption of the Nahuatl word "Nahuatlatos," meaning those who speak clearly or interpreters</note>.

<margin>The Mexicans use pictures in place of letters.</margin>
Furthermore, although the Mexicans lack characters and letters, being ignorant of the art of writing, they nevertheless attempted to express their thoughts through certain pictures. By these means, they recorded for posterity first the chronology of their Kings and the memory of their deeds; second, the revenues and tributes of the kingdom and cities; and finally, the laws for the education of children, as will be seen shortly. Since these characters are constructed from various figures of animals, plants, tools, and similar objects, many have convinced themselves that this literature is entirely hieroglyphic.

<margin>Mexican characters or figures are not hieroglyphic.</margin>
Truly, that this opinion is false will be more than clear from what we shall present shortly. For it is certain that nothing lies hidden beneath them wrapped in arcane meanings; rather, the figures themselves represent actions or a sequence of events, and they exhibit a kind of painting of an event, rather than a secret symbol. To demonstrate this clearly here, I have decided to explain several figures extracted from various writers of Mexican history, so that the nature of our undertaking may be more brightly revealed.

<margin>Signs for numbers among the Mexicans.</margin>
Numbers were shown by the Mexicans in this way: one circle ○ noted unity; two circles ○○ noted the number two; three circles ○○○ noted three, and so on, expressing any number with as many circles as the number contained units. The number twenty <note>The original Latin text omits the word "twenty" but describes the symbol as a small flag</note> was expressed with a small flag symbol, and by multiplying this sign, they reached up to 400; indeed, this sign placed twice meant 40; three times, 60; four times, 80; five times, 100; and ten times, 200. These were placed next to items to indicate how much tribute was to be paid for those things, such as pepper, flour, strawberries <note>original: "fragorum," likely referring to a specific New World fruit or berry</note>, weapons, and similar goods, which are found everywhere in their books concerning the payment of tribute to the King. This figure of a feather or stylized tree signified 400; placed twice, it indicated 800; three times, 1200; and four times, 1600, and so on for the rest.

<margin>Signs for years among the Mexicans.</margin>
The following figure of a large bundle or bushy tree, which is quite complex, signifies 8,000. I could not find any other numbers among their tribute records besides those mentioned. They did, however, have others used in the counting of years, as I said above, which were indicated by circles.

<margin>The Mexicans divided the year into 18 months.</margin>
To make this clear: note that the Mexicans were accustomed to distributing the year into eighteen months, each of which consisted of twenty days, which in themselves...

<margin>The Mexicans expected the destruction of the world at the end of each of their centuries.</margin>
On the last day of their fourth century <note>meaning the 52nd year of the cycle</note> of 52 years, they would break all their vessels and extinguish their fires. For since they had heard from their ancestors that the world would perish in a "secular" year <note>A year marking the end of an age or *saeculum*.</note>, they awaited this event every fifty-second year. Thus they kept watch through the whole night, fearing that the light would never shine again; but at sunrise, they testified to their joy with trumpets and flutes and celebrated a feast, giving thanks to their gods that they had extended a new age to the world. They would prepare new vessels and other furniture for themselves, and seek "New Fire" from the Priest. <margin>Samuel Purchas.</margin> All of this is confirmed by Samuel Purchas in his work on the description of the world and travels, written in English <note>Purchas his Pilgrimes (1625).</note>, volume 3, book 5, chapter 7, page 106, in these words:

> *In the order and rule of the divisions which are numbered for years, that division which has a branch with a foot-like flower signifies a bitter and unfortunate year. This is what the Mexicans had and feared, saying that their predecessors from time out of mind gave them warning that such years, which occurred every fifty-second year, were dangerous, unfortunate, and bitter years. Because in such years there were generally floods, and likewise a darkness of*
