Gómara <note>Francisco López de Gómara, a 16th-century Spanish historian</note> confirms that all these things are true in these words: *They distinguished these same days and years into classes of thirteen days, and by marking a small circle like the letter O, multiplied as many times as necessary, they noted the order and number; they also distributed the years into similar classes and ages; and their age <term>century: the 52-year cycle</term> consisted of four such classes, that is, 52 years; yet in the description of the years they used no more than four figures or signs: House, Rabbit, Reed, and Flint Knife.* See the class of thirteen years above on page 29.

Samuel Purchas <note>An English cleric and compiler of travel reports</note> indeed describes these thirteen years in the third part of his *Pilgrimage* in English with these words:
> Concerning the pictures of blue in the margins of this history it is to be understood that every several space or partition, doth signify one year and they be the numbering of years; it is to be understood that every several space or partition signify the one several year, and so they accounted and numbered every year severally, proceeding to thirteen roundels. And from thence they began again at the beginning in their account from one point or roundel, and so accordingly they did proceed in numbering again, till they came to thirteen; and although that in the partitions or spaces severally, there be diverse figures yet the principal account of numbering, is that of account of the pictures or roundels therein contained; and although the names of years that they give to every partition, from the number of the first point till the thirteenth.

That is, *As for the blue pictures at the margin of this history, it should be noted that the individual places or partitions signify a year, and are the number of years: so that the places or partitions taken individually signify as many years, and thus they proceed up to thirteen circles, and begin again from one point or circle up to thirteen; although in the individual places or partitions there are different figures, the primary method of counting is taken from the number of figures or circles contained in them, although the names of the years, which they attribute to each partition, are from one to 13.*

<margin>Another Mexican picture containing the laws for educating children.</margin>
The Mexicans have certain laws according to which they are accustomed to educate their children, which are expressed in these and the following figures. First, as soon as a woman has given birth, the boy is placed in a cradle; after four days, however, the midwife takes the naked boy and carries him into a garden, in which a grate woven from reeds and wicker is spread out over the waters. When she has washed the boy here, three boys sitting nearby, provided with rice, strawberries, and similar fruits of the fatherland, are commanded by the midwife to bestow a name upon the boy. I would have placed the images of all these things in this location, but since they are easily understood from the preceding sections without any trouble, I judged it to be superfluous to stuff the book with useless figures that are not so relevant to our subject; therefore, it shall suffice to explain the Mexican <term>pedotribic</term> <note>From the Greek 'paidotribes,' referring to the training or education of children</note> history in words only.

After this figure, therefore, they place another, like a certain page, by whose figures it is expressed how a boy or girl of three or four years is to be educated—namely, with the following admonitions. A certain portion of bread is established, specifically a half-portion, when they have reached their third year; but a whole bread when they have completed their fourth year. All these things they explain through images of the actions to be performed. Hence, they place the mother of the infant wrapped and sitting, in that posture which the letter **A** shows in the preceding figure. They indicate three or four years by three or four circles, just as the four circles in the preceding figure show. When the boy has reached these, he is urged with admonitions, and a portion of a whole bread is daily assigned to him, signified by a certain figure.

The mother, however, urges the girl toward exercises suitable to her sex, with a whole portion of bread assigned daily. When they indicate that a boy is to be exercised in the nautical and fishing art, they indicate this by the figure of a skiff with an attached hook. A distaff, however, and the equipment of the weaving art, teaches that the girl is to be exercised in that. Furthermore, when the boy is five years old—indicated by five circles placed near him—his father teaches the boys the way of carrying things to the market; and a whole bread is granted to them daily. The mother, meanwhile, instructs her five-year-old daughter in the method of spinning.

When the boy is six years old—indicated by six circles—his father teaches him the method of selling the fruits native to the country, and the way of making shields; and one and a half breads are assigned to him daily. The mother teaches her daughter the art of spinning. When the boy is 7 years old—indicated by seven circles—his father instructs him in the art of fishing, as the <term>weel</term> <note>A wicker trap for catching fish</note> which he holds in his hand teaches. The mother teaches the daughter the art of spinning cotton; for both, however, the daily portion of food is set at one and a half breads. Here you see that no mystery at all lies beneath the figures; rather, they express only simple actions.

To a boy of eight years—noted by eight circles—his father threatens punishment by the thorns of a certain shrub called *Maquez* <note>Likely referring to the Maguey plant (Agave), whose thorns were used for discipline and ritual bloodletting</note> unless he behaves well; the mother does the same to the daughter; and the daily food of a bread and a half is assigned to both, as all things expressed by the figures themselves show. A nine-year-old boy who is incorrigible and stubborn is tortured by the father with *Maquez* thorns; the mother does the same to the daughter. A ten-year-old boy is punished by his father with a stick for disobedience and negligence in his duties; the mother likewise punishes the daughter for negligence committed in spinning. They proceed no differently in the remaining duties until, as I said, having been released, he takes a wife; all of which things are expressed through the actions of the images themselves. Lest I draw out delays in a matter that is useless and quite ridiculous...

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER. 37 CH. V.

...sent it to me, so that if possible, I might bring some light to such a great darkness of mysteries hidden beneath them; just as it was not right to refuse his friendly wish, so too with the greatest investigation I have applied all the powers of my mind and talent to penetrate the secret sacraments of this tablet. The matter, therefore, stands thus.

<margin>Who were the Melchites?</margin> <note>The Melchites were Middle Eastern Christians who followed the Byzantine rite; Kircher views their practices through the lens of his interest in "oriental" mysticism.</note> It is well established that Christians drawing their origin from Moorish and Arab blood were accustomed to construct sacred images, both in the past and now; which they said were of great virtue, and like certain most powerful amulets against the malignant powers of Demons (doubtless a branch of that ancient Magic which the Gnostics impiously thrust upon the world, propagated by a certain successive tradition to these later times). These they would fix to the walls of infested places and the partitions of houses, or even wear bound to the chest with great veneration; just as has been explained at length in *Hieroglyphic Magic* <term>Hieroglyphic Magic: Kircher's term for the study of symbols believed to have inherent supernatural power</term>, where we also brought forward several not dissimilar diagrams. I know not, however, by what superstition driven askew, they persuaded themselves that sacred images of this kind could by no means achieve their effect unless they deformed them with a certain vain observance of secret characters drawn from the school of the <term>Cabalists</term> <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah), though Kircher often applies the term to any mystical letter-symbolism</note> and Magicians. For among these people, you see nothing rightly performed without characters. Indeed, they had drawn this impious custom from no other source than the superstitious Arab nation, whose company they constantly kept; and lest they should seem to agree with them in their institutions, they thought they had performed something sufficiently great if they applied these portentous characters of great efficacy to the sacred mysteries of the Christian Religion. For they imagined in their simplicity that by joining these, the sacred Image would acquire greater force and strength. The crosses, medals, and sacred tablets—marked partly with Hebrew names, partly with other Magical characters and portentous names of Angels together with images of Christ and the Blessed Virgin—which are sent to me from various parts of the world as if to an Interpreter of such things, and which we shall perhaps produce more opportunely in due time, testify more than enough to this kind of Christian superstition.

<margin>Interpretation of the tablet.</margin> And from the number of these was this present tablet, and that it was a wearable amulet, the hole marked **A**, and its being hung from something, clearly shows. In the front part of this tablet, marked **B A C**, you may first see Christ the Lord sitting upon a throne according to the ancient rite, whose head is surrounded by a radiant circle, which we have said elsewhere the Ancients called a nimbus <note>A halo</note>, with his face veiled, and his hand raised as if imparting a blessing; the other hand is hidden. By the radiant nimbus they signified the majesty of divinity; by the veiled face, that it is inaccessible to human intellect; by the extended blessing hand, his mercy; and by the hidden hand, they hinted at his justice, delaying on account of the hope of repentance. On the corners **B** and **C**, two Angels are placed, likewise with veiled faces, of whom the first, **B**, signifies Gabriel, and the other, **C**, Michael, as the letters placed at the side of each teach; but the Savior has seven characters placed around him, by which the seven Apocalyptic Spirits are signified; whose names are Sebtael, Zedakiel, Madamiel, Shemfiel, Nogael, Co—

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>

Cochabiel, Leuaniel, and others correspond to the Intelligences of the seven planets; these are, however, characters originating from the School of the Gymnosophists <note>A term used by Greeks for ancient Indian philosophers who practiced asceticism</note>. In this manner, they express the Intelligence of <note>Saturn: ♄</note> through <note>Sigil resembling a trident or Greek Psi</note>; the Intelligence of <note>Jupiter: ♃</note> through <note>Sigil resembling a cross with a loop at the top right</note>; the Intelligence of <note>Mars: ♂</note> through <note>Sigil resembling a stylized 'A' or 'Et' ligature</note>; the Intelligence of <note>the Sun: ☉</note> through <note>Sigil resembling a cursive 'L' or '2'</note>; the Intelligence of <note>Venus: ♀</note> through <note>Astrological symbol for Venus: ♀</note>; the Intelligence of <note>Mercury: ☿</note> through <note>Sigil resembling a bird or winged 'V'</note>; and they indicate the Intelligence of <note>the Moon: ☽</note> through <note>Sigil of a cross atop a crescent</note>.

But these matters have been explained here and there in various places throughout this Work. Furthermore, the four characters placed upon the four Angels indicate the Intelligences presiding over the four parts of the World, and they are Mahaziel, Azaël, Sauiel, and Azazel. By the power of these—as is found in the writings of Saint Irenaeus—they impiously believe that Christ, the Word of God, flows into the mystical World of His Church. These things are indeed aptly hinted at through the images of the Blessed Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist with veiled faces, and through the double Moon bound to the cross; by which the influence of the archetypal *Malcuth* <note>Hebrew: "Kingdom," the final Sephirah in the Kabbalistic Tree of Life</note>, that is, the super-celestial Moon, into the mystical World of the Church is noted (as we have taught in the *Kabbalah*), which is suggested to have been accomplished by means of the cross and the Lord's Passion. The characters **α** and **ω** are Greek, and they mean the same as **α** and **ω**, Alpha and Omega: the beginning and the end, the giver of life to all—as the Arabic word <note>original: محي</note> <gloss>Mehi</gloss> <note>Arabic: "The Giver of Life," one of the names of God</note> teaches—and the fulfillment of all things, which the cross or the decussated ten <note>The Roman numeral X, representing the number ten and the shape of a cross</note> indicates, as we explained in the *Arithmetic*; these are attributes appropriated to Christ.

And this is the exposition of the mystery contained under the first part of this table: where you see the mystical, Kabbalistic, Greek, Hebrew, and Arabic characters of the Spirits mixed together with sacred images. This was perhaps not done rashly, but because they believed, out of their usual and inherent superstition, that these characters would acquire greater efficacy when joined to the images; a practice we know is still used to this day by many Christians in Eastern regions.

The other part, however, was so defiled by Magic characters that it was unworthy to see the light of day, especially since it contained nothing Egyptian; thus, it was by no means to be included here. Therefore, let us move on to other things.

-> # CHAPTER VI. <-

-> ### Interpretation of certain characters described on a Cross. <-

**N**ot long ago, Father Franciscus Bonasmorus sent to me from Constantinople a diagram of a Cross, transformed (as he himself thought) by Magical figures. He earnestly requested that I might bring some light to such great darkness with my interpretation. I have done what he asked; and I say that this writing is by no means Magical, but Illyrian <note>Referring to the Slavic languages of the Balkans</note>, of that kind which is commonly called Serbian or the script of Saint Cyril <note>Cyrillic</note>. It is bound and linked together in a monogrammatic style, but the language is ancient Bulgarian, the same as that which the Ruthenians <note>An archaic term for East Slavic peoples, such as Ukrainians and Belarusians</note> use in their sacred rites.

# CHAPTER VII.
## Concerning the Hieroglyphic Characters of the Armenians.

->**W**hile I was writing these things, a certain diagram was brought to me, full of characters transformed into all kinds of animals; since many had persuaded themselves that these were hieroglyphics, I finally, having examined each one with diligent investigation, found that it represented nothing other than the uppercase or capital letters of the Armenians arranged in alphabetical order. The characters proposed to me were the following, of which the first set explains the figured [animal] shapes; the second set shows the uppercase characters of the Armenians. Contemplate the diagram on the following page.<-

But so that the matter may appear more clearly, it should be noted that the Armenians are accustomed to using a threefold kind of letters. The first is called **բոլորգիր** <margin>*Poluerchir*, that is, the orbicular or round letter, which they are accustomed to use everywhere.</margin> The second is called **նօտրգիր** *Noderchir*, that is, the letter of the Notaries, by which name are signified the more expeditious letters, which are called "running" [cursive]. The third kind is called **երկաթագիր** *Ergathachir*, namely the "iron letter," by which are designated the uppercase letters, which like iron endure longer and are more difficult to erase. Truly, because uppercase letters are customarily placed at the beginnings of Chapters or Writings, they are called besides by another name **գլխագիր** *Chelhbachir*, that is, Capital letter. Again, the same, because they are sometimes outlined with a various display of flowers, are also called **ծաղկագիր** *Zakghachir*, namely the "flowering letter." These same are also called from time to time **գազանագիր** *Chaffanachir* <note>Kircher's transliteration of the Armenian 'Gazanagir'</note>, that is, the "beastly letter," because they are indeed presented under various figures of beasts, birds, and reptiles. And of this kind are the letters which follow shortly after. I have thought it necessary to add some of these here, lest anything in this...

In this alphabet, Column A represents the figurative characters of the Armenians, while Column B represents their capital letters <note>original: "maiusculos"</note>. From their outlines, it is easily evident that these figurative characters are exactly what we have said they are: not at all hieroglyphic. Rather, they have emerged from the imagination of the painter for the convenience of the letter and the logic of the strokes. This is clearly evident from the Armenian Rituals <note>Liturgical books used in Armenian Christian worship</note>, where you will frequently find the initial letters expressed in this fantastical scheme of characters.

# CHAPTER VIII.
## Concerning other schemes of false hieroglyphics.

Not long ago, the most distinguished man Mr. Harsdörffer <note>Georg Philipp Harsdörffer (1607–1658), a prominent Nuremberg poet and scholar</note>, a Patrician of Nuremberg, sent me a leaf filled with hieroglyphics which he extracted from a French author and a book which he calls *Polyphilus* <note>The *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*, a famous 1499 book featuring mysterious woodcuts and "hieroglyphic" puzzles</note>. The author asserts that he extracted these from the monuments of the Egyptians. However, by examining each one with the greatest zeal, I have finally found that they are by no means to be placed in the catalog of hieroglyphics. Anyone who is properly skilled in the logic of hieroglyphics will easily convince himself that they were either fabricated by the author or extracted from elsewhere. I wished to warn the reader about these things, lest by a false persua-

# PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE II.

## Concerning the mystical Alphabet of the Egyptians, and the Coptic language.

<margin>Two types of languages used by the Egyptians.</margin>
<margin>The Common.</margin>
Having previously compared hieroglyphics with the writings of various other peoples, let us now return to the path of our intended purpose. It has been sufficiently proven elsewhere that two types of language were in use among the Egyptians; the first was common and used by everyone, established for the use of human commerce, and this was the Egyptian language or idiom which is called Coptic or Pharaonic. The other was used only by the Priests, Prophets, and <term>Hierogrammats</term> <note>Sacred scribes or keepers of the holy records</note>, and others of the priestly order who had hope of ascending to the kingdom; this we call <margin>Hieroglyphic.</margin> hieroglyphic. We shall discuss the former in this place first, and treat the latter thereafter. Nature was so arranged among the Egyptians that, just as nothing in all their institutions was performed without a mystery, so it was in their common language. This is evident from their Alphabet, which was so arranged by a mysterious institution of letters <margin>The Alphabet of the Egyptians is full of mysteries.</margin> that almost no letter is found in it that is not full of hidden sacraments <note>In this context, "sacraments" refers to sacred mysteries or holy secrets</note> on every side. And although we have treated this extensively in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, nevertheless, because many things worthy of consideration have since occurred to me through long experience—the mistress of things—I have thought it timely to interweave them in this place.

Regarding the primeval letters of the Egyptians, there are various opinions of different authors, which we followed at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. All, however, agree on this: that most were taken from the forms of sacred animals, their gait, and the positions and symmetry of other <margin>Egyptian letters taken from the forms, gait, etc., of animals.</margin> parts of the body. Thus says Demetrius Phalaræus <note>An Athenian orator and statesman who supposedly helped found the Library of Alexandria</note>, who, assigning seven vowels, says they were consecrated to seven Gods, while the rest were taken from the forms of animals. Eusebius asserts the same; and the author of the *Scala Magna* <note>The "Great Ladder," a famous medieval Coptic-Arabic dictionary</note>, or Egyptian Dictionary, demonstrates this in plain words at the <margin>Eusebius. Author of the Scala Magna.</margin> beginning of his *Scala* with these words: ϫⲉ ⲛⲓⲭⲁⲣⲁⲕⲧⲉⲣⲉⲥ ϧⲉⲛ ⲡⲓⲭⲏⲙⲓ ⲛⲧⲉⲑⲏⲣⲓⲟⲛ <note>original Coptic: "je nikharakteres khen pikhemi ente-thērion"</note>. "Egypt took its first characters from the figures of animals." But so that the context of our undertaking may appear more clearly, we have thought it necessary to repeat some things concerning the primeval institution of letters from the *Pamphilian Obelisk*.

<margin>Osiris rendered Lower Egypt habitable.</margin>
The ancient writers of Egyptian history relate that the lower part of Egypt was once covered by the sea; but Osiris, the first King of Egypt, when he saw this gulf of the sea bringing forth something terrestrial from the vast accumulation of mud and sands brought down from Ethiopia by the flow of the Nile, led the waters of the Nile into channels. Thus he separated the intervening land from the waters, rendering it not only fit for inhabitants, but even pleasant—

<summary>Kircher introduces the distinction between the common Coptic language and the priestly hieroglyphic script, arguing that even the Coptic alphabet contains hidden mystical meanings derived from animal forms. He cites ancient authorities and the "Scala Magna" to support the theory that Egyptian letters originated from the natural world and the civilizing efforts of King Osiris.</summary>

produced; but since a vast multitude of serpents born from the putrefied mud rendered the place continually infested, and many died daily from serpent bites—among whom was Canopus, the pilot of Osiris—Osiris sent a great force of Ibises into these places. By devouring the serpents, they purged the location in a short time and rendered it immune from danger. Thus, as the Ibises multiplied, and as posterity noted that the said birds transformed themselves into various shapes according to the different positions of their bodies; and with many other benefits received from the Ibis being added, the Egyptians—calling it that Spirit or *Agathodaemon* <note>Greek: "Good Spirit"</note> from the figure it expressed with its feet—enrolled it in the sacred register of animals and called the place itself by the name Agathodaemon. Ptolemy teaches this in these words: <margin>The sending of the Ibis against the serpents.</margin> <margin>Why the Ibis is called Agathodaemon.</margin> <margin>Ptolemy.</margin> *That is called the Great Delta, near which the river called the Agathodaemon flows.* <note>Original Greek: Δέλτα μέγιστον ἐκεῖνο καλεῖ, παρ' ᾧ ὁ μέλας ποταμὸς ῥέει μέρος Ἀγαθὸς Δαίμων</note>. The Ibis, therefore, with its legs spread wide and its beak inserted transversely between them, expresses the first letter of the Egyptian Alphabet in this manner, **A**, which signifies the same as *Agathodaemon*. So says Plutarch in *Symposiacs*, Book 5: *The ibis, by a certain distance of its feet from one another and in comparison to its beak, completes an equilateral triangle.* <note>Original Greek: ἡ ἴβις, φησί, τῇ ποιᾷ τῶν ποδῶν διαστάσει πρὸς ἀλλήλους, καὶ πρὸς τὸ ῥύγχος, ἰσόπλευρον τρίγωνον ἀποτελεῖ</note>. And in Book 9, Question 3: *They say that Mercury was the first of the Gods in Egypt to discover letters; wherefore the Egyptians make the Ibis the first of the letters, as being appropriate to Mercury (the Agathodaemon).* <note>Original Greek: Ἑρμῆν λέγουσι Θεῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ γράμματα πρῶτον εὑρεῖν, διὸ καὶ τῷ τῶν γραμμάτων Αἰγύπτιοι πρῶτον ἴβιν γράφουσιν, ὡς ἑρμῇ (Ἀγαθοδαίμονι) προσήκουσαν.</note> <margin>The first of the Egyptian letters taken from the Ibis.</margin> <margin>Plutarch.</margin>

The second letter was taken from the neck of the Ibis with the beak held across it; since this resembles a square <term>norma</term><note>A carpenter's square or right-angle tool</note>, they called it *gaeele*; for it is clear from our Coptic Dictionary that *gaeele* signifies nothing other than a square or a rule fit for performing measurements. Since Mercury was the author of Geometry just as he was of letters, he aptly established the second letter as the Geometric square, taken from the neck and beak of the Ibis. Clement of Alexandria suggests this in plain words in the 5th book of the *Stromata*: *The Ibis seems to have provided the Egyptians with the very idea of number and measure among living things, just as it does with oblique circles.* <note>Original Greek: Ἀριθμῶν δὲ ἐπίνοιαν καὶ μέτρον μάλιστα τῷ ζώῳ ἡ ἴβις ἀκριβῶς παρεσχῆσθαι τοῖς Αἰγυπτίοις δοκεῖ ὡς τῷ κύκλων λοξοῖς</note>. <margin>The second Egyptian letter taken from the neck and beak is Γ.</margin> <margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin>

The third letter was taken from the spreading of the Ibis's feet, omitting the insertion of the beak: for in this way, it expressed a **Δ** (Delta) exactly against the level of the ground. Consequently, the Egyptians marked this place near the sea with no other name than "Delta," and posterity has retained this name even to our times. For the Egyptians believed that Mercury, under the form of an Ibis, had delivered various forms of letters to the human race, and had taught, among other things through the form of the **Δ**, how the Nile should be divided so that the land submerged by waters and marshes might be rendered fruitful and fit for human habitation. From this, perhaps, the name *aeloutsi* was given to this letter, which I find in Coptic signifies nothing other than "good field." Certainly, Pausanias, cited in Pierius, Book 17, teaches that the Delta was taken from the Ibis in these words: *There is also another reason why they signified Egypt hieroglyphically by the Ibis, namely because that region...* <margin>The third Egyptian letter taken from the Ibis.</margin> <margin>What the letter Δ signifies.</margin> <margin>Pierius.</margin>

<summary>Athanasius Kircher explains the zoomorphic origins of the Egyptian alphabet, arguing that the letters A, Γ, and Δ were derived from the physical postures of the Ibis bird, which represents the god Hermes/Mercury.</summary>

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

The region of the Delta was named for the shape of the Greek letter Δ (Delta); it shares a similarity with the Ibises because these birds seem to mark out that letter with their gait, the space between their feet being drawn into the equal lines of a triangle; the same is signified by their open beak. And in book 47 regarding the seven letters, he says: Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Egyptian wisdom.</note>, who first communicated letters to the Egyptians, wished for the Ibis to be the first letter; for it reflects a triangular shape in its gait, with its legs positioned as has been said in its proper place; and that which is the first letter among us and the Greeks is adapted to the face of an isosceles triangle.

<margin>The fourth letter.</margin>
The fourth letter was V <note>Equivalent to the Greek Upsilon</note>, taken from the opening of the Ibis's beak, as the beak resembled a Y; for that shapes and characters were taken from the beaks of birds is testified by Theogenes in his *Hymn to the Sun* with these words: <gloss>Who taught the lines and letters from the beaks of birds.</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὃς ἐδίδαξας γραμμὰς καὶ γράμματα ἐκ τοῦ ῥύγχους τῶν ὀρνίθων</note> Indeed, the Ibis, by the gaping of its open beak, first taught the Egyptians the use of the compass <note>term: circinus - a tool for drawing circles and measuring distances</note>, which among them was a symbol of the measurement of things and the process of nature from lower to higher things, as will be taught at length in what follows.

<margin>The fifth letter.</margin>
The fifth letter among them was O, and it corresponded to the Greek Omicron: for they observed this animal either purging itself with a clyster <note>A historical belief that the Ibis used its long beak to perform self-enemas with water</note> or arranging its scattered feathers, with its neck twisted into a circle, expressing that figure which they, referring it to the number of letters, called <note>Three symbols: 1) A circle with a horizontal bar and vertical cross (similar to a Coptic or astrological Earth symbol), 2) A vertical bar with a hook at the top, 3) A small cross or plus sign.</note> as the author of our Dictionary mentions, whom we shall cite later; although others wish for this letter also to have been taken from the shape of the Sun. We have, therefore, five letters represented in one Ibis exhibiting different figures, which they included in the number of letters; so that no one should wonder that this animal was held in such great honor among the Egyptians. For first, it is probable that it indicated the whole of <margin>The Ibis in honor among the Egyptians.</margin> Geometry and the progression of quantity to the Egyptians: lines indeed by the various stretching of the neck and the longer legs; angles by the beak and the spreading of the feet; rectilinear triangles through the two legs, which, when spread while it inserts its beak across them, creates an equilateral triangle; and it perfectly expresses the ratio of triangular quantity through the section made; which are the first foundations of both speculative and practical Geometry. Concerning the other mysteries of this bird, they are dealt with at length in their proper places.

<margin>The sixth letter.</margin>
The sixth letter was Λ, which corresponds to the Greek A, and it was expressed by the spread feet of the Ibis, whence it was also called *abōk* <note>original Coptic: ⲁⲃⲱⲕ</note>, which in Egyptian signifies "progress"; for the Ibis walking reflected this character, whence also the invention of the Egyptian or "Ibiac" cubit <note>term: cubitus - a unit of length based on the forearm</note>; for from the tracks of this animal left in the mud of the riverbank, they took the measure of the cubit. It is placed in contrast to the preceding letter V, from the conjunction of which is born X, another letter frequent on Obelisks, by which they indicated the progress of the Soul of the World <note>term: Anima Mundi - the intrinsic connection between all living things on Earth</note> toward lower things and again to higher things. But see these matters treated specifically in their own places.

<margin>The Ibis called the first letter by the Egyptians.</margin>
And from this it is clear why Plutarch, Clement, and others called the Ibis the first letter: for it is said elsewhere that from this bird they learned not only letters, but also the secret reasoning of the hieroglyphics; for the letter is taken among...

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

Among them, it was not considered a simple letter-shape, but an entire hieroglyphic system; although it was a single entity, the Ibis exhibited various and great aspects of itself through its form. <margin>The Ibis dedicated to Mercury.</margin> For this reason, they dedicated it solely to Mercury <note>The Roman name for Hermes/Thoth</note>, as the God and inventor of the greatest things. But concerning the Ibis, see what we have discussed in its own Hieroglyphic Interpretation in Book 4 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*; the other letters, however, are said to have been discovered in this manner.

It is established from all the monuments of the Authors that the Bull was worshipped with divine honors by the Egyptians because of its remarkable benefits, so much so that they believed Osiris, under the form of a Bull, taught men various things necessary for sustaining human life. From this, observing the figure more curiously (as was their custom), <margin>Letters 7 & 8. <note>Coptic characters: ⲝ and symbolic flourishes</note></margin> they derived three characters: from the curvature of the horns <note>Symbol: A crescent moon shape representing the moon/Luna</note>, which they called *Sima*, that is, the symbol of the Moon; then the square forehead <note>Symbol: A small square frame</note> <note>Symbol: a square</note>, which they called the "Great O"; for they related various mysteries through the symbol of this figure. This indeed, when joined with the horns, provided them with another character, which they called <term>Beta (from the Phoenician word for 'house' or 'ox')</term> from the figure of the bull, and it corresponded to the Greek B; for the lowing of the bull produced such a vowel sound. For <term>Beta</term> was not merely a simple letter, but an "ideal" hieroglyphic letter, <margin>What Beta signifies in the language of the Phoenicians. Plutarch.</margin> involving many and various concepts, as will be clear in its explanation. Plutarch asserts this to be the case in Book 9 of the *Symposia*, Question 3, in these words:

->They say that Cadmus placed Alpha as the first of all letters because the Phoenicians call the bull by this name; and they placed it not second or third (as Hesiod does), but first among the necessary things.<- <note>original Greek: "Κάδμον φασὶ, τὸ ἄλφα πάντων προτάξαι διὰ τὸ οὕτω Φοίνικας, ἔτω καλεῖν τὸν βοῦν..."</note>

The third sacred animal among the Egyptians was the Hawk, from which we read that <margin>What letters the Hawk provided.</margin> similar characters, both common and symbolic, were borrowed. And indeed, the head with the beak gave the letter which they called *Scima* in the Alphabet, <margin>Scima, the 9th letter <note>Coptic characters: ⲥ followed by flourishes</note></margin> that is, "vision," because through the head of the Hawk (which expressed this character), they indicated the all-seeing God by a hidden allegory, as was shown extensively in the preceding pages; these things are confirmed elsewhere by various authorities.

The fourth animal was the dog; although they displayed great mysteries under this form <margin>10th Letter. What letters the Dog provided.</margin> and also derived a letter from it, it has not been possible to find exactly which one they deduced from it.

And these were those four most celebrated animals, which they called "the letters," because <margin>Four sacred animals.</margin> they had learned the principal letters from them, and they were accustomed to carry them about in the solemnities of the *Comasiae* <note>A Greek term for a festive procession or ritual parade</note>. Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a Christian theologian who wrote extensively on Egyptian customs</note> confirms all these things in Book 5 of the *Stromata* with these words: <margin>Clement.</margin>

->And in that which is called the Comasia among them, they carry about golden images of the Gods: two dogs, one hawk, and one ibis; and they call the four images of the idols "four letters."<- <note>original Greek: "Ἡ δὲ κἂν τῇ καλομεδίᾳ παρ᾿ αὐτοῖς Κομασίας τῶν Θεῶν χρυσᾶ ἀγάλματα..."</note>

Now indeed, in those things which are called by others the *Comasia* of the Gods, they carry about golden images of the Gods—two dogs, one hawk, and one ibis—and they call those four statues "four let-

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...letters, namely in honor of Mercury <note>The Roman name for the Egyptian god Thoth, whom Kircher credits with inventing writing</note>, who ingeniously and filled with mystical reasons extracted the first elements of letters from their forms.

<margin>
Ten letters extracted from four animals.

The eleventh letter taken from the horns of a Ram.
</margin>

We have, therefore, ten letters derived from the four aforementioned animals. The remaining letters, however, they derived from other living creatures, or even from the likeness of instruments. From the Ram, which they called *Amun*, or the dwelling place of Jupiter Hammon <note>The syncretic Greco-Egyptian god Zeus-Ammon</note>, they took the letter which corresponded to our **B**; the sound and pronunciation of which letter they learned from the voice of that same animal. Certainly, it is likely that the Interpreter of etymologies had this in mind when he sings thus:

-> "But the fool walks along like a sheep saying *be be*." <-
<note>original Greek: Ὁ δ’ ἠλίθιος ὥσπερ προϐάτων βὴ βὴ λέγων βαδίζει.</note>
-> *He walks like a stupid beast saying Be Be.* <-

<margin>
The twelfth letter, Zeuta.
<note>Hieroglyphic/Coptic symbol: A vertical squiggle resembling a serpent or the Coptic letter Ⲋ / ⲋ (Zeta/Zaita)</note>
</margin>

Hence Pierius <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano, a famous Renaissance mythographer</note> also asserts this was the second letter of the Egyptians. Furthermore, from the Serpent they derived another letter, which they called *Zeuta*, that is, "life," because the Serpent was a symbol of life among them; it corresponded to the Greek **ζ** (Zeta). The Copts form it thus: **ⲍ**; all of which things are demonstrated in their proper places.

<margin>
The thirteenth letter, called Thoth.
<note>Coptic text: ⲑⲁⲩⲧ (Thaut) with a cross-like symbol resembling a Theta with a horizontal bar extending out.</note>
</margin>

Moreover, by enclosing a transverse serpent within a fiery circle, they formed a letter which they called *Thauta*, that is, the letter of Thoth; it corresponded to the Greek **θ** (Theta). This was one of the most mystical characters, by which they secretly indicated the World through the fiery circle, and the Preserver of the World through the Serpent. Pherecydes the Syrian <note>A 6th-century BCE Greek philosopher</note> pursues all these matters at length in the book he inscribed concerning the *Ophiones* <note>Serpent-beings</note> and the sacred rites of the Egyptians. But let us hear Eusebius <note>The Bishop of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian</note> in Book 1, Chapter 7, near the end, describing everything word for word:

<margin>
Eusebius.
</margin>

> Taking his starting points from the Phoenicians, Pherecydes also theologized concerning the god he calls Ophioneus, and the Ophionidae, about whom we shall speak again. Furthermore, the Egyptians, depicting the world from the same concept, draw a circular, airy, and fiery-eyed circle, and in the middle a stretched-out hawk-shaped serpent; and the whole figure is like our Theta; signifying the world by the circle, and by the serpent in the middle, they signify this connective Good Spirit <note>original Greek: ἀγαθὸν δαίμονα / Agathodaemon</note>.

Pherecydes also, receiving the formations from the Phoenicians and being divinely taught concerning the God whom they called Ophioneus, and concerning the Ophionidae, discussed them in a wonderful manner; of which we shall speak in another place. Truly the Egyptians, depicting the universal World, led by this very opinion, extend a serpent in the form of a Hawk into an astral and fiery circle spread around the surface, so that it is similar to the figure of the Greek letter **θ** (Theta); signifying the form by the circle, and by the serpent placed in the circle, signifying the Good Spirit <term>Agathodaemon: a protective spirit or "Good Daimon" often depicted as a serpent</term>, the preserver of all things, by whose power the World is contained.

<margin>
The fourteenth letter.
<note>Coptic text: ⲫⲁⲗⲟⲯ (Phalops) followed by a symbol resembling a cross within a circle or the letter Phi (φ).</note>
</margin>

Furthermore, from a symbol or letter of this kind, they formed another, which they called *Phalops*, that is, "Love"; and it corresponded to the Greek **φ** (Phi). Truly, since we have explained the greatest mysteries of this letter in other places, it may suffice here to have merely indicated them; the reader meanwhile may consult the *Prodromus* <note>Kircher's earlier work, *Prodromus Coptus* (1636)</note>, where we have described the secrets of this character at length, as we have also done more extensively in the preceding pages.

Moreover, many characters were derived not from animals, but from the likeness of things...

# THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHICS.

I find that the shapes of the letters were taken from the things they represented; for example, the letter M, which <margin>The fifteenth letter, called *mou*:</margin> they call *mou* <note>original: ⲙⲱⲟⲩ</note>, that is, "water"; for this character represents the flow of water <term>kyriologically <note>In a literal or primary sense, where a sign directly represents an object.</note></term>. Such is also the character Z, which they call *zanken* <note>original: ⲍⲁⲛⲕⲏⲛ</note>, that is, a "chain," for it represents this by its shape and likeness, and it often occurs—as does the preceding one—among <margin>The sixteenth letter, *zanke*</margin> hieroglyphic diagrams. But more on these in their proper place. In the same way, they learned the letters N and P: the former from its likeness to a twin pyramid, the latter from its likeness to a grappling hook. Regarding O and C <note>The lunate Sigma, shaped like a C</note>, they did not learn them only from the Ibis and the Ox, as was said a little earlier, but according to the testimony of Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian</note>, they were <term>kyriological</term> letters <margin>The 17th & 18th letters, as well as the 19th & 20th.</margin> taken from the likeness of the Sun and the Moon. I cite his words from the 5th book of the *Stromata* <note>A major work by Clement of Alexandria; the title means "Miscellanies."</note>: "Those who wish to write 'Sun' make a circle. And when signifying the 'Moon,' they write a horn-like shape, according to its proper form." <note>original Greek: Οἱ βουλόμενοι γράφειν τὸν ἥλιον, ποιοῦσι τὸν κύκλον. Καὶ τὴν σελήνην σημαίνοντες σχῆμα κερατοειδές, κατὰ τὸ σχῆμα κύριον γράφουσι.</note>

Finally follows the letter of Taut <note>Thoth/Hermes Trismegistus</note>, the most mysterious of all, which corresponds to the Greek *Tau*; since we have described its structure and mysteries at length in the *Coptic Prodromus* <note>Kircher's 1636 work on the Coptic language</note>, as well as in the specific *Hierogrammatism* in the fourth book of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, we refer the reader there, lest we lose time in such a great mass of things to be said.

And these are the primary letters and elements of the Egyptians, with which they not only wrote common letters, but also hinted at great mysteries known only to the Priests, filled with mystical symbols. However, so that you may view what has been said so far in a single synopsis, we have decided to provide a table showing each one exactly.

**50 -> THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS <-**
<note>original: "OEDIPI ÆGYPTIACI". Athanasius Kircher’s massive 17th-century work attempting to decode Egyptian hieroglyphs through a mystical and symbolic lens.</note>

that is, the *Good Spirit* <note>original: "Bonus Demon"</note>, with the initial letters combined into one; for here, besides the capital letters of the aforementioned words, it also expresses the figure of that portion which they everywhere call Delta, or in Coptic *Agathos* <note>original: "ⲁⲅⲁⲑⲟⲥ"</note>, that is, the *Good Field*. Letters of this kind were mostly composed of three or six papyrus branches or wands <term>thyrsi: ceremonial staffs associated with ritual processions</term>, adapted into the shape of the first alphabetical letter. They displayed this during the established solemnities of the Gods' processions <term>Comasiarum: from the Greek 'komos', a ritual procession or festival</term>, and especially to Mercury in the form of an Ibis <note>original: "ⲓⲃⲓⲙⲟⲣⲫⲱ" (ibimorpho)</note>, from whose bird-shape the letter had been discovered; they also called this the *Hieralpha* <note>A "Sacred Alpha"</note>. But now let us subjoin the individual letters of the hieroglyphic alphabet.

***

-> **I** <-
<note>Hieroglyphic box showing an Ibis bird bending its neck to touch its feet, forming a shape similar to a capital 'A'.</note>

This character signifies the same thing as the *Good Spirit* <note>original: "Ἀγαθὸς Δαίμων" (Agathos Daimon)</note>, that is, the *Good Genius*; and it is composed of the initial letters **A** and **Δ** <note>Alpha and Delta</note>. For if the letter **Δ** is extended, it becomes **A**, which contains within itself in a monogrammatic way both **Δ** and **A**. This hieroglyphic letter is found in almost all Egyptian inscriptions, most notably on the Barberini, Lateran, Flaminian, Mahutean, and Medicean Obelisks, as will be discussed below in its proper place; we shall henceforth call it the *Hieralpha*.

***

-> **I I** <-
<note>Hieroglyphic box showing the profile of an Ibis head on the left and a right-angle square (norma) on the right.</note>

This character is called in Egyptian *Gammatoi* <note>original: "ⲅⲁⲙⲙⲁⲧⲟⲓ"</note>, that is, the *Square* <note>original: "Norma"</note>, and it properly expresses the Greek letter Gamma. By this, nothing else is indicated hieroglyphically than the Symmetry of the things of this Universe; hence it is seen everywhere inserted into the hands of Horus, the moderator of the sensible World. For just as by a square, or a gnomon, all things are arranged with just measure and proportion in architectural works, so the Genius of the Universe, in the fabric of the sensible World, gives to all things the correct proportion, measure, and weight.

***

-> **I I I** <-
<note>Hieroglyphic box showing a triangular shape or the Greek letter Delta (Δ).</note>

This character is called *Agathos* <note>original: "ⲁⲅⲁⲑⲟⲥ"</note>, that is, the *Good Field*, and it indicates that part of Egypt which they call the *Delta*; because that region, above all other provinces of Egypt, is both extremely healthy and fertile in all things necessary for the human race. It was discovered from the gait of the Ibis dwelling everywhere there; because the abundance of all good things flows from the supreme Powers into these lower realms, they aptly expressed it through a pyramidal shape—an element discovered from the spreading of the Ibis’s feet.

# THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHICS. 51

### IV
<note>Hieroglyphic tableau showing an ibis head with its beak wide open, forming a shape resembling the letter Y.</note>

> The Ibis, by the opening of its beak—which they called the instrument of the compass—provided them with the occasion for **discovering** the letter **Y**. By this character, they correctly indicated the progression from lower things to higher things, namely from the center to the circumference. For while the Ibis keeps one part of its beak fixed in the sand, it leaves a certain circular mark in the sand by the rotation of the other part. Since the Egyptians were most diligent in observing the actions of animals, it is not surprising that they discovered both the instrument of the compass and the occasion for the motion from the center to the circumference from this source.

---

### V
<note>Hieroglyphic tableau showing an ibis with its neck twisted back and around into a complete circle, forming a shape resembling the letter O.</note>

> This character is called <note>original Coptic: Ⲟⲩⲫϯ (Ouphti)</note>, which in Egyptian is the same as "Lord of the World"; it is equivalent to the Greek **O** micron. It likewise emanated from the Ibis; for the Ibis occasionally twists its neck in such a way that it appears to imitate a circle. When the Egyptians noted this, they were most superstitiously persuaded that they were being warned of some remarkable mystery by Mercury <note>The god Thoth, whom the Greeks identified with Hermes/Mercury</note> transformed into an Ibis. Consequently, they bestowed upon it the name <note>original Coptic: Ⲟⲩⲫϯ (Ouphti)</note>, which is the same as "Lord of the World." **Plutarch** alludes to this in his book *On Osiris and Isis*, while explaining the name **Omphis** (or more truly, you would say **Ophta**).
> ->*Plutarch.*<- <margin>Plutarch</margin>

---

### VI
<note>Hieroglyphic tableau showing the lower half of an ibis with its legs spread wide, forming a shape resembling the Greek letter Lambda (Λ).</note>

> This letter is called <note>original Coptic: Ⲗⲁⲃⲇⲁ (Labda)</note> by the Egyptians, and it is the opposite of the preceding one. For just as the preceding one indicates the progression of lower things to higher, so this one indicates the progression of higher things to lower. It is formed from the spreading of the Ibis's feet, from which the Egyptians first discovered the measure of the Egyptian cubit <note>A unit of length based on the forearm</note> impressed in the sand by the stride of the Ibis, as we have mentioned in the *Mechanics*; we have beautifully proved these things in their proper place from Abenephius <note>A reference to an Arabic author Kircher frequently cited</note>. This sign is found everywhere among the hieroglyphics, as will be discussed in its place; and this letter corresponds to the *Lambda* <note>original Greek: τῷ λάμβδα</note> of the Greeks and the Copts.

## X I I

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A circular border containing a coiled serpent, representing the 'Letter of Thoth' and the 'Life of the World'.</note>

This character is called by the Egyptians *Thauth* <note>original: ⲑⲁⲩϯ</note>, that is, the Letter of Thoth <note>The Egyptian god of wisdom, often identified with Hermes Trismegistus</note>; and hieroglyphically it signifies nothing other than the Life of the World, which the serpent enclosed in a circle denotes. This kind of hieroglyphic is seen everywhere on Obelisks and other Egyptian monuments, as we shall show in due time.

---

## X I I I

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A circle (globe) intersected by a vertical axis and a horizontal wavy band, described by Kircher as the 'Sphere of Love'.</note>

From the preceding character, the present character was born; which the Egyptians call *Philos* <note>original: ⲫⲓⲗⲟⲥ</note>, that is, *Love*. For it shows that all members of the World are connected by love through a universal life; whence it is also designated the Sphere of Love. We have treated this at greater length both in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, in the *Coptic Forerunner*, and in other places in this Work.

---

## X I V

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: Two horizontal wavy lines representing water.</note>

This character is called by the Egyptians *Moou* <note>original: ⲙⲱⲟⲩ</note>, that is, *Water*, because it expresses the flow of water, and thus it is a literal symbol of water <note>original: κυριολογικὸν τὸ ὕδατος σύμβολον</note>. It corresponds to the M of the Copts, Greeks, and Latins; nothing occurs more frequently among the hieroglyphics than this.

---

## X V

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A vertical chain-like symbol composed of interconnected small circles.</note>

This character is called by the Egyptians *Halysis* <note>original: ϩⲁⲗⲩⲥⲓⲥ</note>, that is, *Chain*, because it expresses a chain connected by circles; and it is a literal symbol of the "Chain of the Gods" <note>original: κυριολογικὸν δὲ σειρᾶς τῶν Θεῶν σύμβολον</note>, as Psellus <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine philosopher</note> teaches in his exposition of Zoroastrian Philosophy, and it corresponds to the Greek letter Xi (ξ).

### X V I I I

| <note>Hieroglyphic symbols: At the top, a Sun with a human face and rays. Below it, a crescent Moon with a human profile face. At the bottom, a C-shaped character (Coptic Sima).</note> |

What these two literal symbols of the Sun and the Moon represent is recognized from their very shapes—namely, the Sun and the Moon—and they are the same as the Coptic letters <term>ⲟ</term> <note>Omicron</note> and <term>ⲥ</term> <note>Sima</note>. These letters are seen in a very ancient fragment sent by that man of immortal memory, Nicolas Peiresc <note>A famous 17th-century French scholar and antiquarian</note>, which I shall place here. In it, you see four statues enclosed by a serpent twisted into a circle, with the characters ⊕, and a figure in the middle <note>Symbol: A rectangular portal containing a Sun and Moon</note>. Although we have explained these in the *Supplement to the Prodromus* and the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, we have nevertheless decided to explain them more fully in this place as if in their own proper home.

# PREPARATORY DISCOURSE III.
## That the Egyptian letters were first brought into Greece by Cadmus, and concerning the antiquity of the Coptic language.

<margin>The origin of Greek letters and sciences is from Egypt.</margin> **T**here is indeed a great controversy among Authors concerning the Greek letters and from where they took their origin; for some ascribe their invention to Cecrops, some to Inachus, and others to Palamedes. We, to settle the matter in a few words, assert that all knowledge, both of letters and of sciences, was first introduced into Greece from Egypt. And I say that the letters could have been no other than those mystical ones which we have cited just above;

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...mus; <note>The text continues from the previous page, likely referring to "letters" or "characters."</note> which indeed are sufficient for expressing any concept of the mind in writing; although the Greeks, in the succession of time, always added more and more, as is evident from their Alphabet. <margin>Herodotus. Cadmus brought letters from Egypt into Greece.</margin> And that these letters were adapted for common use, neglecting the figures of animals <note>Referring to Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>, and first transferred to the Greeks by Cadmus, is clear from Herodotus in *Terpsichore* and elsewhere; and for that reason they are called Cadmean letters, or to use the words of Herodotus, <term>Phoenician letters of Cadmus</term> <note>original: Φοινικὴϊα τὰ Κάδμου γράμματα</note>. Whence also that most ancient consensus of all Greece sufficiently proves that the Greeks received letters from Cadmus; nor is there any reason why <margin>Cadmus the inventor of Greek letters.</margin> we should either deny so manifest a thing, or agree with Tzetzes <note>Joannes Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine poet and grammarian</note> who denies it; who strives to prove by a double argument that the Greeks had letters before Cadmus. The first is that an Oracle was given to Cadmus: <term>"Flee, you, avoiding the Median... to Cadmus"</term> <note>original: Φεῦζε σὺ μῆδον ἀλύσθων εἴκτοσε Κάδμῳ; this refers to an ancient prophecy</note>. The other argument: that Bellerophon, who was older than Cadmus, carried written tablets concerning his own death. Both arguments are futile, and both were invented by the Poets. For why were they called Cadmean letters, if they are not attributed to Cadmus as the Author? Even if Cadmus is the Author, or at least the first teacher and indicator of them in Greece, how did the Greeks have letters before Cadmus, since they are nowhere called by a more ancient name than <term>Cadmean letters</term> <note>original: Καδμήϊα γράμματα</note>? <margin>Clement.</margin> To all of which Clement of Alexandria subscribes in Book 1 of the *Stromata*: <term>Cadmus the Phoenician is the discoverer of the letters of the Greeks, as says Hor-</term> <note>original: Κάδμος ὁ Φοῖνιξ ἐστὶν, ὁ τῇ γραμμάτων Ἑλλήνων εὑρέτης, ὡς φησὶν Ὁρ-</note>... Whence also Herodotus writes that the letters were called <margin>Herodotus. Cadmus and Phoenix were Egyptians.</margin> Phoenician: but that Cadmus and Phoenix were Egyptians; St. Jerome testifies that they flourished in the times of Joshua, and that Cadmus, together with his brother Phoenix, set out into Syria from Egyptian Thebes, where they had originated; so that it is likely that in the time of Othniel <note>A Biblical Judge</note> he came from Phoenicia into Greece, and there, in memory of Egyptian Thebes, he founded Boeotian Thebes, leaving Phoenicia to his brother Phoenix, from whom it also obtained its name. Moreover, Egyptian men could not have handed down any letters other than those they had learned as children in Egypt. Therefore, there should be no doubt that Cadmus was that first person who perfectly imbued the Greeks with Egyptian letters. However, that there was in Greece before Cadmus some seed or some rudiment of these letters, and that there were already at that time most learned men in Greece, <margin>Philo.</margin> is clear from Philo, who relates in the *Life of Moses* that all the most learned men were called from Greece with great promises for his instruction. Therefore, they either had their own letters at that time, whether brought from Egypt by Cecrops, the first King of the Athenians, or introduced before him by Inachus, from which the story later emerged (that the Greeks had letters before Cadmus). This is likely; since Cecrops himself was an Egyptian, nearly a century older than <margin>Cecrops the Egyptian.</margin> Cadmus, and a contemporary of Moses, according to the testimony of Eusebius; therefore, according to Tzetzes, he was called <term>Two-natured</term> <note>original: Διφυὴς; usually meaning hybrid or of two forms</note> because he was equally skilled in the Greek and Egyptian languages. Pausanias is the authority that he also transferred <term>piety</term> <note>original: εὐλαβείαν</note> from Egypt to Greece along with other ceremonies; <margin>Pausanias.</margin> about which Tzetzes also sings thus:

# THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHICS

The first of all the kings of Attica was Cecrops, and he was the first to be called <term>Diphyes</term> <note>Greek: "of two natures" or "double-formed"</note>, because he possessed the stature of two men in length, and because he was skilled in both the Greek and Egyptian languages.

<margin>Whether the Egyptian language proceeded from the Greek, or vice versa.</margin> It is clear from what has been said that Greek letters first originated from the Egyptians. However, one might rightly doubt whether the Greek language also proceeded from the Egyptian. I asserted the affirmative in the fourth chapter of my <term>Coptic Forerunner</term> <note>Original: "Prodromus Coptus," Kircher's 1636 work on the Coptic language</note>; but, eventually becoming better informed through daily experience, I have found that the Egyptian language is one of the mother tongues <note>original: "maternarum"</note> having no affinity with any other, as far as can be gathered from its unique character, conjugation, and the inflection of nouns. Nor should we be moved by words smelling of <term>Hellenism</term> <note>Greek: "hellenismon," or Greek influence</note> and Greek-style expressions occurring here and there in the Lexicon. Indeed, I teach extensively elsewhere that this kind of mixing of Greek words with Coptic vocabulary happened during the times of Alexander the Great and the subsequent kings of the <term>Ptolemaic lineage</term> who held power in Egypt. This occurred through frequent commerce and the back-and-forth travel with the Greeks that intervened over a space of three hundred years and more; and the Copts whom I consulted on this matter affirm the same thing. Therefore, I would not want my words in the *Coptic Forerunner* to be understood in the sense that I was asserting that the Greek language stands in relation to the Egyptian as, for example, the Chaldean language does to Hebrew, or Italian to Latin, as some have thought. No one, unless unskilled in said languages, would deny that the latter is the daughter of Latin and the former the daughter of Hebrew. For I do not feel that Greek drew its origin immediately from Egyptian; much less do I think the Greek language should be called a corrupted Egyptian. Rather, anyone who compares one with the other <term>more accurately</term> <note>Greek: "akribesteros"</note> will know that the entire similarity between the two happened from a mixing of words, as I have said. For some languages can use the same words common to another language, even if they differ in substance by "the whole heaven," as they say. Thus, German intersperses many Latin, Italian, and French words; Latin also willingly receives Greek vocabulary, even though both are very different from the languages from which they borrow; you will find these matters treated more extensively elsewhere. Indeed, the Coptic language uses not only Greek words, but also Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, and Samaritan ones, arising, I believe, from the fellowship of neighboring nations. But since we have dealt with this argument regarding the Coptic language in a specific work, which we call *The Coptic Language Restored*, we refer the reader to that, from which the wise reader will easily recognize which words are of Greek and which are of Egyptian origin.

<margin>Pietro della Valle.</margin> Truly, I cannot omit in this place to interject those things which that most eminent man, Pietro della Valle—a singular friend of mine while he lived—asserts in the 11th Letter of his *Travels* concerning the Coptic language; these are certainly consistent with what we have already taught in the preceding pages. His Italian words are as follows: *"Since we are on this subject of languages, I want to tell Your Lordship another curiosity regarding my mummies, which I alluded to above when I promised to speak of Egyptian letters. You must know, then, that here in Egypt, among those Christians whom I have mentioned at other times as Copts, I have found a particular language, with a writing system, the characters of which,"*

# EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

which, as much in form as in name, are all Greek (although slightly altered in pronunciation) except for eight, which they have in addition to the Greeks, being of different pronunciation and shape. Among these, as I wished out of curiosity to have some knowledge of them, I found some correspondence with Greek matters, and specifically regarding details for which not even the Greeks could provide a reason. For example: this Coptic language writes its arithmetic numbers with the letters of the Alphabet, just as the Greek language does. But the Greeks, not having enough letters to express all the numbers—as Your Excellency knows—supplement them with other figures; particularly for the number 6, they mark it with a <note>original: "Sigmatau," referring to the Stigma symbol Ϛ</note> Sigmatau. However, I say: if the letters are not enough and the Greeks find other figures, that is fine; but why place the <note>Stigma symbol Ϛ</note> so early at the number six, and not follow the order of the letters as long as they last, since there would be time to supplement those that are missing at the end? Regarding this, I find no Greek who can give me the reason. But I have indeed found it in the writing of the Copts: because their Alphabet has a letter in the sixth place which the Greeks do not have; the shape of which is exactly a <note>Coptic letter So: ⲋ</note>, and they call it <term>So</term> <note>The Coptic numeral for 6</note>, and they pronounce it like an S, but different in some way from the Sigma. And so, quite rightly, this figure comes to occupy the sixth place among the arithmetic numbers. Concerning these matters, see the extensive treatise in the <term>Coptic Prodromus</term> <note>Latin: "Prodromus Coptus," Kircher's earlier work on the Coptic language</note>. Furthermore, the figure that the Greeks use for 90 is not very dissimilar from the letter that the Copts place there.

In short, from these and other signs, I gather that without doubt, either the Coptic script originates from the Greek, or the Greek from the Coptic, although the languages themselves are entirely different from one another. That the Greeks gave the script to the Copts is suggested by their modern name, which is Greek, and according to some means nothing other than "Cut" <note>Greek: "kopto," to cut</note>; and they say they were so called because these Christians, who formerly followed the heresies of Eutyches and Dioscorus, used to circumcise themselves before baptism. From this they also took the name "Christians of the Belt"—that is, from the belt upwards—because from the belt downwards, due to circumcision, they appeared more like Jews. Furthermore, we know that Alexander built Alexandria and left colonies in Egypt, which could have taught the people their script and also, in part, the language; since in Coptic one very often finds some Greek word, but pronounced in the ancient manner, with the same diphthongs, with the H <note>Eta</note> for the sound of E, and with similar circumstances which we know from a thousand signs have been changed by modern Greeks.

But on the contrary, I see that the Copts in their books call themselves Egyptians, as I mentioned at the beginning; and that perhaps the name "Copt" is either corrupted through ignorance, or was given to them by modern Greeks to mock them as "Circumcised," derived from the similarity of the words. For the word "Copt," which in Greek can mean "Cut," is somewhat similar to the name <note>original Coptic script: ⲄⲨⲠⲦⲒⲞⲤ</note> **EGYPTIAN** <note>Greek: "Guptios"</note>, which is what they call themselves in their own language; and even more to <term>Cubti</term>, which is the word also meaning Egyptian by which they are called by the Arabs. This word <term>Cubti</term> could also be that it was perhaps derived by the Arabs from the name of the City <term>Coptos</term>, which in Egypt—that is, in the Thebaid—was once a principal city, common to both Egyptians and <margin>Strabo.</margin> Arabs, according to Strabo. Although it seems difficult to me that this city (which is not known to have ever been the royal seat of the whole country) could have given its name to all Egyptians—even if it gave it to a single Province of which it was the head, which according to <margin>Ptolemy.</margin> Ptolemy took its name from it as the <term>Coptite nome</term> <note>A "nome" was an administrative district in ancient Egypt</note>—nevertheless, it would not be impossible that

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

There is another particular detail, no less beautiful: namely, that the hieroglyphs in those times were not otherwise the common letters of the Egyptians, as perhaps some have thought; but that it was another hidden way to express concepts secretly, almost like our **Devices** <note>Italian: *Imprese*—symbolic emblems or heraldic mottos popular in the Renaissance</note>; or, if they were indeed letters (as I believe), they were <margin>Diodorus Siculus. Herodotus.</margin> sacred characters, not commonly used in all matters; according to what Diodorus Siculus, and much before him Herodotus, has left written for us: that the Egyptians had two kinds of letters, sacred and profane; and that the popular and common Egyptian letter of that time was this **Coptic** <note>original: *Cofta*</note>, of which I speak. For although Herodotus <margin>Herodotus.</margin> in the same place says that the Egyptians, contrary to the Greeks, wrote from right to left—which does not happen in the writing of the Copts—it may nonetheless be that he intends this for the sacred writing of the hieroglyphs, not specifying that he means both. And the order of the hieroglyphs in being written, as they must undoubtedly begin from top to bottom, so perhaps, where there are several lines of them, or a single line across, they must proceed from right to left, as Herodotus says, and as I understand also happens with the characters of the **Chinese**. However, be that as it may, of this Egyptian writing of the Copts, I already have with me a few books, namely the entire **Psalter of David**, the entire **Gospel of Saint John**, and some others, which upon returning to Italy by the grace of God, I will be able to show and read to those who are curious, and keep them at least as an ornament for my library. But among the others, I have one which I considered a great fortune to find, which contains by four authors who write in Arabic (briefly indeed, but perhaps sufficiently among them all together) the **Grammar** of this Egyptian language; and furthermore two **Vocabularies** with about six thousand Egyptian words, the most important ones, faithfully interpreted since ancient times into Arabic. If in Rome, or elsewhere, where some understanding of the Arabic language is beginning to exist, someone were ever found who by means of these could interpret this book of mine into Latin; and, as I shall not fail to use diligence, we could by means of the printing presses propagate it and communicate it to the Learned throughout the world; I would hope that in such a way even this lost and dead Egyptian language of the Copts could be revived in the world, with notable benefit both to literature for its antiquity, and also to the Church, as the few relics that remain of the Egyptians today are very ancient Christians, separated from the Roman Church for a very long time. <note>The following is Kircher's Latin commentary</note> *Whatever Peter della Valle desires in this place, we have provided in the "Treasury of the Egyptian Language," which we also call "The Egyptian Language Restored," <note>original: "Lingua Aegyptiaca Restituta," published by Kircher in 1643</note> based on the original manuscript of the said Peter, which he had granted to me for this purpose, as is evident in the Preface of the said Treasury.* And, as they have all the Holy Scripture in this language of theirs, and many other things besides that belong to religion; everything that is found among them to conform with us will be a great argument against the modern **Heretics** of Europe, who disagree with us in so many things, in which nevertheless the overseas Christians, separated from us for so many centuries, are seen in every way to agree with us. Your Lordship has heard, regarding various subjects, very long digressions, which I would never have made with anyone else but you; because such discourses in the ears of certain people of little understanding seem—and I know it—mere pedantry; and one must accommodate oneself to the taste of others in this world, at least in appearance. *Thus says Peter della Valle. # THE THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHICS

### Whether hieroglyphs consist of a certain kind of reading as in other writings, and how such a reading should be established.

Since hieroglyphs explain symbolic and mystical concepts through certain signs discovered with the highest felicity of genius, they certainly cannot consist of syllables, words, or sentences. We have already proven this many times over against those who—persuaded by I know not what arguments—too simply believe that histories and the praises of Kings are contained beneath the hieroglyphs. For as <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries; Kircher relies heavily on him to justify a spiritual rather than linguistic interpretation of symbols.</note> rightly says: since the Egyptians insert hidden mysteries into manifest symbols, in interpreting them, "dismiss the words, and receive the meanings." I have decided that the following examples will now clarify how this is so. The following figure:

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: An elaborate symbolic figure enclosed in a rounded arch. It features two cobras (aspides) facing outward on the left and right, each balanced on a textured base and supporting a sphere (sun disk) on its head. Between the serpents is a central vertical bundle, described by Kircher as a floral or gramineous cluster, topped by a larger sphere. A smaller circular element is positioned at the base of the central stalks. Kircher identifies this as a "tutulus" or sacred ornament.</note>

is a <term>tutulus</term> <note>Originally a Roman term for a high-piled hairstyle or a conical priest's cap; here Kircher uses it to describe a sacred Egyptian headdress or architectural ornament.</note>, and it is partly placed upon the heads of the Gods, and partly possesses its own hidden significance when standing alone. For I find that the cornice of the Temple of Isis in Rome was decorated with this figure, as seen from the innumerable stones upon which this figure is carved—two of which are still viewed in my Museum. Such "tutuli" are also frequently seen in the border of the smaller characters of the <term>Isiac Tablet</term> <note>Also known as the Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet of Roman origin depicting Egyptian deities, which Kircher believed was an ancient map of secret wisdom.</note>, as will be seen in due time. The figure consists of a flame, two asps carrying spheres on their heads, and a grassy bundle with flower and fruit, upon which a globe is placed. This is a hieroglyphic character; it suggests to the mind not a letter, nor a syllable, nor a word, but an entire ideal sense; and it is as follows: [**The eternal and immortal nature of the Gods, bestowing life, fire, heat, motion, and the abundance of things upon all those who worship them rightly.**] Moreover, it was not only significant of the aforementioned things, but it also possessed an added efficacy, which being granted...

<summary>Kircher argues that hieroglyphs represent complex theological ideas rather than phonetic sounds, using a specific "tutulus" ornament from the Temple of Isis in Rome to demonstrate how a single image conveys the eternal, life-giving nature of the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Egyptian symbolic logic from the previous section, specifically addressing how the physical orientation of hieroglyphs relates to their metaphysical meaning across different media.</meta>

...placed soon after, through a hidden system of symbols wonderfully pleasing to the Gods, they believed they would obtain that which the symbols signified. Furthermore, it signified not only the operations which he <note>likely referring to a specific deity or the creator</note> performed in the **Archetypal World**, but also those in the **Starry** and **Elementary Worlds**. For the <term>Tutulus</term><note>A high, conical headdress or crown often seen on Egyptian deities</note> by itself indicates the principles of the Archetypal World; when placed upon a <term>Hawk</term>, it indicates the virtues of the Starry World; but when placed upon Isis, or Nephthys, or the Elementary Spirits, it indicated Elementary operations. And this is how all hieroglyphics must be understood, as will be explained in the sequence of this Work. Hence, such is the nature of hieroglyphics that whether they are placed downward, upward, to the right, to the left, or in whatever position, they retain their full and perfect sense, according to the condition of the various subjects upon which they were carved, just as we reported above regarding simple characters. For on **Obelisks**, they were most often displayed in a perpendicular position within their columns; but on marble tables, they maintained a flat position parallel to the Horizon; while on statues, they preserved an order mixed from all—perpendicular, horizontal, sloping, scattered, and interrupted; which can also be seen in the <term>Bembine Tablet</term><note>Also known as the Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs that Kircher studied extensively</note>, as will be discussed in its proper place.

When I say this, I would not want anyone to persuade themselves that the characters were therefore placed blindly and without reason: not at all; for there was a supreme connection of these types of symbolic characters, and a wonderful arrangement, by which one concept always followed another. But since these things cannot be sufficiently explained except by practice itself, the curious Reader will see all these things more clearly in the interpretation of the hieroglyphic monuments that will soon follow, and, taught by experience itself, will find that what I have said is true.
