# THE THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHS.
## CHAPTER I.

### -> The Hieroglyphic Significance of the Guinea Fowl and the Goose: <-

<margin>What the Guinea Fowl is.</margin> Various authors have explained what the Guinea Fowl <note>original: *Meleagris*</note> properly is in different ways; some have called the Guinea Fowl a Peacock; several a Turkey <note>original: *Gallum Indicum*, literally "Indian Cock"</note>; others the "Hen of Pharaoh"; others the Stymphalian birds; and others have called them Penelopes. Certainly, what the Guinea Fowl properly is, the hieroglyphic figure of this bird—which is very frequent among the hieroglyphs—shows clearly enough: for it is nothing other than that bird which the common people call the "Hen of Pharaoh." Its entire body is composed of a blue color sprinkled with innumerable black spots, as if by certain most elegant and beautiful patterns; it has a bony head, resembling something triangular, a back protruding somewhat into a hump, a rather long neck, and a slender tail. Birds of this kind are seen here in Rome in the gardens of Princes, and not infrequently on the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet of Isiac mysteries, also known as the Mensa Isiaca</note>, as will be seen in due time. <margin>Pausanias: The Guinea Fowl is sacred to Isis.</margin> Pausanias, in his *Description of Phocis*, testifies that these birds are sacred to Isis. For two fairs were celebrated annually for the Tithorean Isis, namely in Spring and Autumn; on the third day before each, when it was lawful to enter her inner sanctum, the inhabitants of Tithorea purified themselves by a certain secret rite, and they buried the remains of the entrails that had been cast out during the previous fairs, always carried to the same place; and that was the rite of their solemn day. On the following day, the merchants erected stalls for themselves out of reeds and whatever material was at hand; finally, on the third day, those who had come to those fairs sold furniture, every kind of cattle, clothing, and silver. In the afternoon hours, they turned their minds to the sacred rites; the wealthier people sacrificed oxen and goats, while those whose family fortune was thinner sacrificed Geese and Guinea Fowl to the Goddess. <margin>Why they are called Meleagrides.</margin> They are called *Meleagrides* because of the slain Meleager, at whose tomb his sisters lamented; and they say that Diana transformed them into Guinea Fowl. <margin>Ovid.</margin> Regarding these, see the Mythologists and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* Book 8. And this indeed is the opinion of the Greeks concerning the Guinea Fowl; but the Egyptians philosophized about the "Hen of Pharaoh" in a much different manner. <margin>The nature of Guinea Fowl according to the Egyptians.</margin> For when they saw that the entire body of this bird was constituted with a certain ineffable symmetry, and adorned with little stars distributed over the whole body as if in a firmament, they came to the opinion that the World Soul <note>original: *Anima Mundi*</note>—which they themselves called the All-Forming Spirit of Nature <note>original: *Pantamorphum naturae Genium*</note>—had established its seat in the body of this bird. They thought that through this very thing, the bird revealed itself to wise men regarding those matters which they observed to shine with such majesty, order, disposition, and variety. Hence, they attributed this bird as a most fitting symbol to the All-Forming Spirit of Nature, or the "Paternal Depths" <note>A Neoplatonic term for the source of all creation</note>. <margin>The triangular head of the Guinea Fowl.</margin> It has a triangular head to indicate the three triads by which the Paternal Depths were constituted; it has a blue, humped body, or one made in the shape of an arch, by which they noted the arched and blue surface of the firmament, decorated with innumerable stars just like the blue body of this bird. On the Bembine Tablet, it is placed upon the head of the All-Forming Nature, the significance of which...

will be explained in its own time. It is also often seen with its neck contracted as if sleeping. <margin>Abenephius</margin> But let us hear Abenephius <note>An Arabic author frequently cited by Kircher, though often through pseudepigraphal sources</note>:

-> The Pharaoh’s Hen is a sign of the celestial sphere <note>original Arabic: "Al-dajaja Fir'awn hiya 'alamat al-falak al-fuluk"</note> <note>Symbol: A small circle surrounded by eight dots or rays</note> <-

*The Pharaoh’s Hen is that sign of the firmament or of the fixed stars.* For just as the firmament is adorned with various stars, so the Pharaoh’s Hen is variegated with spots like little stars; hence the Egyptians rightly signified by it the firmament and its presiding power. And let these remarks suffice concerning the <term>Meleagris</term> <note>The guinea fowl, named after the sisters of Meleager in Greek myth</note> or Pharaoh’s Hen.

<margin>The sacred writing of the Goose.</margin> The figure of the Goose is also frequently observed among the hieroglyphics; by which the Egyptians indicated nothing other than a cautious and vigilant Governor; for the Goose is a vigilant animal, and at the slightest noise it cackles by raising its voice, and is excellently equipped by nature for swimming. Hence they used to call <term>Cheniscos</term> <note>From the Greek 'chen' meaning goose; a goose-shaped ornament on a ship's stern</note> that part of the ship which they call the stern, adorned with the image of a Goose, according to the testimony of Bayfius. Moreover, that there was a gilded image of a Goose, <margin>Lucian. The figure of a Goose used to adorn the sterns of ships.</margin> Lucian testifies in the Dialogue titled **The Ship, or The Wishes** <note>original Greek: Ploion e Euchai</note>; **as the stern itself rises up slightly curved, with a golden little goose placed upon it.** <note>original Greek: hōs d' hē prymnē men epanestēken ērema kampylē chrysoun chēniskon epikeimenon</note> For the Goose was a ship of good omen in the business of navigation, and just as the Goose easily reaches the shore by swimming, so they believed that by the happy auspice of this bird, the ship would reach the port it sought with successful progress.

<margin>Herodotus. Pausanias.</margin> Hence Aristides, Herodotus, and Pausanias testify that Geese were sacrificed to Isis. Petrus Marsus, commenting on Herodotus, says: *I found that the Egyptian Priests were formerly accustomed to eat the flesh of oxen and geese, by whom Isis is worshipped, whom they maintain to be the Moon, on whose forehead are lunar horns.* For the Goose disturbs the silence of that time which is proper to the Moon, that is, the night. And after a few words, he says: *Truly, Io, daughter of Inachus the King of the Argives, from whom the river took its name, was snatched away by the Phoenicians, as Herodotus pleases, and led into Egypt; after her death she was called Isis, and was held to be the Tutelary Spirit of Egypt, according to Servius; where her image was, holding a sistrum in her right hand and a bucket in her left, provided with bovine horns; she had a temple in Busiris, where the Priests performed divine rites for her with water and fire, in memory of the navigation by which Io was carried into Egypt; for which reason it happened that the Goose was consecrated to Isis, who was accustomed to delight in the waters; just as Isis does in the Nile, of which she is the Spirit and Governess.* But since we shall speak more diffusely of the hieroglyphic of the Goose in its proper place, let what has been said here suffice. It remained to speak of the sacred writing of the fish; but since we have treated this argument extensively in its proper places and occasions, we did not wish to linger on it longer here. See the Pamphilian Obelisk, page 526, and in the following sections on Obelisks.

# CHAPTER II.
# On Hieroglyphic Herbs and Plants.

The Egyptians, the most inquisitive of mortals, were accustomed to dedicate different numbers to different Gods (as we have taught in our sections on Arithmetic); in a wonderful manner, they applied these mystical numbers to natural things to produce marvelous effects. This was most clearly evident in the subject of vegetables <margin>The Egyptians dedicated numbers to their Gods.</margin>. Indeed, they dedicated Unity to the Supreme Deity and the Cause of Causes, from whom all things flow as if from a perennial fountain. They dedicated the number two to Pallas; three to Minerva; four to Apollo; five to Isis; six to Osiris; seven to Mercury; eight to Ammon; and the same judgment applies to the remaining numbers dedicated to as many Gods. After this, they would investigate what number the leaves of herbs possessed; and whichever herb matched in its leaves a number dedicated to a certain Deity, they consecrated that plant to the same, as if it pertained to the household of said Deity. <margin>The Egyptians dedicated flowers and leaves to the Gods according to their numbers.</margin> Finally, they examined flowers according to the number of petals with which they were adorned, together with their shape and color; and if they found any flower corresponding to a Deity in number, shape, and color, they consecrated it to that same Deity as being most appropriate. They performed sacrifices with these plants, believing them most effective for petitioning the Deity; having been taught by long experience, they eventually enrolled these plants in the sacred register of hieroglyphics as belonging to the "chains" <note>Kircher refers to the Neoplatonic idea of "chains" or "series" (catenae), where earthly objects are linked to celestial powers.</note> of the divine Powers. In a similar way, they duly investigated the number of nodes in the stalks of plants, and the shape of the stalks—whether they were round, triangular, or square. By employing these ceremonies according to the analogy of the aforementioned things, they believed they could produce wonderful effects both in Medicine and in divination through dreams. Indeed, when they were about to consult regarding the cure of some disease, before committing themselves to bed, they would place many such <term>characterisms</term> <note>original: "characterismos"; here meaning the distinctive physical traits or "signatures" of the plants</note> of plants and flowers before them, entreating the Deities to show them through dreams which of the said herbs would lead to the healing of the disease. <margin>The Egyptians investigated the powers of plants and herbs through dreams.</margin> Whichever plant appeared in the dream, they considered it to have been divinely demonstrated for the cure of the illness. They proceeded no differently in other consultations, concerning which see what we have brought forward from various authors in our sections on Magic and Hieroglyphic Theology.

Furthermore, they observed with the highest scrutiny the <term>characterisms</term> of individual plants—namely, which member of the human body each responded to and expressed best, as we have handed down extensively in our <term>Hieroglyphic Medicine</term> <note>A concept where plants are used to treat organs they physically resemble.</note>. For they believed that a plant was most suitable for a specific limb if it expressed that limb through its external shape and a certain analogous <term>signature</term> <note>original: "signatura"; the "Doctrine of Signatures" suggests that plants resembling body parts can treat those parts.</note>. But so that we may provide you with some specimen of this, we have chosen to place here several diagrams of herbs, so that the mind of the Egyptians in botanical doctrine might become more clearly known. If, therefore, they discovered any herb similar in shape to the heart, they persuaded themselves with absolute certainty that it would heal the ailments of the heart; for by its hidden signature, the Deity who presides over the heart...

In this same manner, the following herbs were said to heal the teeth, eyes, and bladder: <term>Dentaria</term> <note>Toothwort, named for its tooth-like root scales</note>, <term>Anthemis</term> <note>Chamomile, whose flower was thought to resemble an eye</note>, and <term>Colutea</term>, or the <term>Egyptian Staphylodendrum</term> <note>Bladder senna</note>, because by their roots, flowers, and pods, they expressed the teeth, eyes, and bladder. Indeed, they believed all species of orchids healed the reproductive organs, because they reflected the genital members with their roots, as the following <term>Cynosorchis</term> <note>Dog-orchid</note> teaches. In this way, they said that <term>Hermodactylum</term> <note>Finger-moly or "Hermes' Finger"</note> was beneficial for joint diseases or <term>Chiragra</term> <note>Gout of the hand</note>, because its root expresses the hand, as the figure shows. For the falling out of hair or <term>Alopecia</term>, they used a remedy of <term>Adiantum</term> <note>Maidenhair fern</note> or <term>Polytrichum</term> <note>Hair-moss</note>, because it expressed hair, as is clear from the following figure. If, however, a Scorpion had bitten someone, they cured him with the root of the <term>Scorpion-plant</term>, which herb we call <term>Doronicum</term> or <term>Leopard's Bane</term> <note>original: *Aconitum pardelianches*</note>, because the root of this herb expresses the perfect shape and likeness of a Scorpion by its own form, as the figure [shows].

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER. CHAPTER II.

...lest we defraud the literary Republic of this new addition of materials, we have deemed it necessary to subjoin their genuine significance here.

Certainly, it is demonstrated more than enough from Obelisks, tablets, and statues that the Egyptians gathered a great store of hieroglyphics from the economy of plants; these we have decided to explain in this place as much as possible, lest they bring confusion rather than clarity to the reader during the actual interpretation of the hieroglyphics. And concerning the hieroglyphics of vegetables—the fennel-stalk, the rush, the papyrus, and their thyrsi <note>thyrsus: a staff topped with a pinecone, associated with ritual</note>, branches, and staffs; likewise concerning the lotus, the persea tree, and reeds; likewise concerning the staffs, crowns, and other things usually made from them—since we have treated these most amply in the section on the Obelisk, we shall omit them here and turn our pen to describing other hieroglyphic plants omitted in that place.

->But to the point.<-

<margin>Various Egyptian herbs and plants.</margin>
§ I. **Acacia** <note>original Coptic: ⲁⲕⲁⲕⲓⲁ</note> is an Egyptian plant which the Arabs call **Sant** <note>original Arabic: سنت</note>; it grows in places in Egypt far removed from the sea, and trees of this kind grow to the size of a mulberry tree, spreading their branches widely upward. The trunk is the size of a plum tree, has a black, rough bark fortified with very sharp thorns; it has somewhat long leaves, very minutely incised; it produces small but golden flowers, with downy globules of a most excellent scent, very similar to the globules of a plane tree if you disregard the color; it bears seed enclosed in pods, though smaller than carobs. It is well established that this herb was sacred to the Egyptians and received among the hieroglyphics because, by a certain hidden play of nature, it seeks the Sun; for when the Sun rises, not unlike the lotus and the heliotrope <note>heliotrope: a plant that turns toward the sun</note>, it is accustomed to open its leaves, but at sunset to close them so tightly that they seem more like thorns than leaves. Furthermore, the flower, with its downy head, closely mimics the radiant splendor of the Sun, as we have been able to observe with great admiration in our own domestic garden, where these trees grow very well. Whence the Egyptians, having numbered it among the Solar herbs, used it with the greatest diligence in sacrifices offered to the Solar Deities, as will be said in its proper place; for they believed that just as the solar Deities are greatly delighted by herbs of this kind committed to their trust, so the Deities are effectively drawn to them by a legitimate rite, on account of a hidden natural similarity and analogy. See what we have discussed more fully regarding this plant in the **Bembine Tablet** <note>The Bembine Tablet of Isis is an elaborate bronze tablet with Egyptianizing motifs, famous in the Renaissance</note>.

<margin>Centaury.</margin>
§ II. **Antialleas** <note>original Coptic: ⲁⲛⲧⲓⲁⲗⲗⲉⲁⲥ</note> is an Egyptian plant which we say is the same as that which the Arabs and Syrians call **Qanturiyun** <note>original Arabic: قنطوريوس</note> and the Greeks also call **Kentaureion** <note>original Greek: κενταύρειον</note>. It is the herb which we commonly call Lesser Centaury, concerning which see Mattioli, Fuchs, and other Botanists.

<margin>Serapion the Arab.</margin>
Serapion, the Arab Physician, describes it in these words:

> *Centaury is an herb similar to Hypericum, and it is a certain kind of mountain Mint.* <note>original Arabic: قنطوريون هي حشيشة يشبة هيوفاريقون وهو الفودج الجبلي</note>

<margin>Aben Sina.</margin>
To which **Aben Sina** <note>Avicenna</note> subscribes in almost the same words. The Vatican Codex has it thus:

> *Centaury is an herb and has a stalk longer than a span, and a flower most beautiful, tending toward the color of purple.* <note>original Arabic: قنطوريون هي حشيشة ولة ساق طولة اكثر من شبر وزهر اجمل الى لون الفرفير</note>

The *Centaurium* <note>Centaury, a medicinal herb</note> herb has a stalk whose length is greater than a palm, and a reddish flower like purple; in the flower there appears a likeness to that flower which is called *Lachemdas*; the Egyptians call it *Antims*. However, Chiron, in the cited book of Apuleius chapter 75, is the authority that the Prophets or Egyptian Hierophants <note>High-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> called it <term>blood of Hercules</term> <note>original Greek: αἷμα ἡρακλῆς</note>.

<margin>Apuleius.</margin>
<margin>Plantain.</margin>
<margin>Serapion the Arab.</margin>
§ III. <term>Sout</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲥⲟⲩⲧ</note> is a plant which, according to Apuleius, the Prophets called in the Coptic voice <term>Glory of Heaven</term> <note>original Greek-Coptic: ⲟⲩⲣⲁⲛⲟⲩ ⲇⲟⲝⲁⲛ</note>; we say the same is that which the Arabs call <note>original Arabic: لسان الحمل</note> the tongue of the lamb or ram, the Greeks call <term>many-nerved lamb's-tongue</term> <note>original Greek: ἀρνόγλοσσον πολυνέυρον</note>, and the Latins call the many-nerved plantain. The cited Arabs, the most faithful interpreters of the Egyptians, support this fact. *Serapion*.

<note>original Arabic: "Lamb's tongue is called 'many-ribbed' and it has seven ribs; its leaf is large and its essence is composed of water and earth, and its name is Glory of the Sky."</note>
<note>Symbol: Solar/floral emblem ☼</note>

*Lamb's tongue* is called <term>many-nerved</term> <note>original Greek: πολυνέυρον</note> because of its many ribs, for it has seven sides or ribs, and consists of a large leaf; its nature is composed of the watery and the earthy, and it is called *Glory of Heaven*. The Vatican Codex calls it <note>original Arabic: اسوت</note> *Asuth* by the same name which Apuleius asserted above that the Egyptians named it; the Hebrew interpreter of Avicenna, whose manuscript I possess, reports this same word.

->*Asuth* is the name of the herb in the foreign tongue, *Plantago* [Plantain].<- <note>original Hebrew: אשות שם העשב בלעז פלנטנוא</note>

*Asuth* is the name of the herb, called *Plantago* by the Latins. It is called by the Egyptians the "Glory of Heaven" because it has seven nerves, just like the seven rays of the planets derived into itself, possessing all the power of the planets; it was of great use in medical matters, as well as in the sacred rites which they used to perform for the seven Spirits of the World. You will see this herb everywhere on Obelisks and other hieroglyphic monuments, as we shall explain in its proper place.

<margin>Satyrion.</margin>
<margin>Apuleius.</margin>
§ IV. <term>Sekee</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲥⲉⲕⲏⲏ</note> according to Apuleius, is the same as the herb *Satyrion* <note>A type of orchid</note>, of that kind which the Arabs and the Greeks call <term>Dog's Testicle</term> <note>original Greek: κυνὸς ὄρχιδα</note> from the shape of its bulb. It is called *Panion* by the Hierophants, according to Apuleius, because even when held in the hand it vehemently excites lust and libido; whence it not wrongly drew its name *Satyrion* from the lustful Satyrs, and *Panion* from Pan, the Spirit of fertility. The Vatican Codex states:

<note>original Arabic: "Dog's testicle is what the wise men of Egypt call Panion because it excites the sexual urge."</note>
<note>Symbol: Solar/floral emblem ☼</note>

*Dog's Testicle* is the herb which the Egyptian Sages call *Panium*, because it powerfully excites one to intercourse. To which Aben Sina <note>Avicenna</note> gives his support.

<margin>Aben Sina.</margin>
<note>original Arabic: "Dog's testicle excites the sexual urge so much that it cannot be calmed except by drinking broth of lettuce and lentils."</note>
<note>Symbol: Solar/floral emblem ☼</note>

The *Dog's Testicle* herb so excites intercourse that it is not calmed unless a broth of lettuce and lentils is taken. It is called by the Egyptians <term>Sekee</term> <note>original Coptic: ⲥⲉⲕⲏⲏ</note> after the Moon, because just as the Moon, by the influence of its fertile moisture, is the cause of sublunary and vegetable things, so also among plants *Sekee* is judged to move the genital moisture. I find this herb likewise among the hieroglyphics [associated with] a Goat's <gloss>head</gloss>

# THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHICS. CHAPTER XII.

attached to the head, dedicated to the God of the Mendesians <note>The ram-headed god Banebdjedet, often conflated by Greeks with Pan</note>; by which they aptly signified that no other herb is more rightly dedicated to the goat-like Pan, or the God of fertility, than that herb which both provides fertility and powerfully excites the genetic force in bodies. Hence, nothing was considered more fruitful or more healthful than this herb, as we shall interpret in its proper place.

**§ V.** <note>Coptic: ⲞⲢⲦⲈⲂⲒⲞⲔⲀ / Ortebioca</note> or, as Apuleius corruptly writes it, *Ophitebioca*, is the same as **Cinquefoil** <margin>Cinquefoil</margin> in the Egyptian language, which the Priests call sometimes the "wing of the Ibis" <note>original Greek: πτερύγιον Ἴβιδος</note>, and sometimes the "herb of Mercury" <note>original Greek: Ἑρמוῦ βοτάνην</note>. The use of this herb was very great in the sacred rites of Mercury, which they called *Hermanibim*, that is, the Hermetic Ibis. For since the Ibis was a bird dedicated to Mercury because of his invention of the greatest things—into which bird he transformed himself to reveal various matters to the human race, regarding both letters and Medicine, as we taught in the *Mystic Alphabet*—they rightly consecrated this herb to him. As for why they called it the "wing of the Ibis," I give this reason: because Mercury is the "rival-skilled" <note>original Greek: ἀντίτεχνον</note> deity to Typhon <note>Set</note>; whom they signified by the Crocodile, and whom the wing of the Ibis strikes with a stupor. They claim this herb was used in sacred rites because, just as the wing of the Ibis (according to Horus) strikes the Crocodile and renders it motionless, so did *Hermanibis* <note>A syncretic deity combining Hermes/Thoth and Anubis</note> repel every malignant, harmful, and deadly power of Typhon by its virtue and assistance, rendering it ineffective. But of these things, we speak throughout this entire Work.

**§ VI.** <note>Coptic: ⲚⲈⲠⲈⲚⲈⲤⲦⲪⲈ / Nepenesthphe</note> is the name of the herb which Apuleius corruptly calls *Nemebsphe* <margin>Ground-pine</margin>, others *Nesphe*; in the Egyptian language it is called "Beauty" or "Decoration of the Sky." The Priests, according to Apuleius, called it the "Blood of Minerva" <note>original Greek: αἷμα Ἀφροδίτης - Note: Kircher equates Minerva/Athena with Aphrodite/Isis here</note>; and it is nothing other than our **Ground-pine** <term>Camæpythys: A low-growing plant of the mint family, historically used in herbal medicine</term>. The Vatican Author states:

-> Ground-pine has stalks and red flowers inclining toward black and greenish; the flower has a bitter taste with a little astringency and its sharpness of taste is somewhat bitter; its leaves are grassy, thin, creeping upon the earth; it is called Nespha by the Egyptians. <-

With this, the Hebrew translator of Avicenna <note>Aben Sinæ</note> also agrees:

-> Ground-pine has branches and a red flower inclining toward black <-
-> or toward thin greens; its flower is bitter, and its nature is hot in the second degree and dry <-
-> in the third degree. <-

> *The branches and red flowers of Ground-pine, inclining toward blackness, and its flower is bitter; its nature is also hot in the second degree, and dry in the third. The use of this herb was in the sacred rites of Minerva or the Saitic Isis, because of the hidden properties of nature which they thought the said herb shared with this Goddess.*

**§ VII.** <note>Coptic: ⲀⲚⲈⲚⲈⲚ / Anenen</note> we interpret from the Egyptian as "Good," and it is <margin>Artemisia herb.</margin> nothing other than the herb **Artemisia** <note>Mugwort</note>, which they call so because of its goodness. The Priests, according to Apuleius in chapter 10, called it sometimes *Bubasteoscordium* <note>original Greek: Βουβαστεοσκόρδιον</note>, that is, the "Heart of Bubastus," and sometimes *Artemisia*. Now, Bubastus was a City of Egypt in which the worship of Diana and of Dogs flourished wonderfully; to which the Greek *Artemisia* (that is, "of Diana") corresponds not inappropriately.

# CHAPTER II. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

Whether it was from dogs—who love this herb and, according to the testimony of Antonius Musa, prepare medicines for themselves from it against natural diseases—or whether the power of this herb was first discovered by Diana, it makes no difference; it is enough for us to demonstrate that the <margin>Antonius Musa <note>Physician to Emperor Augustus.</note></margin> **breath of the heart of Bubastis** <note>original Greek: ἀνεσην βουβάϚεως καρδίαν. Bubastis refers to the Egyptian goddess Bastet, often equated with Diana/Artemis.</note> of the Egyptians and the *Artemisia* <note>Mugwort or Wormwood.</note> of the Greeks are exactly the same herb. The Hierophants <note>High-ranking priests of the mysteries.</note> also called this herb **the blood of Saturn** <note>original Greek: αἷμα κρόνου</note>. So says Apuleius in the place cited; and <margin>Apuleius; Aben Sina <note>Avicenna, the famous Persian physician.</note></margin> Aben Sina confirms this, asserting that it possesses a Saturnine nature and a miraculous power against exhaustion. This herb is called **al-damsisa** <note>Arabic: الدمسيسة</note> by the Arabs, and in Coptic also **Artemisia** <note>Coptic: ϯⲁⲣⲧemⲓⲥⲓⲁ</note>, and it was held in great esteem in the sacred rites of the Bubastic Isis; for Philadaemon, in his book *On the Flight of Isis*, testifies that Isis used this against the exhaustion of her journey while she wandered through Egypt searching for the body of Osiris; this has also been discussed elsewhere in this work.

### § VIII.
**Saphseph** <note>Coptic: ⲥⲁⲫⲥⲉⲫ</note>, I interpret this word from the Coptic as "against the God," and I say it is the herb which the Greeks and Latins call *Hyoscyamus* <margin>Hyoscyamus <note>Henbane.</note></margin>. Zoroaster, according to Apuleius, calls it **Typhonion**, because it is of a Typhonian nature—that is, it excites madness and, when consumed, corrupts the most divine part in man, namely the intellectual faculty. For this reason, there was a very great use of this herb in the sacred rites of the Egyptians to appease Typhon; for in the secret rituals of the sanctuaries, they were accustomed to strike the Crocodile three times with this herb and, with a set formula of words, put to flight the malignant power of Typhon, as Serapion of Nicaea is the authority. It is called **al-banj** <note>Arabic: البنج</note> by the Arabs, and **oukeneamoush** <note>Coptic: ⲟⲩⲕⲉⲛⲉⲁⲟⲩϣ</note> by the Copts.

### § IX.
**Saphseph** <note>Coptic: ⲥⲁⲫⲥⲉⲫ</note>, corruptly written as *Sophosph* in Apuleius ch. 19, is the same <margin>Aristolochia <note>Birthwort.</note></margin> herb which the Arabs call **Zeraund** <note>Arabic: زراوند</note>, and the Latins and Greeks call *Aristolochia*. The Vatican Codex states:
-> **The Zeraund is the Saphseph herb of the Egyptians; its length is about a span, and the color of its flower is purple.** <-
-> **It has a foul smell.** <-
*The Zeraund herb is the Saphseph to the Egyptians; its length is a palm, and the color of the flower is purple, with a heavy odor.* But Aben Sina says:
-> **Zeraund is of a cleansing, softening, opening, and relaxing nature; it is attractive, for it draws out thorns.** <-
*Zeraund is of a cleansing, opening, thinning, and attracting virtue, for it draws out thorns and splinters.* The Hebrew translator of Aben Sina says thus:
-> **Zeraund in Greek is Aristolochia; in Egypt, Saphseph; it bears a flower similar to the flower called Habiam (perhaps he means Apium [celery]), and it is a species of Lablab [climbing bean].** <-
The Egyptian prophets called it *Ligea*, as the cited Apuleius is the authority.

### § X.
**Chamaleoups** <note>Coptic: ⲭⲁⲙⲉⲗⲉⲟⲩⲯ</note> in the Egyptian language denotes that herb <margin>Chamælea <note>Daphne alpina or similar spurge-olive.</note></margin> which we call *Chamælea* or *Mezerium*; so says the Vatican Codex:
-> **Black Mezerium is the same as Chamælea, called Samur by the Egyptians.** <-
*Black Mezerium is the same herb as Chamælea, called Samur by the Egyptians.* The Hebrew also confuses it with *Marrubium* <note>Horehound.</note>:
-> **Chamælea is a species of Marrubium, and it is black.** <-

# THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHICS: CHAPTER II.

The Chameleon is a type of Horehound, and it is a plant of black color. Regarding this and the preceding plant, I have found no trace among the hieroglyphics.

§ XI. <margin>Dragon Arum.</margin> <coptic>ⲉⲙⲓⲛⲓⲟⲛ</coptic> <note>Eminion</note> Among the Egyptians, this is the same as the plant <term>Dracontæa</term> <note>Dragon Arum or Snake Lily</note>; so says Apuleius in chapter 14. By the Greeks, he says, it is called <term>Dracontæa</term>, by others <term>Asclepias</term>, by others <term>Pithonion</term>, by others <term>Anchomanes</term>, by others <term>Sancromaton</term>, by some <term>Ancryssa</term>, by some <term>Chereon</term>, by several <term>Sceon</term>: likewise <term>Dorcadion</term>; the Prophets call it <term>Typhonion</term>, others <term>Crocidilion</term>, others <term>Ostanes</term>: Zoroaster calls it <term>Theriophonon</term>, and the Egyptians <term>Eminion</term>; it is said to be born from the blood of a Dragon. It is called <term>Pythonion</term> because it is said to be born from the blood of the serpent Python; <term>Typhonion</term> because it is of Typhon—that is, of a fiery nature; <term>Crocidilion</term> because it is a friend to Crocodiles; and <term>Therophonon</term> <note>original Greek: Θηροφόνον, "beast-killer"</note> because it kills animals that consume it by a certain caustic power. There are those who confuse this Dragon Arum with the <term>Culcasia</term> <note>Taro</note>; they do so erroneously, since the Culcasia, which they also call "native cabbage," provides a most pleasant food for the Egyptians. However, the Dragon Arum, or <coptic>ⲉⲙⲓⲛⲓⲟⲛ</coptic>, seems to them to be the same as what we call <term>Arum</term> <note>Cuckoopint</note>; <margin>Matthiolus.</margin> <term>Matthiolus</term> and <term>Clusius</term> teach that this plant is of the Dragon Arum genus, which excels greatly in a certain fiery bite or caustic force; so much so that it nearly drives those who consume it to madness, from which it seems to have derived its Egyptian name, as if it "moves the mind": although some also confuse Arum with Colocasia. We say, therefore, that *Eminion* is neither Colcasia nor Arum, but the Greater Dragon Arum, which resembles a spotted skin in its stalk, and the tongue of serpents in its flower and leaves; it sprouts from the earth at the same time as serpents, and hides itself at the same time they do. The tradition of the Egyptians is that it was born from the blood of a wound inflicted on Typhon by Horus, as witnessed by Apollodorus; hence it is not without reason called Pythonion, Dracontæa, or Typhonion; its use was in the sacred rites by which they strove to appease Typhon.

§ XII. <margin>Vervain.</margin> <coptic>ⲡⲉⲙⲡⲉⲙⲡⲧⲉ</coptic> <note>Pempempte</note> <note>symbol similar to an anchored cross/coptic cross</note> that is, "Gift of God"; so the Egyptians call <term>Verbenaca</term> <note>Vervain</note>, a well-known plant endowed with a certain magical power, corruptly called <term>Pempsempte</term> by Apuleius. <margin>Apuleius.</margin> Chiron is the authority in Apuleius stating that the Prophets called it "Juno’s Tear": in Greek, he says, it is called <term>hieran botanen</term> <note>original Greek: ἱεράν βοτάνην, "holy herb"</note>, others <term>artemisia orthon</term> <note>upright artemisia</note>, others <term>disdaton</term>, others <term>peristereon</term> <note>pigeon-plant</note>, others <term>panchromon</term> <note>all-colored</note>, others <term>Colletis</term>: Demetrius and Aesculapius call it <term>Cyparisson</term>, Pythagoras <term>Erisceptron</term>, others <term>Aristeron</term>, the Egyptians <term>Pempsempte</term>, and the Prophets <term>Heras dakryon</term> <note>original Greek: Ἥρας δάκρυον, "Tear of Hera/Juno"</note>. It is also called <coptic>ⲡⲉⲙⲡⲉⲙⲡⲧⲉ</coptic> "Gift of God," and "Holy Herb" from its use, because the Egyptians use it in sacrifices; <term>peristereon</term> because it is friendly and sympathetic to doves; <term>panchromon</term> because its use is suitable for all; <term>Erisceptron</term>, or better, <term>ho tou erotos skeptron</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ τοῦ ἔρωτος σκῆπτρον</note>, "Scepter of Love," because its use was employed in love potions; and finally, it found its name "Juno’s Tears" from the mythologists.

§ XIII. <margin>Bugloss.</margin> <coptic>ⲁⲛⲧⲟⲩⲉⲣⲙⲃⲉⲥ</coptic> <note>Antuermbes</note> Apuleius corruptly calls it *Antuermbesus*, that is, "Ox-tongue," or in Greek <term>bouglosson</term>; Chiron, along with the Hierophants, calls this <term>gonon tou ailourou</term> <note>original Greek: γόνον τοῦ αἰλούρου</note>, "Seed of the Cat"; the Arabs call it <term>Lisan al-thawr</term> <note>original Arabic: لسان الثور</note>, "Tongue of the Ox"; see its powers in Apuleius, chapter 41. Since I have found nothing regarding this plant among the hieroglyphics, I have judged it superfluous to say more about it.

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
<margin>Horehound.</margin>
# § XIV. *Asterope* in Egyptian is the same as the Eye of the Star;
and we say this is the herb which the Latins call *Marrubium* <note>Horehound</note>, the Greeks call *Prasion* <term>πράσιον</term>, and the Priests call sometimes *Blood of the Bull* <term>αἷμα τοῦ Ταύρου</term>, and sometimes *Seed of Horus* <term>γόνον τοῦ Ὥρου</term>. So says the Vatican Author.
-> <note>original Arabic: فراسيون حشيشة مرة الطعم لمصريون استرب جاره في الثانية يابس في الثلثه</note> <-
*Phrasium is a herb of bitter taste, called Asterope by the Egyptians; it is hot in the second degree and dry in the third.* This is supported by the Hebrew interpreter of Avicenna <note>Aben Sina</note>:
-> <note>original Hebrew: פראסיון הוא עשב בלועז מרוביום מרה מטעם מפתח וממרק ומתיר וממס ומחתך</note> <-
That is, *Phrasium is the herb Horehound in the foreign tongue, of a bitter taste; it opens, cleanses, dissolves, loosens, and cuts.* It is called the Eye of the Star—that is, of the Sun—because there was great use of this herb in the sacred rites of Horus. Whence also the Initiates called it the *Seed of Horus* <term>γόνον τοῦ Ὥρου</term>, whom we interpret elsewhere as the Sun. The Priests used this herb in the sacrifices of Horus and Serapis, as will be said in its proper place; for it is very powerful in Horian or Phoebeian virtue—that is, Solar—and its use among Physicians was very great.

<margin>The herb Scilla or Mouse-onion.</margin>
# § XV. *Slitha* is how we interpret that herb which is commonly called *Scilla* <note>Squill or Sea Onion</note>;
The Arabs call it *Eskil* <term>اسقيل</term>, or *Mouse-onion* <term>بصل الفار</term>; the Egyptian Priests call it the *Eye of Typhon* <term>ὀφθαλμὸν τοῦ Τύφωνος</term>, as Apuleius says in chapter 42; and Hali also considers it to be Scilla.
-> <note>original Arabic: اسقيل هو بصل الفار سمي بذلك لانه يقتل الفار وهو حريف قوي فقال قوم لانه العنصل لمصريون سليطه</note> <-
*Eskil is the mouse-onion, so called because it kills mice; it is vehemently sharp, and some have wished it to be Scilla; by the Egyptians it is called Slitha.* It is called the Typhonian herb on account of its extreme power to do harm and its thoroughly fiery faculty, the sort of nature Plutarch teaches Typhon possessed in his book *On Osiris and Isis*. Therefore, the Egyptians did not wrongly call this the Eye of Typhon, both from its yellowish-fiery color and from its burning shape and quality. For as Avicenna rightly says:
-> <note>original Arabic: اسقيل لونه اصفر الى البياض ومنه جنسی سمي قتل وطی بغضهم لانه البلبيوس من اجل علامة التي وجدها</note> <-
*Eskil is of a yellowish-whitish color, and from it comes a certain type of thoroughly lethal poison; some thought it was the bulb of the Aconite <note>Napellus</note> itself, because of the sign they found in it.* The Hebrew interpreter confirms these sayings:
-> <note>original Hebrew: אשקיל הוא בצל עכבר חם בשלישית יבש בשנית מתיך וממרק מאוד</note> <-
*Askill is the mouse-onion; it is hot in the third degree and dry in the second; it is dissolving, and draws blood, burning, ulcerating, thinning, and cutting, with a power beyond the power of its own heating.* Who does not see that all these effects are Typhonian? The Egyptian Priests, according to Plutarch, greatly detested this herb as something Typhonian and utterly deadly, both because of the virulence of this plant and because of the opposition it has toward the Moon...

Therefore, regarding what Plutarch relates about onions being held in abomination <margin>Onions which the Egyptians abhorred.</margin> among the Egyptians, you should know that this is by no means to be understood as the ordinary onion—than which no food is more common in Egypt—but rather the squill <note>original: "caepa scillitica"; the sea onion, often associated with Typhon due to its bitter or purgative properties</note>; which they also called, not without reason, the Eye of Typhon.

§ XVI. **Selex** <note>Coptic: ⲥⲉⲗⲉⲝ</note> is the same as our Watercress, concerning which herb <margin>Watercress.</margin> see Apuleius chapter 20, and Ibn Sina <note>Avicenna</note> under the word **جرف** <note>original: "Juruf"</note>, and other Latin botanists.

§ XVII. **Taborin** <note>Coptic: ⲧⲁⲃⲟⲣⲓⲛ</note> is an Egyptian word signifying that herb <margin>Chamomile.</margin> which the Arabs call **بابونج** (*Babungs*), the Latins *Chamæmilla*, and the Greeks *parthenion*, *drykolabon*, or *chrysakalon* <note>Greek: παρθένιον, δρυκόλαβον, χρυσάκαλον; various names for chamomile or feverfew</note>; for its virtues and properties, see Ibn Sina under the cited word, and Chiron in the works of Apuleius.

§ XVIII. **Stemphe** <note>Coptic: ⲥⲧⲉⲙⲫⲏ</note> <term>Care of God</term>, corrupted by Apuleius as *Thephin* or <margin>Bloodwort herb.</margin> *Themphin*; we say it is that herb which the Arabs call *Basielraghi*, the Greeks *polygonon*, *polykarpon*, or *chyliophyllon* <note>Greek: πολύγονον, πολύκαρπον, χυλιόφυλλον; meaning many-seeded or thousand-leaved</note>, the Initiates call it the *offspring of the sun* <note>Greek: γόνον τοῦ ἡλίου</note> or the *seed of the Hero*, and finally the Latins call it *Sanguinaria* <note>Bloodwort</note> or *Proserpinaca*, so named from creeping <note>Latin: "serpendo"</note> through the earth; some also call it *Miserdivinum*, concerning which see the botanists under the word *Polygonon*.

§ XIX. **Pelelia** <note>Coptic: ⲡⲉⲗⲉⲗⲓⲁ</note> or, as the Hierophants <note>Priests of the sacred mysteries</note> name it, **Aspho** <note>Coptic: ⲁⲥⲫⲟ</note> <margin>Sowbread</margin> according to Chiron in Apuleius, is the same as *Cyclaminus* <note>Cyclamen</note>, concerning which a more copious space for discussion will be given in its proper time.

§ XX. **Eshoris** <note>Coptic: ⲉϣⲟⲣⲓⲥ</note>, corrupted by Apuleius as *Etui*, is interpreted as *Maidenhair* <note>Latin: "capillum Veneris"</note>, or *polytrichon* <note>Greek: πολύτριχον; "much hair"</note>, which the Greeks also call *adianton* <note>Greek: ἀδίαντον; "unwetted"</note> and the Arabs **برشوكان** (*Bar-schiaufchan*): it grows in damp places and is familiar to the walls of springs. <margin>Maidenhair fern.</margin>

§ XXI. **Pisine** <note>Coptic: ⲡⲓⲥⲓⲛⲉ</note> or **Pishrintepre** <note>Coptic: ⲡⲓϣⲣⲓⲛⲧⲉⲡⲣⲏ</note> is the herb which we interpret as <term>Offspring of the Sun</term>, <margin>Heliotrope</margin> and it is the *Heliotropium*, according to Chiron in Apuleius, who also calls it *heliotrophon* because it continually turns itself toward the Sun; others call it *heliouran*, that is, <term>Tail of the Sun</term>, because just as an animal makes its tail follow it, so the Sun makes this herb follow him. It is also called *Sideritis*, because just as a magnet draws iron, so the Sun draws this herb. The Egyptians held this herb in the highest honor and esteem, since it exhibited in its flower the most perfect image of the Sun. Among the hieroglyphics, I find this herb depicted with the Hawk with very good right; for <note>Hieroglyphic description: The plant Heliotrope is described as being depicted with a Hawk (Accipiter), symbolizing the solar nature and the plant's constant orientation toward the sun.</note> the Hawk is the Sun: but the flower of the herb exhibits the bride of the Sun, who, ravished by love for the Sun, follows him with a movement full of solicitude, with such constancy that the Egyptians therefore adopted it as a hieroglyphic for the measurement of time.

§ XXII. **Menishne** <note>Coptic: ⲙⲉⲛⲓϣⲛⲏ</note> is the same as <term>Genius of the Moon</term>, corrupted by Apuleius as *Emenipse*, and it is that herb which the Latins call *Dictamnus* <note>Dittany</note>, and the Greeks call *artemision*, namely after Diana <note>Artemis</note>, who is the Genius of the Moon; for the same <margin>Dittany.</margin> reason it is called by Theophrastus *selenogonon*, <term>Sperm of the Moon</term> <note>Greek: σεληνογόνον</note>.

§ XXIII. **Lotometra** <note>Coptic: ⲗⲟⲧⲟⲙⲉⲧⲣⲁ</note>, corrupted by Apuleius as *Lotonietra*, is the herb <margin>Theophrastus's Nymphaea, or Lotus.</margin> which we call the Egyptian *Nymphaea* <note>Water-lily</note>, and it is called *Lotus*, concerning whose miraculous power see Theophrastus. Moreover, it is called *Lotometra* because [it follows] the course of the Heaven...

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

it is, or as if it measures the Sun with its flower, possessed of exactly the same virtue with which we taught the preceding plant was endowed. The Arabs call it نيلوفر *Nilufar* <note>original: "Nilufar"; the water lily</note>; although the Nilufar is distinct from the *Lotometra*; for the latter provides a most sweet food for the Egyptians, yet it is harmful due to its power of extinguishing heat. Therefore, the *Nilufar* is properly the same as our *Nymphæa* <note>Water lily</note>, which they commonly call Seaweed or Marsh Poppy, because of its power to extinguish Venus <note>i.e., sexual desire</note>; some have even called it the "Nail of Venus," and it is called *vikiota* by the Egyptians.

<margin>The herb Nufar or Nilufar</margin>
§ XXIV. *Gratias* <note>Greek: γρὰτιὰς</note> that is, *The Bond of Religion*, because the use of this herb delivers a man from the illicit desires of the flesh: so says the Vatican Author.

->The Nilufar is an aquatic stalk and is called the Seed of the Bride and the Guardian of Women; it is cold and moist in<-
->the second degree, and its drink is very thinning. ۞<-

*The Nilufar is an aquatic stalk, and is called the Seed of the Bride, and the Guard of Chastity; cold and moist in the second degree, and its drink is of powerful extinction.* With this the Hebrew Interpreter of Aben Sina <note>Avicenna</note> agrees in these words:

->The Nilufar or Nenufar is an herb that grows in the waters of marshes and is useful for removing<-
->foulness; it diminishes desire and dries up the drop of seed by a special property within it.<-

*The Nilufar or Nenufar is an herb sprouting in marshy waters; it diminishes luxury, vehemently breaks the desire for coitus, and congeals the sperm by a certain hidden property which lies within it.* With these the words of Dioscorides harmonize: <term>Nymphæa</term> <note>original Greek: Νυμφαῖα</note> grows in marshes and stagnant waters. It has leaves similar to the *ciborium* <note>the seed vessel of the Egyptian bean</note> but smaller and more oblong, with stalks remaining in the water; the root and flowers are a remedy against nocturnal visions <note>wet dreams</note>; moreover, it works a weakness of the private parts for a few days if one drinks it continuously. *Nymphæa, he says, is born in marshes and stagnant waters; it has leaves similar to the Bean or the Egyptian Lotus, but smaller and more oblong, many coming forth from one and the same root: it is drunk against the dreams of Venus, for it takes them away entirely; indeed, if drunk for several days continuously, it so weakens the instruments of generation that, all lust being removed, those who have drunk it are rendered cold and impotent.* Regarding this herb, <margin>Prosper Alpinus</margin> Prosper Alpinus speaks thus in his book on Egyptian plants, chapter 34: *I consider this herb, he says, to be exactly the same as the Nymphæa, which the Arabs call Nuphar; indeed, in the entire Nile river washing the Egyptian lands, no other plant has been found which bears the marks of the Lotus except the Nymphæa itself, which is certainly a plant similar (as Dioscorides affirms of the Lotus) to the Colocasia or Egyptian Bean; and it bears a white flower (I speak of the greater Nymphæa) very similar to a lily, which Theophrastus expressed in these words: "a white flower closest to lilies in the narrowness of its leaves"; for truly this is the flower of the greater Nymphæa, which is closed at sunset and hidden under the water, and at sunrise rises above the waters, comes out, and is opened; which is observed in this plant not only in Egypt, but in many places in Italy, and especially in the marshy and lagoon-filled places around Venice; for the valleys of Marghera and Mestre bear many of these plants, in which anyone can clearly observe what is said by Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and many others concerning the Lotus.* Theophrastus also says that this herb grows in the Euphrates, and that the stalk itself and the flower are submerged in the evening until midnight, and go so deep into the depths that it cannot be found even if one reaches out a hand; then it turns, and gradually rises up, and at the rising of the Sun it emerges—

### § XXV. 
<margin>Wild Mint.</margin> **ⲥⲟⲩⲉⲓⲥⲧⲟⲛ** <note>Coptic: soueiston</note> we also interpret as Wild Mint, called by the Hierophants <note>Priests of the sacred mysteries</note> <term>the fitting things of Apollo</term> <note>original Greek: αἴσιμα τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος</note>; its use was very frequent in the sacred rites of the Egyptians. By the Arabs it is called *Naanaa*, concerning which Ibn Sina <note>The Persian physician Avicenna</note> says:
> <note>original Arabic: نعناع حار يابس في الثانية وفيه رطوبة فضلة فيه قوة مسخنة قابضة يمنع واذا ترك خافات منه في اللبن لم يتجبن</note>
*Mint is hot and dry in the second degree, and in it is a superfluous moisture, possessing a heating and astringent power; and when pieces of it are placed in milk, it will never be curdled into cheese.* It is also called the "Seed of the Sun" by the Arab Ali, in the passage already cited. I also read that Mint is called by the Hierophants <term>the blood and progeny of Ammon</term> <note>original Greek: αἷμα καὶ γόνον τοῦ Ἄμμωνος</note>. See Apuleius, chapter 94. The use of Wild Mint, on account of the sweetness of its scent and the Apollonian <note>solar/healing</note> virtue with which it flourishes, was very great in the sacrifices of the Solar Osiris, as Eubulus the Egyptian testifies in his book on odors.

### § XXVI. 
<margin>Sea Wormwood.</margin> **ⲥⲩⲗⲉⲉⲥ** <note>Coptic: sylees</note> is the same as *Seriphium*, or Sea Wormwood. Ali describes it in these words:
<margin>Ali the Arab.</margin>
> <note>original Arabic: أفسنتين ينبت في المصر كثيرا وهو ماهوي وحشيشة تشبه لورق الصعتر وفيه مرارة وقبض وحرافة</note>
*Wormwood germinates abundantly in Egypt, and is called Sumi; it is an herb similar to the leaf of Oregano, and in it is bitterness, astringency, and the highest sharpness.* This herb is beautifully expressed in the Bembine Tablet in the hand of Isis, to whom it was sacred; its mystical significance was that, just as Isis as the Moon tempers the dryness of the Sun, and dissolves and refines the waters into which she flows by a certain natural sharpness of her rays; so *Seriphium*, placed in waters imbued with a malignant quality, corrects them and delivers them from malice. But concerning this, see what we have written more copiously in the *Pamphylian Obelisk* and the exposition of the Bembine Tablet.

### § XXVII. 
<margin>The herb Mercurialis.</margin> **ⲁⲫⲗⲟⲙⲟⲛ** <note>Coptic: aphlomon</note> by this word, according to the testimony of Chiron in Apuleius, the Egyptians call the herb which we commonly call *Mercurialis* <note>French Mercury</note>, endowed with a purgative power; the Initiates call it <term>Royal Blood</term> <note>original Greek: αἷμα βασιλικόν</note>.

### § XXVIII. 
<margin>Bryony.</margin> **ⲑⲟⲩⲱⲛ** <note>Coptic: thon</note> is the same as Bryony, known in the apothecary shops as White Vine, and to the Arabs as <note>original Arabic: فاشرا</note> *Phasira*, the powers of which you may see among the Botanists.

### § XXIX. 
<margin>Scolopendria.</margin> **ⲫⲉⲡⲣⲉ** <note>Coptic: phepre</note> is nothing other than *Scolopendria* <note>Hart's-tongue fern</note>, which some confuse with *Asplenium*, because when taken in a drink it diminishes the spleen and benefits those suffering from spleen ailments. To the Arabs it is <note>original Arabic: اسقولوفندريون</note> *Isqulufundriyun*.

### § XXX. 
<margin>Cyclamen.</margin> **ⲓⲧⲁⲑⲟⲥⲁⲗⲗⲟⲛ** <note>Coptic: itathosallon</note> is the same as Cyclamen; so says Apuleius following Chiron; in Greek <term>kyklaminos</term>, to the Arabs <note>original Arabic: جويانس</note> *Baians*, concerning which see Ibn Sina, Serapion, and other Arab Botanists.

### § XXXI. 
<margin>Oregano or Pennyroyal. Apuleius. Antonius Musa.</margin> **ⲡⲁⲛⲧⲁⲅⲁⲑⲟⲛ** <note>Coptic: pantagathon</note> is the same as *All-good*, or *good for all things*; it is the herb which some call Oregano, others Pennyroyal. See Apuleius chapter 93, Antonius Musa, Caelius Aurelianus, and other ancient Physicians.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>Butcher's Broom.</margin>
§ XXXII. **Semenate** <note>Coptic: ⲥⲉⲙⲉⲛⲁⲧⲉ</note>, which is corruptly called *Sremeeös* by Apuleius, we say is the shrub commonly called Butcher's Broom <note>Latin: Ruscus</note>. The Greeks call it <term>wild myrtle</term> <note>Greek: μυρσίνην ἀγρίαν</note>. The Arabs call it *Harim* <note>Arabic: حارم</note>. The Egyptians, according to Chiron in the works of Apuleius, call it **Blood of the Titans** <note>Greek: ⲁⲓⲙⲁ ⲧⲓⲧⲁⲛⲱⲛ</note>, or Alexandrian Myrtle <note>Arabic: الكنة السكندرية</note>, or even **Blood of the Ibis** <note>Greek: ⲁⲓⲙⲁ ⲓⲃⲉⲱⲥ</note>. Eubulus, in his book on the metamorphosis of the Gods in Egypt, is the authority for the claim that this herb sprang from the blood of the Titans during the conflict of the Gods. It is called "Blood of the Ibis," however, because the Ibis feeds upon crocodiles, which represent the Titans or the Typhonian <note>Typhon was the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos</note> mob; since this plant possesses the power to overcome such things, it is no wonder it obtained its name from the blood of the Ibis.

<margin>Dodder.</margin>
§ XXXIII. **Anthropophon** <note>Coptic: ⲁⲛⲑⲣⲟⲡⲟⲫⲟⲛ; literally "man-slayer"</note> we interpret as Dodder <note>Latin: Cuscuta</note>, as if you were to say <term>vetch of the trees</term> <note>Greek: ϑηβον τῆς δένδρον</note>, that is, the Bitter Vetch of trees, or <term>the orphan of the trees</term> <note>Greek: ὀρφανὸς τῆς δένδρων</note>, a herb strangling the trees or exercising tyranny over them; no one, unless they are <term>unobservant</term> <note>Greek: ἀϑεώρητος</note>, is unaware that Dodder is of this nature. There are some, however, who wish to claim the Egyptians called Alexanders <note>Latin: Smirnium or Olusatrum</note> by this name, but they are mistaken; for there is a notable difference between these herbs, as is clear to the experts.

<margin>Purslane.</margin>
§ XXXIV. **Motmutin** <note>Coptic: ⲙⲱⲧⲙⲟⲩⲧⲓⲛ</note> signifies the same as "delivering from death": this is what the Egyptians called Purslane <note>Latin: Portulaca</note>. The Priests <note>Hierophantes</note>, however, called it **Blood of Mars** <note>Greek: ⲁⲓⲙⲁ ⲁⲣⲉⲱⲥ</note>, according to the Vatican Author.

-><note>Arabic text: Purslane, the fool's herb, a well-known plant to the Egyptians as Motmut; cold in the third degree and moist in the end of the second.</note><-

*Purslane* is a well-known herb, called *Motmut* by the Egyptians: it is cold in the third degree, and humid at the end of the second. It is called *Motmut* in the Egyptian language because it wonderfully and uniquely assists against malignant fevers and all inflammations peculiar to Egypt. The Initiates <note>Mystæ</note> called it the Blood of Mars, <term>not because of a sacred cause</term> <note>Greek: μὴ τὰ αἱτίερον</note>, but because by its coldness and moisture it tempers the scorched and parched, or "Martial," bile, and expels its malignancy, as *Ibn Sina* <note>Avicenna</note> testifies: <note>Arabic: It is beneficial for hot fevers</note> and because it profits hot fevers in a marvelous way. See this herb illustrated with its mystical reasons in the exposition of the Bembine Tablet.

<margin>Betony.</margin>
§ XXXV. **Irathiorin** <note>Coptic: ⲓⲣⲁⲑⲓⲱⲣⲓⲛ</note>, which *Antonius Musa* corruptly calls *Hierathiorine*, we say is the herb Betony, endowed with—to speak with *Theophrastus*—innumerable virtues; hence, not without cause, it was called "Sacred to Horus" by the Ancients. I read that it is also quite fittingly called <term>nourisher of the soul</term> <note>Greek: ψυχότροφον</note>, because it wonderfully assists the head, which is the seat and dwelling place of the intellectual soul. But he who desires more concerning the powers of this herb should consult the cited <margin>Antonius Musa. Dioscorides. Apuleius. Theophrastus.</margin> Antonius Musa in the specific booklet written about it, as well as Apuleius, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and other ancient botanists.

<margin>Coriander.</margin>
§ XXXVI. **Kotian** <note>Coptic: ⲕⲱⲧⲓⲁⲛ</note> is Coriander: so the Arabic botanists often cited use the word <note>Arabic: كزبره</note> *Kuzbare*, which signifies Coriander.

And these are the things we thought should be said concerning Egyptian plants; of which indeed a fuller mention will be made in the following interpretations of the hieroglyphics.

# TREATISE I. THE ISIAC TABLE,
## OR THE BEMBINE TABLET.
### TO THE MOST SERENE PRINCE
# LEOPOLD WILHELM
### Archduke of Austria, Supreme Governor of Belgium and Burgundy, and Grand Master of the Teutonic Order.

->**MY MOST CLEMENT LORD.**<-

<note>Decorative initial 'I' depicting a central vertical column surrounded by architectural scrolls and floral motifs.</note> In those golden and blessed ages of Egyptian prosperity, Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, author of the 'Deipnosophistae' (Banquet of the Learned).</note> records that after a king was elevated to the height of royal dignity and his inauguration was complete, it was customary for a rich banquet to be prepared. In this feast, for every dish served, there were placed symbolic representations of the royal virtues necessary for the good and blessed administration of the kingdom, adorned with a wondrous transformation of hieroglyphics. Thus, as the King ascended his royal throne, he would be prompted by this unusual display of symbols—as if by a silent lesson—to learn from this subtle and ingenious apparatus what most pertained to the administration of the office entrusted to him. 

In this place, I have seen fit to set before Your August Serenity a Table <note>original: "Mensam"; Kircher plays on the word 'Mensa' meaning both a physical table and the 'Isiac Table' artifact.</note> spread not with a variety of perishable foods or nourishment common to both men and beasts, but, to speak with the ancients, one filled with the nectar and ambrosia of the immortal gods. The Egyptians persuaded themselves that whoever tasted of this would be blessed with the fellowship of the sons of God and would lead eternal dances in the Elysian fields <note>The conception of the afterlife for the heroic and virtuous in Greek and Roman mythology, here applied to Egyptian beliefs.</note>. For whatever wonderful and secret thing exists within the entire scope of Egyptian Wisdom is exhibited here on this Table, as if in a summary, veiled with a certain miraculous majesty of Sacraments. It was, therefore, the unique Mirror of the Priests; by contemplating it, they trusted they would discover—as if from a most fertile Oracle of the divine Power—what should be embraced and what should be avoided in the conduct of human affairs. 

Truly, although these things are not to be greatly cared for by a Christian heart, being as they are involved in their own superstitions; nevertheless, because even in the thickest darkness and the muddy paths of labyrinths, precious Jewels <note>original: "Carbunculi"; literally small coals, used to refer to deep red gemstones like garnets or rubies.</note> occasionally shine—that is, under a certain analogy of types, sacraments shine forth that are not unlike the Christian faith and true religion. These instruct us quite clearly in what spirit we ought to regard the cult of religion, and with what piety and veneration we should behave toward God and the Heavenly Beings; therefore, I have judged that they should not be entirely despised. 

Since, therefore, August Prince, your great mind—by which you draw almost the entire world into fixed admiration of your Virtues—is so disposed that you earnestly indulge in symbolic games of wit when the opportunity arises; I certainly found no one to whom I might more rightly prepare this present Table of Isiac Wisdom than to You. Indeed, I consecrate it to the glorious and heroic title of Your name all the more gladly, as I feel myself bound to You by a greater obligation of gratitude for the innumerable benefits bestowed upon me at all times. Farewell, delight of Belgium and heroic glory of our age; and continue to cherish me under the shield of Your Most Serene protection, as you have begun.

->TREATISE<-

# TREATISE I.
## Interpretation of the Isiac Table, or the Bembine Tablet.

### INTRODUCTION.
<note>original: "ΠΡΟΟΙΜΑΤΙΟΝ" (Prooimation)</note>

<note>Decorative initial E: Woodcut showing an architectural scene with buildings and a town in the background.</note>I present to you at last, curious Reader, the long-promised true and genuine interpretation of that most celebrated Isiac Table—which they call "Bembine" after Cardinal Bembo, its former owner. Before you commit yourself to reading it, I ask a few things of you: First, that you place the Table before you, divided into its many sections and most diligently marked with its own letters, so that you may exactly compare the words with the figures. Next, I ask that you do not weigh the explanations—brought forth according to the mind of the Ancient Egyptians—in a superficial or perfunctory way, but rather ponder and examine them carefully in the deep scales of the mind. Finally, observe the order and the connection of the subjects explained with the diligence that can and should be applied to the study of hidden knowledge. If you perform these things, I am confident that you will give a correct, sincere, and noble judgment, subject to no false objections, regarding the true and genuine interpretation I have completed. Farewell, and enjoy it.

## Concerning the name and origin of this Isiac Table.

Why it is called the Isiac or Bembine Table.

Cardinal Bembo preserved the Isiac Table.

<margin>
The Bembine Table perished in the pillaging of Mantua.

The size, material, and ornaments of the Bembine Table.

<note>Decorative initial E: Woodcut showing a standing figure within the letter.</note>Proceeding <term>methodically</term> <note>original Greek: "ΕΥΜΕΘΟΔΕΡΩΣ" (Eumethoderos)</note> in this book, we have decided to lead the beginning of our interpretation from that Table from which the arguments of the other things following in order depend, like streams from a fountain. It is called the <term>Isiac</term> Table because it contains the sum of Isiac—that is, Egyptian—Theology. It is called <term>Bembine</term> because Cardinal Bembo, for the great benefit of the literary world, was the first to bring it forth to the world after rescuing it from destruction. For he redeemed it at a significant price from a certain blacksmith who had acquired it during the Bourbon sack of the City <note>The Sack of Rome in 1527</note>. He preserved it until his death as a wonderful monument of ancient Wisdom in his Museum, which was most richly furnished with all things pertaining to the knowledge of letters and antiquities. After his death, it finally passed to the Duke of Mantua, in whose Treasury it was kept among the monuments of illustrious antiquities until the year 1630. In that year, during the wretched pillaging of the City of Mantua, it vanished in such a way that, although the greatest effort has been made to find out what finally became of it, no one to this day has been able to discover it. The Table had a length of five palms and a width of four. It is reported to have been entirely of bronze, and [decorated] with figures partly in enamel—which they call <term>Smaltum</term>—and partly with silver plates, by which the figures...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Mensa Isiaca (Isiac Tablet), also known as the Bembine Tablet. Having introduced the artifact, Kircher now details its provenance and the history of its reproduction by Renaissance scholars before arguing for its authentic Egyptian origin.</meta>

# TREATISE I. THE ISIAC TABLET. 81 CH. II.

the ornaments and garments of the figures were wonderfully decorated, being skillfully inlaid; this was first engraved on copper to the size of the original with the greatest zeal and diligence by the eminent engraver Enea Vico of Parma <note>original: "Æneas Vicus Parmenſis"</note>, under the care of Torquato Bembo, and dedicated to Emperor Ferdinand I. Later, as copies became scarce, Herwart <note>Johann Georg Herwart von Hohenburg (1553–1622)</note>, the Chancellor of the Duke of Bavaria, gave orders for it to be engraved anew, and he published it inserted into his *Theater of Hieroglyphics*. From this source, we exhibit it here to the curious Reader, translated into a smaller proportion with all the diligence we could muster. While we do this, no small difficulty arises: was this monument—certainly the most celebrated among all others—fashioned by the Ancient Romans or by the Egyptians? There are those who feel this Tablet was composed by the Romans; others assert it was brought from Egypt along with other monuments of Egyptian affairs (for which the Romans had a unique craving) and placed in the Temple of Isis. And these latter seem to me to conjecture more truly. <margin>The Bembine tablet was transferred from Egypt to Rome.</margin> Certainly, the nature of the figures themselves and their mystical composition—not to mention the craftsmanship and style of painting, which utterly savor of the Egyptian genius—demonstrate more than enough that the Tablet was fashioned in Egypt by the ancient Priests <note>original: "Hieromantis," referring to sacred seers or priests</note>. It was by no means made by the Romans, whose habit it was never to fashion an Egyptian image so pure without always attaching to it something drawn from Latin Theosophy <note>Kircher uses "Theosophy" here to mean a system of divine wisdom or religious philosophy</note>; as has been demonstrated throughout this Work. Since, therefore, this present Tablet is purely hieroglyphic and has nothing mixed in from the literature, sculpture, or painting of other Nations, it is concluded irrefragably that it was fashioned by the Egyptians, in Egypt, and what is more, before the invasion of Egypt by Cambyses <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE; Kircher uses this as a chronological marker for the decline of "pure" Egyptian art</note>—namely, at that time when hieroglyphic letters flourished most in Egypt. Added to this is the fact that it could not have been fashioned except by the Sacred Scribes <note>term: "Hierogrammatistis" — the class of Egyptian priests responsible for sacred writing and temple records</note> themselves, whose duty it was to arrange hieroglyphic inscriptions and hand over the arrangements to be engraved on Obelisks, stones, folding-doors, and Temple tables. Since the knowledge of these characters had already failed by the times of the ancient Romans, it is certain that this could in no way have been completed by the Romans; it was therefore fashioned by the ancient Egyptians.

The walls on every side were full of both hieroglyphic paintings and sculptures, in the midst of which an altar was placed, the surface or slab of which was marked with hieratic letters. # CHAPTER II. 82 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

Indeed, the images of the greatest Deities and the entire concatenated series of Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"; referring to a chain of spiritual beings or demons</note> were displayed through such hidden symbols that they did not merely—as they foolishly imagined—mark the concealed recesses of the highest mysteries, but they also possessed an infallible efficacy for summoning whichever of the Spirits they wished through horrific and cursed adjurations, and analogous rites and ceremonies. In these inner sanctuaries <term>Adyta: the innermost, most secret parts of a temple, forbidden to the public</term>, or recesses removed <margin>Egyptian Theology was taught in their inner sanctuaries.</margin> from the company of all men, that more secret mystical Theology of the Egyptians was taught; described through hieroglyphic symbols, it was handed down to men of the Priestly order. Arnobius <margin>Arnobius</margin> <note>A 3rd-century Christian apologist</note> testifies to all of this when he speaks of an Egyptian Magician: *The Magician,* he says, *performed all those things by his clandestine arts; he stole the names of powerful Angels and remote disciplines from the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptians.* Clement of Alexandria, <margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin> discussing Pythagoras, says: <note>original Greek: Ὁ Πυθαγόρας περιετέμνετο...</note> *Pythagoras was circumcised so that, having entered the inner sanctuaries, he might learn the mystical philosophy handed down by the Egyptians.* Justin Martyr, <margin>Justin Martyr</margin> in his *Questions to the Orthodox*, 25: <note>original Greek: Τίμια δὲ τὰ τότε...</note> *At that time, the hieroglyphic disciplines were held in high esteem among the Egyptians; these were handed down in the inner sanctuaries to the most select individuals, not to men of the street. Astrology, however, was considered a lowly, common, and vulgar study among them.* St. Clement, writing to James regarding a certain Heretical Magician, said: <note>original Greek: Εἰς Αἴγυπτον πορεύσομαι...</note> *I shall go to Egypt, and I shall be joined in friendship with the Initiates, Priests, and Prophets of the inner sanctuaries.* Not only were the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptians highly celebrated by all, but also the Magical books with which the Priests conjured Demons and strove to bring them <margin>Magical Books of the Egyptian Priests.</margin> under their power, as Lucian mentions in *The Lover of Lies*: <note>original Greek: Ἐγὼ δὲ οὖν βίβλους λαβὼν...</note> *The house was infested by a Demon; I, however, took the books (of which they had many such among the Egyptians), came to the house, and with a most horrific chant I drove out the Demon, imitating the Egyptian tongue.* What else are these books of this kind, if not those we have mentioned: tablets furnished with various hieroglyphs, that is, Magical signs? These things are so true that even Holy Scripture itself seems to reproach the Hebrews for such abominations, which <margin>Inner sanctuaries of the Hebrews built in imitation of the Egyptians.</margin> they were accustomed to perform in inner sanctuaries built in subterranean places after the manner of the Egyptians. It should be noted that the greatest mention is made of tables in all antiquity: for they were consecrated to the Gods, and placed in sacred and religious locations, without which nothing was performed; upon these it was customary to slaughter, to sacrifice, and to place vessels of every kind. Hence by the Greeks it was called a <term>thysias</term> <note>original Greek: θυσιάς; a sacrificial altar</note>, or <term>trapeza thysias</term> <note>original Greek: τράπεζα θυσιάς; table of sacrifice</note>, that is, according to Hesychius, a table consecrated for sacred uses <term>or the repositories of offerings</term> <note>original Greek: ἤ τὰ θυηφυλάκια</note>. He says: *The fires of the Gods, the solemn tables, the hidden and innermost hearths.* Furthermore, Festus records that a table fit for divine mysteries was called an <term>Anclabris</term>, just as the bronze vessels which the Priests used in sacrifices were called <term>Anclabria</term>, surely derived from the old Plautine verb <term>Anclare</term> or <term>Antlare</term>, whether that be from the Greek verb <term>antlo</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντλῶ</note>, that is, *I draw water*, or from the ancient word <term>anculare</term>, which signified the same as *to serve*. # CHAPTER II. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

We read that such things existed. Hence, golden tables were designated for Jupiter and Apollo; silver for Diana, Venus, and the Moon; marble for the remaining crowd of Gods; and finally, wooden ones for the lesser deities who followed in the train of the Gods. <margin>Valerius Maximus</margin> Valerius Maximus relates that Dionysius of Syracuse was held in such great hatred for no other reason than that, disregarding religion, he removed the golden and silver tables from the temple of Apollo. <margin>Cicero</margin> And Cicero, in *On the Nature of the Gods*, says: *He now ordered the silver tables to be carried away from all the shrines, upon which, according to the custom of ancient Greece, was inscribed "Of the Good Gods," for he said he wished to make use of their goodness.* The same author said that Verres carried off Delphic tables made of marble, most beautiful bronze mixing bowls, and a vast quantity of Corinthian vessels from all the sacred buildings. <margin>The sacred tables of the Ancients were Altars.</margin> Therefore, to embrace many things in a few words, the sacred tables were nothing other than altars; these were always held in such great veneration among the Ancients that proverbs flowed from them, such as "to fight for altars and hearths" <note>Latin: *pro aris et focis*; a common idiom for defending one's most sacred and home-bound values</note>, meaning that no thing should be valued as highly as that which has been consecrated to the Divine Powers of the immortal Gods. There is also that line of Aristophanes: *In those ungrateful men, neither altar, nor faith, nor oath remains* <note>original Greek: Ἐν οἷς ἀχαρίστοις οἰσὶν οὔτε βωμὸς, οὔτε πίστις, οὔθ' ὅρκος μένει</note>, spoken regarding the utterly treacherous, such as he says the Spartans were. Virgil also teaches that those swearing an oath touched the altar with their hand: <margin>Virgil</margin>

->*I touch the altars, and the fires between, and call the Divine Powers to witness.*<-

<margin>Cicero. Sacred tables as most holy inner sanctuaries.</margin> And Cicero in *Against Flaccus*: *If he were to swear while holding the altar, no one would believe him.* Furthermore, the altars, or sacred Tables, were the most holy asylums and places of refuge for men. Cicero, after his return, said: *Who, unless he had fled to the altar of the tribunate, could not have escaped the violence of the Praetor.* The same in *For Roscius*: *Just as to an altar, so did he flee to his house.* And in the *Tusculan Disputations*: *Bereft of such great progeny, when he had fled to the altar, a hostile hand slew him.* <margin>St. Jerome</margin> It was therefore not permitted to drag suppliants away from the altar, such as the altar of Concord mentioned by St. Jerome, to which if anyone had fled, as if to a statue of Caesar, it was considered a great sin to tear him away.

<margin>The origin of Tables or Altars flowed from the Egyptians.</margin> From these matters, explained perhaps more diffusely than was necessary, it is clear that the origin of altars and tables flowed from nowhere else than from the Egyptians. For them, as I have said, it was a solemn custom to place tables in the inner sanctuaries <term>adyta: the innermost, most sacred part of a temple, restricted to priests</term>, not just any kind, but those skillfully adorned with hieroglyphics, established both to procure reverence for the rites and ceremonies, and to more powerfully and effectively draw the Divine Powers whom they solicited with their incantations, and whose images were displayed there in symbolic garments. <margin>Aben Vaschia</margin> These they placed in the middle of the temple or sanctuary, as witnessed by Aben Vaschia <note>Ibn Wahshiyya, a 9th/10th-century author often cited by Kircher for Egyptian lore</note> in his book *On the Service of Egypt*:

<margin>Sacred tables were placed in the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptians.</margin>
