# CHAPTER III.

->**The Subject Matter of this Tablet, or the Isiac Table.**<-

<margin>Iamblichus. The Egyptians imitated the Gods in establishing hieroglyphics.</margin>Imitating the very nature of the Universe and the craftsmanship of the Gods—as Iamblichus testifies—the Egyptians themselves displayed certain images of secret and hidden notions in the creation of their symbols. Just as nature expresses hidden principles through apparent forms as if through symbols, and as the Gods explain the truth of Ideas through manifest images, so too did the Egyptians work. Therefore, since they recognized that all higher things take pleasure in the likeness of lower things, and moreover desired to be filled with goodness from those above, they strove to imitate them to the best of their ability. They rightly offered a mode of action corresponding to the celestial beings by embedding hidden mysteries within manifest symbols, in the interpretation of which one must *dismiss the words and receive the meanings*. <margin>The Egyptians signified hidden mysteries through manifest symbols.</margin> Since this was the established custom among the Egyptians, they constructed this sacred table; and just as it had the greatest use in sacrifices and the worship of the Gods, so too it seemed fit to exhibit their entire Theosophy <note>Divine wisdom or mystical philosophy</note> upon it through symbols devised with the highest ingenuity. <margin>The Isiac Table contains the entire Theosophy of the Egyptians.</margin> Therefore, just as at a sumptuous table furnished with every preparation of the most exquisite foods, the nutritive faculty of man converts the food into the substance of the one nourished; so in this sacred and mystical table, the Priests—received as if at a banquet of the immortal Gods—would contemplate the nature of eternal and incorruptible substances expressed through wondrous and highly appropriate symbols with the subtle investigation of the intellect. Through the likeness of the actions expressed therein, they were thought to be joined to them in perfect union; which was the very purpose of this tablet. <margin>The purpose of the Isiac Tablet: that Egyptian Priests might be united to God through its teaching.</margin>

Thus, this table teaches first the entire constitution of the triple World: the Archetypal, the Intellectual, and the Sensible. It shows, namely, how the Paternal Mind <note>The supreme divine intellect</note>, or the supreme divinity—as if stirred from a certain center into the entire circumference of the Worlds, both sensible and insensible—moves all things, animates all things, and marks all things with the character of its triad. <margin>The subject of the Bembine Tablet. The Paternal Mind unfolded from the center into the circumference.</margin> Next, it shows how it governs the universe through the "paternal depth" <note>original: *fundum paternum*</note> constituted of three triads (which depth some call *Iynges* <note>Magical or intermediary powers in Chaldean oracles</note>, some a <term>multiform super-principle</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπεραρχὴν παντόμορφον</note>; others, like the Platonists, call the Soul of the World, and Philo calls <term>world-crafting wisdom</term> <note>original Greek: σοφίαν κοσμοτεχνῖτιν</note>). It shows how each triad—consisting of Power, Father, and Mind—exists as a most perfect triad enfolded within the fountain-triad of faith, truth, and love. <margin>The paternal depth constituted of three triads. Each triad consists of Power, Father, and Mind.</margin> You will also see on this table the order, disposition, administration, and protections of the divine Powers. These are the attendants and ministers of the divine and supreme Mind and the Paternal *Iynges*, which are dispersed from the Paternal depth, as if from a most fertile Ocean, into all the paths of the World. <margin>The order of the divine Powers.</margin> Here are seen the individual Rulers of the Worlds marked with their own insignia: the fiery, the ethereal, and the material. <margin>The Rulers of the Worlds and the Fathers of the Fountains.</margin> Here are the Fathers of the Fountains, whose care it is to arrange and preserve the principles of all things and to found the inviolable laws of nature. You will observe, curious Reader, the linked series of those Deities which the Ancients called <term>Zonia</term> <note>Those "with zones" or bound to specific celestial spheres</note> and <term>Azonia</term> <note>Those "without zones" or unattached to a specific sphere</note>—that is, those who are bound to no certain sphere—each adorned with their own insignia and arranged into certain triads under... <margin>The Zonia and Azonia Deities.</margin>

# CHAPTER IV.

## *The Division of the Isiac Tablet or Table.*

<margin>
Division of the Bembine Tablet into intrinsic and extrinsic space; the intrinsic space of the Bembine Tablet is divided into three regions.
</margin>

**F**irst, this entire Tablet A B C D is considered as a parallelogram, according to its internal and external space. The internal space is divided into three regions, following the triple pattern of the Supreme Mind <note>Kircher refers to the Neoplatonic idea of a threefold divine intellect reflected in the physical world</note>; namely, the superior, the middle, and the inferior. The Supreme Region is bounded by the letters E F, and contains twelve human-shaped figures, or sacred inscriptions <note>original: "hierogrammatismos"</note>, divided into four triads and adorned with various and multiform symbols.

<margin>
The first region of the Bembine Tablet.
</margin>

The second or middle region, which is bounded by the letters G H, is again subdivided into three spaces: the middle one, marked with the letters Γ Δ Θ Φ <note>Gamma, Delta, Theta, Phi</note>, contains 7 principal figures O, Q, R, S, X, Y, Z, adorned with a manifold display of symbols; while the two ends—the right marked with the letters G A Ξ Π <note>Xi, Pi</note> and the left marked with the letters P H M N—are arranged with a diverse array of figures and ornaments.

<margin>
The second region of the Bembine Tablet.
</margin>

The lowest region, intercepted by the letters I K, is likewise displayed with twelve principal human-shaped sacred inscriptions, just like the uppermost; the explanation of which we shall bring forward shortly.

<margin>
The third region of the Bembine Tablet.
</margin>

-><-

We have seen the internal arrangement of the figures; now let us also declare the external one in a few words. The border <note>original: "limbus"</note> of the tablet occupies the external arrangement, by which the consistency of the entire Tablet or Table is enclosed. This border is fourfold: superior, inferior, right, and left. We have marked the superior A C, the inferior B D, the right A B, and the left C D with letters: each of which contains various hieroglyphic ideas, as will be seen later.

<margin>
The external space of the Bembine Tablet is divided into four borders.
</margin>

There remains, moreover, another subdivision of smaller borders, which distinguishes the middle region G E H N from the superior and inferior, marked with various hieroglyphics; the upper of these is marked with the letters G H, the lower with Ξ N; while the transverse ones are marked with the letters Λ Γ Π Δ and Θ P Φ M. The base <note>original: "Σηνὲ" (Sene), likely referring to the plinth or footing</note> which is placed below the larger border serves only as an ornament. And with these portions, the Composition <note>original: "Syntagma"</note> of the entire tablet is completed; the secret meanings of which we shall explain shortly in the same order in which we subdivided it.

<margin>
Division of the smaller borders of the Bembine Tablet.
</margin>

-><-

# CHAPTER V.

## *The Anatomy of the Tablet, or concerning the habits, ornaments, headdresses, staffs, and the whole multiform <note>original: "πολυμόρφῳ" (polymorpho)</note> variety of sacred inscriptions and their differences.*

<margin>
Anatomy of the Bembine Tablet.
</margin>

**T**he figures in this Isiac tablet differ chiefly in eight things: namely, in form, position, gesture, actions, clothing, headdresses <note>term: "tutulis" - specialized ceremonial caps or hairstyles</note>, staffs <note>term: "baculis" - ritual rods or scepters</note>, and finally in the sacred inscriptions placed around them, such as flowers, twigs, small letters, and animals; all of which must be explained.

<margin>
Eight things are to be considered in the Bembine Tablet.
</margin>

# CHAPTER V. 88 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE THEATER OF HIEROGLYPHS

...they represent a figure, as is evident in the upper, middle, and lower regions, with a few exceptions; others are transformed by various animal masks, as appears in the fourfold border.

<margin>Posture</margin> They differ in **Posture**, for some are standing, others sitting, some kneeling, others carried in ships, or standing upon variously shaped pedestals <note>original: *abacis*</note>; finally, others are seen in different positions; these are not without a hidden significance, as will be made clear later.

<margin>Gesture</margin> They differ in **Gesture**; for some are seen with arms now raised, now hanging, and with hands effectively contracted; others appear composed for running, and others for worshipping something.

<margin>Action</margin> They differ in **Actions** <note>original: *Operationibus*</note>; for you may see some here as if imperiously ordering and commanding something, some humbly seeking something, others sacrificing, and finally others offering and presenting with a suppliant spirit.

<margin>Dress</margin> They likewise differ in **Dress**, yet all are adorned according to the Egyptian rite. Most are naked over the greater part of the body, and are veiled rather than clothed with a thin garment from the breast or navel down to the knees; and this habit is mostly seen in male figures. Women are seen with a cloak extending from the breasts to the feet, entwined on the shoulders with certain bands. Furthermore, garments of this kind are seen now latticed, now of a feathery texture, or with a covering variously wrapped in bird wings, sometimes woven with stars and crosses, and elaborated throughout with other symbols; all of which will later be shown to be full of mysteries.

<margin>Head-dresses</margin> I come to the **ornaments of the head**; where the greatest variety and diversity of things considered also occurs. For certain statues are seen with head-coverings <note>original: *vittis*</note> now flat, now twisted into a cone, some of which are imbued with a white color, others black; some are covered with a simple veil, some are fashioned with a double-bordered band fixed on the crown. Above the aforementioned veils, however, rise the head-dresses <note>Kircher uses the Latin *tutuli*, referring to high priestly wigs or caps</note>, adorned with no less a variety of things; most are feathered, or made of herbs and flowers, <term>flame-circle-serpent-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: *φλογο-κυκλο-οφιόμορφοι* (phlogo-kyklo-ophiomorphoi). This compound word describes an ornament combining flames, a solar circle, and the form of a serpent or uraeus.</note>, that is, most are distinguished by a spreading of flames and rising vipers, as well as by a spherical body.

<margin>Staves</margin> The **Staves** or scepters which they carry in their hands also differ greatly; there are some with the head of a hoopoe bird, some marked with a Lotus flower, others adapted into the shape of an arrow; there are those who carry plants or feathers in place of a scepter, with most equipped with the <term>Tautic character</term> <note>The *Crux Ansata* or Ankh, which Kircher associates with the god Thoth/Hermes Trismegistus (Taautus).</note>, that is, the **Handled Cross**, as is evident from the table.

<margin>Surrounding Hierograms</margin> Each of the **Hieroglyphic compositions** <note>original: *Hierogrammatismi*</note> has various arrangements of symbols placed near them, which we reduce to three heads. First are animals, both four-footed, winged, and creeping, as well as those mixed from these. Second are small hieroglyphic characters, some of which are simply placed near the figures, others are seen enclosed within an oval shape, which we named "sacred tablets" in the *Pamphylian Obelisk* <note>Kircher’s earlier work on the Roman obelisk now in the Piazza Navona</note>, and they indicate I know not what amulets and protective charms <note>original: *phylacteria*</note>; as will be said in its proper place. Third are altars, columns, and sacred tables, filled with vessels, flasks, urns, bowls, flowers, and plants; all of which, as they swell with the greatest mysteries, so they deservedly merit a singular interpretation.

->And this is the anatomy, which first, before the interpretation<-
->I begin...<-

COLLECTION I. THE ISIAC TABLE. CHAPTER V.

<note>Signature: M 2</note>

...before we began, we thought it necessary to set this before the eyes of the curious Reader, lest we should seem to have approached the exposition of this most mysterious of all tablets in a confused or rash manner, without proper digestion, or with "unwashed hands," as the saying goes. <note>original: "illotis... manibus" - a Latin idiom meaning to approach a sacred task without due preparation.</note> Nothing further remains but to now set our hand to the work and finally fulfill the promise made so many years ago, having at last been released from our debt.

# The True and Genuine Interpretation of the Isiac Table, or the Bembine Tablet.

<margin>
The method to be followed in the interpretation of the Bembine tablet.
</margin>
We begin at last, under the auspices of the Divine Power, the interpretation of the Isiac Table, according to that order into which we divided it in the preceding sections. Lest we encounter confusion in such a great variety and multitude of things to be explained, we have decided to clarify the individual parts of the tablet through eight paragraphs. We will not always provide the authorities for the matters explained right next to them, but will instead direct the Reader to seek them out via marginal numbers in those places where they were cited elsewhere, both in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* and in the preceding Volumes. This is to ensure that, in such a great heap of facts and authorities, the thread of the interpretation is not hindered to the boredom and confusion of the Reader; however, we will always provide the full authorities for matters never proven elsewhere. We wished to advise the Reader of this first, so that the reasoning behind our plan would not be hidden from him. To the matter, then. May God, the Best and Greatest, breathe favor upon our prayers.

## DIVISION I.

### *Exposition of the figures in the middle region of the Tablet.*

<margin>
The middle region of the Bembine tablet is explained.
</margin>
<margin>
The Egyptians considered the divinity diffused through all things in two ways.
</margin>
The Egyptians, contemplating the divinity diffused through all things, understood it in two ways: either as it is established in the solitary unity of the Eternal Mind, far removed from all material fellowship of things, enjoying the everlasting good of its own happiness in the ineffable retreat of the godhead; or as it expressed a certain regard toward the orders of created things. In this latter sense, it is seen as unfolding from a certain center into the universal series of Worlds through the ministers and attendant Spirits <note>original: "Genios"</note> and Secondary Intelligences <note>original: "Secundeos" - a term for subordinate celestial beings</note> subject to it, governing all things, animating all things, making all things fruitful, and finally urging all things toward the sustenance of the Universe. Since, however, they placed a certain triple power in God, and thus established the supreme divinity with a certain triform power (as they themselves say) within one substance—a doctrine handed down to them by Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure identified with the Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> under a great concealment of silence—upon which all things depend, and by which, as if by a certain ideal seal, all the orders of the Worldly classes, both sensible and insensible, are
<margin>
The Egyptians placed a triple power in God.
</margin>

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...they knew these things most excellently; hence they have beautifully expressed the systems of the individual triads shining forth in the Universe, each adorned with its own appropriate symbols in this Tablet, as we shall now explain.

<margin>The Great Gate of the Gods in the center of the Bembine Tablet is explained.</margin>
In the middle of the Tablet, therefore, as if at the center, you behold the Throne *a b c d l m, f i e s*, the "Great Gate of the Gods," as they call it, constructed with a grand architecture of symbols. Its topmost crown or front *a b* expresses flames spread out in the form of rearing serpents. The second crown *c d* is marked by a winged globe; the third *e f*, and the base *l m* of the throne are distinguished by the same emblem. The supports of the throne are marked with eight-part circles circumscribed by squares. <margin>The figure sitting upon the central throne of the Bembine Tablet is explained.</margin> The entire crown rests upon two columns *e l* and *f m*, divided by white and black steps, and equipped with the head of Isis. Seated upon this throne is a figure in female dress; from the navel to the feet she is covered in feathered breeches, and from the navel upward toward the breast, she is crowded with innumerable breasts <note>original: "multimammia" — a reference to the many-breasted form of deities like Artemis of Ephesus, symbolizing nature's fertility</note> (though they are not well-depicted in the diagram). Her head is veiled with an Egyptian fillet, and over the veil is spread a guinea-hen <note>original: "meleagris"</note> that appears to be taking flight; on its back is a basket <note>original: "calathus"</note>, from which emerge two leaves of the persea tree and two horns, which enclose a circle marked with the figure of a Scarab. In one hand she holds a scepter distinguished by a Lotus flower; with the other she makes that gesture by which something is usually commanded imperiously. She sits upon a polished seat marked with the figure of a sitting dog. Beneath the throne a pedestal <note>original: "Abacus"</note> is seen, the border of which is marked with eight-part circles, as mentioned; within the pedestal is placed a reclining figure composed of a Lion and a Hawk, holding a Canopic jar <note>original: "Canopum"</note> with its forefeet; from the back, however, is a serpent-shaped globe <note>original: "ὀφι-μορφος"</note>; above the head of the hawk-headed figure <note>original: "ἱερακόλοντος"</note> is joined a crescent Moon, upon which a star rests. Standing by the throne on both sides are two flowered columns *V W*, by which two asps with swollen, upright chests, adorned with sacred fillets, stand like sentinels of the throne.

<margin>The attendants standing by the central throne of the Bembine Tablet.</margin>
We have seen the Throne or the Great Gate of the Supreme Mind; now let us contemplate the attendants standing around it, turned toward the supreme throne: three are placed on each side, *O, Q, R* on the right, and *X, Y, Z* on the left. Of these, *O* and *Z* are seen standing, clothed in the same habit and dress; the middle ones, *Q* in the form of an ibis <note>original: "ἰβίμορφος"</note> and *Y* in the form of a cat <note>original: "αἰλούμορφος"</note>, are painted in a sitting posture. The symbols they carry, the headdresses <note>original: "tutuli"</note> they wear on their heads, and the throne on which they sit will be explained later. Two images are close to the top of the throne on either side, *R* and *X*, distinguished by that position and the dress of symbols which you see. But with these things thus duly set forth, let us now explain what the Egyptians noted by this hieroglyphic display of symbols. <margin>What the central throne of the Bembine Tablet or the Great Gate of the Gods signifies hieroglyphically. Plutarch. Plato.</margin> The throne described just above indicates nothing other than the diffusion of the triform Supreme Mind into all the paths of the three Worlds, from whose unfolding this World is born—that is, this sensible Universe—which Plutarch calls the "House of Horus" and the Egyptians call the "Great Gate of the Gods"; which indeed was proved elsewhere from Plato to flow forth from the archetypal triangle. The topmost crown of the throne or gate, in the midst of the spread-out serpent-shaped flames, indicates that the Supreme Mind is full of light and life, eternal, incorruptible, and separated from all contagion of matter, <margin>Zoroaster.</margin> according to that saying of Zoroaster: *When you see the sacred fire, without form, shining leaping through the depths of the whole world, listen to the voice of the fire.* <note>original Greek: "Ἡνίκα μὲν βλέψῃς μορφῆς ἄτερ εὐίερον πῦρ λαμπόμενον σκιρτηδὸν ὅλον κατὰ βένθεα κόσμου, κλῦθι..." — Kircher quotes the Chaldaean Oracles attributed to Zoroaster to link Egyptian theology with Neoplatonic light mysticism.</note>

# TREATISE I. THE ISIAK TABLE. CHAPTER V.

"When you see the formless, sacred fire flashing, dancing through the depths of the whole World, then listen to the voice of the fire." <note>original: ὅταν ἴδης τὸ ἄμορφον... This is a fragment from the Chaldean Oracles, ancient mystical texts attributed to Zoroaster.</note> And this is that most abstract fire, hidden in the sublimity of the divine essence, according to that saying of Zoroaster: "The Father snatched himself away, nor did he shut up his own fire in his intellectual Power." <note>original: Ἐαυτῷ ὁ πατὴρ ἥρπασεν... Another Chaldean fragment suggesting God's essence is not contained but shared.</note> For the supreme Parent God snatched himself away, and did not enclose his Fire within his own intelligible Power, but communicated it to the remaining Worlds. "For all things are the offspring of one fire." <note>original: πάντα γὰρ εἰσὶν πυρὸς ἑνὸς ἐκγεγαῶτα</note> <margin>How the supreme triform Mind communicated itself to the triple World.</margin> But let us see how this was done. Unrolling from the center into the Worlds, he first communicated it to the Angelic Intellectual World through the Spirit; secondly to the Sensible World; thirdly to the Elementary World: all of which are beautifully evident from the symbols of the throne. We have said that the supreme *ba* flourish <note>A specific decorative or symbolic mark on the tablet.</note> indicates that Empyrean or Archetypal World, full of infinite light and life, <margin>Symbols of the Angelic World.</margin> from which the triform nature of God (as the Egyptians say) unrolled and communicated its fire and life to the Angelic Intellectual World; these are aptly indicated by *c d*, the second flourish, and by the globe in the form of a winged circle; for this World, purged of all material dregs, can be conceived only by the mind and intellect. <margin>Symbols of the Sensible World.</margin> Then, from this, the nature of the triform divine essence unrolled and communicated itself to the sensible World; and first indeed to the "depth" of the divine and paternal Mind, the <term>Iynx pantomorpha</term> <note>A "multiform" spiritual intermediary or "whirl" that transmits divine will into the world.</note>, which the Platonists call now the First Mind, now the Word, now the Soul of the World, and which Philo also calls "manifold wisdom"; <margin>Symbols of the multiform Iynx, or Soul of the World. Philo.</margin> which they placed with a truly fitting heap of symbols in the middle of the Egyptian throne, as if in the center of all nature, which she governs. She sits first, to imply power and dominion: the seat shines like a dog, because this Isiack Iynx, or paternal depth, shines forth in the star Sothis <note>The star Sirius, associated with Isis and the Nile flood.</note>, as <margin>Diodorus.</margin> Diodorus testifies: with the thighs expressed by a varied texture of wings, she indicates the speed and sublimity of the operations by which she diffuses herself into all the paths of the World: <margin>See appropriate authorities omitted here in the Pamphilian Obelisk, book 4, and Volume I of Oedipus, page 190.</margin> from the navel to the breast she is thickened with innumerable breasts, with which she continually feeds and nourishes the entire machine of the World with an abundance of necessary things: the Zones encircling her neck denote the celestial Orbs, which she agitates with continuous motion: her head is covered with a veil, to indicate the hidden and inaccessible mysteries of nature which she works: she carries a flying <term>Meleagris</term> <note>A guinea-fowl, used here to symbolize the variety of creation.</note> on her head, to signify the variety of beings in all nature, which are aptly indicated by the diverse-colored feathers of the <term>Meleagris</term>: the Basket resting on the back of the Meleagris signifies the abundance which she brings forth; the leaves of the persea tree signify the wisdom with which she administers all things; the horns express the Moon, and the scarab enclosed in a circle expresses the Sun; by which it is shown that she effects that variety of all said things by the aid of the Sun and Moon; <margin>See Pamphilian Obelisk, book 5.</margin> in her right hand she holds a lotus-bearing scepter, by which she shows that she moderates all things according to the pattern of the Paternal Mind; for the flower of the Lotus follows the Sun day and night with untiring motion, as <margin>Theophrastus.</margin> Theophrastus testifies: but by the imperious gesture of the left hand, it is hinted that all things stand under her commands and orders; for as Zoroaster rightly says: "For the Father perfected all things, and delivered them to the second Mind, whom the nations of men call the first." <margin>Zoroaster.</note>

*O mother of all life and of the childless;* <note>original Greek: θ. ω. μῆτερ ἁπαντολ. ζωῆς καὶ ἀτεκνιων; likely a fragment of a hymn or invocation.</note> Isis is the Goddess of all things, according to that inscription previously brought forward in the *Egyptian Politics*: *I am all that has been, and is, and shall be, and my veil no mortal has ever uncovered.* <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ εἰμὶ πᾶν τὸ γεγονὸς, καὶ ὂν, καὶ ἐσόμενον, καὶ τὸ πέπλο ἐμὸν οὐδεὶς τῶν θνητῶν ἀπεκάλυψε.</note> These words can truly apply to no other but the Paternal Depth—that is, the intelligible *Iynx* <term>Iynx: A Neoplatonic term for a "magical link" or intermediary spirit that transmits divine ideas into the material world</term> or the Paternal Word. Concerning these, see the first Volume, page 185, where everything said thus far is confirmed by extensive authorities. This is the storehouse of Worldly Ideas, which is aptly suggested by the supports of the throne or gate marked **g h i k** <note>Letters g, h, i, k refer to a diagram of the Bembine Table found elsewhere in the work.</note> and by the squares in which eight-part circles are inscribed, depicted in a continuous order all around. For we have shown in *Hieroglyphic Geometry* that the number four is indicated by the square, and the number eight by the eight-part circles; these joined together give 12, the symbol of mundane perfection, and they express the ideas of the individual partial Worlds, which you may see explained in the cited place in the treatise on *Hieroglyphic Geometry*.

<margin>
The vicissitudes of Worldly affairs are expressed by the columns of the throne of the All-formed Iynx.

->Since indeed in the elementary World all things are subject to the change of days and nights, of darkness and light, of harmonies and discords; in the ethereal world, to the opposition of motions; and in the intellectual world, to the "counter-craft" of the Divinities <note>original: Numinum antitechnia; referring to the balancing forces of divine powers</note> in harmonious-dissonant ways for the preservation of the Universe; they have quite aptly expressed this constitution of the mundane house, indicated by the throne, supported by two columns distinguished by white and black steps. By this, they aptly indicated the vicissitudes of things and the laws of harmonies and discords, without which the World could by no means exist. See what we have discussed more fully on these matters in Book 4 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. To these columns are placed the serpent-shaped figures <note>original Greek: ὀφιόμορφα</note> of the Ophionian *Agathodaemons* <term>Agathodaemon: A "Good Spirit," often depicted as a serpent, representing protection and vitality</term> **V** and **W**, crowding the throne in the form of Serpents or Asps. They stand upon flowered columns to show that the Ophionian Agathodaemons give consistency to all things through life and animation in the lower World, the ethereal, and in their own way, the intellectual. Within the Abacus is placed **T**, a reclining Lion, notable for a Hawk's head and a black veil, with the remaining hieroglyphics, as you see. ->. . . But Goddess, I pray to you, with fortunate times,<-
->To lead us in peace and health, and the increase of all things.<-

You have here the interpretation of the first and most important part of this table. We see, therefore, how the supreme triform Deity unfolds itself from the Archetype into the Angelic World, and from this into the ethereal, and from here into the hylic <note>material or physical</note> or Elemental World; we have seen how the Father handed over all things to be governed by the Second Mind; and what effects he completes in the worlds just reviewed. Now we must see how, and through which assessors or ministers, the Spirit of the "paternal foundation"—or the now-unfolded form of the universal World—administers all things in the World.

<margin>What the paternal foundation is according to the Egyptians.</margin> The Egyptians held, as was shown copiously both above and in the *Hieroglyphic Theology*, that the paternal foundation is nothing other than the Word of the Father, which the Platonists call the Spirit of the World, the Chaldeans call the *Iynx* <note>a "top" or "wheel" used as a magical mediator</note>, and others entitle by other names. <margin>The paternal foundation is composed of three triads. Psellus.</margin> And they held that this is composed of three triads; which triads are indeed nothing other than certain assemblies of Genii <note>guiding spirits</note> distinguished by a triple order, each of which consists of a Father, a Power, and a Mind. <note>original Greek: "πατρικὸν τίνα βυθὸν, σέβοντ’ ἐκ τριῶν τριάδων συγκειμένων, ἑκάστη δὲ τριὰς ἔχει πατέρα, δύναμιν, καὶ νοῦν"</note> "They worship a certain paternal depth composed of three triads, and each triad has a father, a power, and a mind," says Psellus in the *Zoroastrian Oracles*. Let us now reveal how aptly the Egyptians expressed these things.

# D I V I S I O II.

->*Interpretation of how the paternal foundation—that is, the soul of the universal World—is divided into three Triads in this table according to the Egyptians.*<-

<margin>The paternal foundation is a collection of Genii divided into three triads. The first triad.</margin> The paternal foundation, or the Word proceeding from the essence of the triform supreme Deity, as the Egyptians will it, is marked by the same character of the triad. It has likewise arranged the universal assemblies of Genii or intellectual substances into certain classes of triads, according to the testimony of Psellus. And the first triad indeed shines forth in the figures **V, S, W**, who are the Ophionean *Agathodaemones* <note>Serpent-shaped "Good Spirits"</note>; by these, as we have said, the all-forming <term>pantamorphus: having many shapes or forms</term> spirit of the World, or the paternal foundation, is surrounded, providing life and motion to all things through its process into the triple World—intellectual, ethereal, and hylic or elemental—as we explained a little earlier. <margin>The second triad. The third triad.</margin> The second Triad by which it is surrounded is denoted on the right by the three figures **O, Q, R**; the third indeed on the left by the three figures **X, Y, Z**; who are like certain leaders of their own triadic order. <margin>Each triad has a Father, a Power, and a Mind.</margin> And since each triadic order contains a Father, a Power, and a Mind, the figures **Q** and **Y** are quite aptly understood as the Fathers and Leaders of their order; **R** and **X** as the Powers of their order; and **O** and **Z** as the Minds of their order. All of these stand beneath the paternal foundation, and having turned toward it, they ask for mandates in duly performing their ministries; and thus the all-forming nature is understood to be first constituted from these three triads **V S W**, **O Q R**, and **X Y Z**. But let us explain the workshops and ministries of each.

## TREATISE I. THE ISIAC TABLE. CHAPTER V.

<margin>The Fathers, Powers, and Minds of the individual Triads are explained.</margin>
And so, the two triads O-Q-R and X-Y-Z show, by the position of their faces turned toward it and by their gestures and nods, the desire with which they strive to execute the commands of the "Paternal Depth" <note>original: *fundi Paterni* — a Neoplatonic term for the ultimate source of divinity</note> upon the matters committed to their faith, surrounding the throne of the All-formed Divinity <note>original: *Pantamorphi Numinis*</note>. The two middle figures of these triads, Q and Y, are called "Fathers" within their triads; for they sufficiently declare by their seated posture the authority and dominion which they hold over the choirs of their respective triads. The figures O and Z, however, denote "fecund Minds," as will later be evident from the symbols; finally, R and X are called "efficacious Powers" in the choir of their triad. But let us examine the symbols of each, beginning with the Fathers. <margin>The Fathers of the triads are explained.</margin> The Fathers occupy the middle place in the triad, acting as the leaders of the sensible world (as Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar known for his work on the Chaldean Oracles</note> speaks) and as directors of the minds and powers that surround them. All of them, as I have said, have their faces turned toward the throne of the paternal depth as if toward a center from which they flowed and from which they drew the authority of their dominion, both for the sake of veneration and to execute the commands of the paternal depth.

<margin>Explanation of the Ibis-shaped figure marked with the letter Q.</margin>
Thus, the first figure on the right of the triad, marked with the letter Q, displays an <term>Ibis-shaped</term> <note>original: *ἰβίμορφον* (ibimorphon)</note> figure—that is, in the form of an Ibis—sitting upon a seat woven in various ways with checkered work. Its head supports a two-pronged flame, distinguished by a headband, a circle, and two snakes emerging from either side, and it sustains a bundle composed of feathers and sprouts. In its right hand, it holds the Tautic character of the handled cross <note>The Ankh</note>, while the left hand proffers a scepter marked with the head of Isis. Beneath the seat, two crocodiles turned in opposite directions lie prostrate as if pressed down. The explanation of all these things is as follows: <margin>What the Ibis-formed man signifies.</margin> By the man transformed with the head of an Ibis, the Mercurial Divinity is indicated, whom the Egyptians call Hermanubis; for as was rightly shown in the <margin>Pamphilian Obelisk, folio 348.</margin> *Pamphilian Obelisk* regarding the Sacred Writing of Isis, the head of an Ibis attached to a human figure always indicates Mercury, the Name of the moist substance, as we also taught above in the Astrology of the Egyptians. He sits because he prevails with the highest power. <margin>What the checkered seat of the Ibis-formed Divinity means.</margin> He occupies a checkered seat made of small white and black squares, by which it is indicated that although in the nature of things all are "consonant-dissonant" <note>harmonious yet conflicting</note> and differ by light and darkness, heat and cold, and the greatest vicissitude of things, they are nevertheless so aptly disposed by the virtue of Hermanubis that they now provide the highest symmetry and beauty, without which the World cannot consist, so that the greatest benefit for the World emerges therefrom. Hence Orpheus rightly says of Mercury: *He who holds the reins of the World, splendid on his variegated seat.* <note>Kircher translates a Greek Orphic fragment into Latin here</note> From this, I believe, the Greeks attribute to Mercury a wand varied with white and black; see this mystical disposition described more at length in the *Hieroglyphic Arithmetic* in the treatise on Arithmetical Seals. <margin>The Quail of the Ibis-shaped seat.</margin> On the panel <term>eta-zeta</term> <note>original: *ηζ*</note> inserted into the seat, the figure of a Quail is seen; since this is a symbol of adverse things, nothing else is indicated by it except that by Ibis-shaped virtue, evils are reconciled with goods, cold things with hot, and dry things with moist, so that the greatest benefit for the World emerges therefrom. <margin>The handled cross and the scepter with the head of Isis: ornaments of All-formed nature.</margin> In his right hand, he holds the Tautic character <note>The Ankh</note>, by which it is hinted that he contains within himself the power of the influential virtue communicated to him by the Supreme Mind. In his left, he holds a scepter marked with the head of Isis, by which it is shown that he exercises the power received from Isis—or All-formed nature, or the paternal depth—over the things committed to his faith. He has his head covered with a veil, pertaining to the secrets of the mysteries—

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...[the previous triad] could perform nothing in the management of the moisture committed to its care. Having thus explained the triad O Q R, let us now explain the other triad X Y Z with equal pace.

<margin>
The Triad XYZ of the Bembine Tablet is explained.
</margin>
It must be noted, therefore, that just as the Triad O Q R represents the active principle in a masculine guise, so this triad X Y Z behaves by way of a passive principle, as represented by the feminine guise; and they regard one another in a beautiful order. For the Egyptians, as was related in the first Volume, third Treatise, confused the sexes among their Gods indiscriminately; learning from which, the Greeks also frequently distinguished their Divinities with both sexes.

<margin>
The Egyptians and Greeks expressed their Divinities with both sexes.
</margin>
This distinction of sex is to be understood such that those Divinities who command others subject to them behave by way of an active principle, while those subject behave by way of a passive principle. Thus the Moon, insofar as it is an active generative principle of operations in the Elementary World, was called *Lunus* <note>The masculine form of the Moon</note>; insofar as it is subject to solar influences, it was called *Luna* <note>The feminine form</note>, as has been proven elsewhere.

<margin>
Divinities under a masculine guise signify an active principle; under a feminine guise, a passive one.
</margin>
Therefore, in respect to the Superiors presiding over them, they assumed a feminine sex; in respect to the inferiors subject to them, a masculine one. This occurs in the same way in these triads: for although the triad X Y Z is feminine in respect to the triad O Q R, it nevertheless possesses a masculine force in respect to those subject to it. In this way, figure Y is indeed subject to figure Q as a passive principle; yet in respect to another triad subject to it, it possesses the character of an active principle and is called "Father," as Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a Byzantine scholar often cited by Kircher for Neoplatonic insights</note> most excellently notes.

<margin>
Psellus. Nephta is explained by the letter Y in the Bembine Tablet.
</margin>
But to follow the thread of the explanation begun: the figure Y is called **Nephta** by the Egyptians, the Father of their triadic choir and Ruler of the World, as the symbols demonstrate more than sufficiently. He sits upon a throne with his head veiled and wearing a tiara <note>original: "tutulato," referring to a high priestly headdress</note>, to denote the supreme authority over all things committed to him by "All-Formed Nature." Beneath him stands the figure of a kneeling Genius, formed in the manner of a suppliant, joined to the seat with a Lotus flower; by which it is indicated that the Divinities subject to him perform all their actions according to the example of the Father or leader set before them, just as the Lotus flower, as has been said, follows the Sun with perpetual motion.

<margin>
Momphta, the Presider over moist nature, in the pedestal of figure Y of the Bembine Tablet.
</margin>
The pedestal <note>original: "Abacus"</note> on which he sits contains the figure of a Lion, which in the *Pamphylian Obelisk*, book 4, in the hierogram of the Lion, we called **Momphta**—that is, the Presider over the Nilotic increase and moist nature, from which he takes his name. By this it is indicated that Momphta is subject to the dominion of this Father and director of the World, and receives from him the methods and influences for arranging the increase of the waters, as the Lotus flower indicates. The small table with two Nilotic vessels shows the Nilotic sacrifices, and the Hawk's feather shows the motion of the Sun or Osiris, of whom Nephta is the sister and wife, according to <margin>Plutarch.</margin> Plutarch; by which motion Momphta is incited to promote the increases of the Nile and adapt them for fertility. The small characters above the table express it thus: *The Chain of Nature is derived into the fourfold World, and from there into the management of the substance of water.*

<margin>
The small hieroglyphic characters on the pedestal of Nephta are explained. The dress and gestures of Nephta are explained.
</margin>

# TREATISE II ON THE BEMBINE TABLE. CHAPTER V.

...as we have shown in the great treatise; from the veiled crown a two-pronged flame emerges, by which the power and hidden force of the fiery mind is hinted at; upon this is placed a triple headdress <note>original: "tutulus," a high conical headdress worn by priests or deities</note> of grain, which structure of headdresses a Beetle <note>Scarab</note> with outstretched Hawk-wings binds and connects, as is clearly visible. By the three headdresses, the triple harvest in Egypt is indicated, which Nephta <note>An Egyptian deity associated here with divine providence or the "world-soul"</note> provides through the power and motion of Osiris (or the Sun), indicated by the Beetle with extended Hawk-wings, by vivifying and making all things fruitful. <margin>Figure expressed by the letter Z.</margin> Figure Z exhibits the Nephtaean mind of the triad, and is exactly the same as the figure of the Ibis-shaped triad O already explained; for which reason we deliberately omit its exposition. <margin>Figure expressed by the letter X in the Bembine table.</margin> Figure X exhibits the passive power in the Nephtaean triad; hence it is marked by a feminine habit, a swelling breast, a flower-bearing staff, and a hanging arm with the hand effectively contracted; since their meanings were explained in the opposite figure R, there is no need to repeat them. The headdress of this figure differs from the previous figure R, and is <note>Symbolic icon: A small circular glyph with two serpents emerging from the sides and a feathered or winged top.</note>, that is, it consists of a circle, with serpents emerging from both sides, and a feathered top; by which is indicated the triform power of the Divinity communicated to the Nephtaean power for acting rightly; just as both the speckled Numidian bird <note>labeled alpha in the original</note>, and the Hawk <note>labeled beta</note>, the idea of the solar Divinity, conspicuous by the extension of its wings, along with the scepter and the handled cross <note>the Ankh</note>, sufficiently indicate the idea of the triform Divinity and the Polymorphous Archetypal Sun. Imbued with this idea, Nephta and her Power bring about the variety of worldly things through the efficacy of their influence.

-><-

<margin>Summary of what has been said.</margin> You see, therefore, how the supreme archetypal Mind of minds, unfolded from its own retreat of divinity as if from a certain center, proceeds into the Angelic or intellectual world of minds, imbuing each and every thing with its ideas. From here, through the Word or its "depth," <margin>Zoroaster.</margin> as Zoroaster witnesses, *that ideas are characterized, of which there is one source* <note>original Greek: ἰδέας κεχαρακτηρίσθαι, ὧν πηγὴ μία</note>, gracious with all-encompassing ideas whose fountain is one, it pours itself into the sensible World. Through three triads—of Fathers, Powers, and Minds—which are like the secret and intimate attendants of the All-Formed <note>Pantamorpha</note> nature or the Paternal depth, it governs, animates, fertilizes, and preserves all things. You see the readiness of the attendant minds, turned toward the All-Formed mistress of the World as if toward their own fountain and original spring, to carry out her commands.

<margin>Various names of the Paternal depth.</margin> You have here, therefore, the mysteries of the Paternal depth or the Paternal Word, which the Chaldeans call the *Iynx* <note>A "spell" or "link" in Chaldean Oracles</note>, the Egyptians *Hemphta*, and the Platonists the universal Soul of the World, while others call it by other names. For as we said above, and deduced at length in the *Theology of the Egyptians*, the Egyptian followers of Zoroaster held one principle of all things, and celebrated it as the One and the Good; then they venerated a certain Paternal depth, constituted of three triads; and that each triad has a Father, a Power, and a Mind. By these three names, the first principles are also named. <margin>Proclus, Damascius. From this Archetypal Triad, the triads of all created things subsequently emanate; in these, the highest order of Fathers would be as similar as possible to the supreme Father; the second order of Powers would be as similar as permitted to the Word or Son; and the third order of Minds would be very similar to the Mind; and so on for the rest. Nor should it be thought that in each triad there are only three Spirits, but rather innumerable ones contained under each order; all of which are shown expressed by their symbols on the throne or gate of <term>Pantamorph Nature</term> <note>Nature in all its forms; a title for Isis.</note>; <margin>Many Spirits in each triad.</margin> which Pantamorph Nature Zoroaster also calls <term>Hecate</term>, just as he calls the intellectual minds <term>Synoches</term>. <margin>What Hecate and the Synoches are.</margin> However, Hecate in this place is nothing other than the unity and idea of the forces of all living things; the Synoches are the intellects which, having received from Hecate the influence of that fire which grants life, pour it into the empyrean, ethereal, and material worlds, and they contain, continue, and rule those worlds, and bestow vital motion upon them. And this indeed is the more secret <term>Theosophy</term> <note>Divine wisdom or mystical insight.</note> of the Chaldeans and Egyptians.

## The Azonian Hecatine Triad.

<margin>The Azonian Hecatic Triad.</margin>
This system of sacred hieroglyphs is therefore separate, and is called the Azonian Triad. The spirits of this triad are called <term>Azonoi</term> <note>original: Ἄζωνοι; literally "un-zoned" or "unbound by belts"</note>, because they use their power freely within the zones, being placed above the visible and sensible Gods. This class is distinct from the "Zonary" class of Gods, who inhabit the sensible parts of the World and do not exit their prescribed zones.

<margin>The three Minds of the Hecatine or Azonian triad.</margin>
Thus, the Azonian or Hecatine Triad contains three Minds, whose names are <term>Ekdotis</term> <note>The Giver</note>, <term>Komas</term> <note>The Reveler</note>, and <term>Ekklustike</term> <note>The Pourer-forth</note>. These "Azonian" Gods are said to be Serapis, Bacchus, and the chain of Osiris. So says <margin>Psellus.</margin> Psellus in his commentary on the Chaldean Oracles: <margin>Azonian Gods.</margin> > For among them there are also Azonic ones, such as the Chaldean Ekdotis, and Komas, and Ekklustike; and the Azonian Gods among them are Serapis, and Dionysus, and the chain of Osiris. They are called Azonian because they exercise authority over the zones without being bound by them, and are established above the visible Gods; whereas the Zonary Gods are those who travel strictly around the zones in heaven and govern the things there. <note>original Greek: Εἰσὶ γὰρ παρ’ αὐτοῖς καὶ ἀζωνικοί...</note>

However, different authors refer to these Azonian and Zonary deities in different ways. How the Egyptians understood them is more than sufficiently demonstrated by this hieroglyphic system, which finally frees us from the secret confusion of authors, since their meaning is made clear from the figures themselves.

<margin>The image of the Egyptian Hecate is explained.</margin>
We therefore call the triad L, M, N "Hecatic," because the Father <note>In the sense of the primary source or progenitor</note> of this triad is the Egyptian Hecate. She is called <term>ioiekaustos</term> <note>original: ἰοίεκαυστος; likely meaning "burned by poison" or "fiery-violet"</note> by Psellus, because she becomes a kind of receptacle for the material World; hence she is called the center of all influences. This is indicated by the image M, notable for her female face, canine ears, and the black veil with which she is covered. She has three zones <note>bands or belts</note> wrapped around her breast and neck; on her head she carries the shape of a gate or a worldly house. She stands upon a Lotus flower, whose stalk is like a column marked with white and black steps, ending at the bottom in the shape of a white heart in place of a pedestal. From the middle of this column flow two perfect leaves, and two heliotrope flowers emerge.

<margin>The dress and habit of Hecate are explained.</margin>
Let us explain what each detail indicates: The head of M signifies the "Out-pouring" Hecate or Isis, and is the same as the "Paternal Depth," insofar as she enters into the tripartite boundaries of the terrestrial World. This is aptly indicated by the three zones wrapped around her breast and neck. She is surrounded by a black head-veil because she exerts her hidden powers in the dark parts of the terrestrial World. She has canine ears because Hecate was dedicated to the Dog, as witnessed by <margin>Macrobius.</margin> Macrobius, Natalis Comes, Phornutus, Apollodorus, and other mythologists; and as <margin>Natalis Comes.</margin> <margin>Phornutus.</margin> <margin>Apollodorus.</margin> <margin>Zoroaster.</margin> Zoroaster openly teaches: > From the hollows of the earth leap the terrestrial dogs. <note>original Greek: ἐκ δ’ ἄρα κόλπων γαίης θρώσκουσι κύνες χθόνιοι.</note>

Certainly, the terrestrial Dogs come forth from the ends of the earth. They are attached to Hecate because she is the most faithful guardian and preserver of earthly treasures. Indeed, all these things have been abundantly demonstrated in the "Dog" hieroglyph of the Pamphilian Obelisk. She contains a square gate to show that she is the gate through which all the abundance of superior influences is derived into the worldly house. Because the sensible World is subject to innumerable vicissitudes of things, she is aptly given a column marked with a lotus flower, with...

Assisting the column are the attendant Spirits L and N. The first is called *Epidotis* <note>original: ἐπιδοτὶς — "The Giver" or "Bestower"</note> and the second *Komas* <note>original: κωμας — likely referring to a reveler or attendant</note> by Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and scholar of the Chaldean Oracles</note>. They supply nourishment distributed to each, as if through the veins and receptacles of subterranean passages. These things are indeed aptly suggested by the three collar zones, namely the tripartite kingdom of sensitive, vegetable, and mineral nature. What is signified by the ribbons led down from the Hecatic column, and by the swelling breasts reaching downward, has been discussed throughout this Work.

<margin>Pierius. What the ribbons signify.</margin>
Regarding the ribbons, Pierius <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani, author of a famous Renaissance book on hieroglyphics</note> writes thus in his commentary on Macrobius: *Hence those various and manifold ribbons dedicated to Isis; Heliodorus calls them not only the seven phases of the Moon, but also the "conjunction," "angles," "rising," etc.* <note>original: συνοδον, γωνίας, ἀνατολὴν</note> *but they also indicate the power of that which is occupied with matter—namely, that which begets all things and conceives all things: light and darkness, day and night, life and death, beginning and end.* Therefore, the attendants gird themselves with these ribbons from the Hecatic column, which is marked by white-and-black steps to signify the aforementioned things.

<margin>Plutarch. The Egyptian Hecate, or Isis according to Plutarch.</margin>
For as Plutarch asserts: *Isis, or the Egyptian Hecate, is that part of nature which, being as it were feminine, receives all births into herself; she is called by Plato the nurse and the common receptacle of all things, and by many others "the one with ten thousand names"* <note>original: μυριώνυμος — Myrionymos</note> *endowed with innumerable names because reason turns her into all forms and species. For she intends good and flees from evil, and is the subject-receptacle of both; yet of her own accord she inclines only toward the better, offering herself to be filled and preserved by the influences and likenesses in which the fates, suited for begetting things, rejoice and exult.* The things said up to this point correspond appropriately to these views.

<margin>The headdresses of the attendants of the Egyptian Hecate are explained.</margin>
Indeed, the headdresses <note>original: Tutuli</note> of both figures L and N consist of a crown distinguished by various stones surmounting the head, from which two persea flowers emerge, with a lotus flower leaning on each side and one in the middle propagating straight upward; these indicate the triple nature over which they rule. Sensitive nature is indicated by the lotus flower; for the lotus follows the Sun by an immutable law from the East to the South, and from there to the West, as if sensing the movement of the star. It also indicates that these aforementioned Spirits establish their operations in all their ministries according to the pattern of the archetypal Sun. Vegetable nature is indicated by the leaves of the persea. Finally, the crown distinguished by stones indicates the level of mineral nature.

<margin>The tripartite kingdom of the Hecatic triads, Psellus.</margin>
And this is the tripartite kingdom of the Hecatic triad which is committed to their care, of which the Father or Prince is Hecate *Ecclystice*; the middle is called *Epidotis*, and the power is called *Komas*. ## The Serapaean Triad <margin>Serapaean Triad</margin>

**O**f the triads opposed to this one, the prior or lower is marked with the Greek letters ζ, η, θ, and the superior with the letters γ, δ, ε. The lower triad is called **Serapaean**, because in it **Serapis**, indicated by the monstrous head H, holds the office of the Father; the figure ζ represents Mind and Power. It is the fountain-triad of faith, truth, and love, represented by the head of Serapis composed of every material of the lower World, such as Beroaldus <note>Filippo Beroaldo (1453–1505), a famous Italian humanist and commentator.</note> records to have existed in Alexandria in his commentary on Apuleius. But let us hear Beroaldus: <margin>Beroaldus: The head of Serapis was greeted by the Sun with a kiss.</margin> 

> At Alexandria there was a temple of Serapis constructed with vaulted work, a sight of wondrous art, in which the image of the God was so vast that with its right side it touched one wall and with its left the other. It was said to be composed of all kinds of metals, woods, and roots. There was also a small window, fashioned with trickery and art, so aligned with the rising Sun that a solar ray directed through it would illuminate the mouth and lips of Serapis, so that in the sight of the people he appeared to be greeted by the Sun with a kiss.

Which description certainly shows that it was not a complete statue, but a head, transformed with wondrous industry, of the kind that appears in this place. In it, the beard is joined together by the roots of herbs instead of hairs; the eyes, nose, and ears are seen expressed by every kind of stone and metal and mosaic work. The crown of the head is proud with a tripartite feather, and the head rests upon a lotus-bearing column likewise divided into white-and-black steps. <margin>What the head of Serapis in the Bembine Tablet signifies hieroglyphically.</margin> Serapis, with this apparatus of symbols, indicates nothing else in this place but the **Subterranean Sun**, who is named Pluto and Dis by the Greeks, exercising his dominion over the entire subterranean economy of the World, as the composition of the head from all the materials of the lower World demonstrates more than sufficiently. In his tripartite kingdom, he disposes all things, ordaining the laws of agreement and disagreement by that method which was shown above, through the attendants assisting him; <margin>The attendants of Serapis, and the hieroglyphic explanation of them.</margin> of whom the first, the **Serapic Mind**, is dressed in feminine attire, with a garment reaching to the ankles swelling with innumerable breasts, and she holds in her hands a *thyrsus* <note>A staff topped with a pine cone, usually associated with Bacchus/Dionysus</note> curved at the top. By this, the influence of Serapis is indicated as being poured into lower things through the Serapic Mind, and the abundance of nourishment is expressed through the multiple breasts. From this manifold nourishment, all things in the tripartite kingdom—indicated by three crowns encircling the breast—are animated through the **Serapic Power** <note>original symbol: a circle with a central dot, often representing the Sun or a Monad</note>, whose operations are shared with the third Mind. The third Serapic Mind indeed bestows copious nourishment for the growth of vegetable nature; while the **Serapic Power** <note>original symbol: a circle with a central dot</note> assigns to each thing its own property, life, and motion; these are aptly indicated by the Serpent emerging from the forehead. All these things were demonstrated at length first in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* page 224, and in Volume I, page 194, and in various other places. Furthermore, the Serapic Mind marked **M** has a flower <margin>What the frog sitting on the persea flower signifies.</margin> placed with leaves of the *persea* <note>An Egyptian tree, often identified with the Mimusops schimperi</note>, upon which a frog sits. By the frog sitting on the persea flower, it is signified that the Serapic Mind, mistress of the Nile, presides over imperfect things, and does not immediately advance them to the highest degree of perfection, but leaves that duty to the Serapic Power. To understand this, it must be known that the Ancients indicated material or *hylaean* <note>From the Greek 'hyle', meaning matter</note> imperfection by the Nilotic frog; for one may often see animals of this kind in the mud where they are procreated—one part a frog, the other part something imperfect, earthy, or muddy, attached to the living portion. The inundation of the Nile provides evidence for all these things; for as it subsides, mice and various kinds of animals are found, the work of earth and water having begun in a living part of the body, while the newest form is still earthy. In frogs, however, even when born at full maturity, nature is always imperfect; so it is no wonder that the promotion of imperfect things was indicated by a frog. The frog is placed upon a persea leaf without fruit; for just as the fruit represents the shape of the heart, so the leaf placed here represents the shape of the tongue, <margin>Horus.</margin> according to the testimony of **Horus** <note>Referring to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs</note>. By this it is shown that just as a leaf without fruit is of no use, nor does the speech of the tongue produce any good unless it proceeds from a deep and premeditated heart; so neither does the Serapic Mind act, unless the Serapic Power and virtue are added, by whose help the things which the Mind has wisely disposed, the Power leads to perfection and completion. Moreover, the **Serapic Power** <margin>The Serapic Power signified by the letter <note>original symbol: a circle with a central dot</note> in the Bembi Table.</margin> is represented by the figure marked with the letter <note>original symbol: a circle with a central dot</note>, imbued with exactly the same symbols as the former. By this it is signified that the nourishment which the Serapic Mind inserts into the terrestrial womb does not reach perfection unless the Moon, by the Serapic Power...

## The Osirian Triad.
<margin>The Osirian triad is twofold on the Bembine Table.</margin>

<margin>Apuleius.</margin> Above the Hecatic triad stands the **Osirian triad**, in which first occurs the fertile Divinity of omnipotent nature—by which name **Apuleius** calls him—**Apis**. He is adorned with exactly those symbols by which we described him in the Pamphilian Obelisk under the "Sacred Engraving of the Ox." Moreover, the triad is twofold: one on the right G, I, K, and the other on the left from the opposite part of the table ϛ, η, θ. <note>Kircher refers to diagrammatic letters/symbols G, I, K and the Greek markers ϛ, η, θ likely found on an engraving of the Mensa Isiaca.</note> The Ox marked with the letter I is black-and-white, distinguished by various signs and symbols, all of <margin>What the Apis, or the black-and-white Ox, signifies.</margin> which you will find described in the Pamphilian Obelisk on pages 259 and 260. He signifies the power of Osiris flowing into the Moon. Eusebius reports that this ox, variegated with black and white spots, was called **the living image of Osiris** <note>original: "ζῶον τὸ Ὁσίριδος ἄγαλμα"</note>, because through certain appropriate signs and symbols he taught men and instructed them in things necessary for the human race. For what else do the 29 signs—which **Aelian**, **Herodotus**, **Diodorus**, **Pliny**, and **Eusebius** recount were impressed upon his body—denote, if not the diverse lunar-solar effects upon the earth? What else is meant by the horns, if not rays? What by the rising Asps enclosed by the horns, if not the lunar-solar rays full of life-giving influences? What else did they wish to denote by the wreath fixed to the back of the ox, composed of phalluses and four-part circles, if not the highest fertility which the Sun and Moon confer upon things, diffused into the four-fold World? What does the **Ankh** <note>original: "Crux ansata" (the cross with a handle)</note>, the amulet marked with the **Ankh** hanging from the neck, signify, if not that this is an averting Spirit <note>A "deus averruncus" is a deity that wards off evil or bad luck</note>, by which all adverse powers are put to flight and routed by this charm as if by a powerful spell? Indeed, the star which is placed above the back of the Bull, conspicuous for its expansion of wings, shows the highest fertility of **Nephthe** or the **Egyptian Venus** in her own house—that is, in Taurus—of all things in the three-part annual season of Egypt. This is aptly indicated by the three phalluses attached to the winged star by a thread. See the most ample treatment of these in Volume I, page 357; likewise concerning Apis on page 194, and the **Phallophoria** <note>Festivals involving the carrying of phallic symbols</note> on page 229, and in the Pamphilian Obelisk on page 260, and in various other places as the indices will suggest to the curious Reader. # THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
The Father of the officiating Triad and his attendants.
Psellus.
Diodorus.
</margin>
In this Triad, Osiris is the father, and the others are his attendants: <note>Ink blot over text; appears to contain handwritten Greek characters, possibly added by a reader</note> so the Egyptians call them. Psellus calls them *Masona* and *Tropomon* <note>original: "Μασώνα & Τρόπομον"</note>, as has been said elsewhere; Diodorus calls them Maro and Triptolemus. Although these names are highly corrupted, they nevertheless possess a very close affinity to one another. Diodorus indeed says that Maro, a companion and attendant of Osiris, taught the method of cultivating vines, while Triptolemus taught the method of cultivating fields and committing seeds to the earth; these roles correspond aptly to the attendants of Osiris. For although it has already been proven elsewhere at length, <margin>Osiris is the same as Bacchus</margin> Osiris is the same as Bacchus or Dionysus, the overseer of wine and the founder of agriculture, according to these lines:

<margin>Tibullus.</margin>
> Osiris first made plows with a skillful hand,
> And provoked the tender ground with iron;
> He first committed seeds to the untried earth,
> And gathered fruits from trees not previously known.
> He taught how to join the tender vine to poles,
> And how to prune the green foliage with a hard sickle.
> Bacchus gave to the farmer's heart, exhausted by great labor,
> The means to dissolve its sadness. etc.

<margin>
The Osirian Attendants.
Plato.
</margin>
But let us return to the Osirian attendants. Each appears wrapped in a garment woven of wicker-work reaching to the ankles, which, according to Plato, is characteristic of the farmers of Egypt, and indicates Spirits <note>original: "Genios"</note> who are perceptible and immersed in matter. The first of these, marked with the letter G, is seen urging a bull with his left hand to influence things benignly, while with his right hand he seeks commands to rightly perform the duties of his ministry. That this figure is the overseer of liquids, the small hieroglyphic characters <margin>Small hieroglyphic characters of the Osirian Attendant.</margin> sufficiently teach, the sense of which is this: <term>Propagator of celestial liquid into the lower regions</term>. The attendant K, Triptolemus, displays a cup in his left hand and the phallus of a bull in his right; by the vessel or cup, liquid is denoted, and by the phallus, fertility. By this it is correctly indicated that the fertility of the earth can in no way exist without the addition of liquid, nor can it promise any abundance of things, except by the influence of Osiris through Maro and Triptolemus, who are the Mind and Power of the <term>All-Honeyed Triad</term> <note>original: "Triadis Pammeliæ"</note>. Furthermore, the star upon which a quadrant rests on a small column is a symbol for discerning the hours, and thus of all time, as Clement of Alexandria teaches in the 6th book of his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromatum"</note>. <margin>The astronomical quadrant on the Bembine Table is a symbol of time. Clement of Alexandria.</margin> Since in the business of agriculture the greatest account is taken of time, they rightly placed a quadrant with the triad, by which the opportuneness of time was observed. Furthermore, on the opposite part of the table another triad <note>Astrological symbols: ♈ (Aries), ♉ (Taurus), ♊ (Gemini)</note> occurs, which, since it involves the same symbols, I have decided to omit the explanation; only some difference occurs in this: that the white bull denotes the Sun precisely, the celestial <term>Apis</term> <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, seen here as a solar/celestial symbol</note>, insofar as by its power it provides an abundance of all things. <margin>What Apis, or the white Bull, signifies.</margin> But since the two bulls <term>Mnevis</term> and <term>Apis</term> have been treated very copiously in various places both in this Work and in the hieroglyphic study of the bull in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, we refer the reader there, lest we confuse our proposed goal of explaining things by repeating a multitude of authorities already delivered elsewhere.

# DIVISION IV.
## Explaining that the seven Triads depicted in the middle region are nothing other than the seven Systems of the Genial Worlds.

<margin>
Zoroaster.
The Triad shines throughout the whole World, according to Zoroaster.
</margin>
Rightly and wisely did Zoroaster say: <gloss>The Triad shines throughout the whole world <note>original Greek: ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ λάμπει ἡ Τριάς</note></gloss>; *The triad shines throughout the whole World*: for indeed, according to the pattern of the supreme, three-formed Archetype of the Divine, all the patterns of the Worldly Systems were established. Hence he rightly adds, *the triad is divided into individual patterns.*
<margin>
The seven triads of the Bembine Tablet are the seven Systems of the Genial Worlds.
</margin>
Furthermore, these triads are nothing other than certain Systems of Genii <note>Genii: guardian spirits or intermediate divine beings that govern aspects of nature</note>, which the Egyptians called "Worlds." The seven principal triads explained a little earlier correspond to the seven principal Worlds, all of which flowed forth from the intelligible archetype—the three-formed World, as the Egyptians say, which is comprehensible only by the "flower of the mind." They also call this the Empyrean <note>The highest heaven, associated with pure fire and light</note>, which we have said was signified by the crowning ornament of the throne of "all-formed nature."

<margin>
The three-formed or Empyrean World.
The three triads of the ethereal Worlds.
The first Intellectual World.
</margin>
This is followed by the first triad, the Ophionian or Iyngæan <note>Iynges: In Neo-Platonism, these are "wheels" or "whirls" that act as messengers between the divine and the material</note>, which corresponds to the vital and empyrean World, as was explained; it is the first Intellectual World, which the Ancients also call "ethereal." Regarding this, Zoroaster says: <gloss>O, how this World has inflexible intellectual supporters! <note>original Greek: Ὦ πῶς κόσμος ἔχει νοεροὺς ἀνοχῆας ἀκαμπτεῖς</note></gloss> This is evidently because of their constancy and the inviolable laws and statutes by which they govern the Universe.

<margin>
The second Intellectual World.
The third Intellectual World.
</margin>
The second triad, the Ibimorphic <note>Ibis-shaped, likely referring to Thoth/Hermes</note>, corresponds to the second intellectual or ethereal World, and it contemplates the nature of moisture, according to a certain analogical and archetypal pattern. The third triad, the Nephtæan <note>Associated with the goddess Nephthys</note>, corresponds to the third intellectual and ethereal World, which likewise regards the moist principle, but in its fertilizing aspect. And these are the triads of the ethereal Worlds, which we taught above from Zoroaster constitute the "paternal depth."

<margin>
The four triads of the sensible Worlds.
</margin>
There follow the four triads of the sensible Worlds <note>Sensible: worlds that can be perceived by the senses, i.e., the physical universe</note> which are immersed in matter. The first two of these triads correspond to the Sidereal Worlds G, I, K, and the Sun ☉, the Moon ☽—that is, Osiris and Isis, the Sun and the Moon—indicated by the two oxen; these are the Governors of the lower Worlds. There follow two triads: the Hecatæan L, M, N and Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃; and the Serapæan; these correspond to the sublunary and subterranean Worlds, as has been said. Thus, these are the Triads of the seven primary Genii of the World, by whose administration the whole of nature consists.

<margin>
Psellus.
</margin>
That this is the case, Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a Byzantine scholar who preserved many ancient Oracles</note> openly recites from the mind of Zoroaster, and Sanchuniathon the Phoenician <note>A legendary Phoenician author</note> according to Philo, in these words: <gloss>They say there are seven corporeal worlds: one empyrean and first, and three ethereal after it, then three material, of which the last is the terrestrial, and the hater of light, which is the place beneath the Moon, containing matter within itself, which they call the Depth. <note>original Greek: Δεῖ ποι ἑπτά φασὶ σωματικοὺς κόσμους...</note></gloss> For the Egyptians and Chaldeans establish seven corporeal Worlds (namely, those administered by intellectual powers): one fiery and first, after this three ethereal, then three material, of which the last is called terrestrial and the "shunner of light," which is the place below the Moon, embracing matter within itself, which they name the "depth."

<margin>
The eight primary Worlds according to the Egyptians.
</margin>
And so, including the archetypal triad, or the World far removed beyond every corporeal limit, there are eight Worlds, by which the Universe pri-

<margin>The opinion of the Platonists concerning the eight Worlds.</margin> Concerning these things, Plato—following the mind and decrees of the Egyptians—writes in the *Epinomis* that a Philosopher ought to know how the seven circles revolve under the first; whence in the *Timaeus*, joining the first and exemplary World with the remaining Worlds, he posits eight circuits. # CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

From the first fiery triad, the Heavens were created, and the earth from the waters—that is, from the <term>Ibi-morphous mother</term> <note>A term likely referring to a "thoth-shaped" or "ibis-shaped" primordial matter, from the Greek 'Ibis' and 'morphe'</note>—and the air or "Nephta," as Plutarch himself witnesses, is the mediatrix <margin>The triad of mothers signifies the Paternal Depth composed of three triads. The Kabbalistic maxim regarding the production of the Worlds is explained.</margin> between fire and water. He calls this a wonderful, great, and hidden mystery, because it regards and hints at archetypal properties; he says it is sealed with six seals, because whatever God produced in the World in the space of six days is encompassed by them. He says that fire and waters proceed from these, which are divided into male and female, because fire and water are the principles of all things, such that the fiery force denotes the male, and the watery force the female: and over these preside the fathers, to whom everything in the Universe is believed to have been handed over. And that these are the triads of the paternal depth, he expressly teaches in these words:

-> <note>Hebrew: "Three mothers: He engraved them, hewed them, combined them, and sealed with them three mothers in the world, three in the year, and three in the soul, male and female."</note> <-
<margin>Iochaides <note>Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai</note> in the Zohar and the Yetzirah.</margin>

*Three mothers,* he says, *God carved out, and he engraved them, and combined them, and sealed in them three mothers in the World, three mothers in the year, and three mothers in the soul, male and female.* Where you see that he takes mothers for fathers, and fathers for mothers, male for female, and female for male, indiscriminately; just as the Isiac Table <note>A famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs used by Kircher as a primary source</note> also shows, where you see images shown in masculine dress swelling with breasts, adorned with veils, and those expressed in female appearance feigning masculine dress; by which, as I have said, nothing else is hinted at except that according to a different concept, insofar as they preside, they show themselves as males, and insofar as they are subject, they show themselves as females; and these are they who are established as the presidents of the World, the years, and the times. See all these things explained more profusely in the Kabbalah. The cited author afterwards continues:

-> <note>Hebrew: "And from them were born seven triads: above and below, East and West, North and South, and the Holy Temple in the middle, and it supports them all."</note> <-

*And from these are born seven triads: the supreme, the infernal, the Eastern, the Western, the Northern, and the Southern, and in the middle the holy temple supporting all things.* I do not see what could be brought forward more aptly for our explanation. What else is indicated by the "holy temple in the middle supporting all things" but the house or throne of <term>Pantamorphic Nature</term> <note>All-formed nature</note> expressed in the middle of the table? Which is surrounded on the East, West, North, and South, below and above, by its attendants, the seven triads, or the seven presidents of the Worlds, as was explained; which Iochaides pursues in the Chaldean style in these words:

-> <note>Aramaic/Hebrew: "And it is seven fountains from which all nature flows, and the chains from which all words/things are attached."</note> <-

<margin>Zoroaster. Iochaides. Psellus. Iochaides seems to have taken his ideas on the production of the Worlds from Zoroaster.</margin> *And these are the seven fountains from which universal nature flows; and they are the chains which connect all things.* Which things Zoroaster himself—from whom perhaps Iochaides copied these things—testifies to be most true in his Oracles, as found in Psellus, in these words: <note>Greek: "The Eternal ones worship every Triad of faith, truth, and love, and the seven fountains, and the primordial sun; and from the material spark and the primeval-sweet ones, and the fountains abundantly, the whole judgment, and the thunderous fountain, and the heaven-fallen fountains, and the characters of the fountains embarking upon justice."</note>
