# TREATISE I. THE ISIAIC TABLE CHAPTER V.

...unknown symbols; and sources of holiness; of Apollo, Osiris, and Hermes; but they say the material sources are called origins. <margin>Seven springs which the Egyptians worshipped.</margin> The Egyptians also worship a triad of faith, truth, and love; and seven springs: the Imperial Sun, and from a material source the Archangelic, the source of senses, and the fount of judgment, and the source of lightnings, and the source of mirrors or inspections, the source of characters composed of unknown constitutions, and the fount-like summits of Apollo, Osiris, and Mercury; but they call the material sources those of centers and elements. <note>Kircher is using "Apollo, Osiris, and Mercury" as interpretative names for Egyptian deities, likely Horus, Osiris, and Thoth.</note> Thus, by the Imperial Sun, he understands the Solar World; by the material Archangelic, the Lunar; by the source of senses, the Saturnian; by the fount of judgment, the Jovial <note>Jupiter</note>; by the source of lightnings, the Martial <note>Mars</note>; by the source of mirrors, Venus; and finally, by the source of characters, the Mercurial World. How aptly these are applied to the seven triads, or the seven systems of the Worlds expressed on the table, is clear from the explanation set forth above.

<margin>The seven triads of the Egyptians can be applied to the three Worlds: Archetypal, Intellectual, and Sensible.</margin> It should be noted, however, that these seven triads are so taken by the Egyptians that, according to a certain analogy, they can easily be applied to the three Worlds: the Archetypal (or Ideal and Intelligible), then the Intellectual World of Angels, and finally the Sensible World. In the Archetypal, they are considered as Intelligences, Fathers, and Ideas; in the Intellectual, under an intellectual condition and as they are immediate Virtues flowing from the Archetype, to whose care the sevenfold Worlds are committed; in the Sensible, they are considered under a material condition. But he who desires to know these things more clearly should consult the Class on the Cabala <note>Kircher's section on Jewish mysticism</note> and other treatises presented throughout this Work. And these are the things which I thought should be said concerning the middle region of this table; therefore, let us proceed to explain the remaining regions of the table.

## DIVISION V.

### Interpretation of the Upper Region of the table.

<margin>The upper region of the Bembine Table contains four triads of the World Rectors.</margin> The Upper Region, enclosed by the letters E, contains twelve Rectors of the World, divided into four triads, which correspond to the twelve signs and months. The first triad P, S, V, is called Mendesian; and it corresponds to the three months, Mechir, Phamenoth, and Pharmouthi. The second Triad X, Z, A, is called Ammonian, and corresponds to the three months Pachons, Paoni, and Epep. The third triad B, C, E, is called Momphraean, and corresponds to the three months Mesori, Thoth, and Phaophi. The fourth triad is called Omphraean, and corresponds to the three months Athyr, Choiak, and Tobi. <note>These are the names of the months in the Coptic/Egyptian calendar.</note> And these are the Rectors of the Starry World; whose duty it is to preside over the course of the entire year in procuring the production of things suitable to each. <margin>Rectors of the Starry World and their duty.</margin> They are the administering Spirits <term>Genii<gloss>guardian spirits or minor deities</gloss></term> of all-forming nature, arranged in that order which is fitting for the administration of things: For a Triad, according to Zoroaster <note>Kircher quotes the "Chaldean Oracles" attributed to Zoroaster</note>, *shines in the whole world;* <margin>Zoroaster.</margin> *for the eternal Mind of the Father assigned a Triad to all things to govern all. And there appeared in it Virtue, and Wisdom, and many-minded Truth. From here flows the countenance of the Triad before essence.* <note>original Greek: "Τριὰς γὰρ... ἐν παντὶ τῷ κόσμῳ λάμπει... ἧς Τριὰς γὰρ ἔλαχε πᾶς πατρὸς ἀΐδιος νῶι πάντες κυβερνᾷν. Καὶ ἐφάνη ἐν αὐτῇ ἡ τ᾿ ἀρετὴ, καὶ ἡ σοφία, καὶ ἡ πολύφρων ἀτρέκεια."</note> For the Triad shines in the whole World. For the Mind of the eternal Father spoke into three; governing all things by Mind. And there appeared in it Virtue, and Wisdom, and many-knowing Truth. From here flows the face of the Triad before essence.

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

For after the *Iynx* <note>A Neoplatonic term for a "linking" or "mediating" spiritual force; literally a "whirl" or "spell-binding" power.</note> or the all-shaping nature of the paternal depth has been divided into its cosmic triads, Psellus—drawing from <margin>Psellus.</margin> Zoroaster—shows in these words that the World Rectors are next: *After this come the Connectors: the Father, the Ether, and the Material.* <note>original Greek: μετὰ ταύτην, οἱ συνοχεῖς, ὁ πατήρ, ὁ αἰθήρ, καὶ ὁ ὑλαῖος.</note> Immediately following the intelligible *Iynx* come the World Rectors or Leaders: the fiery, the ethereal, and the material. They are divided into two classes, the watery and the earthly; and these, by their celestial influence, labor at continuous combinations in the four elements of fire, air, water, and earth, adorning various mixtures among natural compositions, intent both on the harmony of the World and on procuring the abundance of all things. These are the Presiders over the signs and months, who administer the World according to twelve <margin>The triads of the World Rectors have their own Father, Mind, and Power.</margin> boundaries. Moreover, each individual triad has its own Father (or mother), its own Power, and its own Mind; two of which always look toward the middle father or mother as if toward their leader <note>original: "choragum," the leader of a chorus in Greek drama.</note>, as is clear from the table. Indeed, that these twelve preside over the months and signs, Iochaides <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Isaac Luria or a similar Kabbalistic authority.</note> shows in these words from the *Book of Formation* <note>The Sefer Yetzirah, a foundational text of Jewish mysticism.</note>, as a genuine disciple of the Egyptians:
<margin>Iochaides. The World Rectors preside over the months and Zodiac signs.</margin>

> He engraved twelve gates, combined them, and formed with them the twelve celestial signs in the World. Their signs are: MSHT, MAIB, S’AQ, GDD. And these are the twelve months that lead, and He made them like a city, and arranged them like a war; and God also made one thing opposite the other, three mothers which are three fathers, from whom come forth fire, spirit, and water. <note>original Hebrew: ויב" שערים חקקן וצרפן וצר בהם שנים עשר מזלות בעולם סימן משת מאיב סעק גדד ואלו חן יב" חדשים מנהיגין ועשה אותם כמין מדינה וערכם כמין מלחמה וגם את זה לעומת זה עשה האלהים שלש אמות שהם שלשה אבות שמהם יצא אש ורוח ומים :</note>

*There are twelve gates; He engraved, combined, and formed in them the 12 celestial signs in the World. Their signs are: MSHT, that is, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, the first triad; the second triad is SAIB, that is, Cancer, Leo, Virgo; the third triad is MA’Q, that is, Libra, Scorpio, and Sagittarius; the fourth triad is GDD, that is, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces. And these are the twelve moderators, whom He disposed in the likeness of a City, and directed them in the manner of war, and made one over against the other, three mothers who are three fathers, from out of whom go forth fire, spirit, and water.* From these things, unless I am mistaken, it clearly appears that the twelve figures denote nothing other than the twelve Intelligences presiding over the year, divided into four triads.

<margin>I. The Mendesian triad.</margin> But now let us explain each part in detail. The first triad, P, S, V, is the Mendesian, and it corresponds to Winter, of which S represents the Father, V the Mind, and P the Power. It is called Mendesian from the Egyptian word <term>ⲙⲉⲛⲁⲛⲥ (Menans)</term> according to the testimony of <margin>Herodotus.</margin> Herodotus, by which they name a goat; whence both the City and the Mendesian Province <note>original: "Nomus," an administrative district of ancient Egypt.</note> obtained their name, and the goat placed upon the altar M demonstrates this sufficiently. <margin>What is the goat hieroglyphically?</margin> The figure S, the Father, seems to be killing this goat. Hieroglyphically, however, the goat is nothing other than the primal fertile power of the earth in the year, by which it produces sprouts as if they were certain first-fruits; which happened in Egypt during the three months corresponding to the <margin>Manetho.</margin> Mendesian triad, according to the testimony of Manetho, in the months of Mechir, Phamenoth, and Pharmuthi, in which the Mendesians sacrificed goats as if <margin>Aelian.</margin> a happy omen for the beginning year. This is supported by Aelian in book 10 of his *History*, chapter 24, where he records that female goats were among the delights on the head of Isis, but the males were sacrificed. From here, the translation of Capricorn into the Heavens seems to have flowed to the Greeks,

The attendant P, however, in masculine dress, with a flower-bearing headdress <term>circularly-encompassing-the-parts</term> <note>original Greek: *amphi-kyklo-perimero*</note>, and a veil with an emerging viper, shining moreover with a scepter in the shape of a hoopoe's head <term>Cucuphamorphe</term>, exhibits the Power which brings into execution the things prescribed by the Mind, supplying life, heat, and other things necessary for the happy growth of sprouts. Through the Nilotic vessel, the protection of moisture is signified; she seems to wish to seek from Osiris that he imbue her with his heat, without which no generation of things can be achieved, seeing as it is perfected by the warm-humid alone; the warm acting by way of the active principle, and the humid by way of the passive principle. <margin>III. The Momphtean Triad.</margin> Now follows the **Momphtean Triad**, corresponding to Summer, exhibited by the three figures B, C, and E. It is called Momphtean because <term>Momphta</term> <note>A name Kircher uses for a specific Egyptian divine power or "Intelligence"</note> is the presiding Deity of the Nilotic increase, as we have taught at length in the Pamphilian Obelisk regarding the <term>Hierogrammatism</term> of the Lion; which the **Nilotic Sphinx** (D) expresses quite aptly. <margin>The Nilotic Sphinx.</margin> But let us hear the words of Horus, who in Book 1, Chapter 21, describes the inundation of the Nile thus:

> <note>original Greek: Νείλου δὲ ἀνάβασιν σημαίνοντες... κ.τ.λ.</note> Signifying the rise of the Nile, which the Egyptians call *Nous* <note>Mind</note>, which is interpreted to mean "new"; they sometimes paint a lion, because when the Sun enters Leo, it causes a greater rising of the Nile. Indeed, while the Sun enters this zodiac sign, half of the new water often overflows. Whence the ancient overseers of sacred works fashioned the water-spouts and the inlets of the sacred fountains in the form of lions, from which even until now, prayers are offered for the floods.

Furthermore, signifying the inundation of the Nile, which they call in the Egyptian tongue *Nun* (more correctly <term>mon</term> <note>Coptic for water</note>), which if you interpret it, sounds like *new* (more truly *waters*); they depict a Lion etc. because when the Sun enters Leo, it makes the Nile's inundation more ample; for as long as the Sun persists in this sign, the water of the Nile itself often grows to double its size, whence the first hieromants <note>sacred priests</note> were accustomed to manufacture the tubes and channels of the sacred fountains in the shape of a Lion. Hence, to this very day, while prayers are poured out on account of an immoderate flood, they are accustomed to use the sign of the Lion. Therefore, the sitting **Sphinx**, conspicuous with wings and the face of the Moon <note>Greek text: on the forehead?</note>, that is, horned and twisted into a circle, into which the character of the <term>Agathodæmon</term> <note>The "Good Spirit" or protective deity, often depicted as a serpent</note> is inserted—this, I say, denotes nothing other than the Intelligence of <term>Momphta</term>, the Presider over the Nilotic increase, who was believed to dominate Egypt most greatly during this three-month period, as we have taught in our Astrology. <margin>The hieroglyphic dress and gesture of the Nilotic Sphinx.</margin> It carries the Moon on its head in a sextile shape twisted into a circle, to show that by the conjunction of the Sun and Moon within the 48 days in which the increase lasts from beginning to end, it is most greatly urged on; it carries the included character on its head, by which it is indicated that the <term>Agathodæmon</term>, delegated to the <term>Momphtean</term> Deity, is most greatly incited by its influences; it grows continuously for the most part for 24 days, and decreases for just as many days; which are indeed aptly indicated by the six four-part circles inscribed on the base, which denote 24, as was said, and this number doubled constitutes 48, the duration of the entire increase. But so that all these things may be more aptly confirmed, let us examine the remaining figures of this **Momphtean triad** in order.

<margin>The three presiders of the Momphtean Triad. The Father of the Momphtean Triad.</margin> There are three presiders, marked by the letters B, C, and E. **C** denotes the father, the <term>Pantopaion</term> <note>All-producing</note> Deity:—he is adorned with a fillet formed in the manner of a *calathus* <note>a basket-shaped hat</note>, from which a serpent emerges around the forehead, with two Hawk feathers and an intermediate circle; all of which are symbols of Solar vigor, and of the life and heat of the world, with which he imbues the moist substance of the World; in his right hand he carries the Ankh <note>original: Crucem ansata</note>, a symbol both of influence and of the averting of evil; in his left he carries a *cucuphomorphous* staff <note>a staff topped with the head of a hoopoe or "cucupha"</note>, a mark of the variety which he produces in the moist substance; he has as attendants **E**, the Isiac Mind, and **B**, the executive power. <margin>The Mind and Power of the Momphtean Triad.</margin> The Isiac mind **E** is covered with a white veil in the manner of a protuberant Nilotic vessel; upon which bovine horns stand with an intermediate star and two feathers: in her right hand she carries a winged scepter, from which two triangular sistrums <note>ancient Egyptian percussion instruments</note> hang on either side.

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

I shall explain what all these things signify. The white veil <margin>The meaning of the hieroglyphic Isis is explained.</margin> indicates the revealed power of divinity; the bovine horns attributed to Isis, emerging from a Nilotic vessel <note>A vessel used to measure or hold water from the Nile</note>, indicate a happy omen for agriculture—over which she presides—following an abundance of growth. The star indicates Sothis <note>The star Sirius</note>, which they called the harbinger of the Nile's rising, and from it they divined the state of the entire coming year; Horus <note>Referring to the author Horapollo</note> confirms all these things in these words in Book 1, Chapter 3: <gloss>Wishing to represent the Year, they paint Isis, that is, a woman. By the same figure they also signify the Goddess. Among them, Isis is a star called Sothis in Egyptian, but in Greek the Dog-star, etc. Furthermore, it is because at the rising of this star we observe signs concerning everything that is to be completed in the year. Therefore, not without reason, they call the Year "Isis."</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἐνιαυτὸν δὲ βουλόμενοι δηλῶσαι, Ἶσιν τουτέστι γυναῖκα ζωγραφοῦσι... Διόπερ οὐκ ἀλόγως τὸν ἐνιαυτὸν Ἶσιν λέγουσι.</note> Furthermore, wishing to signify the year, they paint Isis, that is, a woman, by which they also signify the Goddess; for among them there is the constellation of Isis, which is called Sothis by the Egyptian name, but by the Greeks the "Dog-star," because at the rising of this constellation we observe by certain signs those things which are to be carried out throughout the whole year; <margin>The star Sothis is the harbinger of the Nile's rising. Hyginus. Manilius.</margin> therefore, not without reason, they call the year Isis. We have said that Sothis, the Dog-star, was the harbinger of the rising of the Nile; because at its rising the Nile was said to overflow, as found in Hyginus and Manilius, which was discussed in the first volume concerning the rising of the Nile. In her right hand she carries a winged scepter with triangular sistrums <note>Ancient Egyptian percussion instruments</note>, by whose sound the movement of things (according to Plutarch) and the malice of opposing Typhonian powers <note>Forces of chaos associated with the god Typhon/Set</note> were believed to be driven away. But see the mystical meaning of the sistrums discussed throughout this work. Figure B, likewise dressed in female attire, displays in her right hand *Seriphium* or sea-wormwood, and in her left a staff or papyrus thyrsus <note>A staff topped with a pinecone or ornament, here made of papyrus</note>, by which the plenty of things necessary for the human race is indicated, as was proven in the Pamphilian Obelisk; on her head she supports Thermutis, that is, a <term>hawk-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφον (hierakomorphon)</note> serpent; let us explain what they intended by these symbols. *Seriphium* or sea-wormwood, according to Theophrastus, <margin>Seriphium or sea-wormwood. Theophrastus</margin> grows in greatest abundance in Egypt around the beginning of the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar</note>, and its greatest use was in performing sacred rites and ceremonies; it was a symbol of the antidote against decay; and therefore we read in Pliny and Dioscorides that it was dedicated to Isis and Mophta as guardians of the Nile, and was customarily carried by the Isiacs <note>Priests or followers of Isis</note>. It grew in Taphosiris, <margin>Pliny. Dioscorides.</margin> that is, the City which is called the "Tomb of Osiris," and Plutarch asserts that by its power Osiris, having been killed by Typhon, was recalled to immortality. See more concerning *Seriphium* in the hieroglyphic writing of plants. Thermutis is a type of sacred serpent, of which the veil of Isis, by which it is surrounded, is an indicator; it is painted <term>hawk-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφος (hierakomorphos)</note>, that is, distinguished by the head of a hawk; by this secret resemblance, allusion is made to the life, light, and motion with which the Ophionian <margin>The hieroglyphic significance of Thermutis</margin> *Agathodaemon* <note>A "Good Spirit" or protective deity, often depicted as a serpent</note>—who is always indicated by this kind of Thermutis—flows into this Isiac or Nephtaean power; for while these are imbued with moist substance through Nephtys, the seeds of Mophta are animated as if by a certain hidden force, and are disposed to produce that variety of things which the fertile rising of the Nile is accustomed to bring with it; hence, the head of a hawk was not poorly placed upon Thermutis. <margin>
The IV Triad of Omphtha; Omphtha is the presiding deity of the sign of Libra.

The fourth triad, marked F, G, and H, is attributed to Omphtha and corresponds to Autumn. As has been demonstrated in Astrology, Omphtha is the presiding deity of the sign of Libra <note>The Scales</note>, by which, after the rising of the Nile, the earth—pregnant with moisture—is gradually prepared for fertility through the beneficent power of Omphtha. This is because he decrees a fitting portion of the fertile moisture to each individual thing with exactitude. This Omphtha is indicated by the letter G; he holds a papyrus staff or thyrsus in his right hand and carries an "eyed phallus" <note>original: "phallum oculatum"</note> in his left. These indicate nothing other than that by the ministry of Omphtha, those things which Momphta wisely arranged by the benefit of moisture in the preceding three-month period are finally brought into execution by Omphtha (according to the testimony of Plutarch). That is to say, an abundance of all things necessary for human life results from the "eyed phallus," which represents the provident action of the spermatic <note>generative</note> power. He is assisted by his followers F and H. The first, F, carries in his right hand a <term>Cucuphemorphum</term> <note>A staff shaped like the head of a hoopoe bird, symbolizing gratitude or protection</note> staff, and in his left a <term>black-colored</term> <note>original Greek: "μελάγχρουν"</note> vessel—that is, a vessel of the black Egyptian earth (for thus they call the Egyptian soil hieroglyphically, according to Plutarch). In this vessel, the moisture received is prepared for a variety of things through the staff expressed by the head of the Hoopoe, providing a happy omen for agriculture, which is signified by the bovine tails with which figures G and F are marked. H, however, is an "averting" or protective deity <note>original: "Numen auerruncum seu apotropæum"</note>, distinguished by a lotus-bearing staff and a swelling breast, serving to preserve the aforementioned fertility (over which he stands guard) from all Typhonian <note>destructive or chaotic</note> adversity. Regarding the scepter of the Hoopoe, the eyed phallus, and the lotus, see the various passages provided in the appropriate places of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. And these are the twelve moderators divided into four triads, by whose ministry the course of the entire year is ruled and governed.

**T**he third and lower region of the Isiac Tablet, comprised within the letters I and K, contains twelve figures who are the twelve Fathers of the perennial fountains, also called the "Leaders of the World" <note>original: "Mundi Ductores"</note>. Each triad has been allotted its own part of the World to administer: the triad λ, μ, N presides over the East; the triad opposite to this on the tablet, ψ, F, H, presides over the West; ξ, ο, Σ over the North; and its opposite, τ, φ, χ, rules the South or Midday. ## The Fountain Triad of the Hour, or the Great Gate of the East.

<margin>
The Fountain Triad of the Hour is the Great Gate of the East.
</margin>

**T**he Triad marked by the letters $\lambda$, M, and N is called the Great Gate of the Eastern World. Here you see Horus, enclosed within a gate in the form of a boy, wrapped in a reticulated <note>net-like</note> garment. He is distinguished by a cross-bearing staff in the shape of a Cucupha <note>The "was-sceptre," topped with the head of a hoopoe or similar animal</note>, a gnomon <note>an L-shaped square used for measurement</note>, and a lituus <note>a curved staff or trumpet</note>. Hanging from his back is a triangle from which a globe emerges. A winged globe is set into the lintel of the gate, and the sides of the gate are adorned with alternating four-part circles and five-pointed stars. The base is marked with various hieroglyphics. Let us see what these things indicate.

<margin>
The Great Gate of the East.
</margin>

It is called the Great Gate of the East because through it is indicated the principle of all light, life, and motion (noted by the winged globe) diffused into the four parts of the world and the fivefold order of beings (signified by the four-part circles and the pentagram stars), as has been explained elsewhere. The image M represents Horus under the form of a boy—that is, the Sun—who, having entered through the East as if through his own proper gate, refreshes all parts of the world with rays of life and light. He is depicted as a boy with a visible headband because the Sun, restored daily to the world through the door of life, as it were grows young again, and makes the world grow young along with him. He is wrapped in a net-like garment because the principle of the influence and virtues which he bestows upon the world are hidden, complex, and inaccessible to human ingenuity. The staff he carries is first marked with a Cross; since this is a symbol of the four elements, it aptly indicates that the Sun first communicates his virtues to the four elements, which, impregnated by the flow of hidden powers, bring forth that great variety of things. These are beautifully indicated by the head of the Hoopoe; with the highest order, symmetry, and <term>analogy</term> <note>original Greek: ἀναλογία; meaning proportion or correspondence</note> indicated by the gnomon; and finally with a wondrous harmony indicated by the lituus. The triangle hanging from his back signifies the World, which, according to the testimony of Plato, flowed forth from an archetypal triangle. See the explanation of this figure provided in various places both in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* and in this *Oedipus*. The hieroglyphics engraved on the base upon which he stands yield this sense: *The parent of vegetable nature, the guardian of moisture,* <note>original: ἀναλογία</note> *the sacred tutor of the Osirian Nile, the ruler of the worlds and their master, the multiform spirit* <note>original: δαίμων (daemon)</note> *providing an abundance of necessary things.* And this is the meaning of figure M. I come now to the attendants $\lambda$ and N. Of these, N is dressed in female attire, with a veiled head upon which a Hawk sits; she offers five vessels to Horus. Through her, the Mind of the Triad of the Hour is expressed; for she distributes the light and heat (expressed by the Hawk sitting on her head) participated from Horus into the five vessels of the lower world. These are the nurseries of water, air, and—within the terrestrial globe—of inanimate things, vegetable nature, and sensitive beings, according to the plan prescribed for her by Osiris. She is depicted in female dress because she is, as it were, a certain Idea of the Osirian or Horian intellect, inclined toward bringing forth and showing herself ready to fulfill the will of Horus. *For, as Plutarch rightly says, Isis is nothing other than that power of female nature, the recipient of all generation*, on account of which she is called <term>tithene</term> <note>original Greek: τιθήνη</note>, that is, the nurse...

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>Plato.</margin>The mother, or <term>receptacle</term> <note>original: ἐκμαγεῖον (ekmageion) — a term used by Plato in the *Timaeus* to describe the "matrix" or "waxen mold" of the universe</note>, was so named by Plato; for she admits all ideas and images, and possesses a congenital love toward that which is first and highest among all things, which is surely the Good itself. Toward this she is drawn, this she desires, and this she follows; but that which is evil, she flees and opposes. See the rest of this matter as cited in various places in Plutarch.

<margin>The power of the Horæan triad.</margin>The image indeed shows the **Power of the Horæan triad**, equipped with a lotus-bearing staff, upon whose flower an Asp <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A small circular sign with a tail, resembling an eye or a planetary mark</note> sits with a swollen breast and a star upon its head. In her left hand she likewise holds a Nilotic vessel; she is in female dress, with a swollen breast, and wearing a headdress fashioned in the form of a basket upon her head. By the Asp, or <term>Thermutis</term> <note>The sacred cobra associated with protection and the goddess Renenutet</note>, as has already been said often, the motion and life of things—which the Sun, rising daily, bestows upon the World—is indicated. For the Ophionian Asp <note>The "Serpent-like" Asp</note>, as Arius rightly says in the works of Eusebius: <margin>The Ophionian Asp. Eusebius.</margin> **"An inflammation: whoever looked up, he would fill everything with light in his first-born region; but if he should close his eyes, darkness occurred."** <note>original Greek: Ἐπίκανσις· ὃς ἂν ἀναβλέψῃ, φωτὸς πᾶν ἐπλήσει, ἐν τῇ πρωτογόνῳ χώρᾳ αὐτῶ· ἂν δὲ καμμύσειε σκότος ἐγίνετο.</note> It is a gracious animal; if it raised its eyelids, it filled its entire first-born region; but when it kept them closed, shadows were poured out. **"This one, whenever he opens an aperture of life, also rules over death; because of this, they place him upon the heads of the Gods."** <note>original Greek: Οὗτος ὁπὴν ἀνοίξῃ ζωῆς, καὶ θανάτου κυριεύει· διὰ τοῦτο αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τῆς κεφαλῆς τῶν Θεῶν ἐπιτιθέασι.</note> Wherefore, since he is seen to have power over life and death, he was quite deservedly placed upon the heads of the Gods. By the lotus-bearing scepter, it is indicated that he acts according to the reason prescribed for him by the archetypal Sun. This figure also wears a headdress on the head, fashioned in the form of a basket, by which protection and dominion over the economy of vegetable nature is signified, to which she grants fecundity and abundance, as the female habit and swollen breast demonstrate. Thus **Horus**, or the World, is attended by two followers, one of whom has the care of life and motion, and the other the care of light and heat, committed to them by Horus. Hence the Astrologers, not without reason, called this great Eastern Gate of the World the <margin>The Gate of the World or the Horoscope of the Astrologers.</margin> "Gate of Life, Heat, Light, and Motion," and with greatest zeal they observed the rising of the signs and stars while they scrutinized the natal themes of those being born, as the unique <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: Small loop or decorative mark</note> foundation of their work, which they also called the **Horoscope**, as we have said in our *Astrology*; consult that work for a more profuse treatment of these matters.

### The Fontana Triad, or the Great Gate of the West.

<margin>The Fontana Triad of the Cat-shaped one.</margin>
<margin>The Great Gate of the West.</margin>
<margin>The Father of the Great Gate of the West.</margin>
Furthermore, opposite to this Horæan triad, the triad of the Great Gate of the West opens itself, which is marked by the letters <note>Symbol: resembles the astrological sign for Jupiter ♃ or a stylized Coptic letter</note>, F, H. The **Fontana** parent is included in the gate F, whose lintel is marked with a winged globe, a symbol of the influence of the supreme mind; and the sides with four-part circles, which are the ideas of the quaternary number of which the World consists. In the middle of the gate, the image F is seen, terrifying in female dress and with a feline face <note>Likely referring to a Bastet or Sekhmet-style figure</note>; in her right hand a lotus-bearing staff is fashioned, and in her left the **Ankh Cross** <term>Crux ansata</term> <note>The "handled cross," the Egyptian symbol of life</note>. On her head she wears a circle marked with the image of a **Scarab** and a Serpent emerging from a globe. But let us now reveal what these individual things mean. The Gate denotes the West, through which the Sun, leaving the upper Hemisphere, seeks the lower; that is, the Sun departing below—

# TREATISE I. THE ISIAIC TABLE. 121 CHAP. V.

...seeks the subterranean Horizon; all of which are aptly indicated by Figure F; in which a feline head, marked with the image of a **Scarab**, signifies the setting Sun. For the cat, or *aelurus* <note>original: "aelurus," from the Greek word for cat</note>, is a lunar and nocturnal animal, according to the witness of Horus <note>referring to Horapollo, an author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>, and exercises its operations chiefly at night. That this may be understood, it seemed necessary to trace the matter a little deeper. We know that after the setting of the Sun, the Moon <margin>The Moon is the Sun's deputy.</margin> acts as his deputy, as if in his absence. For, as has already been explained in various places in this Work, the Moon, according to the Egyptians, is nothing other than a kind of mirror of the Sun, into which he reflects his rays upon the earth; so that what he could not cherish with a direct ray, he might at least sustain by the reflected or deputy ray of the Moon. And this deputy power of the Sun through the Moon they aptly expressed through the natural properties of the cat. For this animal, following the daily <margin>The cat is a hieroglyph of the Moon.</margin> solar course, not only expands and contracts its pupils, but changes the pupils of its eyes according to the increases and decreases of the lunar phases, being equally intent on the hunting of mice by night and day. Most truly, however, it seems to undergo these changes at the setting of the Sun: so that even from this, not without cause, they expressed that Divinity which presides over the West with a feline head. But let us hear Horus in Book 1, Chapter 10, confirming these sayings with these words: <margin>Horus.</margin> *The male cat,* he says, *changes its pupils according to the varying habit and course of the Sun; at the rising of the Sun in the morning they are somewhat extended, toward Noon they become as if round, and as the Sun verges toward Setting they appear more blunt and dim.* As if the Sun <margin>The image of a cat at Heliopolis.</margin> had now committed the care of his power to the Moon; hence also the statue of the Sun God which is at Heliopolis, as is held in Pausanias <note>Greek traveler and geographer</note>, expresses the appearance of a cat. <margin>Pausanias.</margin> This appearance and likeness is expressed by Figure F, upon whose feline crown stands a circle marked with the image of a Scarab, by which the Sun is shown, as we have taught with most ample authorities in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* in the chapter on the Scarab. This indeed, joined with the feline head, indicates that deputy power of the Sun in the Moon which we mentioned, which it exercises in the earthly World after the setting of the Sun. This is evident from the fact that the Moon is like a kind of nocturnal Sun, <margin>The Moon is the nocturnal Sun.</margin> which imbues the earth with reflected virtue lest it be destitute of the total influence of Solar light; it refreshes the earthly mass, dried out by the heat of the Sun, with tempered moisture, whence the life of things—indicated by the serpent emerging from the globe—comes forth to all things. It holds a lotus-bearing scepter in the right hand, because <margin>The attire of the lunar statue.</margin> the Moon affects the Sun in all things. Since, however, adverse powers dominate most in the darkness of night, for this reason it carries in the left hand a <term>Crux ansata</term> <note>The Ankh; literally a "cross with a handle," viewed by Kircher as a powerful protective amulet</note>; a most potent amulet and safeguard against them. It is painted in feminine attire, and with a swelling breast, because the force of the Sun flowing from the Lunar body into the earth is fruitful, and with life-giving plenty it nourishes, cherishes, and restores all things; hence it is called both the "fountain father" or "fountain mother," because the Sun at its setting opens a most fertile fountain, by which all things, being irrigated, are preserved in their vigor. But let us hear Plutarch <margin>Plutarch.</margin> beautifully confirming all these things: *The rays of the Sun,* he says, *cast upon the Moon as if into a certain mirror, are reverberated to us with increased forces, whose power and efficacy taught men to commit seeds to the earth at a certain and opportune time, to cut wood fit for building, and to toil in the works of agriculture.* Whence Columella in Book 1 teaches that the arts of life and those necessary for human use arose.
<margin>Columella.</margin>

represents the **Mind** of the cat-shaped Divinity; it carries a flower-bearing staff in the left hand and an "eyed" phallus in the right. On its head, it wears a headdress remarkable for its two-pronged flame, two Aspics, a star, and feathers. Through the phallus, fertility is indicated; through the scepter, dominion over vegetable life; and through the headdress—<note>original Greek: φλεγ-οφι-ας σελαηνι σελμασσην, likely a magical formula or corruption referring to "burning serpent-light"</note>—heat, life, and motion are aptly signified, which are caused by the light of the Sun reflected onto the Moon and other stars after the Sun has set.

<margin>
The Power of the cat-shaped Divinity.
</margin>
The attendant H represents **Intellectual Power**. It holds a papyrus thyrsus <note>a staff topped with a pinecone or ornament, here made of papyrus</note> in the left hand, a sign of the abundance of necessary things; with the right hand, it awaits the commands of the mother or father—the androgynous Divinity—to carry into execution the matters committed to its faith and prescribed by the Mind. It wears an Aspic or <term>Thermutis</term> <note>the sacred cobra associated with protection and royalty</note> marked with a star on its head, by which the life and motion of things are signified, as was explained above. But let us see what the figures of this triad marked with the letters $d, e, \Omega$ denote. The letter $d$ expresses the figure of a **Sitting Dog** with a sistrum <note>a ritual rattle used in Egyptian worship</note>, which in this place denotes nothing other than the guardian of the Horizon when it is destitute of Solar light, or the guardian of the great western gate.

Anubis of ethereal form <note>original symbol: likely a solar or planetary sign</note>.

These things denote nothing other than the vigilance of Anubis on the border of both Horizons, by whose effective operation the economy of the lower World is preserved. Thus <term>Typhon</term> <note>the Egyptian god Set, representing chaos and darkness</note>, attempting all manner of evil in the absence of the Sun—that is, the Crocodilian force of Typhon—is struck and extinguished as if by the

See how aptly that figure $\Omega$ expresses the type of the **Cynocephalus** <note>dog-headed</note> Anubis placed upon an altar or column, watching as it were at the great gate of the setting Sun? From this, therefore, that Hecatine <term>Cerberus</term> <note>the three-headed dog of Hades</note> among the Greeks and Chaldeans found its origin.

<margin>
The Genii of the western region.
</margin>
It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that the display of this triad expresses nothing other than the protection of the **Genii of the western region**. By their protection, the Typhonian and <term>Ahrimanic force</term> <note>referring to Ahriman, the spirit of evil in Zoroastrianism</note> is routed, so that the Sun, although absent, may nevertheless perform the accustomed operations of nature in the Moon and stars. This is done strenuously for the sake of such good by the attendants H and <note>original symbol: ψ</note> who flank it on both sides (of whom one presides over fertility, the other over life, light, and heat, as is clear from the symbols explained a little earlier), while Anubis keeps watch against the adverse schemes of the Powers...

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>
The number nine signifies the North among the Egyptians.

Pandoches, the Genius of the Northern region, and his nine seals.

Psellus.

The attendants of Pandoches.

The antipathy of the Quail toward the Sun and Moon.
</margin>

...was [honored] by the Egyptians, because this number is closest to the number ten, by which the completion of all good things is denoted. For when the Sun traverses this region <note>The Northern sky</note>, the days increase and the nights decrease, from which comes a most bountiful harvest and an abundance of fruits; the rising of the Nile begins, and with it follows a wealth of all good things. They imagine, therefore, that **Pandoches** <note>Greek: "All-receiving," a genius or spirit of the North</note>, the Genius of this region, possesses **nine seals**, by which the gates are opened to the abundance of all goods. These nine seals are noted through symbols with which the figure of Pandoches is marked <note>Symbol: A circle with a cross inside, similar to a theta or earth symbol</note>. 

The **first seal** is the seat, a sign of the change of days and nights; the **second** is a bundle of vegetable nature inserted into the seat; the **third** is the fullness of influences, which are noted by forked crosses; the **fourth** is the **Ankh** <term>Crux ansata: the "handled cross," an Egyptian symbol of life</term>, or the Tautic character, which is a most effective amulet against Typhonian <note>Referring to Typhon/Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and storms</note> powers; the **fifth** is the lotus-bearing scepter, a symbol of working according to the pattern of the archetypal Sun; the **sixth** denotes the Mundane Bowl, over which he presides; the **seventh**, through the Asps, hints at the inner chambers of the vital nurseries; the **eighth**, through the forked cross, the shrines of the Solar **Agathodæmon** <term>Agathodæmon: a "good spirit" or protective deity, often depicted as a serpent</term>; the **ninth**, through the feathers, marks the enclosures of the intellectual virtues. 

All of these things the aforementioned **Psellus** <note>Michael Psellus, a Byzantine scholar</note> confirms with these words: *The all-receiving power rules over the North with nine sacred seals* <note>original Greek: Ἡ δύναμις πανδεχὴς τῷ ἄρκτῳ κυριεύει, ἐννέα σήμαντροις σεβάσ...</note>. These indeed harmonize beautifully with the symbols engraved on the footstool upon which the throne rests; where you see this sign <note>Hieroglyphic inscription: Four vertical bars followed by a circle containing a cross (IIII ⊕), representing the number nine</note>, by which, as we have shown in our Arithmetic, the Egyptians expressed the number nine; it is composed of five units and a four-part circle, for five joined to four make nine. This symbol, expressed nine times on the lower edge of the said seat, silently alludes to the nine seals.

->**But let us proceed to the attendants of Pandoches, of whom $\zeta$, who is on the right**<-

is a protective deity, whose indicator is the **Ankh**. Looking up at the actions from the Ideal World indicated by the *circular-shaped* symbol <note>original Greek: περιϰυϰλόμορϕον</note> which hangs over his head, he undertakes to defend the variety of things (signified by the **Cucupha scepter** <note>A scepter topped with the head of a hoopoe or "Cucupha" bird, symbolizing power</note>) which Pandoches produces against Typhonian storms. 

The attendant $\epsilon$ standing to the left of Pandoches carries a **Quail** in his right hand, with a headdress fashioned in the shape of a basket, upon which a gourd with a tendril rests. By the **Ortygometra** or Quail <note>original: Coturnix</note>, the unlucky machinations of Typhon are signified; for this animal has a certain antipathy toward the Sun and Moon, as **Horus** <note>Horapollo, author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note> shows in Book 2, Chapter 49, and **Hecataeus** notes with these words: *What is more unworthy than the "kikkake" cry of the quail? By this voice it seems to despise the greatness of the Gods* <note>original Greek: Τὸ ἀναξιώτερον τὸ ϰιϰϰαϰὴ ὁ τρυγομήϰας ϰραυγᾷ ἢ ϰαταϕρονῆσα ἐστὶ ταύτης τῇ ϕώνῃ τῶν Θεῶν μεγαλοτητὸ...</note>. What is more shameful than the "kikkake" voice of the quail, by which it seems to some extent to scorn and mock the greatness of the Gods? Hence, not without reason, they adopted it as a symbol of Typhonian pride. 

Therefore, the image $\epsilon$ offers the Quail to the deity Pandoches, the father of the Northern triad; by which is secretly noted that greatest care and solicitude which he employs in driving away, with continuous assistance, those adverse Typhonian powers dwelling in the Northern region. They work together according to the rule of the triform deity's Ideal influence, indicated by figure $\alpha$ (the *circular-shaped* form): $\Sigma$ representing **Power**, $\Xi$ representing **Mind**, and <note>Symbol: Theta-like circle</note> representing the **Father or Mother** of the triad; which also aptly...

# TREATISE I. THE ISIAC TABLET. CHAPTER V.

And it is aptly indicated by a <note>original: "baculum ἀμφικύρτον"</note> curved staff, that is, one which terminates on both sides in a scepter, stretched out toward both the <note>Symbol: circle, representing the Sun</note> and the <note>Symbol: the letter Phi with a bar, a specific Egyptian character in Kircher's system</note>, serving as a symbol of a dominion shared by both sides.

### The Thaustic Triad, Mistress of the South.

<margin>The Thaustic Triad, Mistress of the South.</margin>

Let us proceed to the final triad of this region, which is marked by the letters T, <note>Symbol: Phi with a bar</note>, and <note>Symbol: Chi</note>. It denotes the protection and station of the Southern Genii or Intelligences, placed in opposition to the Triad of the North. The Father of this triad is marked by the image of the <note>Sun symbol</note>, the Mind by T, and the Power by <note>Symbol: Chi</note>.

<margin>The Father of this triad.</margin>

The Father of this Triad—just as the figure <note>Sun symbol</note> in the Northern triad sits upon a uniform checkered seat—appears here in a <term>hawk-headed form</term> <note>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφος (hierakomorphos)</note>, distinguished by a miter or headdress. In his left hand he holds a papyrus staff, while with his right he seems to be commanding his "Mind" <note>referring to the second member of the triad</note>. He sits because he possesses absolute dominion over the Southern region, and also because in this region, at the Tropic of Capricorn <note>literally "the tropic of the South"</note>, he holds the fixed and stable boundaries of his rule. He is depicted as <term>hawk-headed</term> so that they might silently suggest that this Solar Deity moderates all things. For the hawk-like figure is a transformed image—as was proven at length in the *Hieroglyphic Interpretation of the Pamphilian Obelisk*—representing nothing other than the Solar Intelligence, abounding in spirit, light, and life. Hence, according to the testimony of Horus <note>referring to Horapollo, an author on hieroglyphs</note>, the Egyptians called him <term>Baieth</term> and <term>Thaustus</term>. By the compound word <term>Baieth</term>—of which <term>Bai</term> signifies "soul" and <term>eth</term> signifies "heart"—they silently hinted that just as the soul, the source of life, has its seat chiefly in the heart, so the Soul of the World, or this <term>Thaustus</term> present in the Sun, resides in the heart of the <term>macrocosm</term> <note>original: megacosmi; the "great world" or universe</note>. These are the words of Horus, Book 1, Chapter 7:

<margin>The hawk-like image is the Solar Intelligence.</margin>

<margin>Horus. Baieth and Thaustus.</margin>

<margin>The Hawk signifies the Sun among the Egyptians.</margin>

> Among the Egyptians, the hawk is called *Baieth*, and this name, when divided, signifies soul and heart. For *Bai* is the soul, and *eth* is the heart. And the heart, according to the Egyptians, is the enclosure of the soul. Thus the synthesis of the name signifies "Soul-Heart."

Indeed, the hawk is called <term>Baieth</term> by the Egyptians because the name, when split, means soul and heart; for <term>Bai</term> is soul and <term>eth</term> is heart, and in the opinion of the Egyptians, the heart is the vessel of the soul. And in Book 1, Chapter 6, he writes that when they wish to signify God, they paint a hawk, both because this animal is prolific and long-lived, and also because it seems to be an image of the Sun more than any other bird, since by a certain peculiar and occult natural power, it looks directly into its rays with intent eyes. From this it also happens that they sometimes paint the Sun in the form of a hawk, as the guardian and master of sight. For other testimonies cited from every kind of learning, see the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 308 and following. He holds a papyrus staff in his left hand to signify the abundance of all necessary things which he provides. The miter resting on his head, marked by a multitude of small circles, shows his dominion over all worlds; and by the gourd-shape fashioned into a basket placed upon it, he indicates his action upon moisture, as has been demonstrated elsewhere at length. The number seven was anciently dedicated to him, according to the testimony of Manetho, because, as we taught in *Hieroglyphic Arithmetic*, the heptad was consecrated to the Sun; for the Sun is thought to moderate the entire Universe, of which it is the symbol—

<margin>The number seven is consecrated to the Sun.</margin>

Moreover, the subterranean Hecate or Isis is the same in this context as what the Greeks call Persephone or Proserpina, the mistress of flowers, fruits, and all vegetable nature; these are indeed aptly signified by the bowl, and the flowers and ears of grain (1, 2) which she carries on her head, surrounding the head of Hecate. This is not without mystery; for by this is noted the abundance of the southern Nilotic bowl, which, enriched by heavenly influence, allows none of the twelve months of the year to be unfruitful, but rather produces something for the benefit of men in each month through the subterranean Isis, made pregnant by the power of Thaustus. <margin>Isis of the Nile.</margin>
Figure χ <note>The Greek letter Chi, referring to a specific figure on the Table</note> represents Isis of the Nile in female attire; she is seen wrapped in hawk-like

<margin>The Numidian bird as a symbol of southern influences.</margin>
Her head is covered by a Numidian bird or Guinea fowl <note>original: "Meleagride"</note>, because it is a hieroglyphic of astral influences, or of the starry sky, due to the innumerable spots it bears on its body, as has been proven elsewhere. Upon the back of the bird is placed a mixing bowl <note>original: "craterem"</note> which supports two bull's horns with the star Sothis between them. <margin>Sothis is attributed to Isis.</margin>
the Dog-star <note>Sirius</note>, which we read is so attributed to the Nilotic Isis that, according to Horus <note>Horapollo</note>, those wishing to signify Isis would paint <term>Aspherithia</term> <note>original: "Ἀσφερίθια"</note>. Indeed, she
<margin>Horus.</margin>
herself says in the writings of Diodorus: *I am she who shines in the Dog-star* <note>original: "Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἐν τῷ τῷ κυνὸς ἄστρῳ λάμπεσα"</note>. It is placed between the bull-horns of Apis to signify the conjunction of the Sun with the "Star-dog"—that is, with Isis—by which the rising of the Nile, the completion of all happiness, occurs. This is also aptly explained through figure Y, which contains a Scarab with outspread wings holding Sothis (the Dog-star), and through the Ibis C with a Nilotic vessel from which emerges Sea-Wormwood <note>original: "Seriphium seu Absinthium marinum"</note>, likewise an indicator of the Nile's increase. For,
<margin>Theophrastus.</margin>
according to Theophrastus, when this plant blooms, the Nile is accustomed to overflow, acting out of some unknown sympathy with the Dog-star; and therefore, as read in Eusebius, they attribute Sirius to Isis
<margin>Eusebius.</margin>
because she brings the waters. Moreover, the Ibis is the mark of the Nilotic <term>Agathodæmon</term> <note>A "Good Spirit" or protective deity, often depicted as a serpent or bird</note>; from its natural disposition, they promise themselves something great regarding the vital influence, indicated by the attached globe teeming with a Serpent. But concerning Sothis, the Scarab, and the Ibis, see the extensive treatments scattered throughout this Work and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*; for these are certain Ideal patterns of the actions of the supreme Divinity flowing into this Southern triad of Genii. We must now explain why they expressed this triad with these symbols. It should be noted that the Southern region was always held
<margin>The Southern region held in veneration by the Egyptians.</margin>
in the highest veneration by the Egyptians; they called it sometimes the "urn of light," sometimes the "mixing bowl of the World" and its "outflow," as Plutarch testifies. Furthermore,
<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
Egypt is situated in the Southern parts, through the middle of which the Nile—which they call the gift of God and the outflow of Osiris—flows straight from the South to the North. They call the North the right side of the World, and the South the
<margin>Egyptians call the North the right, the South the left of the World.</margin>
left side, because just as the heart is on the left in a man, so the Nile, the source of life, is located on the left part of the World. They also represented it with a fig leaf, whose fruit expresses the likeness of the heart and its leaf the likeness of the phallus, by which they hinted at the fertility of vital flows expressed in the Nile. But
<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
let us hear the words of Plutarch: "For the Egyptians think, according to Xenophon, that the face of the World is the part from which the Sun rises; the North is the right, and the South—where the Nile is—is the left. Whence the Egyptians say not inappropriately of the Nile that it rises from the left and perishes on the right." For the Nile, flowing from the South (the left part of the World), is absorbed into the Northern
<margin>Osiris of a black color.</margin>
tract, mixing itself with the sea. They also say that Osiris, whom they also called the Nile, was of a black color, because it is the nature of water to turn the earth, clothes, clouds, and other things [black]...

# CHAPTER V.

<margin>Egypt is called "black-earth."</margin>
...and other things with which it may be mixed, it turns black; either because of the dark color with which the element of moisture seems imbued; and for this same reason, the Bull Mnevis was also imbued with a black color. But they also called Egypt itself <term>melangaion</term> <note>original: μελάγγαιον; literally "black-earth"</note>, that is, a black vessel, or <term>chemeia</term> <note>original: χημείαν; the root of "chemistry," referring here to the black soil of the Nile</note>, on account of the richness of the soil; although others signify the "heart" by this term as well. For Egypt is hot and humid, and situated in the Southern parts of the world—which we have said above is the left side of the world—just as the hot and humid heart occupies the left side in a human being. Hence, calling Osiris or Dionysus the "Lord of the Worlds," they were accustomed to use <term>nebrides</term> <note>fawn-skins worn by followers of Bacchus/Dionysus</note> by casting them over themselves, and seizing <term>thyrsi</term> <note>staffs topped with pine cones</note> during the Orgyasms <note>ecstatic rituals</note> as if inspired by the God. Moreover, Eudoxus testifies that the Egyptians do not consider the Nile alone,
<margin>The Egyptians called all moisture the "outflow of Osiris."</margin>
but everything that is liquid, to be the "outflow of Osiris." They wish to signify this by a vessel full of water, placed before the doors on a sacred day; and the humid principle by the <term>Thrio</term> <note>original: Θρῖον</note> or fig leaf, which also has the signature or likeness of the genital member, signifying the offering or the discovery of moisture. By this they also denoted the King and the Southern region; from which the <term>phallophoria</term> <note>processions carrying symbols of fertility</note> also took their origin. These things are from Plutarch; in which whatever we have explained concerning the Southern mysteries of this triad are aptly perceived. You see here the figure T <note>referring to a specific location on the Bembine Tablet</note> clothed in a fawn-skin, the sign of Dionysus, the overseer of moisture; you see the thyrsus in the hand of the <term>hawk-formed</term> <note>original: ἱερακομόρφου</note> Thaustus; you see the Divinities covered in black veils, alluding to the words of Plutarch; for as Anticlides rightly sings in his hymn to the Sun:

-> *The Sun is the Lord of the South, the multiform Hawk.* <-
-> *Sol Austri dominator, Accipiter multiformis.* <-

<margin>Why Thaustus is Hawk-shaped.</margin>
For because the power of light and life is the ruler in the South, and from there the outflow of Osiris brings the fulfillment of all good things; quite deservedly is Thaustus seen transformed into the form of a Hawk. For the Hawk delights in places subject to the South, and toward midday, when the Sun is at its highest, it is accustomed, 
<margin>Aelian.</margin>
according to the testimony of Aelian, to seek the tracks of the air with its eyes. Hence, on the front side of his seat, Thaustus holds an engraved, oblong <term>cyathus</term> <note>a cup or ladle</note>, which extends below into the shape of a heart and the appearance of a phallus; which kind of figure we have learned from Plutarch is the <term>Thrio</term> or fig leaf. For the moisture of the Nilotic cup, stored in the heart of Egypt, promises that abundance of all things which the flowers and buds surrounding the cup rightly signify.

And these are the things which I thought should be said concerning the three principal regions of the Bembine Tablet; in which we have intentionally and deliberately omitted the interpretation of the smaller hieroglyphs for reasons to be revealed shortly hereafter. Furthermore, nothing remains except that we explain the figures of the circuit or border with equal boldness.

# DIVISION VII.

->Interpretation of the Border or Circumference of the Isiac Table.<-

<margin>Interpretation of the borders of the Isiac Table.</margin>
<margin>The outer border ABCD.</margin>
The outer border, enclosed by the letters **A B C D**, contains all the systems of the three Generative regions already explained; in it, hieroglyphics are displayed in various figures of living creatures—humans, quadrupeds, birds, insects, plants, and springs—partly whole, and partly transformed by a certain wonderful metamorphosis, as will be seen shortly. This indicates nothing other than the Ideal or Archetypal World, filled with all kinds of forms of Ideas, which the Egyptians call <term>Iynges</term> <note>Kircher uses this term from the Chaldean Oracles to describe divine messengers or "wheels" that transmit the divine will into the material world</note>; before we proceed to the explanation itself, it seemed appropriate to provide a slightly deeper introduction to these.

<margin>What Ideas are according to the Ancients.</margin>
It must first be noted that, according to the mind of the Ancients, Ideas are nothing other than certain patterns of things to be made, held within the Supreme Mind; or we may define it otherwise: an Idea is an eternal pattern of things producible by nature, placed in the Divine Mind, through which all things proceeding from the first Creator are presented to Him and produced outwardly. Since much has been said about these in the *Hieroglyphic Theology*, and in the Sixth Class concerning the *System of Worlds*, and especially concerning the *Ideal World*, I have judged it unnecessary to repeat those things here; therefore, in this place, I have seen fit to bring forward only as much as suffices for our purpose, including some things omitted in the aforementioned places for a greater understanding of the matters to be explained.
<margin>The Egyptians were the first assertors of Ideas.</margin>
The Egyptians, therefore, were the first of mortals to assert the existence of Ideas; they were followed by Orpheus, Pythagoras, and finally Plato, who gave the Academic assembly the greatest material for debate. For, first contemplating the order and disposition of the Universe, they believed it impossible that such a miraculous machine of the World could have proceeded from anything other than a certain supreme and infinite Mind. They gathered, therefore, that the Creator of the World <note>original: "Opificem," referring to the Demiurge or Divine Architect</note>, imitating an eternal pattern that existed in the Creative Mind, had founded the World.
<margin>Ideas of all things in the mind of God according to the mind of the Ancients.</margin>
Furthermore, when they saw the sensible world containing all things, they felt it was necessarily created in the likeness of a single thing; moreover, that "one" to which all things are referred, and which contains all things in itself, they called the Ideal World, shining forth in the First Mind. But since Ideas in the Divine Mind can by no means be considered as accidents in a subject, or as forms within another form—which is said to be truly intelligible—they are therefore found in the Mind, whose proper function is to understand.
<margin>Unparticipated Ideas in the Divine Mind, participated in other Minds.</margin>
And as they are in the Supreme Mind, they are called "unparticipated"; in other minds, they are called "participated." For they are participated in by the soul, without which such minds are not found. Furthermore, in the First Mind they depend solely on God, but in subsequent minds they depend on the First Mind and on the Ideas existing within it. Finally, in the First Mind, the Ideas are less distinct from one another; in others, they are distinguished more and more as they recede further from the First Mind. They thought, moreover, that Ideas were diffused from the First Mind into others, just as rays are diffused from the Sun into other stars; and just as the power of illuminating and heating is poured out from the Sun through its rays...

He traces this metaphysical concept from Egyptian origins through Orpheus and Pythagoras to Plato, describing how divine ideas emanate from the Creator into the material realm.</summary>

# THE THEATER OF EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPHICS

...and other things of a generative nature, which are said to be created by the Sun through light; in the same way, they believed that from the unparticipated Mind, a power and faculty is diffused through the Ideas into the Ideas of other minds to produce similar things. And since all Ideas exist within individual minds, the Intelligible World <note>The "Mundus Intelligibilis" is the realm of pure thought and forms, as opposed to the physical world.</note> will also be found in each one, so that as many intelligible worlds arise from the Ideas as there are minds in existence.

<margin>An Idea is not found outside the boundaries of the Mind.</margin> It should also be known in this place that an "Idea," properly understood, no longer has a place outside the boundaries of the Mind; rather, as we descend from the Mind to the soul, Ideas are changed into "reasons" <note>original: "rationes," referring to the formative principles or logic of the soul</note>. Nevertheless, the soul, having been made a participant of the mind, rises up to the Ideas and is connected to them. They believed that nature was placed beneath the soul, and because nature depends on the soul, traces of these reasons are found in nature, which are called "seeds." Through these seeds, corporeal things are immediately produced, enclosing matter; finally, in that matter, those things which are generated from the seeds and correspond proportionately to the Ideas are called imitations, participations, the closest boundaries of matter, and finally, the shadows of Ideas. Concerning these, see Plato in the *Timaeus* and *Parmenides*, and the other followers of Platonic doctrine: Plotinus, Arnobius, Numenius, Proclus, and in *Platonic Theology*, Marsilio Ficino, and countless others who pursue this doctrine at length.

<margin>Plato: Plotinus: Arnobius: Proclus: Numenius.</margin>

<margin>The Egyptians called Ideas "Iynges" and "Sphinges."</margin> That all these things emanated from the Egyptians will be clear from what follows. They called these "Iynges" <note>Iynges (singular: Iynx) in Neoplatonism are intermediary spirits or "wheels" that transmit divine influence.</note>, which they sometimes called the "reasons" of the supreme Mind, sometimes the "copies" <note>original: "ectypa"</note> of the Paternal source, and sometimes the "seals" of the worldly classes and chains. Others also call them "Sphinges" <note>Sphinges is the plural of Sphinx.</note>: thus **Clement of Alexandria** in Book 6 of the *Stromata* says: *They place Sphinges in sacred places to indicate that discourse concerning God, nature, and similar things is obscure and enigmatic.*

<margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin>

<margin>Sphinges on the thresholds of shrines and inner sanctums. Herodotus. Aristotle.</margin> For they used to engrave these multi-formed images on the thresholds or cornices of shrines, and on the pillars of the inner sanctums, as **Herodotus** testifies; and as **Aristotle** testifies (as will be cited shortly after), they placed them before the eyes of the Sages as "ideal concepts." Thus, those laboring in the sacred inner sanctums and the <term>theoleptoi</term> <note>Greek: θεόληπτοι, meaning "those possessed by God" or divinely inspired.</note> might contemplate the supreme beings of the world, no longer by means of human discourse, but in the manner of minds abstracted from all matter.

<margin>A description of the "Iynges" from Proclus.</margin> But let us return to the **Iynges**. **Zoroaster** describes them in these words in **Proclus's** *On Theology* and in his third commentary on the *Parmenides*: *The Paternal Mind, perceiving with supreme counsel, produces the all-formed Ideas; these, however, flying out from a single fountain, have leapt forth. For from the Father was the counsel and the end, but they are divided, partitioned by intellectual fire into other intellectual things. For the King placed an incorruptible intellectual type over the multiform World, into whose ornament he introduced a trace of form, through which the World appeared, gracious in every way with Ideas. Of these there is one fountain, from which others proceed, flowing without breadth through the bodies of the World, which are carried like swarms around the vast depths, changed here and there, plucking much of the flower of fire from the Paternal fountain in the forms of time; the summit of the first-born Idea flowed first from the Father, the self-flowering fountain of this.*

<margin>Proclus.</margin> Which **Proclus** explains in this sense: *Through these things the ancient Initiates declared where the substance <note>original: "hypostasis"</note> of the Ideas is, and who is the God who contains that one fountain of them, and how the multitude proceeded from this fountain, and how the World was made according to them, and that they are the movers of all worldly systems, and that they are all intellectual by essence, and that through...*

<margin>The paternal Mind produced the Ideas.</margin> But let us explain the individual points. The Paternal Mind, therefore, produced the Ideas; for as Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> rightly says, while God begets himself by observing himself, he simultaneously generates all things in himself, understanding by his supreme counsel the all-forming ideas. For in that offspring of God, as <margin>Plato:</margin> Plato speaks (which he also calls the universal seed of the World), there are present all the specific seeds of the members; which, by his will—as a good that is diffusive of itself—he produces outwardly when he wishes, communicating them to the other Beings in order. Hence Zoroaster rightly says that these leap out, flying from a single source; for just as the Sun, by shining in itself, illuminates all things, so the supreme Mind of Minds, by understanding and willing itself, both knows and effects all things. Indeed, just as these are essentially united in God, so when produced outwardly, they are divided (as Zoroaster says) and poured into other intellectual orders of Minds by an intellectual fire. Thus, what was one and a "multiplicity in unity" in the supreme Mind, becomes all-formed in the World according to the ineffable order of divine disposition, and is distinguished according to certain formal reasons. Furthermore, all things outside the supreme Mind are marked with the incorruptible <margin>God is the source of all things according to Zoroaster.</margin> seals of the divine conception, according to which they operate by an inviolable law. For in this way the World, preserved in its beauty and order of grace, appears charming with all kinds of Ideas: for just as various streams are led down from a fountain, which nevertheless essentially depend on that fountain; so from the most fertile and infinite fountain and sea of the divine Mind, innumerable streams of divine goodness are derived through the Beings and substances of the entire Universe, as Zoroaster rightly perceived, by which the Universe is uniquely preserved, animated, and made fruitful.

### CHAPTER V

...participate in the model, so that all things in the economy of the World are rightly administered; thus the World, imbued with a variety of forms, may present that ornament and beauty of arrangement which we all admire. For the <term>Iynges</term> <note>original: "Iynges"; in Neoplatonism, these are "wheels" or "whirls" that act as divine mediators or messengers between the intellectual and material worlds</note>, moved by ineffable counsels, as Zoroaster says, while they contemplate the beautiful likenesses of the Father within themselves, derive them by a uniform diffusion into the Sensible World and all its universal members. <margin>The Egyptians expressed the Iynges or Ideas through various symbols.</margin> Therefore, so that the Egyptians might aptly express these Iynges or Ideas, they indicated them through various and occult symbols; so that wise men accustomed to contemplation, while looking upon them, might apprehend the series of the entire hidden meaning without discursive speech or consultation, and might emerge as <term>God-formed</term> <note>original Greek: "Θεομόρφοι" (Theomorphoi); meaning those shaped into the likeness of God</note> according to the model of the blessed Minds. Plotinus <margin>Plotinus.</margin> beautifully explains this in Book 8, Chapter 5, in these words: <note>original: Plotinus, Ennead V, 8, 5</note> *One must not think, therefore, that in the Intelligible World there are certain propositions or Gods, nor that those who are there are beyond spirits; but each of the things spoken of there are beautiful statues, such as one might imagine to exist in the soul of a wise man; statues not painted, but truly existing; wherefore the ancients called the Ideas "beings" and "essences."* <note>The Latin text provides a translation of the Greek passage: "Nemo igitur existimare debet..."</note> No one, therefore, should think that in the Intelligible World either the Gods themselves, or the other more-than-happy inhabitants there, contemplate certain rules of propositions; but rather that each thing said to be there offers itself to those gazing upon it as certain models and spectacles or beautiful images; such as someone might perhaps imagine to exist in the mind of a wise man. I say, however, not painted images, but existing ones; for which reason the ancients called the Ideas "Beings" and "Essences." Hence the Egyptian Priests, <margin>Why the Egyptians used hieroglyphic figures to signify divine mysteries.</margin> to signify divine mysteries, did not use a form of characters similar to ours (as has been proven at length above), but rather the complete figures of herbs, plants, animals, or those composed from multiple transformations; this was to indicate that the supreme archetypal Divinity does not possess knowledge of things as a multifaceted thought about a matter, but as the simple form of a single thing.

<margin>Plotinus.</margin> *But let us hear the words of Plotinus:* It seems to me that the Sages of the Egyptians, whether by a certain perfected wisdom or by a natural instinct of the Mind, when they determined to signify the mysteries of wisdom to us, did not use the shapes of letters which signify the discourses of speech and certain properties, and which imitate the voices and pronunciations of rules; but rather they described the images of individual things, and by painting them in sacred places, they silently signified the discourse of the matter itself. This was because each image and model is a certain knowledge and wisdom, and that subject spectacle is a whole collected together, and is neither a certain thought nor a counsel. Afterwards, however, from that model image or wisdom which is all at once, an image is made in something else which is now unfolded and speaking with a certain discourse, finding the causes for why things were so instituted. Indeed, when the arrangement of things—because it is so well-ordered—moves one to admiration, he says that one will admire the wisdom who considers how it, though not having the causes of its own essence for why it is so or acts so, nevertheless exists just as those things do which are produced according to it. This arrangement, indeed, may scarcely or in any way become manifest through inquiry—namely, that it is necessary for things to be so—but it is necessary in the Intelligible World, before all inquiry and argumentation, that it should so exist and be. *Plotinus, Book 8.* Above the corporeal Heaven in the incorporeal Heaven there are two-fold Gods, namely the intelligible and the intellectual; the former are indeed the Ideas, while the latter are all the intellects blessed by the eternal contemplation of the Ideas; for the divine intellect...

# TREATISE I. THE ISIAC TABLE. CHAPTER V.

...derives the divine Ideas into itself in such a way that the whole is preserved in each individual part, but under different and distinct properties. One should not say so much that the ideas are within the intellect, as that the intellect itself exists as those very ideas—manifesting as "all-formed" from its own "Uniform" self in a marvelous way, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage associated with Thoth.</note> speaks. And just as in the Intelligible World all things are intellect, so in the celestial intellectual World, all things are heaven. There, the earth is heaven; there, the sea, animals, plants, and men are heaven. In short, whatever belongs to that <margin>In the celestial intellectual World, all things are Heaven.</margin> heaven is heavenly. Each of the Gods there is the whole; everything there is the Universe. For everything there is great, since even the small there is great. There the Sun and all the stars exist, and a single star is the Sun, and likewise all are stars.

Aristotle himself marveled at this kind of Egyptian doctrine; in his *Mystical Theology* <note>Kircher refers to the "Theology of Aristotle," a work now known to be Neoplatonic (based on Plotinus) rather than by Aristotle himself.</note> <margin>Aristotle's doctrine on Ideas according to the Egyptians.</margin> discussing the mind of the Egyptians in Book 14, Chapter 14, he includes these points among others: *Among the beings of the upper World, none is substantially nobler than another, but all things there exist according to the best form; just as the forms existing in the mind of an architect are equal as causes, and differ from the effects—that is, the figures carved into a wall. Therefore, the ancient Sages of Babylon and Egypt, with sharpness of mind, looked into these upper forms as "exemplars" (which Plato said were the essential substances of lower things). They embraced the intellectual species of the World through knowledge handed down from elsewhere or discovered from within themselves, which they claimed as their own profession. Indeed, when they were about to describe something, they used intellectual teaching, not the discursive speech common to men. Unlike some others who, after consulting them, did not feel they had learned firmly enough from spoken sentences, these Sages wrote down the concepts received in their minds (as we read with the evidence of our own eyes) onto stones through figures.* They did the same in all arts <margin>Why the Egyptians used Hieroglyphic figures, according to Aristotle.</margin> and sciences, which they placed in temples like pages to be read through; such were their first useful books. They did this to indicate that the immaterial "Active Intellect" created all things according to the specific reason and likeness of each essence. This was the best and most beautiful instruction; through which, I wish they had also indicated by what means they reached those marvelous and hidden forms. For then their mystery would be even more worthy of praise—a condition that has happened to few men.*

These words certainly agree so well with those of Plotinus cited above, that it seems Plotinus described them from Aristotle. In these, both allude to the hidden meanings of the hieroglyphs. For as <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> Iamblichus rightly says: *Imitating the very nature of the Universe and the handiwork of the Gods, the Egyptians also show certain images of mystical and recondite actions in the creation of symbols. Just as nature expresses hidden reasons in apparent forms as if through symbols, and the Gods explain the truth of ideas through manifest images. Therefore, when they perceive that all higher things delight in the likeness of lower things, and moreover desire to be filled with goodness from the Higher ones, they offer what they can by introducing certain hidden mysteries into manifest symbols. In interpreting these, leave behind the words and take the sense.*

Therefore, hieroglyphic figures are nothing <margin>What Hieroglyphic figures are.</margin> other than certain external forms of divine notions and signs of "ideal reasons." They are no different from the sensible forms of natural things which exert themselves in stones, herbs, plants, animals, and stars, and which intrinsically mark the reasons of hidden powers and marvelous properties. These are nothing other than the "ideal reasons" of the divine mind, and as Saint Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note> says, they are certain mirrors of divine virtues, of which... <margin>St. Dionysius.</margin>
