# CHAPTER V. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER.

Through contemplation, the mind rises into the hidden secrets of the intelligible World. 
<margin>Hermes</margin> For as **Hermes** rightly says in the **Pimander** <note>original: "Pimandro"; referring to the *Poimandres*, a foundational text of Hermeticism</note>: *Lest the preeminent name of God be lacking to you, do not be ignorant of the fact that what seems hidden to many is actually clear; for if it were nowhere manifest, it would be nothing at all. Whatever offers itself to the sight is created; but that which is hidden exists eternally. For there is no need for this to appear, since it never ceases to be. He places all other things before the eyes, but He Himself remains secret, inasmuch as He enjoys eternal life. He brings all things forth into full light, yet hides in the inner sanctums; nevertheless, He expresses each thing through appearances. For appearance is concerned only with those things that are created, in which nothing exists at all except generation; even when that uncreated thing is incomprehensible to appearance, yet because all things become clear through Him, He shines upwards through all things and in all things; and He appears especially to those to whom He wished to communicate the knowledge of Himself.* What is the name of God, if not power identified with the essence of God diffused through the members of the entire World? And as <margin>Suidas.</margin> **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> says, "walking through the Universe"? Concerning this, it is treated more extensively in the Kabbalah, where whatever has been proven regarding the divine Names and the ten **Sephiroth** <note>The ten attributes/emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself</note> refers back to the divine ideas. But, as I said, consult the Kabbalah on these matters, where you will find everything treated at length. Since, therefore, as Aristotle says in Book 14, Chapter 15 of his *Mystical Theology* <note>Kircher attributes the "Theologia Aristotelis"—actually a Neoplatonic text—to Aristotle</note>, the wisdom of the Egyptians concerning heavenly matters is to be admired, the time and place now demand that we explain what they signified through those many-formed figures expressed on the border of the table.

### ->Explanation of the Border of the Isiac Table.<-

<margin>Porphyry.</margin> **B**efore we begin our interpretation, it seemed appropriate to cite here a passage from **Porphyry**, Book 4 of *On Abstinence*, where in a few words he seems to touch upon the sum of our entire exposition; for he speaks thus: *From this exercise and conjunction with God, the Egyptians perfectly understood that divinity did not pass through man alone, nor did the soul obtain a dwelling on earth in man alone, but it also passes through almost all animals. Whence also, for the representation of the Gods, they adopted every animal <margin>The Egyptians adopted every animal along with man for the representation of the Gods</margin> along with man, in which they mixed the bodies of brutes, men, and birds. For among them, individual images show a human likeness even up to the neck, but the head exhibits the body of a bird, or a lion, or some other animal. By these they clearly signify that these things, according to the judgment of the Gods, have a fellowship among themselves, and that related animals—both the tame and the wild—are not without a certain divine will.* <note>original Greek: Φανερὸν γὰρ ὅτι...; Kircher provides the Greek text followed by his Latin translation, both rendered here into English</note> **For it is manifest that the Egyptian Priests of the Sacred Mysteries wished to signify all the secrets of sacred things from various things established into One, such as by assuming the heads of a Hawk, or an Ibis, or similar things onto a human form.** For in all those things in which divine reason shone forth regarding a certain manifest effect, they adopted that same thing to mark the idea of a divine notion and intellect. And in this way, having wandered through all the paths of the worldly classes, they sought those reasons of the ideal chains by which the divine **Mind** [governs] all things.

The knowledge of these things had as its goal <term>contemplation and divine insight</term> <note>original: "θεωρίαν καὶ θείαν"</note>, the fulfillment of all human and divine happiness, as will be explained below.

### ->Interpretation of the Upper Border.<-

<margin>Interpretation of the upper border of the Bembine Tablet.</margin>
**J**ust as the Border surrounds the <term>enclosure</term> <note>original: "peribochen," referring to the perimeter or circuit</note> of the entire table, in the same way the Ideal World encompasses the system of all nature. It is divided into four parts: the upper, the lower, the right side, and the left side; all of which we shall explain in order, beginning our interpretation from the upper part.

<margin>Interpretation of the Dog sitting in the upper border of the Bembine Tablet.</margin>
The upper border is marked with the letters A and C, in which the first figure is marked with the number 1. It consists of a sitting Dog with a sistrum <note>An ancient Egyptian percussion instrument associated with the goddess Isis</note> resting upon a Nilotic vessel. From its back emerges an eyed phallus, and it is flanked on both sides: on one side by a lotus, and on the other by a leaf of the Persea tree. Receive now in a few words what these things indicate. By the flower of the lotus, the exemplar existing in the divine Mind is indicated, according to which all things produced outwardly conform their rules of operation. This is drawn from a likeness to the nature of the lotus; for, according to the testimony of <term>Theophrastus</term> <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, often called the "father of botany"</note>, it is a white flower, very close to lilies in the narrowness of its leaves. Indeed, this is the flower of the Great Water-lily, which closes at the setting of the Sun and is hidden under the water, and at the rising of the Sun emerges above the waters and comes forth. It opens by measuring the movement of the Sun most accurately, whence it is called by the Egyptians <term>lotometron</term> <note>original: "λωτόμετρον"</note>, that is, the "measuring lotus," about which see the extensive discussion in the treatise of this Work concerning the hieroglyphic herbs of Egypt.
<margin>The lotus flower follows the Sun.</margin>
<margin>Theophrastus</margin>
Therefore, from this wonderful property of the plant, the Egyptian Sages, wishing to exhibit the Idea, painted the lotus flower to indicate that all Ideas and forms of natural things relate to the form of forms and the Idea of Ideas—the supreme Mind and the archetypal Sun—just as the lotus flower relates to the sensible Sun. For all things follow the archetypal Sun by an infallible and inevitable law in the proper administration of the Worldly republic.
<margin>What the Egyptians indicate by the lotus flower following the Sun.</margin>
The lotus flower rests upon a very thin stalk, by which they indicated that the reasons of the Ideas, abstracted from all matter, depend upon the contemplation of the intellectual Sun. Therefore, wherever you find this lotus flower in this tablet (and it is found everywhere and most frequently), let the Reader know that they allude by this symbol to those things which we have said.

<margin>The Persea tree.</margin>
Furthermore, on the other side, a hanging leaf of the Persea is found. To explain this, it must be noted that the Persea tree has a leaf like a tongue and a fruit like a heart, as <term>Horus</term> <note>Referring to Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> testifies and as we have shown in various places. By the heart, they indicated anagogically <note>In a spiritual or mystical sense</note> the intellect of the first and supreme Mind; by the tongue, the word which it produces. For the paternal intellect, or concept, by conceiving itself, produces the word in which all the reasons of the Ideas are unfolded outwardly; for just as the secrets of the heart are expressed through the tongue, so is the intellect through the word, as I have said...

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...as I have said, it displays all the notions of existing things, which it imprints upon all the orders of the World through a certain communicative goodness, so that each individual might cooperate toward the good and preservation of the World according to the notions of the Ideas communicated to them. But because the World must necessarily become sterile without fertility, it therefore employed a guardian of the fecundating power—with which it was imbued by God—necessary for its preservation; and it attributed this exemplar to the Anubic choir of Spirits <note>Geniorum</note>, so that they might operate according to it. And they display this entire reasoning quite aptly through the figure of a seated Dog, swollen with breasts <margin>The Dog signifies Anubis.</margin>, with a sistrum <note>An ancient Egyptian percussion instrument associated with Joy and fertility</note> placed nearby. <note>Hieroglyphic description: A seated Anubis dog with swollen breasts, holding or accompanied by a sistrum, and occasionally a phallus on its back.</note> The Dog signifies Anubis, as has been said very often, while the phallus attached to its back signifies the guardianship of Osirian fertility; the seated Dog with the sistrum and the phallus attached to its back denotes the Anubic power, the preserver and propagator of Osirian fertility, communicated to it by the supreme intellect of the triform Deity. This is clearly evident through the winged serpent-bearing globe together with the scepter placed near the Serpents; since we have dealt with this most abundantly in the *Pamphylian Obelisk* on page 398, we refer the reader there. But because a symbol of this kind occurs very frequently in the border of this tablet, I have thought it best to explain it in this place in a few words <margin>What the winged Globe with Serpents and scepter signifies.</margin>, lest we be forced to repeat the same thing so many times. The symbol <term>kyklo-ophi-pteromorphon</term> <note>original: κυκλο-οφι-πτερόμορφον; meaning "circle-serpent-wing-shaped"</note>, that is, this displayed globe conspicuous for its wings and Serpents, denotes nothing other than the First Mind, and the supreme cause of all causes, from which—as if from an infinite fountain of all lives and all Ideas—all things are derived into all things by a certain eternal efflux. They display this Ideal concept of His not incongruously through the circle, the wings, and the Serpent: for just as all lines are drawn from the center of a circle to the circumference, so from this circle—whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere—through His word (aptly compared to a Serpent) and the all-forming spirit <note>spiritum Pantamorphum</note> (indicated by the wings), the rays of the Ideal reasons are diffused into the universal nature of the Worlds. They mark individual substances, both sensible and insensible, with the seals of their powers; for from this the universal life of the World depends, as was proven above. Thus, they aptly placed this Ideal symbol of the divine Mind above individual images to show that no being exists in the World that has not participated in the reasons of its essence from the supreme influx of all things.

But now to our purpose. The second figure displays the form <margin>Interpretation of the Hawk figure in the upper border of the Bembine tablet. Plutarch. Psellus.</margin> of a Hawk distinguished by the head of Horus, by which nothing else is indicated but the <term>Sphinx of Horus</term> (which Zoroaster also calls the *Iynx* <note>A "Iynx" in Neoplatonic thought is a "spell" or "transmitter" that conveys divine will to the material world</note>), the Idea of the providence of the sensible world, as Plutarch witnesses and Psellus confirms with these words: <term>The Iynx is [the operator] of the perception of the sensible world</term> <note>original Greek: Ἴυγξ ἐστὶ νοήσεως τοῦ κόσμου αἰσθητικοῦ</note>. Indeed, marked by this Ideal seal from the supreme triform Deity, it conceives an abundance of necessary things according to the prescription of the first exemplar; for as Zoroaster rightly says, <margin>Zoroaster. The Iynges, having been understood by the Father, themselves understand. Interpretation of the Lion in the supreme border of the Bembine tablet.</margin> *The Iynges, having been understood by the Father, themselves understand*, that is, being imbued with Ideal reasons by the Father, they provide for the Universe according to their immutable law. Furthermore, because a fiery force is entirely necessary for the World, they placed another Ideal symbol next to this one, marked with the number 3; it is a Lion with a winged globe placed above it, and lotus flowers placed here and there. What is indicated by the lotus flower and the winged globe, I have explained just a little while ago.

# TREATISE I. THE ISIAC TABLE CHAPTER IV.

We have already established the position; let us now explain what is meant by the Lion. The Lion, as we taught in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on page 284, denotes in this context that corroborating force of the archetype acting upon earthly powers, or the fiery power of the Sun, which they also call <term>Mophtæa</term> <note>A name Kircher uses for a supreme intellectual or solar power</note>. This force acts by promoting movement within moisture, by which the impregnated earth recovers as if from a long-lasting decay and is rendered fit and suitable for bearing fruit. For, according to <margin>Horus.</margin> Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note>, the Lion is an earthly animal full of fiery spirits; indeed, if the machinery of the world lacked this fiery moisture, it would necessarily perish and dissolve entirely. Therefore, so that it might be delivered from this destruction, it was necessary for the Intelligence <term>Mophtæa</term>, marked with an ideal seal, to apply itself inviolably to this assigned duty. This is also aptly expressed by the branch of a plant, which is called <term>akantha</term> <note>original: "ἀκανθα"; the Acacia or thorn-bush</note> by the Egyptians, whose leaves are so closed at night in the absence of the Sun's light that it resembles <margin>Branch of a plant.</margin> thorns rather than leaves, yet sometimes they soon expand with joyful growth at the presence of the Sun. The branch stands upon a Nilotic vessel, by which it is indicated that if the fiery spirit is absent from the moisture, all things must waste away; but when it is present, all things flourish fruitfully. Furthermore, since the Intelligence <term>Mophtæa</term> does not work immediately but through an Intelligence sub-delegated to it, it hands over the guardianship and execution of the things committed to it to <term>Nephtæ</term> <note>Nephthys</note>, by whose ministry the interior of the earth is disposed toward fertility. These are aptly shown through figures 4 and 5, where you see an <term>eyed phallus</term> <note>original: "phallum oculatum"; a symbol of generative power combined with divine providence</note> placed upon a flowering basket, <margin>Figures 4 & 5: The Eyed Phallus and Nephtæ</margin> and <term>Nephtæ</term> kneeling with a vessel in her left hand, as if worshipfully receiving the treasure of fertility committed to her faith; so that what was granted to her by <term>Mophtæa</term>, she herself completes by the double-forked flame emerging from her head—that is, by the fiery power of the mind. There follows the figure marked number 6, the <term>Ophionian Agathodæmon</term> <note>The "Good Spirit" in serpent form</note>, visible with the body of an Asp, the head of a Hawk, and outspread wings; it has been proved extensively elsewhere that this is a <margin>Figure 6: The Ophionian Agathodæmon.</margin> symbol of light, life, and motion. Because this fiery spirit cannot exist without moisture, they have aptly placed a bull's head beneath it, which has been said elsewhere in many places to be a symbol of the Moon, as the horns <margin>Figure 7: A Bull's head.</margin> manifest clearly enough. They indicate, therefore, that the spirit of life and light does not achieve the effect of its efficacy until it has been joined to the Lunar body; for the Moon tempers the power of the luminous excesses and fiery spirits with moisture, so that they can obtain their effect in the lower world. See a more diffuse treatment of this symbol in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 514.

-> <-

The figure marked with number 8 is a <term>Frog</term> sitting upon an altar, surrounded on both sides by papyrus thyrsi <note>Staffs or wands</note>, with a globe encircled by a Serpent placed nearby. These <margin>Figure 8: A Frog sitting on an altar.</margin> symbols indicate the lowest matter, the receptacle of forms, which is still imperfect and deprived of all form. The symbol is derived from the likeness of the Nilotic Frog, which they called the most imperfect of all insects, because the Frog alone among living creatures, in the very first cradles of its birth, is half-composed of some earthly matter while the rest is animated, and it is reducible back into mud and slime. But concerning these things, see what we have delivered above regarding the Frog. Hence the Egyptians, when signifying mud, rightly painted a Frog, as it is <margin>The Egyptians, signifying mud, painted a frog. Iamblichus.</margin> born from mud and likewise resolvable into mud; all of which Iamblichus seems to have beautifully suggested in these words: *Whenever, therefore, they name mud in the sacred rites...* <note>Kircher is quoting Iamblichus's "On the Mysteries," explaining the Egyptian use of "mud" as a metaphor for primeval matter.</note>

# CHAPTER V.

...they signify or introduce; understand here the body and matter of the World, and the generative power inserted within it, which is, as it were, equally agitated and flowing; or even the principal cause, placed like a foundation, of the elements and the power of things composed of elements. Since this is the case, God himself is the cause of generation and of all the forces of nature present in the elements, inasmuch as he towers above all these things, being himself immaterial, undivided, immovable, and unbegotten, entirely from himself and entirely within himself, overseeing all these things, he precedes and leads them, embracing all things in himself. <margin>A globe surrounded by a serpent.</margin> The globe surrounded by a serpent and placed upon a frog seems to reflect all these things; for the Supreme Mind, conceiving matter through the ideal influence of its action, imbues it with all manner of forms and renders it perfect from the imperfect; without which things could neither subsist nor be adapted to the generations of things. <margin>The Egyptians consecrated the frog to Isis. Herodotus.</margin> Hence the Egyptians rightly consecrated the frog to Isis, as the fashioner of the Intelligence of all things and the mother of all. In the festival of the finding of the parts of Osiris, according to the testimony of Herodotus <note>Kircher refers to the "Inventio Osiridis," a ritual reenacting Isis searching for the scattered limbs of her husband.</note>, the priests adorn the altars with thyrsi <note>Staffs topped with pinecones or leaves, usually associated with Dionysian rites but here linked to Egyptian reeds.</note> made of papyrus and reeds, among which frogs are most accustomed to dwell. They are secretly suggesting the abundance of generative moisture which they sought from the mother of all things; these are quite aptly indicated by the two thyrsi flanking the frog. Concerning the lotus and the persea <note>An Egyptian tree, likely *Mimusops schimperi*, often confused with the peach or laurel in early modern botany.</note>, which are symbols of ideal influence, it has been discussed above.

<margin>Figures 9 & 10: The Androsphinx and the kneeling figure.</margin> There follow figures 9 and 10, namely a <term>cat-shaped form</term> <note>original Greek: αἰλουρόμορφον (*ailouromorphon*)</note> in a sitting posture, and a kneeling figure, marked on the head with a sixth-day Moon <note>A crescent moon.</note>, carrying the feather of an Ibis in its hand, with leaves of the lotus and persea in between. The Androsphinx, composed of a lion and a human face and conspicuous for its wings, denotes the Solar Intelligence prevailing with a strengthening power. This intelligence, through the ideal influence communicated to it by the Supreme Mind (indicated by the lotus and persea leaves), together with the Lunar Nephta <note>Likely referring to Nephthys, the sister of Isis, whom Kircher associates here with lunar moisture.</note> as a subordinate deity, finally leads the terrestrial moisture—still raw, unpolished, and imperfect—to its intended end.

<margin>Figures 11, 12, 13, 14 placed upon a ship.</margin> Furthermore, the figures marked with numbers 11, 12, 13, and 14 are seen placed upon a ship. These are the Nevian Bull <note>The Apis bull, often depicted with specific markings.</note> with a winged serpent-bearing globe, flanked by persea leaves; the pilot of the ship holding a pole in his hands is marked with number 11; the figure marked with number 14 has a feather in its hand and a crescent moon on its head. The prow of the ship is decorated with a lotus, and the stern with a hawk’s head carrying a feather and an asp in place of a crest. A quadrant with astronomical markings stands near the bull. It seemed best to begin the explanation of what these individual things mean from a slightly deeper perspective.

<margin>The ship Barys, most famous among the Egyptians. Plutarch. Herodotus.</margin> This most famous ship of the Egyptians, the <term>Barys</term> <note>A specific type of flat-bottomed Nile boat described by ancient historians.</note>, is a type of papyrus vessel, according to Plutarch, which they use in sacred rites, as Herodotus testifies. In the table, it holds the central place of the border, toward which all the symbolic animals and ideal arrangements on both sides look, as if toward a supreme Idea. Just as it holds the first place among the figures of the upper border, so it would have been necessary to explain it first of all, had not the method of the order prescribed in the table suggested otherwise. Therefore, all the symbols in the border, partly explained so far and partly yet to be explained, look toward this point.

<margin>The stern of the ship marked with a hawk's head.</margin> But let us explain the individual parts. # TREATISE I. THE ISIAC TABLE. CHAPTER V.

[The figure] occupies [the space], flanked on both sides by the leaves of the persea tree; upon its back rests a globe <note>original Greek: ὄφιο-πὶ σεμνοες — likely a corruption referring to the "venerable serpent-faced one"</note> and it has an astrological quadrant placed near it. Figure 14 is kneeling, carrying a hawk’s feather in its hands and the Moon with an emerging viper upon its head. Finally, the lotus flower resting on the stern closes the arrangement. All these symbols express the **Ideas** by which the entire machinery of the World is continually governed and preserved by the Supreme Deity through his ministers. The ship signifies the vehicle of the supreme emanations diffused into all the paths of the World. The stern, distinguished by the hawk’s head, the feather, and the asp, signifies light, life, and motion— <margin>All the figures of the ship *Baris* express Ideas.</margin> by which [the Deity] completes all things with his own swiftness and fertility. The prow, notable for the flower of the lotus or melilot, secretly indicates the likeness by which all things operate according to the Idea of the Divine Mind, as has been said. The pilot of the ship is **Horus**, namely that power of the World or the Sun which moderates the proper constitution of the parts of the year <margin>Horus, the Pilot of the Ship.</margin> for each individual thing. **Apis**, or the bull, expresses **Osiris**, either as the Soul of the World or the Supreme Mind of the Solar Deity. Isis follows him, wearing the Moon on her head and holding a hawk’s feather in her hand, by which it is suggested she is the consort of the Sun, as has been explained at length elsewhere. For as Diodorus rightly says in Eusebius: *Osiris and Isis are the Sun and Moon <margin>Eusebius. Osiris and Isis are the Sun and Moon.</margin> according to the Egyptians, by whom the World is governed through the three seasons—spring, summer, and winter—conducted in an invisible manner, and all things are born, nourished, and increased.* Hence they aptly placed the astrological quadrant near the bull as a symbol of time, because they chose the times suitable for the works of agriculture, according to Diodorus; although these seasons may oppose one another, they nevertheless complete the year with a wonderful harmony. One of these gods is said to produce the temper of fire and spirit, the other of the moist and the dry, and both of the air, by which all things both arise and are preserved. Moreover, Plutarch testifies that **Osiris** and **Apis** are the same <margin>Osiris and Apis are the same.</margin> in these words: *Those who signify that the Universe is urged by a rapid motion through Apis hold a more tolerable view; but most Priests say that Osiris and Apis fall into the same thing, and they relate and teach us: <note>original Greek: Ὅτι ἔμμορφον εἰκόνα χρὴ νομίζειν τὸ Ὁσίριδος ψυχῆς τὸν Ἆπιν</note> That Apis must be considered the beautiful image of the soul of Osiris.* But concerning the Bull, see the very copious treatment in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, the Hierogrammatism of the Bull, and Volume I of *Oedipus*, Treatise 3, concerning Apis. Therefore, the Egyptians <margin>The hieroglyphic ship, and what it indicates among the Egyptians.</margin> wished to indicate nothing else by this ideal arrangement than the diffusion of the triform Deity (indicated by the winged globe) into all the paths of the World, yet in a certain singular order: First, it exerts itself into the Soul of the World signified by Apis; then into Horus and Isis, that is, the Sun, Moon, and other stars; and finally, it diffuses into all the remaining members of the lower World over which they preside. For by their administration, both the arrangement of time and the generations of all things are facilitated, as has been said. They are carried in a ship because their motion is in the "moisture" <note>A reference to the ancient belief that celestial bodies floated in a fluid ether or "celestial waters."</note>. Thus Eusebius says: *They place the image of the Sun in a ship <margin>Eusebius.</margin> which is carried by a Crocodile, so that motion in the moisture is signified by the vessel, while the Crocodile signifies the drinkable water in which they contend the Sun is carried.* But Iamblichus explains this entire expression of ideal meaning quite appositely to our purpose; he describes all the hieroglyphics of this matter so aptly <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> that he seems to have explained this very thing; for he says: *Accordingly, where they introduce a God, [it is in] a ship...*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Egyptian symbolic theology from Athanasius Kircher's "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," specifically focusing on the philosophical justifications for depicting gods in animal or changing forms, drawing heavily on the Neoplatonist philosopher Iamblichus.</meta>

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

->The pilot signifies leadership; the Governor of the World: For just as a pilot, though distinct from the ship and the rudder, moves, rules, and directs the vessel from a single easy point of momentum; so God himself from above—namely, from the first principles of nature—provides the primary causes of all motion. Since, in truth, all parts of heaven, the celestial animals <note>referring to the signs of the Zodiac</note>, the motion of the entire Universe, and time itself (according to which the World moves), and finally all things contained within the whole, receive powers descending from the Sun—some indeed mixed within themselves, others surpassing any mixture—therefore, the symbolic method of representation introduces these things. By words alone, it designates that the Sun is figured according to the celestial animals, and that its forms change in turn through the seasons; meanwhile, however, it demonstrates the Sun's immutable and simultaneous transmission of its whole self through the entire World. But since the things that receive this transmission are carried in different ways around the indivisible gift of God, and they themselves—on account of the diversity of their natures and motions—receive multiform powers from the Sun, therefore the symbolic tradition intends for the one God to enter through a multitude of gifts, and for the one power of God to be present through multiform powers. Wherefore, it says that the One and the same remains consistent; yet it asserts that the changes of forms and transfigurations result from the recipients. Therefore, it says he is changed according to the animals and the seasons, as if such mutations vary around God according to the different vessels that receive Him. The Egyptians use such methods not only in the actual visions of the Gods, but also in their lighter prayers, which hold the same meaning; and through such symbolic and mystical cultivation, they approach the Gods in supplication. Thus far Iamblichus <note>original: "hactenus Iamblichus"; Kircher is quoting from 'On the Mysteries of the Egyptians'</note>; see these things explained more fully in Class III, folio 183.<-

Figures 15, 16, 17.
</margin>

Following the ship are three other diagrams, marked with the numbers 15, 16, and 17. The first of these shows the figure of a kneeling Horus; the second, a Hawk or *Thaustus* <note>a term Kircher uses for a specific solar aspect</note>, upon whose back is a Serpent coiled around a globe; the third, a Goat’s head placed upon an altar, with thyrsi <note>ritual staffs</note> and flowers surrounding it. By these, nothing else is indicated except the force and efficacy of the Solar Divinity upon the sensible World. And the Hawk indeed, as has already been said often, is a symbol of the life and light which stands out in the Sun, and is expressed through the Serpent coiled around the globe; for by light, heat and life are brought together in the World, which is denoted by the kneeling Horus. He is kneeling because this sensible World relates to the Soul of the World (which fixes its seat in the Solar body) just as the body relates to the soul; hence Horus desires to subject himself, in a certain way, to the *Thaustus* and its influences. What the Melilot flower with its six leaves and the acacia branch placed by the Hawk indicate has already been said often. There follows the Goat’s head placed upon an altar, by which the Mendesian power is hinted at. Now, to the Egyptians, Mendes, <term>ϣⲉⲛⲉⲧⲏⲃ</term> <note>Coptic: shenetēb</note>, is the same as a Goat, which they also call <term>ϣⲉⲛⲉⲧⲏⲃ</term>, that is, the "Sacred Goat"; and thus, whom the Greeks call <term>Πᾶνα</term> <note>Greek: Pana/Pan</note>, the Egyptians call <term>ϣⲉⲛⲉⲧⲏⲃ</term>, that is, the president of fertility. It is joined to the *Thaustus* because those things which the *Thaustus* has wisely arranged in the worldly house of Horus through heat, light, and motion, this *Simendes* or Pan, by his fertilizing virtue—arousing each thing according to the conditions of their seminal reasons—causes them to sprout forth into a most abundant plenty of all things.

Therefore, by the wise counsel of the Supreme Mind, it was established that the hot should be aptly tempered by the moist, and thus the World should be preserved by a mixture of this kind; which is appropriately indicated by the said symbols. <margin>The World is preserved by a tempering of the moist and the hot.</margin> The tri-formed winged globe, as was already said above, shows the influence; and first indeed into the Sun and Moon, or what is the same, into the Intelligence of the Sun and Moon, whose symbol is the <term>hawk-shaped</term> <note>original: "ἱερακόμορφος" (hierakomorphos)</note> Sphinx, with the Moon on its head, and an Asp included within the circle between the horns of the Moon. Ibis with the winged globe.</margin> into which the archetypal triform Deity infuses a moistening power; and thus it is necessarily joined to the Leontosphynx, so that it cannot exist without it; for from here the system of all vegetable nature is governed and ruled; these things are hinted at by the herbal bundle full of flowers placed near the Ibis.

The ten ideal marriages of the Gods.

**T**he lower border contains the ideal marriages of ten Gods, and their operations and faculties by which they administer the Universe. You will see here, always next to the individual figures, leaves of the lotus-measure, the persea, and the acacia; since these signify the conversion of lower things to higher things, I shall say nothing more of them here, as they have all been explained in the preceding sections.

<margin>
Figures 47 and 38. The marriage of the Asp-Sphinx with the Power of Hora.
</margin>

The first marriage is of the Asp-Sphinx with the Power of Hora, marked with numbers 37 and 38; their meanings have been set forth in the preceding pages.

The second marriage is of the Intelligence of Hora with Momphta; <note>Momphta is Kircher’s name for a specific Egyptian creative force, often associated with a lion-headed deity or the "Hemi-Sphinx."</note> they understood by Horus and Momphta, as has already been frequently explained, that corroborative strength of the Archetype (as the winged globe indicates) acting upon terrestrial powers—or rather, the fiery force of the supramundane Sun. By this force, the Sun acts upon moisture to promote it, whereby the impregnated earth recovers as if from a long-lasting decay, and, being comforted, is rendered fit to bear fruit. This ideal marriage is excellently exhibited in figures 39, 40, and 41, where we behold Horus covered in a latticed garment, with the head of a boy, reclining as if upon a bed. The front leg of this bed's frame is a Lion’s foot, and it is joined to a Lion’s head in such a way that they seem to form a single statue; the back frame of the bed represents the hind foot of a Lion, with the tail bent back into the shape of a crescent Moon. Beneath the bed are placed three Canopic jars or polymorphous water-vessels, the first of which is distinguished by a human face, the second by a Hawk’s face, and the third by a Dog’s face. All these things signify nothing other than the descent of the triform Divinity, or the Soul of the World, into Horus (or the Sun), and of the Sun into the Nile through the Leonine virtue of Momphta. When the fiery joins with the moist upon the "Bed of Momphta," the births of all things are awakened and disposed toward the generation of reality. The attendants and guardians of this Bed of Momphta are: Canopus <gloss>of the nature of ether</gloss> <note>original Greek: αἰθεροειδὴς</note>, Osiris <gloss>hawk-shaped</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφος</note>, the Nilotic, and Anubis <gloss>dog-shaped</gloss> <note>original Greek: κυνομορφος</note>, the Genii of the Nile. Through Anubis, providence and guardianship are indicated; through the Nilotic Osiris, the power of the Moon mixed with the Sun (either Osiris, or the Nile with Isis, or the earth); through Canopus, the beneficial Spirit of moisture is indicated, according to the testimony of Plutarch. Horapollo also testifies with these words: *“The three water-jars placed there signify either heaven or earth, or whatever gushes forth in abundance, making the Nile similar to a heart, endowed with a tongue: to a heart indeed, because this is held among them to be the principal part of the whole body, just as the Nile is the leader and prince of all Egypt; and to a tongue, because this...”*

And by its ministry, the source or <term>Hemphtaean</term> bowl—that is, the bowl of the supreme Deity of the Worlds—is opened, from which flows an abundance of all good things; the dispenser of these goods is the Horaean Genius expressed by number 44, the minister of the <term>Mnevian</term> Mind; for he diffuses the moisture, which he has drawn from the supramundane bowl, into all the members of the World, as is evident from the operation.

The fifth is the <term>Ammonia Ship</term>, by which <term>Ammon</term> and Horus, joined together and carried through the Universe, fill it with fertility. The <term>two-headed Ram</term>, shining with a double-forked flame, represents <term>Ammon</term> as the presiding officer of fertility; figure 47 expresses Horus as the pilot of the ship. The Ram is two-headed because it looks toward both the upper and the lower World; for as we correctly taught in the "Hierogrammatism of the Ram" in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 273, Ammon not only disposes the secret powers of hidden reasons in the upper intellectual World, but also takes care of the Mundane heat in the sensible World, by which the generations of things are promoted through a perpetual ascent and descent; hence, not without cause, he is painted two-headed with a double-forked flame on his head, which notes the diffusion of fiery power and heat both in the said upper and lower World. But concerning these things, see the cited place in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* at length. The stern of the ship shines with a Hawk's head and a crown <note>original: tutulo</note> placed upon it; by which Horus and Ammon are indicated to be the carriers of light and fiery heat through the inner recesses of the entire World; these achieve their operation and effects at appointed times, which are hinted at by the attached Astronomical quadrant.

<margin>Figures 50 & 51. The union of the Momphto-Mendesian Mind.</margin> The sixth union, that of the Momphto-Mendesian Mind, is indicated by figures 50 and 51; figure 50 denotes Momphta <note>Kircher's name for a specific solar-creative spirit</note>, while the Goat placed upon the altar marks Mendes. Just as the fertility of the hot or fiery principle is denoted in Ammon, so the fertility of the moist principle is denoted in the Goat. This, being joined to the Nilotic Momphta—the Leonine <note>lion-like</note> guardian of moist heat—demonstrates the fertility of the lower World.

<margin>Figures 52, 53, & 54. The Lunar-Solar union. The Moon-shaped Ibis signifies the Lunar Intelligence.</margin> The seventh union, the Lunar-Solar, is expressed through figures 52 and 53, where Horus, carrying a two-pronged flame on his head and a pyramid in his left hand, gazes at an Ibis marked with a lunar character. Note here that the Ibis does not signify this material Moon, but a supramundane Intelligence <note>a spiritual being or celestial governor</note> immediately subject to the influence of the triple-formed Deity (as the winged globe shows). Horus is subordinate to this Intelligence and, by his very gesture, seeks to be filled by it with "ideal moisture," since a fiery substance can by no means subsist without moisture. That the Ibis denotes the Lunar Intelligence has been explained at length using every kind of learning in the *Pamphylian Obelisk* <note>One of Kircher's previous major works on hieroglyphs</note>. How the Priests used to attract these Spirits in their sacred rites is indicated by the headdress of figure 54.

<margin>Figures 55, 56 & 57. The union of the Anubic Mind.</margin> The eighth union, indicated by numbers 55 and 56, is that of the Anubic Mind with the Lunar-Solar Cynocephalic <note>dog-headed</note> Mind. This Intelligence, marked with the "ideal" influence from the supreme Deity, is said to preside over time, wherein it provides to each thing its own proper and fitting influence. <margin>Horus. The Cynocephalus signifies the Lunar-Solar Mind.</margin> For, as Horus says <note>referring to Horapollo, an ancient author on hieroglyphs</note>, the Cynocephalus measures the hours by its urination, knows the time of the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, and rejoices and exults at the rising of the star; conversely, it grieves and is saddened at its setting. Thus, it was not without reason that they expressed the Mind presiding over these things through the Cynocephalus. Figure 55 exhibits Anubis, whose duty it is to take those things which the Cynocephalic Mind has wisely arranged according to the time proper to each, and through sagacious counsel and industrious invention, convert them to the good of the World. Hence, for the sake of either appeasing or <margin>Pausanias.</margin> summoning these Spirits, the Priests used various herbs, flowers, and fruits in their sacrifices, as witnessed by Pausanias and Simocatta <note>Classical and Byzantine historians</note>; the altar 57, adorned with a flowery bundle, sufficiently indicates this.

<margin>Figures 58 & 59. The union of the World-Soul with the sensible World. The Scarab.</margin> The ninth union is that of the Soul of the World with the sensible <note>perceptible by the senses</note> World. Figure 59 marks the Soul of the World; figure 58 the sensible World. The Soul of the World, or the Spirit of the Universe, consists of a Scarab and the head of Horus, with claws holding a tablet, on which is read the word **φγλοϰ** <note>original: "phylok", a Coptic term Kircher interprets as "the end" or "completion"</note> in Coptic letters. The firmament was signified by the Scarab; the five planets by the five circles attached to the neck; the Sun by the head of Horus; the Moon by the lunar figure placed upon the head; and the Elements by the Cross placed upon the circle. By these things, nothing else is hinted at but the aforementioned Spirit, penetrating all members of the World by its virtue, animating them, and connecting them with love. However, since we have explained this "Hierogrammatism" <note>sacred symbolic writing</note> in its individual parts in a full treatise in the *Coptic Prodromus* and in other places in this Work, we refer the curious Reader there. It also contains the arrangement of the sensible World according to the orders of the celestial globes, as is evident from the cited passages.

->**Interpretation of the right lateral border.**<-

<margin>
Interpretation of the right lateral border of the Bembine Tablet.

Apotropaic or averting deities.
Figures 61 & 62: The Genius Horus, and the Ophionic Mind.
</margin>
This border contains Deities endowed with apotropaic or averting power <note>Apotropaic: intended to turn away evil or bad luck</note>; by their help, whatever in the World is corrupted by excess or defect is brought back to a middle state. Figure 61 indicates the Genius Horus, who tempers the excess of the Ophionic Mind <note>Ophionic: related to the serpent-god Ophion</note> expressed by Figure 62. Its symbol is the lotus flower, the fruit of which is of such a nature that if it were always exposed to the Sun, it would be destroyed by excessive dryness; on the other hand, if it always remained hidden under water, its power would be suffocated by excessive moisture. Hence, by day, seeking the motion of the Sun, it is freed from the moisture contracted under the waters by his presence; and lest it be entirely deprived of all moisture, it seeks the water again at night as if to be soaked, until it attains its perfection through an equal temperament of heat and moisture. Regarding Figure 63, which is the same as Figure 30, since it has already been discussed, let the Reader refer to the cited figure.

<margin>
Figure 63.

Figures 64, 65 & 66. The sacred Hawk.
</margin>
Fig. 64, remarkable for its Hawk's face, human clothing, and the crown placed upon its head, holds a sacrificial knife <term>secespita: a long iron knife used by Roman priests</term> in its right hand in a threatening gesture. With this, it seems to put to flight the Agathodaemon Orimazius <note>Agathodaemon: a "good spirit"; Orimazius is a Latinized form of Ormuzd/Ahura Mazda</note>, or to prune away the superfluities of light and warm-moisture in the Universe (indicated by the Bull Mnevis) at appointed times, signified by the added quadrant. This has been discussed throughout this Work and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. The character of Orimazis placed above the Lunar horn, Α, is the mark of the Agathodaemon, as we have said elsewhere. The Moon joined to the Hawk's face denotes the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, by which great alterations in the World usually occur, filled with a certain Arimanian <note>Arimanian: referring to Ahriman, the Zoroastrian spirit of darkness/evil</note> power, which Orimazes, the lord of light and life, destroys for the good of the World with the sacrificial knife. Therefore, the Priests about to perform sacred rites venerated this Agathodaemon with a headdress <note>original: "tutulo"</note> composed of Hawk feathers, a star, bull horns, and leaves of the persea tree, as the headdress of figure 65 shows.

<margin>
Figures 67, 68 & 69. Horus and the Nilotic Genius.
</margin>
Fig. 67 and 69 following: the former signifies Horus, the latter the Nilotic Genius in the form of an Ibis. They indicate that the rising of the Nile is brought to a proper temperament by the Horaean Daemon. Just as its excess or defect brings necessary poverty, so its temperament brings the highest fertility. They hint at this by a truly most occult symbol: the Lunar herb placed near the Ibis, which they say brings forth fifteen leaves daily until the full moon, and loses just as many until the New Moon. If it bears more or fewer, they hold it as certain that a notable imbalance will follow. Hence the Priests, in rites to appease these Genii, place three Nilotic vessels (according to Horus); in one of these, the flower of the heliotrope bindweed is a symbol fit for attracting both Agathodaemons, as we have taught in the section on hieroglyphic herbs.

# TREATISE I. THE ISIAC TABLE: CHAPTER V

...they call it the blood of Mars; and it is said so because it wonderfully tempers the scorched, parched, or Martial bile through its own coldness and humidity; concerning which, consult the treatise on hieroglyphic herbs.

<margin>Figures 71 & 72. The Man-Scorpion.</margin>
Figure 71, composed of a scorpion and a man, indicates a malignant and scorching power latent in the Sun, represented by the Scorpion. This power is dissipated and put to flight by the Spirit Anubis <note>original: "ἀποπᾶς"; likely a reference to a Coptic or Hellenized name for a protective deity</note>, the guardian of Osiris, whose symbol is the herb *Motmutin*. However, the Momphtaean Power indicated by number 72, sensing the earthly body to be weighed down by excessive moisture, diverts the immoderate heat and scorching rays of the Sun toward it. By this process, the Sun is emptied of its excessive heat, while the Momphtaean substance—cut down and diminished by the Sun's superfluous heat—is freed from its excessive moisture, and thus a temperate balance is brought to both. For this is nature's unique remedy, by which caustic poisons are occasionally adopted by nature for intended uses; for nothing in nature is so superfluous, as <term>Proclus</term> <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the harmony of the cosmos</note> says, <margin>Proclus.</margin> that it cannot be substituted for the deficiency of another worldly body to its benefit, as has been treated elsewhere. All these things are administered by the wise counsel of the protective Spirit <note>original: "apotropaei Genii"; a guardian spirit intended to ward off evil</note>.

<margin>Figures 73 & 74. Horus piercing the Hippopotamus.</margin>
Figures 73 and 74 exhibit Horus, who pierces a Hippopotamus dwelling among flowering shrubs. By this, the <term>correspondence</term> <note>original: "ἀντίστοιχα" (antistoicha); things that stand opposite or correspond to one another</note> between Horus and Typhon is indicated. For when they wished to express Typhon as the <term>opposing deity</term> <note>original: "ἀντίθεον" (antitheon); an adversary or rival god</note> to Horus and Osiris, they painted a Hippopotamus. Since they recognized this animal as harmful and born to inflict damage—and furthermore, immense in its cunning and impiety—it perfectly expressed the nature of Typhon. They noted, not incongruously, that Typhon was tamed and pierced by Horus or Osiris through this image. Indeed, they secretly hinted at the Nile through Osiris, and through Typhon that malignant, putrid, and pernicious force by which crops and fruits are infected, which either Horus or Osiris, the protective Spirit of the Nile, destroys. But see those things which we have discussed more abundantly regarding the Hippopotamus in its own Hieroglyphic study in the <term>Pamphilian Obelisk</term> <note>Kircher's 1650 work interpreting the hieroglyphs on the obelisk in the Piazza Navona, Rome</note>.

And this is the sum of the Isiac Table, or of Egyptian Theology, whose hidden meanings I have seen fit to explain through as many chapters, so that they might be explained a little more at length, lest we should seem to have omitted anything necessary to hidden erudition.

<meta>This page introduces the "Anagogical" or mystical interpretation of the Bembine Tablet (also known as the Isiac Tablet). It establishes the metaphysical framework of the four Egyptian worlds—Archetypal, Intellectual, Sidereal, and Elementary—which Kircher uses to decode the tablet's symbols.</meta>

# Supplement on the Anagogical, Magical, and Ethical senses, and other uses for which this Tablet served.

## Section I.
->Concerning the Anagogical sense lying hidden beneath the tablet.<-

<margin>The Anagogical <note>The "anagogical" sense refers to the highest level of spiritual or mystical interpretation, leading the mind upward toward divine realities.</note> sense of the Bembine tablet.</margin>
<margin>The fourfold World of the Egyptians.</margin>
<margin>The Archetypal World.</margin>
<margin>The figures in the middle region of the Bembine tablet are mirrors of divine virtues.</margin>
<margin>The figures in the highest region of the Bembine tablet are Ideas of divine intellections.</margin>
<margin>The figures in the lowest region of the Bembine tablet are the Fountain-Fathers.</margin>
<margin>The border of the Bembine tablet contains the Ideas existing in the divine Mind.</margin>

We have taught in various places throughout this Work that the Egyptians established a fourfold World: namely, the Archetypal, the Intellectual, the Sidereal, and the Elementary; within which the entire universe of things was contained. The Archetypal World—divine, infinite, immutable, eternal, and incorporeal—was called the divine intellect of the triform Deity <note>original: "triformis Numinis"; likely referring to Kircher's conception of an Egyptian Trinity (Osiris, Isis, Horus).</note>, containing all other lower Worlds within itself under a simple and essential unity of nature. It is from this world, as if from a creative vein of all things, that whatever is, was, or shall be, proceeds. From the Ocean of its immense goodness all things flow forth, all things exist, all things are animated, and all things are preserved. In its intellect, all Worlds—both intellectual and sensible—exist so united under ideal and archetypal principles <note>original: "rationibus"</note> that there is nothing in the nature of things, nor can there be, which does not lie hidden therein like an effect within its cause.

Indeed, all these things are displayed in this tablet through material symbols joined together in a varied fabric of figures and through hidden chains of similarities. This heap of emanations was first participated in by the "all-formed" <note>original: "pantamorpha"</note> nature of the World, or the paternal source constituted from three triads, as the sacred figures of the middle region of the tablet show. These are nothing other than mirrors of the divine virtues which shine in the intelligible archetype, and the seals of the ideal notions with which the first minds after God are marked, so that they may operate according to the pattern of the divine model. From these, the twelve Governors of the World <note>original: "Mundi Rectores"</note> contained in the highest region of the tablet participate in all influences; in the archetype, they are nothing other than the Ideas of divine intellections emanating from infinite goodness and beauty, according to which they administer the lower realms. There follow the Fountain-Fathers <note>term: Fontani Patres. In Neoplatonic and Hermetic thought, these are primordial generative principles or "fathers" who act as sources for specific chains of being.</note>, the preservers of the great gates of the Universe, who are all displayed in the lower region of the tablet; they receive influence according to the Ideas existing in the paternal Mind and communicate that influence to the regions of the World. The border <note>original: "Limbus"</note>, moreover, contains the Ideas existing in the divine Mind, through which all the particulars of the Worlds are regarded, as has been said. By all these things, they indicate nothing other than the concatenations of beings from the highest point down to the lowest matter. Let us see, then, how this is demonstrated through hidden symbols.

->It is known from the Theology of the Egyptians, that all things in whatever way good<-

# TREATISE I. THE ISIAC TABLE. CHAPTER V.

...things that participate in it, the Good must first precede them; which is indeed nothing other <margin>The first and unshared Good is God.</margin> than that very Good which all things desire. Just as there is no other being beyond it, so there is no other Good; it is, namely, the first Cause of Causes. Truly, this Cause can neither exist nor be conceived by any reasoning without goodness, since the Good is diffusive of itself <note>A central Neoplatonic idea: goodness naturally overflows and creates.</note>; from this comes the production of all things. However, it could not produce anything at all unless it contained within itself the multitude of all things already produced, as well as those yet to be produced, since no one can give what they do not possess. All these things are beautifully hinted at through the **Lotus-measure of the Lotus, the Acacia, the Heliotropes, and the flowers and leaves of the Persæa** <note>The Persæa was a sacred Egyptian tree, often identified with the Mimusops laurifolia</note>, which are carried and turned toward the celestial bodies by a certain hidden motion, and with which the entire Table is filled. From this it is clearly evident that all things are in God, God is in all things, all things are the same in all, and any one thing is in any other. For indeed, in <margin>Lower things are contained in higher things.</margin> the Angelic or Intellectual World, there exist the same beings that are in the sensible <note>The world perceived by the senses.</note> World, but in a spiritual and invisible manner. In the Divine Archetypal World—which is supramundane, uncreated, infinite, and incomprehensible—both the Angelic and the Sensible worlds are one and the same, existing together in a divine and most perfect way. Therefore, the lowest things show the highest, corporeal things declare the intellectual, and the invisible things are perceived through those things which have been made. And this was the reason why the Egyptians used the sensible images of the lower World, established in various transformations: <margin>The Egyptians ascended to higher things through the lower.</margin> for through the natures and properties of lower and earthly things, the Egyptians ascended into the natures and properties of the superior and celestial. For these lower things are external and visible patterns, marks of the superior, and symbols of the invisible internal realities, by which they were led from corruptible things to the virtues of incorruptible beings. For they knew <margin>The visible world is the shadow of the invisible God.</margin> that the whole of creation, and this vast machine of the World—in which God, the invisible Creator of all, exhibits Himself to us to be seen, heard, tasted, smelled, and touched—is nothing other than the shadow of God, and the figure and <term>ectypon</term> <note>original: "ectypon" - a Greek term for a copy or reproduction of a model.</note> of the internal paradise. Indeed, the light of nature itself proved to them that all things which appear in the sensible World clothed in a corporeal garment are contained in the archetypes in an invisible and spiritual manner. Since they established a fourfold World—**the Archetypal, the Intellectual, the Sidereal <note>The world of the stars and planets.</note>, and the Elemental**—and saw one within the other, they necessarily recognized that the lower are ruled by the higher and receive the influence of their powers. Thus, the Archetypal Mind itself and the Maker of all things pours out the virtues of His infinite power, first through His own depth, then through the "fecund Gods" (that is, the Intelligences), <margin>The Egyptians understood that lower things are governed by higher things.</margin> the heavens, stars, elements, living creatures, plants, metals, and stones. And so, through a continuous ascent or descent, they revolved now from God to the creatures, from intellectual things to external forms, as if from the center to the circumference; and at other times they were carried from the lowest visible forms of things to invisible forms, as if from the circumference to the center. Thus, they even beheld the entire Universe in a single grain of seed; for just as they saw the whole tree—with its root, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits—folded within a single invisible grain of seed, so in the Intellectual nature, they saw the forms and seeds of all lower things folded in a spiritual or intellectual manner...

He argues that Egyptian symbols like the Lotus and Acacia were used to contemplate the divine unity present in all creation.</summary>

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...they contemplated these things in a folded state <note>original: "plicata"; referring to the Neoplatonic idea that all effects are "folded" within their cause</note>; the symbol of this was the phallus so often displayed in the Tablet, which the images of the Intellectual World <note>The realm of pure angelic thought above the physical world</note> carry before them or have attached to them. By this, all things were indicated to be filled with "seminal reasons" <note>term: seminal reasons (rationes seminales); the hidden spiritual blueprints or seeds from which all physical things grow</note>.

<margin>The Angel folds all things into itself, but in an Angelic manner.</margin>
For the Angel carries and possesses all things within itself in an Angelic and spiritual way; indeed, it folds the entire machine of the World within itself. Whatever nature can do, or whatever art can do through nature, the Angel—being established and elevated above nature and art—can do in a more excellent way. Since such is the nature of the 

<margin>God, as the first cause of all, contains all things.</margin>
Angel, then certainly the first and supreme Cause, existing from itself and independent, must be judged to fold all things within itself in an invisible and incomprehensible way, within the abyss of its divinity and in its fountain-like unity, in the simplest manner. For He is the one who is all in all, namely the first and last cause of things.

<margin>Every effect remains in its cause, proceeds from it, and returns to it.</margin>
For every effect <note>original: "causatum"</note>, as the Egyptians say, remains in its cause, proceeds from it, and returns to it, just as the lotus flower turns toward the Sun; since all progression is brought about through the likeness of the secondary things to the primary.

<margin>The bringing forth of all things from God.</margin>
For from the supreme intellect, through its paternal depths, light first proceeds—that is, the Angelic World. From that light come the invisible virtues of things, which some call the stars; from the stars comes the sensible World composed of the four Elements. And thus all things are in all things in their own way, and one remains in the other, just as the seed is in the tree, and the tree is in the seed. All visible bodies or elements are in the invisible stars or spiritual elements, and the stars are in the bodies; the stars are in the Angels, and the Angels are in the stars;

<margin>Higher things are in the lower, and these in the higher.</margin>
the Angels are in God, and God is in the Angels. Therefore, just as all things are in God divinely, and in the Angels angelically, so all things are in the World corporally, and vice versa. The entire machine of the World is in God, God is in the Angels as an Angel, and in the stars as the stars; and just as the seed is a folded tree, and the tree is an unfolded seed, so God is the World folded <note>original: "complicatus"</note>, and the World is, so to speak, God unfolded <note>original: "euolutus"</note>.

<margin>Proclus.</margin>
For as Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note> rightly says: *The property of every divine order permeates through all things fruitfully, and gives itself to all lesser kinds.*

<margin>The fertilizing power of God is in all things, in a manner proper to them.</margin>
[That is, in the supreme Mind of all, the fertilizing power, for example, is in the Angels in their own way, in souls, in the heavens, the elements, and in things composed of these—animals, plants, stones, and the other grades of beings—in each in its own way. For each thing carries a property from its own nearest cause, according to which it has been allotted its substance. For a stone participates in the fertilizing power insofar as it is suited to be multiplied by material fertility; but a plant participates in it vitally, an animal sensitively, the heavens movingly, a soul rationally, an Angel intellectually, and God super-essentially, uniformly, and divinely. The entire series possesses the same power from one divine cause, as the <term>Egyptian Theology</term> <note>A reference to the "Theologia Aristotelis," a text then attributed to Aristotle but actually based on Plotinus</note> shows in Book 10, Chapter 2. The same must be said of the remaining divine emanations; for all the series of divine progressions are assimilated to their own principles, maintaining a circle without beginning or end through the return to their principles. All these things are indicated in the Tablet through an ingenious weaving of most hidden symbols, as we have explained. And that the Egyptians felt this way, their <term>Theology</term>—first explained by their disciple Plato and written down by Aristotle—shows in these words in Book 8, Chapter 3.

<margin>Aristoteles.</margin>

We say, therefore, that this entire sensible world <note>The world perceived by the senses.</note> is an image of another; <margin>The visible world is an image of the invisible.</margin> for which reason, since this world is full of life, it is all the more necessary that that other world lives; for if this one exists as perfect, that one is even more perfect, since it imparts life, power, perfection, and perpetuity to this one. If the highest sphere is supremely absolute, without doubt its beings are also more absolute than the others existing here. There, therefore, stand other heavens endowed with stellar virtues, just like the heavens of this world, except that they are of a higher species, more lucid and greater, and they are not distant from one another as these are, for they are incorporeal; there also exists a land, not an inanimate substance, but vivid; in it are animals, all natural and terrestrial, <margin>Lower things exist in a more excellent way in higher things, according to Aristotle.</margin> just as here, but of another species and perfection; there are sown plants, and gardens, and flowing water, as if animate; there are likewise aquatic animals, but more noble; there exists air, and in it animals proper to it, living simply and entirely immortal; and although those animals are of the same nature as these, they are nevertheless more honorable than them, being intellectual, perpetual, and unalterable. If anyone should object and ask from where the plants of heaven and the other aforementioned things come to be in the superior world, we shall respond: all things exist within the perfect superior world because they were produced in it by the first Author, absolute and inherent; therefore, all intellects and souls are present there, nor is there any defect such as want or corruption; for the beings there are full of abundance, strength, and contribution, being sublime in life, and having sprung from one source, and marked by one quality embracing all others, such as sweet tastes, fragrant odors, clear colors, harmonic sounds, tactile things, and other perfections; nor do the parts there vex one another, nor are they mixed together, nor do they mutually corrupt; but each is preserved perfectly according to the best reason of its essential habit, distinct; and since they are simple, they nevertheless contain many reasons without an internal plurality of themselves or increase, as bodies are multiplied and increased. Thus far the Author of Egyptian Theology; <note>Likely referring to the "Theology of Aristotle," a Neoplatonic text attributed to Aristotle in the Renaissance.</note> but not everything he says here is to be approved.

### §. II.

-> **On the use of the Ideas of this Table, and the benefit emerging therefrom in Medicine, Physics, Astrology, and Ethics.** <-
<margin>The use and utility of the Ideas of the Bembine Table.</margin>

As Ideas are of a noble and most eminent nature, so the Egyptians recognized many <margin>Three grades of the Ideas of the Bembine Table.</margin> and distinguished benefits through them; all of which are divided into three grades, according to the triple region of the table. The first pertains to the uncreated mind; the second to the order of things, the last <margin>The first grade pertains to the uncreated Mind.</margin> to man. If we turn to the first, we shall see that the Ideas contribute greatly to the knowledge of the mind and the functions of its duties; for the Mind, turned into itself, knows all things through Ideas; knowing them, it produces them; and having produced them, it cares for and preserves them; if the Ideas were removed, one could not think rightly concerning the knowledge of the divine Mind, nor the state of things depending on it, nor providence—

<margin>The second grade pertains to the order of things.</margin> we are able to perceive. If we consider the second grade according to the Egyptians, we shall find that fate and immutable laws are derived from the Ideas; for since there is a constant and upright order in nature, not falling to it by chance, it must depend upon some first, firm, constant, and immutable order; such is the order of Ideas in the primary Mind. Furthermore, they thought that the Ideas contributed greatly to the connection of the things which depend upon them, to the ascent and descent of the grades of nature, and consequently to the antipathy and sympathy of the individual parts of the World, which are viewed by us not without admiration. <margin>Ideas contribute to the connection of things.</margin> From this sympathy arises the origin of natural magic <term>magia naturalis: the study of hidden natural forces and their correspondences</term>; which among the Egyptian Sages was at all times held in the highest esteem. <margin>Natural magic among the Egyptians took its origin from the knowledge of the sympathy and antipathy of things.</margin> Moreover, Ideas contribute to the generation of things; <margin>Ideas contribute to the generation of things.</margin> for females would not give birth to animals, or plants <note>original: "animalia, aut plantas"</note>, unless they included a forming power, as was proved a little while ago; but they would not include it, unless they received it from the soul; they cannot receive it from the soul, unless it were contained within it; it would not be contained, unless the soul received it from the mind by the gift of the Ideas, and the Mind finally from the very single head of the Ideas. It follows that the first beginnings of mortal things must be eternal; otherwise they would not be beginnings; however, proper eternal principles of things would not be given, unless Ideas were given. Furthermore, Ideas serve so that things, which are but shadows in matter, may truly exist somewhere; that those which flow in Matter may remain firm somewhere; that those which are insensible with the body alone, may be rendered intelligible; and that those which lack perfection with matter may be finished and perfected through something else. Finally, if we turn to the third grade, we shall see many utilities shine forth from the Ideas within it: for they contribute to its knowledge; <margin>The third grade pertains to man. Ideas contribute to understanding.</margin> nor could man, by understanding the essences of things, reach them unless there were inserted into his soul reasons <note>original: "rationes," referring to the rational principles or blueprints of things</note> corresponding to the Ideas; for only external accidents are offered to the senses. Whence, unless the soul be elevated through these reasons to the Ideas, and joined with the mind, it can neither be said to properly know nor understand, but only to opine rightly or wrongly. From this connection of the soul with the mind and the Ideas, it depends that a man devoted to contemplation dominates and commands the body, not only his own, <margin>Ideas contribute to divination according to the Egyptians. Plotinus.</margin> but also the nature of other constant things. Finally, from the series of reasons and Ideas, divination and Prophecy take their origin in man, which the Egyptians pursued with such great zeal, as will be said later; so that it ought not to seem a wonder that it was said by Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) whose works heavily influenced Kircher's interpretation of Egypt</note>, that the intellect of a contemplating man, although it seems to be in the East, can nevertheless behold those things which happen in the West; and while he is in one place, he can work miraculously in another very distant one, and moreover move others by his knowledge; for a man then truly contemplates when he is joined with his principle, and is found in it through the soul, in which those things which seem distant to us are not distant, but are joined in an eminent way, so much so that he sees through causes those things which it is scarcely given to others to behold in effects. <margin>The Ancients thought a double matter existed in things.</margin> From this wonderful connection of lower things with the middle and supreme, and the conversion of Ideas to the Idea of Ideas, the ancient Sages deduced that a double reason <note>or "account/nature"</note> exists in each grade of Beings; one visible, the other invisible; but the visible proceeds from the invisible just

For this sensible, earthly body is not (as they themselves think) properly an element, but the *body* of an element; however, the element properly so-called is life and spirit, in which the stars—or the invisible virtues of things and the "spermatic reasons" <note>The formative spiritual blueprints of physical things</note>—lie hidden, by which all things are produced, each according to its own species. The fiery element, from its internal and astral element, confers light and heat upon all the remaining bodies of the world. For as the Egyptians say, just as the earth brings forth leaves, flowers, and fruits from its internal element, so the fiery element, from its internal element, produced the sensible stars in the nature of things, in the firmament, and in the other Heavens. ### § III.

->**Concerning the Theurgic or Magical sense, by which the Priests, in this Isiac tablet, exhibited the method of instituting sacrifices, and the arrangement of rites and ceremonies through an occult context of symbols.**<- <margin>The theurgic or magical sense of those things contained in the Bembine Tablet.</margin>

**T**he ancient Priests thought that something great and ineffable lay hidden beneath the correct and uncorrupted <margin>The power of sacrifices rightly performed according to the Ancients.</margin> exhibition of sacrifices; hence, if they did not rightly perform even a single ceremony of the rites, they were certain that the entire theurgic work would fall into failure, as Iamblichus <margin>Iamblichus</margin> <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the Egyptian mysteries</note> testifies. Hence there was such great care in instituting sacrifices rightly and legitimately, such great preparation of soul and body, such great purifications, washings, and expiations. For since <margin>What those about to sacrifice attended to.</margin> sacrifices [have] a great, indeed necessary [connection] with the orders of things and the chains of the Gods...

...they recognized that they possessed a dependency and connection through these chains; certainly, they believed they would achieve their prayers by no other means more effectively than if they established their sacred rites according to the patterns of each rank and the ideal principles. They also knew that the first <term>Hieromants</term> <note>Priests or initiates who interpret sacred mysteries</note>, seized by a certain divine frenzy, had discovered these things arranged in such an order and adorned with such mysteries, so that the very primary ideas of things, exhibited through a mystical weaving of symbols, would signify the work to be performed. <margin>The Bembine Tablet contains the method for sacrificing correctly.</margin> All these things they placed before the eyes of those sacrificing in the <term>adytas</term> <note>The innermost, most sacred shrines of a temple, restricted to priests</note> by means of this <term>Isiac Tablet</term> <note>Also known as the Bembine Tablet, a famous bronze tablet depicting Egyptian deities and rituals</note>, so that from it they might learn the principles of the individual Gods and perform sacrifices according to the prescribed laws. For since the individual ranks of the Gods were established with their own symbols, gestures, garments, and ornaments—by which they might express the nature, property, and action of each—it was therefore judged right to appear in the sight of the Gods while performing sacred rites with an analogous and entirely similar condition of things. This was done so that they might finally obtain what they sought through this symbolic apparatus, than which they believed nothing could be more powerful, nothing more effective, and nothing more forceful for attracting the Gods and Spirits. <margin>The higher things rejoice in the lower, and the latter in the former.</margin> For the higher things rejoice in the lower, as causes do in their effects; and the lower things rejoice in the higher, as those upon whom they solely depend and by whose influences they subsist. The floor and walls of the Adytas, etc.</margin> And so the Initiates established their <term>adytas</term>—which were hidden places, removed from all human company—with such industry that there was almost nothing in the nature of things that was not contained therein. And first, indeed, the floor exhibited the economy of the lower or <term>material world</term> <note>original: "hylæi Mundi"</note> with a symbolic apparatus suited to it, being adorned with every kind of mineral and stone and fertile with small streams; the walls were expressed with symbols of the Sidereal World; the Dome exhibited the principle of the World of Spirits; in the center of which an altar was placed, representing as it were the center of the emanations of the Supreme Mind, which were then diffused into the periphery of all the Worlds. Thus, the adytas represented nothing other than the universal series of the Worlds, for the knowledge of which no one was deemed fit unless, having left behind the senses and cast aside the care for fleeting things, he withdrew himself entirely within himself; which the adytas themselves signified by their hidden recesses. <margin>The dress of those sacrificing among the Egyptians. The dress of the figures on the Bembine Tablet teaches the disposition of those sacrificing.</margin> In sacrifices, therefore, they appeared in a similar dress to that by which they represented the Gods. The half-naked and lean bodies of the figures taught that the Priests ought to be naked from all care for sensible things and devoted to abstinence, by which the lust for pleasures is restrained. They keep their private parts covered to indicate the purity of mind and body with which they ought to be equipped. They have their heads shaved to indicate that the care for earthly things—which was marked by the useless hairs, the excrements of the body—must be utterly rejected, which is why it was necessary for the Priests to be shaven. They wore <term>tutuli</term> <note>High, conical ornamental headdresses</note> on their heads, composed of flowers, feathers, snakes, stars, animals, flames, circles, vessels, and other similar things, by which the properties of the Spirits and the ideal principles are expressed. The Priests likewise imitated these in sacrifices, and by them it was noted that the Priest must continually contemplate the celestial ideas of the Gods, which are signified by the <term>tutuli</term>; for by doing this, they [transform] themselves into that intelligence...

They persuaded themselves that they were transformed into, united with, and in a certain way identified with that very essence which they continually revolved in their minds. Once united and enrolled in the company of the Gods, they believed they had reached the very goal of happiness as <gloss>God-bearers</gloss> <note>original Greek: θεοφορήτους (theophorētou), meaning those possessed or carried by a deity</note>. Thus, through the similarity of their operations and the use of analogically composed hymns, they judged they could infallibly draw the World Soul to whatever they desired. They established similar rules for the other regions of the table and the images of the Gods. Hence, from the entire series of worldly things, they asserted that only those were fit for drawing down a specific God which the individual objects expressed under said series. Since all these things lay hidden, involved and complicated under the Idea to which they looked, they thought that by a necessity of nature, the Spirits <term>Genii; intermediary spirits or guardian entities</term> could present themselves when drawn by those things which were analogous to them.
