Furthermore, while they contemplated the Idea expressed by the gathered objects, their mind was connected to the principal Idea; and having been rendered "God-form" through intellectual union, the mind came to know all things in the primary Idea of Ideas <margin>How the Egyptians sought the science of divination.</margin>. From this, they believed, there was born in their souls prophecy and divination, by which they believed they could give a determined judgment regarding the outcomes of future events, the successes of distant places, and impending evils. For since in the Supreme Mind all things are simultaneous and indistinct, and future things are as if present, they judged it necessary that as soon as the mind—or human intellect—was absorbed in the contemplation of the Supreme Mind and Intellect, it could consequently acquire the knowledge of all future things through this deifying union. Furthermore, all the images expressed on the table were nothing other than amulets, or certain protective <margin>All the images of the Bembine table are Amulets.</margin> charms <note>original: periapta; objects worn around the neck for protection</note>, which, as soon as they were consecrated by the said analogical arrangement of things, caused the virtue of the superior Powers they represented to be derived into them by a certain inevitable necessity. They believed that by the aid of the Spirits they noted, all occurrences of evil were turned away. Since we have treated these matters with curiosity in our *Hieroglyphic Magic and Theology* based on every kind of authority, we refer the reader there. In the cure of hidden diseases, they thought magic diagrams of this kind were of great efficacy and power <margin>The power of the Bembine table's figures in healing among the Egyptians. Isis appearing in sleep teaches the method of healing.</margin>. For the Spirits, to whom they paid sacred dues with the stated rites and ceremonies, were thought to appear in sleep to those who had been purified by previous preparation, and to teach them the healing of diseases; just as Astrampsychus <note>A legendary Egyptian priest and magus often cited in Hermetic literature</note> relates concerning the Sacred Scribe. ### Section IV.
#### ->*Concerning the hieroglyphic significance of the small character, which is placed everywhere near the images; and by which the two interior borders are seen to be inscribed.*<-

<margin>
The significance of the small hieroglyphic characters on the Bembine Tablet.
</margin>
In this tablet, certain small hieroglyphic characters are seen written next to almost every individual image; the middle circuit of the central region of the tablet, marked G H I K, is also marked by them. These must be dealt with in this place, lest we seem to have hidden anything from the curious Reader in the exposition of this table. It must be noted, therefore, as we have hinted elsewhere, that the Egyptian characters were so arranged that they did not exhibit a latent sense through a context of letters in the manner of the Greeks or Latins; rather, there was hidden beneath them a certain <term>Ideal concept</term> <note>Kircher's core theory: hieroglyphs represent complex divine ideas directly to the mind, rather than phonetic sounds or words.</note>, so that as soon as they looked upon one of them, they would come into the knowledge of a hidden meaning. For example, if the figure of a Hawk <note>original: "Accipitris"</note> occurred, they would form a judgment concerning the hidden properties of the Solar Divinity based on the innate faculties of this bird, without further discourse, as we have taught in the specific <term>Hierogrammatism</term> <note>A sacred symbolic description or "sacred writing" of a specific figure.</note> of the Hawk.

<margin>
Hieroglyphic characters as marks of concepts.
</margin>

<margin>
Hieroglyphic characters assumed from all things pertaining to sacrifices.
Various uses of hieroglyphic characters.
</margin>
Secondly, it must be noted that these characters were assumed from all things whose use was in sacred rites, as if they were the recondite symbols of the Gods: for just as they looked toward the analogous chains of the Worlds and were connected by them, so too they were believed to contain great power and efficacy in <term>Theurgic operation</term> <note>Theurgy: "God-working" or rituals intended to invoke the presence or action of a deity.</note> for soliciting the Gods. And first, indeed, their use was in forming the said concepts of Ideal notions; secondly, in the manufacturing of amulets, which we see marked everywhere with similar characters, as we shall reveal in the following; thirdly, they stood in the place of hymns and adjurations, by which they solicited a certain specific Divinity <note>original: "Numen"</note>; and those small characters, which you see placed near almost all the images, signify hymns or adjurations of this kind. The inscription marked with the letter Q, enclosed within the sacred table, denotes an amulet which they used to propitiate the <term>Mendesian Deities</term><note>Gods associated with the Egyptian city of Mendes, often linked to fertility and the ram-god Banebdjedet</note>. The second inscription, marked with the letter R, contains these characters: the first signifies the bandages of Osiris; the second, the Heavens; the third, a <term>Canopic vessel</term><note>A jar used to hold internal organs, or here, a symbol of water and the Nile</note>; the fourth, a semicircle; the fifth, a Serpent; and the sixth, a bird in a Nilotic vessel. <margin>Interpretation of several hieroglyphic characters.</margin> The meaning of these is as follows: *The variety of the operations of the Sun and Moon descends from the celestial World into the moist substance of Canopus, by which influx life is given in the lower World; and the Nilotic Spirit adapts and disposes this for the fertility of things.* Furthermore, the Priests, when about to sacrifice to the <term>Ammonian choir</term><note>The assembly of gods or priests associated with Amun</note>, would pronounce the reading of these characters in words conceived in this manner: <margin>The reading of hieroglyphic characters among the Egyptians.</margin> *By the bandages of the celestial Osiris, by the motion of Canopus, by the <term>Ophionian power</term><note>original: "Ophioniam vim" - referring to serpentine or primordial creative force</note>, by the sacred Hawk of the Nile, we adjure thee to grant us this or that.* Then, they would inscribe those same things upon some appropriate stone, or an idol, or some other material; by the wearing of which amulet, they persuaded themselves through Magical superstition that they held the invoked Demon to be propitious. Indeed, what the Egyptians expressed through characters, their disciple Orpheus observed throughout his hymns; <margin>Orpheus followed the Egyptians in his prayerful hymns;</margin> who, after describing the virtues of the Gods at great length, finally adds a form of prayer at the end, in these and similar conceived words: *But I pray to the Goddess, the august queen, to come deeply to the sacred initiate.* <note>original Greek: Ἀλλὰ Θεὰν λίτομαι σεμνὴν βασίλειαν ἐλθεῖν βαθύτην ἐκ' ἱερῷ τῷ μύστῃ.</note> For all antiquity attributed a great deal to hymns, as the sole incitement for either appeasing or petitioning the Gods. I would explain more extensively that these minute hieroglyphic characters exhibited such things, if the growth of this Work permitted it in any way; for to confirm the meanings of each of these symbols with authorities, it would be necessary to build a new Work. Therefore, lest the Reader be confounded by such a great multitude of things, it seemed best in this place not so much to explain their significations as to point them out. It adds to this that I deliberately do not explain every detail; for since they involve the hidden adjurations and entangled invocations of Demons, I judged them more worthy of darkness than light, lest I might seem to give the incautious Reader an occasion for learning ancient Magic.

But before I conclude this present argument, another matter no less worthy of consideration occurs in the present table; and that is the inner border, situated between the uppermost border (distinguished by a variety of figures, which we have already explained) and the three interior regions which it encloses, remarkable for its mysterious circuit. There you see, intertwined in various paths after the manner of writings, images now of flowers, now of stars, and a little later of various faces; where among the rest appears the head of Serapis with a <term>modius</term><note>A grain-measure basket worn as a crown, symbolizing abundance</note> on his head, which a little later, with flowers and small stars mediating, is followed by the head of Isis, or <term>All-formed Nature</term><note>original: "Pantamorphæ naturæ"</note>, in exactly the same way as they are seen expressed below the oxen on the two columns of the middle region, M and H; and they are repeated again and again in this order around the circuit of the border. It is asked, therefore, whether this border was instituted merely for the sake of ornament, or to signify something more sublime? I respond that the genius of the Egyptians was so disposed that they wished nothing, however small, to be devoid of mysteries; and this is evident from the said border:

# CHAPTER V. 144 THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>SYN-</margin>

...it holds: which, although it may seem to have been added merely for the sake of ornament, nevertheless also possesses a certain hidden allusion to the characteristic <term>Theosophy</term><note>Divine wisdom or the study of God's presence in the world</note> between which it mediates. Indeed, by those lines with which the principal images of the Gods are interconnected, they hint—as if by certain silent signs—that from the supreme <term>All-Forming Mind</term><note>original: "Pantamorpha Mens"; a Neoplatonic concept of the divine intellect that contains the forms of all things</note> down to the final Serapis (namely the subterranean Osiris, whom we have called Pluto), all the series of intermediate Worlds are bound together by a certain wonderful concatenation. They are joined in such a way that from the first Divinity of all, down to the very last through the intermediaries, the influences—expressed by the likeness of agents and patients—are diffused in a marvelous order into all the paths of the Worlds. Thus, there is nothing that does not participate in the principles of its own life, motion, and action from such a beneficial and necessary diffusion. You have, therefore, the interpretation of the proposed border, expressed not so much as an ornament, but as a type of mysterious significance. Nothing remains, then, except that, having completed the exposition of the Isiac Table, we now begin—with God's blessing—the explanation of the Obelisks with equal pace and daring.

# TREATISE II.
->**The Ramesseum Obelisk, or the Lateran Obelisk.**<-

### PREFACE.

Since the form, mysteries, proportions, measurements, and other properties of obelisks were treated at length in the section on the Pamphilian Obelisk, it seems nothing further remains for this section except to first set forth the history of each individual monument proposed here, and then to explain their mysteries and secret meanings; this we promise to do in this Treatise. May God, the Best and Greatest, favor our daring efforts and prosper what we have begun.

## CHAPTER I.

### Historical account of the Ramesseum or Lateran Obelisk.

<margin>
History of the Ramesseum Obelisk.
</margin>

In the year 1097 after the Flood, and 1297 before the salvation of the human race <note>i.e., 1297 BC</note>, there arose in Egypt King Rameses, son of Sothis. Following his father's example, he had erected several obelisks, but remained unsatisfied. Nursing thoughts in his deep breast worthy of so great a King, <margin>
Rameses, son of Sothis, erects the greatest obelisk of all.
</margin>he set his mind to erecting another—one that would be the most mysterious and the largest of all those ever established in Egypt, whether you consider its mystical proportions or the vastness of its bulk. It is said that twenty thousand men labored in its cutting, carving, and erection. And <margin>
20,000 men expend their labor on erecting the Ramesseum Obelisk. Rameses ties his son to the tip of the Obelisk. Pliny.
</margin>because he feared that during the raising, such a mass might be broken by its extreme weight, he saw to it that his own son was tied to the pinnacle. He did this so that the architects, spurred by reverence for the prince and a desire for his safety, would perform a work of such great importance with more caution and circumspection. So says Pliny in Book 36, Chapter 8. The life and character of this King are treated abundantly in the section on the Pamphilian Obelisk.

And this indeed was the first erection of the Ramesseum Obelisk, which took place at Thebes in the Temple of the Sun, where it remained until the time when Constantine the Great shone upon the world.

<margin>
Constantine the Great builds a circus at Constantinople.
</margin>Thus, in the year 334 after Christ, the Emperor Constantine the Great—driven by the greatness of spirit in which he excelled—was laboring to make the city of Byzantium (afterwards called Constantinople after his own name) entirely similar to Rome in all things, whether you consider its size or the magnificence and majesty of the wonderful works to be seen therein. Among other memorable things, he <margin>
Constantine the Great sends to Egypt to seek an obelisk.
</margin>decided to build a Circus after the model of the Roman Circus Maximus, which he indeed completed. But since all the Roman circuses were adorned with their own obelisks, he did not wish his newly constructed Circus to lack its own; he soon sent architects to Egypt to find those of the better sort...

# TREATISE II. THE RAMESSEAN OBELISK. CHAPTER I.

...Obelisks, they might bring them to Constantinople, their "New Rome." But since the predecessor Emperors—Augustus, Caius Caligula, and Caracalla—had already brought all the larger and more intact ones to Rome, and they saw that those remaining were either useless to them, corroded by the long passage of time, or too small; they were nearly ready to abandon the business in frustration. Finally, they were informed by locals skilled in antiquities that one still remained at Thebes, the largest of all that had ever been made in Egypt, standing in the Temple of the Sun. <margin>The Ramessean Obelisk was spared from fire by Cambyses.</margin> Even the extreme fury of Cambyses <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE; he was notorious for destroying temples.</note> had spared this one alone, though all the others had been ruined by fire. For while he was storming and burning the City, and the fire had reached the base of the Obelisk, he ordered the flames to be extinguished out of reverence for the massive structure—he who had shown no mercy to the City itself. This Obelisk, preserved thereafter either out of religious awe or fear of an unlucky omen <note>original: "inauspicatum... augurium"</note> that might befall them, remained whole and unharmed by both the Ptolemies and the Romans themselves. But Constantine, imbued with the new light of faith and burning with zeal for divine glory, considered the superstitions of the Heathen religion to be of no account. <margin>Constantine the Great cares for the Ramessean Obelisk to be carried to Alexandria.</margin> Once it was torn from its place, he took care to have it transported to Alexandria, intending it to be a fitting monument to his glory, to be moved soon after to Constantinople as soon as a ship capable of carrying such a massive weight could be built. But as the arrangements of human affairs are uncertain, so too was Constantine prevented by death, and he could not bring the work he had conceived to execution.

Thus, the Roman Empire having been divided among his three sons: Italy, Illyricum, and Africa fell to Constantine <note>Constantine II</note>; Gaul, Spain, and Britain to Constans; and Asia, Thrace, and Egypt to Constantius. Constantine was killed at Aquileia in the third year of his reign, leaving his brother Constans as successor to the Kingdom. But after Constans himself was slain by Magnentius at the Pyrenees mountains, Constantius, to avenge the death of his brothers, gathered an army and attacked Magnentius, defeating and prostrating him so utterly that, having lost everything and driven by despair, he died by his own hand. Constantius, elated by such a solemn victory and having brought the whole Roman Empire under his law by subjugating his enemies, hastened to Milan. After staying there a short while, he burned with a great desire to visit Rome, which he had never seen. <margin>The Emperor Constantius comes to Rome.</margin> Having entered it with the highest pomp and magnificence, and having contemplated the City so beautiful and splendid with its monuments of palaces, temples, porticoes, baths, amphitheaters, circuses, and fountains, he found everything to be greater than its reputation. Astonished by the wonder of such great works, he was fired with the desire to leave some monument of his own magnificence in the same City, as a sign of his achieved victory and his first arrival. Therefore, after various plans were considered, he remembered the Obelisk left by his father Constantine, which had been moved from Thebes to adorn the city of Constantinople. Since it was judged to be larger and more intact than all the Roman Obelisks, it seemed fitting that <margin>He orders the Ramessean Obelisk, left at Alexandria, to be transported to Rome.</margin> the one which no power of Augustus Caesar or the other Roman Emperors had been able to move from its place, the lofty soul and greatness of power of Constantius should bring to Rome and erect. And so, with his intention...

# CHAPTER I. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

After consulting with the architects, it was concluded that it should be brought to Rome as quickly as possible. Therefore, with the greatest speed, they constructed that ship—memorable for all ages and equipped with three hundred oars—to carry such a massive weight; they brought the loaded burden with the greatest success to the Roman port adjacent to the mouth of the Tiber. From there, it was carried up the Tiber <margin>The Obelisk is erected in the Circus Maximus.</margin> as far as the village of Alexander <note>The "Vicus Alexandri," a landing place on the Tiber about three miles below Rome.</note>; from here, however, the burden was placed upon carriages and rollers <term>scytalis: cylindrical rollers used for moving heavy stones</term> and was finally moved into the Circus Maximus by an infinite multitude of men. There, after the Obelisk erected by Augustus (which had been placed by him in the middle of the Circus) was set aside, Constantius erected his own in its place. He then re-erected the displaced Obelisk of Augustus at a distance of three paces, so that it might be demonstrated to anyone comparing the two how much more powerful Constantius was than Augustus, just as his Obelisk was more eminent than the other. Truly, concerning the laborious erection of this Obelisk and the multitude of men and machines, see Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 17, whom we quote at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 84. The symmetry of the parts of this Obelisk <margin>Measurements of the Ramesseum Obelisk and its parts.</margin> erected in the Circus Maximus—as is evident from the dimensions given by Michele Mercati, who measured it exactly at the time of Sixtus V when it was uncovered—is as follows: Above the pavement of the Circus Maximus, after a foundation was first laid, a base was spread, and above this a pedestal <term>abacus: the flat slab forming the top of a pedestal or column capital</term> of white marble; this, together with the base, reached a height of ten palms from the pavement. Above this, another pedestal of variegated pyrite <note>Likely referring to a speckled hard stone like granite or porphyry</note> was placed, in the shape of a cube, though somewhat wider compared to its height; specifically, it had a height of 13 1/4 palms and a width of 16 palms, composed of fragments since a single piece of such great size was not available. Following above this cubic base were four supports, which they call Astragals <term>astragalos: small moldings or supports, here likely bronze feet</term>, cast from metal and 1 1/4 palms high, arranged here and there in the four corners, upon which the entire mass of the Obelisk rested; the measurement of which is as follows:

<margin>
1st Pedestal of white marble.
2nd Pedestal of pyrite.
Astragals.
Height of the entire Obelisk.
</margin>

->The length of the entire Obelisk, exactly measured, contained 148 palms;<-

to which, if we add the astragals, the pedestals, and the bases, we find that the entire Obelisk from the ground to the summit in the time of Constantius was approximately 173 2/4 palms, which, when converted into feet, gives 132; Publius Victor also teaches that the height of the entire mass was this great. It is said that a golden ball was placed atop the Obelisk, which, after being struck down by lightning, was later replaced by Constantius with a figure made of gilded metal in the shape of a flickering flame. On the base were contained 24 hexameter verses, six on each side; since we have produced these in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, I have decided to omit them here for the sake of brevity.

<margin>The Ramesseum Obelisk is thrown down by the Goths.</margin>

And so this Obelisk of Constantius, thrown down by the savagery of the Goths, sank by the greatness of its weight into the marshy soil to a depth of 24 palms; thus it vanished from both the eyes and memory of men until the time of Pope Sixtus V, so much so that nothing but certain obscure indications from historians gave testimony that it had stood in this place.

# TREATISE II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. CHAPTER I.

Therefore, Pope Sixtus V, endowed with an incredible greatness of soul, <margin>Pope Sixtus V inquires after and finds it in the Circus Maximus.</margin> while his mind seethed with the desire to perform great deeds according to his innate genius, and as he set about restoring Rome to its ancient splendor, after many stupendous monuments left within the City in just a few years, finally turned his attention to the erection of all the Obelisks. This included this specific one, which he had learned from experts in antiquities lay hidden, buried in the earth somewhere in the Circus Maximus <note>The ancient Roman chariot-racing stadium</note>; he therefore commanded the Architects that it be sought without delay. For this purpose, a very long and sharp iron tool was first prepared, <margin>It is dug out broken into three pieces.</margin> shaped like a massive awl, which, when driven into the marshy soil, would allow a judgment to be formed regarding the hidden Obelisk from the resistance of the iron. The attempt met with a success more fortunate than anyone expected: for within a very short time, the Obelisk was detected by the aid of the iron. Soon, after the earth was dug out by a great multitude of men applying themselves tirelessly day and night, it was uncovered, broken into three pieces. However, due to the overflow of subterranean waters and the instability of the marshy ground, it rightly caused the Architect <note>Domenico Fontana, the lead engineer for Sixtus V</note> the greatest fear of successfully completing the task. Nevertheless, by his supreme industry and the strong hand of the laborers—of whom part were occupied in digging out the earth, part in draining the floods of water, and finally part in continually lifting the Obelisk by means of capstans <term>ergatas: mechanical winches used for hoisting heavy loads</term>—it came to pass that the Obelisk, dug out piece by piece, finally saw the light. Indeed, it was a work of no less expense and labor to dig it out than to erect it. The first fragment was 65 1/2, <margin>The size of the individual fragments.</margin> the second 43 1/2, and the third, together with the small pyramid at the top <term>pyramidium: the pointed capstone of an obelisk</term>, was 39 palms <note>The Roman "palmo" was approximately 22.3 cm</note> in length; these added together give the height of the Obelisk as 148 palms. The base of the Obelisk, worn down by its own fall, mutilated, and extremely decayed, was hardly sufficient to support such a mass; hence it was necessary to cut it back to a length of four palms, so that a base fit for supporting it could be obtained. Thus the Obelisk, <margin>The Ramesside Obelisk is shortened by 4 palms.</margin> having been shortened, received a lesser height than it had before, which it retains to this day: 144 palms. Once the Obelisk had been dug out with the labor I have described, there remained the no less difficult task of transporting it to the Lateran Field <note>The Piazza di San Giovanni in Laterano</note>, <margin>And it is erected in the Lateran Field.</margin> due to the long, sloping road and the arrangement of 650 perches <note>A unit of length</note>; however, with every difficulty overcome, it was conducted to the designated place, where it remains erected to this day, in that figure, form, and disposition as is evident in the illustration placed here; the summary of its measurements is as follows.

### CHAPTER III.

->Interpretation of the Lateran Obelisk.<-

->*The Subject Matter of the Lateran Obelisk.*<-

<margin>Trismegistus established the hieroglyphic doctrine.</margin>
Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure conflating the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth, regarded as the author of a vast body of sacred texts.</note>, as we have already shown in the *Politics of the Egyptians*, was the founder of the doctrine regarding not only secular but also sacred worship of the Gods. At a time when the Kingdom of Egypt was not yet stabilized by solid and firm laws—as often happens in the earliest beginnings of things—and finding it unequipped with any political discipline, he felt he was born for the common good. Thus, he seriously considered how he might introduce an exact form of living to a Kingdom that was still free and utterly disorganized. He believed this could only be achieved through the establishment of most wholesome laws, by which the unrestrained impulses of the people might be held back as if by certain barriers. However, with the great sharpness of his intellect, he noticed that no law can endure unless it is ordered and arranged according to the archetypal Idea latent in the Divine Mind, and that divine law cannot be obtained except through a religious life composed according to every norm of justice. Therefore, with the greatest zeal and no less subtlety of mind, he established a certain sacred and exceedingly mysterious Doctrine—which posterity called "hieroglyphic"—comprising 42 books, as witnessed by Clement of Alexandria <note>original: "Clemente Alexandr." Referring to the 2nd-century Christian theologian who described the 42 essential books of Hermes.</note>, in which the entire system of Egyptian Politics and Philosophy was contained.

<margin>And he delivered it to the Priests.</margin>
<margin>Prohibiting them from teaching it to any outside their own order,</margin>
<margin>And they were to engrave it in stone,</margin>
But truly, since he well knew the frailty of humans in observing laws, he established a College of Priests—men of the greatest sagacity, highly practiced in wisdom and long experience of affairs—who alone would have access to the succession of the Kingdom after the death of a King. To them he delivered the norm of the laws and bound them by oath that they should not communicate the same to any other person outside their order. To these he added Assistants of the Kingdom divided into five Classes. Furthermore, lest the laws be lost in the storms of wars or similar unhappy events of Kingdoms, he engraved them upon incorruptible stones as if to endure forever; concerning these, see Volume I of the *Politics of the Egyptians*, page 113.

<margin>Rameses orders the largest Obelisk to be adorned with hieroglyphics relating to politics.</margin>
And among these Obelisks, this Lateran one is one created by Rameses <note>Likely referring to Ramesses II or III; Kircher often attributes these monuments to "Rameses" as a central figure of Egyptian power.</note>. Having been instructed in the priestly doctrine by his father Sothis <note>A name Kircher uses for a ruler, likely derived from the Sothic cycle or lists of pharaohs</note>, the restorer of Obelisks, he excerpted from the Mercurial books <note>The "Books of Hermes/Mercury" mentioned above.</note>—which we proved were surviving in the time of Sothis in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on the authority of Sozomen, Eusebius, Africanus, and other authors—all the best dictates regarding the arrangement and preservation of the politics of Kingdoms. Because these were of the greatest importance in human affairs, he engraved them upon the largest of all Obelisks ever made, as if to last for eternity.

<margin>The Ramesseum Obelisk contains the method of ordering the Political and Archetypal World.</margin>
This Obelisk therefore shows, first of all, how the political World is to be ordered according to the principles of the archetypal and sidereal World, so that it may be able to subsist, since...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Obeliscus Ramessaeus within Syntagma II of Kircher's Oedipus Aegyptiacus. It establishes the philosophical and political foundation for the obelisk's inscriptions, linking the Egyptian state structure to a cosmic hierarchy.</meta>

# TREATISE II. THE RAMESSEAN OBELISK. CHAPTER II.

Since no Kingdom or Empire can stand unless it is founded upon religion, the **Egyptians** <note>original: *Ægyptij*</note> knew that the fear of the Gods was of the greatest value in keeping subjects bound to their duty. Furthermore, just as the Ideas of the archetypal World are infallible and embrace all parts of justice—subject to no error—through a certain ineffable reason; <margin>Human laws established according to the norm of divine laws have power.</margin> so they believed that human laws, established according to the norm and immutable exemplar of the first law existing in the Divine Mind, would likewise obtain an infallible effect. For the Supreme Deity of all Deities, while He governs the Universe with such equity of laws, disposes it with such providence, and preserves it with such love and benevolence—what else does He exhibit to us but a certain most absolute exemplar <margin>God is the exemplar of the Monarchical state.</margin> of the **Monarchical state**? What of the Genial or Angelic World, distributed into so many Classes, distinguished into such various duties and ministries, and conspicuous for such an admirable disposition of orders? In this world, although there are various and disparate degrees of dominion <margin>Angels are the exemplar of the Aristocratic state.</margin> and subjection, all nevertheless seem to busy themselves with this one thing: that, linked together by one will and purpose, they conspire toward the preservation of the Universe. What is this but a most absolute exemplar of **Aristocratic dominion**, whose entire happiness is union and the harmony of the Best Men <note>Kircher uses "Optimates," referring to the ruling aristocratic class</note>; its stability being the love and care for the common good in each individual? Finally, what does this sensible machine of the World—composed of the orbits of the stars and the mobile and unstable mixture of corruptible elements—exhibit, <margin>The sensible World is the exemplar of the Democratic state.</margin> if not the form of a **Democratic state**, which we see is as much more dangerous as it is exposed to the tumults of factious men?

<margin>The Egyptians care for the Monarchical state.</margin> Therefore, the Egyptians, considering these things more attentively, judged that state to be more fit for preservation which was more similar to the archetypal Monarchy and less subject to changes; in which the Angelic Spirits obey the nod of one Monarch, the supreme moderator of things, and in which each individual class of created things in this sensible World is subjected to an absolute and perfect dominion. They applied themselves with the greatest zeal to adorn their own Monarchy according to this norm of the Monarchical state, as if after a certain exemplar. In this, the King as Monarch, in the place of the supreme Deity, moderated all things with a certain architectonic intellect; the Priests <margin>The members of the Egyptian Monarchy: King, Priests, People.</margin> were the Aristocrats, or Citizens of the political World, who were distributed into a fivefold order: the **Singers**, the **Horoscopes** <note>Priests who observed the hours and stars</note>, the **Hierogrammatists** <term>Sacred Scribes: experts in hieroglyphic writing and religious law</term>, the **Stolists** <term>Robers: priests responsible for dressing the sacred statues and maintaining ritual purity</term>, and the **Prophets**. The people, however, although distinguished into various duties, were left to the judgment of the one Monarch. And the Obelisk exhibits all these things. For they persuaded themselves that if these things were rightly arranged, the Egyptian Kingdom would endure in its peace and unshaken happiness. Moreover, the Egyptians exhibit all these things on the Obelisk through twelve columns, of which <margin>The subject matter of the Ramessean Obelisk.</margin> each side contains three, which correspond to the three aforementioned Worlds. In this, it is taught how, according to the reasons of the archetypal intellect, the Priests (who might have hope for the Kingdom) ought to be inaugurated, and with what rites and ceremonies they are to be consecrated; then, how all-forming nature insinuates itself into the three Worlds, from which the life and happiness of said Worlds result.

This is proposed, moreover, as a certain prototype, so that according to it, the laws—

# CHAPTER II.

<margin>
What Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon signify in the political world.
</margin>
...that they may establish laws beneficial to the Kingdom; and that they may understand by what means Osiris and Isis resist the tyranny of Typhon, and how Horus—as well as Osiris, who was slain by Typhon—may be restored to life. By **Osiris**, they indicate the *architectonic intellect* <note>The "master-building" or governing mind</note> of the King; by **Isis**, they mean *prudence*; by **Horus**, *salutary laws*; and by **Typhon**, they understand everything troublesome that disturbs the Kingdom. Therefore, if the state of the Republic should at any time fall from the height of its prosperity through discord and the treasons of factional and rebellious men, the Obelisk teaches by what methods they ought to guard against similar damages to the common good, or by what rites and ceremonies the presiding Spirits <note>original: *Genij*—local guardian spirits or tutelary deities</note> of those places are to be appeased against all dangers of adversity. For just as the Supreme Deity, through a many-formed spirit, insinuates itself into all members of the world-machine, brings harmony to disagreements, and grants life to sluggish and nearly desperate affairs—being "all in all"—so too the King, through the care and vigilance of the governors he has appointed over the individual provinces of the Kingdom, ought to be present and inherent in each and every thing through the dictates of his subjects, conforming to the King's intellect. For from this, love and concord are born; from this arises a unanimous conspiracy <note>In the Latin sense of "breathing together" or uniting</note> to overthrow whatever rebellious machinations are harmful to the Kingdom, which is the safety and sole support of the Realm.

<margin>
The King ought to be present in all affairs of his Kingdom.

The source of concord in kingdoms.
</margin>

Yet it happens from time to time that, on account of the iniquity and injustice committed by a King, the dictates of the subjects become distorted; from this, Typhonian conspiracies contrary to the common good are soon born. Just as these gradually withdraw from the law of the Supreme Deity, so they are like the immediate stages leading to the ruin and destruction of the Kingdom. For the presiding Spirits appointed by the Supreme Mind, being deterred by the deformity of human law when it strays from the divine, soon desert the protection of the province committed to them; and once the character of the divine intellect and will is erased in the Prince, everything is turned upside down. The authority of the Prince toward his subjects perishes; and when that perishes, what else will remain for the Kingdom but the greatest confusion, desolation, and a total <term>disorder</term> <note>original: *ἀταξία* (ataxia)—a Greek term for lack of order or anarchy</note> of all things?

<margin>
The source of discord in kingdoms.
</margin>

Hence the Egyptians, when about to consult on matters of great importance, first purified themselves with sacrifices and sought the Oracles of the Gods through preliminary rites and ceremonies to know what should be done. For they knew that laws are inspired into men by God, a point which **Plato**—having been taught by the Egyptians—deduces most fully in his dialogues *On Laws*; for they reasoned thus from the discourses handed down by **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with Egyptian wisdom</note> on that matter:

<margin>
The Egyptians appeased the Gods with sacrifices before consultations.

Plato.
</margin>

If Nature, which is nothing other than the lowest instrument of Divine Providence, is seen to proceed so providently that she does not lead herself, but is led by Providence itself—prescribing the ends and orders of all things both within herself and inscribing them upon nature as she wills; if, I say, such a Nature neither abounds in superfluities nor fails in necessary things; then certainly it is confessed that Divine Providence will never fail in necessary matters. Now, mutual gathering <note>social assembly or society</note> is necessary for the human race, which is otherwise unable to live; and for a gathering that would otherwise quickly perish without law, law is supremely necessary. Furthermore, divine authority is equally necessary for laws, lest they either become obsolete through negligence or be shattered by fraud and violence; and to acquire this divine authority, there was a need for both sanctity of life and a punishment more to be feared than the loss of human life. For if Divine Providence...

## TREATISE II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. CHAPTER III.

He provided the necessary uses for each of the elements, plants, animals, and limbs; much more diligently, through providence, He could not fail the species of animals that participates to some extent in divinity <note>referring to humanity</note> in ordaining laws so necessary for the safety of men. For as Plato rightly says: <margin>Plato</margin> *No Prince can lead the ship of the State, tossed by whatever whirlwind, storms, and innumerable dangers, safely to port without a heavenly breeze.* Therefore, God the Best and Greatest, both through the hidden inspirations of souls and through manifest miracles, as often as <margin>God gives laws to men.</margin> necessity demands, both reveals the mysteries of laws and openly ordains and promulgates them, as the first beginning of laws and their ultimate end; without whom it is certain that human public affairs can neither be rightly composed, nor endure once composed. Hence, they strive with such great zeal to imitate the Author of laws in this present Obelisk, both in rites and ceremonies, and to care so expensively for divine worship, as will be seen in the course of the interpretation. And this is the sum of the contents in this Mercurial column <note>original: "Mercuriali columna"; a reference to Hermes Trismegistus, to whom the wisdom of the obelisks was attributed</note>. Nothing further remains, except that we undergo the risk of this most difficult and very arduous argument with the help of the good God.

# CHAPTER III.

->*Note to the Reader concerning the method of establishing the interpretation.*<-

<margin>The method of interpreting the Obelisks.</margin> We begin at last, with the help of the good God, the interpretation of the Obelisks, for the sake of which we have constructed the mass and apparatus of so great a work. And so that we may preserve a proper method in it, we shall start with those which have attained the highest fame in the monuments of ancient authors, in which the first place is deservedly claimed by the Lateran Obelisk. In its interpretation, I may perhaps run into certain "Aristarchuses" <note>severe critics, named after the Greek scholar Aristarchus of Samothrace</note> who will pierce me with their harsh "obelisks" <note>a pun on the word 'obelus', a critical mark used in ancient manuscripts to indicate doubt or error</note>, even on this account: that I have not established each and every point at length with their own authorities. But I do not fear the insolence of peevish men, since I am confident that he who knows these difficult and inaccessible sanctuaries <note>original: "adytus"; the innermost, most sacred parts of a temple</note> will rather give due thanks for the difficulties overcome by the grace of God, than <margin>The interpretation of the Ramesside Obelisk is difficult due to the very obscure matters it contains.</margin> condemn the Author for ignorance. This Obelisk is filled with so many and such abstruse matters that if I had wished to derive each point at length, a huge and vast Volume would not have sufficed to contain them; although this would not have been difficult for me if the consideration of time had permitted, yet I saw it would happen that, from such a heap of Authorities, the thread of the interpretation would be so entangled and rendered so confused that he who read the later parts would by no means perceive the connection to the earlier ones. Thus, readers might be more truly alienated by excessive boredom than attracted to the reading. Therefore, after maturely weighing the matters, it seemed more advisable to explain the great medley of things contained in this present Obelisk succinctly and briefly, so that the connection of the matters <margin>The method of interpreting the Ramesside Obelisk.</margin> to be treated in it might present itself more clearly to the Reader's mind, and the uninterrupted thread, with things arranged in order, might direct the Reader's understanding without hindrance or disturbance; which I saw would be <unclear>impeded</unclear> in a great heap of authorities. And since hieroglyphics very often...

# P R E L U D E

->*In which some things are set forth for a better understanding of the matters to be treated on the Obelisk.*<-

<margin>The nature of the figure on the Ramesseum Obelisk. The sacred hieroglyphic tablet.</margin> There occurs very frequently on the present Obelisk an oval figure, furnished with the apparatus of hieroglyphics which you see here; this we have been accustomed to call the **sacred tablet** <note>original: "sacram tabulam"; this refers to what modern Egyptologists call a cartouche.</note>. Now, the sacred tablet was a certain complex of specific hieroglyphics of great efficacy and power, because they persuaded themselves that the Deities could be reconciled to them by no better means than this or something similar. Moreover, these types of tablets differed according to the diversity of the subjects with which the Obelisks were marked. And they are called "sacred tablets" because, for the most part, having been excerpted from the Obelisks, they were carved onto separate tablets of either wood or stone for use as **prophylactics** <term>prophylactic: a protective charm or amulet intended to ward off evil or disease</term>. But let us reveal what this present oval scheme signifies.

<margin>Interpretation of the oval figure.</margin> First, there is placed inside an **Ibis** <note>The Ibis was the sacred bird of Thoth, whom Kircher identifies with Hermes/Mercury.</note> atop a **gnomon** <term>gnomon: originally the blade of a sundial; here used to mean a carpenter's square or a mechanical standard</term>, or a rule, or a mechanical support, transformed into the shape of the letter Alpha; to this is joined now a curved staff, now a hook, and sometimes an agricultural spade; below these is joined a triple inverted branch with three boundaries, in place of which the figure of a **Scarab** is very often placed, and sometimes it is even omitted, as is seen in column 1, in the region of Θ and Ρ. <margin>Laws and sciences necessary for the preservation of kingdoms. Therefore, the Ibis or Hermes rightly stands upon the gnomon: <margin>Plutarch.</margin> first because, as Plutarch witnesses, he is the *Agathodaemon*, which the figure of the gnomon composed of Α and Α <note>Kircher interprets the shape of the support as two Greek 'A' letters, symbolizing the beginning or the "First Mind."</note> sufficiently demonstrates, as was said elsewhere at length; secondly because...

And indeed, the branch of the persea was sacred to Hermes, Isis, and Osiris, as we showed in the *Pamphylian Obelisk*, folio 364; and each is conspicuous for its circuit of four leaves, by which the time of the year was divided into three parts—Spring, Summer, and Winter—each of which was likewise divided into four months, marking the course of the entire year. It was triple because it was consecrated to the three moderators of the whole year: Isis, Osiris, and Mercury—that is, the Sun, the Moon, and Mercury. # EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

GABAIM

...all things are joined together; and also to Mercury <note>The author refers to the Egyptian god Thoth, whom the Greeks and Romans identified with Hermes/Mercury</note>, who is the reason directing all things to their proper end; hence the leaves of the **Persea tree** <note>An Egyptian evergreen tree, often identified with *Mimusops schimperi*</note> take the shape of a tongue, and its fruit the shape of a heart, by which the wisdom of Mercury is aptly noted in directing the laws of nature as well as those to be imposed upon the political world. <margin>Diodorus.</margin> **Diodorus** reports that Mercury was the author of this division. By this, it was aptly suggested that all actions and operations of natural and human affairs are subject to time, in which, under fixed boundaries, the laws of all nature and the politics of the world turn as if upon a certain hinge. <margin>Theophrastus.</margin> Moreover, he is noted by the branches of the persea because, according to **Theophrastus**, the persea brings forth new fruits in each of the three portions of the year, enjoying perpetual greenness. But concerning this symbol, see the very extensive treatise in the *Pamphylian Obelisk*, page 363. There follow three boundaries <note>original: "termini"</note>, by which first the three-part division of the year, established by the laws of the supreme world, is indicated; concerning these, see at length in the *Pamphylian Obelisk*, page 425. In the political world, however, these three boundaries <margin>The three boundaries on the Rameassean Obelisk signify laws.</margin> indicate laws established according to the laws of the higher world. Hence, by the same Egyptian word, both "laws" and "boundaries" are named; the reason for this was the division of all Egypt by frequent boundary stones, because of the inundation of the Nile which confuses all things, so that in this way through boundaries—as if by certain positive laws—that which belonged to each person might be distributed by an exact measure of justice. <margin>Boundaries sacred to Mercury.</margin> For the same reason, boundaries were sacred to Mercury, so that from this you may recognize the origin of the **Herms**, which were quadrangular statues of Mercury usually placed in fields in stead of boundary markers; concerning these, see page 392 of the first volume. Finally, the eightfold mark truly denotes the face of the upper land or the Horizon.

From these things, unless I am mistaken, it is clearly evident why the Egyptians held this <margin>The sacred Hermetic tablet held in honor among the Egyptians.</margin> sacred Hermetic tablet in such high honor: because it mystically signifies all the benefits conferred upon the human race by the Hermetic power through a most hidden context of symbols, and was therefore thought to be of the highest virtue and efficacy for propitiating and attracting the said Deity.

<margin>The sacred tablet is explained.</margin> The **Sphere** indicates the essence of the supreme, invisible, and most abstract Deity, as we have taught in the *Hierogrammatism of the Circle*; from which all good things flow into all worlds, and emanate as if from a certain incomprehensible center. <margin>The twelve-towered wall.</margin> The following mural figure, the <term>dodecapyrgos</term> or "twelve-peaked" wall, first notes the twelve measurements of heaven, or the twelve houses of the Zodiac, which are called the limits of the Starry World; the guardians of these are individual Spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note> deputed by the supreme Deity, to whom the government of the whole year is committed, according to the laws prescribed to them by the Author of nature. ...the table shows the figure of the <term>seven-towered wall (heptapyrgos)</term>, by which the citadel and bulwark of the seven planets, equipped with their presiding guardians, is signified. Sometimes it is <term>four-towered (tetrapyrgos)</term>, by which <margin>The seven-towered wall; the four-towered wall.</margin> the kingdom of the four elements is indicated. Since the whole of nature is defended against harmful powers by these three bulwarks, they quite aptly expressed it through the figure of a <term>many-towered (polypyrgos)</term> wall. For just as the supreme Deity first flows into the twelve virtues and powers of the Starry World, so do these flow into the kingdom of the seven-towered [planetary] realm, and both of these into the fourfold Elemental World; it is necessary that the entire machine of the World be preserved by this union and the perpetual communication of mutual influence. Therefore, the Egyptians, turning to the laws of these three bulwarks—the Starry and the Elemental Worlds—as if to a certain model, arranged their own politics, as we shall now show.

Thus, when the Egyptians wished to represent a kingdom or a city, they placed the figure of a wall, <margin>The figure of a wall signifies a kingdom or a city on Obelisks.</margin> distinguished by twelve, seven, or four peaks <note>original: "apicibus," referring to the battlements or points atop the wall symbol.</note>, which are indicated by just as many rays, like those of a crown, expressed in the figure; and they very frequently place this figure at the base of the Obelisk. By the <term>twelve-towered (dodecapyrgon)</term> wall, or one of twelve towers or peaks, they indicate an analogy <margin>What the wall of twelve, seven, or four peaks signifies.</margin> to the celestial twelve-towered structure, both of the Ideal World and of the Zodiac in the Starry World, which are distinguished as if by twelve mansions. By the seven-towered wall, they signify the mansions of the seven planets, according to whose idea the Republic must be established. By the four-towered wall, they signify the Regions of the four Elements, which are like a certain model according to which the Republic must be governed. For just as one Sun traverses the twelve mansions of the Zodiac, which are equipped with various and differing properties, and animates them to preserve union in the World; so also a Prince in his Kingdom must, with the greatest care, animate the temperaments of diverse peoples and the minds of those differing in their diversity into unity and concord. One must reason no differently concerning the seven-towered and four-towered structures.

Plato demonstrates all these things so aptly in the 5th Dialogue of the *Laws*, that he seems to have looked back upon hieroglyphics of this kind. For from the <margin>Plato. <note>original Greek: "ἐν ἑκάστῳ τῷ θεῷ... οὕτω τέλος ἔχειν." This is a passage from Plato's *Laws*, Book VI, discussing the ideal distribution of land and tribes.</note>

That is to say: *Furthermore, the villages are to be distributed into 12 parts, just as the other resources of the citizens are; so that from the constitution of 12 parts, the purifications of the circuits may be more conveniently carried out. Twelve parts are likewise to be attributed to twelve Gods; and each part shall be named after the name of that God to whom it falls, so that the Tribe itself may be of the same name as its tutelary God. Moreover, the twelve members of the city, just as was done in the rest of the region, shall be individually divided into two habitations, one of which is near the center, the other near the edge; and the order and logic of the habitation shall be shaped in this manner.* And this is the method for establishing a city and a region according to **celestial ideas**, which Plato judged ought to be founded. But why into twelve parts? So that you may understand that so great and laborious a mass requires the help of the Universe itself, which is distributed into twelve spheres; in exactly the same way, a terrestrial city or kingdom must be managed according to the image of the **Heavenly Kingdom**. For the Heavenly City, says Plato, is distributed into twelve signs, as if into twelve tribes; and not without reason did the Greeks—just as the Egyptians did for their Kingdom—consecrate their own to their twelve Gods, who preside over the twelve signs. Indeed, there are six Gods and six Goddesses, whose names are:

Now, assign each to each: the signs to our individual limbs, and furthermore the Gods to the signs; and through these things you will understand that a city or an entire kingdom ought to be nothing other than one body made of many members, just as it is one made of citizens and inhabitants. Some Deities are called masculine and others feminine, so that you may know that both those things pertaining to **matter and passions**, and those pertaining to **forms and actions**, are governed by the Powers Above. But why does Plato give the principal citadel of the city to Vesta, Jupiter, and Pallas <note>Athena</note>? So that you may understand that in divine matters, three sources of all things exist: **Vesta** as the source of *being*, **Jupiter** as the source of *living*, and **Pallas** as the source of *understanding*; and in all these things, help must be obtained from the Powers Above. That all these things flowed from the discipline of the Egyptians will be revealed in what follows. For those things which the Greeks indicated through the triple assistance of the deities Vesta, Jupiter, and Pallas, the Egyptians indicated through **Isis, Horus, and Osiris**; for they taught that all things are governed by these. Hence they mystically dedicated three boundaries, three circles, three urns, <margin>Three boundaries, circles, urns, axes, feathers.</margin> three axes, three feathers, and similar things; signifying celestial and terrestrial laws through the boundaries; the triple divine power over all things through the three circles; dominion over moist substance through the urns; and penetration through all and into all things through the feathers. # TREATISE II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. CHAPTER III

This sacred table is, therefore, nothing other than a certain Idea of the polity of the Celestial Deities, according to which they indicate that the lower political World must be established so that it may be able to subsist. <margin>Plato. Every human law comes from God, according to Plato.</margin> For as Plato rightly shows in *Dialogue 11* on Laws, every human law was discovered and established by God, appointing a reward for those who keep it, but a proportionate punishment for those who transgress. For God is the artisan of the whole World, and embraces the whole within himself; therefore, he inspects every single thing, lest anyone trust that they can remain hidden while transgressing; and he revolves through all things, lest anyone hope to escape his hands after a crime. He is the founder of all laws, *Defining and completing the Right* <note>original: "Recta definiens, & peragens"</note> (these are the words of Plato), that is, he determines each thing by a certain right rule. And first, indeed, he determines for each thing the measure of its nature—what, of what kind, how many, and how great they are, and where, and when, and how they are moved; then he determines for souls what must be done and what must be avoided. It is established that this determination is the law of all things in the power of God, the author of all, and that it is sanctioned by <margin>Plato's opinion on God as the lawgiver.</margin> God himself by the same act by which all things are understood and made by him—namely, by a circular act. Timaeus <note>A character in Plato's dialogues representing Pythagorean philosophy.</note> says this is natural to the divine Intelligence, arising from itself, looking back upon itself, and by looking back upon itself, always beholding all things. Perhaps, indeed, beyond the circular motion internal to God, he also hints at a straight motion—the proceeding of things from God and the influx of God through all things; therefore he said he "defines and completes the right [straight] path." He signaled that the straight motion depends on the circular, by which both the keepers of the law and the transgressors are perceptively discerned, and what is most especially owed to each is effectively decreed. Because this judgment both powerfully discerns and decrees, an inevitable vengeance for sins and a reward for those who observe the law follows. Moreover, the observation of the law consists in this: that the subject renders himself <margin>The observation of the law consists in making the subjects similar to God.</margin> perfectly similar to God—similar, I say, through the purity of temperance, by which, as if by a rule and a square <note>A "square" or "amussis" is a builder's tool for ensuring straightness.</note>, he may measure all his affairs. For measure, as Pythagoras also says, is judged the best of all things and makes the soul most similar to God; He is the measure of all things, especially for us, who must pursue or flee individual things to the extent that they are judged either congruent or dissonant with the divine Mind and will. Hence that saying in Plato’s epistle: *To a wise man, God is the law; but to a fool, his lust is law.* <margin>Plato.</margin> All these things are beautifully displayed in the sacred table, where an oval figure denotes the World, and the architectonic intellect of the divine Mind stands there upon the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow; here used to represent a central pillar or standard of measurement.</note>. By the <margin>The meanings of the sacred table.</margin> arrangement of this, all things that are in the World acquire symmetry and the most exact proportion, and they attain a harmonic construction indicated by the reed-staff. Here, he bestows life, measure, and the efficacy of operations through influxes to the celestial "many-towered" regions <note>original: "polypyrgis cœlestibus," likely referring to the tiered or fortified levels of the heavens.</note> and their guardians. Toward this, the intellect—the legislator of the lower World, indicated by the <term>Scarab</term> <note>The dung beetle, an Egyptian symbol of the creator and the sun's movement.</note> and three boundaries—must look in all actions and be supported by them, lest in human actions (which are otherwise utterly deceptive) he fall into the precipice of errors. # CHAPTER IV.
### Concerning the inscription and division of the Obelisk.
### P R E L U D E.

<margin>Division of the Rameßean Obelisk</margin>
This present Obelisk has four sides, arranged according to the fourfold division of the World, each of which is further distinguished into three columns. This division is preceded by an inscription contained in three compartments, two of which, A and B, are in the pyramidion <note>The small pyramid at the very top of an obelisk</note>, and the third, C, is contained at the beginning of the column; it is the same on all sides of the Obelisk for this reason: so that the Authors of the Obelisk might immediately strike the eyes from all parts of the World, and so that people might be encouraged to preserve with the greatest zeal the doctrine handed down therein by the favor of the immortal Gods.
<margin>The inscription or Epigraph contained in three compartments.</margin>

<margin>The first part of the inscription of the Rameßean Obelisk.</margin>
The first inscription is held immediately below the peak of the pyramidion under A, enclosed in an oval figure <note>A cartouche</note>, with this display of symbols. <note>Hieroglyphic inscription described: An Ibis sitting on a gnomon shaped like the letter 'hieralpha' (a chevron or Greek lambda), with a wall-like base, a curved staff, three vertical lines/limits, and a scarab.</note> An Ibis sits upon a gnomon <note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow; here used to describe a geometric support</note> composed in the form of the letter <note>Symbol: Hieralpha/Lambda-shape</note>, under which is placed a figure resembling the form of a wall, and across from this a curved staff; to these are joined three limits, together with a Scarab; by which symbols indeed nothing else is indicated but Mercury <term>Agathodæmon</term> <note>The "Good Spirit," a protective deity often identified with Thoth or Hermes</note>, a powerful ruler, founder of political laws, and institutor of hieroglyphic doctrine, from whose books this column was extracted and prepared. But that this is so, it now falls to us to establish with all our effort.

<margin>The Ibis signifies Mercury.</margin>
That the Ibis signifies Mercury has been shown in countless places in this Work, and was demonstrated with copious authorities in the *Hierogrammatism of the Ibis* of the Pamphilian Obelisk. For Mercury was thought to appear to men under the form of an Ibis, and by various gestures of its body, to teach the invention of various things; whence an animal of this kind was held sacred to Mercury by everyone. Certainly Plato in the *Protagoras* says openly that under the name of Mercury, the human race first received laws. See Horus <note>Horapollo, author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs</note> Book 1, chapter 10 at the end, and chapter 36; Plutarch on *Osiris and Isis*, and the *Mystic Alphabet of the Egyptians* shown above. ### TREATISE II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. CHAPTER IV.

We have shown in the "Mystic Alphabet" and elsewhere that the letter Alpha, composed of <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A gnomon or square-rule</note> from <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A smaller gnomon</note> and <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A shepherd's crook or lituus</note>, denotes the *Agathodaemon* <note>The "Good Spirit," often identified with Hermes/Mercury</note>; he was regarded as such by all the Egyptians. It is shaped into the form of a gnomon <note>A carpenter's square or right-angle tool</note> to show that he is the author of all justice, by which alone human actions are directed, and that this is especially necessary in the political administration of affairs, which is aptly denoted by the symbol fashioned in the form of a wall. But because one cannot administer these things without strength and power, <margin>The curved staff is a sign of dominion.</margin> a curved staff is appropriately joined to it from the opposite side, a symbol of power and dominion over lower things; beneath these, three boundaries are placed with a Scarab. By the three boundaries is indicated the nature of the archetypal Intellect, which acts upon the triple World—Intellectual, Sidereal, and Elemental—no differently than the Sun. Thus, I say, the "political Sun," who is the Lawgiver in the archetypal intellect and is aptly expressed by the Scarab, must act upon three classes of men: upon himself, upon the Nobles, and upon the people, by exercising his power, by which the body of the world <margin>The Scarab is a symbol of the Sun.</margin> is uniquely sustained. For as Porphyry says in his book *On Abstinence*: <note>original Greek: Αἰγύπτιοι δὲ ἱέρακα τὸν καὶ δαίμονα, ὡς εἰκόνα ἡλίου ἔμψυχον.</note> "The Egyptians worshipped the Scarab as a living image of the Sun." This symbol must be attributed by a certain analogy not only to this sensible Sun, but also to the Archetype, and to the Political Sun from which it emanated. Furthermore, when the meaning is transferred to moral character, the same Scarab <margin>Horus.</margin>—according to Horapollo, Book 1, Chapter 10—denotes a father and masculine virtue, which is uniquely necessary for administering a Kingdom; by which, with paternal affection and warlike fortitude, a King removes all things adverse to the Kingdom. Hence Aelian (Book 10, Chapter 15) and Plutarch <margin>Aelian. Plutarch.</margin> in his book *On Isis and Osiris* clearly teach that the engraving on the rings of warriors was a Scarab, because all males must fight for their country. <margin>What the Scarab engraved on a ring signified.</margin> In the same way, the Egyptians thought Mercury <note>Thoth</note> to be not only the Lawgiver, but also the supreme tutelary Deity and *Agathodaemon*, upon whose worship and veneration the safety of all Egypt depended. Hence the present epigraph or inscription was not incongruously made for Mercury, adorned with those symbols which would both display the divine virtues of Mercury and, at the same time, solicit him to defend the Egypt committed to his faith, as if by this most powerful *periamm* <note>A protective amulet or charm worn around the neck</note>.

The second space on each side of the pyramidion displays the figures of two men wearing mitres and dressed in linen cloaks, who seem to be discussing matters of great importance. It is certain that these are the Priests <margin>The second part of the inscription of the Ramesside Obelisk.</margin> of the Egyptians, as is clear from Apuleius and Plutarch, who clearly teach that they were conspicuous for their mitred heads and used linen tunics—the latter in *Isis and Osiris*, the former <margin>Apuleius. Plutarch. Mitred Egyptian Priests. Eucherius.</margin> in his *Metamorphoses*. Moreover, as Eucherius asserts, the *cidaris* <note>original Greek: κίδαρις</note> was a priestly cap made of fine linen, which some call a tiara and others a mitre. And Hesychius of Jerusalem is the authority that this was a symbol of wisdom, because the organ of wisdom was placed by nature in the brain. <margin>The cidaris or priestly mitre is a sign of wisdom. The linen cloak of the Egyptian Priest is a symbol of purity.</margin> By this it was shown that the Priests, as those chosen for the administration of the kingdom, ought to devote themselves perpetually and uniquely to the study of wisdom; they were dressed in linen, not woolen garments, because the latter originate from wool, the excremental superfluity of animals, which is contrary to the purity of Priests...

# CHAPTER IV. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER.

<page-num>180</page-num>

...they did not take up [garments of wool]; but rather those made of linen, because it springs directly from the bountiful mother earth, first producing a blue flower similar to the color of the heavens, then a stalk <note>original: *thyrsum*</note>, which, when variously prepared, finally provides the fabric most suitable for making Priestly vestments, as witnessed by Plutarch and Porphyry. For these small cloaks were a symbol of brightness and extraordinary purity, which ought to shine forth in Priests who enjoy the perpetual company of the Gods. There is no doubt, therefore, that the two mitre-wearing figures represent Priests to anyone who has correctly understood what we discussed concerning the habit of Priests in the first Volume. Indeed, it is likely, as Michael Mercatus also thinks, that these <margin>Michael Mercatus.</margin> figures of Priests represent Sothis and his son Ramesses, Kings and Priests <margin>Figures of Sothis and Ramesses on the Ramesside Obelisk.</margin> of Egypt. For these were the first who—after the slaughter to be remembered through all ages, when God through Moses avenged Pharaonic stubbornness by the drowning of the Egyptians in the Red Sea—restored the Egyptian Kingdom to its former splendor and magnificence nearly two hundred years later. For they were continually conversing with the Priests and were Priests themselves; they unrolled the Hermetic books (which they held as an inestimable treasure, having sought them out from everywhere) with the greatest zeal to restore the dogmas of the ancestral religion, which were contained under hieroglyphic symbols. For as Plato rightly shows in his book *On Kingship* <note>The *Statesman* or *Politicus*</note>, no one among <margin>Plato: Among the Egyptians, Priests were Kings and Kings were Priests.</margin> the Egyptians was admitted to the administration of the Kingdom unless he enjoyed the title of Priest; indeed, if anyone from another class had usurped the Kingdom by force, it was necessary for him to be initiated into the sacred rites after the assumption of the Kingdom, so that he might be both King and Priest. For, to use Plato's words, *the character of Priests and Prophets abounds in magnanimity, intelligence, and clarity, because of the magnificence of the things they handle.* Hence, as Pliny testifies, through their combined study and labor, these two Kings and Priests <margin>Pliny.</margin> were the first who constructed eight Obelisks, which we enumerate in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. But Ramesses, being excellently instructed by his father Sothis, and turning something more sublime over in his mind since the aforementioned Obelisks did not equal the greatness of his soul, erected this greatest of all Obelisks at Thebes, furnished with the political doctrine necessary for preserving the safety of the Kingdom. Pliny reports that things are so in these words: *Afterward,* he says, *other Kings in the aforementioned City [erected them]: Sothis, four in number, forty-eight cubits in length; and Ramesses, in whose reign Troy was captured, forty cubits; the same man, departing from there where the Palace of Mnevis is, placed another eleven feet in length and four cubits along the sides; 20,000 men are said to have performed that work.* That these things we have said concerning Sothis the father and Ramesses the son are so, Manetho teaches in Africanus, in a fragment from the Peiresc Library: <note>original Greek: Σῶθις ἐβασίλευσεν ἔτη ξγ΄, ὃς ἔτειψε πολλὰς τὰς πυραμίδας. οὗτος καὶ τὰ πρὸς τοὺς Θεοὺς ἐξεῦρε, καὶ τὴν ἱερὰν ἐν Τάναϊ γράφει βίβλον, ἣν ὡς μέγα χρῆμα ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ γενόμενος ἐκτὸς ἔλαβεν.</note> *Sothis reigned for 63 years; he built many pyramids (understand these as Obelisks); he was the first contemplator of the Gods, spoke wisely about the Gods, and ordered a sacred book to be written, which he possessed as a thing of vast price while being in Egypt.* All of which is confirmed by Abenephius the Arab, <margin>Abenephius.</margin> whose words you may see in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* in the prologue to the history of the Obelisk. Since, therefore, Sothis and Ramesses, Kings and Priests of Egypt, [held] the uniquely sacred...

# TREATISE II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. 181 CHAP. IV.

...since they promoted the sacred doctrine of hieroglyphics by unanimous consent, it is likely that Ramesses wished to engrave himself and his father upon this present Obelisk for the eternal memory of the matter. Thus, by casting their eyes upon this unusual mass of the Obelisk, Egyptian posterity might revolve in their minds, with perpetual gratitude of remembrance, how much they owed to them.

<margin>The square compartment marked on the Ramesside Obelisk.</margin>
After this inscription, there occurs in the first place on the Obelisk a square compartment marked with the letter C. In this, a figure is conspicuous, wearing a miter <note>a tall, ceremonial headdress</note> on its head and appearing naked, seated upon a throne. It has another figure before it, prostrate on its knees with arms extended in the manner of one seeking and beseeching something; to whom the seated figure seems to impart a blessing. On the wall, indeed, four various figures are seen, which we call "sacred tablets"; these are nothing other than certain sacred amulets established for the purpose of propitiating the Gods. We say, therefore, that these arrangements on the four faces of the Obelisk—which are exactly the same—denote nothing else but, first, the World of Genii <note>the "Mundus Genialis," or the realm of guardian spirits and divine influences</note> and its protection as a sort of model for politics; and secondly, the very inner sanctum <term>adytum: the most sacred, restricted inner chamber of a temple</term> of the Egyptians, in which the Priests were inaugurated with those rites and ceremonies which you see, and indeed in that manner which we shall explain.
<margin>Rites by which the Egyptian Priests were inaugurated.</margin>

<margin>Hemphta, the supreme Deity.</margin>
First, the supreme Priest, conspicuous in a tiara or headdress—a symbol of wisdom—sat upon a throne, the symbol of highest power, representing the role of the supreme Deity, Hemphta <note>Kircher's name for a creator-god, often associated with the "Divine Intellect"</note>. For they held this Deity in the inner sanctum, portrayed with an equal display of symbols. By this they indicated the supreme right and most absolute dominion of this highest Deity over all kinds of things produced by Him, and the necessary dependence of all things subject to Him, without whose concurrence and benign influence nothing could subsist. He is shown naked because He is most far removed from all contagion of material things, lacking nothing, and sufficient unto Himself alone.

From Him, the Intellectual, Sidereal, and Political World participates in whatever good it possesses, according to a certain analogy. Hence the Priests, so that their actions might be more conformed to this supreme Deity, performed their inaugurations and other sacred rites in their inner sanctums according to the likeness of the supreme Deity already mentioned. They persuaded themselves that these rites obtained no force or efficacy unless they were performed with an analogous display of symbols. And so that their operations in the solicitation of the Gods might have greater power, they used to place in the sanctums certain sacred tablets adorned with those hieroglyphics which most suited the Deity they were petitioning. They thought these tablets acquired great power for obtaining what was sought from the Deity, both from the hidden virtue of the sacraments performed there and from the particular influence of the Gods. But concerning the secret arrangement of the sanctums, see page 393 of the first Volume, and other places throughout both the *Egyptian Oedipus* and the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, the optical drawings of all of which you may contemplate as exhibited in the treatise on *Egyptian Mummies*. These things having been prefaced, let us now at last, with the favor of the Divine Power, begin the particular interpretation of the Obelisk.
