<meta>This page continues the analysis of the Lateran Obelisk (Obeliscus Ramessaeus) by Athanasius Kircher. It establishes the structural framework for interpreting the hieroglyphic columns, which Kircher divides into three distinct "worlds": the Archetypal, the Sidereal, and the Political.</meta>

# Section I.

## Interpretation of the first column of the first Northern side;

<margin>Each side of the Ramesside Obelisk is divided into three columns.</margin>
<margin>First column.</margin>
It must first be noted, therefore, that the individual sides of this Obelisk are divided into three internal columns, separated from one another. The first of these is denoted by an Asp emerging from a globe, which, having made a turn, appears to wind itself toward a Crux Ansata <note>original: "Cruci ansatae"; the "handled cross" or Ankh</note> or Tautic character <note>A symbol associated with the god Thoth/Hermes</note>. This figure occupies the highest place in the column and shows us the Archetypal World of the supreme Divinity; emerging from this into all classes of beings, the Divinity animates, gives life to, and preserves them.

<margin>Second column.</margin>
<margin>Third column.</margin>
The second column is denoted by a Hawk <note>original: "Accipitre"; representing Horus or the Sun</note>, by which the Sidereal World <note>The world of stars and celestial bodies</note> is indicated. Its moderator is the Sun, who exerts his power upon the economy of the Elemental World subject to him, according to the Idea of the Archetypal Divinity. By the third column, marked by the figure of a Priest, the Political World is denoted, in which the Priest-King orders the Political World and the state of public affairs according to the principles of both the Archetypal and Sidereal Worlds. And these three figures, representing the triple World—Archetypal, Sidereal, and Political—occupy the first place on every side of the Obelisk, each in its appropriate column, and serve as a kind of inscription for the aforementioned triple World.

It must be noted secondly that, since we could not distinguish every single figure with its own letter due to their great multitude, we have—to avoid confusion—marked the individual sides in the margin with letters of the Alphabet. These are common to the three spaces of the columns, so that in each column, parallel figures would correspond to the same letter. With these warnings given, let us now explain the first column of the Northern side, whose first space is marked with the letter **D**.

<margin>An Asp emerging from a globe and winding itself into a Crux Ansata.</margin>
The first figure in the column of Northern side **A**, in the region of **D**, is an Asp emerging from a globe and as if winding itself into a Crux Ansata; by this, the supreme archetypal Divinity is noted. The Asp unrolls from the globe because God, unrolled as if from a certain center of a divine and boundless sphere, first winds into the Angelic World, then the Sidereal (which two Worlds are aptly indicated by two small circles impressed on the sphere). From these, He finally descends into the lower <term>Hylaean World</term> <note>From the Greek 'hyle', meaning the material or elemental world</note> or Elemental world, which is beautifully noted by the Crux Ansata or Tautic character; and from here, finally raised upward, He is restored to His own sphere. Even Virgil <note>The Roman poet (70–19 BCE)</note> seems to have alluded to this:

<margin>Virgil.</margin>
> ->In the beginning, the Spirit within nourishes the Sky,<-
> ->the lands, the watery plains, the shining globe of the Moon,<-
> ->and the Titan stars; and Mind, infused through the limbs,<-
> ->stirs the whole mass and mixes itself with the great body.<-
<note>original Latin: "Principio Coelum, ac terras..." from the Aeneid, Book VI</note>

Furthermore, that this Asp is the supreme Divinity, which by its power permeates all—

# COLLECTION II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. 183 CHAPTER IV

<margin>Horus</margin> <note>Horapollo, a 5th-century author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> Horus expressly teaches how [the divine power] pervades [the universe] in Book 1, Chapter 2: "When they wish to represent the World, they paint a serpent biting its own tail, marked with various scales." <margin>A serpent biting its own tail.</margin> By the scales, they obscurely hint at the stars with which the Heaven and the World are distinguished. Furthermore, this animal is very heavy, not unlike the earth, yet very light and extremely slippery in the manner of water. Moreover, just as the serpent sheds its skin every year and puts off its old age, so also the revolving year, which is produced by the rotation of the World, is renewed by a change and, as it were, grows young again. The fact that it uses its own body as if for food signifies that whatever things are produced in the World by God’s providence are again resolved into the same, and undergo a kind of transformation. By this symbol, they seem to have expressed not only this sensible World, but also the insensible archetype, the intellectual world of Spirits, the sidereal world, and the elementary world according to a certain analogy. The circle indeed denotes the outward movement of the divine Mind; the asp, distinguished by a manifold order of scales, rightly designates first the stars in the archetype (which are divine attributes and perfections), then in the intellectual World the various armies of blessed Minds, then in the sidereal world the stars, and finally in the elementary world the various grades of beings of the lower World. And as the supreme Deity pervades all these things, He governs them by His wisdom and preserves them by that same supreme providence. See all these things explained at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 370.

Immediately following the Asp in space **D** is the **dragon-shaped butterfly** <margin>**D** Dragon-shaped butterfly with a papyrus staff.</margin> with a papyrus staff <note>original: "thyrso papyraceo"</note>, by which they denoted the "all-formed" <note>original: "Pantamorpham"</note> nature or power, into which the supreme Deity flows most closely and immediately. The Platonists call this the **World Soul** <note>original: "animam Mundi"</note>, but the more secret Egyptians call it the "paternal depth," composed of three triads, as we explained in the *Bembine Tablet*; this is because, having been introduced through the three triads of the Worlds, it grants life and motion to all things. However, how and why the Egyptians attributed so many and such great excellences and prerogatives to this butterfly—a most lowly animal—we have shown amply in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 500, to which we refer the curious Reader, lest we be forced to always transcribe the same things with an excessive increase in the size of this Work. The butterfly has an attached papyrus or reed staff, by which is noted the abundance of necessary things which the "all-formed" nature, filled with Ideas, confers upon the beings of the aforementioned Worlds. <margin>Papyrus or reed staff.</margin> See the cited location. Therefore, the supreme "naturing nature" <note>A philosophical term for God as the creative source of all things.</note> first communicates itself to this all-formed nature, which transfers the participated power into the lower Horizons of the Worlds, which the two semicircles placed below the butterfly denote. The **Agathodæmon** <note>The "Good Spirit" or protective deity.</note> of three sections participates in the virtue of the All-formed nature, as the Egyptians call it; and indeed the figure **A** denotes the Agathodæmon, as we have taught in the *Mystic Alphabet* and elsewhere in various places; the three following axes <note>original: "secures," referring to the flag-like hieroglyphs often interpreted as axes or banners.</margin> indicate the triple power of the said Agathodæmon, by which whatever is **Typhonian** or **Bebonian** <note>Referring to Typhon/Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and destruction.</note> in the triple World is cut away and uprooted. <margin>The Agathodæmon is signified by the letter A.</margin> And that this is so is shown by the statue of this Agathodæmon, which is encountered quite frequently among hieroglyphic schemes; it is under a human form, wrapped in a long garment, holding a leveling-square in the right hand and an axe in the left; by which symbols the office of this Agathodæmon is indeed beautifully expressed, which is to level injustices, <term>inequality</term> <note>original: "ἀνισότητα" (anisotēta)</note> or <margin>Three axes.</margin>

**D** IN the second column of the first Northern side, the crested Hawk holds the first place; he who acts as the leader of the dance in this Sensible World, namely the Solar Divinity, whom they call Osiris, as has already been said often. He sits upon a parallelogram square, in which are inserted a bull, an arm conspicuous with an extended hand, along with a <term>hieralpha</term> <note>A sacred letter 'A' or symbol used by Kircher to denote a primary divine principle</note>, to which is placed a circle with an I. The square denotes the material World, which the Bull Apis dominates—the earthly Osiris sub-delegated to the Celestial one—from whose beneficial power, noted by the extended arm and participated in by the Celestial Osiris, the abundance of all necessary things in the lower World flows. Hence, he is not incongruously called by the Egyptians the Agathodæmon of the lower World, as the figure A with the globe and the I placed beneath it teach. But since we are about to explain this same figure in almost all the following Obelisks, and have explained it in the Pamphilian Obelisk on page 442, we refer the reader there.

The Asp and the sleeping Hawk.

There follows a square with an Asp reared up with a scaly breast, frequently met with in this as in other Obelisks, behind which sits a Hawk, which with a contracted neck seems as if to sleep. # SYNTAGMA II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. 187 CHAPTER IV

...he kept his eyes closed, and darkness was poured out. But let us explain the mystery. <margin>The worship of the Asp among the Egyptians.</margin> The celestial Osiris, offended by the wicked life of mortals, occasionally seems to sleep regarding the matters entrusted to his faith; from this, great inconveniences and disturbances are born in the World. However, when he is awake, it is necessary that all things be filled with joy, as it were. While Osiris sleeps, the Asp, his sub-delegated <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>Greek: "Good Spirit," a protective deity often depicted as a serpent</note>, the arbiter of life and death, tears apart all lower things; he scatters them, and as <term>Horus</term> <margin>Horus.</margin> says in Book 1, Chapter 2, he kills all things with a single breath. But when Osiris is worshipped with the appropriate ceremonies, all good things come to the World; for this reason, the Egyptians rightly used to soothe such an implacable Deity with singular worship. If he had kept his eyes closed during the sacred rites, it was an omen of the greatest misfortunes that the kingdom had to undergo; but if he were seen with open, kind, and pleasant eyes, it promised a great abundance of goods in the Kingdom.

Therefore, the divine symbols are appropriately placed in this location; of which the Hawk denotes the clemency, goodness, piety, and beneficence of Osiris. The Asp, however, shows by its breast swollen with Martial rigor, as well as the scales it raises, the fates, the justice, the severity, and the supreme rigor of Osiris. This rigor first emerges when, the clemency and piety of Osiris having been set aside, the rigor of justice flows into the World. For then, in Heaven, a massing of malignant <margin>F.</margin> influences occurs; in the world of elements, the greatest discord of things, sterility on the lands, contagion in the air, and in public affairs, tumults and seditions are soon born. These are truly aptly indicated by the following Owl in the region of the letter F; which, as has already been said often, is the symbol of <term>Typhon</term> <margin>The Owl is the symbol of Typhon.</margin> <note>The Egyptian god Set, associated with chaos and storms</note>, that is, the symbol of all evils. For he, prevailing with a triple scepter, labors in every way to dry up the mixing bowl of Osiris, which the Hawk expresses with the bowl placed beneath it. <margin>G.</margin>

When calamities of this kind are imminent, the Priests of Osiris are accustomed to solicit the <note>original: "$\sigma\varepsilon\iota\rho\grave{\alpha}\nu$" (seiran)</note> *chain* <margin>The chain of Osiris.</margin>—which the Priest expresses with the attached figure of a chain—that is, the chain of Spirits arranged according to the triple laws of the threefold World, through continuous sacrifices. For by these sacrifices, first, the polymorphic nature of the World is attracted, indicated by the winged Butterfly <margin>H.</margin> <note>original: "$\delta\varepsilon\sigma\mu\omega\tau\rho\acute{\alpha}\phi\omicron\nu$" (desmotraphon), meaning "nurturer of the bond"</note>, and an abundance of necessary things, indicated by the papyrus staff, is granted once the evils have been expelled.

To <margin>I.</margin> which the following amulet of the sacred table, enclosed in an oval figure, greatly contributes; it is a circle, a wall conspicuous with seven points, with a Scarab. Through the circle, the supreme divinity is expressed; through the seven-pointed wall, the protection of the seven principal Spirits of the World, over whom the Solar <margin>Amulet of the second column of the North side at letter I.</margin> Deity, expressed through the <term>Scarab</term>, uniquely rules. We have seen the amulet; now let us examine its effects as well. Following the oval figure is a wall marked with twelve points, which the Egyptians call "citadels," the Arabs <note>Arabic: "بروج" (burūj)</note> *towers of the zodiac*, and the Greeks <note>Greek: "$\pi\acute{\upsilon}\rho\gamma\omicron\upsilon\varsigma$" (pyrgous)</note> *towers*, as shown elsewhere and especially in the Pamphilian Obelisk on page 510. By this is noted the protection of the twelve Spirits who preside over the signs of the Zodiac; they believed that by the use of this amulet, the series of seven planetary Deities concatenated with these twelve masters <margin>Figures contained between letters K and L.</margin> was drawn down. There follows a feather, with a double water-scheme <margin>K.</margin>, a goose in between, and a scepter with testicles, which is followed by <margin>L.</margin> a Serpent, a curved staff, and a persea tree conspicuous with three branches, with two water-schemes...

->*Interpretation of the third column of the Northern side. It exhibits the Political World:*<-

<margin>Opposite D</margin> <margin>Clement of Alexandria on the office of the Stolistae.</margin> **D** In the first place on the third column of the first Northern side is placed the figure of a Priest from the number of those whom they call <term>Stolistae</term> <note>Priests in charge of the sacred vestments and ritual purity</note>, according to the testimony of Clement of Alexandria in the 6th book of the *Stromata*. Their office was to urge the preservation of all things pertaining to sacred disciplines and institutes with inviolable rigor, and to guard them with untainted vigor. Furthermore, they were to draw from the sacred books decrees concerning the administration of public affairs and political business, which were profitable for the common good and conducive to the stability of the kingdom. To perform this rightly, two things were chiefly required: the cubit of justice—a symbol of the distribution of the kingdom's burdens, offices, and rewards with the highest equity and just measure; the other was divine worship, the end and ultimate goal of all political happiness. ...with an extended hand, he appears as a figure exploring their will, as it were; <margin>D 4 <note>Refers to a diagram in the preceding section.</note></margin> by the "cubit of justice" <note>The *Maat* cubit, a symbol of divine order and measurement.</note> he shows himself ready and prepared to fulfill all parts of justice, placing all his zeal into this: that he might rightly adapt all things according to the pattern of both the Archetype and the Starry World. <margin>The eight Hermetic laws.</margin> Through these figures, the initiate Priests indicate the Hermetic or Isiac columns, on which eight laws of the greatest importance were inscribed, as <margin>Iamblichus. Plato. 1st Law</margin> Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> testifies, and as Plato records in the 4th book of his *Dialogues on Laws*, according to the tradition of the Ancients; and they are: First, that providence is never <margin>2.</margin> lacking to men, provided they are not lacking to themselves. Second, that Kings must greatly avoid pride and wantonness, which for the most part take their origin from the greatest license and power in affairs. <margin>3.</margin> Third, just as beasts cannot be governed by beasts without a human shepherd, so neither can men be governed by men in the best way without God as Leader; without whom all life is made miserable and full of labors. Therefore, above all other things, divine worship and religion, as the ultimate end of the state, must be uniquely loved and sought. <margin>4.</margin> Fourth, the very distribution of the Mind is a certain law, which must be obeyed in every private and public governance. <margin>5.</margin> Fifth, let no constitutions be called laws unless they procure the common good. <margin>6.</margin> Sixth, let the offices of the magistracy, and especially the duties of divine worship, be committed to those who more observantly obey the laws. <margin>7.</margin> Seventh, destruction is prepared for a City or Kingdom in which the laws do not rule the Magistrates, but the Magistrates rule the laws. <margin>8.</margin> Eighth, the Magistracy must not be committed to any except those conspicuous for prudence and to the Elders. And these are the Hermetic laws, or the laws engraved on the Isiac columns, which Plato interspersed into his *Dialogues on Laws*, just as <margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin> Marsilio Ficino <note>The famous Renaissance translator of Plato.</note> demonstrates at length in his prefaces, and <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> Iamblichus openly teaches in his book *On the Mysteries*; which eight laws we shall exhibit more clearly in the following Treatises, expressed hieroglyphically just as they are here. However, since <margin>Herodotus.</margin> Herodotus mentions four laws usually placed on a column in *Clio* <note>Book I of Herodotus' Histories.</note>, and these are excellently expressed by the hieroglyphics in this place, I have thought it timely to explain them here.

<margin>The four laws of the Egyptians from Herodotus.</margin> It was a custom among the Egyptians, according to the testimony of Herodotus in *Clio*, to show fourfold laws inscribed on a column to be studiously observed, which two columns adorned with four transverse scepters show; the first of these suits the Starry World, the other the Political World, which receives its laws from the Starry one. Moreover, the law is fourfold: Royal, Sacerdotal, Nilotic <note>Relating to the Nile and its management.</note>, and of agriculture...

The sacred tablet indicates divine worship; <margin>I</margin> the oval figure indicates the "Reason of the World," which the Archetypal intellect of the Prince <margin>Political documents</margin> ought to imitate in all things. For what the divine intellect is in all things, so is the intellect of the Prince in the Political World. That which the wall indicates in the Sensible World through the governance of the seven planets, it indicates in the Political state through seven diverse classes of men. From the priestly order there were: Singers, Horoscopes <note>Time-keepers/astrologers</note>, Sacred Scribes, Robers <note>original: *Stolistæ*, those in charge of sacred vestments</note>, and Prophets. Indeed, by the Scarab, the King was indicated—endowed with masculine virtue, supreme fortitude, and prudence. By his direction, the whole mass of the political state was set in motion, as if by the fixed boundaries of the laws. By the cord which follows the oval figure, the laws are hinted at; by the extended <margin>I</margin> arm, the liberality and beneficence of the Prince are shown, by which alone all Typhonic conspiracies are dissipated. # CHAPTER IV. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...established, it must necessarily perish. Therefore, Osiris and Momphta <note>Momphta is Kircher’s name for a creative Egyptian deity, often associated with a formative or "plastic" power in nature.</note>—those two Nilotic Spirits indicated by the Hawk and the Lion-like statue—must be worshipped with the highest honor. This is due to the beneficence of moisture, from which the life of all things overflows, and the beneficence of laws, from which the life of the State's condition likewise emerges. For without laws, it is impossible for a state to be preserved. All these things are aptly suggested through the symbols contained between K, L, and M, as will be clear to the reader comparing one with the other.

<margin>M</margin> There follow further: a Hawk with a whip; beneath which is placed a <term>hydroschema</term> <note>original: "hydroschema" — a symbolic representation of water or fluid essence</note>, a Serpent, two Owls, a Scarab, a Serpent, an Owl, a <term>testiculate scepter</term> <note>original: "sceptrum testiculatum" — a scepter symbolizing fertility or generative power</note>, three boundaries, a <term>hydroschema</term>, and an Ibis closes the line. I interpret these symbols as follows: Osiris, the averting Spirit (for the Hawk with the whip placed before him aptly expresses this), being thrice-powerful in vital moisture (indicated by the <term>hydroschema</term>, the scepter, the Serpent, and the three scepters), thus puts to flight the Typhonian force <note>Typhon represents chaos, drought, and destruction in Kircher's system.</note> dwelling in the South and North (indicated by the two Owls and the two boundaries), together with the earthly Osiris subordinate to him (indicated by the Scarab), yet he allows him to live.

<margin>Adversity is occasionally beneficial to the political state.</margin> By this very thing, they allude to the political state of the Kingdom, for which it is occasionally good to be pressed by adversaries. Such adversities render Kings vigilant, prudent, and circumspect in penetrating all the engines of their opponents; on the contrary, lasting peace and an abundance of all good things render them improvident, sluggish, and somnolent. For they knew that Typhon performs the same role in the Political World as Mars does in the Starry World when compared to the Sun and Jupiter; although Mars may be malignant, virulent, and utterly pernicious, he nevertheless contributes his own benefits to the celestial economy, as was treated at length in the section on the Politics of the Egyptians.

For Typhon is not so sterile that he does not have his own fecundity; which is indeed nothing other than the most exact observation of the laws prescribed by Hermes among the subjects. When this is in force along with the rigor of justice, while all are vigilant for the common good and against Typhon, a right administration of affairs in the Political World must necessarily result. Hence, they expressed these things very appropriately through the Scarab, the Serpent, and the <term>testiculate scepter</term> (with an Owl in between), as well as through the three boundaries, the Momphtaean scepter, the <term>hydroschema</term>, and the Ibis.

Thus the ideal discourse is concluded by the diagram of the sacred table between O and P; since we have explained this in the preceding pages, we do not wish to dwell on it longer here. The symbols following the sacred table are: a wall with a feather, a Bull, an Ibis, a Serpent, an Alpha with two feathers, and a pyramid with a <term>handled cross</term> <note>original: "Cruce ansata" — the Ankh symbol</note>. By these, the effects of the sacred rites are indicated, which are the attraction of Apis, the Hermetic Good Spirit <note>original: "Agathodaemon"</note>, and the influx of the vital Soul of the World, as has been proven elsewhere. Do you see, therefore, from this ideal discourse of the third column, how the Egyptians endeavored to aptly adapt their laws both to the Archetypal laws and to the laws of the Starry World?

# CHAPTER V.

->*Interpretation of the second Southern side of the Lateran Obelisk.*<-

<margin>Southern side of the Ramessean Obelisk</margin>
This Southern side of the Ramessean or Lateran Obelisk contains figures A, B, and T, which are entirely common and the same as the figures of the first Northern side A, B, and C; since their meaning has been explained at length in the preceding pages, we have decided that it should by no means be repeated here. After the inscription <margin>A</margin> A, and the consultations B of the two Kings of Egypt, Sothis and Ramesses <margin>B</margin> (the erectors of this Obelisk), and the inauguration of the Priests in the inner sanctuary T, <margin>T</margin> a point worthy of note occurs: the Priest to be inaugurated, with bended knees, <margin>Pomegranates and poppy heads denote the union of Kingdoms.</margin> appears to supplicate the mitered Priest sitting upon a throne (who acts in the place of the Supreme Deity) so that he might imbue with his influence two pomegranates, or more truly poppy heads, which he carries in his hands. It is asked, therefore, what they intended by those two pomegranates or poppy heads? I answer, that they understood nothing other than the Kingdom: for just as in the pomegranate or the poppy, nature has fashioned a most perfect crown, and yet within the rind has enclosed innumerable grains distributed into various distinct receptacles, all of which are truly enclosed together by the rind as if by a wall; so in the political state, under one single crown, different ranks and men of different conditions are contained, distinguished by their offices and duties. As long as these are contained together under the rind of the kingdom—which is the observance of the laws—the public states flourish and are preserved; but if, the rind being damaged, even one receptacle is harmed, the whole must necessarily rot. So says <margin>Eusebius.</margin> Eusebius <note>original: "Papaver Civitatis symbolum fuit..."</note>: *The poppy was a symbol of the City, because just as many men live in a city, so in the head of a poppy, as if within the same walls, there are many seeds; and as a City is distributed into neighborhoods and houses, so also the head of the poppy is divided into many parts within, and has many interstices.* Pierius, moreover, comments on this <margin>Pierius. The poppy as a symbol of the earth.</margin> passage thus: *The poppy, in its hieroglyphic, referred to Ceres, and thus to the whole earth inhabited by human commerce; nor was this for one reason only: for its shape is orbicular, just as the earth bulges out, with certain valleys as if sinking down, in the manner of mountains and acres, and the likeness of remote places; finally, it carries its interior divided by certain small sacs, just as the nations of men are separated by rivers, mountains, and cities: furthermore, it includes innumerable seeds like men, who are governed by justice and the giving of laws.* Regarding the pomegranate, he discusses it thus: *That was <margin>Symbol of the pomegranate.</margin> the chief symbol of that fruit, to signify various peoples and races gathered into one College; they think this was done for the reason that those grains, separated from others in some number by certain membranes, seem to present the boundaries of Provinces; and to distinguish individual groups of men, or rather Nations, separated from others by laws; for the various little chambers described around it with their grains indicate various nations there, each bounded by its own borders.* In the solemnities...

# CHAPTER V. 194 THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
The Egyptian Priests offered pomegranates or poppies.
</margin>
Therefore, on all feast days, the Priests who were to consult on the state of public affairs in the inner sanctuaries offered either poppies or pomegranates to the Supreme Deity. This is evident from the diagram provided here, where a figure offers such things to the Deity on bended knees, suggesting through a hidden symbol that the greatest care must be taken for those matters expressed by the occult meaning of the poppy or the pomegranate, and which they were to discuss regarding this Obelisk. With these things having been prefaced, let us now begin to interpret the three columns of this Southern side.

V.
<margin>
The first column of the second side of the Ramesside Obelisk.
</margin>
In the first place of the column, marked by V, a Priest dressed in mystical robes sits upon a throne, receiving a Hawk <note>The hawk often represents Horus or the sun-god</note> as if with outstretched arms. By this, it is indicated that the Prince of the Political World receives the principles of laws from Osiris—that is, from the soul of the Starry World—just as here he receives all things from the all-persuading Spirit of the World, who is signified by the Asp. On the preceding side, the Archetypal World <note>The world of divine ideas</note> holds the first place in the first column; it communicates its power to the Starry World of the second column, and finally flows into the Political World of the third column, as if by a descent made through two series of Worlds. On this side, however, the Political World—by making an ascent from the Political to the Starry, and from there to the Archetypal—elicits from each the necessary principles and laws for the good and blessed administration of kingdoms. How it does this remains to be explained.

-> §. I. <-

-> *Interpretation of the first column of the second Southern side, which expresses the Political World.* <-

<margin>
The end for the sake of which man was created by the best God.
</margin>
Since God and nature produce man for the sake of acting, they certainly produce him so that he may act; and let him act, I say, for the sake of divine things. Just as there is one end for the sake of which nature creates a thumb, another for the hand or foot, and yet another toward which it creates the whole man; so too there is one end toward which it directs the individual man, another for the family, another for the City and Kingdom; and finally, that end must be considered the best for the sake of which God procreated the entire human race. Let no one think that while there is an end for every individual <unclear>act</unclear>, there is none for the whole; or that while there is order in the parts of human life, there is confusion in the universal kind of life; or that while the parts have a union among themselves for the sake of one intention, the Universe lacks it and remains scattered and disjointed. Therefore, it is necessary <margin>The end of man consists in action regarding the best things.</margin> that there be a certain end for the human race, and that it consists in a certain action regarding more perfect things, through which he may both imitate higher things by his powers and diligently govern lower things—scrutinizing natural things through science, disposing of human things through prudence, and worshiping divine things through piety. Indeed, this absolute perfection requires so many and such great supports that neither...

# TREATISE II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. CHAPTER V.

...which can be fulfilled neither by a few individuals, nor by the many, but only by the entire human race together; for it is impossible for such diverse nations to be led through such diverse means to one common end for all, unless they are guided by one person through a single law that brings everyone together into unity. <margin>The Egyptians approve of the Monarchical state.</margin> Hence the Egyptians always held the Monarchical state in high esteem above all others, as it was adapted to the pattern of the divine Deity, whom the King most closely resembles. Plato also approves of this in his book *On Kingship* <note>original: "de Regno"; likely referring to the *Statesman* (Politikos)</note>, where, while seeking the Monarch of the World, he brings forward the Architect; by whose judgment and direction men of diverse conditions—even if they differ in various artificial crafts—conspire toward one end under the judgment and direction of this one leader: namely, the construction of the building and its preservation. 

Hence, immediately in the first column, the symbol of the **Dragon-shaped Butterfly** <note>original: "Papilio Dracontomorphus"</note> is placed with a papyrus staff <note>original: "thyrso"</note>, through which they refer to all those things we have discussed up to this point. <margin>The Butterfly.</margin> This animal is subject to the laws of various metamorphoses, as we have shown regarding the Pamphilian Obelisk; hence it is deservedly the most fitting symbol of the <term>Pantamorphic</term> <note>All-forming or all-shaping</note> spirit. For in this way, the principal Monarch of all nature, working all things in all people, governs innumerable beings differing in diversity with the highest peace, gathers disjointed things into one with the highest union, and leads each one to its desired happiness. And this was the first model of political dictate proposed by the Egyptians, which the King was required to keep always before his eyes, so that he might derive the principles of his governance from it and act according to them. 

<margin>The King must work all things in all his subjects.</margin> They suggested by this symbol, therefore, that it belongs to the Monarch King to work all things in all his subjects by his command, becoming "all things to all" in the manner of **Proteus** <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will</note>; which they aptly express through the metamorphosis of the Egyptian Butterfly. For by this, the uniform reason of the subjects became one with the reason of the King, without which uniformity it is impossible for a Kingdom to stand, as Plato rightly teaches in the cited book. This dictate is indeed nothing other than the singular providence of the Monarch, by which provision is made for each subject regarding every use of necessary things; which is aptly denoted by the papyrus staff placed near the Butterfly. 

<margin>The worship of God must be employed for the preservation of kingdoms.</margin> Furthermore, since the borders of a Kingdom are infested by various snares of enemies, and not all dangers can be evaded by human counsel, the worship of the immortal Gods must necessarily be employed. Their anger, if ever the iniquities of the people should boil over, must be appeased by the usual religious rites; or rather, their supreme innate readiness to help must be summoned by the religion of the people. 

<margin>X</margin> And indeed, the borders of the Kingdom are aptly indicated by the four segments, and the middle segment, corresponding to the four horizontal segments of the Sensible World to which they are analogous, and arranged through the next sacred table which we have explained here and there in the preceding pages. Following the sacred table is a wall <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: A rectangular crenelated enclosure, likely representing a city wall or temple precinct</note>, a symbol of the **Celestial Kingdom**, which indicates that civil government should be composed according to its model. 

<margin>Y</margin> There follows the curved staff <note>The heka or crook</note>, a symbol of dominion granted by the Powers Above; then follow three feathers with the figure A, a symbol by which it is hinted that the virtues of the <term>Agathodaemon Momphtaeus</term> <note>A "Good Spirit" or protective deity in Kircher's system, associated with the creative breath</note> must be imitated in executing the affairs of the Kingdom. For he, as the minister of the supreme <term>Osiris</term> <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife and rebirth, often equated by Kircher with a primary solar deity</note>, towers above all things by the sublimity of his condition, and penetrates all things by his subtlety...

<summary>Kircher explains that the Egyptian monarchy was modeled after divine order, using the "Dragon-shaped Butterfly" as a symbol for a King who, like a "Pantamorphic" spirit, adapts to the needs of all subjects to maintain unity and peace.</summary>

# CHAPTER V: THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS
### Page 196

...it spreads, and with speed of motion accomplishes all things; these are the properties of the said Agathodaemon <note>The "Good Spirit," often depicted as a winged serpent or protector</note> indicated by the three feathers. The Momphaean Deity <note>A local Egyptian manifestation of a god</note> is also to be imitated through a lion-shaped statue; here he indicates the Agathodaemon through the **hieralpha** <term>hieralpha: a sacred symbol resembling the letter Alpha, used as a sign of divine power</term>, which he carries in his hand. This indicates that the dominion committed to him by the Powers Above—as shown by the curved staff placed over him—exerts the greatest force upon the moist substance of the Nile. From this flow great benefits for the Cities and for agriculture, as the symbols **Z** suggest. Hence, every year, <margin>Plutarch.</margin> according to the testimony of Plutarch, they used to lead his statue in a **Baris** <note>original: "Bary"</note> along the Nile, as the beneficent Deity of the Egyptian earth, as the <margin>The Baris ship.</margin> depicted Baris and the two extended hands sufficiently indicate.

**A** Through the Baris ship, they indicated that a political Kingdom ought to be governed with the highest care, so that the said advantages might result from it. Like a Vulture, the ruler must constantly brood over the political sky and keep watch against Typhonian <note>Referring to Typhon/Set, the god of chaos and destruction</note> machinations. There follows the figure of a globe, from the bottom of which two feet emerge; by this <margin>A globe from the bottom of which two feet emerge.</margin> symbol, as was shown in the Pamphylian Obelisk, the hidden movement of the Supreme Deity through all the paths of the World is expressed, which is to be uniquely imitated by Kings. For a King, physical movement into the innermost recesses of his realm is hardly necessary; rather, his "feet" ought to be the dictates of right reason. While through these, healthy institutions for the Kingdom are established and promulgated, the King is rightly judged to pervade the whole Kingdom and to animate everyone with his presence; and this is to imitate the hidden movement of the Supreme Deity through the paths of the entire World. And yet, though this movement of the Supreme Deity is hidden, it shines forth most clearly and in a sensible manner in the All-Formed nature of the World through the variety of effects it produces, which is indicated by the following <margin>Butterfly.</margin> Butterfly; this hints that a Prince ought to shine forth chiefly through his executors of constitutions, his Counselors, and Prefects, through the effects caused by justice and the observation of laws. Whence the sacred tablet is prescribed as an image of these things, and a most powerful **periapt** <term>periaptōn: an amulet or protective charm worn on the body</term> for attracting the divine Legislator Osiris, which was explained in the preceding pages.

**C** Following the sacred tablet are two Owls, between which is a globe with two segments. These indicate that those carrying the tablet warn Osiris and Isis of dangers and dire events threatening the Kingdom (which are aptly indicated by Owls, as we have taught more extensively in the "Hieroglyphics of the Owl"), so that they may look into matters in a timely fashion. (For as Manetho <margin>An Owl seen in a dream is a bad omen.</margin> reports, if any of the Priests had seen an Owl in a dream, it was considered altogether dire and ill-omened). Thus, Kings are to be informed to some extent of Typhonian plots by the aforementioned tutelary Deities, so that they might foresee in time the ways in which they might resist them. So says <margin>Abenephius.</margin> Abenephius the Arab in his book *On Egyptian Servitude*.

-> [The text refers to a figure] conspicuous with a Lion’s head and a whip; for it was believed that this Deity turned away all the dire things which the Owl portends with its grim omens for the earth, waters, cities, and altars, and converted them into good, as is evident from the symbols at **D**. There follow these three gates with five boundaries; by which it is indicated that upon the three gates <margin>Five laws carved on three gates. Pausanias.</margin> of Agathodæmon Ophioneus <note>A "Good Spirit" often depicted as a serpent; Kircher links him to the Greek "Ophioneus."</note> five laws had been carved, which Aristaeus of Memphis recites, as found in Pausanias; the first of which was, *pull the chain of the Gods*; the second, *guard the papyrus bundle*; the third, *bind the celestial and terrestrial Horus, the beneficent Deities*; the fourth, *imitate the two Hawks well*; the fifth, *bind yourself by the beneficence of Horus, which will happen if you offer sacred rites to him at the fourfold quarter of the World*. Let us reveal how aptly these five laws are displayed through symbols. The cycloid figures placed above **E** with five limits indicate the three gates of Agathodæmon Ophioneus, who was one of the ministers <margin>E</margin> of Momphta <note>Kircher's term for the supreme creative intellect of the Egyptians.</note>, as Aristaeus asserts; upon these, the five laws to be observed above all were carved by the Priests, and they regarded the prosperity of public administration.

The first law, *Pull the chain <margin>Hieroglyphic of the first law.</margin> of the Gods*, is fitly displayed by figure **E**, formed in the manner of a chain, which ended in an eye-like shape; by the chain was indicated the concatenation of the Spirits of the World, whose vertex is the eye—the archetype of the supreme Mind, namely divine providence—which the law prescribes must be "pulled." To pull the chain of the Gods is nothing other than to know the order of things in the World and to contemplate the same assiduously; for from this contemplation, as if by a certain attraction, the followers of the Gods present themselves as obedient to all your requests; especially if you establish sacred rites for them analogous to the operations of the Spirits of the World, as we have taught throughout this entire Work.

The second law, *Guard the papyrus bundle*, which the staff <margin>Hieroglyphic of the second law. A papyrus staff signifies abundance.</margin> opposite the chain expresses; we have shown in previous sections that the papyrus staff indicates nothing other than the abundance of all things; and this is because the Egyptians prepared everything necessary for human use from papyrus, and it was a symbol of <term>Pantamorphic</term> <note>All-forming or taking many shapes.</note> nature, which the Butterfly, swollen in the manner of a Dragon, suggested, and to which you will always find it attached. Therefore, to guard the papyrus staff signifies nothing else than that the leaders of the Kingdom must apply themselves with the greatest zeal to provide for all things necessary for human life, if they wish to keep their subjects in peace and tranquility.

The third law was, *Bind the celestial and terrestrial <margin>Hieroglyphic of the third law.</margin> beneficent Deities of Horus*; which are indeed most aptly indicated by the noose joined to the head of Horus, to which a little further down, by means of a Serpent, another head is placed with two hands extended. Horus, as we have taught throughout this entire Work, is nothing other than the Sensible World, which, according to Plutarch, is twofold: <margin>Horus is twofold: superior and inferior.</margin> the superior Horus, that is, the Starry one, and the inferior, that is, the Elemental one. The law therefore commands to "bind" him; by which nothing else is suggested but to apply the orders of the things of the lower World to the orders of the upper through a certain fixed analogy, and finally to establish the political state according to the analogy of said things through a disposition of laws adapted precisely to both.

The fourth law is, *Imitate the two Hawks*; <margin>Hieroglyphic of the fourth law.</margin> which are aptly expressed by the two Hawks opposite **F**; for two Hawks, according to <margin>F</margin> Horapollo <note>The supposed author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs.</note>...

There follows this Serpent, and the statue of <term>Isis the Averter</term> <note>original: "Isis averrunca," a deity who wards off misfortune</note>, as the whip in her hands teaches, with a poppy-scepter; by which symbols the worship of Isis the Protectress is chiefly urged. In this, what the crown is to the head of the poppy, the King or Prince is to the political state; what the seeds contained in the head are, the subjects are in politics; and finally, what the distinct little chambers are in the poppy, the different jurisdictions are in the political state; and thus Isis appropriately holds the poppy-scepter. If you observe these laws, raised up by the Hawk’s feather via the Hermetic ladder, you shall obtain the happiness of dominion, which is expressed by the wing, the ladder, and the curved staff; the vital moisture will confer an abundance of all things, as the water-symbol with the Serpent and the papyrus staff indicate. Finally follows the Ibis with the Serpent and the Nile-vessel, the three-knotted scepter, and two boundary stones; these indicate that the Hermetic laws described in this column provide life and health to the entire Nilotic dominion, which is the goal of Egyptian happiness.

# TREATISE II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. CHAPTER V.

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

It increases; it removes all parching and <term>Bebonian</term><note>Referring to Bebon, a name for Typhon, the god of chaos and drought</note> nocturnal force; furthermore, it perpetually flows into the Zodiac by its own power. From there, it flows into the Nilotic streams through three vessels—marked, according to the witness <term>Horus</term><note>Likely referring to Horapollo, author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note>, as receptacles of the vital moisture—and finally transmits the desired life through the influxive motion of the <term>dodecapyrgos</term><note>A "twelve-towered" structure or astrological device representing the twelve signs of the Zodiac</note> into the subterranean cisterns or <term>fauissae</term>, passing through three receptacles placed beneath a semicircle. <margin>Sacred cisterns.</margin> These <term>fauissae</term> or sacred cisterns were certain receptacles in the subterranean inner sanctums of the shrines, which derived their origin from the Nile through hidden channels. Just as their waters were consecrated to the immortal Gods, so they were thought to possess the greatest energy above all the waters of the world. Truly, concerning the construction of these cisterns, see what we have handed down copiously in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 473. In these cisterns, the Nilometric columns were placed, from whose steps the Priests, at the time of the Nilotic increase, <margin>Nilometric columns.</margin> would divine the future condition of the year. But these things are expressed, not incongruously, by the Nilometric scale divided into certain steps, which the Priest standing beside it <margin>Nilotic laws.</margin> is seen to contemplate. Through these Nilotic laws of great importance, they judged above all else that an abundance of necessary things must be procured for any Kingdom; while this lasted, the Kingdom would stand firm, the subjects would live in peace and tranquility, and they would honor the Prince with due love and benevolence for his providence toward his subjects. But when these things failed, they believed that nothing else but murmurs, seditions, and similar injuries to the Republic could lead the Kingdom to ultimate ruin. But now, back to the thread of the argument.

**F** Following the Nilometric column is a <note>Reference to a schema or diagram marked 'F'</note> diagram composed of water and a <margin>The Hydrophrium diagram.</margin> Serpent, and it represents the vital moisture. Since the <term>Typhonian</term> nocturnal force is contrary to this, the Gate of the inner sanctum must be marked with the pole of <term>Canopus</term><note>A reference to the star or the Egyptian deity associated with water</note> and adorned with the celestial laws of the triple World, using the image of a vulture—the passive principle of nature—at the altar where the customary ceremony is to be performed according to the four quarters of the World.

**G** & **H** In this manner, Typhon shall be driven out from the Kingdom. All these things are signified by those symbols contained between F, G, and H. You see in the region of H something like the figure of a crown, adorned with three poppy <margin>A crown adorned with poppies and peach leaves.</margin> heads and two intervening peach leaves. By these it is shown that the King ought to be always mindful of his subjects, so that he may govern them with union **I**, direct them with wisdom, and win them over with beneficence; he must see to it that the Nilotic laws are exactly observed as the pillar of the Kingdom. Thus, with Typhon—the adversary of Egyptian fertility—repelled by the providence of the King, the life of things is granted to the highest benefit of all, brought about through the influx of the supernal powers into the lower <term>hylaean</term><note>From the Greek 'hyle' (matter); the material or physical world</note> World.

The summit of this column is held by an Asp, emerging from a circle and penetrating all members of the Universe; it presents a symbol of <term>Pantamorphic</term> <note>meaning "all-shaped" or "all-transforming"</note> nature, or, as the Platonists would have it, the *Anima Mundi* <note>the "World Soul," an intrinsic spirit believed to animate all nature</note>. Since this symbol has already been explained quite often, we have chosen not to dwell on it here. Beneath it, it has a goose standing upon a sacred tablet, by which they signified that the power of the World Soul flows immediately into Osiris. Here, it flows into the Mercurial economy, as shown by the oval figure of the sacred tablet, conspicuous with an Ibis sitting upon an <term>Alphamorphic</term> <note>shaped like the letter Alpha, symbolizing a beginning or primary form</note> gnomon; this is a <term>periapt</term> <note>original: "periaptū," a protective charm or amulet</note> of great virtue, as has been said. <margin>The office of Mercury.</margin> For the office of the supramundane Mercury, granted by Pantamorphic nature and Osiris himself, is to weigh all things in the balance of reason, to adapt them to symmetry, and to arrange the benefits of the seasons of the year. Mercury performs this same function in the sidereal kingdom, as does the King, the minister of Mercury, in the Political World. Thus, there is nothing in the lower World that does not exist in a certain more eminent way in the superior Worlds; and therefore the Ideas of the superior World are certain patterns to which the lower things, and even the political World, must be adapted. Without these, the lower could not subsist, depending upon them as causes "essentially," as the Schools <note>referring to Scholastic philosophers</note> say. And such a pattern is this sacred tablet, so often proposed on this Obelisk, the effects of which we shall now <margin>**Y**</margin> explain. They are as follows: first, a happy omen; second, the supply of necessary things; third, the flight of evils. The first is explained by the Nilometer itself with its joined signs; the second by the Hawk with a papyrus staff; the third by the Owl. Then follows the care of sacred things, signified by the altar and the attached feather, as has been said elsewhere. For by these, divine providence is indicated through the eye, while it pervades all the paths of the World with a hidden motion (indicated by two feet). It derives the vital moisture—which the <term>hydroschema</term> <note>a symbolic representation of water</note> and the Serpent denote—after the Typhonian Owl has been put to flight, from the Mendesian bowl <note>a symbol of fertility and the overflowing Nile</note> filled with fecundity. This flows from the three Worlds (signified by three circles) <margin>**Z**</margin> into the Political World, which is denoted by the scepter upon which a poppy-shaped head <margin>**A**</margin> is placed and a transverse Serpent rests. By this, it is indeed aptly indicated that life is drawn from the supramundane bowl into the Worlds subordinate to it, and finally into the political state. The "life" of such a state consists of upright dominion and the observation of laws among the subjects, as well as the study of agriculture, which is pursued diligently for the preservation of the kingdom. From this, fecundity results in the fourfold face of the World, which is indicated by three shovels, the scepter with a goat's head, and the cross-shaped figure. <margin>**B**</margin> Osiris and the celestial Horus, the overseers of the vital moisture, are drawn down through two sacred tablets C and D, which possess great virtue; and to them, the providence of Pantamorphic nature is <margin>**C**</margin> reconciled. But see the meanings of these things already declared above. Following the sacred tablet are the water-symbol, the Serpent, the Genial Alpha, and the cycloid <margin>**E**</margin>...

# TREATISE II. THE RAMESSIDE OBELISK. CHAPTER VI

...from the Sparrow, and it also disagrees with the Crow. Let us demonstrate both. Pierius <margin>Pierius Valerianus.</margin> <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani (1477–1558), author of the influential "Hieroglyphica."</note> speaks thus concerning the Owl and the Crow: *If the Egyptian Priests wished to signify two enemies driven by a capital hatred, plotting damages and snares against one another with everlasting indignation, and staining their hands with the blood of mutual slaughter, they decided to place the Owl and the Crow. The enmities between these two are so immortal that both the former and the latter continually exercise their hatred to their mutual ruin. For by day, the Crow snatches the Owl's eggs and takes them for itself, being aware that the Owl is blind during the day; and the Owl, in turn, attacks the Crow's eggs by night, stealing them to eat. Thus, one is more powerful by day and the other by night; because of this, there are those who persuade themselves that the mingled blood of the two cannot even be made to mix.* So says Pierius. <margin>The disagreement of the Owl and the Crow.</margin> Regarding the Sparrow and the Owl, Horus <note>Horapollo, the purported author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs.</note> discusses it thus: *Desiring to show a man who flees to his own patron but is not relieved by his help, they paint a Sparrow and an Owl; for while the Sparrow is hunted by the fowlers, it runs to the Owl for protection, by whom it is soon crushed.* <margin>Horus.</margin> Is it not aptly suggested by these symbols that there is a tyrannical administration of political affairs, appropriately expressed through the Typhonian <note>Associated with Typhon/Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and evil.</note> Owl? What else does the Sparrow denote but the simple common people, who, agitated by various afflictions, seek refuge with an unhealthy Prince? Far from finding a safe refuge there, they are instead soon crushed by him, either by the unjust extortion of money or by the imposition of other intolerable burdens. From this, an utterly irreconcilable hatred of the people toward the Prince is born, and consequently seditions, riots, slaughters, and other damages to the Republic, which portend the ultimate destruction of the Kingdom. <margin>The Sparrow denotes the simple people.</margin> This tyrannical mind of a King is expressed even more aptly by the following symbol **F** in this region: a Quail with a papyrus scepter <note>original: "thyrso papyraceo"</note>, a symbol of the lack of things necessary for the kingdom due to the depravity of the King. <margin>The Quail is a symbol of a Tyrant. **F**</margin> Horus graphically describes the malice of this bird in Book 1, Chapter 49, with these words: *And writing of impudence, they paint a quail* <note>original Greek: "ἀναίδειαν δὲ γράφοντες ὄρτυγα"</note> (for the better manuscripts have it thus, as has been demonstrated by us elsewhere, not "oryx") *they paint it.* <margin>Horus.</margin> Furthermore, noting an impious and wicked mind, they paint a Quail. <margin>Properties of the Quail.</margin> Indeed, this bird was considered by the Egyptians to be as ill-omened as it was irreverent toward the immortal Gods; it was infamous not only for its impurity, but because it joined to that impurity a contempt for the Gods and a hatred of religion, which was so greatly execrated by the Egyptians. For as often as the Moon rises, it raises ill-omened cries against her, according to Horus—not to bid the Goddess hail, nor to pursue her with the praises due to the Gods, but it gives the most manifest signs of indignation against her. This was considered a great impiety among them, since they pursued the Moon with the highest worship. Above all, it digs in the earth and repeatedly scratches its own pupils, as if impatient of the Moon, whom it does not even deign to look upon; it does the same at the rising of the Sun, that divine star. Likewise, in the solitary places it frequents, if it finds any spring of clear water, as soon as it has drunk, it strives to corrupt the remaining water with its beak and feet and make it muddy by casting dust into it, lest it be sought for drink by any other animal. By this, they secretly and aptly taught the malice, avarice, and depravity of a tyrant, who does not have the common and political good as his goal, but follows his own advantages in all things.

# CHAPTER VI. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
Tyranny according to Aristotle
</margin>

For as Aristotle rightly showed, Tyranny is nothing other than Kingship degenerating into ruin and corruption through the impiety of the Ruler; when a Ruler, though <term>self-sufficient</term> <note>original: "αὐταρκὴς" (autarkēs) - a Greek philosophical term for one who is independent or lacks nothing</note> and overflowing with an abundance of all goods, seeks not the benefit of the needy people, but his own. From this follows the restlessness of the people; from restlessness, murmuring; from murmuring, sedition; from sedition, war; and from war, the final destruction of the Kingdom lies open. A Tyrant, like a Quail, despises the laws of the Sun and Moon while he imposes laws contrary to the dictates of right reason. He digs into the earth while he consumes treasures owed to the public good for his own uses. What else is it to disturb clear water and make it muddy, if not to disturb public tranquility with intolerable burdens, to envy the goods of others, and thus to seek every way and means to seize them? But all these following symbols included between F, G, H, and I teach this sufficiently: <note>Hieroglyphic description F: An eye (oculus), a knotted scepter (sceptrum tuberosum), a square (quadratum), two segments (one smaller, one larger), and three axes (tres secures).</note> namely, the knotted scepter, the square, two segments (smaller and larger), and three axes. Through the eye and the scepter, the providence of the Kingdom is removed; the highest things are confused with the middle, and the middle with the lowest, bringing about the destruction of all things through a triple cutting-away, as it were, by the three axes. <note>Hieroglyphic description G: A sparrow (Passer) flying toward an owl (Noctua).</note> The Sparrow flying toward the Owl is soon overwhelmed, which is beautifully indicated by the bird with the feather from region G; the celestial life, the standard of Osiris's Kingdom, is thrown into confusion, as the Serpent, the coils, <note>Hieroglyphic description H: A coiled serpent (Serpens cycloides) and two opposing pestles (pistilla).</note> and the two opposing pestles denote. The three rudders of H, established for the Kingdom according to the pattern of the triple World and the symbol of prosperous conduct, are perverted through the transgression of laws—which are like certain boundaries established for human actions—by an action of life contrary to them, noted by the opposing movements of the Serpents. <note>Hieroglyphic description I: Osiris as the intellect of necessary things.</note> Osiris, the intellect providing for the abundance of necessary things, is confined by the heavens; hence, with the laws of the upper and lower worlds confused, the beneficent power necessarily ceases both from the cities and from the vital moisture of agriculture. For these evils, no other remedy seems to remain except the religious worship of the triform Deity, as the tripod <note>Hieroglyphic description K: Religious cult of a triform deity, a tripod (tripus), and Nilotic vessel amulets with a mitered statue.</note> and the amulets of Nilotic vessels with the mitered statue indicate. The statue of Hemphta, powerful in dominion over the tripartite division of the year, and the lion-formed Momphta, the principle of vital motion and providence, will eliminate the Typhonian Owl—that is, all adversities—both from the <term>twelve-gated</term> <note>original: "δωδεκαπύλῳ" (dōdekapylō) - referring to the twelve signs of the Zodiac</note> celestial Zodiac of the three Worlds, and from the lower Elementary and Political World established according to its model. Isis, the overseer of vital moisture and the Good Spirit <note>original: "Agathodæmon"</note> of necessary things, will resuscitate the crushed life of the Worlds through both munificence and blessing, by the provident progress of nature. This is properly attributed to Isis (from whom she takes her name), and the foot placed between boundaries sufficiently hints at this, as does the statue M with the papyrus staff <note>Hieroglyphic description M: A statue with a papyrus thyrsus between two serpents and two pestles; one arm extended, the other in a blessing gesture.</note> positioned between two Serpents and two pestles, and the two arms, of which the first holds a hand extended, and the other

# TREATISE II. THE RAMESSEAN OBELISK. 205 CH. VI.

...the things of the provider and guardian will be fulfilled; for which the following preventative measure, already often explained, will be effective.

### §. II.

->*Interpretation of the second column of the third Western side.*<-

<margin>Interpretation of the second column of the third side of the Ramessean Obelisk. The evils of the Starry World, and their antidotes.</margin>
In this column, the evils of the Starry World and their antidotes are indicated, and an example is proposed for the Political World <note>The "Political World" refers to the organized human society and its governance, mirroring the celestial order.</note> to imitate. For there is in the starry economy a certain malignant force, resulting both from the disposition and radiation of the stars, and from the influence of opposing presiding Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"</note>, by which all lower things are repeatedly vexed in a horrendous manner. How indeed this fatal necessity, which the Egyptians asserted, must be met, and how they can be released from fate, the column explains. And first, a Hawk sitting upon a square, as has already been often said, indicates the Elemental World, over which Osiris, the soul of the Starry World, rules. Moreover, within the said square are placed an ox, with an extended arm, an Owl, and a statue of <term>Momphta</term> <note>A Kircherian term for a specific divine manifestation of the creative intellect, often associated with water or humid nature</note>; by which is indicated I know not what antipathy of fire and water, of which if either prevails, it is certain that great calamities are brought in; and it is a certain fatal necessity, as they say; concerning which it seemed fit to discuss a little more deeply.

<margin>Iamblichus. The Egyptians seem to have subjected free will to the motion of the stars.</margin>
Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD)</note> teaches that the Egyptians subjected our free will to the motion of the stars; how this is to be understood, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote "On the Mysteries"</note> explains in his book on the mysteries from the Mercurial opinions or Hermetic doctrine. *Man has two souls,* he says, *as the Mercurial letters—that is, the Hieroglyphics—teach; one indeed is from the first intelligible, which is <term>Hemphta</term>* <note>The supreme divine intellect or "Creator" in Kircher's Egyptian theology</note> *the highest and first intellect of all, partaking of the power of the Maker himself; the other truly is bestowed upon us from the life of the celestial beings, into which the soul, the observer of divine things, also creeps. Therefore, the soul descending into us from the Worlds also follows the circuits of the Worlds; but that which comes from the intelligible is present in an intelligible way, and it stands above the circuit of generation; and through this we are released from fate, and we ascend to the intelligible Gods, and we hold a religion tending toward eternal things.*

<margin>Our soul is not subjected to Fate.</margin>
By no means, therefore, should it be thought that all things are bound by the insoluble chains of necessity, which they call fate; for the soul has a principle proper to itself, by which it may betake itself to the intelligible; and it descends indeed from those things which are born, but it approaches toward Being itself and the divine; nor does fate properly apply to the Gods, as Iamblichus says, whom the Egyptians worshipped in temples, sacrifices, and statues as those who release us from fate; but certain lowest natures descending from the Gods, and involved in generation and the mixture of the corporeal World, carry out fate. Hence the Egyptians, not without reason, applied all sanctity to the Gods, so that they alone, ruling over necessity through intellectual persuasion, might loosen the evils threatening them from fate: For not everything in nature is bound to fate, but there is also another principle of the soul, superior both to nature and to generation, through which they could join themselves to the Gods...

<summary>Kircher explains how the Egyptian soul can escape the "fatal necessity" of astrological influence by connecting with the supreme divine intellect (Hemphta). He uses Neoplatonic philosophy to argue that while the body is subject to the stars, the higher soul remains free.</summary>

**F** <margin>The Butterfly, or Egyptian fly, and the multiform Demon of the Sensible World.</margin> After the quadrangle, therefore, in region **F**, the Dragon-shaped Butterfly or Egyptian fly is encountered, under whose feet is a Serpent, followed by the sacred table—found everywhere and already frequently explained. By the Butterfly, as we have taught elsewhere, the multiform Demon of the Sensible World <note>The "Sensible World" refers to the physical world perceived by the senses, as opposed to the "Intelligible World" of pure thought and spirit.</note> is indicated, powerful in his dominion over the lives of things and master of all fate. For since he involves and entangles himself in all bodies of the Sensible World, and governs each thing by his influence, as the sacred table shows; they denote the presiding Intelligences by the globe, the economy of the Starry World and the celestial spheres (especially the Zodiac) by the <term>dodecapyrgon</term> <note>original: δωδεκάπυργον; literally "twelve-towered," referring here to the twelve signs of the Zodiac</note>, and the lower Osiris by the Scarab. Moreover, since fate is bound to the conversion and disposition of the stars, no one, according to the opinion of the Egyptians, can escape its fatal influence according to the laws prescribed by necessity; for this multiform Demon is inferior only to the Intelligible World. Hence the Egyptian Priests, in times of impending fate, would betake themselves entirely to the Intelligible World. And indeed, according to the testimony of Horus, they expressed fate through the figure of a Star, but the Intelligible World through a globe resting upon a tripod, governed solely by the office of the triple-formed supreme Deity, the ruler of the vital and intelligible World.

**G** <margin>Horus.</margin> <margin>The hieroglyphic of Fate.</margin>

**H** This Deity the Priests—whom the human figure depicted with extended arms in the manner of a suppliant denotes—would solicit against the fatal machinations of the Bebonic Owl <note>The "Noctua Bebonia" or Bebonic Owl represents a destructive or chaotic force in Kircher's system, often associated with Typhon or ill-fortune.</note> through rites and ceremonies that were not physical, but through various internal intellectual operations. To this Deity, as the following symbols—the three boundary stones, the altar, the feather, the square, the segment, and the circle—show, they performed mystical rites. By the feather, they signified the elevation of the mind; by the bare altar, they bore witness to a mind immune from every stain of human contagion; by the square, the stable rest of a mind directed toward God and unshaken constancy, according to the testimony of Pierio. By the three boundary stones, with the segment and the globe, they signified the untarnished observation of the divine or Mercurial laws.

<margin>The discord of things in the Sublunary World.</margin>
<margin>**Y**</margin>
<margin>A Political lesson</margin>
**A** hawk sits upon a quadrangle, in which a statue of <term>Isis</term> <note>The Egyptian goddess representing nature and the earth</note>, and a <term>Quail</term>, is included with an Alpha and two feathers. By this, indeed, nothing else is indicated at first glance but the dominion which <term>Osiris the Hawk-like</term> <note>Osiris represented as a hawk, symbolizing solar and divine authority</note> holds over the Elemental World, of which Isis—that is, the earth—holds the principal seat, the support of all inferior and <term>hylic</term> <note>from the Greek 'hyle', meaning material or physical matter</note> nature. However, those who take Isis for the Moon understand through her the chief dominion over the material world (inasmuch as she is adjacent to it) and the principle of the actions of all things subject to the Moon. To her, as I have said in preceding sections, the Quail—that is, a certain Typhonian force <note>Referring to Typhon/Set, the principle of chaos and destruction</note>—is contrary to the Lunar moisture. By this is understood nothing other than the strife of things in the sublunary world, which are subject to the greatest alterations and contrary qualities; where cold things fight with hot, and moist things with dry. These are so necessary to the contrariety and antipathy of the material realm that the lower world could by no means consist without them. From this, let politicians learn that to maintain vigilance in a Kingdom and to strengthen the vigor of the mind, troublesome enemies of the realm are sometimes necessary. For in this way, laws are more exactly observed, the King is rendered more vigilant and cautious in the care of administering the kingdom, and more circumspect toward the schemes of the opposing faction. For if only cold, or heat, or moisture, or dryness reigned alone in the lower world, it would be necessary for all things to fail; so in a kingdom, where there is no enemy, there is languor and idleness; where there is no fear, there is luxury and discord, which are like certain nearby precipices of the entire kingdom, portending its ultimate ruin. The Egyptians hint at this beautifully, <margin>Why Isis did not kill Typhon.</margin> according to the testimony of Plutarch <note>A Greek philosopher who wrote 'On Isis and Osiris'</note>, through Isis and Typhon. For Isis, although she had captured <term>Typhon</term> (who was plotting the ultimate destruction of the Egyptian kingdom) by the strength of <term>Horus</term>, was so far from killing him that instead—though she did not set him entirely free—she detained him as a necessary incentive for care and vigilance in administering the kingdom. All of these things are expressed thus far in the quadrangle by the statue of Isis with the Quail. But concerning these matters, see what we have dealt with at greater length in the *Politics of the Egyptians*, Volume 1, Section 2, folio 30.

<margin>**Y**</margin>

### §. III.

### Interpretation of the third column of the fourth Oriental side; containing the origin of evils:

<margin>
Interpretation of the third column of the fourth side of the Rameseum Obelisk.
</margin>

<margin>
The Archetypal World contains no evil. Plutarch.
</margin>

In order for this to be understood, it must be noted that in the **Archetypal World** <note>The divine realm of pure ideas</note> there is no evil, nor does any evil or defect proceed from it effectively. Rather, all evil follows the operations of the Sensible World—which are otherwise good—just as rust, according to **Plutarch**, follows iron. Therefore, the Egyptians believe that the cause of all evils and adversities lies in the disposition of the Starry World (as fate), by reason of its arrangement, as we have taught in our *Politics*. These evils cannot be countered by any other means than the exact practice of religious worship, as prescribed in this column.

In the first place, following the Asp and the symbol of the **All-Formed** <note>original: "Pantamorphi"</note> spirit of the Ideal World, there occurs a curved staff with a Goat’s head, a Nilotic vessel, and three feathers. These are followed by the **Owl**, beneath which are placed three arms with three boundaries between them. By these symbols, it is aptly indicated that in the Supreme World, there is a certain Mendesian <note>Fertile or generative</note> fecundity of the All-Formed nature, corresponding to the supra-mundane Nile and proceeding from the mind of the triform Deity, from which an abundance of all good things flows. However, as soon as this is propagated into the Sensible World, it contracts a certain malignancy, indicated by the Owl, which is contrary to the triple vital benevolence of the Divine Mind (as shown by the three arms). This malignant force is evident in the dominion of the Heavens, which are agitated by contrary motions; by this, the benevolence of the Deity is to some extent coerced in the material worlds. This malignant force shines forth in the laws of the **twelve-towered** <note>original: "δωδεκαπύργου" (dodekapyrgou)</note> zodiac, in which, just as signs are found contrary to signs, so houses are contrary to houses and mansions to mansions of the Gods. Indeed, by their influx into the lower Political World, evils are subsequently multiplied as if carried in a triple vehicle, through the power of the **Opposing Fortunes** <note>original: "ἀντιτύχων" (antitychon)</note> of the deities. These, when communicated to the moist substance, bring various species of pestilential contagion to the political state, signified by the figure of the Scorpion. Nevertheless, celestial providence will heal all things by its virtue, if they pull the chains of the Genial Deities—that is, if the Priests solicit the said Genii with frequent ceremonies according to the disposition of the year and the laws of the Kingdom. For by these, the Owl shall be crushed; the troublesome Quail shall be put to flight by the industry of the Priests; the three Watchmen—
