# TREATISE II. THE RAMESSEUS OBELISK. CHAPTER VII

The guardians <note>original: "cubitores"</note>, Chenosiris, Anubis, and Hermanubis, indicated by three geese, together with Isis, the averting Spirit <note>A protective deity who turns away evil</note>, being filled with life-giving influences, shall dispel the Typhonian Owl <note>A symbol of darkness or Typhon, the principle of chaos</note> which is contrary to the providence of celestial life; <margin>G</margin> Osiris, fertile with life-giving beneficence, shall bestow the vital moisture of the lower world upon Osiris <margin>H</margin>; he, in turn, shall attract the polymorphic spirit of the world for the aid of the sacred power of the following table, and through the observation of the laws described on the Isiac column; and in this manner, once the Owl of all evils has been routed, an abundance of things shall be restored to the fourfold world.

From all these interpretations proposed thus far, it is clearly evident that this Obelisk, marked with its hieroglyphics, shows nothing other than the rational method for establishing a political Kingdom according to the model of the supernal minds; for they did not believe that any Kingdom could endure unless it were founded upon religion, which is the worship of the supreme Deity. Plato explains all of these matters so clearly in the 10th book of *The Laws* that he seems to have looked toward the Egyptian standard. For we have found that the order of things shining forth in nature depends everywhere upon reason; and indeed, an order that is nowhere and never interrupted emanates from a most powerful reason; finally, an order that is beneficial, harmonious, and connecting all things in a wonderful union emanates from the highest reason. Since, therefore, both the disposition and the progression of the Universe are most orderly, and are always and everywhere so, and not without the highest benefit; it is necessary that the World be disposed and moved by the highest and most powerful reason. 

But since the Universe is one, and a unity is not made from diverse things except by a single source, it follows that this kind of reason is supreme. Furthermore, there are many divine reasons under the supreme divine reason, just as in a single work of the World, ordered by the highest reason, there are many spheres distinct from one another in appearance and manifold in virtue, all ordered by a wonderful reason, so much so that in a certain way many worlds seem to be contained within the most ample circumference of the one World; likewise, many rulers of these narrower worlds, as it were, are arranged in succession and encompassed under the one Ruler of the most ample World. He, surely, since he is not merely more orderly, but is himself, so to speak, immense order, rejoices much more in the ordainer than in the ordained. Wherefore, if he is undoubtedly delighted by the many ordered things in the Universe, it is necessary that he is also delighted by many ordainers; for the most excellent greatness of the most ample King consists in this: that he has beneath him not only lowly servants, but also many great Kings. 

Furthermore, since the supreme Deity acts by understanding what he does; and if he makes the whole, he also understands the whole; if he knows the whole, he shall also know the parts of which the whole consists; if the parts, then also the necessary particles from which the parts coalesce: he is therefore able, and knows how, to govern the Universe, he who knows and is able to provide for the same. But he cannot govern the whole unless the parts are governed; therefore, he who did not neglect to make the smallest things does not neglect to govern the smallest things. Nor is governance difficult for him for whom procreation is easy. # TREATISE III.
# THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK,
## FORMERLY KNOWN AS THE OBELISK OF SENNESERTAEUS.

<note>Decorative woodcut ornament consisting of symmetrical leafy vines and floral motifs</note>

### TO THE MOST AUGUST
# FERDINAND IV.
->King of the Romans.<-

**F**OR YOU, Ferdinand the Fourth, August King, I raise this present Obelisk—one long ago brought out of Egypt by Augustus Caesar and erected in the <term>Circus Maximus</term><note>The largest stadium in ancient Rome, used for chariot racing; Augustus placed the obelisk on its central barrier.</note> as a kind of trophy of honor to the immortality of his name. It is fitting for August Emperors to erect Obelisks, and just as fitting to consecrate them to August Kings. Just as Obelisks, by their extraordinary height, seem to strike the very heavens, so too should mortals learn from this symbol that Kings—raised above the common condition of men—should savor nothing but what is high, sublime, glorious, and noble. Because you, **MOST AUGUST KING**, excel in these qualities, I have been driven by a certain hidden premonition of the mind to prove to posterity, through this Flaminian Obelisk (as if through a hidden and recondite symbol), how much the World promises itself from your Heroic virtue. Farewell.

# TREATISE III.
## The Flaminian Obelisk, formerly called the Sennefertean.
### CHAPTER I.
->*Historical account of the Flaminian Obelisk.*<-

<margin>The Flaminian Obelisk was erected by King Sennefertes of Egypt, according to Pliny.</margin>PLINY asserts in Book 36, Chapter 9, that this Obelisk was erected by the Egyptian King Sennefertes <note>original: "Sennefertæo"</note> in these words: *“Furthermore, that Obelisk which the Divine Augustus erected in the Circus Maximus was cut by Sennefertes, in whose reign Pythagoras was in Egypt; it is 125 feet and nine inches tall, excluding its base of the same stone.”* Pliny therefore thinks that this Obelisk was erected by Sennefertes, and that he was the last King after the devastation of Egypt by Cambyses <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE.</note>. <margin>Herodotus. Diodorus.</margin> However, since others—such as Herodotus—assert that Amasis was the last, and others—such as Diodorus—claim it was Nectanebo, I do not see how these accounts can or should be reconciled. It is by no means likely that such a famous Obelisk was erected at a time when the Egyptian Kingdom was already declining toward its end, since Kings in such a desperate state of affairs could not have applied their minds to the erection of Obelisks, let alone even thinking about them. <margin>The Flaminian Obelisk was erected by Psammirtas.</margin> Therefore, I have seen fit to reveal when and by which King this Obelisk was actually erected. I say, then, that this Obelisk was not erected by Sennefertes, but by Psammirtas; it is certain that Pliny, deceived by the similarity of the names, substituted one for the other. For it is established from our Chronology that the third King of the twenty-sixth Dynasty, whom Manetho calls Psammus and Ctesias calls Amirtes, held power over Egypt. <margin>From where Psammirtas was named and the time in which he lived.</margin> It is probable that from the two names, Psammus and Amirteus, fused into one, "Psammirtas" emerged, which was then corruptly written as "Sennefertes." This King lived about 1527 or, as others say, 1622 years after the Flood, around the beginning of the Olympiads and the founding of the City <note>Rome</note>, roughly 340 years after the reign of Sesostris, as is clear from the Chronology of the Kings of Egypt presented in the first Volume and Treatise. And this Psammus Amirteus, or Psammirtas, erected this Obelisk at the very time when hieroglyphic learning was in full bloom in Egypt, <margin>The time when Pythagoras was in Egypt.</margin> regardless of what Pliny says. Most chronographers of better reputation teach that Pythagoras did not study philosophy in Egypt under this king, but under King Amasis, specifically four years before the invasion of Egypt by Cambyses. However, concerning these matters, as well as Pliny's error regarding the measurement of the Obelisk, we have treated more copiously in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, pages 72 and 73.

<margin>Sixtus V erects the Sennefertean Obelisk on the Via Flaminia.</margin>This present Obelisk was first erected by Psammirtas in Heliopolis; from there, Caesar Augustus took it and erected it in the Circus Maximus in Rome. Finally, having been cast down by the injury of time and buried in the earth, Sixtus V (of happy memory) had it excavated and erected in the Flaminian Field <note>The Piazza del Popolo</note> in the manner which we shall describe.

->Afterwards<-

### TREATISE III. THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK. 215 CHAPTER I.

After the Supreme Pontiff Sixtus V, together with the Ramesseum Obelisk <note>The Lateran Obelisk</note>, had uncovered this present Obelisk buried in the earth in the same Circus Maximus, and various fields of the City of Rome were being considered for its placement; it finally seemed best to erect it in the Flaminian Field <note>The Piazza del Popolo</note> near the primary gate of the City and the Church of St. Mary, commonly called *del Popolo*. This was decided both because it established the supreme majesty of the City of Rome in that location—at the very first entry of foreigners—and because it looked out toward the three principal streets of the City. Therefore, once the Ramesseum Obelisk had been erected in the Lateran Field, the beginning of the erection of this one in the said Flaminian Field was soon given. And first, indeed, a foundation was laid, proportioned to support the mass; then a wooden structure <note>The complex scaffolding and machinery designed by Domenico Fontana</note> necessary for raising the Obelisk was built. Furthermore, upon the foundation, a base of Tiburtine stone <note>Travertine</note> 15 palms in height and 22 palms in width was placed; so that six steps of width were assigned to the three stair-steps surrounding this base, and thus the *abacus* <note>The flat slab on top of the pedestal</note> emerging beyond the stairs maintained a width of only sixteen palms. <margin>Base of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> Upon this base, a square *abacus* fifteen palms high and thirteen wide was placed; this was the same *abacus* upon which the Obelisk had formerly been erected, distinguished by its ancient and new inscriptions, as will be seen shortly hereafter. Thus, the entire base from the surface of the ground to the base of the Obelisk is 38 palms, if you add the height of the cornices surrounding the base and the *abacus*. Upon this substructure, therefore, the Obelisk was placed, which formerly was 100 palms [tall], but now reaches a height of 97 palms up to the *pyramidion* <note>The small pyramid at the very top</note> (on account of three palms of the lower part having been removed, which, corroded by the injury of time, had left the Obelisk unfit for founding). <margin>Height of the same alone, and together with the pyramidion.</margin> Since the *pyramidion* is ten palms, the entire Obelisk today has a height of 107 palms; if you add 38 palms to this, the entire structure from the surface of the earth to the apex reaches a height of 145 palms. The measurement of the parts of the Obelisk is as follows: The two larger and opposite sides of the lower base have a width of 10 and 1/4 palms; <margin>Measurements of the individual parts of the same</margin> the smaller opposite sides are 9 and 1/2 palms. At the *pyramidion*, however, the two larger opposite sides are nine and a half palms; the two smaller opposite sides are 6 and 2/3 palms; from which symmetry the weight of the entire mass can easily be deduced. Moreover, this Obelisk was dedicated to the Holy Cross by Sixtus V on the 25th day of March in the year 1589, as the sign of the Cross placed upon the gilded bronze ball sufficiently demonstrates, and as is evident from the figure placed above on page 213 and the following inscriptions. <margin>In what year and day it was erected.</margin>

# CHAPTER II.

->## The Subject Matter of the Flaminian Obelisk.<-

<margin>The subject of the Flaminian Obelisk is the excellence of the number twelve.</margin>Since the Egyptians perceived a great force and power to be stored within the number twelve <note>Latin: *duodenarius*</note>, they adapted almost all of their symbols to it. For the number twelve is, as we have said elsewhere, a symbol of the entire Universe; by it they expressed the Angelic World divided into twelve parts, the twelve Spheres, the twelve signs of the Zodiac, the twelve regions of the Heaven, and the twelve portions of the Elements. Over these they placed one supreme Deity as the moderator of all things. <margin>Plato.</margin> Plato, a disciple of the Egyptians, especially approves of these things in his sixth Dialogue on *The Laws*; and <margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin> Ficino clearly demonstrates in the preface which he prefixed to the said sixth Dialogue of Plato’s *Laws* that these matters are contained within the mysteries of the Egyptians. *Plato praises,* he says, *the number twelve and that Universe which is exactly adapted to that twelve-fold arrangement, for the reason that there are, according to him, twelve spheres of the World, and twelve signs in the Zodiac, and twelve parts in the Elements; for each of the four <margin>Virtues and qualities of the Elements</margin> Elements is divided into three regions—the highest, the lowest, and the middle—differing not only in position but also in virtue. Add to this another twelve-fold set of the Elements, by which both the four substances of the Elements and the eight qualities are encompassed. Some of the qualities are masculine, namely heat, cold, lightness, and heaviness; of which the first two are the principles of alteration, and the following two are the principles of local motion. Four, however, are feminine, which are more subject to passion <note>In this context, "passion" refers to being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note>, namely moisture, dryness, rarity, and density. <margin>Iamblichus.</margin> Iamblichus asserts that all of this is contained within the mysteries of the Egyptians. Furthermore, in the twelve-fold number of months, the Sun, the lord of the planets, both completes his own course and produces various effects. Finally, he wishes the individual parts of the City, according to the Egyptian norm, to be considered consecrated to God—specifically to the twelve Gods, that is, to the souls of the twelve Spheres, likewise to those ruling the twelve signs of the Zodiac, and again to the twelve orders of Demons <note>In the classical sense, *daemones* were intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences, not necessarily evil.</note> following the celestial signs. Hence <margin>Plato.</margin> Plato asserts that the twelve gates of the City ought to imitate the circuit of the Universe, and then that the army of Gods and Demons is arranged into twelve orders under the leader Jupiter. He concludes at last that the parts of the City—both through the twelve-fold number of tribes and through the divine worship solemnly renewed for these in each of the twelve months—are so prepared for the divine powers of God that they are governed by the Gods themselves as if they were presiding over them.* These are Ficino’s words on Plato. These things certainly agree so well with our Obelisk that Plato seems to have described them from these very monuments. To show this, it must be known that the Egyptians were accustomed to divide the World into twelve regions, according to the testimony of Iamblichus; <margin>The Egyptians divided the World into 12 regions.</margin> over which they placed one Moderator of all, whom they called Hemphta or the supramundane Osiris. <margin>Hemphta or the supramundane Osiris.</margin> They asserted that he acts as all in all things, and that he, continually flowing into the three Worlds below him, bestows life and motion upon all. And since he established a certain "hot-moist" quality in the nature of things shining forth in the Sensible World <note>The physical world perceivable by the senses.</note>, as if it were the fountain of all production and the principle of all things;

From this, they quite aptly indicated these things through the hierogrammatism <note>original: "hierogrammatismum"; refers to the sacred writing or symbolic arrangement</note> at the very top of the **Obelisk**, as if it were a kind of inscription; and they consecrated it to the supramundane **Osiris** and to the supreme **Momphta** <note>A term used by Kircher to describe the "hemic" or creative spirit of the world</note>, the moderator of the moist-warm principle. Although these two are the same in the Intelligible World, they differ in the Sensible World due to the diversity of their effects. <margin>**Momphta** the supreme flows into the World through 12 Solar Genii;</margin> This being, therefore, first flows into the twelve-part World through twelve Solar Genii, who are denoted by twelve **Hawks**. Just as the protection of the entire machinery of the World is committed to them, so too do they moderate everything within it according to different laws. And first, they exert their power upon the twelve signs of the **Zodiac** and the months corresponding to them, and then upon the twelve regions of the sky. Hence, each individual **Hawk** sits upon a specific column corresponding to a region, where the effects which the presiding Genius works in such and such a region are indicated through hierograms in a hidden manner. And since the judgment of all worldly things was established among them, they followed these Genii with great care and religion, lest by omitting the due worship and neglecting religion, the Genii might suspend their beneficial influences and thus subject them to the dominion of contrary powers.

-><-

Wherefore, in this **Obelisk**, the sacred and Hermetic laws are arranged, by which <margin>Sacred laws contained in the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> the manner and reason, and the rites and ceremonies by which divine worship must be instituted in their inner sanctuaries, are set forth. It contains the ways in which the twelve sacred Solar Genii are to be propitiated, and if ever they should incur indignation due to neglected religion, how they are to be appeased, and how the efforts of opposing powers are to be repelled—in a word, the whole is contained, marked through appropriate symbols. <margin>Twelve Solar Genii.</margin> Thus, through the twelve Solar **Agathodaemones** <note>term: Agathodaemones; "Good Spirits" or noble guardian deities</note> of the Starry World, nothing else is signified than the various virtues of the one **Osiris**, by which he acts upon the lower World. To these correspond the twelve terrestrial **Osirises** of the Elemental World, indicated by the twelve **Apis-bulls**, who are the presidents of the twelve regions of the Horizon, dispensing the power received from the highest virtues into the remaining economy of the lower World. Therefore, when the Egyptian Sages saw a certain admirable order of the sensible things of this World toward their invisible virtues, they established a certain sacred and priestly doctrine under the leadership of **Trismegistus** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of Egyptian wisdom</note>, which they wished to be known only to men of their own order. Starting therefore from the World, as **Iamblichus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> teaches, and proceeding to the Mundane Gods, by the distribution of the four Elements in the World <margin>**Iamblichus.** Mundane Gods worshiped by the Egyptians</margin> from a common lot made according to the measures of the Elements, revolving in order from the circumference around the centers, they trusted they would have easy access to the truth of the sacrifices. For since they were in the World, and were contained in it as parts—indeed, understanding that they were generated by it, perfected by its total powers, and had obtained a certain portion of life and nature from it—they concluded that in divine worship, the World and the Mundane orders should by no means be bypassed. <margin>Laws concerning the proper institution of sacrifices established by the Egyptian Priests.</margin> For since they saw that around any part of the twelve-fold World there was indeed some body, and that there were furthermore incorporeal forces distributed in order within those bodies; hence they distributed the laws of the sacred rites—that is, like to like—with such industry that all things might progress from the highest to the lowest through the middle, applying bodies to body...

# TREATISE III. THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER II.

by applying them, namely by rendering to each what is its own. Thus, the sacred laws teach that sacrifices to the Gods must be established with the greatest diligence; for they believed that when the Gods descend to earth, all the powers subject to them are moved together, and as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on Egyptian mysteries and theurgy.</note> teaches, they precede them like heralds and ceremonial processions. Therefore, they persuaded themselves that whoever does not sacrifice correctly and legitimately to each of these, nor distributes what is suitable to each, nor follows each with a specific honor and worship, does not attain the presence of the Gods. But they imagined that he who has rendered all the Divinities favorable to himself, offering pleasing and most similar gifts to each, is by no means frustrated in his hope, but receives the divine Choir in its whole and full presence. 

<margin>The Egyptians appeased individual Divinities with similar gifts.</margin>

Hence, from this principle of religion, the rite ought by no means to be simple, but <term>pansmikos</term> <note>original Greek: πανσμικῶς; meaning "universally" or "in a world-encompassing manner." Kircher uses it to denote a ritual that reflects the entire cosmic order.</note>, and constituted from every harmony and from all the species of the World, as Iamblichus says. For they knew how great a multitude of forces is usually excited when the Gods descend; which indeed was deprived of all effect if the circumstance of even one rite or one ceremony were omitted from the sacrifice. 

<margin>Why the Egyptians chose the number twelve for the Spirits.</margin>

Because they knew the number of the Gods to be incomprehensible to human wit, they therefore encompassed the entire series of Spirits within the number twelve, thinking it sufficient if they worshipped the individual classes of the <term>duodecads</term> <note>Groups of twelve.</note>—both of the Intellectual, the Starry, and the Elemental World—by the aforementioned religious rite for that which they intended. Just as this Obelisk teaches, where the individual classes of the Generative Spirits have their own columns, in which the rite due to them is described, as will be clear from the context of the interpretation. 

<margin>Public worship of the Gods required certain gifts, private worship others.</margin>

This prescribed worship looks chiefly toward those benefits which concern the abundance of things necessary for the human race: the healthiness of the air, and the beneficial increase of the Nile (which they call the munificent rain of the Gods). These things could not be obtained except through the best disposition and temperament of the annual space, which they hoped to achieve solely by the gift of the Gods presiding over it. Private worship, however, followed the private benefits of the Gods whom each person worshipped, such as the benefits of health, prosperity, wisdom, divination, and finally <term>eumorphia</term> <note>original Greek: εὐμορφίας; meaning "beauty" or "goodness of form."</note>. 

<margin>The wearing of amulets.</margin>

The worship was carried out by the religious wearing of sacred amulets; which they judged to possess such great virtue and efficacy that, even when merely worn, they were believed to powerfully draw the Divinities to grant their prayers. From these things it is clear how, from this apparent sanctity of religion, the Devil wove long chains of superstitions to drag souls into eternal ruin, and how greatly we are bound to God the Best and Greatest, because through the incarnate Word He deigned to rescue us from such great blindness. But let us now begin the interpretation.

# CHAPTER III.

->*A preliminary interpretation of certain things which occur very frequently on this Obelisk.*<-

<margin>Sacred tablets or oval figures on Obelisks.</margin>
**T**here occur quite frequently, both on this present Obelisk and on those to follow, certain diagrams of an oval shape which the Egyptians called "sacred tablets." It seemed best to provide their interpretation here at the outset, lest we cause confusion for the reader within the main body of the interpretation due to the variety of things to be said about them. Therefore, in the following pages, we shall always refer anyone wishing to know the reasoning behind these hidden symbols back to this chapter. These sacred tablets were certain arrangements of more illustrious symbols which, just as they regarded the hidden operations of the Gods, were also believed to possess great power for drawing those Gods down. For this reason, they carved them separately as something extraordinary, both on the public monuments of Obelisks and Sphinxes and on the walls of the inner sanctuaries. Later, these were extracted from these original models, as it were, and carved into various stones to be carried for private use as certain sacred amulets <note>original: "periata marta," likely a corruption of "periapta," meaning charms or amulets worn on the body</note>.

<margin>Two more famous sacred tablets, AB and CD.</margin>
There are, however, two types of greatest consideration which occur on almost all Obelisks, and very frequently on this one in particular (as will be evident to anyone examining it), adorned with the array of symbols shown in the following two diagrams. The first we call the *Momphto-Mendesian* tablet; the second we have decided to name the *Osiriac* for greater distinction. And just as we almost always find the Momphto-Mendesian tablet topped by a Butterfly (marked A), the symbol of the multiform Spirit <note>original: "polymorphi Daemonis"</note>, so we find the Osiriac tablet (marked C) topped by a Goose, the symbol of Osiris and Isis.

## § I.
->*Explanation of the Momphto-Mendesian sacred tablet.*<-

<margin>The Momphto-Mendesian tablet.</margin>
**T**his diagram, marked with the letter B, is distinguished by an oval shape because, just as they indicated the World by an egg, so by the oval shape of the figure in which the hieroglyphic diagrams were enclosed, they secretly suggested the operations of those Gods (whom the symbols signify) within the World. There are three figures inserted into this same shape: the first is a staff <term>goat-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: "αἰγόμορφος" (aigomorphos)</note>, that is, marked with a Goat's head; the second is a statue transformed with a Lion-like face, signifying Momphta—the presiding deity of the "moist-warm" principle as well as the rising of the Nile; the third is a Nilometer <note>A tool used to measure the depth of the Nile's flood</note>, by which they indicated Momphta's particular dominion over the Nile. <margin>Significance of the Goat-scepter.</margin> The Goat-scepter denotes the Divinity whom the Egyptians call Mendes (for so they named the God of fertile generation), and he is equivalent to the Divinity whom the Greeks call Pan; concerning whom we have written extensively in the [treatise on] Obelisks—

He specifically defines the Momphto-Mendesian tablet, identifying its symbols as the goat-headed staff of Mendes (Pan) and the lion-faced Momphta who governs the Nile's fertility.</summary>

# TREATISE III. THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER III.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A large vertical engraving of a single face of an obelisk, likely the Flaminian Obelisk. At the top (pyramidion) is a winged sun disk. Below are several registers of hieroglyphic symbols. Register 1: Two cartouches under the winged disk. Register 2: A hawk (Horus). Register 3: A quadruped, possibly a bull or lion. Register 4: A seated figure and a bird-headed figure. Register 5: A large cartouche labeled 'A' and 'B' on the left, containing a seated leonine figure (Momphta) with a feather on its head, holding a scepter and ankh. Register 6: A bird (swan or goose). Register 7: A second large cartouche labeled 'C' and 'D' containing seated figures and an eye symbol. Register 8: Stylized floral or plant motifs at the base.</note>

<margin>
The significance of the lion-like statue.
</margin>

As was shown in the Pamphilian Obelisk on page 274, and especially in the Mendesian <term>Nome</term> <note>A 'Nome' was a territorial division in ancient Egypt.</note> in the first volume on page 18, this figure was worshipped. The **lion-like statue** denotes **Momphta**, that is, the Spirit of the waters. This table is viewed separately as its own piece because it contains mysteries of greater importance; and therefore, because of this mysterious arrangement of symbols, they were thought to possess great power for summoning the Spirit which it represented—a most common amulet. Having recognized this, the time requires that we reveal the principles from which those symbols were constructed, so that the genius of the Egyptians in devising symbols might be more clearly seen, along with the intention and end for which they established them in this manner. But to the point.

<margin>
Why the figures of the Obelisks are carved roughly and crudely.
</margin>

The first place in this heap of hieroglyphs is held by two images. The first image is **lion-shaped** <note>original: "λεοντόμορφον" (leontomorphon)</note>, crude indeed and unpolished, but one which displays a no obscure proof of divinity by the feather on its head and the symbol of the **handled cross** <note>The Ankh symbol, which Kircher interpreted as a 'handled cross' representing life or divinity.</note>. Indeed, they used to work those hieroglyphic images with a certain crude skill on purpose, both because it was difficult to engrave tiny proportions of limbs in such hard stone, and because if they had made the sculpture thinner with subtle artistry, it could easily have been obliterated by the long duration of time (the devourer of things) and by the injuries of the air and sky. Therefore, since the Egyptians aimed for eternity in their works, they were content only with the outward outlines of the bodies and a certain bare likeness of things, and they engraved the symbols so deeply into the stones that, nevertheless, what the sculpture hinted at would easily become known to those more skilled in such matters; which is well worth noting.

Table C D: The sacred Osirian rites.
</margin>

Moreover, that this is a statue of Momphta, the Nilotic Spirit, according to our interpretation made above, is shown first by the feather rising above the head, the mark of the **handled cross**, and the lion-like form.

<margin>
Momphta is twofold: supramundane and material, though one in effect.
</margin>

It must be noted, however, that a twofold Momphta can be considered here: the **supramundane** and the **material** <note>original: "hylæus", from the Greek 'hyle' meaning matter.</note>. Just as the supramundane Momphta exercises absolute dominion over the substance of the Universal moisture, so the material Momphta, his substitute in the lower world, takes up the protection of the moist substance—

### CHAPTER III

<margin>The attire of Momphta is explained.</margin> ...undertakes. We see both expressed in this place: truly one Deity, though diverse in his effects. By the feather rising upon the head, they signified that his nature is difficult to find and visible to no one, being sublime not only above the senses but even above the grasp of human intelligence. However, by the human form, they indicated the same Author and Mover of life, who can be understood by the intellect through a circular motion. <margin>The effects of God can be seen; his nature cannot be seen by us at all.</margin> Just as the body of a man is seen, but the mind itself—which distinguishes man from other living creatures—can be seen by no one; so also the actions and movements of God the Supreme Architect (which he himself calls "the back parts" in the sacred scriptures <note>A reference to Exodus 33:23, where Moses sees God's back but not His face</note>, just as Aristotle calls effects "posterior" and causes "prior") can be seen by the human intellect. But the Mind itself and the divine nature that governs created things cannot be absolutely known while in the prison of this body. This is beautifully hinted at among the more secret Hebrew theologians through the "fifty gates of light," all of which they say Moses entered except for one, as we have taught in the *Kabbalah*. And therefore, according to the testimony of <margin>Why God is painted dressed in a blue garment.</margin> Porphyry <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian religion</note>, they painted him dressed in a blue garment to signify that he is celestial and dwells in Heaven, participating in no color or accident, and clothed in no shroud of earthly mixture—even if he might seem to us to take such things on, appearing now angry, now appeased. This is just as Heaven itself, though it has no color, appears blue because of the vastness of the distance. <margin>Porphyry.</margin> But let us hear the words of Porphyry; for he says: *“The symbols of the Egyptian Gods are such: they call the Creator of Egypt Emepb (better Momphta), whose image they make in the form of a man of a blue color, holding a belt and a scepter, on whose head they place a feather, signifying that the Creator is difficult to find and visible to no one, yet also life-giving, a King, and moved by an intelligible circular motion. This God,” he says, “produces an egg from his mouth, from which is born the God whom the Egyptians call <term>Phta</term> (Ptah), and the Greeks call <term>Vulcan</term> (Hephaestus); moreover, the egg signifies the World to the Egyptians.”* You see, therefore, the summit sublime with a feather; you see the scepter; you see the mysterious mark of the <term>handled cross</term> <note>The Ankh, often called the "crux ansata" in Latin</note>. <margin>What the feather on the head of Momphta signifies.</margin> By the feather, they signified not only—as Porphyry wishes—that God is difficult to find, but that the knowledge of the divine essence is most remote from the human intellect. For just as the feather lifts the bodies of birds into the high air where we cannot reach, so that ineffable essence of God is so high and so exceeds the capacity of the intellect that we can in no way reach it with full knowledge. Whence also the Psalmist, intending to show how much the divine essence exceeds the smallness of our intellect, says that God "flies upon the wings of the winds" and "made darkness his hiding place." Moses also, to show high mysteries, placed two Cherubim with extended wings over the mercy seat <margin>Exodus 37. Jerusalem Targum.</margin> by a certain symbolic method. Where the *Jerusalem Targum* <note>An Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note>, besides those things in the Vulgate edition, has it thus:

->In the wisdom of the spirit of prophecy, he made the Cherubim on both sides:<-

-><note>original Aramaic: בחוכמת רוח נבואה עבד ית כרוביא סתרין סתרין</note><-

->*In the wisdom of the spirit of prophecy, he made the Cherubim from each side:* by which words certain great hidden mysteries are signified. That great Dionysius...<-

# TREATISE III. THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER III.

Dionysius, the Prince of mystical Theology, compares a soul stripped of all earthly influence to a feather; <margin>Dionysius the Areopagite</margin> *A feather*, he says, *signifies both the speed of guidance, and that which is celestial, and that which moves, and that which shrinks from all zeal and desire for earthly things; because it is carried upward; moreover, the lightness of the feather raises that which is in no part earthly, but entirely without admixture or weight, toward the heights.* <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist; Kircher uses his definitions of celestial symbols to explain Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> Furthermore, they fashioned the aforementioned statue seated, implying by this—as Porphyry says—a stable and unchangeable power; <margin>Momphta is fashioned sitting, and with a Leonine face.</margin> for it is fashioned to sit so that a stable and unchangeable virtue may be expressed. In its hand it holds a scepter, about which much has already been said extensively in the preceding pages. It has a **Leonine face**, indicating the force and power which it holds over the moist substance <note>The "moist substance" refers to the element of water, specifically the Nile.</note> by its own corroborative virtue, and thus indicating the Nile, over which it presides; concerning this, see the extensive discussion in the Hierogrammaticism of the Lion on the Pamphilian Obelisk, which you should consult. It has a **Goat-shaped Scepter** <term>Aegomorphon: shaped like a goat</term> placed near it, by which the Mendesian power is indicated; for the Egyptians called **Mendes**, or the **Goat**, the Deity presiding over the genital moisture. It is aptly joined to Momphta, since unless the moist element abounds in fertility, its institution in the nature of things seems in vain, as the generation of all things consists in the moist and the warm, as has been said: thus the Momphtaean power is rightly joined to the Mendesian as necessary for the generation of things. But concerning these, see the *Pamphilian Obelisk* folio 283 and elsewhere, where we have discoursed most abundantly on both Momphta and Mendes.

## §. II.

->Explanation of the Nilometer.<- <margin>Explanation of the Nilometer.</margin>

Beneath the Goat's head in the hieroglyphic arrangement occurs an instrument which Abenuaschira <note>A reference to the medieval Arabic author Ibn Wahshiyya.</note> mentions, and which some not incorrectly interpret as a **Nilometer** <term>Niloscope/Nilometer: a structure for measuring the height of the Nile's annual flood</term>, traces of which are still seen in some places. His Arabic words are these:
*When they wished to test the Nile, they would depict the measure for the increase of the Nile in the form of the lion's chin.* <note>original Arabic: فلما كانوا يريدون اختبار النيل كانوا يصوّروا المكيال لزيادة النيل بصورة الذقن الاسد</note>

*To show the fertile nature of the Nile, they place that structure by which the increments of the Nile are measured.* Strabo describes the same Nilometer in these words: <margin>Strabo</margin>
*The island of Syene, in which are the "miladia" <note>likely a corruption of "niladia" or Nilometers</note>, and in this a city having a temple of Kneph, and a Nilometer constructed of a single stone on the bank of the Nile, which marks the greatest, the least, and the middle [increments]...* <note>original Greek: Συήνης νῆσος, ἐν ᾗ μιλάδια, καὶ ἐν ταύτῃ πόλις ἔχουσα ἱερὸν Κνήφιος, καὶ Νυλομέτριον ἐν μονόλιθω κατασκευασμένον ἐπὶ τῇ ὄχθῃ τοῦ Νείλου σημειοῦται τὰς μεγίστας δὲ καὶ ἐλάχιστας, καὶ τὰς μέσας...</note> This is: *Another Island placed a half-stadium in the Nile before Syene, in which is that City which has the temples of Knaphis and a Nilometer: here, moreover, is a certain well on the bank of the Nile constructed from a single stone, in which both the maximum, minimum, and average increments of the Nile are denoted.* Following Herodotus, Diodorus, Apuleius, and Plutarch, Joannes Leo Africanus <margin>Joannes Leo Africanus, book 8.</margin> also mentions an instrument of this kind, who says he is an eyewitness of this structure: for he says thus: *Opposite the old city in the middle of the Nile is seen the island of Michios, that is, of the measure, from which, by the proportion of the inundation of the Nile, the harvest of that year...*

# CHAPTER III. 224 THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...they gather [this data] throughout all of Egypt by a most certain method invented by the ancient Egyptians. However, I shall not dwell on describing the *Nilometer* <note>original: "Niloscope," an instrument or well used to measure the Nile's water level</note>, as it is a matter well known everywhere. One thing in the Arabic text of Aben-Wahshiyya <note>original: "Abenuaſchiæ," referring to the 9th-century author Ibn Wahshiyya</note> concerning Egyptian agriculture kept me in great suspense and perplexity; I was unable to understand what he meant by the image of a "lying and long-tailed animal," until, by consulting various antiquities, I finally sensed the truth and investigated the hidden context of his words. For Aben-Wahshiyya intended to say nothing other than that it was in the likeness of a **Sphinx**, which is found among authors as the symbol of the Nile's inundation.

<margin>What the Sphinxes were among the Egyptians.</margin> Now, the Sphinxes (as is evident from those brought from Egypt that are seen here and there throughout the City of Rome) were biform statues, the front of which represented a human face and the rest a Lion, as we teach in the treatise on Sphinxes. These figures were expressed by the Egyptians not because they believed such animals were found anywhere, but to denote the more recondite <note>hidden or profound</note> meanings of the mind. Thus, the Sphinxes expressed in this way denoted the "station" or standing of the Nile flooding Egypt.

<margin>The Sphinxes will demonstrate the Nile's inundation among the Egyptians; on what occasion they were devised by the Egyptians.</margin> For since the increases of the Nile lasted throughout all of July and August, and the Sun during said months mostly traverses **Leo** and **Virgo** <note>The zodiac signs of the Lion and the Virgin</note>, it was easy for a people otherwise very inclined toward portentous and many-shaped compositions of things to form monsters from a Virgin and a Lion, which they called Sphinxes. These were properly statues consecrated to the Nile, resting on their bellies, by which they represented the stationary peak of the flooding Nile. Sphinxes of this kind can still be seen today in the Quirinal Garden, at the Capitoline fountain, and in the Villa Borghese.

<margin>Pliny.</margin> A great number of these Sphinxes, according to Pliny (Book 36, Chapter 13), were in Egypt; some of these, of immense mass, were worshipped in the more famous places of Egypt, especially around the places where the Nile is accustomed to overflow, such as Heliopolis and Sais, and in the Memphite desert. In that desert, among others, is one of prodigious magnitude, 143 feet long and 62 feet wide. They seem to have also had the office of designating the increases of the Nile, as appears from the words of Aben-Wahshiyya. Indeed, I will say something more: that very figure of the *Nilometer* <note>original: "Nilometrij"</note> which the Egyptians placed here as a symbol of the Nile's fertility seems to insinuate nothing else by its bare image.

<margin>Pierio, Book 1.</margin> Pierio <note>Pierio Valeriano, a famous 16th-century mythographer</note> confirms our opinion, saying that the Egyptians used the hieroglyphic of a "lying Lion" to signify the increase of the Nile—which in the Egyptian language signifies *Nun* <note>A reference to the primordial waters</note>. He says that when the Sun reaches the back of the Herculean Lion, it excites the deluge of the Nile, and a double amount of fresh water often overflows while the Sun stays in that sign. This force of water, spread widely through the spacious Egyptian plain, renders the soil pregnant with that fertility by which not only the natives gather food for themselves, but relieve a great part of the World from hunger. Because of that redundancy of waters, which they experience every year through the "benefit of the Lion,"

<margin>Why Lion heads are applied to fountains.</margin> it was established, and is now a custom received among all nations, that channels, pipes, and siphons which belch out water should emit it through holes bored into **Lion heads**, which are customarily sculpted for this purpose in suitable places, so that the water appears to be vomited from the Lion's gaping jaws. And that these things are so is testified by not a few [statues] seen to this day in Rome, Lions at the base...

<summary>Kircher explains that the Sphinx is a composite of the zodiac signs Leo and Virgo, symbolizing the Nile's peak flood during those months. He also traces the common architectural motif of lion-headed water spouts back to this Egyptian solar-hydrological symbolism.</summary>

# TREATISE III. THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER III.

...the roots of the Capitoline Hill, and the fountain next to the Church of the Blessed Virgin of Victory <note>The Church of Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome, near the Acqua Felice fountain</note>, which belch forth water from wide-open mouths. Lest they be forced to always paint the entire figure of a Lion or a Sphinx in hieroglyphic inscriptions to denote the increase of the Nile, they judged it more prudent to represent it through that same character by which Egyptian Astrologers prefigured the sign of Leo—that is, by <note>Astrological symbol for Leo: ♌</note> the tail of the Lion. It was shown above that the astronomical characters of the signs and planets were first devised by the Egyptians, and <term>Dee</term> <note>original: "Deenus"; referring to John Dee (1527–1608) and his work *Monas Hieroglyphica*</note> <margin>Dee.</margin> proves this at length in his *Hieroglyphic Monad*; we also discuss this specifically in our *Egyptian Astronomy*. But the sign placed below (<note>Astrological symbol for Aquarius: ♒</note>) also demonstrates this clearly; for it has been most abundantly demonstrated elsewhere <margin>The signs or characters of Aquarius and Leo.</margin> that this is a symbol of water, derived from the likeness of the figure of undulating water. For this same reason, it was adopted by the Egyptians—and by the common consent and approval of astrologers—as the symbol for waters: consequently, wherever it occurs in hieroglyphics, it refers to moisture. But more on these matters in their proper places.

->But someone might object here: what does Aquarius have to do with Leo?<- 

To this <margin>The Egyptians denoted the excellence of things by the juxtaposition of opposites.</margin> I respond: when the Egyptians wished to demonstrate the excellence of a thing, they did so chiefly through the juxtaposition of opposites. For they perceived the Nile to be enriched beyond all other rivers of the world by certain marvelous gifts of nature; it not only showed evidence of the greatest fertility throughout the entire course of the year, but did so most especially at the very time when the Sun, inflamed by the heat of Leo, scorches all things. When all other rivers fail due to a lack of moisture, the Nile seems to fill everything with its own fullness. Conversely, in Aquarius, it reaches its greatest state <margin>Why the signs of Leo and Aquarius signify the Nile’s inundation.</margin> of diminution, while other rivers are subject to floods only in Aquarius, the sign opposite to Leo. Therefore, to symbolically express this preeminence of the Nile, they seem to have wished to place the opposite sign of Aquarius beneath the sign of Leo.

Wherefore, whether this symbol refers to a <term>Nilometer</term> <note>original: "Nilometrium," a device for measuring the height of the Nile</note>, or a Sphinx, or a Lion, it is all the same; the reader cannot err, whichever he chooses. For we have demonstrated shortly before that the Nilometer, the Sphinx, and the Lion were each hieroglyphs of the inundation. It may even be that they constructed those structures to represent both the Sphinx and the Lion while performing the function of a Nilometer; that something of this sort existed is suggested not only by the words of the Author, but also by Strabo in Book 17, Herodotus, and other Ancients—indeed, by as many statues of the Nile as are found today. But we leave all these things for the subtle reader to investigate further. Let us therefore proceed to the interpretation of the second sacred table.

# CHAPTER III. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

# § III.

->**Exposition of the second sacred Osiriac table.**<-

<margin>Exposition of the second sacred table of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> If, according to the rule of Xenophon <note>Referring to the Greek historian’s views on social and divine obligations</note>, we are bound by a certain due gratitude toward those from whom we receive even the smallest benefits, surely reason itself dictates that we ought to be most grateful toward the most beneficent God, by whose favor we possess all things. The sacred page clearly teaches that we are bound to this by divine law. <margin>Gratitude toward God for benefits</margin> Certainly, the Egyptians recognized this more than other nations. Their gratitude, love, reverence, inclined mind, and their zeal and care in worthily worshipping the divine powers are brilliantly demonstrated by that "never-sufficiently-sought" Osiris, the many portentous rites performed in sacrifices, and the many representations of multiform deities. It appears they wished to leave these to posterity in the present hieroglyphic <term>composition</term> <note>original: "Syntagmate"</note> as a unique testimony of their will to honor the Gods. For after they had represented that divine power of Osiris and his majesty shining forth in the theater of nature—most especially in the fertile nature of the Nile—<term>symbolically</term> <note>original: "symbolicῶς"</note>, they joined to his side another hieroglyphic <term>composition</term> as a reflection of divine worship. By this, they expressed hieroglyphically that he, from whom they received such great benefits, must be honored with worthy praise. In this hieroglyphic <term>diagram</term> <note>original: "Schemate"</note>, six figures are primarily to be considered: two statues, a ritual litter, a triple branch, a staff or thyrsus, and a sea-rush.

->**On the two Statues.**<-

<margin>Exposition of the sacred table.</margin> The first figure is in the form of a seated <term>hawk-headed</term> <note>original: "ἱερακόμορφος" (hierakomorphos)</note> being; that is, transformed with the head of a hawk, supporting a globe upon its head and holding the <term>Tautic character</term> <note>The "Ankh" or T-shaped cross, which Kircher associates with the letter Tau</note> in its hands. By the <term>hawk-headed</term> hawk, they understood Osiris, as has already been shown many times; by the globe on the head, they understood divinity; and by the Tautic character, they understood the movement or influence into the innermost reaches of the universal world. The other figure has a human face, which varies both here and on other obelisks; for sometimes it is seen with a basket <note>original: "calatho"</note> placed on its head, and sometimes with a feathered crown. In its hands, it holds now the letter <note>Symbol resembling an Alpha or A</note>, and now a scepter marked with the head of a <term>hoopoe</term> <note>original: "Cucuphæ"; the Cucupha scepter was a common Egyptian motif</note>. By this image, they denoted nothing other than the attendant of Osiris, namely the solar <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>The "Good Spirit," a protective deity often associated with the sun or life-force</note>. The symbol it carries in its hands is the Alpha <note>Symbol resembling an Alpha or A</note>; and since this same figure is the presiding officer over worldly variety, it therefore sometimes holds the <term>hoopoe-shaped</term> <note>original: "Cucuphomorphum"</note> scepter in its hands as its symbol. The basket or tiara denotes power over all things committed to its protection; the feathered crown signifies the sublimity of the operations it performs, as we have said above. Osiris is placed directly opposite this figure to show that every variety of virtue derived into this <term>Agathodaemon</term> proceeds immediately from that very influx of all good things—from the supramundane Osiris, I say; which is also the conversion of the one toward...

He argues that these images reflect the Egyptians' profound gratitude and religious duty toward the source of life and nature.</summary>

# TREATISE III. THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK. / CHAPTER III.

...to the other, and the Tautic sign, which Osiris holds in his hands, clearly teaches the symbol of this divine influx. <margin>The Tautic character borrowed from the Hebrews.</margin> But concerning these things we speak elsewhere more at length. He bears in his hand the symbol of the Handled Cross <note>The Ankh, which Kircher calls the *Crux Ansata*</note> or the Tautic seal, which is a symbol of the divine mind diffusing itself into all the paths of the world. It is likely that the Egyptians borrowed this character from the Hebrews, being curious observers of figures; it was indeed mystical to both, but differing in the significance of the mysteries. Yet it is false that this character among the Egyptians signified the "life to come," as Ruffinus <note>A 4th-century Christian monk and historian</note>, Suidas <note>The author of a 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>, and other authors would have it. <margin>What the Tautic character signified among the Egyptians.</margin> Instead, it is likely that this whole rumor arose from the Jews, who at that time wandered through Egypt as exiles; for seeing this sign "T" <note>The letter Tau</note> repeated so many times in their images, they interpreted it everywhere as their coming salvation according to the tradition of their Fathers. We say that this character signified nothing else among the Egyptians than, as I have said, the movement and diffusion of the divine Mind in the production of all things.

### Concerning the Tray, or Litter.

<margin>The tray or litter, and its hieroglyphic significance.</margin> **H**aving now explained the images, there immediately follows the tray, called a *litter* <note>original: φέρετρον (*pheretron*)</note> by the Greeks; which was a symbol of exhibiting divine honor to the Gods. For the Egyptians were accustomed for the most part to take those instruments, the use of which was in sacred rites, as hieroglyphic symbols. For it is clearly evident from Lucian and from Apuleius <note>An author who provided a famous description of the procession of Isis in *The Golden Ass*</note>, who graphically describes the Isiac procession, that they used the litter for carrying around the statues or images of the Gods in solemn procession. Moreover, that litters of this kind were like chests is apparent from their shape on many Obelisks; and it is gathered from Apuleius that it was a chest capable of holding secrets, <margin>Lucian. Apuleius. Sacred hidden things.</margin> because the Egyptians were accustomed to hide in them the "sacred hidden things," <note>original: *opertanea sacra*</note> which were so called because they were covered and not exposed to the eyes of the profane. These are also called "mysteries" by the Greeks, according to the testimony of Suidas, <term>from the closing of the mouth</term> <note>original: ἀπὸ τοῦ μύειν τὸ στόμα (*apo tou myein to stoma*)</note>; namely, because it befits those who hear divine ceremonies and the secrets of religion to stop up their mouths and not announce them to any mortal. Moreover, included in them were the phalli or fig-wood members <note>original: φάλλα (*phalla*)</note> <margin>Basket-bearers, sacred chests.</margin> of Osiris and Isis; what these properly were has been discussed at length elsewhere. Whence also chests of this kind are called by Suidas <term>sacred chests</term> <note>original: κίσται ἱεραὶ (*kistai hierai*)</note>, and those who carried them were called <term>basket-bearers</term> <note>original: κιστοφόροι (*kistophoroi*)</note>, who were chosen from the most select persons for this blessed ministry. So much so, indeed, that Lampridius and Aelius Spartianus <note>Historians of the *Augustan History*</note> note that the Emperor Commodus once did not disdain the honor of the sacred ceremonies, even appointing himself the leader of this procession; for he observed the rites of Isis, so far as to shave his head and carry the statue of Anubis. <margin>Ithyphallia. Plutarch. Basket-bearers.</margin> And Plutarch testifies that from this solemnity of the "Comasiae" <note>Processions</note> flowed the *Ithyphallia*, the Dionysian rites of the Greeks, where he says a phallus was usually carried behind the "Basket-bearing Virgins" <note>original: Canophoras</note> and a phallic song was sung; for the "Basket-bearers" <note>original: Canophoras / Kanephoroi</note> were free-born Virgins who carried baskets on their heads in which all the first-fruits were placed.

It is said that there were four letters <note>original: "literas," likely referring to symbolic characters or figures</note> among the Egyptians representing, as it were, the four Elements; for by this conjunction, the diverse concepts of all things are expressed. From this blending of the four Elements, whatever exists in the nature of things comes to be. ### Concerning the Inverted Branch.

That the Egyptians carried branches in the aforementioned solemnity of the <term>Comasiae</term> <note>Processional festivals involving the carrying of sacred objects; from the Greek 'komazein', to revel or process.</note> has been sufficiently shown above from Clement and Apuleius (who called these solemnities <term>Oschophoria</term> <note>A Greek festival of "carrying vine-branches." Kircher is identifying Egyptian rites with Greek names.</note>). Clement testifies to this in these words: <gloss>Through symbols, such as that wheel which is turned, which was drawn in the precincts of the Gods among the Egyptians, and the branches given to those who worship.</gloss> <note>original: "Διὰ δὲ τῶν συμβόλων ὡς ὅ τε τροχὸς ὁ στρεφόμενος, ἐν τοῖς τῶν Θεῶν τεμένεσιν εἵλκετο μέρει παρὰ Αἰγυπτίοις, καὶ τῶν θαλλῶν τῶν διδομένων Τοῖς προσκυνοῦσι."</note> So also says Orpheus:

> But of the branches, for those men whose concern is earthly things,
> All things are rolled in the mind around more than one place,
> Nor is it right for them to stand in one part,
> But they keep all things in the part where they began their course.

<margin>The festival of branches in honor of Bacchus. Pausanias.</margin> Certainly among the Athenians there was a feast day distinguished by the name of "branches," on which, according to Pausanias, they carried forward <term>oscha</term>—that is, slender branches, especially of the vine—in honor of Bacchus. From this comes the term <term>Oschophoria</term>, which is the celebration of the carrying around of branches; and the <term>Oschophoroi</term>, or "branch-bearers," were the name given to the young boys serving the sacred rites. These boys, having received small vine branches from the temples of Bacchus, carried them to the temple of Athena Skiras, as the Scholiast of Nicander clearly testifies: <gloss>Those called Oschophoroi at Athens are boys with both parents living who compete by tribes; taking vine shoots from the temple of Dionysus, they ran to the temple of Athena Skiras.</gloss> <note>original: "ὀσχοφόροι δὲ λέγονται Ἀθηνησι παῖδες ἀμφιθαλεῖς ἁμιλλόμενοι κατὰ φυλὰς, οἱ λαμβάνοντες κλήματα ἀμπέλου ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ τοῦ Διονύσου ἔτρεχον εἰς τὸ τῆς σκυρράδος Ἀθηνᾶς ἱερόν."</note> Because those worshipping the Gods moved both their hand and a branch according to the ancient rite of order, St. Jerome correctly translates: *And they applied the branch to their hands*, <margin>The Feast of Tabernacles of the Jews.</margin> namely as a sign of the adoration they were performing to the Sun. The sacred scriptures relate that the Hebrews also used these same ceremonies in the worship of God during the Feast of Tabernacles, and Josephus clearly testifies to this in the third book of *Antiquities* with these words: <gloss>As for the burnt offerings, and sacrificing to God when they bring thank-offerings, they carry in their hands a bundle of myrtle and willow, with a palm branch, and also the fruit of the Persian apple.</gloss> <note>original: "Ὁλοκαυτώματα δὲ, καὶ θύειν τῷ Θεῷ ὅτε χαριστήρια φέροντας ἀνὰ χεῖρα ὁρισιωνων μυρσίνης, καὶ ἰτέας συνερράδην Φοίνικος πεποιημένη τε μίλα τε τῆς περσίας φερόντων." The "Persian apple" refers to the Citron or Etrog.</note>

# SECTION III. THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK.

While sacrificing victims to God and sanctifying them in an act of thanksgiving, they meanwhile carry in their hands branches of myrtle and palm, from which "Persea apples" <note>This refers to the fruit of the *Mimusops schimperi*, often confused in antiquity with the peach or "Persian apple."</note> hung. Whether the Egyptians imitated the Hebrews in this, or the Hebrews the Egyptians, is clear from the fact that they worshiped Horus with branches of Persea and lotus, to signify that the <margin>Horus. The Egyptians worshiped Horus with branches of Persea and lotus.</margin> heart and the tongue must be dedicated to God. For as was said above, the Persea has leaves pointed in the shape of a tongue, but its fruit is shaped almost in the image of a heart. That the Ethiopians also imitated these is clear from Heliodorus, who says that when kings or great nobles were received, the people came to meet them crowned with lotus and <margin>Heliodorus. The Ethiopians received their Kings by carrying branches in their hands.</margin> shaking palm branches in their honor; his words are: <term>Τὰς κεφαλὰς τοῦ Νειλώου λωτοῦ καταστέψαντες, καὶ Φοινίκων θύρσους τῇ χερσὶ κατασείοντες</term> <note>original Greek: "Having crowned their heads with the lotus of the Nile, and shaking thyrses of palms with their hands."</note>. Therefore, if they wished to signify someone honored by the remarkable favor of the people and received with the most celebrated applause and joy of all, they called this person <term>φυλλοβολούμενον</term> <note>Greek: *phylloboloumenon*, meaning "one showered with leaves."</note>, because they not only displayed those branches, but also scattered leaves and flowers upon those who had served well. This kind of offering, he says, involved neither incense nor any other victim, but leaves—like the first down of budding nature plucked by hand—from which herbs, fruits, and all things born from the earth are produced and grow. And thus far concerning the branches usually carried in public ceremonies; now the subject requires that we discuss our hieroglyphic branch, and what it signifies in this context. This symbol is very frequent, so much so that one can hardly inspect a pyramid without its frequent occurrence. Since we have dealt with these most extensively in the *Hierogrammatism on Egyptian Herbs* regarding the Pamphilian Obelisk, and previously regarding the Lateran Obelisk, I thought some of these points should be repeated here for a greater understanding of the matters.

The branch is triple and inverted. That it was a branch of the Persea tree, and <margin>Triple and inverted branch on the Obelisks.</margin> that it had various symbolic meanings, will be clear from what follows. The Persea is a tree peculiar to Egypt, <margin>The Persea tree.</margin> so much rejecting every soil except its native land, and having such discord with other lands, that if grafted into them, it produces neither buds nor fruit, as if indignant; see the description of it in Theophrastus <margin>Theophrastus book 4, chapter 2.</margin>: *“There is also another tree in Egypt called the Persea, great in appearance and form, and in its leaf, flower, branch, and whole figure it is most similar to the pear tree; except that one has perpetual leaves, the other deciduous. It bears fruit abundantly and perfects it at all times, for it always occupies new ones; its maturity is completed by the breath of the annual winds; they take away the rest while still raw and store it; from this they make statues, tables, and other similar things.”*

From this it is clear that the opinion of those who think it is the same tree brought from Persia to Egypt is false; false also is the opinion of Pierius and others who confuse it with the "Persian apple" <note>The peach (*Prunus persica*), which Kircher distinguishes from the Egyptian Persea.</note>. Therefore, the Egyptians used these branches in ceremonies; they used them in place of symbols; they consecrated this tree <margin>Why the Egyptians use the Persea branch in ceremonies and hieroglyphics.</margin> to Isis, according to Plutarch, and to Harpocrates <note>The Hellenistic god of silence and secrets, derived from the Egyptian Child-Horus.</note>, because it was first planted in Egypt by them, not by the Persians (as some wrongly interpret). Rather, it was honored because of the great usefulness of this tree, which they calculated according to the number of leaves inserted on the triple branch. First, because images of the Gods, according to Theophrastus (book 4, chapter 2), were made from it; second, by the same witness, the tables of the temples; third, trumpets; fourth, the throne of Harpocrates was constructed from it; fifth, because of its fruit, which is most pleasing to the taste; sixth, because of the oil from it—

### CHAPTER III.

...from which oil of great use was expressed; seventhly, because of the seeds used for various sacred purposes; eighthly, they decorated temples with the leaves; ninthly, they spread them before the statues; tenthly, when dried, they served as fuel for the fire; eleventhly, they used it as an ornament for Harpocrates <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian child-god Horus, often depicted as a child with a finger to his lips.</note>, as it seems it is never absent from the Bembine Tablet <note>Also known as the Isiac Tablet, a famous bronze plate depicting Egyptian deities and symbols.</note>; twelfthly and finally, they signified many secrets through these things, which will be discussed in the following pages.

<margin>The Persea is ever-green.</margin>
First, therefore, the Persea is ever-green, never losing its leaves, and always full of fruits and flowers. The Egyptians seem to have aptly represented the remarkable nature of this tree through that triple branch, each of which is notable for a series of four leaves or flowers, with the leaves turning downward and three fruits or "apples" of the tree protruding upward. By this, they seem to have placed before our eyes the entire sequence of the planting or sowing of things. 

<margin>What the triple branch of the Persea and the four leaves of each signify.</margin>
For what else did they signify by the three branches, if not the three parts of the year (into which, according to <margin>Diodorus.</margin> Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BC historian who wrote extensively on Egypt.</note>, the year was divided by the Egyptians, in addition to the fourfold division of three months)? These were summer, winter, and spring; each of which is again divided into four months, signified by those four series of leaves depicted on each of the branches. By these branches, the generation of plant life is signified. 

<margin>The leaves of the Persea hieroglyphically signify the generation of plant life.</margin>
For just as the seed of the Persea (or the leaves placed in the earth) is decomposed over four months—that is, in the first part of the year, namely winter—it is gradually prepared for sprouting by the conception of vital heat; in the second part of the year, that is, the four spring months, it bursts forth into shoots, leaves, buds, and flowers; and finally, in the third part of the year, that is, the four summer months, it swells into fruit, which are brought to maturity by the blowing of the Etesian winds <note>Strong, periodic Mediterranean winds that blow in the summer.</note> and provide a new abundance of seed for the rest of the year; so, I say, does all generation of plant life occur. For first, the buried seed is gradually prepared for life within the earth; once this is done, it soon breaks forth into sprouts, leaves, and flowers; thirdly, it produces fruit, which is the goal of the <term>vegetabilis anima</term> <note>The "vegetative soul," a philosophical concept describing the basic life force responsible for growth and reproduction in plants.</note>. 

<margin>What the inverted leaves and branches of the Persea signify.</margin>
They also seem to have expressed this circular motion of vegetation quite well through an inverted plant; for unless every tree and plant is in some way inverted, and the upper parts become the lower, according to the saying of Hermes <note>Referring to the *Emerald Tablet* of Hermes Trismegistus: "That which is above is like that which is below."</note>: "that which is above was that which is below; and vice versa"; that is, unless the fruit and seed are returned to the earth, it will never produce fruit, as the very source of all Wisdom <note>A reference to the words of Jesus in John 12:24.</note> testifies: *Unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, etc.* <note>original: "Nisi granum frumenti cadens in terram mortuum fuerit &c."</note> Therefore, the fruits on these branches are in the upper position, from which the seed is then committed to the earth, so that from the new little branches, leaves, and flowers that grow up, new fruits also gradually arise. From these things it is now clear why they used branches of Persea in public solemnities. Truly, however, the seed is committed to the earth in vain unless that celestial Osiris approaches and animates it with his fertile influence; therefore, they establish Osiris and Isis as the inventors of the planting and sowing of this tree. 

<margin>Why the Persea tree is a symbol of sowing and planting. Abenephius.</margin>
For this reason they accepted it as a symbol of sowing and planting; indeed, the author Abenephius <note>Kircher's name for Ibn Wahshiyya, a 9th/10th-century author whose works Kircher believed contained ancient Egyptian wisdom.</note> claims that Osiris and Isis discovered the method for all other sowing from the character and nature of this tree, as was shown above. Since, therefore, a plant of this kind brings with it so many and such great benefits...

But since every sowing and every planting is in vain unless the celestial Osiris approaches and vivifies it with his motion; and unless Isis, through her fecund influence, also moistens, enlivens, and increases it as it grows; or unless, according to Plutarch <note>Plutarch was a Greek philosopher whose work "On Isis and Osiris" is Kircher's primary source for Egyptian myth.</note>, Isis—that is, the earth pregnant with seed—is animated by the Nile—that is, by the alluvium and fertile overflow; hence, lest either Osiris or Isis be lacking, they strived to entice them with such a great apparatus of sacrifices. ### ->Of the curved scepter.<-

<margin>The curved scepter:</margin>
**W**e interpret this sign of the curved scepter as the thyrsus made of giant fennel <note>original: "thyrsus ferulaceus." A thyrsus is a staff topped with a pine cone, carried by followers of Dionysus/Bacchus.</note>, because it is certainly curved in the manner of an augur's staff <note>original: "litui." A curved wand used by Roman priests (augurs) to mark out the sky.</note>. In the Arabic of Abenephe <note>Kircher's name for Ibn Wahshiyya, a 10th-century author he believed was an ancient Egyptian authority.</note> it is <note>Arabic text: القصبة</note> *elkasbe*, for by this name in Arabic, a thicket, a thyrsus, a fennel-stalk, a spear-like instrument, a pole, a rod, or a whip is signified, as appears from the *Al-Qamus* <note>A famous 14th-century Arabic dictionary.</note> of the Arabs and the Granada Lexicon.

<margin>The fennel thyrsus.</margin>
We call the fennel-stalk a "fennel thyrsus" because a thyrsus was not necessarily made from vine branches, but was called a "spear" when taken from any long and smooth stalks of plants, such as the giant fennel <note>The *Ferula communis*, a tall plant with a sturdy stalk used in antiquity for canes and staves.</note>. Likewise:

### CHAPTER III.

> *I invoke the law-giving, Fennel-bearing Dionysus,*
> *The praised seed of Eubulus, who has many names,*

> *Near the river of Egypt.*
<note>original: "Invoco legiferum Narthicophorum Dionysium..." This is a Latin translation of an Orphic Hymn to Dionysus. Kircher uses it to show that even in antiquity, Dionysus was identified with the Egyptian Osiris and the Nile.</note>

Various authors give various reasons why the fennel-stalk staff <term>thyrsus: a staff topped with a pine cone or ivy, carried by Dionysus and his followers</term> is assigned to Father Liber or the Egyptian Dionysus—whom we have shown to be the same as Osiris or the Sun in my work on the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. <margin>Eusebius. Why the fennel is attributed to Bacchus or Dionysus.</margin> Eusebius calls him <note>original: "ναρθηκοφόρον" (narthēkophoron)</note>, that is, the "fennel-bearer," and gives the reason that if men, when drunk, are driven into a frenzy and strike one another, they should use fennel stalks so that they may stab each other without causing mortal wounds, for the blow of a fennel stalk is slow and not lethal. <margin>Plutarch.</margin> Plutarch, in his *Symposium*, assigns another reason: that fennel and forgetfulness are given to Bacchus because it is hardly appropriate for those drinking to remember every error committed between cups; or if a fault is committed, a light and childish reprimand should suffice, just as children are punished with a fennel switch. Others say that the fennel is most suitable for Bacchus so that <margin>Fennel [ferula] named from "bearing" [ferendo]. Theophrastus.</margin> those unsteady on their feet from drunkenness might guide their staggering steps with this light support. Among the Latins, the fennel is named *ferula* from the word for "bearing" <note>original: "ferendo"</note>, because its stalks served as walking sticks and staves for the elderly. Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> describes it thus: *The fennel rises quite tall, with a single stalk, and is jointed at the nodes of the stem; its leaves are large, alternating, and divided into many fine segments like hair; the largest leaves are those closest to the ground, clasping the stem like reeds; the seed is like that of dill, etc.* In Egypt, it grows with great abundance; the Egyptian varieties are hollow, while most others contain a spongy pith inside. But leaving these things aside, let us see why the Egyptians used these fennel-stalk <margin>Why the Egyptians used fennel staffs as symbols.</margin> staffs as symbols. First, it is attributed to Osiris (the Egyptian Dionysus) because he was the first to teach how to plant the vine and how to use the fennel thyrsus as a support or stake most suitable for holding up the vine. For since fennel stalks, according to Theophrastus, often grow to five or six cubits <note>About 7.5 to 9 feet.</note> in great numbers in Egypt, it is likely that Osiris first used them as supports when planting vineyards. Therefore, that fennel thyrsus was a symbol among the Egyptians for the use of wine and the vine; hence it is attributed indiscriminately to both Osiris and Isis in the *Bembine Table* <note>The "Mensa Isiaca," a famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs that Kircher studied extensively.</note>. <margin>Pliny.</margin> Pliny writes that for this same purpose, the reed was primarily cultivated in Italy; or perhaps because from its joined intervals, a flute with seven pipes was constructed, as Ovid says. For the ancients used to call the joined reed <note>original: "ζεύγην" (zeugēn)</note>, making pairs and <note>original: "μεσόγλοια" (mesogloia)</note> "middle-pith" pieces suitable for crafting musical instruments. In the hollows of these stalks, according to Macrobius, they placed tender clusters of grapes and ivy, which caused the stalks to curve at the upper part—a feature that was not without its own mystery. Furthermore, Herodotus testifies that they fashioned curved staves <note>original: "lituos," a curved ritual staff or trumpet.</note> from fennel stalks just as they did from reeds. Since, however, Osiris is credited through these staffs not only with the invention of wine... <margin>Staffs made from fennel stalks. Herodotus.</margin>
