...fennel-like stalks <note>original: "ferulaceos"</note>, as has been said, were not only signified, but they also attributed them to Music, as Diodorus reports; certainly they could express it through no other symbol better than through stalks and reeds, from which Pliny and Theophrastus testify that Music drew its first origin in Egypt; since both are capable of being bent, and both grow hollow in Egypt. <margin>Herodotus. Why the Reed is attributed to Bacchus.</margin> <margin>Music invented in Egypt.</margin> <margin>Pliny book 16, chapter 36.</margin> <margin>Theophrastus book 4, chapter 12.</margin> For since Egypt abounds in marshy places, and therefore is by no means lacking in the plants of said places, where stalks and reeds usually grow, they discovered among other things many types of stalks and reeds that were flexible and hollow inside, and they saw they were suited for producing sound; finally, through frequent experience in inventing flutes and trumpets with both, it provided the occasion, according to that line of Ovid:

->*And he plays a light song on the waxed reed.*<-
<note>original: "Et leue cerata modulatur arundine carmen." From Ovid's Metamorphoses, referring to the Pan-pipes.</note>

Hence also in Greek it is called a <term>κάλαμος</term> <note>kalamos: a reed or cane</note>, a word which has been widely adopted by Latin poets as well, as Manilius says when dealing with the power of Music:

->*And slender reeds, and words set to the strings.*<-
<note>original: "Et graciles calamos, & neruis insita verba." From Manilius's Astronomica.</note>

Concerning these, one may see countless poets everywhere. The reed is called <term>ζυγίτης</term> <note>zygites: the "yoke-reed," from the Greek "zygos" for yoke</note> in Theophrastus, which Gaza <note>Theodorus Gaza was a 15th-century scholar famous for translating Greek botanical works into Latin</note> translates as "straw-like," and thinks it should be named "yoke-like" because vines were tied to a yoke with it; Columella teaches this method of weaving the vine. <margin>Gaza. Columella book 4, chapter 17.</margin>

Furthermore, Theophrastus in the cited place identifies two kinds of reeds: <margin>Two kinds of reeds.</margin> the first is <term>αὐλητικός</term> <note>auletikos: "flute-like," referring to reeds used to make musical instruments</note>, which Pliny interprets as "tibial" <note>pertaining to the tibia or flute</note>; and the other is <term>πλόκιμος</term> <note>plokimos: "woven"</note>, that is, "textile," in Gaza’s interpretation, perhaps because mats, coils, and other things of that kind were made from its leaves; where Pliny, due to the similarity of words in Theophrastus, reads <term>πλοίας</term> <note>ploias: "floating"</note> instead of "woven," as if it were a "floating reed." For there are Egyptian reeds, according to Pliny, and Cretan ones, which they call <term>Θῆβας</term> <note>Thebas: Theban</note>, because the best arrows were also made from them. Theophrastus testifies in the cited place that these were usually cut in season before the time of Antigenes <note>A famous Greek flute player</note>, when flutes still played more simply, under the constellation Arcturus in the month of September; for he says that those cut thus were useful many years later, and required much practice in sounding, but the "mouths of the tongues" <note>referring to the reed's vibrating tip</note> were pressed together, which was more useful to them for signaling things to the people. But after variety and artifice were added, the time of cutting was changed. Apuleius mentions these reeds being used in Egyptian solemnities <margin>Apuleius.</margin> in these words: *There went also the flute-players dedicated to the great Serapis, who, through a slanted reed held toward the right ear, repeated the familiar tune of the temple and the God.* Indeed, to embrace many things in a few words, the Egyptians seem to have denoted nothing else by this symbol of <term>fennel-stalk thyrsi</term> <note>thyrsorum ferulaceorum: staffs made of giant fennel, a plant with a pithy center</note>—which are seen partly placed in the hands of the Gods, and were partly accustomed to be carried around in the more solemn festivals— <margin>The symbol of fennel-stalk thyrsi among the Egyptians.</margin> except the planting of the vine and the invention of Music. They did not take this so literally, but applied it entirely to mystical and anagogical <note>anagogical: a method of spiritual interpretation that detects allusions to heaven or the afterlife</note> senses; for in each of the orders of the Worlds there are their own "plantings," their own "vines," and "harmonies," to which they were chiefly alluding.

<margin>Three things to be considered in the thyrsus-scepter of Osiris.</margin> Therefore, this reed-like scepter or thyrsus is attributed to Osiris to denote his power. Three things must be considered regarding the hieroglyphic thyrsus-scepter. First, the power of Osiris, whose symbol was a scepter of this form; then, the method of planting the vine and the technique of training it to a staff or reed, which we have proved above from various sources to be his own invention. Second, the construction of flutes and curved trumpets <note>original: "lituorum"</note>, which it has also been shown in various ways that Pan or Mercury first fashioned from reeds of this kind; from these, the proportions of Music later flowed. Third and finally, in place of the scepter, it is also seen in the hand of Osiris and Isis; in this manner, such a reed-like thyrsus and a curved scepter, stretched out in the fashion of a slanted reed, is represented six times on the Bembine Tablet <note>The Tabula Bembina, or Mensa Isiaca, is a famous bronze tablet of the 1st century AD covered in Egyptian-style imagery that Kircher studied extensively.</note>. By this, they intended to signify in no obscure way their power and the excellence of the things they invented: wine and Music, or harmony. This sign, therefore, is nothing other than a staff made of fennel or reed—a hieroglyphic symbol of the aforementioned things, as we have demonstrated. But let us now proceed to the third symbol.

## ->Concerning the Nilotic Rush.<-

<margin>What the Nilotic rush or papyrus signifies in hieroglyphs. Pliny. Hermolaus. Donatus.</margin> The third place in order is held by the Nilotic Rush, or if you prefer, the smooth and knotless papyrus, which is confused with papyrus or byblos <note>The inner bark of the papyrus plant used for writing.</note> by Pliny, Hermolaus, and Donatus. By this, the Egyptians seem to have intended to signify first nothing other than the noble invention of letters and writing, first discovered by the Egyptian Mercury <note>Thoth, often identified by Renaissance scholars with Hermes/Mercury.</note>, or rather, Osiris and Isis, as Diodorus testifies. Second, it signifies the provision of all necessary things; for from papyrus and bulrushes, a supply of nearly all things necessary for human use was provided. Hence, we always see it placed near the "many-formed Spirit" <note>original: "Dæmoni polymorpho"</note>, indicated by a dragon-shaped Butterfly, acting as a guardian of necessary things.

<margin>What kind of plant the papyrus or bulrush is.</margin> It is a light plant, <term>azygon</term> <note>original Greek: ἄζυγον; meaning "unpaired" or "solitary," referring here to its single-stemmed growth.</note>, which produces upright, round, thin, knotless stalks or stems or rods in place of leaves. These are a cubit and a half high, green in their grassy color, with sharp points, filled with white pith, resembling and serving as a wick <note>original: "ellychnium"</note>.

<margin>Theophrastus</margin> Theophrastus says: *The bulrush is a certain species of rush, smooth and knotless, from which they make sieves in Egypt.* Others reserve the use of rushes for sea-traps; others, as Pliny testifies, use the pith of the rush for the lights of lamps as a wick. However, since we have treated these matters at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Another of Kircher's major works, published in 1650, focusing on the obelisk in the Piazza Navona.</note>, we refer the reader there.

<margin>Meanings of the Nilotic Rush.</margin> Furthermore, this Rush has as many meanings as the objects it is placed with: for it has one meaning when placed alone, another with a sieve, another with a fly, and another with other symbols. In this place, with the symbols added, some think it indicates the invention of things made by Osiris, and nothing else...

...to be signified, other than the noble invention of letters; for what reason this is so, we must briefly consider.

<margin>The rush, the bulrush, or the papyrus signifies the invention of letters.</margin>
It is well established that the Rush, or bulrush—or if you prefer, the papyrus (for these are confounded by most authors, as Hermolaus Barbarus and Donatus demonstrate from Pliny)—is a plant. The Rush is the light, common sharp-rush <note>original: "oxyschænus"</note>; in place of leaves, it puts forth shoots, or reeds, or rods that are straight, round, thin, smooth, and without knots. They grow a cubit and a half high, are green with a herbaceous color, sharpened into acute points, and filled with a white pith, resembling and serving the purpose of a lamp wick. That such is the papyrus, and that it grows nowhere more frequently than in Egypt, is testified by all the botanists who have written about it. And this Rush, because of its remarkable and manifold uses, has been adopted everywhere as various symbols, as will be seen at length in the following pages. But in this place, it is placed as a symbol of the letters invented by Osiris, as Horus <note>Kircher is referring to Horapollo, the purported author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note> himself testifies in Books 1 and 38: *“When the Egyptians wish to signify Egyptian letters, or a sacred Scribe, or an end, they paint ink, a sieve, and a rush.”* <note>original Greek: "Αἰγύπτια δὲ γράμματα δηλοῦντες ἢ ἱερογραμματέα, ἢ πέρας · μέλαν, καὶ κόσκινον, καὶ σχοῖνον ζωγραφοῦσι."</note> All of these have different meanings. It signifies Egyptian letters because all writing among them is completed with these; for they write with a rush and not with any other thing. They gladly adopted as a symbol of letters that instrument which first gave them the occasion for writing; for the rush supplies not only the pens <note>original: "calamos"</note> but also the paper, for both are made from the same source, as Theophrastus and Pliny testify, and after them Prosper Alpinus.

And these are the two patterns of the sacred tablets which, since they occur not only everywhere else but also on this present Obelisk and the others, I thought it timely to explain in this place, lest a more extensive explanation of them in the context of the interpretation should cause some delay.

### CHAPTER IV. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

the supreme Creator of the World, that supramundane Sun who bestows life upon all. He is seated because he holds power over all things; he is naked because he is clothed in no shroud of bodily passion; he appears with a **hawk-shaped head** <term>hierakomorphos</term> <note>original Greek: ιερακόμορφος. The hawk was a primary symbol for solar deities like Ra and Osiris.</note> <note>symbol: ☉ (Sun/Gold)</note> because he is the cause of all life and vital motion; he is veiled because his essence can never be investigated by any human wit; he supports a globe upon his head because he is eternal, lacking any beginning or end; and he holds a **Cucuphe scepter** <term>cucuphe</term> <note>A scepter topped with the head of a hoopoe bird, symbolizing power or guardianship.</note> because, although he possesses the simplest essence of all, he is nonetheless the cause of all the variety that shines forth in the world. He is placed in a **hawk-shaped** <term>hierakomorphos</term> form on the first Meridian side because, as <margin>Plutarch.</margin> Plutarch testifies, the southern region is the "right side" of the world, the kingdom of Osiris—that is, the Sun—which is most abundant in life and fertility. From this, Plutarch also claims the Nile is nothing other than the outflowing of Osiris, the cause and origin of all good things. These things must be understood according to a certain analogy, not only regarding the Sensible World, but most especially regarding the supramundane Archetype <note>In Kircher’s philosophy, the "Archetype" is the divine realm of ideas that precedes the physical world.</note>.

<margin>The mitred Androsphinx.</margin> The second figure is an **Androsphinx** <note>A sphinx with a human head and a lion's body.</note> wearing a mitre and resting upon a pedestal <note>original: "abaco"</note>. By this is signified that Divinity which they called **Momphta** <term>Momphta</term> <note>Kircher's term for a creative intelligence or "World-Soul" associated with the humid or watery principle.</note>, the Mind of the supreme Divinity, the powerful Artisan presiding over all moist substance. It is depicted with a human face to show the power of intelligence; it has a lion’s body because when the Sun enters the sign of Leo, it exerts its greatest effect in Egypt through the abundance of moisture (the Nile flood) with which it blesses the Egyptian land. It reclines because Osiris, whose minister it is, shows his supramundane power through this posture; it is mitred to suggest the power over all moist things granted to it by Osiris.

<margin>What the Inscription of the Flaminian Obelisk signifies.</margin> Thus, the inscription of this Obelisk signifies nothing other than a dedication to Osiris and Momphta; the former presides over the Heat of the world, and the latter over its Moisture. By these two, the machine of the entire world is preserved in its perfection. Furthermore, this figure is placed within the **pyramidion** <note>The pointed capstone of an obelisk.</note> to indicate that he towers above the entire circuit of created things, and remains hidden in the infinite abyss of his essence alone, insofar as the "moist-heat" over which he presides is knowable—purely and simply—only within the hidden concept of his ideal reason. He is placed on the four faces of the pyramidion so that his identical power might be shown throughout the fourfold world.

<margin>B The space marked with the letter B on the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> Furthermore, in the space of the pyramidion marked with the letter **B** on the southern side, Osiris appears again in **hawk-shaped** <term>hierakomorphos</term> <note>symbol: ☉ (Sun/Gold)</note> form sitting upon a throne, adorned with the same symbols as above. By this arrangement of figures is signified the procession of the supramundane Osiris toward his external work. This occurs when he communicates himself to the Genial or Intellectual World, which is the supramundane **Isis**, represented here by the kneeling image. She is painted kneeling both to show her prompt readiness in obedience toward the supramundane Osiris, and because she is, as it were, a passive principle into which Osiris continually flows his virtue. She is veiled because she is the Intelligence of insensible substance, whose veil <note>original: "peplum"</note>, according to Diodorus, no one has revealed. which is the triform seal of the supreme Divinity, by which the female consort of Osiris is established as the administrator of worldly affairs; she displays small images of **Canopus** <term>Canopus</term> <note>A jar-shaped deity representing the Nile water or the element of moisture.</note> to Osiris as a symbol of moisture. First, he is considered as in the first compartment **A**, and thus he is the same as **Hemphta** <note>A name Kircher uses for the supreme, Egyptian creator-god.</note>, the supreme triform Deity of Deities, the supramundane and archetypal Sun, the supreme Jupiter, and the Ruler and Moderator of all things.

Third, there is the **celestial Osiris**, the life and soul of the Sidereal World, a Solar Divinity to whom the administration of the **Sensible World** <note>The physical world we can perceive with our senses.</note> has been entrusted. <margin>Osiris of the Sidereal World.</margin> The number twelve, over which he presides, is most especially consecrated to him; for he presides over the twelve dwellings of the great circle and the twelve regions of the World through twelve powers most similar to himself. It is one and the same power of Osiris which, diffused through twelve Powers or Intelligences that attend the Solar Divinity in the twelve paths of the World (over which each presides), produces different operations according to the effect, just as they differ by their "dwellings" or zodiac signs. They have a **Cidarin** <term>Cidarin</term> <note>A royal Persian or Egyptian headdress or tiara.</note> placed on their heads to demonstrate the supreme power over all things communicated to them by Osiris.

This bull distributes the power—which flows from the supreme Osiris into the Sidereal realm, and from there by a linked dominion into the material realm—through twelve material Intelligences into the entire mixture of the Elementary World. From this, the abundance and variety of all things are born. All these things are aptly suggested by the **twelve Bulls** that preside over the twelve regions of the Horizon and act as moderators of the Elementary World. By the Bull, the material Osiris is understood because, according to <margin>Twelve Bulls on the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> Egyptian tradition, having been changed into a Bull, he first taught agriculture, planting, grafting, and the other arts necessary for human life, as we have shown in various places.

Kircher refers to the aspect of the god governing the physical world.</note>, distinguished by a triple dominion granted from heaven, guardian of Cities, the fertilizer of the material storehouse according to the threefold disposition of the year, and the giver of life.* In the symbols of the third quadrangle, this sense is held: *Material Osiris, the generous giver of vegetable nature, impregnating the lower Isis with the influence communicated to him from the supreme Divinity.*

<margin>Three quadrangles of the second side.</margin>
In the first quadrangle of the barren side is a bull, an arm, a goose, and a lion-like statue with a **Tautic character** <note>A symbol associated with Thoth (Hermes), often the Ankh or "handled cross."</note>; their meaning is: *Material Intelligence, follower of Osiris, the beneficent guardian of things, the material Momphta, communicates the influence received from above to the rest of the material world.* In the [second] barren quadrangle, this sense is contained: *Material Intelligence, follower of Osiris, the beneficent Momphta, minister of Horus.* The third quadrangle has this sense: *Material Intelligence, follower of Osiris, the beneficent Good Spirit <term>Agathodemon</term> of the supreme Divinity.*

<margin>Three quadrangles of the third side.</margin>
In the first quadrangle of the third side, as the same symbols occur as in the first quadrangle of the first side, they reflect the same meaning. In the second quadrangle of the third side, this sense is contained: *Material Intelligence, follower of material Osiris, beneficent minister of Horus, Momphta, the Good Spirit.* In the third quadrangle of the third side, the significance of the symbols is this: *Material Intelligence, follower of Osiris, the beneficent Momphta, distributes the influence of the supreme Divinity, communicated from above, into the air.*

<margin>Three quadrangles of the fourth side.</margin>
In the first quadrangle of the fourth side, the symbols are explained thus: *Material Intelligence, the beneficent minister of Osiris, Momphta, spreads the influence communicated to him into the air.* In the second quadrangle of the fourth side, it is held thus: *Material Intelligence, minister of beneficent Osiris, Momphta, the Good Spirit, inserts fiery qualities into the moisture of the elemental world.* In the third quadrangle of the fourth side, this is the significance of the symbols: *Material Intelligence, minister of beneficent Osiris, drives away the harmful and excessive power of fire and provides power that is moderate and proportioned to things.*

<margin>Twelve material intelligences, and 12 amulets.</margin>
Behold, these are the twelve duties of the material Intelligences, by which each provides for the lower world; and these quadrangles are like so many **amulets and phylacteries** <note>Protective charms or scrolls containing sacred texts used to invoke divine favor or ward off evil.</note>, established both to appease the said Intelligences and to ward off harmful ones.

Thus, having set forth the universal inscription of the Obelisk, let us now prepare ourselves for the particular interpretation of the individual columns.

## *Interpretation of the Second Column of the Southern Side.* <margin>Second column of the southern side of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin>

# § V.

### ->Interpretation of the first column of the second Northern side.<-

<margin>
First column of the second Northern side of the Flaminian Obelisk.
</margin>

**I**n the first position occurs an ax placed above a sacred bowl. To understand this, it must be noted that among the leaders of the World, according to the testimony of **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary Persian prophet, often cited in Renaissance occultism as a source of "ancient theology"</note>, three **implacable Powers** are placed, which they call the <term>Amilicti <gloss>The Unrelenting Ones</gloss></term>; and these were represented by three axes because of the supreme violence and severity with which they administer affairs according to the rigor prescribed by the highest Divinity. These figures were said to preside over the "fountain-bowl," according to **Psellus** <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar who wrote on the Chaldean Oracles</note>; that is, the immense supramundane pool from which all members of both the sensible and insensible World are watered. Therefore, the ax placed in the first position denotes an **Amilictic power**, the ruler of the pool or bowl, by whose cutting the opened bowl flows into the **Mendesian Kingdom** <note>Mendes was an Egyptian city associated with fertility and the ram-god Banebdjedet</note>. Now, since Mendes is a Deity of fruitfulness, he distributes the moisture spread from the pool with a kind hand into the three parts of the year, for the abundance of the harvest and necessary things. All these things are signified by the ax, the bowl, the reed-like thyrsus <note>A ritual staff associated with Dionysian or fertility rites</note>, and the staff marked with a human head, through the three boundary-markers, and the added sea-rush, the leaf of the **Persea** <note>A sacred tree in Egyptian mythology, often associated with the sun and the recording of history</note>, the water-symbol <note>Original: hydroschema</note>, and the two extended arms. Truly, lest any harm should arise from the excessive vehemence and severity of the Amilicti, they again consecrate two following amulets of the sacred tablets—the **Momphto-Mendesian** and the **Isiac**—to the many-formed Deity who presides over the fruitfulness of things and who dispenses all that is carried out by the Amilicti. After the sacred tablets follows a scepter, an extended hand, and a square in which a **swallow** is enclosed. Let us see what these indicate. **Herodotus**, **Diodorus**, and **Eusebius** relate that in the temples of the Egyptians there were certain enclosures established for the feeding of sacred animals; these enclosures were held in such great veneration among that superstitious nation that they even moved them into their inner sanctums <note>Original: adyta</note>, having deemed them worthy of sacred honor. In these, they were accustomed to place not living animals, but their images, adorned with mystical symbols, as **Pausanias** testifies; for they believed they could include the Divinities they represented within them through various ceremonial preparations. This square represents such an enclosure in this place, in which we see a sacred swallow enclosed. Now, the swallow, according to **Pierio** <note>Pierio Valeriano, author of a famous 16th-century work on hieroglyphics</note> folio 162, was a symbol of the benefits conferred upon the human race by **Osiris** and **Isis**; namely, that from them they received the laws of the World and the precepts of cultivating the fields, the rules of the art of Architecture, and learned to live their lives rightly with the rest of men. All these things the character and nature of the swallow teaches, as **Horus** <note>Referring to Horapollo, the purported author of a treatise on hieroglyphics</note> hands down. Therefore, by the use and application of these sacred tablets, well-

### § VI

->Interpretation of the second column of the second Northern side.<-

<margin>Second column of the Northern side of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin>
**I**n the first place of this middle column, the Genii **Ibiacus** and **Ophionius** are positioned, under which is placed the **dodecapyrgon** <term>δωδεκάπυργον <gloss>a twelve-towered structure, representing the twelve mansions of the zodiac or celestial spheres</gloss></term>, along with a water-scheme, snares, and a statue of **Momphta**, accompanied by a **Goose**. The Egyptians call this goose **Chenosiris**, not from the word for "reed," 
<margin>Chenosiris or the sacred Goose.</margin>
which the Greeks call **choiron** <note>original: "χοῖρον"; while usually meaning "pig," Kircher here relates it to a "reed" used in Dionysian rites</note>, because they were accustomed to perform the solemnity of **Dionysus** (or Osiris) with reed thyrsi <note>ritual staffs</note> wrapped in ivy; but they name it from the Egyptian word **shenos** or **shen** <note>original Coptic: "ϣⲉⲛⲏⲟⲥ" or "ϣⲏⲛ"</note>, which signifies a **Goose**. Therefore, they called Osiris "Chenosiris," as if you were to say "the Goose-like Osiris," because he is accustomed to watch over the things committed to his faith with the highest care, just like a goose. They indicate, therefore, that the two Genii, Ibiacus and Ophionius, the presiding spirits of the mansions of the *dodecapyrgon*, are first constrained by the statue of the Lion-headed Momphta and Chenosiris for the care and preservation of the beneficial **favissa** <note>A sacred reservoir or underground storage; here referring to the source of life-giving waters</note>, as the water-scheme—the figure of the reservoir—and the extended arm sufficiently show. 

Next follows the **Hawk**, above which is an **Astronomical quadrant**, and below the Hawk is a statue of **Horus** with a tiller <note>or rudder</note>, followed by cycloids, a scepter, a water-scheme, and finally the statue of Momphta with a feather and a **Scarab**. By the quadrant, as we have said elsewhere, the opportune time is indicated; by the Hawk, **Osiris** or the **Solar Soul** is signified, who, having descended into the "lower Horus" (that is, into the sensible World, according to the testimony of 
<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
**Plutarch**), imbues the heavens with life. Momphta, the lion-headed guardian of the water, is filled by the fertile motion of the Solar operations—indicated by the Scarab—with a power that the **polymorphous Spirit** <note>A "many-formed" deity or demon</note> then transforms into all things according to the nature and property of each, propagating them into an innumerable variety and abundance of things. 

From this, the sacred tablet is arranged, in which 
<margin>Explanation of the sacred tablet in the second column of the second side of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin>
the lion-headed Momphta, conspicuous with a feather on his head, presides over the lower *dodecapyrgon*. Here, the circle clearly signifies participation in divinity, the feather signifies the subtlety of operations, and the **Ankh** <term>Crux ansata <gloss>The "handled cross," representing life or the flow of the spirit</gloss></term> signifies the downward flow of the World Spirit, derived from the upper *dodecapyrgon* into the lower *dodecapyrgon*, which is analogous to the one above. Indeed, the divinities reviewed thus far are the same in substance, differing only in their operations: for what the Genii Ibiacus and Ophionius perform in the **Intellectual World**, the lion-headed Momphta and Chenosiris perform in the **Elementary** (or material) **World**. Both of these latter govern the "moist-warm" principle: Momphta, excelling in fiery quality, tempers the harmful cold inherent in moisture; while Chenosiris, with a moderate coldness, tempers the excessive force of heat inherent in moisture.

### SYNTAGMA III. THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER IV.

...performed; the same is achieved in their own way in the upper World by the **Ibis-like** and **Serpent-like Spirits** <note>original: "Ibiacus & Ophionius Genij"; Kircher refers to spirits associated with the Ibis (Thoth) and the Serpent (Ophion)</note>; of these, the latter, filled with fiery power, provides life and motion to the humid element, while the former tempers it by its own surpassing virtue; in the lower world this occurs under material conditions, and in the upper World under a certain analogous condition appropriate to those realms.

Furthermore, what Osiris—the Hawk-like or Solar Deity—performs in the worldly **House of Horus**, that is, the Starry World, the lower or material **Momphta** <note>Kircher's term for a creative divine force or world-soul</note> performs in the material World. For this reason, the hawk's feather and the **Scarab** are aptly joined to him, to indicate that Momphta directs all his operations according to the prototype or model of the Hawk, which is Osiris, the Solar Deity. I have chosen to explain these matters more extensively here so that if the reader encounters such monstrous forms of the Deities, they may be persuaded to understand them in the manner I have described; and so they might not think I have run into a contradiction if I should occasionally confuse one with another, which I wish to be understood also for what follows.

<margin>Y</margin> Next follows the sacred tablet of the **Ibis** perched upon the **twelve-towered fortress** <term>dodecapyrgos <gloss>from the Greek 'dodeka' (twelve) and 'pyrgos' (tower), representing the twelve signs of the zodiac or celestial spheres</gloss></term>, by which the Mercurial Deity is denoted as the presiding power of the Nilotic twelve-towered structure, as the three Nilotic urns demonstrate. For here, the vanquisher of Typhon’s <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos</note> malice, having been carried down into the lower regions, moves the chains of the Worlds, whereby the machinations of Typhon—broken and crushed by his manifold dominion in the upper and lower World—cannot stand. All these things are indicated by the symbols enclosed between **Z** and **A**; for once the chain of celestial life is moved, the **Arimanian** <margin>Z</margin> <note>original: "Arimanium"; referring to Ahriman, the Zoroastrian spirit of evil, whom Kircher identifies with Typhon</note> dominion of the **Quail** must necessarily be weakened, obviously because of the supreme providence he holds over both the upper and lower bodies existing in the worldly <margin>A</margin> **House of Horus**. Indeed, he is the guardian of all things with his vital eye, <margin>B</margin> and therefore they consecrate the following sacred tablet to him as an amulet of the highest efficacy. In this, <term>A</term> represents the Ibis-like **Agathodæmon** <gloss>the "Good Spirit"</gloss>, the figure of the chain represents the mover of the chain of Deities, and the two feathers with the water-symbol <margin>C</margin> denote the divine motion in the humid element. For through this chain, the **Ibis-shaped Spirits** of the upper, middle, and lower Worlds—according to the required analogy—conspire as one for the preservation of the World. Moreover, the letter <term>A</term> is placed in the preceding <margin>D</margin> sacred tablet because it was discovered from the posture of the Ibis, the living habitation of **Mercury** <note>Mercury is the Roman equivalent of the Egyptian Thoth</note>. The chain is placed there because, just as Mercury is called the Messenger of the Gods by the Greeks, so he is said by the Egyptians to be the adapter of the **chains of Geniuses**, which they call **Seras**. The two feathers are placed there because the feathers of the Ibis are said to strike fear into the **Crocodile**, the symbol of Typhonian malice in the water; the remaining symbols will be explained more fully at the end of this Obelisk.

->**§ VII.**<-

The ruler of the third Northern region is the **Lion-like Momphta** <term>Momphta Leoninus; Kircher’s name for a creative divine force or world-soul, here depicted with a lion's features</term>, who holds dominion over the constitution of the three parts of the year, as indicated by the reed-like staff and the inverted branch. # § VIII.

<margin>First column of the third side of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin>

->*Interpretation of the first column of the third Western side.*<-

<margin>The figure of this column is the same as the figures of the first column of the first side, but in a different order.</margin>
The first part of this column, from I to M, is composed of the half of the first column of the first Southern side, from E to H. The second part of this first column of the third side, however, from M to Q, is composed of the third part of the column of the first Southern side, as before, from E to H; and so, just as the whole consists of the halves of the first and third columns of the first Southern side joined into one, so too the symbols have exactly the same meaning. However, they differ in the effects that the mixture produces, as I shall explain. For just as the first region of the Southern side of the World and the first region of the Western side are similar in their effects due to their proximity, yet differ in their actual result; so also must we judge the protections of the **Spirits** <note>original: "Geniorum"; refers to the guiding spirits or minor deities associated with places or forces</note>. For just as modern Cosmography has assigned different qualities to the individual regions of the World—for example, cold and dry to the **North** <note>original: "Boreæ"</note>, hot and dry to the **South** <note>original: "Austro"</note>, hot and moist to the **East** <note>original: "Orienti"</note>, and finally cold and moist to the **West** <note>original: "Occidenti"</note>—so too the <margin>Spirits assigned to the individual regions of the World by the Egyptians.</margin> Egyptians assigned presiding Spirits of similar qualities to each region. From the various combinations of these, different effects emanated. They would erect statues of these spirits composed of those animals that represented the said qualities, and once erected, they worshipped them with entirely analogous ceremonies. Thus, by the **Ibis** with its neck contracted, they denoted the Spirit of the cold-moist; by the **Asp**, the spirit of the hot-moist; by the **Lion-like Momphta**, the spirit corroborating the hot-moist; and by the **Dog**, they denoted a protector of a mixed nature, as is evident from the symbols placed on the first faces of the columns. Such mixtures are found everywhere in these two sides, the Western and Eastern, as will be said shortly—

The first column in its first place has a hawk perched on a bowl <note>original: "Accipitrem crateri inſidentem"</note>, which is followed by a reed staff, along with a fennel staff, three boundary markers, and a goat-shaped staff; there follow then two arms, etc. These symbols mostly correspond to those of the first column of the second side from T to <margin>Y</margin> Y, with a few exceptions, as well as the symbols of the third column of the third side from M to Q. # Recapitulation of the entire exposition.

<margin>Recapitulation of the exposition of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin>
In our study of this Obelisk, we have first demonstrated the method by which the supreme Deity, Hemphta <note>Kircher's name for a supreme, creative Egyptian spirit, often associated with the 'kneph' or world-egg</note> or the supramundane archetypal Osiris—the cause of all causes—who is visible now with a Hawk’s face and now with a human face, flows into the world. Together with his Sphinx, who is the Maker of the World, he influences first the **Genial World** <note>The world of generation and production</note>, which the figures in the second spaces <margin>APFT</margin> <margin>BQGV</margin> exhibit. From there, he flows into the twelve Solar Intelligences, who are the presidents of the entire twelve-fold order of nature, and finally into the "Hylean" <note>From the Greek 'hyle', meaning material or elemental</note> Intelligences of Osiris within the Elemental World. Having sent this ahead as a sort of summary inscription, the text afterwards descends to particulars. It teaches by what reasoning, and through which sacrifices, rites, and ceremonies, these linked choirs of Divinities—the <term>dodecapyrgi</term> <note>Literally "twelve-towered," referring here to the twelve divisions of the Zodiac as celestial fortresses</note> presidents—are to be petitioned against the Typhonian powers <note>The chaotic or destructive forces associated with Set/Typhon</note> and drawn down to grant an abundance of all necessary things. Not long ago, I found among the coins of the Ancients taken from the <margin>Coins from the Museum of Pietro Stefanoni.</margin> Museum of Pietro Stefanoni <note>Pietro Stefanoni was a well-known 17th-century Italian antiquarian and collector of gems and coins</note>, a Coin on which the Zodiac was inscribed. Within it, like presidents of the twelve-fold order of nature, were inscribed Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, and Vulcan, as is clear in the following diagram. This undoubtedly

<note>Engraving of a zodiacal medallion. The outer ring shows the twelve signs of the Zodiac. The center features Greco-Roman gods: Jupiter (seated with an eagle), Mercury (with his staff), Mars (in armor), and Vulcan (at his forge). A large hawk, representing the Egyptian Osiris, stands prominently in the center, symbolizing the Egyptian source of these later gods.</note>

proceeded from the Egyptians; for the doctrine is the same, even if it was sketched differently by the Greek Astronomers. For what else is the Hawk-like Osiris <note>original: "Osiris Accipitrinus"</note> but Jupiter? And what else is the Ibis-shaped Deity <note>original: "Ibimorphon Numen"</note> but Mercury?

### VOLUME III. THE FLAMINIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER IV.

...for what else is the implacable power of Amilictus <note>Kircher identifies Amilictus as a fierce, martial aspect of the divine, corresponding to the planet Mars.</note> but Mars? And what else is Momphta but Neptune? To these two, the twelve-towered fortress <note>original: "dodecapyrgum"</note> of all nature has been entrusted. You see Jupiter placed in the middle, between Mercury and Mars, as the attendant of the supreme Divinity; while Neptune, conspicuous with his trident, rejoices in his watery empire. Indeed, each of these twelve columns of the Obelisk corresponds either to one of the twelve regions of the world, or to one of the twelve mansions of the great celestial arc. For this reason, their inner shrines <note>original: "adyta"</note> were arranged as twelve-sided (as here), or sometimes octagonal, four-sided, or even triangular, according to the worship of different deities, so that each side corresponded to one portion of the natural "twelve-fold" order. In these shrines, the mystical images of the deities were painted in the same order as seen on the Obelisk. They persuaded themselves that by this arrangement—which mirrored the layout of the world—and through specific, competent sacrifices, the gods could be moved in a wonderful way to favor their prayers. Consequently, they quite appropriately called these connections <margin>Chains among the Egyptians.</margin> **chains**; and upon this "hinge," so to speak, the entirety of their more secret way of philosophizing was balanced.

Thus, in the first column of the first side, <margin>Summary of the first column of the first side of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> whoever drew down the Mercurial Divinity through the proper sacrifices would, as a consequence, also draw down Isis, the many-formed Momphta, Mendes, Chenosiris, and so on, as has been explained. They believed that by drawing down all of these, they would be filled with the happiness of every good thing. Once these were drawn down, they believed no adverse power could withstand them; by drawing them down through the study of contemplation appropriate to each, they promised themselves knowledge of all things. Finally, they imagined that by drawing them down, they could especially acquire **prophetic knowledge** <note>original: "manteuticam notitiam"</note>, which consists in the science of future events, as has been discussed at length in my work on *Hieroglyphic Magic*.

These ideas are beautifully confirmed by those sacred writings <note>original: "Hierogrammatismos"</note> seen at the bottom of each side of this Obelisk, the explanation of which we have intentionally delayed until this point. <margin>Figures at the end of the columns of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> Those on the first side are contained within the letters **N** and **O**; on the second side, **D** and **E**; on the third, **R** and **S**; and on the fourth, **G** and **H**. These spaces indicate nothing other than the inner shrines of the Egyptian priests, in which—through legitimate and highly appropriate sacrifices, rites, and ceremonies described elsewhere at length—they intended nothing but the "attraction" of the aforementioned Divinities.

Therefore, in these shrines, they first placed the statues of the principal Divinities transformed in various ways. These are indicated in the first and second columns by Osiris standing in a <term>hawk-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: "ἱερακόμορφον"</note> form and ready to show favor, as well as by the Hawk and the three Ibises in the second column. Before these, the priests prostrate on their knees offer **Canopic jars** <note>original: "Canopulos," vessels representing the deity Canopus, often used to hold Nile water or viscera</note> fashioned in the shape of vessels. By this very act, they suggest that they desire from Osiris the beneficial protection of moisture and the fruitful preservation of watery substance, seeing as nothing in the world can exist without it.

-><-

However, because moisture is of no use without heat, in the final spaces of the third and fourth sides, <margin>What the naked priests on the Obelisk signify.</margin> they paint Osiris with a human face, before whom naked priests prostrate themselves. The first priest offers a globe, and the second a pyramid, which are symbols of heat fertilizing the moisture; for from these two elements, the generation of all things arises. They are seen partly veiled and partly bound with ceremonial ribbons...

<meta>This page continues Chapter 4 of the "Theatrum Hieroglyphicum" section. ...[of the priests], of whom the former, in female attire, present the moist Divinities as the passive principle of things, while the latter present fire in male form as the active principle of things through their minor deities. They are naked because, as was stated in the treatise on the inner shrines <note>original: *adyta*; the most sacred, restricted parts of a temple</note>, the Priests for the most part performed their sacrifices naked, so that they might represent the Divinities they were petitioning—who are clothed in no covering of earthly mixture—by a similar nudity, or rather, by a nude likeness. Moreover, upon the walls of the inner shrines they placed various diagrams of sacred tables <margin>Sacred tables at the end of the columns of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> as items of great importance for more powerfully attracting the Divinities. These kinds of tables can be seen on each of the four sides, marked with letters a b c d, e f g h, etc. All of these have been extracted from the side of the Obelisk as most powerful amulets. Once the Priests had extracted them from there, they instructed the superstitious common people to carry them for private use, engraved upon particular statues of the Gods, vessels, sideboards, stones of various kinds, and vessels of metal or earthenware, as will be explained more fully in the course of this Work. Indeed, we do not explain these sacred diagrams <note>original: *hieroschemata*</note> here, since anyone who has rightly understood the preceding matters can interpret them with no trouble; for they have all already been explained and, as I said, extracted from the various columns of the Obelisk and transferred to the bottom of the sides, which mark the inner shrines of the Egyptians.

->**Conclusion regarding the interpretation made by Hermapion.**<-

<margin>Ammianus Marcellinus.</margin>And here is that most celebrated Obelisk, which Augustus brought from Egypt and erected in the Circus Maximus; whose interpretation, made by Hermapion, Ammianus Marcellinus recounts in these words: *Moreover, the text of the marks on the Obelisk, etc., following the book of Hermapion, we set down interpreted in Greek letters.* For a long time, Augustus had desired to know the doctrine contained on this Obelisk, and for that reason he had searched throughout all Egypt by means of learned men to see if he might find someone skilled in this hieroglyphic literature. At length, Hermapion the Grammarian offered himself, whom they call the "Cymbal of the World" <note>original: *Cynabalum Mundi*. This was likely a disparaging nickname implying Hermapion was loud and talkative but lacked true depth.</note>; although he promised much regarding these matters, he was nevertheless laughed at by everyone, according to the testimony of Strabo. Nevertheless, trusting himself more than was right, he provided the interpretation of this present Obelisk, which is inserted into the books of the previously cited Ammianus Marcellinus, and which we provide in Greek and Latin on page 149 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. This interpretation contains a dedication of the Obelisk made by Ramesses to the Sun, wherein the praises of both are contained. However, that this interpretation is entirely false, counterfeit, and does not contain even a trace of the things actually contained on this Obelisk, only he will be able to know who compares our interpretation with the exposition of Hermapion <term>more accurately <note>original: *akribesterōs* (Greek: ἀκριβεστέρως), meaning with greater precision or rigour.</note></term>. He first explains six verses, though I have not been able to discern what kind they are on this Obelisk, unless perhaps he thought the columns were verses; but since the Obelisk displays twelve of them, I do not see why he only presented six. Secondly, I find no mention of the first figures of this Obelisk, which serve as the *epigraph* <note>The introductory inscription or title.</note>; where...

# SYNTAGMA III. FLAMINIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER IV.

Where the twelve Hawks and as many Oxen, which are contained at the upper extremity of the Obelisk (and whose mention ought to have been repeated twelve times), remain in Hermapion's interpretation, it has not yet been possible to discover. Added to this is the argument of the Obelisk itself, which can in no way match his interpretation, since the deeds of Ramesses, Heron, and the other Kings named therein are expressed nowhere. Of the thirty-nine diagrams of the sacred tables—which we call amulets—seventeen are similar to the Momphtho-Mendesian <note>Kircher refers to local Egyptian deities or districts (nomes) he associates with specific symbolic systems</note>, sixteen to the Isiac Horon and Osirian, three to Momphtha, and three are consecrated to the great chains of the Agathodaemon <note>The "Good Spirit," often depicted as a serpent in Greco-Egyptian mythology</note>. Although the whole Obelisk is filled with these, where, I ask, is there any mention made of them? Not even a <term>jot</term> <note>original: γρῦ (gry); a Greek expression for the smallest sound or "a grunt," meaning "not a single word"</note> is to be found. Since, moreover, these same kinds of sacred tables are found on most other Obelisks, I certainly do not see how that history of King Ramesses and the account of the erection of his Obelisk sacred to the Sun can be expressed there. Hence, it is more likely that this interpretation by Hermapion, brought forward by Ammianus, is either counterfeit and fictitious, or it is the interpretation of some other hieroglyphic fragment that was falsely attributed to this Obelisk. 

However, lest we seem to do an injustice both to Hermapion and to Ammianus—who relates this same interpretation in his histories as something worth remembering—I will here repeat Hermapion's interpretation once more from my work on the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher's 1650 book *Obeliscus Pamphilius*</note>, so that the Reader, by comparing my interpretation with Hermapion's composition, may finally recognize how absurd and dissonant a doctrine this interpretation of Hermapion contains, so far removed from the genius of the Egyptians.

### First Verse.

> *The Great Celestial God Apollo from the City of the Sun, son of the strong Heron, whom the Sun educated, whom the Gods pursued with honor, who rules over the entire Orb of the Earth, whom the Sun selected, a King renowned on account of Mars, whom Ammon loves, and he, who shines totally, commanded to be a long-lived King.*

<margin>Hermapion’s interpretation is false, and why.</margin>And this is the interpretation of Hermapion; but when we examined it with a more exact scale against the hieroglyphics carved on the Flaminian Obelisk, we found at last what we had long suspected: that this interpretation simply cannot hold up by any means. And lest we seem to do an injustice to an Author celebrated in the records of so many other writers, look diligently yourself at the four sides of the said Obelisk, compare the words with the figures, and you will see how foolishly they match, how with difficulty they cohere—in short, how poorly the whole thing stands, and how far it is from the truth. Thus, I strongly suspect that Hermapion, in place of an interpretation of the Obelisk, substituted some other random inscription; he did so more boldly because there were so few men—indeed, almost none—who could accuse him of such a deceptions.

In the Obelisk, therefore, four things must be considered: first is the Argument or theme of the Obelisk; second, the figures; third, the four sides; fourth, the order and position of the figures. We show by these arguments that Hermapion touched on none of these. And first, indeed, the Theme of the Obelisks: it has been stated extensively in various preceding places that they by no means contain the praises, victories, triumphs, and extraordinary deeds of Kings. <margin>Hieroglyphic doctrine does not contain the praises of Kings.</margin>For since the hieroglyphic doctrine was obscure, enigmatic, mysterious, and far removed from the understanding of the profane—which only those who had hope of the Kingdom, and those to whom the care of sacred things was committed, might know—and since they were forbidden under the strictest silence and penalty of death to reveal it to any other person outside their order; certainly the Obelisks could not contain the mere deeds of Kings. Therefore, in everyone's opinion, he would be a reckless, if not foolish, person who would consign the deeds and magnificent actions of some Prince or King to posterity—things which by their very nature seek the light, either to be imitated or to excite admiration and memory of virtues in descendants—through such symbols.

## CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Herodotus is refuted regarding the subject of Obelisks</margin>...if they were to hand down their propositions for preservation, they would use a certain impenetrable kind of writing. We can form a similar judgment about the Egyptians: if the obelisks contained only the praises and deeds of Kings, why would they be so obscured? Therefore, when Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, Pliny, and others say that the deeds of Kings were expressed in Egyptian monuments—and that expenses for various buildings and expeditions undertaken throughout the world, and even the costs of garlic and onions, are contained therein—they certainly do not mean the Obelisks. Instead, they were referring to the pyramids, or columns, or tablets and stones set into the walls of temples. For on columns and similar structures, they were accustomed to engrave noble deeds and histories in the common character used by the Egyptians, which we call <note>original: "Coptum"</note> Coptic <note>Kircher erroneously identifies the late Egyptian/Demotic script or Coptic language as the "vulgar" script used for history, distinguishing it from the "sacred" hieroglyphs on obelisks</note>; many such examples can be seen in Herodotus and Diodorus. In Obeliscis, however, they exhibited only ideal and intellectual matters, difficult to grasp, and hidden under the most obscure veils of figures, as will appear in the following pages. Since, therefore, Hermapion describes nothing in the said Obelisk but the praises and glory of King Ramestes <note>Ramesses II</note>, it immediately becomes clear from this very point that the interpretation cannot possibly correspond to the mind of the Egyptian Priests. But let us come to the figures.

<margin>The praises of King Ramestes cannot be contained in Hermapion's Obelisk.</note>

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A rectangular woodcut divided into three horizontal registers. The top register shows two human figures kneeling in ritual adoration. The middle register depicts three standing hawks (Accipitres) wearing crowns. The bottom register shows three bulls (Boues) in profile. Kircher uses this to show the repetitive, symbolic nature of the carvings.</note>

->Here you see, at the beginning of the Obelisk, human figures are placed, signifying the actions of those sacrificing by their position and gestures; since these correspond to the four parts of the World, each is seen to be provided with different things. Afterwards, on each side, three Hawks follow, conspicuous by their small crowns <note>original: "tutulis"</note>, as appears here in the figure (for it suffices to have placed the figures of one side here). These are followed by as many bulls, and then three extended arms; so that on each side three orders and series, or columns, are contained. Since these contain the mysteries and secrets of the twelve Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum Mundi"; Kircher interprets these repeating animals as celestial guardians or spirits</note> of the World indicated through the four sides of the Obelisk, let anyone who possesses even a tiny grain of judgment see how Hermapion's interpretation could be adapted to them. For since there are twelve Hawks and as many Bulls carved around the obelisk, which undoubtedly signify one and the same thing—differing only in their various effects—he [Hermapion] ought to have named the same thing twelve times. Since he did not do so, and indeed not even a trace of these things shines through his translation, his interpretation will rightly be judged false.<-

<margin>Another error in the interpretation.</margin>

It follows that since there are four sides on the Obelisk, but he [Hermapion] posits six <note>Hermapion's translation, as preserved by Ammianus Marcellinus, is divided into sections that Kircher finds difficult to map onto the physical four-sided monument</note>, it is impossible for the interpretation to agree with the facts. But if someone were to say that he described three orders contained on only one or two sides, the difficulty would still not be resolved, since even then the words would not cohere with the figures. And indeed, on the first side which looks toward the Southern region, he describes not three, but five orders; yet on the side looking toward the East, he describes only one order, as is evident in the context of the interpretation. I do not see how these can cohere. Therefore, the entire series of the interpretation is confused and <term>inconsistent <note>original: ἀσύστατος (asystatos), a Greek term meaning logically incoherent or having no standing</note></term>. Furthermore, the words of the interpretation...

<sig>Kk</sig>

...[interpre]tations attached to each row, they are so inconsistent with the style and character of hieroglyphs that it is apparent at first glance; it cannot be true, for it is so discordant and remote from the teachings of the Priests of the Sacred Mysteries <note>original: "Hieromystarum"</note>. For it is by no means possible to discover which figures show King Ramesses <term>Ramissem</term>, which show such glorious titles, or which show such a beautiful construction of words. For I do not see what Ramesses, Apollo, Vulcan, or the son of Heron <note>Hermapion's translation, preserved in the writings of Ammianus Marcellinus, identifies certain hieroglyphs as referring to these Greek/Egyptian deities and a specific lineage of kings</note> have in common with the rites of those sacrificing, or with Hawks, Oxen, and the rest. I would even dare to solemnly affirm that so much material concerning hidden matters is contained in each of the twelve rows of the Obelisk that it could not be explained sufficiently for its dignity in—I will not say a single page—but not even in an entire volume. All these things we have sufficiently and more than enough proven in the interpretation of this <term>Sennefertes</term> Obelisk <note>Kircher erroneously attributed the Flaminian Obelisk to a fictional King "Sennefertes," whom he believed was a contemporary of the biblical patriarchs</note>.

Thus, from this entire discourse, unless I am mistaken, it is clearly evident that the interpretation of Hermapion handed down by Ammianus Marcellinus cannot stand by any reasoning; which is what we had undertaken to prove. Whether Hermapion copied this description from some other Egyptian monument, which was later falsely attributed to this Obelisk, let whoever wishes believe; it was our task to demonstrate in these few words that this cited interpretation by Hermapion does not fit or adapt to the hieroglyphs of the Obelisk at all, so that if critics were to cast this interpretation against us, it would be known what should be decided concerning it. And from these things it is openly clear how cautiously one must proceed in explanations of such hidden matters, and that "it is not granted to everyone to visit Corinth" <note>A Latin proverb meaning that not everyone has the skill or fortune to achieve a difficult task</note>. Similar interpretations are found in the apocryphal Berosus of Annio da Viterbo <note>Annio da Viterbo was a 15th-century friar notorious for forging "ancient" texts to create a fictional history for Europe</note>; but since those were fabricated by the author himself, I consider them unworthy of wasting time and paper by citing them. Of this same sort is the interpretation of the discovered Etruscan letters by Volaterranus, which appeared not long ago.

Another "Egyptian Oedipus" <note>Referring to one who solves riddles, like the mythical Oedipus and the title of Kircher's own book</note> of later times was a certain eminent man, <term>Herwart</term> <note>Hans Georg Herwart von Hohenburg (1553–1622), a Bavarian scholar who proposed eccentric theories about ancient wisdom</note>, who, having attempted an interpretation of the <term>Bembine Table</term> <note>A famous bronze tablet, also called the Mensa Isiaca, covered in pseudo-Egyptian hieroglyphs; it was once owned by Cardinal Bembo and is now in Turin</note>, managed the business so unsuccessfully <margin>Herwart, another interpreter of the Bembine Table, misses the mark</margin> that I even greatly wonder what came into the mind of such a distinguished man, that he should have labored over an interpretation so discordant with the intention of the Egyptians. The title of his book is: *Wonderful Mysteries of Pagan Theology Disclosed*. In it, the author attempts to demonstrate with all his might that the lodestone <note>The natural magnet used in early compasses</note> was worshiped as a God by ancient nations everywhere, and that the art by which voyages were undertaken throughout the entire world with the help of the magnet was hidden with the greatest zeal by the ancient Egyptian Priests under the veils of Gods and Goddesses, and likewise under the bark of other myths. And first indeed he claims that through that hieroglyphic Bembine Table, most famous throughout the whole world, the ancient Egyptians intended nothing other than navigation across the entire globe, performed by the help of the magnetic compass and the aid of a nautical or hydrographic map; so much so that by the character-markings of that hieroglyphic table, they meant nothing <margin>The Bembine Table contains neither the mysteries of the magnet nor the art of navigation.</margin> other than the regions of the world and the winds; but in order to prove this,

CHAPTER IV. 256 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS. HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER.

<sig>SYN-</sig> <note>Catchword for the following section, likely "Syntagma IV"</note>

It is truly a wonder how, in the whole history of antiquity, he exhausts himself in twisting [the evidence] to suit his own purpose, and with what zeal and effort he labors to apply whatever he finds—whether they fit or not—to his own subject matter. I greatly marvel that a man otherwise wise, most skilled in antiquity, and of such extensive reading, could even conceive such things in his mind. Indeed, I do not assert these things because I wish to detract anything from a great man, most learned and well-deserving of the **Republic of Letters** <term>Rep. Literaria</term> <note>The "Republic of Letters" was the long-distance intellectual community of scholars and writers in the 17th century</note>; for in such a great man, his supreme effort in a matter of the utmost obscurity is to be praised. But I would wish these things said only so that the Reader may recognize how interpretations ought to be congruent with the mind of the Ancients, so that they might be able to withstand the polished ears and the keen senses <note>original: "emunctas Criticorum nares," literally "the wiped noses of the critics," a classical idiom for sharp-witted discernment</note> of the Critics.

# LEOPOLD IGNATIUS
### Archduke of Austria, Son of the Great Emperor Ferdinand III.

<note>Decorative initial O: A circular historiated initial featuring a landscape with a prominent tree under a cloudy sky, symbolizing growth and stability.</note>I raise this OBELISK to YOUR Imperial Serenity, a trophy worthy of the virtues blossoming at such a tender age; by which virtues, indeed, you so captivate almost the entire world that it promises to itself something great, sublime, and heroic from that innate joy of YOUR vivid character, from the mature wisdom in a young body, from the unusual strength of spirit, and from your dexterity in conducting affairs. And thus, to the wonder of all, you already begin to dictate themes to the world that are full of evidence of right governance—themes worthy of the talents of historians to exercise themselves in explaining when the time comes. Just as I have heard these things celebrated more than once with the highest admiration, so by some happy omen, I have judged that this monument, more lasting than cedar <note>original: "cedro perennius," an allusion to the Roman poet Horace, implying the work is immortal and incorruptible</note>, should be consecrated as a forerunner of YOUR glory, and at the same time a symbol of my most sincere respect for YOUR Imperial Serenity. Farewell, delight of the Imperial house and of the World.

CH. I.

# TREATISE IV.
## The Sallustian or Ludovisi Obelisk.

### CHAPTER I.
->**On the origin, erection, and transport of the Sallustian Obelisk.**<-

<margin>
The Sallustian Obelisk was brought to Rome by Gaius Caligula and erected by Claudius.
Ammianus Marcellinus.
</margin>

CLAUDIUS CAESAR, following the example of his predecessors, in order to adorn the City with a monument of new magnificence, decided that—besides the two plain <note>original: "rasos," literally "scraped," meaning without hieroglyphs</note> obelisks erected in the Mausoleum of Augustus—this present one also should be raised in the most delightful spot in the whole City. Ammianus Marcellinus suggests this in Book 17: *“And succeeding ages brought over others, of which one was erected in the Vatican, another in the Gardens of Sallust, and two in the monument of Augustus.”* <note>original Latin: "Secutæque ætates alios transtulerunt, quorum vnus in Vaticano, alter in Hortis Sallustij, duo in Augusti monimento erecti sunt."</note> But who its first erector in Egypt was, or from what place it was torn away, all the records of historians are silent. However, it is likely that it was transported to Rome together with the Vatican Obelisk by Gaius Caligula on a special ship of astounding size constructed for this sole purpose; and, after Gaius had met his fate, it was erected by his successor Claudius in the said place which they call the Gardens of Sallust, as is clearly evident from the cited Ammianus Marcellinus.

<margin>
The Ludovisi Obelisk in the Villa of Prince Ludovisi is the same as the Sallustian.
</margin>

Now it lies in the Villa of the most excellent Prince Nicolaus Ludovisi, Duke of Piombino, a place most remarkable for its charm and magnificence. It is almost buried in the earth and broken into two parts. Calling it the “Ludovisi Obelisk” after the owner of the place (and not inappropriately), we have judged it should be established as a kind of perennial monument of the favors bestowed upon our Society <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits)</note> by Pope Gregory XV, and a perpetual trophy to the honor of the Ludovisi family. Posterity, we hope, will in its time see and admire this illustrious monument of the City erected before the Ludovisi church consecrated to St. Ignatius.

<margin>
The symmetry of the Ludovisi or Sallustian Obelisk.
</margin>

The symmetry <note>In this context, "symmetry" refers to the proportional measurements and physical dimensions</note> of the Obelisk, being of a size between the larger and smaller ones, has a length from the base to the pyramidion <note>The small pyramid-shaped capstone of an obelisk</note> of 72 palms. Each side of the lower base has a width of six and a half palms; for it is square and <term>isopleuros <note>original Greek: ἰσόπλευρος, meaning equal-sided</note></term>. The pyramidion from the corners to the apex is four palms, as are each of the sides of the base of that same pyramidion where it is joined to the Obelisk; and thus the height of the whole Obelisk is exactly established at 76 palms.

# CHAPTER II.

->**The Subject Matter of the Obelisk.**<-

<margin>The subject matter of the Sallustian or Ludovisi Obelisk.</margin>
This present Obelisk (which was erected in honor of the fountain-like triad, or the three summits known as Osiris, Horus, and Isis-Momphta) contains a description of how these fountain-like summits flow into the triple World. It explains what effects they produce therein, and how, or by what sacrifices, they are to be worshipped so that these effects may be more easily obtained. To make these matters clearer, it seems appropriate to begin from a slightly deeper perspective.

<margin>Psellus. The fountain-like summits of the Egyptians.</margin>
Psellus, in his exposition of the *Oracles of Zoroaster* <note>Referring to the Chaldean Oracles, which Michael Psellus, a 11th-century Byzantine scholar, commented upon.</note>, relates that the Egyptians and Chaldeans worshipped three "fountain-like summits" from which all the goods of the World emanated as if from an eternal spring. He calls these three fountain-like summits those of Apollo, Osiris, and Hermes. *“They revere also the fountain Triad of faith, truth, and love, and the fountain summits of Apollo, Osiris, and Hermes.”* <note>original Greek: "Σέβουσι δὲ καὶ πηγαίαν Τριάδα πίστεως, καὶ ἀληθείας, καὶ ἔρωτος, καὶ πηγαίας ἀκρότητας Ἀπόλλωνος, Ὀσίριδος, καὶ Ἑρμοῦ."</note> They venerate the fountain triad of **Faith**, **Truth**, and **Love**; and the three fountain summits of Apollo (who is the same as Horus), Osiris, and Hermes. From the inscription on the Obelisk, we call these Horus, Osiris, and Isis-Momphta. The faces of the Obelisk contain this first triad. And just as the sacred mystery of this philosophy is hidden, so too did they adorn it with wonderful symbols. For they carved the mysteries of the highest things into obelisks—both this one and others—to indicate by the very shape of the Obelisk that the information displayed with such an unusual array of symbols was by no means trivial.

<margin>The Horæan Triad carved on the Sallustian Obelisk.</margin>
This, then, is the <term>Horæan Triad</term> <note>Kircher links the name of the god Horus to the "Horæ" (the Hours or Seasons), suggesting a divine influence over time and nature.</note> to which they saw fit to consecrate the Obelisk. It is a Triad transformed according to the Archetypal pattern; a Triad analogous to the triad of the Paternal Source, of which it is the minister, and from which it is distinguished only by the diversity of its effects. To this Triad is granted all power over the remaining choirs of triadic deities: the power of faith, truth, and love. It is a true Triad, such that faith beautifully suits Horus, truth suits Osiris, and love suits Isis-Momphta. Indeed, all the symbols contained on this Obelisk seem to refer to this triad, in which Horus provides for the "Worldly House" and each and every being with faithful care, as if they were entrusted to him; Osiris disposes all things in truth; and Isis-Momphta binds each and every thing together in a fellowship of love.

<margin>The fountain triad flows into the three Worlds.</margin>
You will see in this place how this fountain triad flows first into the <term>Genial World</term> <note>The Archetypal or Intellectual world of ideas.</note>, then from this into the <term>Sidereal World</term> <note>The Celestial world of stars and planets.</note>, and finally into the <term>Hylæic World</term> <note>The Material or physical world; from the Greek 'hyle', meaning matter.</note>, with the administrative duties distributed among the three summits. Here it will be revealed how they descend from the Worlds into the management of particular beings, according to the four quarters of the world indicated by the sides of the Obelisk, and what operations they perform in each. You will gaze, as if into a mirror, at how the Priests—through mystical symbols of this kind, through sacred tablets, and through rites and ceremonies performed in the inner shrines—appeased this Horæan triad, and once appeased, drew it down to obtain every kind of happiness. This is the subject matter of the present Obelisk; therefore, nothing remains but for us to demonstrate that this is the case through the following interpretation.

# CHAPTER III.

-> **The Division and Interpretation of the Sallustian Obelisk.** <-

<margin>The division of the Sallustian Obelisk.</margin> Note first that this Obelisk consists of four sides, each of which is divided into three columns or rows distinguished by hieroglyphic patterns. Thus, the entire Obelisk—whether you consider the inscription or <term>periochen</term> <note>From the Greek *perioche*, meaning a summary or an outline of the main points of a text.</note>, or the patterns of the sacred tablets—is so similar to the Flaminian Obelisk that it may rightly be called an abridgment of it. Only some slight differences occur in the smaller figures, which nevertheless do not introduce a great diversity of meanings, nor do they change the intention of the Priests so much that it could be called different in substance and essence from the things indicated, as will be clear to anyone comparing one with the other.

<margin>The Sallustian Obelisk is an abridgment of the Flaminian.</margin> The four sides of the Obelisk are marked with the letters **A**, **B**, **C**, and **D**. All the triangular sides of the pyramid at the top, if you except the first side **A**, are marked with exactly similar hieroglyphic writings expressing the aforementioned triad.

<margin>Hieroglyphics carved on the pyramid of the Sallustian Obelisk.</margin> In the first triangle of the Eastern side **A B C**, you see a statue sitting on a throne, with a headdress and a <term>Cucupomorpho</term> <note>Kircher's term for "hoopoe-shaped" (from the Latin *upupa* or *cucupa*), referring to the "Was" scepter often held by Egyptian deities, which he believed depicted the head of a hoopoe bird.</note> scepter. It has the head of Horus attached to its side, with a circle surrounded by two hooks. This is followed below by another figure <note>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφος</note> <gloss>hawk-shaped</gloss>, that is, distinguished by a hawk’s head, across from which is a <term>Sphinx</term> with a headdress, resting upon a pedestal. On the Southern side, in the first place, is the head of Horus, surrounded by two hooks with a circle placed above; then exactly the same figures as in the preceding side. On the remaining sides, **C F G** and **D H I** (the Northern and Western sides), the very same three figures that appear on the Southern side **B D E** present themselves.

<margin>Hieroglyphics carved on the sides of the Sallustian Obelisk.</margin> Below the triangle of the pyramid are placed four spaces **B C E F**, **D E G H**, **F G I K**, and **H I L M**, in which the hieroglyphic writings are exactly like one another. Specifically, there is an image sometimes <note>original Greek: ἱερακοπρόσωπον</note> <gloss>hawk-faced</gloss>, and sometimes <note>original Greek: γυπαικόμορφον</note> <gloss>vulture-shaped</gloss>, sitting upon a cube, with a kneeling image holding forth two statues. There is no difference between these images, and various marks are interspersed among them, as you can see.

These are followed in the immediate space on each side by three Hawks which press down upon Serpents with their feet, and three Bulls. On the first side, the Bulls are followed by three statues deformed with Hawk-like faces, with a bier placed under each. On the second side, after the Bulls, follow symbols intercepted between the letters **P** and **Q**. On the third side, the Bulls are followed by figures shaped in that posture which you see. Similarly, on the fourth side within space **T V**. Thus, on all sides, the very same figures exhibit themselves; we shall now attempt to explain this mystery so that it may be revealed.
