# CHAPTER IV.

*The interpretation of the hieroglyphic inscriptions contained on the four sides, which, according to the preceding division, are exactly the same, if some minor details are excepted.*

<margin>Explanation of the triangle on the Eastern side of the Sallustian Obelisk.</margin> Note, Reader, that although we have explained all these things in the section on the Flaminian Obelisk—which we have found to be entirely the same as this one, as will become clear shortly—nevertheless, because several things seem to differ here and there, it seemed appropriate to explain them in this place.

In the first triangle **A B C** of the Eastern side, in the first position, a figure appears seated upon a cubic throne, armed with a <term>Cucuphomorpho</term> <note>original: "Cucuphomorpho"; Kircher's term for a scepter topped with the head of a hoopoe (Cucupa), referring to the Egyptian *Was*-scepter.</note> scepter; at its side is the head of Horus marked with a circle and flanked by two hooks, and before it, it displays a <term>hieralpha</term> <note>A term coined by Kircher for a symbol shaped like the letter Alpha, which he believed represented the first principle or "sacred A."</note>. This, within the triad of Horus, signifies the Father distinguished by power. From here, sitting with a commanding right hand, he rules; by the <term>Cucuphomorpho</term> scepter, he hints at the variety of things over which he holds dominion. He conducts all things with unshakable sovereignty, as the seat full of majesty teaches; he is truly the great <term>Agathodæmon</term> <note>A Greek term meaning "Good Spirit," often associated by Kircher with a benevolent divine intellect.</note>, as the hieralpha demonstrates. He has the head of Horus placed nearby, flanked by a hook and a curved staff, because he is the Horean Intellect, the averter of all evils. His Power is represented by a Hawk-like figure, likewise sitting on a cubic seat and armed with a hooked scepter; this is the Power of the divine Osiris-Horus, reaching all things through his own penetrating virtue and governing all with unshakable dominion.

Opposite him, he has a <term>Sphinx</term> reclining upon a pedestal, which is <term>Isis Momphtæa</term> <note>Kircher's specific name for the "Mundan Mind" or the feminine aspect of the divine hierarchy.</note>, the Horean Mind, the executrix of all things that are within the intellect and power of Osiris and Horus. She is composed of a human head with a headdress and the body of a Lion, by which strength and fortitude in executing the commands of Horus and Osiris are especially denoted, as we taught in the section on the Flaminian Obelisk, which you may consult.

<margin>Plutarch: Isis Momphtæa, mistress of the three Worlds.</margin> For as Plutarch rightly teaches, this <term>Isis Momphtæa</term> is nothing other than that feminine force of nature, the receiver of all generation, whence she was called <note>original Greek: "τιθήνη"</note> the "nurse" and <note>original Greek: "πανδεχής"</note> "all-receiver." For she admits all ideas and images; she has an innate love toward that which is first and highest among all things—namely, the Good itself. Toward this she is drawn, this she desires, and this she follows; but that which is evil, she flees and opposes. Hence, she is appropriately called the mistress of the three Worlds, just as the symbols placed above teach: <note>Hieroglyphic symbols: a triangle $\triangle$, a semicircle with three dots, and the Coptic-style characters $\Pi\Omega C$</note> and <note>Hieroglyphic symbol: the characters $\Pi\Pi C$</note>.

Here the Reader should notice <margin>What the Coptic words $\Pi\Omega C$ and $\Pi\Pi C$ mean.</margin> that these symbols **POS** <note>$\Pi\Omega C$</note> and **PPS** <note>$\Pi\Pi C$</note> placed in the space **A B C** are Coptic words and signify "dominion," indicating that she exercises her power most especially in the Sun and the Moon. The word is of the feminine gender, just as **PPS** is of the masculine. But since we have explained these words extensively in various places, we refer the Reader there. See concerning these in the *Astrologia*, folio 192.

<margin>What the Horean Triad is, and why it is so called.</margin> And this is the Horean Triad, consisting of Father, Power, and Mind. It is called "Horean" because Horus is primarily occupied in the intelligible World concerning the administration of the Worldly house; it is a "Triad" because, marked with the seal of the triform supreme Divinity, it carries out its administration just as—

He uses Coptic linguistic theories to explain hieroglyphs as symbols of divine dominion over the celestial bodies.</summary>

# CHAPTER IV

Zoroaster.

...and it performs just as the other choirs of the Triadic Divinity do. <gloss>For in the whole world a Triad shines, of which a Monad is the principle <note>original Greek: "Παντὶ γὰρ ἐν κόσμῳ λάμπει Τριὰς, ἧς μονὰς ἀρχὴ"</note></gloss>; for in the entire world the triad shines, whose unity is the beginning, as Zoroaster wisely teaches.

<margin>
What the Horean head of the Sallustian Obelisk denotes. Explanation of the remaining triangles of the Sallustian Obelisk.
</margin>

->In the remaining sides, however, there always appears in the first position a head distinguished by a circle and flanked by two hooks. In this same way, they denote the Father of the Horean <note>Referring to the god Horus.</note> Triad, the driver-away of all evils. It is marked with a circle to suggest his divinity. It is fashioned with a child’s head because the World, as Plutarch says, daily rejuvenates itself, as if with a new offspring of things capable of being generated. It is expressed by a head alone because the Horean intellect knows the entire sensible World—which it represents in a physical sense—and provides for the things it has known; it is the protector against all evils threatening from any side, as the two hooks by which it is flanked (symbols of warding off evil) clearly teach.<-

<margin>
Why Horus is expressed in a youthful form.
</margin>

Wherever, therefore, a child’s head is seen protected by a circle, it must be considered to belong to Horus. I said "child’s," because hardly any statue of Horus is found that does not display something youthful, yet adorned with different symbols according to the diversity of effects he works in the World through the rejuvenating generations of things. For sometimes they fashion him with a reticulated garment ending in a whirlwind; sometimes in a child’s form held in the arms and bosoms of Priests as if at the breasts, whom they nourished with milk and gruel (since these things have been reviewed elsewhere, I did not wish to be longer here). They certainly formed him with strange rituals of superstition and worship by the Priests, and this for the reason that unless the World grew up daily with a new birth of generation, it would necessarily perish. Hence he is recorded as having been nourished in the marshes of Buto <note>A city in the Nile Delta famous for a shrine to Leto/Wadjet; in myth, Horus was hidden there by Isis.</note>, because moisture released through vapors raised on high is necessary for the World. But since moisture without heat is useless, it is therefore the part of the Horean power to temper the moist-heat in the World, as that in which the genesis of all things consists. This Power is aptly represented by the Hawk-statue sitting upon a cubic seat, which we explained a little earlier and often elsewhere. The Horean Sphinx, however, exhibits Isis-Momphtaea, as we said above, the executrix of the Father’s concepts and of the Power: hence, in her Leonine crouching, she wonderfully strengthens, cherishes, and animates the heat and moisture—with the Sun passing through Leo and Virgo and the Nile flooding—toward a copious bringing forth of offspring. And hence Isis is called Momphtaea because, insofar as she presides over the moist-heat, she is the wife or the passive principle receiving into herself the seeds of things to be generated, belonging to Momphta <note>Kircher's term for a creative Egyptian deity often identified with Hephaestus or Ptah.</note>, who is for the most part confused with the Nilotic Osiris, whose dominion is most vigorous at this time.

<margin>
Isis Momphtaea.
</margin>

But why is this Horean triad placed in the triangle of the pyramid's side? Because this Horean triad is one of the three triads of which the "paternal depth" <note>A term from the Chaldean Oracles referring to the source of divine emanation.</note> is composed, standing immediately under the influence of the supreme triform Deity; concerning this, see the copious treatise in the exposition of the Isiac Table, page 94.

<margin>
The hieroglyphs on the four sides of the Sallustian Obelisk are the same. Explanation of the first side.
</margin>

Furthermore, having explained the first section and title of the Obelisk, let us now proceed in order to the remaining <term>hierogrammatisms</term> <note>literally "sacred writings" or hieroglyphic inscriptions.</note>, which, since they are entirely the same on the four faces of the Obelisk, it shall suffice to have explained one of them.

In the space **BCEF**, therefore, an image occurs, transformed with a Hawk’s face, sitting upon a cubic throne, protected by a hooked staff, and in the left hand something...

# SYNTAGMA IV. SALLUSTIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER IV.

...he seems to command something; in whose region a genuflecting [kneeling] statue with bovine horns presents two hawk-shaped statues to the Deity; by these, the <term>Genial World</term> <note>Kircher uses this term to describe the "World of Genii" or spirits, which in his Neoplatonic system sits between the divine and the material worlds.</note> is indicated, into which the triad of Horus flows immediately.

And through these figures, the Intellectual, Genial, or Angelic World is aptly suggested, in which there are Leaders or Choreographers of individual orders, to whom the remaining lower orders are joined. In this way, figure E is placed below figure F, which it confirms sufficiently by its genuflection, humbly requesting his commands. And indeed, the image—holding a hooked scepter in its right hand, naked and sitting upon a square seat—indicates the supreme Prince of the Genial Choir, pre-eminent in virtue and power, surveying all things with hawk-like eyes, and formidable against Typhonian evils <note>Typhon was the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, representing chaos and destruction.</note> with his protective scepter; with his left hand, he seems to command his subjects somewhat. Undergoing his divine and most powerful force, the Genius E, his subordinate, humbly requests commands; he presents two <term>Canopuli</term> <note>Commonly known as Canopic jars. While these held organs in burials, Kircher interprets them here as symbolic vessels representing the element of water or "moist substance."</note>—which were oblong, swollen vessels fashioned in the form of a child wrapped in swaddling clothes—to his protector who prevails with fiery power. He does this with the intention that the leader, by his life-giving heat, may grant the power of animation to the moist substance indicated by the vessels, and continue by his influence what was begun by Genius E regarding the matters committed to him. This was a certain model of things to be performed by the Priests in the inner sanctuaries. The method of operation is found expressed at the bottom of the sides, as will be seen later.

And figures of this kind are the same on each side, if you except the smaller characters; for these were added out of a certain indiscriminate piety, either for ornament or to facilitate the attraction of the Gods.

<margin>The remaining figures of the same first side are explained.</margin> Now follow, in the space E F N O, three Hawks, three Bulls, and three statues in a sitting posture, each with a <term>Tautic</term> <note>Referring to the "Tau" or Ankh symbol, which Kircher associates with the god Thoth (Taut).</note> character in their hands; on each side there are three, which make 12. And indeed, by the three Hawks, the twelve-fold number of the great citadel of Solar Genii is expressed. As they survey all the regions of the twelve-fold divided World indicated through the four sides of the Obelisk (each of which contains three Hawks, and joined together they constitute the number twelve), they animate all things by their influence and incite them to fertility. <margin>Twelve Bulls of the Sallustian Obelisk.</margin> There follow three Bulls on each side, by which the twelve-fold number of the material <note>original: "hylæorum," from the Greek word for matter, *hyle*.</note> Solar Deities, administrators of the Elemental World, is expressed, analogous to the celestial twelve. For as I remember having said elsewhere, <term>Apis</term> or <term>Serapis</term> was visible in a bovine form, like a certain Solar Deity of the lower World, the **material Osiris** <note>original: "Osiris hylæus"</note>, who—participating in the influence from the celestial Osiris—administered all lower things with fiery vigor according to the regions of the twelve-fold divided World; hence all his followers were expressed in the figure of a Bull. See the more extensive treatment of this in the Flaminian Obelisk and the other following Obelisks.

But the three hawk-like statues belong to the tutelary <term>Agathodæmons</term> <note>From the Greek for "Good Spirits."</note>, whom the ceremonious industry of the Priests busied itself to place for the sake of warding off evil and propitiating the aforementioned Deities of a higher order, and to honor them with the exquisite cult which the litters [shrines] demonstrate.

In the second side B, after the three Bulls, different symbols are seen, wh-

On the third side in space R S, various symbols are placed, the meaning of which is: *The presiding ruler and master of the Moist Element, providing life to all and an abundance of necessary things through his beneficence; he is drawn in through the statue of the <term>Agathodaemons</term> <note>From the Greek "agathos" (good) and "daimon" (spirit); these were protective, benevolent spirits in the Greco-Egyptian tradition.</note>, who act as his ministers.*

<margin>
Interpretation of the fourth side.
</margin>

On the fourth side in space T V, four hawk-like statues marked with <term>Tautic characters</term> <note>Symbols associated with Thoth (Hermes), often appearing as cross-like or looped figures.</note> are placed; these are images of Agathodaemons or beneficent Genii, as their extended arms denote; they were thought to have great power for attracting the aforementioned Deities.

You see, therefore, how from the symbols unraveled just a moment ago, the <term>Triad of Horus</term>—which is closest to the paternal source <note>In Kircher’s Neoplatonic view, the "paternal source" is the ultimate divine mind from which all things flow.</note> and acts as its administrator—flows according to the archetypal plan: first into the assemblies of the <term>Genial World</term>, then from these into the Solar Deities of the <term>Sidereal World</term> [the stars], and through these into the lower Agathodaemons of the <term>Hylean World</term> <note>From the Greek "hyle" (matter); this refers to the physical, material world.</note>, following a specific chained order. Since this is the case, it now remains to be seen how these same Deities flow into particular levels of being, what they perform, and by what rites and sacrifices they are attracted; we shall demonstrate this as briefly as possible through twelve paragraphs, corresponding to the series of twelve columns.

# TREATISE IV. THE SALLUSTIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER IV.

## Ll 2 § II.

The following sacred table B serves for propitiation. It contains the figure of Horus enclosed in an oval shape with a feather on his head; beneath his feet is the figure of a <term>Nilometer</term> <note>A device used by the ancient Egyptians to measure the water level of the Nile during the annual flood; Kircher interprets it here as a symbol of the "moist substance" or life-giving water of the world.</note>. This figure, as we have said elsewhere, indicates the World, of which Horus is the "Mind," according to the testimony of Plutarch. This Mind seems to be held within this form primarily so that it may distribute a sufficient supply of moisture to the individual members of the World; this is aptly signified by the Nilometer upon which he sits, a symbol of the Mundane liquor. This was a solemn <term>prophylactic</term> <note>original: "prophylacticum"; here meaning a protective amulet or talismanic image used by priests.</note> for the priests dedicated to Horus, just as the following one is suited for drawing in Osiris, the interpretation of which you may see above on page 220, where you will find everything most amply explained.

Next, in region C, follows a Serpent with the "cloister of the Hawk," <margin>The Hawk was worshipped at Heliopolis.</margin> which is called the "cage of life." To understand this, one must know that the Egyptians at Heliopolis, in the portico of the temple, worshipped Hawks as sacred to Osiris according to a secret religious ordinance. By this, they showed that life is by no means granted by Osiris unless he is first, as it were, conquered and bound by the services and religious rites of sacrifices and ceremonies. Indeed, by this act of religion, the <term>Typhonian Owl</term> <note>The "Typhonia Bubo," representing the destructive forces of Typhon (Set), which Kircher believes are cast out by these rites.</note> was driven away from the twelve houses of the great citadel. Once this was done, <term>Chenosiris</term> <note>original: "Chenosiris", interpreted by Kircher as "Anserine Osiris" or the "Goose-Osiris."</note>, that is, the Goose-Osiris, conferred life upon the three lower worlds by the help of the triple world of intelligences, just as the symbols included between C and D indicate. The same was also drawn through the following protective symbols of the sacred table, the first of which, E, contains the <term>Mendesio-Momphtaeum</term> <note>A complex term used by Kircher to describe a specific combination of divine influences (Mendes and Momphta).</note>; it has a gnomon with a globe, a <term>Crux ansata</term> <note>The "handled cross" or Ankh, the Egyptian symbol of life.</note> with the letter M, and then the usual Hawk-statues with the head of an Ox below. Directly opposite is a vial placed upon a Nilometer. These symbols express this meaning: *The symmetry of the World is derived from the influence of Momphta and Osiris into the sacred humor and the substance of the Mundane liquor, communicated to the terrestrial Osiris.* Furthermore, the protective symbol of the sacred table marked with the letter F has already been explained more extensively a little earlier in the cited place; there it should be noted that the Goose with the Serpent, which it holds in its beak, signifies the same thing as the guardian of Mundane life.

Now follow, in region G, various small symbols together with three protective or sacred tables. Since we have explained these throughout the preceding sections, the reader will easily be able to explain them by his own effort. What the smaller images at the base of the Obelisk signify will be explained later.

Note, Reader, that all the symbols shown in this column from C to the end are exactly the same as the symbols in the first column of the second side of the <term>Flaminian Obelisk</term> <note>This refers to the obelisk now located in the Piazza del Popolo in Rome, which Kircher used as a primary reference for "translating" other obelisks.</note>, which begin in that same place from the letter Y to the end.

# HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

### § II.
->*Exposition of the second column of the first side.*<-

<margin>Second column of the first side.</margin>The influence of the twelve-fold Deities mentioned shortly before is first poured into the <term>Pantamorphus</term> <note>Literally "the all-formed one," a name Kircher uses for a cosmic deity or force that provides all the various necessities of life.</note>, the bestower of all necessary things. This is indicated at the top of the second column by a fly <note>A small hieroglyphic insect symbol</note> together with a papyrus staff, as we have shown in countless places, and it is drawn in by the two following <term>prophylactics</term> <note>original: "prophylacticis"; protective or talismanic sacred tables used to attract divine power.</note> of the sacred tablets. Since these have already been explained on page 220, there is no need to repeat it here. Through the religious cult of these prophylactics, the providence of the said Deities, and the beneficial help of <term>Chenosiris</term> <note>A Kircherian compound name for Osiris, often associated with the generative power of the Nile.</note>, the gates of the mundane house are opened by the influx of the Hawk-headed statues. The following sacred propitiatory table at region B represents this: namely, Horus the child, that is, the Mind of the Sensible World, in an oval figure—that is, enclosed within the World. All these things are hinted at by the symbols included between the letters Y, Z, A, and B. For by these, the sacredly moved <term>Chenosiris</term> takes up the care of the three Worlds; he drives away the Typhonian owl <note>A symbol of darkness or the destructive god Typhon/Set.</note> by these same rites of sacred ceremonies; the chains of the Typhonian powers are shaken off; and the gate of the great house of the Sun and Moon is opened. The scepters of the Gods are erected, the chain of life and the providence of Osiris are carried down through a hidden channel into the lower kingdom of Horus. To propitiate this, the following <term>prophylactic</term> is established; it is a <term>Chenosiric</term> figure, in which are contained a <term>hieralpha</term> <note>A sacred symbol resembling the letter 'A', often interpreted by Kircher as a sign of the first cause or beginning.</note> with a chain, two feathers, Horus the child with the character of Thoth, and a <term>hydroschemate</term> <note>A symbolic representation of water or fluid.</note>. Their meaning is: *May the chain of the Good Spirits flow into the moist kingdom of the Elixir.* <note>original: "Agathodæmonum catena humidum Elixi regnum influat." The 'Agathodæmon' is a protective "Good Spirit" or serpent deity.</note> To this end, the legions of the <term>Chenosiric</term> Deities of the earth also contribute their effort. All these things are signified by the symbols enclosed between B, C, D, E, F, and G. <margin>Column 2 of side 1 of the Sallustian Obelisk is the same as column 2 of side 2 of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> Note, Reader, that where three Geese are placed in this location, three Ibises are placed in the same spot on the Flaminian Obelisk. This column is exactly the same (with a few exceptions which, however, change nothing in the meaning of the things described) as the second column of the second side of the Flaminian Obelisk.

### SYNTAGMA III. THE SALLUSTIAN OBELISK. CHAPTER IV.

The other section, marked B, with **Chenosiris** <note>A name used by Kircher for Osiris, representing the generative power of the Nile.</note> placed above, contains the head of **Horus**, a hawk-like statue with a **Tau Cross** <note>original: "Cruce Tauca"; refers to the Ankh symbol, which Kircher interprets as a T-shaped cross representing the four elements or life.</note>. Below these is a curved scepter with an inverted triple branch; the meaning of these is: *The influx of Horus into the Sun, the ruler of the year, confers abundance in that year; the providence of the Divinity governs the <term>dodecapyrgon</term> <note>original Greek: "twelve-towered"; referring to the twelve stages of the sun's path or the zodiac.</note> with such industry that both the higher and lower worlds are imbued with life and the beneficence of the Divinities through this twelve-fold system.* To summon these influences, the following two amulets, already explained above, are effective. All these things are indicated by the symbols contained in the letters B, C, D, E, and F. The remaining smaller symbols are likewise signs established for procuring the protection of the Divinities.

<margin>This column is extracted from the third column of the second side of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin>
The reader should note, however, that this column is extracted from the third column of the second side of the Flaminian Obelisk.

But in this place, let us explain the larger figures positioned at the base of the Obelisk; these are exactly the same as those contained within the upper spaces of this Obelisk (B C E F, D E G H, F G I K, H I L M). The only difference is that the <term>hierakomorphos</term> <gloss>hawk-shaped</gloss> figure, which sits in those designated spaces, stands here, carrying a handled tripod in its left hand; in all other respects, there is no difference at all. <margin>The method by which the Egyptians instituted sacrifices.</margin> In order to explain this mystery, note that the Egyptian Priests instituted all their sacrifices in their inner sanctuaries according to the pattern of archetypal reasons, or supramundane Powers. They believed these rituals would be more effective the more they were exhibited <term>analogikotera</term> <gloss>more proportionally</gloss>—that is, more similar to the true exemplars—through that mystical apparatus of symbols. Therefore, to more effectively draw down those chains of Ideal Minds, they were accustomed to adorn their actions in their sanctuaries, at the hour and time most opportune to the Gods, with a dress that was as similar as possible to the symbolic dress of the Divinities. Hence, semi-naked, covered with a Hawk-mask, and equipped with scepters and staffs, carrying in their hand the handled tripod <note>Kircher's term for the Ankh, which he views as a "tripod" symbolizing the triple-power of the deity.</note> that indicates the influx of the tri-formed Divinity, they exhibited the mystical <term>mania</term> <note>original: "mania"; in this context, the ritual performances or "sacred frenzies" meant to mimic the gods.</note> of the Gods. Around them, other ministers representing the Genii <note>protective spirits or minor deities</note> of a lower order would prostrate themselves, likewise naked and on their knees, offering vessels similar to <term>little star-deities</term> <note>original: "Deastrunculis"; small idols or representations of minor gods.</note>. They persuaded themselves that nothing could be more effective for drawing down the Divinities than these ceremonies and masked representations. But since we have described all these things at length in our treatment of the Flaminian Obelisk, we refer the reader there.

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the Sallustian and Flaminian obelisks. ### SYNTAGMA IV. SALLUSTIAN OBELISK. 269 CHAPTER IV.

### First Corollary.

<margin>The Sallustian and Flaminian obelisks are derived from one another.</margin> From what has been said, it is clear that of these two Obelisks, the Sallustian and the Flaminian, one was extracted from the other as if from a certain prototype. Which of them is truly the older cannot be easily determined; however, it seems more likely that this one <note>The Sallustian Obelisk, which stands today at the top of the Spanish Steps.</note> was taken from that one <note>The Flaminian Obelisk, now in the Piazza del Popolo.</note>, as I also suggested above. The Flaminian Obelisk displays the great skill of the sculptor in genuinely expressing the images; <margin>Difference between the Sallustian and Flaminian Obelisks.</margin> this present one, however, did not receive such a skilled hand from its sculptor, for he sometimes transforms certain figures so much that they seem foreign to the truth. Conversely, in the Flaminian Obelisk, some marks are seen to be omitted, such as the head of Horus with two hooks in the triangles of the <term>pyramidion</term> <note>The small pyramid at the top of an obelisk.</note>; whether these were omitted by design, or whether the armature of the coat of arms of Sixtus V <note>Pope Sixtus V (reigned 1585–1590) recovered and re-erected many obelisks in Rome, often topping them with his heraldic symbols (mountains and a star).</note> covered them, I do not know. Furthermore, in the figure of the sacred table which holds the final place on the first three sides of the Flaminian Obelisk, the figure of the boy <note>original: "pueri figura," referring to Harpocrates or the infant Horus.</note> after the two feathers of Horus—which in the corresponding places on the Sallustian Obelisk is inserted as if into a certain cave—is omitted in the Flaminian Obelisk. But what has been omitted or added in either Obelisk, the curious reader will be able to recognize better and more easily through a diligent comparison of the said Obelisks with one another than I could demonstrate even with many and superfluous words; hence, it should suffice for us to have indicated that these two reviewed Obelisks contain one and the same argument.

### Second Corollary.

<margin>The hieroglyphs of the obelisks contain the Theology of the Egyptians.</margin> Since similar chains of symbols are found on almost all Obelisks, it is certain that the subject matter of all of them regards Egyptian Theology. From this it follows necessarily that the Obelisks by no means contain histories, deeds, and the praises of Kings—as many have persuaded themselves until now—but most are symbols of the divinity lurking everywhere, and marks of the concatenation of <term>Genii</term> <note>In Kircher’s system, these are intermediary spirits or divine forces linking the celestial and terrestrial worlds.</note>, displayed according to the multiple series of the Worlds. Thus, it is no wonder that no one until now has dared to attempt an exposition of the hieroglyphs; for which thing I find no other reason than that no one has rightly compared the Obelisks (as well as other Egyptian monuments) with one another, nor studiously combined figure with figure. If others had done as we have, perhaps that more secret literature would have long ago become known to the world; since from the identity of the figures shining forth on almost all the Obelisks—and the arrangement of the images, their position, properties, and the distinctive character <note>original: "idiotismo"</note> of the other figures—it would not have been so difficult to arrive at a perfect knowledge of the meaning of them all. And thus would have long ago ceased that controversy, so greatly torturing the wits of Historians, concerning the true meaning of hieroglyphic literature, while most, following Herodotus, Diodorus, and Pliny, have been of the opinion that the Obelisks contain nothing but the historical commemorations of ancient Kings; which, however...

# TREATISE V.
## THE OBELISK FORMERLY CALLED VERANO, NOW THE BARBERINI.

<note>Decorative woodcut ornament: A central mask-like face flanked by symmetrical acanthus-style scrolls and floral motifs.</note>

->TO THE MOST EMINENT PRINCE<-

# FRANCESCO
->**Cardinal Barberini, Vice-Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church.**<-
<note>original: "S. R. E. Vicecancellario." S.R.E. stands for "Sanctae Romanae Ecclesiae."</note>

<note>Decorative initial 'P': A large woodcut drop cap featuring an eagle or large bird perched within ornate foliage and scrolling vines.</note>

At last, Most Eminent Prince, your very own Obelisk comes forth, most desired now for the course of several decades. It is yours, every bit of it. For you were the first, from time immemorial, to discover it buried in the earth in the Verano field <note>The Ager Veranus, an area in Rome near the Basilica of Saint Lawrence; the obelisk was found there in the circus of Varianus.</note>; you purchased it and brought it into the light. And lest its mystical carvings remain buried in darkness even now that it has been exposed to the light, for this one reason you summoned me from France to the City [Rome] in the year 1635 to be its future interpreter. Just as it seemed right to present the first specimen of interpretation to you in this monument, so it was the first cause, occasion, and origin for the subsequent explanation of the Obelisks, and indeed for this entire present work. Lest I yield to the labors of the arduous task imposed upon me, you encouraged me with your continuous benevolence; you soon dispatched the *Coptic Forerunner* <term>Prodromus Coptus</term> <note>Kircher's 1636 work, "Prodromus coptus sive aegyptiacus," which was the first Coptic grammar published in Europe.</note> to the literary world at your own expense; and lest a work of such great daring suffer delay through a lack of necessary resources, you wished the Vatican Library, and your own—most celebrated for its abundance of hidden Codices and monuments—to be always open, and you unlocked access to your own museums, filled with every kind of antiquity. Thus, I feel myself most deeply indebted by such a heap of benefits. May this Barberini Obelisk therefore redound to the eternal honor of your Name, and like a trophy of your great mind, may it triumph in the literary world for years that will never perish.
**Farewell.**

# TREATISE V.

## The Verano, or Barberini, Obelisk.

### CHAPTER I.

#### A Historical Account of the Barberini Obelisk.

<margin>
The Barberini Obelisk found in the Verano field.
</margin>
When Cardinal Francesco Barberini understood, through certain conjectures of Roman antiquarians, that a noble obelisk lay hidden somewhere in the Verano field <note>The *Ager Veranus* is an area in Rome, now famous as the site of the Cimitero del Verano near the Basilica of Saint Lawrence.</note>, he "moved every stone" <note>An idiom meaning he spared no effort or resource.</note> with a truly praiseworthy effort so that it might be found and uncovered. This was accomplished in the year 1633. Indeed, in a certain vineyard owned by Curtius Saccoccia—in the exact location where the Circus of the Emperor Aurelian <note>Ancient Roman sources often confused the circuses of Rome; this obelisk actually stood in the Circus of Varianus, which Kircher identifies here as the Circus of Aurelian.</note> was once seen, and where even now no small remains of it can be discerned among the ruins—it was detected and dug up. After a significant sum of money was paid to its owner, it was brought to the courtyard of the Quirinal Palace, which they call the Barberini [Palace], where it remains even today, broken into three fragments.

<margin>
The Author is summoned to Rome to interpret the Barberini Obelisk.
</margin>
Meanwhile, the aforementioned Cardinal was informed by Nicolas Peiresc <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a celebrated French scholar and patron who was one of the first to attempt a systematic study of hieroglyphics.</note>, a man of immortal memory, regarding the project I was undertaking for the new restoration of hieroglyphics. He immediately urged our Reverend Father General Mutio Vitelleschi of the Society of Jesus to call me from France to Rome shortly, relying on the hope that once a specimen of interpretation was provided for this newly discovered obelisk, he might promise himself something certain about explaining the rest with equal boldness; and so it was done. As soon as I arrived, he handed over the obelisk, which had been drawn with the greatest diligence, to me, the newly arrived interpreter, to be explained. But since I saw that my credibility might falter in the demonstration of such an unknown science without preliminary foundations,

<margin>
The occasion for preparing the Egyptian Oedipus.
</margin>
I decided that after the <term>Coptic Forerunner</term> <note>Kircher's *Prodromus Coptus* (1636), which argued that Coptic was the descendant of the ancient Egyptian language.</note> and the restoration of the Pharaonic idiom or Coptic language, the *Oedipus* must finally be prepared. In this work, I strove to establish those things which seemed in any way to pertain to the attempt of such an unusual work, unearthed from every kind of Oriental tradition. I did this so that at last, this "offspring," wrenched from many years of midnight labors, might see the light with that equipment of facts which an arduous, difficult, and unattempted work demanded as if by its own right; which was done with God giving and guiding. I thought these things should be detailed more extensively so that posterity might know that there was no other origin or occasion for this work than this present obelisk (which we have therefore not inappropriately called the "Barberini"), and might accordingly give thanks to him to whom it is inscribed, as its first promoter. But now receive these few things, according to our conjecture, concerning the first builder of this obelisk in Egypt.

## CHAPTER II.

### On the Builders of this Obelisk.

<margin>
The builders of the Barberini Obelisk: Sothis and Rameses.
</margin>

Although no ancient writer has made specific mention of this obelisk, it is nevertheless probable that it is one of those eight obelisks which Pliny reports were erected in the City of the Sun <note>The "City of the Sun" refers to Heliopolis, a major religious center in ancient Egypt dedicated to the sun god Ra.</note> by Sothis and his son Rameses. Pliny’s words in Book 36, Chapter 8 are as follows: <note>original: "Postea & alij Regum in supradicta Urbe, Sothis quatuor numero quadragenûm octonûm cubitorum longitudine; Ramesses verò, quo regnante Ilium captum est, 40 cubitorum, alios scilicet quatuor erexit."</note> *“Afterwards, other Kings in the aforementioned city [erected obelisks]: Sothis, four in number, forty-eight cubits in length; and Rameses—in whose reign Troy was captured—erected four others of forty cubits.”* We have shown in our work on the Pamphilian Obelisk (page 58) that eight were erected during the joint administration of the kingdom by both rulers, and that of these, four were brought to Rome by various Emperors. These include: the one in the Campus Martius, intended by Augustus for the marking of hours <note>This refers to the Obelisk of Montecitorio, used as a gnomon for a massive sundial.</note>; the Sallustian, which Ammianus Marcellinus testifies was brought by Claudius; the Pamphilian, by Caracalla; and this Barberini one, brought by Aurelian. The remaining four stay in Egypt even now. We are led to the conjecture that this is one of those four brought to Rome because the builders of the other obelisks are known to us from historians, whereas no mention of this one appears in their records. Thus, it is highly likely that this is the smallest of the four listed, which the Emperor Aurelian—following the examples of his predecessors—brought to his Circus <note>Kircher identifies this as the "Circus Veranus" or Circus of Aurelian; modern archaeology identifies it as the Circus of Varianus.</note> when no other was available. For as we showed in the passage cited, since in ancient times no Circus was without an obelisk—the Circus representing the form of the World, and the obelisk within it representing the Sun or the "Soul of the World"—it seems likely that Aurelian brought this one (the largest among the surviving obelisks in the city not yet erected) to his Circus so that the Verano Circus would not lack this mystical symbol. But regarding these matters, as I said, see the cited passage on the Pamphilian Obelisk.

<margin>
The Barberini Obelisk appears to have been erected in the Verano Circus by Aurelian.
</margin>

<margin>
The size of the Barberini Obelisk.
</margin>

Among the obelisks of the middle rank, this one is the smallest; it reaches a length of 66 palms <note>A "palm" was a common unit of measure in Rome; 66 palms is roughly 16 meters or 52 feet.</note> and a width of 5 palms at the base. It has been variously damaged in many places by the ravages of time, as is evident from its cast. Where the figures are intact, they are carved so vividly to the life that it might seem to have been engraved in our own times.

## CHAPTER III.

### The Subject Matter of the Barberini Obelisk.

<margin>
The subject matter of the Barberini Obelisk.
</margin>

<margin>
Why the Author calls it the "Barberini" Obelisk.
</margin>

Just as we name each of the obelisks brought from Egypt to the city of Rome after the places where they were later erected or where they still lie broken—such as the "Flaminian" from the gate and Via Flaminia, and the "Lateran" from the church over which it looms—so too it is fitting to call this obelisk the BARBERINI, which we present here for viewing adjacent to the Palace of the most Eminent Barberini family. It is an obelisk admirable for the all-encompassing variety of its figures,

# CHAPTER III. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...surpassing all others, it is especially mysterious and filled with a deeply hidden literature of symbols.

<margin>To which Deities it is dedicated.</margin> This obelisk was erected by the ancient Egyptian Priests and <term>Sacred Seers</term> <note>original: "Hieromantis"</note> to the Supreme Deity—whom Hermes Trismegistus and Plato call the <term>all-formed one</term> <note>original: "παντόμορφον" (pantomorphon)</note>, others call Osiris or the Egyptian Mithras, and others call the Soul of the World, invoking him by various <term>synonymous</term> <note>original: "ἰσοψήφους" (isopsēphous), literally "equal-voted" or having the same numerical value</note> names—and to the 48 Spirits of the World who serve as ministers to said Deity and as guardians, so to speak, of the Universe. To understand this:

<margin>48 Stations of the Gods noted in the Heavens by the Egyptians. Aratus. Hyginus. Plutarch. The Southern and Northern side of the World.</margin> Note that the Egyptians observed 48 stations of the Gods in the Heavens, which the Greeks, following them, later called <term>constellations</term> <note>original: "ἀστερισμοὺς" (asterismous)</note>. Aratus and Hyginus recount these according to the Egyptian system, and we ourselves have displayed them in the two hemispheres within our work on Egyptian Astrology. They placed 24 of these in the Southern Hemisphere and an equal number in the Northern. Plutarch calls the Southern side the "Urn of Light," the "Kingdom of Osiris," and the "Right Side of the World," describing it as healthy and beneficial. This is indicated by the first side of this Obelisk, where in the first position Osiris appears, notable for his Hawk-head, as we shall see later. However, the opposite Northern side—the "Left Side of the World"—is called by the Egyptians malevolent, poisonous, feminine, the origin of darkness, and the kingdom of Arimanius <note>A Latinized form of Ahriman, the spirit of evil and darkness in Zoroastrianism.</note> or Typhon. It contains the station of the 24 deities who are the <term>rivals</term> <note>original: "ἀντίτεχνον" (antitechnon), meaning "opposing craft" or "rival"</note> of Osiris. Damascius mentions these, as recorded in Bulengerus’s *Astrology of the Chaldeans*, where he speaks thus:

<margin>Bulengerus.</margin> > *Beyond the circle of the Zodiac, they define 24 other stations of the stars; one part of these they place to the North, the other to the South. Those stars which are visible to the senses in the radiant region, they assign to the Living; those which escape our sight, they claim belong to the kingdom of darkness and the dead. Thus they establish these orders of the universe. Consequently, as the Sun traverses them in its annual revolution, <term>alternating</term> <note>original: "ἐξαλλάξας" (exallaxas)</note> between them with the pyramids of its actions, they are the cause of great changes everywhere in this World.*

<margin>The Zoroastrian Egg.</margin> And this is that "Zoroastrian Egg"—that is, the World—in which Oromazes <note>A Latinized form of Ohrmazd or Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of light in Zoroastrianism.</note> created 24 Gods, and Arimanius created as many <term>rivals</term> <note>original: "ἀντίτεχνους" (antitechnous)</note> for the sake of mixing good and evil. See this fable in Plutarch’s book *On Isis and Osiris*, and treated more extensively on page 176 of my work on the *Pamphilian Obelisk*; the Chaldeans also displayed this under the following symbolic form.

<margin>The Barberini Obelisk contains 48 stations of the Gods.</margin> The Egyptians, however, show on the four sides of this Obelisk the stations of the 48 Spirits—some beneficial, some malevolent—such that each side contains twelve of them. These are indicated by as many stars on the face of each side. They are nothing other than the stations of the Gods which we displayed above according to the mind of the Ancients in the two hemispheres of Egyptian Astrology. For the Egyptians believed that all things in the World are subject to these, and by these all things are governed and contained.

<margin>Subject of the Barberini Obelisk: the All-Formed Deity and the 48 servant Spirits.</margin> Therefore, the **BARBERINI OBELISK** contains, expressed in hieroglyphic marks, the effects and operations of the <term>All-Formed Deity</term> <note>Pantamorphos</note> and the 48 World Spirits who are his ministers; these operations they exercise in the lower World through the mediation of the four primary natures or elements.

### SECTION V. THE BARBERINI OBELISK. CHAPTER III.

-> **THE ZOROASTRIAN EGG** <-
<note>original: "Ovum Zoroastream"</note>

<note>
The diagram illustrates the "Zoroastrian Egg," a symbolic representation of the universe. At the center is a personified Sun radiating light. The egg is divided into twelve segments representing the paths of the planets. On the left side are the spheres of Saturn (♄), Jupiter (♃), and Mars (♂). On the right side are Venus (♀), Mercury (☿), and the Moon (☽). The outer boundary is a ring of stars, signifying the firmament. This diagram visualizes how celestial influences descend into the material world.

Secondly, within the hieroglyphs of this arrangement, one is implicitly taught the <margin>Rites and ceremonies by which they are to be appeased.</margin> rites and ceremonies by which each of the aforementioned Spirits <note>Genii: In this context, protective or intermediary spirits associated with celestial bodies.</note> are to be attracted, conjured, and bound into statues through sacrifices and adjurations. Likewise, it shows which instruments or furnishings are to be used in the sacred rites, and from <margin>The reasoning of magical figures.</margin> what material those statues—which the Greeks call <term>elements</term> <note>original: "στοιχεῖα" (stoicheia); here referring to talismans or animated statues believed to be "elemental" embodiments of spiritual power</note>—must be constructed in certain places. These were to be adapted <term>according to analogy</term> <note>original: "κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν" (kata tēn analogian)</note> to the properties of the Spirits, so that, being thus enticed, they might more easily obey the Magicians who call upon them.

Thirdly, it shows which <term>amulets</term>, <term>phylacteries</term> <note>protective charms or scrolls worn on the body</note>, and <term>charms</term> <note>original: "periaptis"; objects tied around the neck or limbs as protection</note> should be used for the <margin>The reasoning of amulets and phylacteries with which they are to be worshiped.</margin> worship and invocation of each of those Spirits, both publicly and privately, for the warding off of all evils and the attainment of happiness. All these things are contained within the artful architecture of symbols presented on this Obelisk. Some of these reveal exquisite mysteries in the natural Philosophy and <margin>The Devil mixed himself with Natural Magic.</margin> Theology of the Ancients; others are entangled in Magical and superstitious arts—for as Demons secretly mingled themselves with these operations, they opened a path to all impiety for blind minds, leading toward the precipice of total destruction. However, all these things will be explained by us with such <margin>The author’s goal in interpreting the Obelisks...</margin> caution and circumspection that our interpretation will not cause offense to tender minds, nor will it provide an opportunity for the treacherous and the curious to learn the magic of the ancients.

# CHAPTER IV

->*A brief interpretation of the four primary and principal systems of the Obelisk.*<-

<margin>The end and intention of the erected Obelisk.</margin>
**B**efore all else, it must be known that the end and intention of those who erected this Obelisk was twofold. The first was that they might leave these signs for posterity as a <term>memorial<note>original: "μνημόσυνον" (mnēmosynon)</note></term> of their deepest wisdom and a certain <term>proof<note>original: "τεκμήριον" (tekmērion)</note></term> of their skillful minds, leading all future generations into admiration of that primeval Wisdom.

The second intention was that, by this "prophylactic" or protective image, they might ward off all sinister and unfortunate things from the place or region in which it was erected. This was achieved either by the attraction of the good Spirits <note>Genii: In Kircher's worldview, these are celestial intelligences or spirits that mediate between the divine and the physical world.</note> of the World, or by the driving away of harmful Spirits, whom they believed were directly opposed to the good ones.

<margin>The 48 Spirits of the World under the figure of 48 stars. The 48 constellations on the Barberini Obelisk.</margin>
With this presupposed, we approach the explanation of the Obelisk under favorable auspices. First, at the very top of the face of the Obelisk, there appear 48 <term>five-rayed<note>original: "πεντακτινοειδείς" (pentaktinoeideis)</note></term> or five-pointed stars, carved into the sides in such a proportion that each side contains twelve of them. By this hieroglyphic scheme, ancient wisdom points to 48 "faces" which correspond <term>in parallel<note>original: "παράλληλοι" (parallēloi)</note></term> to the 48 faces of the sky, or the images of the Constellations. (For, according to the testimony of Haly Rhodan <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, a famous 11th-century Egyptian astrologer and physician.</note>, the ancient Astrologers of the Egyptians described as many faces in the celestial World as there are grades of beings in the Elementary world, acting as terrestrial faces standing beneath the celestial ones). We shall speak extensively of the properties, offices, actions, influences, and mystical reasons of all these, and why they attributed five rays to each star, when we reveal the particular declaration of each individual mark; for now, it suffices to have indicated these things in passing. <margin>The principal presiding governors of nature.</margin> And these are the 48 principal Spirits who preside over all of nature, arranged into four <term>groups of twelve<note>original: "δωδεκάδας" (dōdekadas)</note></term> in such a way that each group of twelve Spirits corresponds aptly to each of the four parts of the World and the subject Elements, according to the analogy of properties common to both.

<margin>Hieroglyphic arrangements of the four elements.</margin>
Furthermore, since the <term>all-formed<note>original: "παντόμορφος" (pantomorphos)</note></term> World Soul cannot act upon lower things through the stars or celestial Spirits without a medium; beneath the stars themselves, which we have called symbols of the Spirits, the Egyptians immediately placed the hieroglyphic arrangements of the four primary natures or Elements, from which everything in the Sensible World is composed, and which are, as it were, the first objects and subjects—

<summary>Kircher explains that the Barberini Obelisk was designed both as a memorial of ancient wisdom and a protective talisman to attract good spirits. He identifies the 48 five-pointed stars at the top as symbols of celestial governors (constellations) that influence the four elements of the material world.</summary>

# DIAGRAM I.

## The Spirit of Fire.

<margin>A</margin> And first, in what manner and what the World Soul works through Solar or fiery Spirits in lower nature; likewise, by what sacrifices, ceremonies, and preparatory dispositions it is to be attracted, the following hieroglyphic diagram shows. It is marked with the letter A on the Obelisk and faces the Southern side, which is conformable to it in quality <note>In ancient theory, the South was associated with heat and the element of fire.</note>.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A rectangular frame containing an engraving. Figure A is a hawk-headed deity (Osiris/World Soul) seated on a square throne, wearing a solar disk with a snake. He holds a handled Cross (Ankh) in one hand and a hoopoe-headed staff (Was-scepter) in the other. Figure B is a standing human figure in a long tunic with arms raised in a gesture of adoration or offering. Between them is an altar or incense burner (L). Above the altar is a vertical column of hieroglyphs (M) including a disk, a bird, and other symbols. Below the scene is a decorative border of vertical strokes.</note>

<margin>A systematic demonstration of the method for performing rituals for the Spirit of Fire.</margin> Here Osiris, or the World Soul, <term>appearing in the form of a hawk<note>original: "ἱερακόμορφος" (hierakomorphos)</note></term>, or masked with a hawk’s head, sits upon a square throne. In his right hand he carries a <term>hoopoe-headed staff<note>original: "κυκουφάφαλον" (kukouphaphalon)</note></term>, that is, marked with the head of a hoopoe; in his left, the Nautical seal, or the handled Cross <note>The Ankh</note>; on his head he bears a sphere, from the hollow of which a Serpent emerges. All these are symbols, as we have shown at length from every kind of learning in the preceding pages, of the power and efficacy which the World Soul exercises in the World by the aid of its ministers and through the medium of the element of fire.

<margin>What is signified by the head of the Hawk.</margin> And indeed, through the Hawk—a bird gleaming with fiery eyes, swift, lively, and of lofty and sublime flight—they symbolically denote the individual properties of both celestial and elementary fire. Through the staff <margin>What is meant by the hoopoe-headed staff.</margin> <term>marked with the hoopoe’s head<note>original: "κυκουφάφαλον"</note></term>, they prefigure <term>hieroglyphically<note>original: "ἱερογλυφικῶς"</note></term> both the Royal power and the variety of things produced in the World by the force of heat, which is represented by the hoopoe's crest, imbued as it is with every variety of color. Through the handled Cross—which is joined from two parts, <margin>What is meant by the handled Cross.</margin> namely a circle and a Cross—they denote the motion of Ptah, that is, of the World Soul, which skillfully arranges all things that exist in the World. And by the circle, they signify the circular motion of the celestial bodies, by which it animates them to a certain extent and makes them fit to influence lower things; while by the Cross or crossed lines, they signify the motion which it performs in the lower World for the generation and production of things, according to the condition of elementary bodies. For the motion of sublunary <note>Objects below the moon, i.e., on Earth</note> things is according to straight lines, as appears in the motion of heavy and light things, or those of a middle nature; of which the former are carried partly downward and partly upward <term>at right angles<note>original: "πρὸς τὰς ὀρθὰς" (pros tas orthas)</note></term>; the latter, participating equally in both gravity and lightness, have obtained a middle nature and are diffused, as it were, to the sides, aptly expressing the crossed lines of the Cross. And by this single character, for the reasons stated, they not inconveniently denote the process of all nature; for which reason they also considered this character the most mysterious of all hieroglyphics—

<margin>The great mysteries of the handled Cross.</margin>

### CHAPTER IV.

...most mysterious, and they believed it possessed a power greater than others, both for attracting good Spirits and for warding off evil ones. Hence, designating it as a symbol of health, a supreme charm, the <term>Monogram of Phta</term> <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian god Ptah with the Ankh, or "handled cross."</note>, and by other names, they placed it engraved upon all Obelisks, statues, and tablets. Time would fail me if I wished to declare all the mysteries of this character now; therefore, he who desires more should consult the *Pamphili Obelisk*, in which I have written an entire treatise on it, and Chapter 5 of our *Coptic or Egyptian Forerunner*, where we have likewise dealt with it at length.

<margin>What is meant by the circle on the head of the Idol.</margin> Now let us return to our purpose. Furthermore, by the circle from whose depths the Serpent emerges, they signify that divine power which preserves all things, lying hidden everywhere, or the spirit which nourishes everything within with vital heat and mingles itself with the great body of the world. By the square seat, they denote the unfailing constancy of actions in all things. <margin>What is meant by the square seat?</margin> By the base of the seat, marked with a fivefold character of the <term>Handled Cross</term> <note>The Ankh symbol.</note>, they wish to signify the five subjects upon which its power is chiefly exerted: which are stones, metals, plants, animals, and rational beings. And these are the symbols regarding the <term>World Soul</term> <note>original: "Anima Mundi"</note>, or the Solar or fiery Spirit. All of these will indeed become more clearly known when each is established by appropriate testimonies and authorities.

<margin>The Isiac Priest clad in linen.</margin> Opposite the Idol representing the All-Formed <note>Referring to the "Pantamorphon" or universal deity.</note>, there appears the figure of an Isiac Priest, clad in linen, in the gesture of one praying, holding a small statue in his right hand, and distinguished by a varied headdress. Because of the Serpents raising their steep necks on either side, the sphere in the middle, the flame fanned on both sides, and the crest of feathers, we have deliberately chosen to name this headdress with a single word: the <term>serpent-circle-flame-feather-formed headdress</term> <note>original: "tutulum ὄφι-κυκλο-φλογο-πίε-ρόμορφος"</note>. <margin>The serpent-circle-flame-feather-formed headdress.</margin> By this hieroglyphic scheme, nothing else is denoted but the method of sacrifices which the Priests and <term>Sacred Diviners</term> <note>original: "Hieromantæ"</note> were accustomed to perform in their inner shrines with various ceremonies and rites, as has already been said many times, to appease and attract the Solar and fiery Spirits, like all others. And indeed, by the linen garment, they denote the supreme purity required for the appeasement of the Gods by those who were to preside over the sacred rites. <margin>What the linen garment denotes. What the posture of standing and praying denotes.</margin> By the posture of standing and praying, they denote a serious, constant, and devoted will in performing the sacred duties. By the small statue in the likeness of a little man in an adoring pose—which he carries in his hands and seems to offer to the All-Formed Spirit sitting opposite—is denoted how, or by what ceremonies, or by what mixture of things the <term>consecrated statues</term> <note>original: "τερθερῶμαι" (tertheromai); referring to talismans or animated images.</note> are to be constructed, whether for other useful purposes or to be presented to a Spirit, so that, animated by a divine spirit, they may henceforth possess a <term>prophylactic</term> <note>protective or preventative</note> power against the incursions of evil. Regarding all these matters, consult the "Hieroglyphic Magic."

<margin>What the headdress signifies.</margin> Moreover, the headdress which he supports on his head, the <term>serpent-circle-flame-feather-formed</term> one, indicates the properties or virtues of the <term>World Soul</term> which it is necessary to have known, so that by adapting things <term>analogously</term> <note>original: "ἀναλόγως" (analogos); in due proportion or correspondence.</note>, the petty priests may more easily attract the Gods. And for this reason, it is placed upon the head of the Priests, to suggest that sacrifices of this kind must be performed with reason and intelligence. For they believed nothing pleased the Gods more than a serious and constant application of the whole mind and intellect toward knowing, honoring, and in any way uniting oneself to the Gods; of which action, as we have said, the symbol was...

...most [mysterious], that multiform crown. <margin>Circle. Flame. Serpent. Feathers.</margin> And indeed, through the circle, or the central Orb, they signified the immense majesty of the divinity; through the flames, the subtle power of persuasion; through the Serpents, vital fecundity; and through the feathers, readiness in providing aid, speed in action, and finally, supreme excellence in dignity, as if confessing these truths through a silent hymn. <margin>Column with a fire bowl.</margin> Finally, the column with a fire bowl placed between Osiris and the Isiac Priest signifies the sacrifices usually made to the Fiery Genius, which can by no means be performed without fire; for the Genius of fire delights in it as a thing similar to himself, just as he does in all other things analogous to him, as we have previously suggested.

# DIAGRAM II.
## The Aerial Genius.

<margin>B The second diagram is a representation of the rituals to be performed for the aerial spirit.</margin> Furthermore, the present second diagram looks toward the Eastern quarter, which is analogous to the Aerial Genius, and contains the rites and ceremonies by which their Aerial Genius must be appeased and enticed in sacred matters. <margin>What does the egg represent?</margin> One should not sacrifice to the Aerial Spirit <note>original: "aëreo Genio"; the elemental spirit or "genius" of the air</note> except with things of an aerial nature; for the Aerial Spirit delights in such things, as they are analogous to it. For the Egg, besides being of an aerial substance, also perfectly mimics the sphere of the air, and is like a seed of aerial living beings. That the Olive is also aerial is too well known to need further explanation. <margin>Olive. Oil vessels.</margin> Truly, <term>lecythi</term> <note>original: "Lecythi"; ancient Greek oil flasks</note> or vessels full of oil were used in sacred ceremonies, either for the use of lighting lamps or for anointing Idols with oil. Indeed, the Lotus flower surrounding the column of the table signifies <margin>What the lotus flower means</margin> that sacrifices are to be carried out according to the pattern of nature. ### DIAGRAM III.

->**The Spirit of Water.**<-

<margin>A diagram declaring the method for performing rites for the water spirit.</margin> The third diagram marked on the Obelisk with the letter **C**, looking toward the damp and cold Western region, demonstrates the method of performing rituals for the Water or Lunar Spirit. Its symbols are an Ibis-shaped face (<margin>Ibis, Crescent Moon</margin> for the Ibis is a bird of the Nile) supporting the horns of a crescent moon <note>original: "sextilis Lunæ"; literally the moon of the sixth day</note> on its head, by which the dominion of the said Spirit over the water is shown; this is confirmed by the Nile reed <margin>Nile Thyrsus. Frog.</margin> along with the frog, the daughter of the stagnant Nile. Since all their mysteries have been explained in preceding sections, we pass over them; therefore, leaving these things behind, let us proceed to the Isiac Priest **D**. He is dressed in female attire, holding in his <margin>Nile Vessel. Mast of the Baris boat.</margin> right hand a Nile vessel, with the mast and sail of the <term>Baris</term> <note>original: "Baridis"; a sacred Egyptian boat or barge</note> or sacred ship; through these, they wished for prosperity regarding the waters, the Nile, the winds, navigation, and similar things. Indeed, the intermediate table, <margin>Sacred table.</margin> filled with <term>Canopic jars</term> <note>original: "Canopis"; vessels used to hold sacred Nile water or internal organs</note>, Nile vessels, and other symbols of the Nile, shows that sacrifices to the Water Spirit must not be performed without the liquid of the Nile; for they believed the spirit to be drawn by these. Hence, individuals kept the sacred water of the Nile at home for <term>lustration</term> <note>ritual purification</note> and <term>expiation</term> <note>original: "expiationem"; cleansing of sins or ritual impurity</note>, not only in Canopic jars but also in other vessels, as Plutarch testifies. Hence that arm **H**, with the vessel <margin>Arm of Osiris.</margin> which it holds in its hand, placed on the Table by the banks of the Nile, they positioned as a protective <note>original: "auerruncatiuum"; an object intended to ward off evil</note> sign, symbolically denoting the arm of Osiris. Therefore, this entire hieroglyphic diagram signifies nothing other than the method of sacrificing to the Water Spirit. This is attested by the Ibis, the crescent Moon, the Nile reed with the frog, the Nile vessel, and the traces of the sacred ship of the Baris, together with the table filled with Canopic jars, <term>simpula</term> <note>original: "sympulis"; ritual ladles or small cups used for libations</note>, and other vessels. Let the reader consult this figure carved on the Obelisk, which expresses everything more exactly; it occupies the first place **A B** on the first side. In this diagram, however, some things were omitted due to the sculptor's carelessness.

# DIAGRAM IV.

## The Spirit of the Earth.

<margin>A diagram presenting the method of sacrificing to the earth: Isis as the Spirit of the Earth.</margin>
The fourth diagram, looking toward the Northern region of the Obelisk, follows and shows by what rites or by the display of what things the Spirit of the earth, or Isis, is to be drawn forth. Since this diagram is halfway worn away on our Obelisk, we have borrowed it from the Bembine Table <note>original: "tabula Bembina"; the Mensa Isiaca, a famous Roman-era bronze tablet featuring Egyptian-style motifs that Kircher used as a primary reference</note>; it is the central figure in the Bembine Table, which in this place represents Isis as the Spirit of the Earth, or the Great Mother. All these things are indicated by the <term>calathus</term> <note>a basket-shaped crown often associated with fertility deities</note> placed upon her head with ears of grain, a flowered headdress, and the horns of a cow. Likewise, it is shown by her swelling breast; for among the Egyptians, Isis is the same as the earth, according to the testimony of Plutarch. To her is attributed the invention of grain and agriculture, which are aptly signified by the grain-filled basket and the Bull-like horns. The swelling breast shows her to be the nourisher of all things. So much for the symbols of the Spirit of the Earth, which are explained more extensively in the aforementioned table.

<margin>Her symbols are the grain-basket and the horns of the ox.</margin>

<note>Hieroglyphic illustration: A framed woodcut depicting a female figure (Isis/Priestess) in profile. She wears a distinctive headdress (calathus) with horns and ears of grain. In her right hand, she holds a staff topped with a symbol. To her left is an altar with an incense burner and a cross-like symbol (ankh). Above her is a vertical column of hieroglyphs including an eye, a seated figure, and various strokes. Kircher labels parts of the image with "G" and "H".</note>

<margin>The monograms of Phtha and Mu.</margin>
The Priestess, indeed, in feminine attire, holds in her right hand the monograms, which are Phtha and <term>Mu</term> <note>original: "μὺ"; Kircher interprets these as mystical phonetic symbols</note>: the former signifies the Soul of the World <note>original: "Animam Mundi"</note>; the latter signifies the Spirit of the earth, or the earth itself. They represent the actions of Phtha upon the earth. Furthermore, what that many-shaped headdress, what the Cross, the seat, and other symbols signify, has already been said many times. This one thing must be well noted: through the feminine attire of the Priests, the feminine Elements are signified; through the masculine, the masculine. Hence, for the stated reason, the Priests sacrificing to the fiery and aerial Spirits are clothed in masculine garments; but for the watery and terrestrial, they wear feminine; for those Elements are masculine, while these are feminine. From this it is clear how the Priests placed nothing in these sorts of hieroglyphic Treatises without a mystery. And these are the things which we thought should be briefly explained in these four diagrams.

<margin>The feminine attire of the Priests.</margin>

CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...I wished to make it clearer, so that you would not be confused at the first sight of the Obelisk.

The first side of this Obelisk, the Southern one, is the principle of life, heat, and all moisture, just as the first <term>Hierogrammatismus</term> <note>a sacred hieroglyphic composition</note> marked **A B**, explained above, demonstrates more than enough through its appropriate symbols. After this, the side is divided into two columns, as are all the other sides; we are now undertaking their explanation, beginning our discussion with column **C**.

->**NOTE**<-

->***On the diagrams of the first Southern side, which contain the stations of the Southern Gods.***<-

<margin>
The Southern side of the first Barberini Obelisk.

It explains the stations of 48 Gods and their effects.

Six Spirits in each column of the Barberini Obelisk.
</margin>

**T**his side explains the stations of the Gods who influence the success of agriculture, to be understood according to the physical, mystical, and <term>anagogical</term> <note>a method of spiritual interpretation that leads the mind toward higher, heavenly realities</note> senses; it describes by what ceremonies they are to be attracted and appeased for the benefit of humanity, as well as what effects they produce in the lower Worlds. Six <term>Genii</term> <note>spirits or guardian deities</note> are shown in each column; to these, the Egyptians offered honor and worship with the greatest zeal and care to obtain the aforementioned agricultural bounty, specifically to <term>Omphta</term>, <term>Isis</term>, <term>Apis</term>, <term>Momphtha</term>, <term>Nephtha</term>, <term>Horus</term>, or <term>Harpocrates</term>, as will be clear from the interpretation.

<margin>
Two shovels, a human figure holding a scale and a measuring rod.
</margin>

**C** In the first column, at position **C**, two shovels (instruments of agriculture) are seen, together with a human figure holding a scale in one hand and a measuring rod in the other. This denotes the Divinity they call <term>Omphta</term>, according to the testimony of Plutarch; this was a beneficial Divinity believed to distribute to each person what was their own according to the laws of justice. Its symbols are the scale and the measuring rod. They celebrate its festival in the month of <term>Paophi</term> <note>the second month of the Egyptian calendar, roughly October</note>; for in this month, after the flooding of the Nile, they especially recognized the benefits of this Divinity. Therefore, they quite properly numbered it as one among the twelve presiding signs of the <term>Zodiac</term>. We have dealt with this extensively in our work on Astrology and in the description of the <term>Sothic</term> year <note>the "Sothic cycle" is a period of roughly 1,460 years based on the rising of the star Sirius, which the Egyptians called Sothis</note>, to which we refer the Reader.

SYNTAGMA V. THE BARBERINI OBELISK. CHAPTER V.

The power of <term>Omphta</term> <note>Kircher's term for a mediating divine force that maintains cosmic equilibrium</note> overcomes the Typhonian <note>referring to Typhon, the god of chaos and destructive heat</note> forces of the Sun and Moon through its own virtue. It does this by irrigating what is scorched by excessive heat, or by drying what is smothered by too much moisture, thus restoring everything to a state of moderation. These qualities are aptly represented by the Owl and the Quail. The former signifies the scorching Typhonian power and harmful dryness associated with the Sun; the latter signifies the excessive overflow of moisture or a stifling force associated with the Moon.

<term>Omphta</term> overcomes both of these extremes, tempering excessive moisture with heat and excessive dryness with moisture, reduced to a middle ground. It holds power over the Sun and Moon, as shown by the two scepters in section **D**; the first is Moon-shaped, denoting power over the Moon, and the other is Hawk-shaped <note>the hawk was a solar symbol</note>, denoting power over the Sun. These are the moderators of the lower world, as the following segment notes.

<margin>**D** Scepter in the shape of a Moon and a Hawk.</margin>

Regarding the Owl and the Quail, however, see the discussion in the specific "Sacred Scripts" <note>original: "Hierogrammatismis"</note> on the Pamphilian Obelisk, and *Horapollo*, Book 2, Chapter 24.

Because the earth is subject to the workings of all these forces, they placed <term>Isis</term> immediately below, seen sitting with her head veiled. They depict her holding a <term>Cucupomorph</term> <note>shaped like the head of a hoopoe bird, symbolizing gratitude or filial piety in Kircher's system</note> staff in her left hand. This indicates that she is a fellow-worker of <term>Momphta</term> and the cause of the variety of things in the three lower worlds—the animal, vegetable, and mineral. She acts as a preserver of the influence flowing from <term>Momphta</term> into these worlds, arranged according to the law of justice. These concepts are aptly indicated by these symbols <note>Hieroglyphic symbols: two triangles, three circles, one triangle</note> placed near <term>Isis</term>.

<margin>**Horus.** Isis sitting veiled, holding a staff.</margin>

However, because beneficent <margin>What the two pyramids and three circular figures denote.</margin> Deities are thought to accomplish nothing unless they are petitioned through constant religious devotion and observance, we see the Priests at **E**. In the month of <term>Paophi</term> <note>the second month of the ancient Egyptian calendar, roughly October</note>, they scatter seeds in the inner sanctuaries, invoking the "paternal depth" composed of three triads—the fertile Deity of all providence, the fire of all nature from which all things are born. They arranged their bodies in a posture corresponding to a mystic number, and then, with their hands lowered behind their backs and kneeling, they made their petitions. All these things are exactly signified by the symbols: three globes and two <term>pyramidal</term> <note>original Greek: "πυραμιδοειδεῖς"</note> figures. But let us hear <term>Damascius</term> <note>a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> discussing this in his *Theology*:

<margin>**Damascius.**</margin>
> <note>original Greek: "Ἱερεῖς καὶ μυσταὶ ἐν τῷ μηνὶ Παωφὶ ἐν ἀδύτοις σπέρματα προβάλλοντες βυθὸν πατρικὸν, καὶ Ἄμμωνα δὲ πάσης φύσεως, καὶ πολυτοκίας θησαυρὸν ἐπικαλοῦνται· καὶ τούτοις σημαίνουσι, πάντα ἀπὸ πυρὸς ἑνὸς γεγονέναι."</note> *The Priests and Initiates, casting forth seeds in the inner sanctuaries at the beginning of the month of Paophi, invoke the Paternal Depth and Ammon, the overseer of all nature and fertility; by this they signify that all things have been brought forth from a single fire.*

Accordingly, they place three figures near **E**, as if scattering seeds. <margin>**E**</margin> But why do they paint three? Clearly to secretly signify the three triads from which the "paternal depth" was composed, according to the testimony of <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>the ancient Persian prophet, often cited in Renaissance occultism</note> (concerning which, see *Sphinx Mystagoga* page 147 and the explanation of the *Bembine Tablet*). ...of the Nile; by which it is indicated that through the hidden progress of the aforementioned Gods, the inflow to the fields is promoted, life is granted, and the chain of existence is maintained by the Nilotic protective charm. 

<margin>Plutarch. The hidden progress of the Gods is signified by footsteps.</margin> 

Plutarch teaches that the hidden progress of the Gods is signified by human footsteps; he states that Isis denotes nothing other than the prudent progress of nature, which is why two footsteps were always added to her, as is clearly evident from various surviving Roman marbles. 

<margin>The arura and the Nilotic vessel.</margin> 

Furthermore, Horus <note>Kircher refers to Horapollo, author of the *Hieroglyphica*</note> teaches in Book 1, Chapter 3, that a field, or <term>the arura</term> <note>original: τὴν ἀρούραν; a Greek term for an Egyptian land measurement</note>, is signified by a quadrangle. The Nilotic vessel tied with an attachment denotes a protective charm <note>original: *phylacterium*</note> suitable for propitiating the Nilotic Divinity; hence, as Plutarch says, in the procession of Isis, a water vessel preceded, the shape of which the Priests would fix to their hands, neck, and chest. 

But these and the remaining symbols have been explained elsewhere. The following symbols follow, where Isis is again seen veiled in a seated posture with two scepters and a shovel, followed by three boundary stones <note>original: *termini*</note> with a curved scepter and a Scarab; below which are a cycloid, a square, a Serpent, and the hind part of a Lion.
