Isis, powerful with double dominion and fruitful of the Worlds, **F** receiving the inflow through the annual course of the ruling Sun, distributes the beneficial increase of vital strength into the fourfold face of the earth. **G** The Cornucopia, having driven away the hostile <term>Bebonian</term> <note>original: *bebonia*; referring to Bebo or Typhon, associated with chaos and drought</note> Quail, under the guidance of the supreme Divinity **H**—aptly signified by the winged globe placed upon feet—bestows vital moisture upon the material worlds and its receptacles. By this benefit, Horus—that is, the Sensible World—is brought back to life.

Then follow, between the letters **I K**, **K L**, and **L**, the stations of <term>Momphta</term> <note>Kircher's name for a demiurgic or protective deity who guards the cosmic order</note>, the guardian of the Isiac enclosure, and of the Apis bulls consecrated to the Sun and Moon. 

<margin>The enclosure in which the sacred bulls were nourished. Pliny, Herodotus.</margin> 

We have dealt with these extensively on page 258 of the Pamphilian Obelisk, which you should consult. According to Pliny, they call the four pillars in the region of Momphta a "chamber," and according to Herodotus in his book *Euterpe*, it was nothing but an enclosure in which the sacred Bulls—the omens of the people—were nourished. But see all these things treated at length in the cited place. 

Of these Bulls, the first signifies the Sun or Osiris, the other the Moon or Isis. From their cult, various divinations were established regarding the three stations of the year, as the three boundary stones note. The Egyptians believed these celestial inflows and the outflow of the mixing bowl were linked, as the intermediate symbols show: namely, a chain enclosed in a cycloid with the neighboring figure of a mixing bowl. By this, the presiding officer of the sacred enclosure distributed the inflow into the moist substance and into the fourfold face of the world with a hidden motion, as the master of the chains of moist substance.

**X** represents the Universe or the four parts of the world. And since they believed the Crocodiles to be the genuine <term>ectypon</term> <note>original: *ectypon*; a Greek term for a "living image" or "replica"</note> of Typhon, it happened that the Crocodiles would inflict no damage upon mortals during this time, but as if tamed, they would approach the sacred pits, as the figure shows, licking the water from there as if voluntarily subscribing to the worship of the day. For the rest, he is kept in secret, but when he bursts forth into the assemblies, he walks with the lictors moved aside, and a flock of boys accompanies him singing a hymn in his honor; he seems to understand and desire to be adored; these flocks, suddenly inspired, foretell future things, etc. and they sink a golden and silver bowl in the place called the "phiala" [vial/basin] during the days of the Birth of Apis. This is sufficiently shown by the painted scepter, the symbol of dominion over them. That scepter was made of reed, for which Crocodiles have a natural antipathy, as Theophrastus relates; they are even stopped by the sound of its rustling. With the globe, divine providence in the World is signified by the figure of the cornucopia, representing the flow of elementary things. Note in this place, as we have advised elsewhere, that the cornucopia is depicted by the Egyptians in this three-fold manner. When it is depicted with four small squares placed in its opening, as seen here, it then signifies the flow of Elementary things, which we have therefore called <term>hylæum</term> <note>From the Greek 'hyle', meaning matter; referring here to the material or elemental realm</note>; but when it is marked with seven small squares, it then denotes the flow of celestial things caused by the seven planets; finally, when it is marked with twelve small squares, it indicates the flow of the twelve signs of the Zodiac, as has been said elsewhere.

By the Serpent, the spirit of life is shown; by the ribboned boy, <term>Horus</term>, who is everywhere indicated by the figure of a child; by the globe and the Young Goat, the world of plants is meant; and by the feather, motion is indicated. It is as if one were saying: by the <term>causal</term> <note>original Greek: αἰτικὴ (aitikē)</note> power of Horus—that is, the sensible World (for so Plutarch calls him)—the world seems to grow young again continually through the generation of plants, by means of the vital force infused into the Universe, which is marked by the Serpents and the Cross or <term>chiasm</term> <note>original Greek: χιασμὸν (chiasmon), referring to an X-shaped crossing or intersection</note>, or decussis <note>The Roman numeral X, used here to represent a cross-shaped symbolic intersection</note>.

...they were depicted in angles. By these, nothing else was indicated but the supreme and invisible triform Divinity <note>referring to the Triple Deity or Trinity in Kircher’s Neoplatonic interpretation of Egyptian religion</note>, teeming with Ideas: for as we have explained in the *Pamphylian Obelisk*, the globe was the symbol of the divine Power and the supreme cause of causes, hidden in the eternal abyss of its own unity. The triangle, however, was the symbol of the divinity diffusing itself outward; likewise, the triangles spread out in a triple order in the manner of rays were symbols of all things conformed to the eternal exemplar, which are extended from the center of the globe into the whole circuit of created things. Just as in the lower world the gourd—in the middle of which seeds are seen spread out in a triple order—was an index of this, so indeed they assumed a symbol suitable for signifying occult mysteries through this tripod. Since, moreover, the Mercurial gourd

is of a [specific] nature, they determined, not without reason, that it should be dedicated to Mercury, the interpreter of the triform Divinity, as its analogical reasoning suggested. The tripod consisted of three series of connected triangles; by these, they noted the connection of the starry and elemental World in the form of chains derived from the supreme God, the archetypal World, the cause of causes, from whose center they were also derived. To each of these a specific fate was destined, of which Mercury was the herald and interpreter; but the Owl was considered the messenger of Mercury, which Abenephius calls the <term>Prodromos of Hemphta</term> <note>original: "Prodromam Hemphta"; the "Forerunner of Hemphta." -> it foretells everything that is to come upon the children of men. ۞ <-

> *The Egyptians said that the Owl is the messenger of Hemphta, their God, who is the first Deity among them, and they believed that it announced all things which were to happen to the children of men.* 

<margin>What the Owl signifies among the Egyptians.</margin>
The Egyptians, therefore, did not only indicate the operations of an adverse Power through the Owl, but also the name and Power of Hemphta, that is, of universal providence. This deity would send the Owl—that is, its messenger—to men at certain times, and through it signify future things, warn of sinister events, and teach through its song what should be done prudently in the face of an impending calamity. They judged wisdom—over which Mercury presides and which is also indicated by the Owl—to be the only thing capable of meeting and resisting all sinister events.

<margin>The Mercurial Prothyraeum.</margin>

# SYNTAGMA V. THE BARBERINI OBELISK. CHAPTER V.

They stood before the tripod, petitioning the supreme Deity for the aversion of calamities. Finally, one would whip an Owl <note>original: *Noctuam*; the owl was often seen as a bird of ill omen</note>, the herald of dire events, while another repeatedly intoned the aforementioned adjuration. Through the staff of the **Polymorphic Genius** <note>A "shape-shifting" spirit or guardian representing the diverse forces of nature</note>, they indicated an abundance of all necessary things; through the feather of the **Hawk**, the turning away of evils; through the ear of the **sacred Bull**, the favorable generation of things, which occurs through the "hearing" of the Bull. (For the Bull, upon hearing the voice of the Cow, is immediately moved to fertile union with her, as Horus witnesses in Book 1, Chapter 47.) <margin>Horus, Book 1, Ch. 47.</margin> Through the cycloid <note>A circular or curved path</note> with an extended hand and a **twined basket**, they showed the beneficent power of the celestial **Osiris**, who has power over all things; through the **winged scepter** and the **three boundaries**, they indicated dominion and influence over the three-part division of the year caused by the motion of the Sun. Since all these things could not be obtained without the influence of **Hemphis** <note>A name Kircher uses for a supreme, all-encompassing divine spirit</note>, in whom all stated things are contained, the Priests—transforming themselves by the positioning of their entire bodies to express the name of said Deity—performed the sacred rites before the tripod, just as the father [stands] in his region. They whipped the Owl at the three divisions of the day <margin>**E** Effects resulting from the placation of the Gods through the rites of the Priests.</margin> to avert horrors, as the figure shows.

We have thus seen the rites and ceremonies; now let us see the effects denoted by the following symbols. First, through the **small cord** to which a globe is attached, placed below a bowl, is signified the influence of the divine Deity into the **Bowl of Osiris**. Through the **egg**, beneath which a **Roe-deer** is placed, is signified the fertile generation of things. Through the **bowl**, which is placed upon the figure of **Zanati** (that is, a chain), is signified the **Mercurial influx** <note>The influence of Mercury/Thoth as a messenger and connector</note>, which they intended to reach all things subjected to its chain. <margin>**X** **M** **N** **O**</margin> The beneficent power is shown through the two arms of **Anubis**, who is represented by a reclining dog, as if watching over affairs. Liberality in supplying a store of necessary things is indicated by the **triple moisture**, two papyrus thyrsi <note>ritual staffs</note>, and a triple water-pattern. Dominion and power are shown through the twined basket; the direction of vegetable nature in the fields through the bolt; the celestial providence over the fields through the **supplicating figure** and the eye with the cycloid. Finally, through the **Chenosirin** <note>An Egyptian goose</note> or Goose, vigilance is implied.

There follows now the station of the **Polymorphic Demon**, who is signified by a **winged Dragon** and a papyrus thyrsus; he is the indicator of the abundance of things necessary for the human race, as we have interpreted at length elsewhere. Two statues announce the ceremonies to be performed for him, by which the soul rises toward unknown things, the scepter of the sacred Bull is penetrated, and the chain of the celestial Deities is drawn. The damages caused by **Typhon** <note>The god of chaos and storms</note> are warded off by the **Quail** and the **Hawk** (that is, the Moon and the Sun), and the moisture of the Nile is administered by celestial justice and providence regarding agriculture; all these things are noted through the symbols included between P and Q, the meaning of which is already clear from the preceding. <margin>**III. Station of the Polymorphic Demon.** Ceremonies to be performed for the Polymorphic Demon. **P**</margin>

A station now follows in the region of Q, that of the **Terrestrial Genius**, indicated by the front part of a **Dog**, with the letter H and a basket as a head ornament. In this manner they placed **Nephthys**, whom authors say is the same as **Proserpina** <note>Goddess of the underworld</note>, distinguished by a canine head. For, as the very ancient author **Demophilus** rightly says: <term>The Egyptians depict Nephthys in the form of a dog</term> <note>original Greek: Νεφθὺν Αἰγύπτιοι κυνομόρφον ζωογραφῶσι</note>. The letter H signifies the Earth, firmly compacted as if by two columns, one of water and one of earth, over which Nephthys rules; it is established upon three foundations, which are indicated by three boundaries. <margin>**IV. Station of the Terrestrial Genius.** Nephthys or Proserpina.</margin>

<margin>V. The Station of Momphto-Ammon.</margin>
The Station of Momphto-Ammon <note>A composite deity name typical of Kircher’s syncretic style</note> is found in region **T**, whose dominion is said to be over the hot and the moist; the former is indicated by the figure carrying a pipe on its head, the latter by the head of a Ram, the power of which is put into action by the Scarab-Osiris: for by these the generation of all things is perfected, and all adverse and contrary things are driven away through the worship of the said divine powers.

<margin>VI. The Station of Anubis.</margin>
The Station of Anubis in region **V** is shown by the figure of a crouching Dog, keeping watch over the things committed to him—that is, the moisture diffused through the four-fold face of the earth. He is the guardian of the three elements (fire, earth, and water) and the conductor of the same through the paths of the Universe. For this reason, statues of Harpocrates <note>the god of silence and childhood</note>, the tutelary dog-headed Hermes, and Ammon were placed at the entrance <note>original: *prothyro*</note> to turn away evil, with their appropriate symbols, as is evident in region **X**.

<margin>Horus.</margin>
And here is the context of the symbols contained on the first Southern side of the Obelisk, which indeed indicate nothing else but the operations and protections of the twelve tutelary Genii <note>guardian spirits or minor deities</note> presiding over this part, as indicated by the twelve stars placed at the top of the Obelisk; these symbols belong to the twelve Genii. For, as Horus <note>Kircher refers to Horapollo, a late-antique author whose work "Hieroglyphica" was the primary resource for Renaissance scholars trying to decode Egyptian writing</note> rightly says, when the Egyptians paint a star, they sometimes denote a Genius, sometimes fate, etc. You also see six of these Genii placed in the first column of the side, and just as many in the second: having demonstrated these, let us now explain the other side.

**F**irst, in the region marked **A**, the Dove with the star is an absolute symbol of an aerial Genius <note>In this context, a "Genius" is a guardian spirit or a divine entity that mediates between gods and humans</note>. Horus asserts in Book 2, Chapter 1, that a star indeed signifies a Genius: <note>original Greek: "Ἀστέρα παρ’ Αἰγυπτίοις γραφόμενον Θεὸν σημαίνει."</note> *A star depicted by the Egyptians signifies a God or a Genius.* And in Book 1, Chapter 13: <note>original Greek: "Θεὸν δὲ ἢ κόσμον σημαίνονtes ἢ εἱμαρμένην..."</note> *When they wish to signify God, or the world, or fate, or the number five, they paint a star. They use it for God because the providence of God decrees and commands through the stars, by which the movement of the celestial bodies and the entire universe is carried out; for they believe that without God, nothing at all can exist. They use it for Fate, because fate is established by the course and disposition of the stars. And for the number five, because although there are many stars in the heavens, only five of them, by their motion, complete the most beautiful distribution of the world.* <note>Kircher is referring to the five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> By the Dove, however, Horus Apollo understands the air in Book 1, and he gives the reason there: it is of such a sincere and pure nature that it cannot be infected by any contagious air, as other animals are. Thus, the Dove with the star most excellently indicates an aerial Deity, and this is the first station of the aerial Deity.

### SYNTAGMA V. BARBERINI OBELISK. CHAPTER VII.

...a scepter marked with the letter M, which signifies the station of Momphta <note>Kircher uses "Momphta" to refer to a supreme generative or demiurgic power he identifies in Egyptian hieroglyphs, often associated with moisture and life-giving force</note>, as is clear from the symbols and has already been frequently declared. The vessel represents the humid substance, while the Lion’s head represents Momphta himself, as we have taught at length regarding the Lion hierogram in the Pamphilian Obelisk. The scepter <margin>Scepter marked with the letter M.</margin> marked with the M denotes his dominion over the humid element; for M, as we have taught elsewhere, is the same in Egyptian as *Moi*, which indicates water, and also expresses its flowing nature. The Priests uniquely venerated him—his body's form transformed into his very name—as the one who moves all things with a hidden motion and as the bestower of vital moisture. Note here that the feet always denote the hidden movement of the Gods, as has been demonstrated everywhere in the preceding pages from various authorities. 

Now follows in the region of H: a young buck, a thyrsus, and a cup shaped in the figure of Canopus, which, ending in the head of a Hawk, vomits forth water. <margin>H Canopus is the same as Momphta.</margin> To understand this, you must know that Canopus is the same as Momphta; for this reason, they expressed him sometimes with a Lion’s head, and sometimes like a pot-bellied vessel. Expressed in the Lion-like form of the head, it noted that his triple power is most greatly exerted when the rising of the Nile is imminent, which happens when the Sun enters Leo. Here, however, he is like a pot-bellied cup, on whose summit the lid is marked with a Hawk’s head, which expresses water; by this, he indicates the abundance of warm moisture which the Hawklike Momphta imparts to all things according to the chain of material beings <term>hylæorum catenam: a Neoplatonic concept of a "chain" of existence connecting the spiritual to the material</term> and the vital statue of himself, <margin>I Station III of the Polymorphous Demon.</margin> as the statue with the Serpent between H and I denotes.

The station of the Polymorphous <note>many-formed</note> Demon is indicated by the winged Dragon in the region of I, as we have already often explained. His duty is to adorn the World with a variety and abundance of forms, with the assistance of Horus, and to preserve the vital moisture. With the hidden protection of life—which the feet moved toward the seat with the Serpent suggest—he opens the gate to the dominion of Momphta.

Through the three feathers in the region of K, the station of three Intelligences <note>In Kircher’s system, "Intelligences" are spiritual or angelic beings that govern aspects of the cosmos</margin> <margin>K Station IV. What the feather signifies in hieroglyphics.</margin> is indicated in this place. For the feather occasionally signifies wind, sometimes the air, and sometimes—as with the feather of the Ibis with the Crocodile—a restraining power; for the Crocodile is struck motionless by the touch of an Ibis feather. Sometimes, as here, when added to images, it signifies the Mind or Intelligence; because, as Saint Dionysius also testifies, just as the bodies of birds are raised on high by feathers into places inaccessible to men, so do the Intelligences dwell within the perpetual contemplation of the highest and most divine things. But of these things, we speak everywhere in this Work. Therefore, the first Intelligence is represented by the Ibis with a veiled <margin>Hieroglyphic of the Lunar tutelary Genii.</margin> statue equipped with a whip <note>original: "scutica," a lash or scourge used as a symbol of authority or protection</note>; that is, the Lunar tutelary Genius. In the region of L, however, is an image armed with a whip and veiled, sitting upon a throne: the <margin>L Hieroglyphic of the terrestrial tutelary Genii.</margin> terrestrial and tutelary Intelligence. The feather signifies the Intelligence, the seat signifies the terrestrial (that is, the stable and firm); the figure is either Nephthys or Isis; and the whip indicates the protection <margin>Hieroglyphic of the Solar Genii.</margin> of the things committed to its care. The following figure, likewise ribboned and surrounded by nine squares, denotes the Solar Intelligence, which <margin>Plutarch</margin> Plutarch, in his book *On Osiris and Isis*, calls Apopis, the brother of the Sun. Regarding this, Phlegon also writes in his work on Zoroaster: <note>original Greek: *Ἄπωπας δύναμίς ἐστὶ τεταγμένη παρὰ τῶν Χαλδαίων ἐκ τῶν τριῶν τριάδων, καὶ τῶν τριῶν δωδεκάδων συνθημένη.*</note> "Apopas is a power established by the Chaldeans from three triads, and composed of three dodecads." Apopas is a Solar Demon, composed by the Chaldeans from three triads and as many dodecads <note>groups of twelve</note>. So that these things may be understood—

The veiled figure between **L** and **M** denotes **Apopas**, the Solar Demon <note>In traditional Egyptian mythology, Apep (Apophis) is the chaos-serpent and enemy of the Sun; Kircher here interprets him as a 'Solar Demon' or a genius associated with the Sun's cycles</note>, who is surrounded by nine quadrangles: three below, three in the middle, and three above. These are the three triads from which he is said to be composed; they represent the nine Classes of Genii <note>Spiritual beings or guardians</note> subject to him. Let us see how he is composed of three dodecads <note>Groups of twelve</note>. Each quadrangle consists of four sides, which, when multiplied by 9, results in the

number **36**. This is the number which **Plato** so greatly praises (as was explained above regarding the Lateran Obelisk); it was a "circular" number, specifically suited to the Sun. See what we have discussed most abundantly concerning this number in our *Arithmetica* regarding the seals of the planets. The **Hieromants** <note>Interpretive priests of sacred mysteries</note> wish to signify by this number both the triads and dodecads of all nature, from which he draws the fulfillment of his perfection. This is expressly taught by the scepter with an eye and the figure of lightning, by which they indicate the penetrating power of the Sun. Hence, the Sun is rightly called the "fiery source" by **Zoroaster**, as we have taught in the preceding pages. This Genius is likewise indicated by the figure in the region of **M**, conspicuous for his <term>serpent-circle-wing-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: ὀφι-κυκλο-πτερο-μόρφῳ (ophi-kyklo-ptero-morphō)</note> headdress. He opens the gate of moisture, and having driven away the Owl <note>A symbol of darkness or night</note>, he exercises dominion over the fourfold face of the World.

<margin>
Station V. The station of Horus, and an explanation of his attire.
</margin>
In the region of **N**, a boy is seen placed in a receptacle, prostrate and wrapped in a robe: this is called the **Station of Horus**. For the Egyptians recount that **Horus** was nourished near Buto <note>An ancient city in the Nile Delta</note> among the stagnant lagoons of the Nile, by vapors and exhalations, according to the testimony of **Plutarch**. By this they secretly hint that this sensible world cannot possibly exist without the nourishment of a humid substance. He is depicted as a boy because the world, nourished by moisture, is daily rejuvenated, as it were; and he is strengthened by the fluid element (which clearly shows itself surrounding the figure of Horus, as if expressing the flow of water). By the beneficial power of **Osiris** (whom the following Hawk denotes) and the direction of his dominant motion, the moisture is gathered into its receptacles by the power of the rays (which the attached horns denote), where by the industry of **Mophta** <note>A Kircherian term for a supreme demiurgic or generative force associated with the Nile</note> he establishes the

<margin>
Sacrifices made to Horus.
</margin>
beginnings of new generation. Hence, the Priests of Mophta, in order to obtain this so beneficial moisture, were accustomed to establish sacrifices to Horus—that is, to the sensible World—carrying Nilotic vessels on their heads, as **Plutarch** testifies. They expressed the 

<margin>
Plutarch.

Since the remaining symbols are worn away, I have deliberately decided to omit their interpretation, although they could easily have been restored from those that remain.

## § II.

### Second exposition of the column of the third side.

In this column, the **water-divine** <term>hydrothea</term> chain is contained: by which the protection of six Divine Powers, who guard against things contrary to human nature, is displayed. And first, indeed, one encounters the station of Providence, indicated by an eye, a seat, a statue, and two arms. The first of these, having two wings beneath it, indicates a beneficial providence over the air; the other indicates providence over the water via an eye placed beneath a **water-symbol** <note>original: "hydroschemati"</note>. For by this aerial vehicle—signified by an oar and a wing—Providence carries the moisture of the water-vessel into the World and the celestial regions. These regions are indicated by the **Scarab** (according to the testimony of Horus) and by a cycloid with two rhomboids. Despite the machinations of the **Typhonian Owl** <note>Kircher often associates the owl with Typhon/Set as a symbol of darkness or obstruction</note>, the guardian of the water-chain remains watchful, as the Hare figure with its added symbols teaches across from **E**. <margin>First Station: Water-divine Providence.</margin>

### First Corollary .

<margin>The 48 stations of the Genii correspond to the 48 stations of the Gods in Heaven.</margin>
You see, therefore, how on each side twelve Genii <note>Protective or guiding spirits</note> are shown on the top of the Obelisk, indicated by as many stars; these, joined into one sum across the four sides, constitute 48 Genii of the entire celestial and elementary nature. This is the same number of stations or mansions of the ancestral Gods that they were accustomed to place in the firmament; consequently, these 48 stations of the Genii correspond perfectly to those which we have shown in both the Egyptian celestial hemispheres in our section on Astrology. 

<margin>Stations of the Gods in the firmament.</margin>
For the Egyptians believed that there were certain stations in the firmament for the Gods presiding over all of nature, by whose influence all lower things were managed; so much so that there is no level of being among the lower things which does not have its own president and preserver in the firmament. However, because whatever exists in the World consists of a mixed communication of the four Elements through a joining together, they placed the presidents of these four Elements as their <term>Archons <note>original Greek: ἄρχοντες (archontes), meaning rulers or governors</note></term> at the very beginning of the obelisk’s faces and fronts. These were the Leaders and Princes of the chain of Divinities that follow in each column; thus, each Archon had a chain of Divinities linked to himself, as was clear from the interpretation. By their care and guardianship, the specific parts of the economy of the <term>material World <note>original Latin: "hylæi Mundi"</note></term> were managed. Hence, from the Southern Archon of Fire, the remaining twelve are called Presidents of a fiery nature; from the Eastern Archon, the President of Air, come the guardians of the aerial World; from the Western Archon, the President of Water, the guardians of the watery World; and finally from the Northern Archon, the President of Earth, the twelve Presidents of the terrestrial economy are named. For they believed that by the administration of these, the entire machine of the Sensible World was preserved.

### TREATISE V. THE BARBERINI OBELISK. CHAPTER VIII.

->*Second Corollary.*<-

Note, Reader, that we have interpreted the individual contents of this Obelisk according to the physical sense alone—that is, insofar as they regard the face of the sensible World. However, as we have warned elsewhere, the greatest mysteries of the Archetypal World <note>The "Archetypal World" refers to the divine realm of pure ideas or blueprints that Kircher believed preceded the physical creation</note> lie hidden beneath these symbols; all of these, nevertheless, can easily be applied to that same world through a certain analogy. For whatever things are seen in the Starry or Material World exist in the Archetypal World in a divine condition—that is, they are intelligible and reachable by the mind alone. Since these matters have been treated most abundantly in the <term>Hebrew Cabala</term> <note>Kircher often linked Egyptian wisdom to Jewish mystical traditions</note>, Music, and Hieroglyphic Theology, we refer the Reader there. Hidden within these are also the mysteries of the Political World, which I leave to others to apply according to the intended analogy. Yet it is a wonder that the Egyptians, under one and the same set of symbols and through a certain method of analogical consideration, exhibited such varied and diverse meanings. See the places cited a little earlier, and the remaining arguments of this Work, where we discuss this subject throughout.

->*Third Corollary.*<-

Finally, it is clear from these points that the Egyptian Hieromants <note>original: *Hieromantas*; sacred interpreters or priests of the mysteries</note> alluded both to those things already explained in the preceding pages and, most especially in the Starry World, to the 48 Asterisms <note>The 48 constellations recognized in the ancient Ptolemaic system</note>, which they call the "stations of the Gods," and which we displayed under two hemispheres in the *Egyptian Astrology* on page 208. For if you correctly compare the two hemispheres explained in that cited place with the diagrams of this Obelisk, it will appear clearly that the Obelisk and the said Iconisms <note>symbolic images or celestial figures</note> contain the same information, even if represented under a different position, arrangement, order, and names. For they represent the stations of the Divine Powers, in which they were thought to act through a particular influence upon the lower things committed to their faith and protection; hence they were called "monads or gateways" <note>original Greek: *μονὰς ἢ πυλῶνας*</note> and "stations" or "mansions of the Gods," as I said, because in them they attended to the things committed to them with watchful care.

->*Conclusion.*<-

Thus, you have the arrangement of the 48 <term>Iconisms</term> <note>from the Greek *eikonismos*, meaning a depiction or symbolic representation, here referring to the 48 constellations</note> placed in the heavens by the Egyptians, and the physical interpretations of the same, which they also adapted through a certain analogy to archetypal and moral reasons. In this way, through the symbols of the said Iconisms, the Intellectual World might be understood; in this realm, they subtly suggested the distribution of duties fitting for each choir of Genii <note>protective or governing spirits</note>, upon which they impress effects both in the triple series of Worlds and especially in the spheres of souls; for from here they derived the order of fates. <margin>The impious superstition and divination of the Egyptians and Chaldeans derived from the Iconisms of the 48 stars.</margin> From these ascending Iconisms of the Genii, they believed they could know an infallible conjecture regarding the fortune or fate of anyone’s birth. For this reason, they solicitously observed the individual stations of the Gods as soon as they emerged from the Horizon, or culminated in their ascent, at which point the sacred—

<summary>Kircher concludes his study of the Barberini Obelisk by linking its symbols to the 48 constellations (Iconisms) and the spiritual hierarchy of the "Archetypal World." CHAPTER VIII. 302 HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...they strove to appease them, partly through sacrifices and partly through rites and ceremonies. For just as they believed that all the misery and calamity of a newborn child depended on the unfavorable rising of the Spirits <note>original: *Geniorum*</note>, so too they promised themselves fortune and happiness from the benevolent and propitious rising of the <term>Agathodaemones</term> <note>From the Greek 'agathos' (good) and 'daimon' (spirit); these were "good spirits" believed to bring luck and protection</note>. For this reason, they strove to appease the former with sacrifices so that they would not cause harm, and to attract the latter through appropriate objects and sacrifices so that they might be beneficial. Since, however, the seven principal planetary Powers <note>original: *Numina*</note> are continually joining good things to the good, then good to the wicked, and subsequently evil things to the evil, they made pronouncements about favorable or unfavorable outcomes based on the nature of the planetary conjunction. This entire collection of symbolic images <note>original: *Iconismorum*</note> featured four principal Powers, which are indicated by the first four diagrams <note>original: *schematismos*</note> on the four sides; by their flowing influence, both the series of linked Spirits <note>original: *Geniorum*</note> described on the sides and the order <note>original: *oeconomia*</note> of the lower world are governed. But let these remarks concerning the Barberini Obelisk <note>Now known as the Obelisk of Antinous, currently located on the Pincian Hill in Rome</note> suffice.

I dedicate and present the Theodosian Obelisk to you, most eminent Prince **ANTONIO**, you who represent a *Theodosian* <note>original: *Theodosianam*; a play on the name of Emperor Theodosius, implying the Cardinal shares his imperial virtues</note> soul. For indeed *Emperor Theodosius*, endowed with a great soul, erected that monument in *Constantinople* <note>original: *Constantinopoli*</note> so that he might consecrate a symbol of his glory; in like manner, I erect it again, expressed through an accurate drawing, but with printing types, not machines; not for *Byzantium* <note>Istanbul</note> alone, but to be viewed by the whole world, so that it may be a perennial tribute to your glory. Although you do not need this document to become known to posterity, nor this Egyptian mass to appear before the world; your own character and your soul, striving for great things, will raise a theater worthy of you. I wished rather to look after my own duty, lest in this work, by which I restore hidden Antiquity, I should pass you by unpraised, you who deserve so well of our Society <note>The Society of Jesus, the Jesuits</note>: for nothing ought to be more ancient to us than to show a grateful will toward our Benefactors. Farewell, glory of the Ecclesiastical Principality, and delight of the *City of Rome*.

# TREATISE VI.

# The Obelisk of Constantinople, formerly erected by Emperor Theodosius in the Byzantine Hippodrome.

## CHAPTER I.

### A historical account of the origin and erection of the Obelisk of Constantinople.

<margin>The Obelisk of Constantinople.</margin>
**A**fter I had obtained nearly all the surviving Obelisks both in Rome and in Egypt, only the Obelisk of Constantinople—which I had read was once erected with the greatest magnificence by Emperor Theodosius in the *Great Circus* <note>The Hippodrome of Constantinople, a massive stadium for chariot racing and the social center of the Byzantine Empire.</note> of Byzantium—was still missing for the completion of this work. And just as I was possessed by a great desire for it, I "turned over every stone" <note>An idiom meaning he spared no effort.</note> so that I might gain possession of it; for with all others now obtained, it could be said that only this one was lacking. Therefore, I soon sent letters to the most excellent Lord Simon Reniger, who at that time was serving as the Ambassador of his Imperial Majesty to the Emperor of the Turks <note>The Ottoman Sultan</note> at Constantinople. In these letters, I earnestly entreated him to contribute his efforts toward finishing this Imperial Work in all its parts; I informed him that my wishes and prayers would be satisfied if he would soon transmit a drawing of the Theodosian Obelisk, which still survives in the Byzantine Circus. The Imperial Ambassador, out of his great kindness and his zeal for promoting the *Republic of Letters* <note>The international community of scholars and intellectuals in the 17th century.</note>, decided that my wishes ought to be granted. He immediately entrusted the entire matter to Panagioti Nikousios, a Greek who was then serving as the interpreter for the Imperial Legate at the Ottoman Court—a man truly distinguished both for his skill in languages and for his all-embracing erudition. Nikousios himself, thinking that this was an opportunity to serve the Republic of Letters that should by no means be neglected, soon drew the Obelisk, and once drawn, transmitted it to me in Rome shortly thereafter. Truly, so that it may be revealed with what care and diligence both men promoted this work, I have thought it proper to include the letters of both here for the memory of posterity.

Having set forth these authentic letters, we shall now begin the historical account, which proceeds as follows.

<margin>Historical account of the Constantinople Obelisk.</margin>
**Emperor Theodosius**, following the glorious undertakings of Caesar Constantine the Great, understood that Constantine had constructed the Great Circus of Byzantium <note>The Hippodrome of Constantinople</note> in the likeness of the Roman Circuses. Constantine had intended to gift the Circus with the largest of all obelisks—which he had already transported from Thebes to Alexandria—as a lasting monument to his glorious memory. However, upon Constantine’s death, that obelisk (which had been left in Alexandria and destined for the Byzantine Circus) was instead brought to Rome by his son Constantius and placed in the Circus Maximus. Emperor Theodosius, lest the Byzantine Circus—which had been built by Constantine with such great magnificence and was entirely equal to the Roman one in all respects—should remain undecorated and unseemly without the ornament of an obelisk, is said to have sent men skilled in such matters to Egypt. He ordered them to bring back to Constantinople whatever obelisks of better quality they could find remaining after the Roman spoils. Once these were brought back, the more famous locations of the City were assigned to them, among which was the Great Circus, which received this present obelisk. Regarding its magnificence, size, and its colossal nature, consult the Frenchman **Pierre Gilles** in his *Topography of the City of Byzantium*, Book 2, Chapter 11, where all these matters may be read, treated with the greatest diligence and keen study. We shall quote here from his *Topography* only those things that concern the obelisks, about which he brings forward these points among others:

<margin>Pierre Gilles.</margin>
> "In the middle of the Circus, which the Greeks call the *Hippodrome*, there stands an obelisk made of Theban stone. Since the ancient description of the regions <note>The 'Notitia Urbis Constantinopolitanae', a 5th-century list of the city's landmarks</note> does not mention it, yet does mention a square Theban obelisk located in the Fifth Region, I would have thought this one had been overturned by an earthquake and moved to the Hippodrome by Theodosius after that description of the regions was published—were it not for the fact that the description mentions many other works of Theodosius."

The other, however, in the middle of the Hippodrome as a turning-post <margin>Base of the Constantinople Obelisk.</margin> <term>meta</term> <note>The conical posts at the end of a Roman circus track that chariots had to turn around</note> stands to this day upon four bronze blocks <term>tesserae</term> a foot and a half wide in every direction and just as high, supported by a base and a pedestal. From the ground, the pedestal has two steps, of which the lower is one foot high from the earth, with a width of one foot; the upper step is another two feet, projecting four feet and four inches beyond the pedestal; the underlying steps are not part of the pedestal itself, but are added and built on like a platform, as appears from the joints. Above these, the pedestal projects 12 feet on each side to a height of 4 feet and 8 inches, and extends a foot and a half beyond the base. Beyond these four feet and six inches, the pedestal exceeds a foot in height where it does not project beyond the base; for from the top of the pedestal emerges a four-sided molding, a foot and thirteen inches high, consisting of a single, continuous, and identical stone as the pedestal. For the pedestal sends out its uppermost part not only a foot and a half narrower than the lowest part, but also with the corners cut away; in place of these four diminished corners stand four square stones of red Thebaic marble, each a foot and a half high—exactly as high as the molding of the pedestal—enclosed by these four corner stones. These, together with the intermediate uppermost part of the pedestal, support a base 7 feet and 13 inches high, projecting a foot and a half beyond the bottom of the Obelisk's shaft, extending nine feet and as many inches in every direction. This entire base is carved, as is the pedestal, which has all its sides engraved with prominent statues. <margin>Symmetry of the Constantinople Obelisk.</margin>
From this account, the symmetry of the entire Obelisk is clear. Since, by assumption, each side of the Obelisk’s base measures six feet, and a foot contains 1.5 palms, the width of the base on each side will necessarily be 9 palms. Furthermore, as we demonstrated regarding the Pamphilian Obelisk, the height of obelisks up to the <term>pyramidion</term> <note>the small pyramid at the very top</note> is ten times the width of the base; 9 multiplied by 10 will give 90 palms for the height of the said Obelisk. And since the pyramidion usually has a height equal to the side of the base, and the base is 9 palms, the Obelisk will necessarily reach a height of 99, or nearly 100 palms. If to this we add the <term>stylobate</term> <note>the platform or pedestal</note> and its fluting, which rise 9 feet high above the pavement, the height of the entire Obelisk will be nearly 114 palms—provided that the measurement by Pierre Gilles is accurate and it were certain to us that a "Gyllian foot" is equal to one and a half Roman palms. Whatever the case may be, the reader should meanwhile accept the assigned measure based solely on this hypothesis, until that eminent man Panagiotis Nikousios <note>A prominent 17th-century scholar and diplomat</note>, praised above, provides us with a more exact symmetry of the said Obelisk through his own diligence. But let us now proceed to unfold the interpretation of the said Obelisk.

# CHAPTER II.
## The Meaning of the Obelisk.

<margin>The meaning of the Constantinople Obelisk.</margin>
This Obelisk contains, first, how rites and ceremonies are to be ordained by the Priests according to the pattern and exemplar of the Intellectual or Genial World <note>A Neo-Platonic concept referring to the realm of pure spirits and divine ideas</note>, both for the proper and blessed administration of the political state of the kingdom, and for obtaining an abundance of all good things. For, as we showed above in the exposition of the Lateran Obelisk, they recognized that any kingdom could by no means persist for a long time unless founded upon the principles of the divine Power. Moreover, they had learned from the Hermetic books that nothing could be more pleasing or acceptable to God and His attendant spirits and ministers than if they aligned all their actions, both private and public, with those ideal principles. Certainly, all their study and effort was turned toward this end: to perform everything as exactly as possible according to the laws prescribed for them by Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and scientific texts were attributed</note>. They persuaded themselves that it was impossible for the Divinities to ever fail their prayers, provided they had won them over with such a grand display of rites and ceremonies.

<margin>Figures of the first section.</margin>
All these things are contained on this Obelisk, where on sides A, R, H, and Y, figures appear in the first position. Some of these are seen kneeling, others partly standing and partly kneeling with mitered heads, and with various gestures, as if they were about to consult on great matters. These figures indeed have a double significance: the first exhibits the operations of the supramundane <term>Agathodaemons</term> <note>original: "Agathodæmonum"; literally "good spirits," often depicted in Egypto-Greek magic as protective deities</note>, some of whom seem to sit because they are immediately subject to the influx of the supreme Divinity, while others are

# CHAPTER II

...are subject to higher powers set over them, as if to authorities, in order to carry out the commands of the supreme Deity. Some are distinguished by a mitred head and staffs, because they excel in the power communicated to them by the supreme Deity. Nearly all have the <term>hieralpha</term> <note>A sacred symbol, often identified by Kircher as a type of cross or the 'Ankh', signifying divine life or power</note> attached to them because they are <term>Agathodaemones</term> <note>original: "Agathodæmones"; from the Greek for "good spirits" or "benevolent divinities"</note>, as I have said: supramundane beings marked with the beneficial character of the supreme Deity. They are seen in various gestures as if about to consult on some matter of great importance, by which gestures is signified the utmost concern, care, and diligence with which they desire to promptly execute the commands of the Divinity. And this is the first meaning. 

The second meaning presents a certain model proposed to the Priests, by which they might establish their rites and ceremonies. Those who were about to consult the Gods in their inner sanctums regarding matters of great importance were advised to perform the sacred rite in exactly that habit in which the symbolic representations of the Divinities are seen; so that if their operations were <note>original: "ἀναλογωτέραι", meaning "more analogous" or "proportionate"</note> to the operations of the Gods, the sacrifices thus instituted would also obtain a greater effect by this means. Hence, they were accustomed to perform the sacred rites naked, mitred, equipped with scepters, now standing, now kneeling, and transformed into various appearances by different gestures. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> beautifully teaches that all these things are true in his *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, and we have demonstrated this at length from every kind of authority in our *Magic and Theology*, as well as in the exposition of the <term>Bembine Tablet</term> <note>A famous bronze tablet with Isiac symbols, also known as the Mensa Isiaca</note>, to which we refer the curious reader.

<margin>Figures of the second compartment.</margin> Truly, since the operations of these supramundane Agathodaemones would be idle unless they tended toward something else, for this reason, in the second compartment of the four sides B, S, I, and Z, they express another series of Intelligences, which they call Mundane, and which undertake the care of administering the sensible World. These are immediately subordinate to the supramundane beings, and, illuminated by their influences, they provide for the abundance of all necessary things. The symbol of this is the beetle-shaped butterfly <note>original: "Papilio σκανθαρομορφος"</note> placed upon the heads of almost every individual. These are also Mundane Agathodaemones, as the hieralpha attached to them teaches. Yet, because in these choirs of Intelligences—as the necessity of order demands—some preside and others are subject, the Presides are rightly indicated by the tiara and the seat (symbols of power), while the subjects, performing the duty of ministers, are deprived of the tiara and kneel before the Presides. By the very position of their bodies, they more than sufficiently signify their obedience, subjection, and readiness in executing those things commanded by the Preside. By this very act, they secretly indicate what ought to be done in the proper administration of any Kingdom. Since all these things have been most amply explained in our *Egyptian Politics*, as well as in the exposition of the <term>Lateran Obelisk</term>, we refer the reader there.

<margin>Figures of the third compartment.</margin> Again, since the Mundane Intelligences, in their earthly administration, flow most closely into the Sidereal World, they chose to exhibit the third receptacle, C, directly below the second. This represents the Sidereal World <note>The world of the stars and planets</note>, shown by no better means than through the Hawk—that is, the celestial Osiris, the Solar Deity, who by his power instills life, motion, and heat into all parts of the sensible World. For here he propagates his virtue into the <term>hylic</term> <note>material or elemental</note> or elemental Osiris—who is aptly indicated by the Bull and the Asp, and by the statues of the lower Agathodaemones—and, as if through his ministers, he animates, fertilizes, and preserves all things.

# TREATISE VI. THE OBELISK OF CONSTANTINOPLE. CHAPTER II.

Rr

But since we have explained these matters in our discussion of other Obelisks, we shall not dwell on them here. <margin>The Bull as a symbol of the Solar Divinity.</margin> At this point, a doubt might perhaps arise in someone’s mind: why, on the third side in space K, is the figure of a Bull placed instead of a Hawk? I respond that not only was the Hawk a symbol of the Solar Divinity, but so too was the bull, as we have taught at length regarding the Pamphylian Obelisk, in the <term>Hierogrammatism</term> <note>The symbolic or sacred system of writing</note> of the Bull, and in the interpretation of the Serapaic triad in the Bembine Tablet. The Hawk and the Bull were symbols of one and the same Sun, distinguished only by the diversity of their operations. Hence, just as Porphyry called the Hawk a <term>living image of the sun</term> <note>original Greek: ἔμψυχον τοῦ ἡλίου ἄγαλμα</note>, so Plutarch called the Bull a <term>living image of Osiris</term> <note>original Greek: ἔμψυχον Ὀσίριδος εἰκόνα</note>, as has been said throughout this work; thus the Egyptians frequently used these symbols interchangeably. Although these things are most true, because the Egyptians did nothing without the highest reason, they seem to have been led by a deeper plan to place the Bull on this side instead of the Hawk, which I shall now explain.

In the Northern region, toward which this side was turned—namely, in Lower <margin>Why the Egyptians placed the Bull instead of the Hawk.</margin> Egypt, which is fertile with pastures and greening fields—the cult of the Bull flourished most greatly, as we have taught most amply in the Treatise on the Chorography <note>The description or mapping of regions</note> of Egypt. For the celestial Osiris, indicated by the Bull, exerted his power most especially in providing an abundance of things and granting other benefits of nature, as is beautifully shown by the arm with the <term>Capreolus</term> <note>A vine-tendril</note> of the vine placed beneath the Bull. Hence, they not inappropriately carved the Bull on this Northern side instead of the Hawk, so that they might secretly hint at the benefits of the Sun in the works of agriculture, of which the Bull was the symbol; whereas they turned the Hawk toward the remaining regions, which abound in heat and spirit. The reader, however, may hold either of the reasons proposed here without error.

And this is the <term>Inscription</term> <note>original: Epigraphe</note> of the Obelisk, by which they indicated that just as a flow from the <margin>The Idea of the Political State.</margin> supreme Divinity is given through the superior Powers in a truly wonderful order of continuity through the various constitutions of the Worlds, so too should it happen in the Political World. In this world, a King, holding the place of the supreme Divinity, flows through the Nobles of the Kingdom into the men of the middle station, and through these into the common people, providing for the necessities of each. They persuaded themselves that only in this way could an established Kingdom be preserved in its vigor. Having explained these things in order, let us now proceed to explain the columns placed in sequence.

Let us reveal what these things signify.

We have already explained how the inscription indicates the influence of the Universal Divine Power upon the worlds subject to it—the Intellectual, the Starry, and the Material <note>original: *Hylæum*</note> worlds. It follows now to show how this power flows into particular Divinities, and how these provide for the things entrusted to them. Among these, the **Polymorphic Spirit** <note>A spirit that takes many shapes</note>, indicated by the Butterfly, certainly holds the primary place. Its specific duty is to grant an appropriate form to each individual thing, as much in the Starry and Elemental worlds as in the Political world. Therefore, the ancients silently indicated through this symbol that just as there is a certain power in the World which the Platonists call the *venerable power* <note>original Greek: <term>αἰδοίαν</term>, referring here to a generative or preserving force</note>, which grants to each being what is necessary for its self-preservation; so too in the political world there is the Archetypal Intellect of the King, which, through life-giving laws, grants to each subject what is his own. For, as Plato witnesses, in order for the political body to be preserved in its vigor, the intellect of the subjects must be made to conform to the intellect of the King; by this conformity, it is brought about that everyone labors to provide for the common good. The Butterfly beautifully marks this political administration, for according to the conditions of its different ages, it is transformed into one form after another, just as the necessity of its nature demands. You may see all these matters treated most abundantly in my work on the *Pamphylian Obelisk*, and in other places in this present work.

<margin>Duties of the Polymorphic Spirit.</margin> Furthermore, this polymorphic spirit seems to have fixed its seat chiefly in the Sun, as if in the principal instrument of nature; this is indicated by the two following statues at F: the hawk, and the hawk-headed statue. For it is said to transform itself into a Hawk in the Sun because, by the aid of Solar life, heat, and motion, it effects a great variety of things in the lower worlds (which are indicated by the segments). Worship was offered to it under the image of the Hawk at position <margin>F</margin> F. For it is powerful in its dominion, as the statue with the curved staff teaches; and it is an **Agathodaemon** <note>A "Good Spirit" or protective deity</note> penetrating all things, renowned for its double scepter, <margin>H</margin> as the two feathers with the *hieralpha* at position H demonstrate. However, because this spirit is occasionally moved to indignation, a sacred <margin>I</margin> tablet I is placed as a kind of propitiatory monument to appease it. It consists of the Orb, indicating the supreme Divinity; the seven-towered structure <note>original: *heptapyrgo*</note> into which the power flows; the Scarab, indicating the material Osiris; and the Nilometer, upon which it acts and of which it is thought to be the guardian. Next, in the same region, follow **O**, the curved lines, the water-symbol, the circle, and the bier. Hence the Priests, before the **Mercurial Gate** (indicated by the letter **W** and guarded by two dogs), used to keep watch to propitiate the Divinity, intent on various sacrifices which are indicated by **X**. The letter **X** signifies an altar expressed in the likeness of a celestial bow, in the middle of which is a bowl, the symbol of sacrifice, which they were accustomed to perform according to the **Hermetic laws** indicated by the three boundary marks **Y**.

<margin>Explanation of the 4th side of the Constantinian Obelisk.</margin>
<margin>E</margin>
Having already explained the diagrams **V**, **Z**, **A**, and **B** on this fourth side above, let us now declare the rest. Therefore, in the region of the characters, the **Butterfly** <note>original: Papilio</note> with its staff <note>original: thyrsus</note> occurs everywhere, which follows immediately from the sacred tablet **E**. It indicates the influence of the many-shaped Spirit into the political world, just as the sacred tablet **E** shows, marked with a circle, a **seven-towered fortress** <note>original: heptapyrgus</note>, a **Scarab** with a circle, and an **eye**. By these it is indicated that, just as in the sensible world the supreme Divinity flows into the celestial seven-towered structure of the seven planets (of which Osiris is the leader and the eye of the world), so it also flows into the **political Sun**—that is, the master-building intellect of the King—and into the sevenfold ranks of the Kingdom, which we have explained in the *Egyptian Politics*, according to the intended analogy.

<margin>F</margin>
<margin>GH</margin>
The following signs show how this occurs: the **serpent-circle-wing-shaped globe** <note>original: ὀφι-κυκλο-πτερόμορφος</note> **F**, the sacrificial pit, the eye with the Nilotic vessel and scepter, the **Hawk** **G** sitting on a bier, the **seven-towered fortress** **H**, the pool, the cycloids, the crown, and the **Owl** sitting on a **twelve-towered structure** <note>original: dodecapyrgo</note>, etc. Thus, the winged globe, as has already been said often, indicates the triform Divinity, or the three powers in God, as Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> teaches; since these are the single principle of all things, all things rightly emanate from it as if from some overflowing Ocean. But as these things are worthy of consideration, it seemed fit to philosophize about them a little more deeply.

It has been explained quite often that the Egyptians were the first founders of Theology, and that all later thinkers who emerged as Philosophers of the first rank embraced the most sacred dogmas of the Egyptians, as it were. Among these were the Platonists, who, following the Egyptians to a man, confessed a divine triad. To make this apparent, we will cite **Plato** <margin>Plato.</margin> in this place, who in Book II of the *Laws* expressly asserts that a certain trinity of Divinities, which he calls **creative craftsmanship** <term>demiurgia</term> <note>original: δημιουργίαν</note>, always stands by Jove, the supreme Architect of the World. In this trinity, **Pallas** is the first, **Vulcan** the second, and **Mars** the third. But just as the whole trinity is referred back to Jove himself, from whom it originates, so Vulcan and Mars are generally referred to Pallas. Power flourishes in Mars, wisdom in Pallas, and in Vulcan...

### CHAPTER II. EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS'S HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER.
### SYN-

...a fiery spirit; these three things are required for the very art of Jove <note>Jupiter, the supreme Roman deity, used here to represent the primary Divine Mind</note>, by which he completes the Universe. First, indeed, is the **reason** itself, through which he is to make individual things; second is the **effective execution** of those things which he had conceived; third is the **safety and defense** of those things which are to be executed into effect. They name the Idea of the first **Pallas**; of the second, **Vulcan**; and of the third, **Mars**. 

And because both—namely, conservation or defense, as well as the execution or expression of things—require reason and wisdom; therefore Pallas presides over both Vulcan and Mars. For whatever is fabricated by Vulcan, or defended by Mars after it is fabricated and preserved in its form, is carried out under the leadership of Pallas. 

Of these three ruling principles in the divine art, we also see three traces in nature. Through **Pallas**, we see the order by which individual things are arranged; through **Vulcan**, the effective progress and a ready "port," as it were, toward which all things hasten; finally through **Mars**, the most fortified structure applied by the parents <note>original: generantibus; those things that bring others into being</note> to the offspring, and the various ramparts protecting their specific nature from opposing forces. 

Similarly, these three things ought to exist in every human art, but most especially in the **civil art** <note>the art of governance and politics</note>; so that individual things are thought out wisely before they are done, are executed maturely and vigorously, and are preserved and bravely defended in that form in which they were conceived and brought forth. 

Do these things not fitly correspond to the supreme Trinity which the Egyptians call <term>Hemphta</term>? <note>Hemphta is Kircher’s name for the Egyptian supreme divine intellect, often equated with the spirit or breath of the world.</note> Certainly, those whom Plato places as the attendants of Jove—Pallas, Mars, and Vulcan—the Egyptians, according to Iamblichus in his book *On the Mysteries*, identify as **Hemphta**: <term>Amun</term>, <term>Phta</term>, and <term>Osiris</term>. Of these, **Amun**, the Creator-Intellect and Lord of truth and wisdom, brings the hidden power of latent reasons into the light; **Phta**, performing all things without falsehood, artistically establishes all things together with truth (him they also call **Vulcan**); **Osiris**, indeed, the worker of good, strengthens, defends, and preserves all things by his power.

<margin>F</margin> But to return to our purpose: from that **F** triform Deity (to speak with the Egyptians), from that supreme pool <note>original: piscina; likely referring to the Neoplatonic "Source" or "Font" of divine influence</note>, from that super-celestial eye providing for all, from that **G** Archetypal <margin>G</margin> Osiris who is to be worshipped in every way, that **H** civil <margin>H</margin> "seven-towered city" <note>original: heptapyrgum; a symbolic representation of a perfectly ordered state</note> is strengthened by heavenly protection. The **K** Typhonian Owl <note>original: Noctua Typhonia; a symbol of chaos, darkness, or ignorance associated with the destructive god Typhon</note> <margin>K</margin> is driven away by the civil "twelve-towered city," which represents the Magistrates; by the beneficence of the Deities presiding over them, all <margin>N</margin> adversities are also called back from the civil seven-towered city. Through the **N** heavenly watchful **Anubis**, **Horus** the ruler of the Universe bestows life diffused into all the boundaries of the political World; from this, all things are animated, and all members keep watch over the care of the common good, which is the ultimate end of human happiness.

And these are the things which are contained and expressed in hieroglyphic figures on this **Obelisk of Constantinople** <note>The Obelisk of Theodosius in modern-day Istanbul</note>; by which Priests and men suited for the throne of the Kingdom were warned that they should establish their Republic according to the exemplar of super-celestial reasons, and should undertake to adorn it according to the economy of the sensible World, if they wished it to endure and enjoy continuous goodness. For by this pact, they trusted they would have the presence of the Deities, and assistance against adversities, as a firm and perpetual protection.

# TREATISE VII.
## The minor Obelisks: the Monticaelian, Medicean, and Mahutaean.
### CHAPTER I.
->*On the origin of these Obelisks.*<-

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting foliage and scrolls.</note>IN the *Pamphylian Obelisk* <note>original: "Obelisco Pamphylio" — Kircher's 1650 work on the obelisk now in Piazza Navona</note>, it was demonstrated at length that just as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure credited with inventing writing and science</note> was the author and founder of the hieroglyphic doctrine, so too was he the first builder of obelisks during the time of Mizraim <note>The biblical grandson of Noah, traditionally identified by Kircher as the first king of Egypt</note> and Misramuthis. However, even if it cannot be strictly proven what kind of obelisks these were, we are led by a very likely conjecture to believe they were smaller ones, and certainly not the larger ones. For we know from experience that the first principles of things take their origin not from the great and perfect, but from the small and imperfect. 

Indeed, in succeeding times, as the pride and magnificence of Kings grew, they were always erected larger and larger—not so much for the sake of displaying hieroglyphic doctrine, as for the sake of winning glory among posterity through the magnitude and vastness of such insolent masses. Since no other obelisks of this lower class are found except for the Monticaelian, the Mahutaean, the Medicean, and some fragments built into the houses neighboring the Roman College <note>The Jesuit headquarters in Rome where Kircher established his museum</note>, we conclude that all these were made at the same time. We gather this partly from the identity of the doctrine and symbols with which they are marked; they were, as it were, multiple copies of the first and new doctrine invented by Hermes. For they all possess nearly the same characters and the same doctrine, as will become clear from the interpretation of them. 

Furthermore, since the substance of the stone into which they were carved was extremely hard, and in those early times—when the arts had not yet reached their proper perfection—it seemed difficult to work, it is quite likely that they began with small obelisks. This continued until the art of sculpture, advanced by frequent practice, finally incited Kings to cut larger and larger stones after the model of these. 

A significant argument is added to our conjecture: among almost all the obelisks, none are carved with a cruder hand <note>original: "rudiori Minerva" — a Latin idiom meaning 'with less skill,' referencing Minerva as the goddess of wisdom and craft</note> or less artifice than these; this is a very clear sign of the first rudiments of the work. Indeed, Pliny openly teaches that this is the case in Book 36, Chapter 8, with these words: 

*“Near Syene in the Thebaid <note>Upper Egypt</note> is found <term>Syenite</term> <note>A type of granite from Aswan, often reddish in color</note>, which they previously called <term>pyropoecilan</term> <note>original Greek: "pyropoikilos," meaning 'spotted with fire' or 'red-speckled'</note>. The Kings made beams from it in a certain competition, calling them Obelisks and dedicating them to the Divinity of the Sun. The form of the obelisk is a representation of the sun's rays, and this is what the name signifies in the Egyptian language. The first of all to institute this was Mestres (understand this as Mizraim), who reigned in the City of the Sun <note>Heliopolis</note>, having been commanded by a dream; and this very fact is written upon it.”* 

Let us examine the individual points. First, he says the material of the obelisks...

However, the claim that Mizraim was incited to do this by a divine instinct in a dream is mere conjecture and a fiction added by the Historian; unless we say that this instinct was planted in the King's mind by Mercury, who because of his wisdom was regarded at that time as one of the Gods; as this is likely, I would not easily deny it. But when Pliny says that this very story is shown on the first obelisks via hieroglyphic symbols, it is false and invented; for, as will be clear from the course of our interpretation, nothing of the sort is contained in them, nor could it be. But for more on these matters, see the extensive treatment in Book 1 of the *Pamphylian Obelisk*. # CHAPTER II.

->**The Subject Matter of the three minor Obelisks.**<-

<margin>The subject matter of the minor Monticellian, Mahutean, and Medicean obelisks.</margin>
**T**hese three Obelisks are so similar regarding their inscriptions—except for a few details—that he who has explained one can be said to have explained the others. But let us begin with the subject matter.
First, these Obelisks are inscribed to the Sun, or the Archetypal Osiris <note>Osiris represented as the original divine source or "blueprint" of the universe</note>, and they show the manner in which he flows into the Worlds subject to him: the Genial <note>The world of spirits and intellect</note>, the Sidereal <note>The world of the stars</note>, and the Elemental <note>The physical world of the four elements</note>. Second, they show how, through this influence upon moisture and heat, both a variety and an abundance of things necessary for human life emerge. Third, through the ovated schemes <note>Referring to the oval "cartouches" that surround certain hieroglyphs</note> of the sacred tablets, they not only correctly and ingeniously indicated the manner of the influences of that supramundane Sun into the Genial World, as I have said, but they also believed the power and efficacy of these figures—which they wore both publicly and privately in appropriate worship—to be a support of great importance for drawing down the affections of that supramundane Osiris and the Genial World. # CHAPTER III.
## The Monticellian Obelisk, and its explanation.

<margin>The Monticellian Obelisk.</margin>
**I**t is called the Monticellian Obelisk because it is seen erected in the gardens of the Mattei family, which overlook the Caelian Hill <note>Latin: *Mons Coelius*; one of the seven hills of Rome</note>. This was first located in the garden of the Altar of Heaven <note>original: *Aræ Cœli* (Santa Maria in Aracoeli)</note> on the Capitoline Hill; from there, by the permission of the Roman People, it was removed and transferred to his own gardens on the Caelian Hill, near the Slope of Scaurus, where the most excellent Duke Ciriaco Mattei erected it and consecrated it for posterity. It was one of the forty-four smaller Obelisks that Publius Victor records as having been brought to Rome by the early Emperors. To make it appear more magnificent, the craftsmen placed it atop another column made of similar Memphite stone <term>Memphite stone: a type of red granite from Egypt, often associated with Memphis or Syene</term>, variegated with red spots. Thus, the Obelisk, which when considered by itself measured only 10 palms <note>approximately 7.3 feet or 2.2 meters</note>, is now found to have a height of 36 palms from the pedestal to the very top, including the column placed beneath it. Setting aside the figure of the entire Obelisk, we have seen to it that only the part marked with hieroglyphs be engraved in wood, as the following figure shortly hereafter will show.

<margin>The hieroglyphs of the Monticellian Obelisk.</margin>
The four sides of this Obelisk are A, B, C, and D, and if you except one or two figures, they are, as I said, entirely similar. Beneath the peaks <note>original: *apices*, referring to the pyramidion or the pointed top</note> in the first position on each side, there occurs the figure of a Scarab with outspread wings, expressing the act of flying, with a sphere placed upon its head. Then follow two oval diagrams—which we call "sacred tablets" <note>modern term: cartouches</note>—enclosed within each side of the pyramidion, filled with various images. Next follows the hooded figure of a Hawk <note>representing Horus or a solar deity</note> immediately below the pyramidion; it sits upon a quadrangle adorned with the figures you see. After this is a dragon-shaped fly, or a much-celebrated Butterfly, together with a papyrus thyrsus <note>a ritual staff</note>, which is immediately followed by an oval diagram adorned with the same figures as the third diagram within the pyramidion; a sacred Goose succeeds this, sitting upon another oval diagram, which is indeed exactly the same as the second diagram within the pyramidion. Let us now explain what all these things signify.

<margin>1. Meaning of the flying Scarab.</margin>
The figure of the Scarab marked with a circle, which is placed on the four sides immediately below the peak of the Obelisk, holds the place of an inscription and indicates nothing <margin>The Scarab signifies the supramundane Sun. Plutarch.</margin> other than the Supramundane Sun <note>The spiritual or archetypal source of light, as opposed to the physical sun</note>, the Archetypal Osiris hiding in the darkness of his own divinity as if in a center. It has a circle or sphere placed above its head to indicate eternity, immensity, and all those things which are proper to divinity, as we have demonstrated more than sufficiently in our dedicated study of the hierogrammatism <note>sacred writing system</note> of circular figures and with a wealth of various authorities. ### SYNTAGMA VII. THE MONTICELLIAN-MEDICEAN-MAHUTEAN OBELISK. CHAPTER III.

After the Scarab, two diagrams of sacred tables appear; <margin>Explanation of the 2 sacred tables placed beneath the Scarab.</margin> and they are called sacred tables because they were not only indicators of the highest mysteries, but were furthermore thought to have a singular power and efficacy for either attracting or appeasing the Spirits <note>Latin: *Genii*; presiding spiritual forces in Kircher's cosmology</note>; for their explanation, see the Flaminian Obelisk, page 221. They are placed immediately beneath the Scarab, so that the order and series of the divine influence into the Spirit-World <note>original: *Mundus Genialis*</note> might be indicated as being both closest and most similar to itself. Indeed, let us see who those Spirits are.

In the first place, within the oval table which we call "Osiriac," <margin>The Spirits of the Monticellian Obelisk adorned in the first diagram.</margin> marked with the number 3, two statues are seen in a sitting posture. The first, notable for its human face and a veil, holds two feathers on its head; with its hand resting on its knees, it holds a <term>Cucuphomorphon</term> scepter <note>a scepter topped with the head of a hoopoe bird (Cucupha), symbolizing gratitude or filial piety</note>. By this apparatus, they indicated nothing other than the Spirit presiding over the **moist-warm** quality. <margin>The Spirit presiding over the moist-warm.</margin> It is depicted with a human face to denote the power of intellectual potential and its providence in looking out for the necessities of the World; it wears two wings on its head to indicate its wondrous agility in communicating itself to both the upper and lower Worlds. Its posture is <term>Ypsilomorphos</term> <note>shaped like the Greek letter Ypsilon (Y)</note>, <margin>The Spirit presiding over the dry-warm.</margin> that is, in the form of the letter Y, to indicate the reception of the influence sent from the supreme Divinity and its diffusion into the lower World, as has been proved extensively elsewhere; in its hands, it holds a scepter in the form of a <term>Cucupha</term>, by which is indicated the variety of things that it communicates to the World, dispersed by the power of heat, as we have explained elsewhere. The other statue is *hawk-headed* <gloss>original: ἱερακόμορφος</gloss>, that is, shaped with a hawk’s face, in the same position and habit as the former, with a globe looming over its head, holding in its hands a <term>Tautic character</term> <note>a symbol shaped like the letter Tau (T), often representing life or the distribution of divine power</note>. And through this statue, they denoted the Spirit presiding over the **dry-warm**: the <term>Ypsilomorphos</term> posture is the same as that of the previous statue; the globe looming over the head signifies participation in divinity; the <term>Tautic character</term> notes the distribution of the shared influence through all the members of the World. A litter is placed beneath them, by which they suggested that the said Divinities should be worshipped with the highest honor. Why they judged them worthy of such great honor, they aptly demonstrate by the following three symbols: first, a papyrus branch, signifying the abundance of all things necessary to the human race; second, a reed staff or hollowed wand, by which a proper temperament and harmony are to be brought into things; third, a triple branch of persea, by which they signified the three parts of the year, which the said Spirits fostered by their administration, stirred toward the generation of things, and defended against every adverse force; all of which have been confirmed from every kind of erudition in the section on the Flaminian Obelisk. And this is the meaning of the first oval diagram. The second oval diagram, which we call <margin>The other oval diagram of the Monticellian Obelisk.</margin> <term>Momphto-Mendesian</term>, and is marked with the number 2, is constituted by an image that is *lion-shaped* <gloss>original: λεοντόμορφος</gloss>, that is, visible in the figure of a Lion; obtaining the same posture as the previous ones, it holds a <term>Tautic character</term> in its hand; a scepter follows that is goat-headed <note>original: *ægimorphon*</note>, or marked with the head of a goat.
