### CHAPTER III.

...[Osiris], indicated by the flying Scarab, flows into the Genial World, and from here into the Sidereal World, whose soul they call Osiris, noted by the mitred Hawk; and from here into the Genii of the Elementary World, Apis and Mophta; now let us see what they indicate through the chain of symbols that follow.

<margin>The realm of Morpheus shines forth in the Elementary World.</margin> Since, therefore, the realm of Morpheus <note>Kircher uses "Morpheus" here to refer to the "shaper of forms," derived from the Greek word *morphe*</note> properly shines in the Elementary World—in which, according to the Egyptians, the principle of generation is the watery Element, aptly expressed by the Nile, where the generations of things are perfected by the fertile power of warm moisture—it is for this reason that, after the inscription of the fourfold World, they placed in the first position for this realm of Morpheus the **dragon-shaped butterfly** <margin>Dragon-shaped Butterfly. 9</margin> <term>dragon-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: δρακοντόμορφον (*drakontomorphon*)</note> with a papyrus stalk. By the Butterfly, they noted the presiding spirit over the diversity of forms, namely a <term>many-formed</term> <note>original Greek: πολύμορφον (*polymorphon*)</note> Genius <note>a guardian or guiding spirit</note>; by the papyrus stalk, they noted the abundance of all things necessary for the human race, about which see the extensive treatment in countless places in this Work. But because this diversity of things and forms shines most clearly in the <margin>Sacred Tablet of Momphta-Ammonia. 10</margin> watery Element of the sublunary World, they aptly placed an oval figure, in which is the statue of Mophta with a goat-headed scepter, by which Mophta and Mendes are denoted. Of these, the latter is the presiding spirit of fertility, and the former of the Nilotic moisture, as the Nilometer <note>a structure for measuring the Nile's flood level</note> placed below accurately teaches; by their work and continuous providence, both the fertile generation of things and an abundance of necessities are supplied.

<margin>Sacred Tablet.</margin> For this reason, the <term>Hierogrammatism</term> <note>a sacred arrangement of symbolic characters</note> of Mophta and Mendes was fashioned into the shape of an oval tablet, to show that this symbolic character possesses such power and efficacy that, when inscribed and established in infested places, no violent force of <term>opposing</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντιτέχνων (*antitechnon*), referring to hostile or "crafty" spirits</note> Divinities can prevail, as the beneficial Genii keep a watchful eye over the things committed to their trust, attracted by this secret and mystical structure of symbols, which is analogous to the nature and property of the Genii. Again, although the many-formed Spirit, a follower of the Solar Genius, duly carries out the diversity of forms through the powers of Mophta and Mendes, he cannot bring it to the desired <margin>Goose placed upon an oval figure. 11</margin> perfection without the help of Isis or the Lunar Genius. Therefore, they quite fittingly placed a **Goose**, which we call Chenosiris—that is, the Goose-Osiris <note>original: *Anserinum Osirin*</note>—upon another oval figure, by which the influence and vigilance of the Solar Divinity upon the Lunar disk was aptly noted. They believed that this influence could not be more effectively attracted <margin>Sacred Tablet. 12</margin> than through the following sacred tablet of an oval scheme, in which the <term>festive image</term> <note>original: *Comasia*</note> of Isis—conspicuous by the two feathers on her head and supported by a <term>cuckoo-shaped</term> <note>original: *Cucumorpho*</note> scepter—denotes prompt, swift, and sudden aid in the procreation of a variety of things. Opposite the statue of Osiris, this tablet has a Hawk-like figure marked with a <term>Tautic character</term> <note>a symbol resembling the letter T, often associated with life or divinity</note>. This signifies that once the Solar influence has entered all members of the lower World, and after the required ceremonies of honor and worship (signified by the bier) have been performed, the desired abundance of necessary things is finally achieved—signified by the papyrus branch; the proper tempering of things and the happy constitution of the three parts of the year are signified by the shepherd's crook and the triple branch. And this is the sum of the ideal concept which they signaled through the figures shining forth on the **Montecitorio Obelisk**, which we have firmly established above in the cited place from every kind of learning. The Reading of the ideal concept follows.

<meta>This page transitions from the analysis of the Montecitorio Obelisk (referred to here as the Monticellian) to the Medicean Obelisk. <margin>Reading of the Ideal concept of the Monticellian Obelisk.</margin> The supramundane Osiris <note>Osiris "above the world," representing the highest divine principle</note>, hidden in the center of eternity, flows into the Genial World <note>the realm of presiding spirits or "Genii"</note> as if into a neighboring, most similar, and immediate subject. <margin>1</margin> From here, he flows into Osiris as the deity and soul of the sensible World—that is, the Sun. <margin>2</margin> From here, into the Osiris of the elementary World, the beneficent **Agathodæmon** <note>original Latin: *Agathodæmonem*; Greek: *Agathos Daimon* or "Good Spirit"</note> Apis, <margin>3</margin> who distributes the shared power of Osiris into all members of the lower World <margin>4</margin>. His minister and faithful follower, the many-formed Spirit <note>original: *polymorphus Dæmon*</note>, through the variety which he creates and over which he presides, provides <margin>5</margin> an abundance and plenty of all necessary things. But because the beneficent power of the many-formed <margin>6</margin> Spirit can be hindered in various ways by opposing forces, for this reason the sacred <margin>7</margin> **Mophto-Mendesian** tablet <note>Referring to the spirit Momphta and the generative power associated with the district of Mendes</note> is ordered to be carried, through which he acquires the watery strength of the Nile <margin>9</margin> and fertility, to provide an influx of goods without hindrance <margin>10</margin>. Yet, because the many-formed Spirit is entirely insufficient for completing this business, the cooperation of **Isis** is necessary, by whose moisture the dryness of Mendes <margin>11</margin> may be tempered. To obtain this, the following sacred <margin>12</margin> **Osirian tablet** is arranged, which teaches what must be done in sacrifices and how to proceed in the **Gomalian** solemnities <note>Kircher's term for certain Egyptian festivals of joy or renewal</note>. Indeed, through this tablet and the contemplation of it, the supramundane Osiris finally provides the intended plenty of necessary things.

# CHAPTER IV.

## The Medicean Obelisk and its interpretation.

<margin>The Medicean Obelisk.</margin> The Medicean Obelisk is so called because it is seen erected to this day in the Pincian gardens of the Grand Duke of Tuscany <note>The Villa Medici in Rome</note>. It was one of forty-four smaller obelisks once brought from Egypt to Rome on the occasion of the larger ones, as witnessed by Publius Victor; it is thought to have been first placed in the Circus of Flora, from whose ruins it was excavated and moved to the Pincian Gardens, where it was erected as an ornament for the greenery. We here subjoin its four sides, engraved in copper, for the reader to contemplate along with their interpretation.

It should be noted, therefore, that the first nine **hierograms** <note>sacred inscriptions or symbol-groups</note> of this obelisk are exactly the same as the hierograms of the Monticellian Obelisk explained just a little while ago; and therefore I have judged it superfluous to repeat them in this place. For this reason, we shall proceed with the context of the hieroglyphics immediately following the nine mentioned hierograms, which are indeed different on each side of the obelisk.

We explained just a little earlier how Osiris, or the supramundane Sun, flows into the systems of the three worlds subject to him: the Genial, the Sidereal, and the Elementary. We have further explained what use, power, and efficacy the inscribed sacred tablets have in attracting the Spirits of the said Worlds. Now, in the remaining context, there follows an account of what effects the said Spirits provide when they have first been attracted by an analogous worship; these effects are noted differently on the different sides of the obelisk. Let us therefore begin from the first side.

Following the sacred tablets, then—that is, the oval patterns reviewed above—there follows:

### CHAPTER IV. 326 THE THEATER OF EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPHICS OF THE OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS

<margin>Interpretation of the first side, A.</margin>
There follows [figure] 21, a **hawk-shaped** <term>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφος; having the form of a hawk</term> statue, with 22, a papyrus branch, by which the Sun, providing the use of necessary things, is noted; the Ibis 23 succeeds this as a symbol of Isis; 24, a sacred sledge <note>A "traha" or sledge was used in Egyptian ritual processions to carry heavy religious objects</note> receives this. By these, they indicate that the Isiac power, set in motion by Osiris and carried into the hidden inner-sanctums of nature (the sign of which is figure 25, the labyrinth, with 26, a cycloid <note>A circular or curving path</note>), is propagated. This power is received from Osiris and Isis by the 27 Lion-like **Mophta** <note>A spirit or deity Kircher identifies as a creative force</note>, with 28 the **material Horus** <term>original: hylæo Horo; "hyle" is Greek for matter</term> as Leader, and distributed into the subterranean folds of the World, being powerful with a 30 double dominion, as if by a scepter both heavenly and infernal. To obtain this good more easily against opposing powers, the sacred tablet is prescribed; by its use and worship in granting 34 the gifts of the sacred Nile, 32 Mophta and the 32 goat-headed Mendes <note>The Egyptian god of the district of Mendes, often depicted as a ram or goat</note>, together with 35 Osiris, are **attracted** <term>original: allectantur; enticed or drawn in</term> as if by a powerful incantation, once the required worship has been performed.

<margin>Interpretation of the second side, B.</margin>
And this is the explanation of the first side. The second side, after nine sacred scripts <term>original: Hierogrammatiſmos; priestly writings or symbolic arrangements</term> and the amulets <note>original: phylacteria</note> of the sacred tablets, contains these figures: a circle, a quadrangle, and a **hawk-shaped** statue with a scepter. There follow 2 scepters, a semi-cycloid with three squares, the material Horus with a quadrangle, a three-horned beam, two semi-cycloids with two scepters, and the Mophto-Mendesian sacred tablet with a Hawk equipped with two scepters. But let us explain each one. The Hawk-like statue with the circle and quadrangle indicates that the power of the material Osiris is propagated from the Starry World into the material world through prior worship; from here, it is diffused by a double benefit into the three seasons of the year. The material Horus—that is, the elementary Sun—communicates this through a continuous revolution from Sunrise to Midday and even to Sunset, activating it in the subterranean parts of the Horizon, as he is powerful with a double dominion. So that this may happen in the best possible way, the Mophto-Mendesian sacred tablet is prescribed to be worshiped and carried along with the sacred statue of Osiris.

<margin>The third side, C.</margin>
The remaining corresponding symbols of the third side, which follow after the first nine sacred scripts, are two Ibises separated by a Nilotic vessel, with a water-symbol <term>original: hydroſchēmate</term>, a quadrangle, and a globe; which is immediately followed by a Hawk-shaped statue, with a quadrangle and a globe; and the yoke of a balance, under which are placed two arms with a quadrangle, a segment, a cycloid, and three quadrangles, and the symbol of a sacred chest. Then follows the **Comasia** <note>Likely referring to a "Comasia" or processional tablet used as a protective charm</note> sacred tablet, which is followed by a segment, a steering oar <note>original: temo; the tiller or rudder of a boat</note>, a sacred sledge, another segment, and a bier <note>A stand for a corpse or a coffin</note>. Let us explain each one.

The Ibis (or the Moon, the Guardian Spirit of the Nile) and the Ibis (or Isis), by means of the Nile and the watery element, [act upon] Osiris. He, through power transferred from the Starry World into the material realm, tempers every excess; being stirred by the constant worship of hymns, he blesses the three seasonal stations of the year in the lower World with an abundance of things. To obtain this against opposing powers, the following **Comasia** sacred tablet is prescribed, by whose protective use every happy progress of affairs is promised. What worship they ought to apply is beautifully shown by the last four symbols added: the steering oar, the sacred sledge, the segment, and the bier. By the steering oar, they noted the carriage of Osiris through the moisture; by the sacred sledge, works concerning agriculture; by the segment, the birth of subterranean offspring; and finally, by the bier, the due burial...

<margin>The fourth side, D.</margin> The remaining symbols of the fourth side begin from the figure marked with number 21; and it is an eye, to which are joined the figure of a labyrinth, with two cycloids <note>circular paths</note>, which a hawk-shaped statue followed by an owl succeeds; then a sacred Alpha with two other cycloids, and three quadrangles, a Serpent, and four other quadrangles, which, as in the preceding, are followed by the same oval schema of the sacred tablet, with a sledge, a pole, a segment, and a bier. Just as they judged great power was obtained by this symbol, so they believed the Typhonian power and <term>antitechnon</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντίτεχνον; an opposing force or 'rival in art'</note>, which was indicated by the Owl, was utterly put to flight by them. Once this is routed, the <term>Agathodaemon</term> <gloss>the 'Good Spirit'</gloss> or the good Genius of the heavens disposes the virtues in the material <note>Latin: hylæis; from the Greek term for matter</note> Worlds, and life in the lower parts of the earth according to the systems of the three seasons of the year; to obtain which, the sacred Comasian tablet etc. will be of great use, as was said on the preceding side. And this is the summary <note>original: perioche</note> of the matters contained on the Medicean Obelisk; so that you may more easily understand the context, we place here before the eyes of the curious Reader the method of the Ideal Reading.

# CHAPTER V.

->*The Mahutaean Obelisk and its exposition.*<-

The Mahutaean Obelisk is so called because it is seen erected at the Church of St. Mahutus of the Bergamasque Nation (for so the Orientals call St. Bartholomew, although there are some who would have it called corruptly under the name of St. Mahutus from St. Maclovius <note>St. Malo</note>, Bishop of Brittany, to whose honor it was first consecrated; concerning which see Pancirolus on the topography of the City). Its Northern side faces the said Church of St. Bartholomew; the Eastern, the new Basilica of St. Ignatius, founder of the Society of JESUS; the Southern, the square that lies between the Roman Gymnasium of the Society of JESUS and the Monastery of the Dominicans; while the Western side looks toward the Roman Seminary and the square leading to the Pantheon. And this Obelisk, excavated from the foundations of the Isiac temple, is thought to have been one of the 44 minor Obelisks about which we have dealt in the preceding sections. We have seen fit to present its proportion, symmetry, as well as the hieroglyphics contained on its four sides—engraved in copper with as much diligence as possible—here to the curious Reader together with their interpretation.

Note, Reader, that this Obelisk has all things in common with the Obelisks...

[THEATER OF EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPHS]

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

...the Montian and Medicean obelisks explained shortly before, except for those figures which are marked on the four sides by the letters **A B, C D, E F, G H**. The figures on side **A B** are: 21 Goose, 22 spear, 23 water-scheme, 24 Lion-like statue, 25 circle with a boundary-marker, 26 Nilotic channel, 27 Serpent, 28 an arm holding a flame in its hand, 29 cycloids <note>circular paths or patterns</note>, 30 segments, 31 scepters; and they produce this meaning: <term>Chenosiris</term> <note>Kircher's name for an aspect of Osiris, likely "Goose of Osiris"</note> guards the moisture; <term>Momphta</term> <note>Kircher’s term for the Divine Intelligence or the soul of the world</note>, the divine Intelligence, introduces life into things through the Nilotic channels with beneficial heat, to the heavens and the lower members of the World by the power of the following amulet.

The symbols on the second side, included in space **C D**, are: 30 twelve-towered castle <gloss>dodecapyrgon</gloss>, 31 water-scheme, 29 two feathers with three 28 Nilotic vessels, 27 Crocodile, 26 three boundary-markers, 25 twelve-towered castle, 24 three Nilotic vessels, 23 storehouse, 22 pool, 21 segment 32 with three boundary-markers. Their meaning is this: By the power of the preceding amulets, the twelve-towered castle <note>original: "dodecapyrgon"; representing the zodiac or celestial power</note> of moisture is led by motion into the Nile; with <term>Typhon</term> <note>the Egyptian deity Set, whom Kircher views as a destructive or chaotic force</note> defeated, the twelve-towered castle fills all the storehouses and pools of the Nile, by the virtue of the following amulet and the power of <term>Osiris</term>, who is always to be worshiped with the highest honor.

The symbols on the third side included in space **E F** are: 40 a Hawk standing upon 39 a cycloid, 38 the leaves of a gate, 37 three boundary-markers, 36 a handled vessel <gloss>vas ansatum</gloss>, 35 a Hawk-shaped statue; 33 a human head with 34 an altar, 32 a sledge, 31 segments with three boundary-markers, which involve this meaning: The celestial Hawk <term>Osiris</term> opens the gates of the three parts of the year; the Solar <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>A "Good Spirit" often associated with the sun or protection</note> and <term>Horus</term>, duly worshiped, bestow moisture upon the lower regions, all by the power of the following amulet and the singular honor of worshiping <term>Osiris</term>.

The symbols contained in the fourth side, the **G H** space, in order, express this meaning: The beneficial 22 moisture 24 of 25 <term>Horus</term>, who is the 28 author of planting, 27 sowing, and 26 the arrangement of the year, is inserted by 29 a hidden motion into the 30 vital 31 pools; from which both the 32 earthly and 33 airy elements are imbued with a fecund spirit by the power of the following amulet.

And this is the exposition of the Macuteo Obelisk <note>original: "Obelisci Mahutæi"; an obelisk originally from Heliopolis, moved to the church of San Macuto and later to the Pantheon square in Rome</note>; since many of the symbols already explained here are also contained on the Lateran Obelisk, I did not wish to be any longer in explaining them here.

### THE END OF THE SEVENTH SECTION.

<note>Decorative initial 'S' entwined with vines and flowers.</note>
IF it is true, Most High Prince, that Greek exclamation, <term>worthy of being carved</term> <note>original: "αξιογλυφος" (axioglyphos); a term used for men whose glorious deeds deserve to be immortalized in stone</note>, which is used for men distinguished by the glory of their achievements; then certainly anyone who deeply weighs the greatness of Your merits will see that this can be quite aptly applied to You above all others. The world knows with what undaunted constancy of spirit You conducted Yourself during the calamitous state of the Empire <note>likely referring to the devastation of the Thirty Years' War and its aftermath in Germany</note>, how prudently You eluded the snares of the enemies plotting against the Abbey of Fulda, and with what diligence You watched over the good of the Catholic religion in Your Principality—indeed, in such a great perversion of minds, You preserved it immune from every contagion of heresy. Since, therefore, there is so great a heap of Your merits; lest I be found guilty of unseemly ingratitude—both toward Your Highness, to whom I am subject by natural law <note>Kircher was born in the territory of the Abbey of Fulda</note>, and toward my homeland, from which I drew the beginnings of both my life and my knowledge—behold, I have seen fit to erect this present Obelisk as an eternal monument of glory to the splendor of Your name. Upon it, the honor of Your virtues may shine in the indelible carving of letters, as an example to others, and as an ornament of a name that shall never perish for our homeland. Farewell, Most High Prince, ornament of the Empire.

# SECTION VIII.

## The Heliopolitan Obelisk, which to this day is still seen standing near Matarea, a village near Cairo in Egypt.

### CHAPTER I.

->On the origin of the Heliopolitan Obelisk.<-

<margin>
By whom the Heliopolitan Obelisk was drawn.
</margin>

The first account of this Obelisk was offered to me by the most illustrious and noble Lord Matthias Balbiski, who is especially distinguished for his knowledge of various nations and the customs of peoples. While he was traveling through Egypt, he found it in a certain swamp near Matarea—a place famous to this day for the stay of Christ our Savior and the Virgin Mother <margin>Matarea of Egypt.</margin> <note>Matarea, or Matariyah, is traditionally associated with the "Holy Family's" flight into Egypt, specifically the "Tree of the Virgin."</note>—and he drew it with his own hand. The same was viewed by Father Marcus de Luca of the Order of St. Francis of the Observance, who, while I am writing this, told me in person that it stands in a certain lake, remarkable for its <term>hieroglyphics</term> <note>Kircher viewed hieroglyphs as symbolic repositories of ancient mystical wisdom rather than a phonetic writing system.</note>. However, it can only be reached at certain times of the year, namely when the waters of the <term>Nile</term> flood that were received in the said lake have dried up. 

He was the companion of a certain noble Architect often praised in this work: Lord Titus Livius Burattini, most skilled in mathematics, antiquities, and Oriental languages. To him, the reader will likewise credit whatever new material from Egypt has been brought into this work <margin>Titus Livius Burattini communicates many hieroglyphic monuments brought from Egypt to the Author.</margin>, as will be mentioned here and there in both the preceding and following sections; he even today acts as the Architect to the Most Serene King of Poland. When I asked him to communicate what he had observed in Egypt regarding hieroglyphic monuments that was worthy of note, he did so with the greatest readiness and kindness. He not only sent drawings of the remaining Obelisks made with the greatest industry and exact care, but also supplied many other things with which this work has been greatly enriched. Among other monuments, he sent me drawings of two Obelisks: one Heliopolitan, the other Alexandrian. We shall reason about the former first, and the latter afterward. But so that the reader may see the extreme diligence of this man, I will place here his words, which I have extracted from a letter <margin>Letter of Titus Livius Burattini concerning the Heliopolitan Obelisk.</margin> sent to me:

<note>original: "Doi ſtadij lontano dalla Matarèa..." — The following is translated from the original Italian.</note>
> Two <term>stades</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance; two stades is roughly 370 meters or 400 yards.</note> away from Matarea—a place famous for the Balsam tree, which died a few years ago (though there is more common fame that the Most Blessed Virgin Mary stayed there with our Lord and Saint Joseph when they fled the persecution of Herod)—one sees the remains of a very great city. In the forum of this city, one finds this Obelisk standing, which was measured and drawn by me; the hieroglyphs are the same on all four...

The text establishes the obelisk's location near Cairo and its association with the Holy Family's flight into Egypt.</summary>

...four parts; something that this one from Alexandria <note>Kircher is likely referring to the "Cleopatra's Needles" then still in Alexandria.</note> does not have. This ancient city the Arabs call <margin>Ancient site or location of Heliopolis.</margin> **Ain Shams**, which means *Eye of the Sun*; and it may be that this is the ancient Heliopolis, which was called the City of the Sun, being also on the eastern side of the Nile, just as it is said that Heliopolis was in ancient times. But let us hear the Arab geographer <margin>Abu'lfeda</margin> Abu'l-Fida <note>Abu'l-Fida (1273–1331) was a Kurdish geographer and historian whose works were highly valued by 17th-century European scholars.</note>, whose words explain the whole matter.

There are in it remarkable monuments of antiquity, constructed of very large stones and rocks; among other things, indeed, there is a square column which is called the Needle of Pharaoh (that is, an Obelisk). Its length is 30 cubits, and it is about a half-day's journey from Cairo. There is also in the same place a village called Matarea, situated on the left side of the Eastern Nile.* It is called the "Eye of the Sun" because of the worship of the Sun in that city, and because in the Temple of the Sun a mirror was constructed with such art that it reflected the radiant face of the Sun all day long, and thus illuminated the entire sanctuary with its light; concerning this, see my *Egyptian Mechanics*, and the first volume of *Oedipus*, pages 29 and 30, where you will find many things worthy of note regarding the Heliopolitan <term>Nome</term> <note>A 'nome' was an administrative district in ancient Egypt.</note>.

# CHAPTER II.
## On the erection & measurement of the Obelisk.

<margin>The erection and measurement of the Heliopolitan Obelisk.</margin> **W**ho exactly the erector of this Obelisk was is difficult to assert with certainty; since in such darkness of antiquity, nothing remains to us but conjectures. However, as far as I can determine, I would say it is one of those eight which <margin>Pliny.</margin> Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author who wrote the encyclopedic *Natural History*.</note> records that Sothis and his son Ramesses <note>Pliny’s "Sothis" is a historical corruption; "Ramesses" refers to Ramses II.</note> erected at Heliopolis. The words of Pliny are: *Afterward, other kings in the City of the Sun [erected obelisks]: Sothis, four in number, forty-eight cubits in height; and Ramesses, during whose reign Troy was captured, forty cubits:* that is, four others. From this testimony of Pliny, it is clearly evident that this present Obelisk is truly one of those four of forty-eight <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18–22 inches.</note>. If you convert 48 cubits into <term>palms</term> <note>A 'palmus' or palm was a smaller Roman unit of measurement.</note>, you will obtain a total of 96 palms; and <term>Titus Livius Burattini</term> <note>Tito Livio Burattini (1617–1681) was an Italian polymath who provided Kircher with accurate measurements from his travels.</note> found the height of this Obelisk to be exactly that many palms, excluding the <term>pyramidion</term> <note>The small pyramid at the very top of an obelisk.</note>; assuming that Pliny understood the height of 48 cubits to refer only to the shaft of the Obelisk. <margin>Measurements of the Heliopolitan Obelisk.</margin> And first, indeed, he places the height of the entire mass at 63 Capitoline Roman feet, plus 150 of those parts into which the entire Obelisk is considered divided. Furthermore, he places the base of the Obelisk at 6 and 644/970 of said feet, which when converted into palms are approximately...

<summary>Kircher uses Arabic geographical accounts and Pliny's Roman histories to identify the Heliopolitan Obelisk, concluding it is one of the monuments mentioned by Pliny and providing specific measurements taken by the traveler Burattini.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the Heliopolitan Obelisk (the obelisk of Senusret I at Matariyya), moving from the general measurements provided by Arab geographers to the specific architectural data recorded by the traveler Tito Livio Burattini. ...give 10 <note>This continues a measurement from the previous page, likely referring to cubits or palms.</note>. Indeed, the uppermost width of the side, where it meets the pyramidion <note>The small pyramid-shaped capstone of an obelisk.</note>, is 4 and 234/970 feet, which makes nearly 7 feet <note>Kircher's math or transcription of Burattini's units here is complex; he is likely converting between different regional standards of feet and palms.</note>. Finally, the pyramidion is 5 and 49/970 feet, which makes approximately nine palms; and thus the entire Obelisk is 105 palms high. Truly, all these things will become clearer in the exact symmetry of the Obelisk placed here, as it was drawn by the aforementioned Burattini.

<margin>The Heliopolitan Obelisk is crudely carved; why?</margin>As Titus Livius Burattini <note>Tito Livio Burattini (1617–1681) was an Italian inventor and traveler who provided Kircher with many measurements from Egypt.</note> observed, the Obelisk contains exactly the same symbols on each of its sides. These were carved into the stone with a fairly "unrefined Minerva" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "without much skill" or "crudely."</note>, which has led some to believe that this Obelisk could not possibly have been erected by Sothis <note>A legendary figure Kircher associates with a golden age of Egyptian wisdom.</note>, since all the Sothic Obelisks are carved with symbols of great elegance, as is evident in the Pamphilian Obelisk <note>The obelisk now in the Piazza Navona, Rome.</note>. To these people I reply: just as there are good and bad sculptors today, so too this Obelisk—due to a lack of better artists—happened to have a <term>hieroglypta</term> <note>original: "hieroglyptam"; a stone-carver specializing in hieroglyphs.</note> who was not so skilled, as the conditions of the time allowed. It does not follow, however, that it was not carved by the same King. This could also have happened because of the unrefined hand of the <term>hierogrammatista</term> <note>original: "hierogrammatistæ"; a sacred scribe or designer of the symbols.</note>, whose poorly drawn symbols resulted in an awkward carving even by a skilled craftsman, as he carved them exactly as the prototype dictated. For we should not believe that the same <term>hierogrammatistas</term> and <term>hieroglyptas</term> always applied their labor to the carving of symbols; rather, various ones did, just as is common today. We are taught by experience that in the Chancery of any Prince, just as there are different scribes, they also carry out the duty of writing the public documents committed to them with very different hands and styles. And this is the reason why a different and unequal style of hieroglyphic carving is maintained across all the Obelisks.

# CHAPTER III.
### The Theme of this Obelisk.

<margin>The theme of the Heliopolitan Obelisk.</margin>This Obelisk is dedicated to the Solar Intelligence and its Mercury-Lunar attendants. First, it shows how the Solar Intelligence flows into the three-part division of the year and fills the heavens with a vital influence; and how from this, through the care of a many-formed power, an abundance of all necessary things flows forth. <margin>Dedicated to the Solar Intelligence.</margin>Second, it shows how this power is to be won over through the sacred table; and how, from that, the Mercury-Lunar force, which had been dormant, is awakened and preserved by the aforementioned influence. Third, it shows how through the Mendesian <note>Referring to Mendes, an ancient Egyptian city associated with specific fertility rituals and the ram-god Banebdjedet.</note> sacred table, three Mercurial Powers are joined to the Agathodaemon <note>original: "Agathodæmoni"; literally the "Good Spirit," a divine intellect or protective power in Hermetic philosophy.</note> Intelligence to continue the vital influence into both the higher and lower worlds. Fourth, it shows how, again through the sacred table, the strength and power of Anubis, the guardian of the temples, is reconciled by providence and vital influence. That all these things are true will be clear from the interpretation.

He introduces the obelisk's symbolic theme as a dedication to the "Solar Intelligence" and its role in animating the world.</summary>

# C H A P T E R IV.

## ->Interpretation of the Obelisk.<-

<margin>
**A**
Interpretation of the Heliopolitan Obelisk.

The Hawk is the hieroglyph of the Sun, or the Solar Intelligence. *Horus <note>Kircher refers to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs that was highly influential during the Renaissance.</note> Book 1, Chapter 6.*
</margin>

In the first position of the Obelisk, marked **A**, the Hawk appears; you will find this placed in the first position above the quadrangle on almost every single Obelisk. See the Flaminian, Mahutean, Medicean, and Monticœlian Obelisks, and others: it always denotes the Sun or its governing intelligence. For as Horus rightly says: <note>original Greek: "Θεὸν σημαίνοντες Αἰγύπτιοι, ἱέρακα ζωγραφῶσι..."</note> *When the Egyptians wish to signify God, they paint a hawk; God, both because the animal is prolific and long-lived, and also because it seems, above all other birds, to be an image of the Sun, looking into its rays with a gaze of peculiar and hidden natural power.*

<margin>
**B**
The Vulture signifies the heavens.
</margin>

Above the quadrangle **B** sits a figure in which a triple inverted branch, the *Crux ansata* <note>The "handled cross," better known today as the Ankh, the Egyptian symbol for life.</note>, and a Vulture are seen, by which dominion and protection over lower things are denoted. By the inverted branch is denoted the three-part division of the year, dedicated to the three deities Osiris, Isis, and Mercury <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian god Thoth with the Greco-Roman Mercury.</note>; for these "Leaders of the Year" convey the influence of the supreme Deity (which the *Crux ansata* signifies) into the first of the heavens, which the Vulture represents. Horus clearly shows in Book 1, Chapter 11, that the Vulture signifies the heavens, which, like a mother and a passive principle, receives every offspring of nature into itself: <note>original Greek: "Καὶ γὰρ γυναικῶν γένος θηλυκῶν ἐστὶ..."</note> *Because the genus of Vultures consists only of females, the Egyptians assign the Vulture to any female creature as its chief and primary symbol; from this, they also signify every Goddess. Furthermore, wishing to indicate a 'mother,' they paint a Vulture; for she is the mother of the female nature.* He adds that it signifies the "heavenly" <note>original Greek: "οὐρανίαν" (ouranian)</note>, that is, the heaven (for it does not please them, as I said, to speak of the heaven in the masculine gender *ouranos*, but in the feminine), because the generation of all things is from there. You see, therefore, how the Solar Intelligence first communicates its influential power to the heaven (indicated by the Vulture), and in it, as if in a womb, it forms the patterns of feminine things; these are then brought forth by the three-part division of the year, under the protection of Osiris, Isis, and Mercury, who are noted by the triple branch. But see what we have demonstrated most amply concerning the triple inverted branch, the *Crux ansata*, and the Vulture, based on every kind of authority, both in the Pamphilian Obelisk and in this final Volume.

<margin>
**C**
The hieroglyph of the multiform Spirit.
</margin>

Next follows **C**, the dragon-shaped butterfly with a papyrus staff (*thyrsus*), by which we have shown throughout this work the "multiform Spirit" <note>original: "Dæmonis polymorphi"; in Kircher's Neoplatonic view, these were mediating spirits that shaped the physical world.</note> is signified. Attached to it is a papyrus staff, a sign of the abundance of necessary things. See the mystical reasons for all these things described at length in the Pamphilian Obelisk, page 500, and throughout the fourth Discussion of this Volume. Whatever, therefore, the Solar Intelligence in the heaven (acting as a womb) through...

He uses the writings of Horapollo to justify these associations and connects them to his broader theories of divine influence.</summary>

# SYNTAGMA VIII. HELIOPOLITAN OBELISK CHAP. IV.

Vu

...disposes [nature] through a tripartite time with its own influences. This is the multiform Spirit, the true "Chalcodea" of the Arabs <note>Kircher often references "Chalcodea" as a term from Hermetic or Arabic magic, referring to a mediating spirit that governs the material world.</note>, which, while it attributes proper forms to individual things existing in the material worlds, leads them out into the light; and for this reason, they hoped to be able to attract this spirit by means of the **sacred table D**.

<margin>
**D**
An amulet for attracting the Multiform Spirit.
</margin>

Now, the sacred table contains a Scarab and two statues placed below it; the Scarab presents an image of the Sun, whose mystical significations have been dealt with in an entire treatise drawn from almost all the monuments of ancient authors, as well as in innumerable places in this Volume. The Scarab was a most powerful amulet for drawing down the Solar Deity; and it was worn everywhere on the neck, chest, and arms. But we shall discuss this more fully further below. As for the two statues, although they are shown in crude sculpture, we have gathered what they were from the Lateran and Mahutean Obelisks, and other smaller ones, where they are represented more distinctly. One shows a lion's face, the other a hawk's face, which also indicate the Solar Genii <note>In this context, "Genii" refers to tutelary spirits or governing intelligences of the planets.</note>.

<margin>
Images of the Solar Genii. : **E**
</margin>

They are placed beneath the Scarab so that they may acquire power from it, as subordinates and substitutes from a superior. Following directly across at **E** are two figures, the first of which represents an Asp <note>The uraeus or cobra symbol.</note>, conspicuous for its scaly and swollen chest, and the other an Ibis with a contracted neck. These two figures are seen very often and more accurately sculpted on the top of the Lateran and Flaminian Obelisks, where you may also see their significance more fully explained.

<margin>
The Serpentine and Ibis-shaped Deity.
</margin>

For they indicate the Serpentine <note>original: "Ophionium"</note> and Ibis-shaped Deity—that is, the Luni-Solar Deity. Through the Asp, the efficacy of Solar influence is signified; through the Ibis, the Lunar; without the mixing of these two, the world cannot be preserved. For since the generation of things consists of the moist and the hot, neither the moist without the hot, nor the hot without the moist, can obtain a great effect in the nature of things. Therefore they are joined, so that the excessive dryness caused by the heat of the Sun may be tempered to some extent by the Lunar-moisture, and the excessive moisture by the Solar-heat, and thus the generation of things may reach its intended end.

These Deities, therefore, having shared in the influence of the supreme Deity, arrange the fourfold season of the year by "seminal reasons" <note>A Stoic and Neoplatonic concept (*logoi spermatikoi*) referring to the formative principles that govern the growth of living things.</note> within the celestial hollow as if in a womb, and they hand them over to be distributed by the Chenosiri <note>A term Kircher uses for a lower-world deity, likely a variant of Osiris.</note> of the lower world. These are aptly indicated by the symbols **F G H**, which are an inverted branch, a *Crux ansata* <note>The Ankh, the Egyptian symbol of life.</note>, a Vulture, and a Goose; the first three of these symbols are the same as those contained above in the quadrangle **B**.

<margin>
**F G H I**
The Mendesian sacred table and its hieroglyphics.
</margin>

Next follows the Mendesian sacred table **I**, in which are contained a curved scepter along with an "aegomorphic" scepter (that is, one marked with a goat’s head), as well as figures of an egg, a sacred fern, and a "water-shape" <note>original: "hydroschematis"</note>. By the two scepters, the dominion of Mendes is indicated (for so the Egyptians call the sacred Goat and the Deity of fecundity, according to the testimony of Herodotus, Strabo, and Eusebius). By the egg, the hidden <term>mixture <note>original Greek: "συγκρασία" (synkrasia), meaning a blending or temperament of different elements.</note></term> of things in the world is denoted; by the sacred fern, fire; by the water-shape, water.

<margin>
Herodotus and Strabo. Eusebius.
</margin>

These denote the same thing as before: the conjunction of the hot and the moist, without which the Mendesian power (indicated by the goat-scepter) cannot be preserved. They believed this amulet to be likewise most effective for attracting the said Deities. Now, the sacred flint <note>original: "silex sacer"</note> was an instrument with which they drew out fire in the inner shrines; of which we have spoken elsewhere. There were two of them, shaped in the form of pestles, the first of which was made of steel, the other of iron, by which...

<margin>
What the sacred flint is.
</margin>

# HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Pausanias</margin>...when struck together, the tinder would catch fire; Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler and geographer famous for his "Description of Greece."</note> makes mention of these in his *Aeolics*, where he also calls it a "chrysolith" <note>original: χρυσόλιθον; literally "gold-stone," likely referring here to a spark-producing mineral.</note>: <gloss>A fire-starter made from Chrysolite and steel.</gloss> **Fire is kindled from both chrysolite and iron.** <note>original: Ἔκ τε χρυσολολίθου καὶ σιδήρου τὸ πῦρ ἐξαπτόμενον</note> For the Egyptians numbered all those instruments used in their sacred rites among the sacred symbols of their sculpture—as has been said elsewhere—since they were constructed as certain secrets through a likeness to the nature of the Gods they were entreating.

**K** <margin>Three Ibises expressing three Deltas by the spreading of their feet.</margin> Across from this, at **K**, there follow three Ibises, expressing three **Δ Δ Δ** <note>The Greek letter Delta.</note> by the intricate movement of their feet. (These Ibises, which here appear joined into one body, are seen separately on the Lateran and Barberini Obelisks; thus, no other mystery lies hidden here except the choice of the sculptor or the <term>Hierogrammatista</term> <note>A sacred scribe or priest responsible for writing and interpreting hieroglyphs.</note>.) By these, a triple influence of the Mercurial Genii <note>In Kircher’s system, "Genii" are spiritual intelligences or "daemons" that govern specific parts of the natural world; "Mercurial" refers to those associated with the planet Mercury or the god Hermes/Thoth.</note> is expressed. For to these was committed the care over the "moist nature" (as the Nilotic vessel placed below indicates), which they distributed into all the members of the World, indicated by the figure **L**. By the tiller attached to the Nilotic vessel, they noted that water is the vehicle of all hidden forces existing in moisture. Note, reader, that three Mercurial Genii are mentioned because they participate in equal virtue and power from the <margin>Mercurial Genii.</margin> Solar and Lunar Genius; for Mercury mingles himself with the duties of all Genii. Hence, these three Mercurial Genii are the same as those we brought forward a little earlier, differing only in their specific solar effects.

**M** Furthermore, across from **M**, there follow two feathers with a <term>hieralpha</term> <note>A Kircherian term for a sacred "A" or monogram representing a primary divine principle.</note>, by which—as we have already often said—the <term>Agathodaemons</term> <note>Literally "Good Spirits"; protective or benevolent spiritual intelligences.</note> or Intelligences are indicated, such as the three mentioned Mercurial Genii. For these, as the **N** symbols show, **N** first instill vital influences into the sky, by which the tripartite season of the year, impregnated by this influence, then provides the desired effects. These are indicated by the symbols at **O**, **O**, consisting of a Vulture, an inverted branch, and a Cross, now repeated for the third time. From this, the sacred table **P**—suitable for propitiating them—is the same **P** as that which we explained above in **D**. For this, according to the dominion of the deity Mendes <note>An Egyptian god associated with fertility and the ram.</note> **Q**, **Q** as explained above in **I**, acquires the turns <note>The cyclical power or succession.</note> for filling the World with a great variety of things. The guardians and preservers of these things in the Worldly House are the <term>Anubian Genii</term> <note>Spirits associated with Anubis, often depicted as jackals or dogs.</note>, which are skillfully shown by the figure **R**, **R**, which expresses a house at whose gates two dogs recline. Indeed, this most clear figure is seen on the Southern side of the Flaminian Obelisk across from **B**; see the explanation of its mystical meaning there.

Next follows **S**, the house of Ammon, with a scepter in the middle conspicuous for its **S** Ram’s horns. By this is noted, through the mediation of the preceding sacred table, the <margin>How Mendes differs from Ammon.</margin> attraction of the Ammonian virtue—that is, spermatic fecundity. However, Mendes and Ammon differ only in this: that the spermatic force which Ammon contributed, Mendes leads forth into a most fertile offspring of luxuriant nature. They relate to each other as the disposer and the executor, although in truth they are held by the Egyptians to be the same Deity of fecundity. Therefore, by their providence, a vital influence is derived into the entire World, as the eye **T** and the serpent **T**, the <term>handled Cross</term> <note>The Ankh (crux ansata), a symbol of life.</note> with a pyramid, and the serpent with a segment and scepter—symbols already often explained—teach us.

Thus you see presented on this Obelisk a certain chain <margin>The chain of Lunar, Solar, and Mercurial Spirits.</margin> <note>original: "catena"; Kircher uses the Neoplatonic concept of a "Golden Chain" to describe how divine power descends through various ranks of spirits to the physical world.</note> of Lunar-Solar Spirits together with Mercurial ones. # TREATISE IX.
## THE ALEXANDRIAN OBELISK.

<note>Decorative vignette: A small ornamental scrollwork flourish.</note>

->TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND REVEREND<-
->LORD, LORD<-
->**JOSEPH MARIE SUARÈS**,<-
->**Bishop of Vaison in Narbonnese Gaul.**<-

<note>Decorative divider: A horizontal fleuron or floral ornament.</note>

**I** would undoubtedly incur the mark of ingratitude, Most Illustrious and Reverend Prelate, if I did not offer you some small bundle from this literary harvest, which I have cultivated and gathered primarily through your favor and support. For I have not been seized by such a profound forgetfulness that I would fail to remember the sincerity of your affection toward me—specifically, how ardently you acted to ensure that I should come to Rome for the sake of gathering this very harvest. You obtained what you desired, and at the same time you satisfied the wishes of Nicolas Peiresc <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637) was a renowned French scholar and "Prince of the Republic of Letters" who coordinated much of the era's scientific and antiquarian research.</note>, that man who was a sanctuary of all wisdom, and who, through you, ardently requested this from the Most Eminent Cardinal Francesco Barberini <note>Francesco Barberini (1597–1679) was a powerful cardinal and nephew of Pope Urban VIII; he was Kircher’s primary patron in Rome.</note>. Thus, you simultaneously stirred my own industry and imposed upon me a law by which I cast myself into this labyrinth of labors <note>original: "laborum labyrinthum"</note>, even against my own will. It seemed a Herculean work, clearly not to be completed by any ordinary strength; and so, I could not help but fear my own weakness. But the whisper of a divine breeze was present to help me in my struggle. We have plowed through an immense and untried Ocean; we have reached the goal; and therefore, if there is any praise to be found in this Work, I owe no small part of it to you. I was destined for other cares elsewhere, albeit literary ones: but you, at the persuasion of Peiresc, brought it about that I should apply myself solely and tirelessly to this task. Antiquity praised Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, the Greek goddess of wisdom and war.</note> because she aided the audacity of the Argonauts: should you not also be praised in this Work, Most Illustrious Prelate, you who provided both the ship and the skill? Let this, therefore, be an enduring monument of my grateful will toward you; modest indeed, but offered from the heart. Farewell.

# TREATISE IX.
## The Alexandrian Obelisk and its Interpretation.

### CHAPTER I.
#### On the Origin and First Erector of this Obelisk.

<margin>Two Alexandrian obelisks remain.</margin>
Two obelisks are still to be seen in the city of Alexandria, one standing upright, the other half-buried; concerning which the *Arabic Geography* <note>Kircher is likely referring to the work of the 12th-century geographer Al-Idrisi or a similar medieval Arabic compilation.</note> says the following:

-> "In Alexandria there are two obelisks of Pharaoh, which are two square stones along their length," <-
-> "and their tops are narrower than their bottoms. The length of one of them is five *qiyam*," <-
-> "and the width of their bases on each side is ten spans; the total circumference being" <-
-> "forty spans. The author of the *Book of Wonders* related that they were carved from Mount Turkam in" <-
-> "the west of the land of Egypt, and upon them is written: 'I, Ya'mar bin Shaddad, built this city.'" <-
<note>original Arabic: وبالاسكندرية المسلتان فرعون وهما حجران على طولهما...</note>

*There are in the City of Alexandria two Obelisks, namely square stones, whose upper parts are narrower than the lower ones, and their length is 5 rods (which the Arabs call <term>qim</term> <note>original: <term>قيم</term>, a unit of measurement</note>), while the base on every side or face is 10 palms, and the circumference is 40 palms; and Sahab says in the *Garden of Wonders* <note>Kircher refers to the *Kitab al-Aja'ib* (Book of Wonders), a common title for medieval Arabic compendia of marvels.</note> that Iaamar son of Schadad <note>A legendary figure in Arabic lore, often associated with the lost city of Iram and ancient architectural feats.</note> built this city. Now, a <term>qim</term> is a reed consisting of 20 palms, which when multiplied by 5 *qim* makes exactly 100 palms in height, which both consist of; and indeed, the width of the base of 10 palms fits this dimension appropriately in both Obelisks, provided that the width of the base is established in a tenfold proportion to the height. And of these two Obelisks, one is that which Titus Livius Burattini <note>Tito Livio Burattini (1617–1681) was an Italian polymath and traveler who provided Kircher with precise measurements and drawings from his travels in Egypt.</note>, whom I praised above, measured and sketched with his own hand with the greatest diligence and sent to me in Rome not long ago; concerning which he writes in these words:* <margin>The Alexandrian Obelisk sent to the Author by Titus Livius Burattini.</margin> > "I copied these hieroglyphs from the Western side of the Obelisk of Alexandria, which remains standing; as for the other three sides, because they were damaged by the air <note>i.e., eroded by the elements</note>, it was not possible for me to draw them. They are all different, and therefore I do not believe that among all the Obelisks found today, there is another more adorned than this one."

The pyramidion <note>The small pyramid-shaped capstone of an obelisk.</note> is five Roman feet with $6 \frac{74}{970}$, the Obelisk from the base up to the pyramidion is $57 \frac{17}{970}$ feet, and the base is $7 \frac{746}{970}$ feet, as appears in the figure.

<note>Diagram: A geometric sketch to the right of the table shows a triangle representing the tapering body of the obelisk. Points E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, and D are marked to show how the physical dimensions of the stone relate to abstract geometric principles.</note>

To determine the quantity of the individual parts, I <term>subtracted</term> <note>original Latin: *sustuli*</note> G H from IK, and there remain 190 parts, half of which is 95; this is the length of side M K of the tiny triangle M H K. By the help of this proportion, I found side L K of the larger triangle L D K, since as K M is to M H, so L K is to L D. Thus, this space L K, when doubled and subtracted from IK, leaves L P, which is equal to C D, the base of the pyramidion. And this is the <term>symmetry</term> <note>in the classical sense of proportional harmony between parts</note> of the entire Obelisk as observed by **Tito Burattini**, and calculated with no small praise for his geometric skill. So as not to seem to have omitted anything worthy of consideration, he added the orientation of the Obelisk, which was found not to face the four cardinal directions of the world precisely, but declines slightly, as the following figure shows.

# CHAPTER III.

-> Interpretation of the Alexandrian Obelisk. <-

<margin>Interpretation of the Alexandrian Obelisk.</margin>
This Obelisk was produced by the same unskilled hand—whether of a <term>Hierogrammatist</term> <note>a sacred scribe of ancient Egypt</note> or a <term>Hieroglyph-carver</term>—as the Heliopolitan obelisk described in the preceding section. Indeed, the symbols are so crudely carved that they could only be recognized by comparing them to other obelisks. Only one side of this monument was drawn by <term>Tito Livio Burattini</term>, and it contains three columns of text, just like the Lateran and Flaminian Obelisks; the other sides have been destroyed by the passage of time and the wear of the elements, as was made clear from his letters cited a little earlier. <margin>Only one side of the Alexandrian Obelisk displays intact hieroglyphics.</margin> It is likely, however, that the remaining three sides contained nearly the same symbols; so much so, that if I had wished to reconstruct them according to my own judgment, it would not have been difficult. For it is certain that the other sides would have had the same primary inscription, as well as the same arrangements of sacred panels. As I said, this would not have been hard to do, had I not feared that I might incur a reputation for bad faith among future generations. Therefore, to proceed with greater integrity, I have undertaken to interpret only the drawing of the side transmitted to me. <margin>The theme of the Alexandrian Obelisk is the same as that of the Flaminian Obelisk.</margin> The subject matter of this side is exactly the same as that of the Flaminian Obelisk (about which the Reader may see above). It contains the effects and operations of the twelve Solar Genii <note>protective or guiding spirits associated with the sun</note> in the <term>worldly economy</term> <note>original: *Mundana œconomia*, referring to the divine administration or structural order of the universe</note>, resulting from their protection and influence. It also describes the ceremonies and rites by which each of them must be appeased; for each genius looks toward its own region of the world in the circuit of the four sides, which they defend and preserve from the incursions of evil. But to the matter at hand.

<margin>Inscription of the Alexandrian Obelisk. A B C D</margin>
Thus, on this Western side of the Obelisk, there are contained in the first place three crested Hawks **A B**, carved with a rough chisel, which indicate the Solar Genii presiding over the western region, as we explained regarding the Flaminian Obelisk. They sit above three squares, in which there are first three Bulls, with as many extended arms, indicated by the letters **C D**. By the Bulls are indicated the lower <term>material solar divinities</term> <note>original: *hylæa Solaria Numina*; "hylaea" refers to the physical or material realm as opposed to the spiritual</note>, in which the "Material Osiris" dwells. Through the influence shared from the higher powers, he animates and preserves the entire lower economy of the material world with a benevolent hand.

<margin>E F Z</margin>
Figure **E** marks the <term>Hemphtaean</term> image <note>referring to a specific Egyptian creator deity in Kircher's system</note>; **Z** denotes the Mendesian power, which drives away the fertility of evils; and **F** denotes the <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>a "good spirit" or protective power</note>, a power that supplies warmth. These three Genii are substituted for the three material Solar Divinities, as was said regarding the Flaminian Obelisk, where you will also find the authorities for each. Thus, through the three upper Hawks, three Solar Genii in the Sidereal World are understood; through the three Bulls, the same in the material world; and through the three remaining images, their specific effects are understood. <margin>The three columns of the Western side of the Alexandrian Obelisk.</margin> Indeed, if the figures of the remaining sides were added to these, the entire machine of the universe would be seen to be administered and supported by these twelve chains of Genii, according to the connection of corresponding beings.

There now follow three columns, with their sacred panels or <term>votive offerings</term>...

Indeed, the illustrator of this work writes that the lateral spaces **T S** and **T V** were filled with very tiny hieroglyphics; since it was not possible to discern them due to extreme corruption (for they had been eroded by the voracity of time), it did not seem appropriate to offer our judgment concerning them.

->### Corollary I.<-
**H**ence it is clear that this Obelisk is almost entirely composed of figures from the obelisks reviewed above, so that the identity of the figures clearly demonstrates an identity of meaning.

->### Corollary II.<-
**H**ence it is clear that all the diagrams seen engraved on specific images are taken from the obelisks as if from prototypes, differing only in their placement from time to time; however, this placement induces no difference in meaning, as we taught at the beginning of this work concerning the property of symbolic literature.

# TREATISE IX.
## THE FLORENTINE OBELISK.

<note>Decorative floral ornament</note>

->TO THE MOST EMINENT PRINCE<-
->**GIOVANNI CARLO**<-
->**Cardinal de' Medici of the Holy Roman Church.**<-
->MY MOST MERCIFUL LORD.<-

I call this the Florentine Obelisk because it was first discovered in the Museum of that most celebrated City <note>Florence</note>; for which reason I have judged that it should be dedicated to no one with better right than to You, who are most expert in fine literature. For just as in the past <term>Athenian things were for Athenians</term> <note>original Greek: Ἀθηναῖα Ἀθηναῖοις (Athenaia Athenaiois)</note>, so Florentine things are owed to none but Florentines. Thus, in the same place where the gardens of hidden literature have been cultivated at all times, the uncovered inner sanctuaries of Egyptian Wisdom might now become famous to the world. Nor is it a wonder, since over that most celebrated Florentine Academy <note>The "Athenæum," referring to the intellectual circle of Florence</note> presides a truly reborn <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>original: "Trismegistus," meaning "thrice-greatest," a title for the mythical founder of Egyptian wisdom, Hermes Trismegistus; here Kircher applies it as a compliment to the Grand Duke</note>, the Supreme Grand Duke of Tuscany. He is "thrice-greatest" in religion, in wisdom, and in his Royal connections. By his encouragement, the Sages of Your Illustrious City are not only able to perform great things, but are able to prove them to the world through their deeds. Receive, therefore, this new restoration of the present Obelisk, established in Your honor; and if anything should fall short of Your most refined judgment, I trust entirely that, in accordance with Your innate prudence, You will excuse it rather than take it in a bad light, mindful of that saying: *In difficult matters, it is enough to have willed them.* Farewell.

<note>Large decorative tailpiece ornament in a heart-shaped scrollwork design</note>

# T R E A T I S E  X.

## The Florentine Obelisk, and its interpretation.

### C H A P T E R  I.
### ->Concerning the origin of this Obelisk, the method of its inscription, and its subject matter.<-

<margin>The Florentine Obelisk sent by Nardi.</margin>
The most noble Giovanni Nardi, physician to the Grand Duke of Tuscany, first sent this present Obelisk to me, together with countless other hieroglyphic fragments (of which mention will be made throughout the following pages), for the sake of his own promotion of the common good in the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>The "Respublica Literaria" was the international community of scholars and intellectuals in the 17th century</note>. However, so that all things may be established by their own authentic testimonies, I shall subscribe his letter here, from which the occasion of the discovered Obelisk will be clearly revealed.

->**To the Most Reverend Father Athanasius Kircher**<-
->**Giovanni Nardi, [Scholar] of the Fine Arts**<-

<margin>Nardi’s letter to the Author.</margin>
I willingly delay your extraordinary efforts with a recent service, most learned man, and the glory of this passing age. For I, who watch you sweating long and hard over the turning of Egyptian rocks, entice you for the present with a <term>slight little gift</term> <note>original: "levidensi munusculo"</note>; indeed, I call you away and soothe your relentless labor, being unable to move my own helping hands to such a great work, as much as I might wish to. <term>Leisure gives strength</term> <note>original: "Dant otia vires," a quote from the Roman poet Ovid</note>, as the Prophet-Poet sang; and perhaps from our scraps you, most sharp-eyed investigator, who pierces through immense stones with your <term>lynx-like eyes</term> <note>A common metaphor for keen sight, referring to the mythological Lynceus</note>, will gather pearls. I shall delay you no further. I give you images of Egyptian furnishings, marked on seven copper plates and formerly printed at the end of my work on <term>Lucretius</term> <note>Giovanni Nardi published an edition of the Roman poet Lucretius in 1647</note>. To these are added, by way of extra weight, a three-cubit <note>about 4.5 feet</note> model of the Obelisk, an image of three bands, a fragment of a robe, and figures expressed from engraved gems—neither few in number, nor gathered without care. The boredom of the journey will be lightened by the ridiculous nine-inch face of <term>Ammon</term> <note>The Egyptian god Amun, often depicted with ram's horns</note>, a tireless gladiator, and a token carved with hieroglyphic characters. These last treasures are with us, along with the engravings, which we indicated at that time when we assigned the rest to their rightful owners. The most illustrious Carlo Strozzi, the <term>steward of all antiquity</term> <note>original: "Promus condus," a Roman term for a household manager; here meaning a curator or great collector</note>, freely lent the gems, he being honored by the praise of "living history" with envy remaining silent; and such is the singular humanity of the man toward all, that he conspired eagerly for your benefit, Kircher. Having opportunely met the most distinguished Senator Philippo Vecchietti, the most deserving heir of a very celebrated Museum, he communicated everything to us with the greatest kindness as soon as the business was explained. First to be encountered was a marble Obelisk made of <term>Basalt</term> <note>original: "Praſalte," likely a variant of "basalt" or "basalte," a hard volcanic rock favored by Egyptians</note>, carved with letters not unknown to you, which Giovanni Battista Balatri, the distinguished Architect of the Most Serene Grand Duke, faithfully transcribed. The diligent craftsman also bestowed equal labor on the belts—

...garments, which are made of linen and marked with ink; two are complete with sacred characters, while the third, which is mutilated, is marked with <term>popular letters</term> <note>original: "popularibus... literulis"; Kircher is referring to what we now call Demotic script, the "hand of the people"</note> (if I am not mistaken). Farewell, my Kircher, and love me in return. *Florence, the Ides of February [February 13], in the Year of our Salvation 1651.*

<margin>How the Florentine Obelisk was transported.</margin>
It remains unknown how the Obelisk displayed here reached Florence from Egypt; it is likely that in later times it was transported together with <term>mummified bodies</term> <note>original: "Mumiis cadaueribus"</note> and other Egyptian monuments. Those great leaders of learned men <note>The Medici family, Grand Dukes of Tuscany</note> have at all times acquired a great supply of these from Egypt to adorn the Florentine Museum, which is famous throughout the whole world.

<margin>The running characters of the Florentine Obelisk.</margin>
Although the Obelisk is small in size, it is furnished with such a wealth of details that it seems in no way inferior to the larger ones. However, just as the signs were carved in an unusual type of characters (which are nevertheless truly hieroglyphic) which they call "running" <note>original: "currentes"; today known as Hieratic or Demotic script</note> because of the <term>cursive hand</term> that wrote them, so too has this unusual and intricate business exercised my talent. I confess that I have applied more difficulty, more labor, and more ingenuity to this Obelisk than to any other. It seemed impossible to reach an understanding of such an unknown literature, had not the more polished figures of other Obelisks—which agree with these in various places—lent "midwife hands" to my laboring talent. By comparing one to another, it was finally granted to me, with the cooperation of divine goodness, to cut this <term>Gordian knot</term> <note>A metaphor for an extremely difficult problem, famously "solved" by Alexander the Great</note>.

->### Division of the Obelisk.<-

<margin>The division and subject matter of the Florentine Obelisk.</margin>
This Florentine Obelisk, swelling on all sides with hieroglyphs, has four sides, each of which is divided into two columns. The <term>pyramidion</term> <note>The small pyramid at the very top of an obelisk</note> is smooth and worn, marked with no hieroglyphic design that could serve as a title, as can be seen commonly on others. Therefore, the sequence of symbols follows immediately without a prior title. Its subject matter is a certain linked series of <term>Divine Powers</term> <note>original: "Numinum series"</note>, which strive either to attract the good they intend to obtain, or to appease evil to be driven away, through a certain sympathetic structure of symbols.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: The bottom of the page contains the top portion of an engraving showing the faces of the Florentine Obelisk. The characters are not traditional monumental hieroglyphs but what Kircher calls "running characters," representing his early attempt to analyze Hieratic or Demotic script. The symbols are arranged in two vertical columns per side, featuring simplified human figures, birds, and abstract cursive shapes.</note>

<summary>Athanasius Kircher introduces the Medici Obelisk in Florence, noting the extreme difficulty of deciphering its cursive 'running' characters compared to monumental hieroglyphs. He describes the obelisk's physical structure as having four sides with two columns of text each, intended to invoke or appease divine powers.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>

# CHAPTER II.

->*Exposition of the First Side.*<-

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: This page contains a large, detailed woodcut illustration of the hieroglyphic carvings found on the first side of the obelisk. To make his "translation" easier to follow, Kircher has divided the vertical column of symbols into two manageable segments and indexed every individual sign with letters from both the Latin and Greek alphabets.</note>

<note>The first segment (on the left) represents the top of the obelisk. At the very peak is the <term>pyramidion</term><note>the miniature pyramid-shaped capstone of an obelisk</note> containing a single circular emblem, possibly representing the sun. Below this, the symbols descend in a single column, but Kircher has applied two sets of indices—Latin letters (A through M) on the left side of the symbols and Greek letters (α through μ) on the right side. This allows him to pinpoint specific parts of a complex symbol group.</note>

->*The remainder of the side.*<-

<note>The second segment (on the right) continues the inscription where the first left off. It follows the same indexing method, using Latin letters (N through Z) and Greek letters (ν through ω). # TREATISE X. THE FLORENTINE OBELISK. CHAPTER II.

# Section I.

## The characters and exposition of the first column of the first side.

### Characters or figures.

<margin>Characters of Column 1, side 1.</margin>
In this Obelisk, we shall first explain here what these very poorly fashioned letters denote, and to which figures in other Obelisks they correspond. In this way, once the strokes of each individual character have been untangled, we may more easily reach the goal of our interpretation.

Across from **A**, a figure of a **Serpent** appears with an outstretched arm, which is followed by another **Serpent** with a **Persea leaf** <note>The Persea was a sacred Egyptian tree often associated with the heart or immortality</note>. Across from **B**, a **cycloid** <note>a curved or circular shape</note> follows, with two **Serpents** attached on either side; these figures are found equally in the Barberini Obelisk, though more elegantly formed. **C** denotes a **Vine-shoot** <note>original: *Capreolum*</note> with a **basket-shaped tiara** and a **Serpent**. These are followed by two **parallelograms** with the figure of a **flail** <note>original: *flagelli*; likely the Egyptian *nekhakha*</note>; a similar figure in the first column of the Pamphilio Obelisk across from **B** shows that this is the correct reading. Next follows a **Serpent**, under which is a **globe** from which two **Serpents** emerge. **E** is an **eye** with a **staff** and a **Serpent**. **F** is a **footprint** with a **Serpent** and a **channel**. **G** is a **basket-shaped headdress** <note>original: *tutulus calathoides*</note> with a **funnel**, the kind of which can be seen in the first column of the Pamphilio Obelisk. This is followed by a **cycloid-shaped phallus with an eye**, and **H**, an **image** with raised hands, along with **I**, a **Nilotic vial** and two circles. **K** is a **sacred pool** with a **subterranean chamber** <note>original: *fauissa*</note>, and **L** is a **water-pattern** <note>original: *hydroschemate*</note>. Then follows a **vine-shoot** with a **goat-headed scepter**. **M** is a **gnomon** <note>the part of a sundial that casts a shadow, often used by Kircher to describe upright pointed symbols</note> with a sphere. **N** is an **image** of the kind that appears throughout the Pamphilio and other obelisks; below it is a **foot** with raised arms and a **tetrad** <note>a grouping of four</note>. **O** is a **vine-shoot** with a **goat-headed scepter**, a **gnomon**, and the **character of Momphta** <note>Momphta is Kircher’s name for a specific Egyptian deity or creative force</note>. **P** consists of a **cycloid**, a **right-angled triangle**, and the **figure of the Moon**. These are followed by **Q**, a **Goat** and a **boy seated in a gateway**, which the second column of the Pamphilio Obelisk represents in this same arrangement of symbols. Following these are a **hoopoe-headed scepter** <note>original: *sceptrum Cucupomorphum*</note>, a **hook**, a **Serpent**, and a **Hawk**. **R** is a **kneeling image** with an outstretched arm. **S** is a **triangle** with the **figure of the Moon** and a **Serpent**. **T** is a **cycloid** and an **eye**. **V** is the **scepter of a Hoopoe** and a **vine-shoot** with a scepter passing through a cycloid. **W** is the **figure of a Scarab** drawn in a cursive style, with a **globe** from which a channel emerges, and a **Serpent**. **X** is a **Hawk** with a circle. **Y** is an **averting image** <note>original: *simulachrum averruncum*; a protective figure meant to ward off evil</note>, below which is a **baris-ship** <note>a type of Egyptian river boat</note>. **Z** is an **inverted triple branch** with a square and a gnomon. Behold, these are the figures drawn in a cursive hand. Comparing them with the diagrams of the other obelisks with which they agree will more than sufficiently prove that my descriptions are accurate. Nothing further remains except to subjoin the interpretation in brief words.

CH. II. 352 THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

->*Explanation of the figures.*<-

<margin>Interpretation of the 1st Column of the 3rd side.</margin>
**A** is beneficent life; **B** is fruitful life, the fountain of lives, flowing into vegetable nature; **C** is the life capable of ruling the material <note>original: *hylæorum*; from the Greek *hyle*, referring to the physical matter of the universe</note> worlds; **D** is the life that penetrates the whole world; **E** is vital providence; **F**, by a hidden motion, fills the worldly channels; **G**, through the "funnel of nature," fertilizes the year; **H**, through the statue of **Hemphta** <note>Kircher's name for the supreme demiurge or creator spirit</note> flowing into **I**, the vial of the Worlds; **K**, into the sacred pools and temple pits <note>original: *fauissas*; underground cellars or pits in temples where sacred objects were kept</note>, by a hidden process of the Divinity; **L**, it is derived into the moist nature; from which **M**, the fertility of vegetable nature and the symmetry of the World, results through **N**, the worship of the statue of **Nephthys** <note>original: *Nephtæi*</note> and the legitimate ceremonies in the power of the **tetradice** <note>original: *tetradicis*; likely referring to a plant Kircher identifies as a species of Seriphion or wormwood</note>. **O**, the fertility of **Mendes** <note>referring to the sacred Ram of Mendes, a symbol of virility and creation</note>, together with the celestial **Momphta**, **P** move the genetic operations in the sensible World, which is **Horus**; from which a harmonic variety is born. As **Osiris** flows in, and **R**, his follower, the beneficent **Omphta**, **S**, the genetic influences of **Isis** are derived into **T**, the lower World, for which **V**, the Divinity of variety and fertility, provides. Truly, the subterranean **Osiris** transfers the life communicated to him from the superior celestial **Osiris**—by the help of **Nephthys**—into the stations of the tripartite year, from which comes the fulfillment of happiness in the lower World.

->*Commentary on the explanation provided.*<-

**T**he statues located at letters **H, N, Q, R, Y** are all of "averting gods" <note>original: *Dijs auerruncis*; deities tasked with turning away evil or misfortune</note>, each of which we have explained in the Pamphilio Obelisk. They are shown kneeling because they are of a lower order, subject to and ministers of some greater Divinity. They express various gestures, sometimes raising and sometimes lowering their hands; by this efficacious gesticulation, they signal an intense and most faithful desire to administer the matters committed to their trust; thus, they seem to be ardently praying for the commands of the Divinity set over them. See our *Treatise on Averting Gods* <note>original: *Syntagma de Dijs auerruncis*</note>, in which we have discussed them at length.

<margin>The symbol of the Serpent, when attached to various things, signifies various things.</margin>
No symbol occurs more frequently on this Obelisk than that of the **Serpent**. We have demonstrated in many places, following **Horus** <note>Horapollo, an ancient author on hieroglyphs</note> and countless others, that the Serpent is a symbol of life. This symbol expresses different meanings depending on what it is placed next to: for a Serpent placed near a **cycloid** <note>a circular or curved shape</note> indicates celestial life; near a **water-symbol** <note>original: *hydroschemati*</note>, vital moisture; joined to a temple pit, a Nilotic vessel, or a sacred pool, it indicates the vital liquid of the Nile; and so on for the rest.

<margin>The Florentine Obelisk is consecrated to the supreme Hemphta.</margin>
Therefore, although this present Obelisk displays no inscription from which it can be said with certainty to be consecrated to a specific Divinity, it is nevertheless certain—from the meaning of the symbols and the context of the marks—that it is consecrated to the **Life of lives**, that is, to the supreme Divinity of all, **Hemphta**. Throughout this entire Obelisk, nothing else is dealt with other than the vital influence of the supreme Divinity and the life-giver of all virtues, as will become clear from what follows.

<margin>What kind of herb the Tetradice is.</margin>
Between the letters **N** and **O**, a figure appears placed like a rod, which we call the **tetradice**. Plutarch mentions this, saying that **Isis** hid the body of **Osiris** from the machines of **Typhon** <note>the chaotic enemy of Osiris</note> among the currents of the Nile with it, and that it is the same as...

He also discusses the apotropaic nature of kneeling statues and the versatile meaning of the serpent symbol as a representation of "vitality."</summary>
