# § II.

## ->Exposition of the figures, ω, of the second column of the first side.<-

### ->Characters, or figures<-

<margin>Characters of the 2nd column of the 1st side.</margin> **I**n the first place in this region, **α** occurs: a circular shape with a quadrangle, and two **β** extended arms; there follows **γ**, a boy standing upon a sacred pool, with **δ**, a Serpent, a human foot, a Crocodile, and a handled cross <note>The *crux ansata* or Ankh</note>. **ε** is a Statue equipped with a hook, a tendril of a vine with a small disc. **ζ** is the figure of an **Ibis**, with **η**, three Serpents. **θ** is a circular shape, with **ι**, a crowned Pyramid, and **κ**, a "four-fold sprout" <note>original: *germen tetradix*; Kircher's term for a specific vegetal hieroglyph</note>, with three staffs. **λ** is an <term>averruncan</term> statue <note>From the Latin *averruncare*, meaning "to ward off" or "to avert" evil or bad luck</note>, **μ** is a <term>Nilometer</term> <note>A tool or scale used to measure the rising waters of the Nile</note>, **ν** is a Hawk, with another Hawk, and a right-angled triangle. **ξ** is a statue of <term>Momphta</term> <note>Kircher's name for a creative divine force or deity</note>, with two upright arms. **ο** is a basket-shaped headdress and a Serpent. **π** is a walking Ibis and an averruncan statue. **ρ** is a Square, a vine-tendril, a foot, and segments. **σ** is two upright arms and a handled cross. **τ** is a <term>Hydroschema</term> <note>Literally a "water-figure" or symbol of the element of water</note>, **υ** is a Hawk, a <term>baris</term> boat <note>An Egyptian river boat often used for transporting the dead or sacred objects</note>, and a funeral litter. **φ** is a Statue, **χ** a four-fold sprout, and a rising Asp. **ψ** is a sacred Pool. **ω** is a circular shape with a Hawk. We have seen the figures; let us now add the explanation of each.

->### Explanation of the figures.<-

<margin>Explanation of column 2, side 1.</margin>The celestial **α** ruler of the pool **β**, the munificent **Horus γ**, guardian of the sacred pool, by the power of his own occult motion, defeats **Typhon δ** <note>original: *Typhonem*; the Greek name for Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and storms</note>; the influence of the supreme Deity, by the power of the Tautic seal <note>original: *Tautici sigilli*; refers to the 'Seal of Thoth' or the Ankh, often associated by Kircher with Hermetic secrets</note>, is derived into the **ε** warding spirit <note>original: *averruncum Genium*; a protective deity intended to avert evil</note>, the ruler of the vegetable World; the **ζ** Ibis-deity <note>original: *Ibiacum Numen*; the god Thoth, often depicted as an Ibis</note> completes all things by **η** vital operations, preceded by **κ** religious worship; the **Power of Momphta λ** <note>Kircher uses 'Momphta' to refer to a creative, demiurgic power, often linked to the god Ptah</note> gives strength and support to the **μ** channels of the sacred Nile; **ν Osiris** stirs up genetic motions through **ξ Momphta**, incited by the prayers and ceremonies of the **π Priests**; whence also the **\*** Mercurial Deity <note>Thoth or Hermes Trismegistus</note> with a hook wanders through the **ρ** material World <note>original: *hylæum Mundum*; from the Greek *hyle*, meaning matter</note> by an occult force; by **σ** hymns and protective rites the **τ** moisture of nature is attracted; the beneficent **υ Osiris**, carried into the lower regions by a vehicle, through the **φ** warding image and the operation of the **χ** wormwood <note>original: *Seriphij*; referring to the Seriphion plant mentioned on the previous page</note>, sends the **ψ** serpent-like <note>original: *Ophionium*; from the Greek *ophis*, serpent</note> bestower of fruitful life into the sacred pool, whence by the power of the **ω** celestial heat, all things are preserved.

->### Scholium on the explanation.<-

Figures **α β γ** are also found on the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, but carved more finely and elegantly; from which I have gathered that a **Crocodile** is denoted by character **δ**, though it is sketched rather than fully depicted by a rough stroke on this Obelisk. The same judgment is made regarding the figure between **ζ** and **η**, as well as the figure in the region of **π**, both of which denote the **Ibis** there, as I have observed from other Obelisks where these same figures are seen expressed more completely. The letter **ξ** has a figure in its region which presents a letter similar to the Coptic **σ** <note>sigma</note>; in reality, however, it expresses a **Lion’s head**, of which kind two are seen in the first column of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, conspicuous with a veiled crown. The figure between **χ** and **ψ**, however, traced with a rough stylus, shows an **Asp** risen up with a swollen belly, of the kind seen everywhere on all Obelisks, and especially on the *Bembine Table* <note>The Isiac Table, a famous bronze tablet with pseudo-hieroglyphs studied extensively by Kircher</note> placed next to the throne of **All-Formed Nature** <note>original: *Panamorphæ naturæ*</note>; so that, for that reason, I have penetrated into the knowledge of these "running" characters <note>i.e., cursive or simplified hieroglyphs</note> by no other means than by the combination of similar marks from other Obelisks.

Reader, take note: the letters or numbers placed on the right side of the Obelisk's faces pertain to the first column of the side; while those on the left pertain to the second column of the side; each of these indicates the figures corresponding to them in that region.

### Commentary on the explanation provided.

<margin>Horus.</margin>
**B**etween figures 8 and 9, the four-footed figure refers to the Hyena, a symbol of alternation and change in the lower World, according to the testimony of Horus <note>referring to Horapollo, author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs</note>, Book 2, chapter 65:
> <note>original Greek: Τινὰ δ’ ἄστατον, καὶ μὴ μένοντα ἐν ταὐτῷ, ἀλλ’ ὁτὲ μὲν ἰσχυρὸν, ὁτὲ δὲ ἀσθενῆ βουλόμενοι σημῆναι ὕαιναν ζωογραφοῦσι· αὕτη γὰρ ὁτὲ μὲν ἄρρην γίνεται ὁτὲ δὲ θῆλυα.</note> When they wish to signify someone unstable and not remaining in the same state, but at one time strong and at another weak, they depict a hyena; for this animal is sometimes male and sometimes female.

<margin>The Hyena as a symbol of the inconstant.</margin>
When they wish to signify someone unstable, not staying in the same condition, but meanwhile robust and bold, and at other times weak and timid, they paint a Hyena; for this creature is sometimes male, sometimes female. Although Horus assigns this symbol to a human being in this passage, the Egyptians, in their usual manner of universal analogy, preferred to apply these symbols to the actions of nature—most especially in the <term>sublunary World</term> <gloss>the earthly realm below the moon, thought to be the only place subject to change and decay</gloss>, which is subject to a continuous succession of alterations. In this realm, all things exert themselves through mutual change, performing the roles now of the male, now of the female. For as <margin>Oppian.</margin> Oppian rightly says in Book 3 *On Hunting*:

->A marvel is told, and this I have heard regarding the hyena's haunts:<-
->That it alternates between male and female with the passing year.<-

They report an even greater miracle: that Hyenas renew the laws of nature in alternating years, so that the ambiguous creature becomes now a male, now a pregnant female. Since the other symbols are well known, I deliberately omit their explanation.

<margin>Interpretation of column 2, side 2.</margin>
**B**y the beneficent providence (22) of the <term>Momphtaean Divinity</term> <gloss>Kircher’s name for a supreme, creative Egyptian deity</gloss>, the vegetative power of the Moon (23) is carried down into the bowl of the sacred pool, and (25) into the Nilotic vessels through the (24, 25, 26) appropriate protective statues; the (26, 27) Mercurial Divinities, brought through the gates of the World in a (28) vital vehicle, bestow a (29) life-giving influence upon the Worlds of vegetable nature. (30) By the power of the protective statues and the rites performed via the sacred boat, the influence of the supreme celestial Divinity is drawn down; from which, by the influence of <term>Chenosiris</term> <gloss>a composite name for Osiris as a god of renewal</gloss> into the lower World, the constant change of things flows forth, through the worship, (34) rites, and ceremonies of the following images. (33, 35, 36) For through these, the celestial moisture is channeled into lower things at the appointed time of 22 days; (36) these symbols stir the beneficent moisture with a hidden motion according to (37) the laws of generation; while the (38) Ophionic Demon, Hermanubis, and the Ammonian Intelligence bring the work to completion.

->*Scholium*<-
<note>A scholium is an explanatory note or commentary added to a text to provide deeper context.</note>

<margin>What the sacred boat is.</margin>
**W**hat the <term>sacred boat</term> <note>original: "sacra barra"</note> was has been shown more than enough in the work on the Pamphilian Obelisk; for it was a wooden instrument, like a box, intersected crosswise by scepters, in which the Priests of the Mysteries used to perform both their sacrifices and their divinations, in order to obtain something from the Divinity to whom they were making an offering. From this comes the proverb, <gloss>he divines in the boat</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ βάρριδι μαντεύεται</note>, which was said of those who investigate difficult matters with watchful care and untiring labor.

<margin>The right-angled triangle as a symbol of generative power.</margin>
See Demophilus on Egyptian rites. That the right-angled triangle was a symbol of generative power among the Egyptians has already been demonstrated in many places in this work by quoting Plutarch; the base of the triangle is the sign of the passive principle, the vertical line (the cathetus) is the active principle, and the hypotenuse or third side signified the <term>offspring</term> <note>original Greek: ἔγγονον</note>, that is, what is generated from these two. But see the discussion on these matters in the *Hieroglyphic Geometry* and in various other places.

<margin>What kind of instrument the sled is.</margin>
The second-to-last figure of this column refers to a <term>sled</term> <note>original Latin: "traha," a heavy frame for dragging loads</note>; it was a sacred instrument by which the holy images were carried in a type of triumph at certain times of the year, so that it eventually became a symbol of divine worship when recorded in the sacred register of hieroglyphs; as did the bier, about which we have discussed most extensively elsewhere.

<margin>Two cross-marks as a numerical symbol.</margin>
Between 34 and 35, two <term>decusses</term> <gloss>X-shaped marks representing the number ten</gloss> appear; these were numerical symbols, and by them the number 22 was expressed, as we have shown in *Hieroglyphic Arithmetic*. Furthermore, there were 22 days appointed by that ancient Oracle, during which the Divinities would demonstrate their effects; if they did not obtain these effects within the space of this appointed time, they believed either that the Divinity was not at all appeased, or that the sacrifice had not been properly performed. Hence, to appease the Divinity...

## Anatomical Exposition.

<margin>Exposition of Column 1 of the 3rd side.</margin>
Supreme Providence derives the celestial moisture *b* full of life into the Ophionian <note>serpent-like</note> *c* beneficent <term>Agathodæmon</term> <note>A Greek name for a "Good Spirit," often depicted as a serpent</note>, by which provision is made for vegetable nature through the influx of the Divinities *d, e, f, g, h* (explained above; for they are the same as those reviewed a little earlier in the anatomy). The religion of the Priests *b* solicits the provident care of these through *i* statues presiding over the vital moisture, from which *k* change and variety is born into the World, through the hidden *l* motion and vigilance of Anubis. The celestial *m* mixing bowl *n* is brought by that dominant worship *o* of the Priests *p* to the Spirit Momphæus; whence both the genital and vital influx is consigned to the beneficent *q* Hermanuphta <note>A composite deity combining Hermes and Anubis, symbolizing the guide of souls and secret knowledge</note>; who *r* propagates this influx by his hidden motion into the worldly *s* channels of life's dominion, and governs with beneficent providence, through the *t* most powerful influxes of the statue; for which the worship and religion of the Priests will be of benefit through sacrifices duly and legitimately instituted, and appropriate to the Divinity.

## Scholium.

<margin>Monogrammatic characters of the Divinities.</margin>
There occur here and there certain symbols, which we call <term>monogrammatic characters of the Divinities</term> in our *Treatise on the Canopic Jars* <note>original: "Syntagmate de Canopis"</note>, where we have also explained them with the greatest diligence: characters of this sort are those which occur in this column across from *o, s, u*. But see Figure III of the *Canopic Illustrations*, where you will find all things of this kind, as well as their structure, explained. The rest of the marks, as they almost always recur the same as explained in the preceding sections, I would waste time if I repeated them in this place. We call them monogrammatic, however, because they are symbols of the Gods explained in the cited place, and they were held to be of great efficacy among those who were accustomed to carry them according to the required religious worship. Truly all these things—that is, the composition of characters of this sort and the mystical reasons—see fully explained in the cited place, that is, in the *Treatise on the Canopic Jars*.

### § VI.
### Declaration of the Second Column of the Third Side.

<margin>
Exposition of Column 2 of side 3.

**I**n this second column of the third side, from *z* through to *f*, with a few exceptions, the contents are almost the same as those placed in the second column of the second side, from 21 to 28. Most of the symbols in this section are equivocal <note>having multiple meanings or being interchangeable</note>, being equivalent in meaning to the symbols of the other column already reviewed. This practice of using varied symbols for the same concept is characteristic of the Egyptians for the sake of variety, as has been made clear from other Obelisks. Indeed, the remaining symbols were explained in the preceding sections and fall into nearly the same meaning; therefore, they do not require further exposition.

<margin>Exposition of Column 1 of Side 4.</margin>
**T**he power of the vital fluid in the Worlds is preserved by the virtue of the Genius Momphta <note>In Kircher’s system, Momphta is the "divine hemi-sphere" or creative mind</note> (for this is indicated by the monograms 3 & 4, and the "Bed of Momphta," regarding which see the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 284); 5. for he imparts the life of vegetable nature to the pool; this is animated by celestial life through the power of the <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>The "Good Spirit," often associated by Kircher with the life-giving intellect or Mercury</note>. By the force of the Ophionian <note>serpent-like</note> monogram, the influence is also carried down into 11. the basin of the Ophionian pool 12. by an occult motion and the providence of the hawk-shaped Divinity, indicated by the 13. statue very poorly formed with linear strokes alone. 14. He dispels <term>Bebonia</term> <note>Kircher's term for "evil" or "Typhonian" obstacles, likely derived from the name of the Egyptian demon Babai</note> evils from the well-ordered economy of vegetable nature; 19. he binds the influx of celestial life, 20. through the monogram of the Isiac Divinity 21. by the sound of the sacred sistrum driving away all things inauspicious, which therefore ought to be cultivated with all honor; 23. she promotes generations by the virtue of the moisture over which she presides; 24. she brings life into the gate of the material World, which she supports, and restores Osiris to life by the virtue of the tetrad <note>the number four, representing stability and the elements</note>; 25. sustaining the Universe by a wise disposition of things, which are indicated by the leaf and fruit of the <term>persea</term> <note>A sacred Egyptian tree, often identified as *Mimusops schimperi*</note>.

->*Scholium*<-

**A**lthough these marks might seem to be the true strokes of letters because of that crude sketching, they must by no means be thought of as such. Rather, they are marks entirely similar to those which we see everywhere both on Obelisks and other Egyptian monuments—that is, a certain type of "minuter hieroglyphic." Thus, in this present Obelisk, you may find lines put for scepters, dots for circles, and any sort of twisted lines for the figure of a Serpent; even human feet can be seen as nothing but lines. This most worthy of consideration increases the difficulty: that it is in no way possible to discern what composition the scepters, statues, and birds have, from which...

Kircher also explains that the crude, linear style of the carvings is a shorthand form of hieroglyphics rather than mere alphabetical letters.</summary>

...through which, however, the true sense of hieroglyphic literature is extracted; and thus it would have been impossible <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατον</note> to attempt this so uncertain and doubtful interpretation, unless long practice and experience gained through many years of labor by the constant application of the **combinatoric art** <note>The *ars combinatoria*, a method of relating symbols and concepts across different systems, heavily influenced by Ramon Llull</note> had brought some light from similar schematic inscriptions found here and there on Obelisks and other Egyptian monuments. From the hunting of these, while I direct the sharpness of my mind as if to the **thread of Ariadne** <note>A reference to the mythological thread used to navigate the Labyrinth, symbolizing a logical path through a complex problem</note>, I have finally achieved that which at first I thought could scarcely be done. And so, if sometimes the "water has stuck" <note>An idiom meaning to be at a standstill or facing a difficulty; original: *aqua hæsit*</note>, the Reader should not for that reason judge the interpretation to be faulty, since the reason for the essential ideal concept always stands firm. The same thing happens in these matters as in our common descriptions of things, in which even if the words, sounds, and different positioning of phrases seem to bring some change, the essential meaning of the things described nevertheless remains the same. I wanted to bring these points forward in this place so that if any **Aristarchus** <note>A stern or pedantic critic, named after the Greek grammarian Aristarchus of Samothrace</note> should attempt to mark this interpretation of ours with more severe obelisks <note>Kircher is punning here: in ancient manuscript editing, an "obelisk" was a mark (÷) used to flag a passage as doubtful or spurious</note>, he would not be ignorant of the reasoning behind this undertaking of ours.

->CHAPTER V. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS'S HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER.<-

### *Conclusion.*

From the interpretation of this Obelisk, it is therefore clear how life—without which the World cannot exist in any way—is infused into its various members by the ministry of linked **Divinities** <note>original: *Numina*; referring to the hierarchy of gods or spiritual forces in Kircher’s Neoplatonic system</note>, through particular outpourings <note>original: *influxus*; the Neoplatonic concept of divine energy flowing from the heavens down to the earth</note> shared by the **Supreme Divinity**. It is also shown how all things perceived by sight are fertilized, animated, and multiplied by them; and how the higher Divinities always derive their influence into the lower ministers subject to them. These lower spirits, who are the presiding <term>Genii</term> <note>guardian spirits or minor deities believed to oversee specific natural processes</note> of things, each convey that influence into the parts committed to their care—which they called <term>reservoirs</term> <note>original: *piscinae*</note>, <term>mixing bowls</term> <note>original: *crateres*</note>, and <term>sacred vaults</term> <note>original: *favissae*; these terms are used metaphorically for the different levels of the physical world that "catch" divine energy</note>—for the good of the World. Yet, because these Genii are sometimes offended by human wickedness, it is also beautifully demonstrated by what rites and sacrifices they may be appeased and made favorable, so that mankind may thereafter enjoy the desired happiness with the favoring Divinities; this is the end and ultimate goal of the hieroglyphic description.

# TREATISE XI
## THE OBELISKS KNOWN AS THE ESQUILINE AND THE VATICAN.

->TO THE MOST EMINENT PRINCE<-
->**FRANCESCO ANGELO RAPACCIOLO,**<-
->Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Bishop of Terni.<-

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring floral motifs</note> SO GREAT is the eminence of virtue, Most Eminent Cardinal, so powerful is its <term>Magnetism</term> <note>Kircher frequently uses magnetic attraction as a metaphor for the spiritual and moral influence that great individuals exert over others</note>, that it carries away even those who are unknown and however far distant into admiration of itself; it soothes with its sweetness, and gently composes the manners even of the wayward and stubborn. Indeed, I have learned with pleasure from various people on many occasions of the supreme innocence of Your Life, of the example of holy conversation by which You shine before all, and of the cultivation of all the disciplines which You possess in Your most capable intellect—a cultivation truly all the more illustrious because it is so closely joined to the great affection of Your humanity and benevolence, which You pour out upon the learned. Consequently, I might not undeservedly seem envious of such a gathering of virtues if I were to pass over such an illustrious prototype of an Ecclesiastical Prince without the erection of an immortal Obelisk due to Your merits. I therefore erect a double Obelisk worthy of Your virtues: the <term>Esquiline</term> and the <term>Vatican</term> <note>These are two of the major obelisks in Rome; the Vatican obelisk stands in St. Peter's Square, and the Esquiline stands behind Santa Maria Maggiore. Neither contains Egyptian hieroglyphs</note>. Although these are not distinguished by any arrangements of hieroglyphic literature, they nevertheless contain within themselves something divine, and are to be venerated for the majesty of hidden sacraments. In these, whatever Oracles of ancient wisdom the other obelisks display through an innumerable variety of figures, these also express—as if under the guise of a <term>Silenus</term> <note>A reference to "Silenus boxes," an ancient metaphor for something that appears plain or ugly on the outside but contains beautiful, divine images within</note> or by the recondite concepts of the mystical figure alone. They are, therefore, a true <term>ectypon</term> <note>original: *ectypon*; a reproduction or visible manifestation of an inner form</note> of Your most eminent mind; for although You may cover Your virtue under an external veil, according to Your innate modesty, so great is the force and efficacy of the brilliance diffused in the inner center of Your soul, that You seem not undeservedly to kindle the hearts of all as if with a most luminous ray. Let this, then, be a monument of triumphant virtue established as an example to others, for the immortal glory of Your name, and at once a <term>token</term> <note>original Greek: *τεκμήριον* (tekmērion); a proof or sign</note> of my sincere affection for You. Farewell, honor and glory of the Ecclesiastical Principality.

# TREATISE XV.
# THE OBELISKS WHICH ARE THE ESQUILINE AND THE VATICAN.
# CHAPTER I.

->*The Claudian, or Esquiline, Obelisk.*<-

<margin>What are called "smooth" obelisks.</margin>
<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' featuring a portrait of a bearded man</note> OBELISKS are called "smooth" <note>original: *rasi*, literally "scraped" or "shaved"</note> when they are provided with no display of hieroglyphs. The reason for this was either because the Kings—whose intention was indeed to honor them with this distinction—were either prevented by death or distracted by other impediments and business, and could not complete them; or because the <term>Hierogrammatists</term> <note>Sacred scribes responsible for the knowledge and composition of hieroglyphs</note> or <term>Hieroglyphs</term> <note>Kircher here uses *Hieroglyptæ* to refer to the specialist stone-carvers of sacred symbols</note> were lacking in a rude age to perform the work; or because they thought the very shape of the Obelisks, being profoundly mysterious, was sufficient for suggesting the secrets hidden beneath them to intelligent and skilled Priests. For, as was demonstrated at length regarding the <term>Pamphilian Obelisk</term> <note>The obelisk now in the Piazza Navona, which Kircher had recently helped restore and interpret</note>, the shape of Obelisks was so full of mysteries that there was no mystery in the mundane economy that they did not express either by the number of sides, lines, or angles; as we have demonstrated most abundantly in the cited place, so here we did not wish to be longer in repeating them. However, among the other Obelisks, three smooth ones in particular were brought from Egypt: two of these Claudius Caesar erected at the Mausoleum of Augustus, and the third Gaius Caligula erected in the Vatican Circus. We will speak first of the former, and afterwards discourse more fully on the third.

<margin>Two smooth Obelisks brought by Claudius Caesar. Ammianus.</margin>
Thus, Claudius Caesar placed two smooth Obelisks, brought from Egypt, at the Mausoleum of Augustus. So says Ammianus Marcellinus in Book 17: <note>original: *Sequutaque ætates alios transtulerant, quorum unus in Vaticano, alter in hortis Sallustij, duo in Augusti Mausoleo erecti sunt.*</note> *“And subsequent ages had transferred others, of which one was erected in the Vatican, another in the gardens of Sallust, and two in the Mausoleum of Augustus.”* And although nothing is read among the Historians concerning this effort by Claudius, it is nonetheless evident that he erected no others besides these from the fact that Strabo, a contemporary of Augustus, although he described the Mausoleum most exactly, nonetheless made no mention of the Obelisks. Therefore, it is most certain that they were erected by his great-grandson Claudius, in eternal memory of his ancestor from whom he had received such great benefits, as we also showed regarding the Pamphilian Obelisk. This can also be established from the testimony of Pliny himself, who mentions them in these words: <margin>Pliny.</margin> <note>original: *Sunt et alij duo, vnus à Smarre positus, alter ab Eraphio (veriùs Vaphrio) sine notis, 48 cubitorum.*</note> *“There are also two others, one placed by Smarres, the other by Eraphius (more correctly Vaphrius <note>Likely referring to Pharaoh Apries or Wahibre</note>), without markings, of 48 cubits.”* Since Pliny, who lived nearly 70 years after Augustus, mentions them, and between him and Augustus no other Caesars intervened besides Nero and Claudius, and we read of Nero—intent on other things—undertaking nothing regarding Obelisks, it is clearly evident that Claudius erected them. Therefore, of these two Obelisks, which Claudius [dedicated] to the honor and immortality of his ancestor, in the Mausoleum...

<margin>Pope Sixtus V sees to the erection of the Vatican Obelisk.</margin> I do not wish to dispute the truth of this inscription; certainly, it can easily be shown from the timeline of history that the name "Florentine" was not yet in use during the time of Caligula <note>Caligula (12–41 AD) was the emperor who originally brought this obelisk to Rome; Kircher is pointing out that "Florence" is a later medieval/Renaissance designation, making the "ancient" inscription suspicious.</note>. This monument, which was finally almost half-buried in the earth and torn from its original site, was erected in the Vatican Field in the region of St. Peter’s Basilica by the architect Domenico Fontana, by order of Pope Sixtus V—a feat to be remembered in all ages. After the Lateran Obelisk, it is the largest of all those seen to this day, remaining whole and unbroken. Having seen its massive bulk in previous centuries, Popes Nicholas V, Paul III, and Gregory XIII did everything they could to erect it in a more suitable place; however, they were never able to bring the plan to execution, deterred either by the magnitude of the expense or the perceived impossibility of the work. Nevertheless, Sixtus V, out of the great magnitude of his spirit—truly worthy of such a Great Pontiff—and relying on the supreme power of genius and the industry of the aforementioned architect, erected it in the manner that follows.

### The Method and Reason for the Erection of the Vatican Obelisk.

<margin>The erection of the Vatican Obelisk</margin> **P**ope Sixtus V, always intent on the most massive of architectural undertakings, was turning the erection of the obelisks over in his mind. When he found that architects were too timid because of the difficulty of the task, he is said to have used this single argument to prove the work was possible: "What was once done by the Egyptian Kings and the Roman Emperors is by no means to be considered impossible in these times." Indeed, it is clear from history that the Egyptians erected not just one, but many—nay, innumerable—and even larger obelisks; the Roman Emperors followed them, bringing these stones from Egypt and re-erecting them for the adornment of the City. Therefore, no one should doubt that what was done once can be done today, given such an abundance of fertile minds. If anyone should plead the excessive quantity of the costs, I would not have him persuade himself that we suffer from such a poverty of money that it should divert our mind from such things. Rather, it should sharpen and stimulate us to perform, I will not say similar, but even greater things, provided we are not found wanting in zeal and diligence. Come now, Domenico Fontana, whose genius has already become known to us on many previous occasions, attend seriously to this

### CHAPTER II. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

“...do not cease to apply yourself to this task, and let not the magnitude of the expense be a concern to you; if one million gold coins should not suffice, let two be added, or however many may be needed, provided that what we command is carried out.” <margin>Domenico Fontana raises the Vatican Obelisk.</margin> Inspired by these words, Domenico Fontana, Knight and Architect, from that time applied himself seriously to this business. And first, indeed with very prudent judgment, he determined the mass of the said Obelisk through the most exact measurement; having obtained this, he turned to the principles of mechanics. Among these, he found no machines more suitable for expediting this business than the <term>Capstans<note>Original: *Ergatas*. These are vertical-axle winches used for winding heavy ropes, powered by men or horses walking in circles.</note></term>; of which he gathered such a number that the combined power of these machines surpassed the weight of the Obelisk by many <term>parasangs<note>Original: *parasangis*. An ancient Persian unit of distance; Kircher uses it here metaphorically to mean that the mechanical advantage exceeded the weight by a vast margin.</note></term>. Furthermore, the method of erection was as follows.

<note>Engraving: A massive wooden scaffolding structure (Castellum) surrounding a central obelisk. The structure is reinforced with cross-beams and a complex system of pulleys and ropes. Letters A, B, C, D mark the top beams; N, O, P, Q, R, S, T, V, X, F, G, H denote various technical components and base points of the mechanism.</note>

<margin>The method of erecting the Vatican Obelisk.</margin> First, the foundation, placed according to the requirements of the site, was a square, one side of which was three times the width of the largest side [of the obelisk], that is, it was 36 <term>palms<note>Original: *palmorum*. The Roman palm was a unit of measure roughly equal to 22.3 centimeters or 8.8 inches.</note></term> across.

Second, in the middle of this square foundation, which was brought up from the depth to the level surface, an <term>abacus<note>In this architectural context, a flat slab or pedestal serving as a level base for the monument.</note></term> was placed; upon this was the square base with all things necessary for supporting the Obelisk.

**Fourthly**, in these eight holes—of which we said four were left on each side—an equal number of columns were founded. That is, four on each side, such as the beams of the first order shown by **F A** and **C G**. Just like the holes, these columns were equidistant from one another, yet in such a proportion that the two middle columns on each side, by their distance, matched the width of the Obelisk at its widest part. These columns, having a width of four <term>palms<note>Original: *palmorum*. A Roman "palmus" was a unit of measure approximately 8.8 inches or 22.3 cm.</note></term>, exceeded the height of the Obelisk by some distance, as appears in the figure. However, because beams of such great width and height are not always available, each individual column (**F A**, **G D**) was tightly bound together from four other beams using iron <term>clamps<note>Original: *retinaculis*. Specifically iron bindings or tie-rods used to hold the composite beams together.</note></term> and hemp ropes—not unlike the masts of a ship—so that they would be strong enough to sustain the weight. Yet, because the Architect did not trust these columns alone, he arranged four other beams at the summit of these eight columns, which connected the two corresponding columns on each side with a tight joint. Thus it happened that the columns opposite each other, joined by this tight bond, suffered no inward bending from the weight of the hanging Obelisk.

To these beams, four other transverse beams, **A B C D**, were inserted, whose duty was to support the hanging Obelisk. But because this entire machine did not yet seem to have obtained sufficient strength for a mass of such great weight, then:

**Fifthly**, the four middle columns—two on each side—were braced by four other beams applied like <term>Rams<note>Original: *Arietibus*. In this context, these are diagonal shoring beams or "rakers" used to provide lateral stability to the vertical columns.</note></term>, marked in the figure with the letters **F T V X**. The eight outermost corner columns were braced by beams set at right angles; according to the partitioning of the columns, some were larger and some smaller, their thickness matching the thickness of the columns. These were most firmly secured with various bindings, iron hoops, ropes, and transverse timbers. The entire structure was open and passable in the middle for the directing of the Obelisk. This is the construction of the **Castle**, which it was necessary to set forth as the foundation of the entire mechanical operation—a machine equally suitable for pulling the Obelisk from its first site and for erecting it in its second location.

**Sixthly**, after these things were completed by the labor of many workers, a <margin>The layer or ramp for moving the Vatican Obelisk.</margin> path was made from the original site of the Obelisk to the place prepared for its erection. This <term>ramp<note>Original: *Agger*. A raised embankment or causeway used to transport the heavy monument across the uneven terrain of the Vatican field.</note></term> was constructed from piled-up earth, firmly reinforced on both sides with wooden beams and planks so that it could not give way. It was arranged in such a way that it rose in a higher and higher slope until it reached the base upon which the Obelisk was meant to sit. After these things were also finished:

**Seventhly**, came the planting of the <term>capstans<note>Original: *ergatarum*. Literally a "grille" or "lattice," referring here to the heavy timber sled or framework used to slide the obelisk.</note></term> fashioned from four huge timbers with other transverse beams inserted, and with wheels arranged beneath it. With the help of the capstans, it was rolled along the said ramp to the established place. The Obelisk was bound with twelve very long iron...

CHAPTER II. 374 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER.

...and it was clothed with very strong poles, three of which were extended along each side of the Obelisk; to these, three other very thick iron hoops were fitted around with singular industry using iron hooks and strong restraints, which were attached to the longer poles for the purpose of preventing the hoops from being moved from their place. Furthermore, lest the Obelisk, bound by this iron armor, should suffer any damage, it was wrapped beneath this iron garment in an under-jacket woven from mats. Additionally, <term>pulleys<note>Original: *trochleæ*. These are the blocks used to multiply the force of the ropes.</note></term>, each of which was equipped with two small wheels, were hung from the iron hoops on the side facing the columns; the number of these pulleys matched the number of <term>capstans<note>Original: *ergatarum*. A capstan is a vertical-axled rotating machine developed for use on ships to apply force to ropes or cables.</note></term>. An equal number of pulleys were also arranged on the four highest beams (**AB** and **CD**), and just as many others at the base of the machine; we have placed only two in the diagram to avoid confusion.

Once these three rows of pulleys were properly arranged, the <term>cables<note>Original: *rudentes*. Heavy-duty hemp ropes used for the lifting.</note></term> were applied, each to its own section. The cables wound through the pulleys on the Obelisk were then taken up by the pulleys fixed to the beams, and from these they were directed to the pulleys fixed at the base of the machine; finally, from there, they were wound around the drums of the capstans. If a capstan at position **S** pulled a rope wound around the nearby pulley **G**, which is seen to be wound around the upper pulley **N** and the pulley **M** on the Obelisk, the capstans would gradually move the Obelisk by the pull of the machine. The capstans had four long levers, which, by the help of both men and horses, turned the machines in a circle, gradually winding the cables around the drum; by this revolution, the Obelisk was slowly raised.

Lest, in a work of such great importance, the capstans be moved with unequal motion, everyone was warned to drive the machine at the sound of a trumpet; then, at the sound of a bell attached to the machine, they would all stop the motion together. In this way, it happened that the Obelisk raised its head little by little with equal movement and over an equal duration of time. But if one of the capstans was found not to be working because the rope was slackening, that one alone would be driven while all the others remained still, until it obtained a cable of equal tension with the rest. By this skill, they now raised the Obelisk, now lowered it, and tilted it wherever they wished at the Architect's discretion; finally, they placed it upon the four leaded lions at the base of the Obelisk in that position which we behold today with admiration. And this was the manner and method by which both the Vatican Obelisk and the others were erected as ornaments for the City of Rome by <note>Pope Sixtus V (reigned 1585–1590) was famous for his urban planning and for re-erecting several ancient Egyptian obelisks that had fallen into ruin.</note> Sixtus V, a Pontiff of immortal memory, with truly immense daring.

->### On the Power of the Capstans Compared to the Weight of the Obelisk.<-

<margin>How the weight of the Vatican Obelisk was determined.</margin>
It is well established in every mechanical business that the power of the machines must exceed the weight that is undertaken to be lifted. Hence, the Architect of this present machine necessarily had to have the weight of the Obelisk exactly discovered and explored first; then, he had to organize the number of capstans to overcome it. The weight of the Obelisk was found in this way: from the stone which they call <note>Original: *granito rosso*. Red granite, the primary material of the Egyptian obelisks in Rome.</note> red granite, which is the common material of all Obelisks, he formed a cube one <term>palm<note>A Roman unit of measure, approximately 8.8 inches.</note></term> in size, which with the most diligent...

# SYNTAGMA XI. THE ESQUILINE AND VATICAN OBELISKS. 375 CHAPTER II.

Once the weighing was completed, it was found to be 86 pounds <note>The author is calculating the weight of a single cubic unit of the stone to determine the total mass.</note>; with this data, the weight of the entire Obelisk was discovered using the same method of geometric reasoning that we demonstrated for the Pamphilian Obelisk on pages 50 and 57. Specifically, it was first found to contain 11,118 cubic <term>palms<note>Original: *palmi*. A Roman palm was a unit of length approximately 22.3 centimeters or 8.8 inches.</note></term>, which, when multiplied by 86, weighed 956,148 pounds. This is the mass of the entire Obelisk, and it contains enough material to fill 370 <term>carts<note>Original: *carrucis*, or *carrettatas* in the local Roman dialect. These were standard heavy-load wagons.</note></term>.

<margin>The power of the capstans must exceed the weight.</margin> Furthermore, experience established that each individual <term>capstan<note>Original: *ergata*. A massive vertical winch turned by spokes to pull heavy cables.</note></term> had a power of roughly 33,000 pounds. Therefore, the 30 capstans arranged for this task, multiplied by 33,000, produced a force of 990,000 pounds. Subtracting the weight of the Obelisk (956,148) from this leaves 33,852, which is the excess by which the power of the capstans exceeds the weight of the Obelisk. Additionally, the iron armor with which the Obelisk was clothed—along with the attached pulleys and wooden planks—reached a weight of nearly 50,000 pounds. When added to the Obelisk’s weight of 956,148, these constitute a total mass to be raised of 1,006,148 pounds. Hence, there was a need for 40 capstans, each of which, as stated, had a power of 33,000 pounds; these, multiplied by 40, provide a motive force of 1,320,000 pounds, which exceeded the weight of the Obelisk by 313,852 pounds.

<margin>The actual raising of the Vatican Obelisk.</margin> With these preparations made, on the last day of April 1586, after first invoking the aid of the Divine Power, the beginning was given to the raising of the Obelisk. It was moved using five levers, 40 capstans, 75 horses, and 900 men, consisting partly of officials and partly of craftsmen and those driving the machine. At first, with twelve rotations of the capstans, the Obelisk was lifted from the pavement to a height of two palms, and subsequently, by 648 rotations of the capstans, it was led into its designated place. Each capstan was driven by two horses and the application of nearly 20 men. The total weight of the Obelisk, together with the armor, iron poles, belts, pulleys, and wooden planks, reached a weight of nearly 2,060,000 pounds. <note>This final figure likely includes the weight of the entire apparatus or accounts for the friction and tension across the massive complex of ropes and scaffolding.</note>

### *Proportions of the supports and pedestals.*

The Obelisk is supported above the foundation by three <term>pedestals<note>Original: *abacis*. In this context, Kircher uses "abacus" to describe the large, flat rectangular blocks or tiers that form the base of the monument.</note></term>.
The first pedestal, placed upon the foundation, is made of white marble and is 4 1/2 palms high.
The width of this pedestal’s two opposite sides is 22 1/4 palms.
The remaining 2 opposite sides are 15 palms wide.
Where it narrows through certain steps: 13 palms.
The second pedestal has a height of 13 palms.
Its width: 12 2/4 palms.
The <term>molding<note>Original: *coronis*. An architectural crowning or cornice that wraps around the pedestal.</note></term> placed around this is 4 palms high.
Wide in the upper part: 15 palms.
Wide in the lower part: 13 palms.
The third pedestal is 11 1/2 palms high.
The side: 17 3/4 palms.

Four bronze lions are placed atop this and support the Obelisk; the height of this space: 4 1/4 palms.

This entire structure of pedestals, from the pavement to the base of the Obelisk, is 38 1/2 palms.

The entire Obelisk, from the pavement to the ultimate point of the pyramid, is 152 1/2 palms high.

The total structure, however, from the pavement to the ultimate point of the Cross, is 178 1/2 palms.

### Concerning the subterranean Obelisk of the Field of Mars.

<margin>The subterranean Obelisk of the Field of Mars <note>original: "Obeliſcus Campomartius ſubterraneus"</note></margin>
<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'O': A square block containing a stylized multi-petaled flower (rosette) centered within the letter.</note>This obelisk is truly massive, not yielding in size to the Flaminian one <note>The "Flaminian Obelisk" is the one currently in the Piazza del Popolo.</note>, and to this day it can be seen in the Field of Mars at the base of Monte Citorio, near the church of San Lorenzo in Lucina. This is where its base begins, and its remaining mass extends as far as the cellar of the Palace commonly called "de' Conti." Although it is entirely buried in the earth, several of its parts can still be discerned through the wine cellars of neighboring houses. It was originally erected at Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in ancient Egypt.</note> by King Sothis <note>Kircher's "King Sothis" is likely a reference to Pharaoh Psammetichus II, who modern scholars believe commissioned this obelisk.</note>. Later, Augustus had it torn from its place and transported to Rome. To honor such a noble mass with the respect it deserved, he erected it in a very spacious and famous location in the Field of Mars, so that just as the ancient builders intended it to be dedicated to the Sun, it might also serve the Sun in marking the hours. This was achieved by setting it within a vast solar clock <note>The Horologium of Augustus, a massive meridian sundial.</note> marked with bronze lines, where the obelisk served as a <term>gnomon</term> <note>A gnomon is the part of a sundial that casts a shadow to indicate the time.</note>. Its peak was seen raised to a height of 115 palms <note>Roughly 25 meters or 84 feet.</note> from the ground and was distinguished by a golden globe.

SYNT. XII. FRAGMENTS OF OBELISKS. 379 CH. II.

But concerning the origin, the erection, and furthermore its duty in showing the hours <note>This obelisk served as the gnomon (the shadow-casting pointer) for the *Solarium Augusti*, a massive ancient sundial in the Field of Mars.</note>, the form and reckoning of the horology, the size and symmetry of this Obelisk, and other matters, since we have treated them most extensively in the *Pamphilj Obelisk* <note>referring to Kircher's 1650 work *Obeliscus Pamphilius*</note> on folio 76, we refer the reader there. Therefore, in this place, we shall only present that small portion of the Obelisk which we were permitted to see through a cellar, drawn together with its symbols, and it is that which follows.

<margin>Several hieroglyphs of the Campus Martius Obelisk.</margin>

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A vertical column of Egyptian symbols. At the top is a cartouche containing a hawk (Accipiter) with a crook (heka), a flail, and a segment. Below the cartouche, arranged vertically, are: a serpent, a semi-circular segment, two crossed sceptres, a wide bowl or crater, two arms outstretched in opposite directions, an eye (Wedjat), a wavy line representing water (hydroschema), a bird (quail chick/Coturnix), and two triangular/pyramidal shapes at the base.</note>

Where, in the first place, within the oval figure of the sacred tablet <note>original: "tabulæ sacræ ouatam figuram," referring to a cartouche</note> occurs the Hawk, with a curved staff, a flail, and a segment; and it is the amulet of Osiris the averter of evil <note>original: "Osiridis auerrunci"</note>. There follows then a Serpent, a segment, two sceptres, a bowl, two arms reaching out in opposite directions, an eye, a water-pattern <note>original: "hydroschema"</note>, a Quail, and two pyramids. The meaning of these is: *Osiris, the Ruler of all things, draws life into the bowl, benevolently and miraculously for all in abundance, by his providence immune from all malignant and Bebonian power.* <note>Kircher uses "Bebonian" to refer to Typhon or Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and enemy of Osiris.</note> And these were the only few symbols that could be obtained from the said Obelisk. And since each side of the Obelisk has only a single column of inscriptions, and therefore the figures appear very large and distinct; certainly such a distinct expression of all the figures could have been of no small help in clarifying many doubts with greater light. Therefore, it is truly a cause for sorrow that, while almost all the Obelisks surviving in the City have now been elucidated by the help of this Oedipus <note>Kircher refers to himself as "Oedipus," the solver of the Sphinx's riddles.</note>, this one alone—greater than the others in both mass and fame of name, as it was ennobled by the praises of so many ancient writers—could not see the light, but is condemned to perpetual darkness as if submerged in a certain Lethean pit <note>a reference to Lethe, the river of forgetfulness in the underworld</note>, defrauding the literary world of the hidden secrets of its teachings. But I do not doubt that in his own time a Prince of great and wise spirit will come, who, reflecting on the nobility of a mass despised and buried for so many centuries, shall restore it to that rank of honor of which it is worthy, while the entire literary world applauds. And these are the things which I thought should be said briefly about this Obelisk; for the rest, see more extensively in the *Pamphilj Obelisk* at the cited place.

### SYNTAGMA XII. FRAGMENTS OF OBELISKS. CHAPTER IX.

...has been discussed in the exposition of the others. Therefore, it remains to explain what the fish signify. The fish are placed here according to a symbolic logic that I do not recall observing on any other Obelisk or Egyptian monument. <margin>What the fish on the fragment of the Tiber Obelisk signify.</margin> These fish allude to nothing other than the warding off of those evils over which the Hawk-shaped Osiris, the author of life, keeps a watchful eye to avert. For the fish was a symbol of Osiris <note>original: "τοῦ Ὀσίριδος αἰνιγματικῶς" — symbolically of Osiris.</note>; indeed, the Oxyrhynchus, the Phagrus, or the Lepidotus <note>The Oxyrhynchus is a sharp-nosed elephantfish, the Phagrus is likely a sea bream, and the Lepidotus is a species of carp-like fish. All were sacred or taboo in different regions of Egypt.</note>, which these fish represent, were held in the highest abomination by the Egyptians at all times. This was because they devoured the private parts of Osiris after they were cast into the Nile by Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for Set, the god of chaos and brother/murderer of Osiris.</note>. As <margin>Plutarch.</margin> **Plutarch** teaches: *Of all the parts of Osiris, Isis failed to find only the male organ, for it had been cast into the river, and the lepidotus, the phagrus, and the oxyrhynchus had eaten it; it is because of this that the Egyptians especially avoid these fish. But Isis, making a replica in its place, consecrated the phallus, in honor of which the Egyptians still hold festivals today.* <note>original: "Μόνον δὲ τῶν μερῶν τοῦ Ὀσίριδος τὴν Ἶσιν οὐχ εὑρεῖν τὸ αἰδοῖον..."</note> Of all the members, only the penis of Osiris was not found by Isis; for it had been immediately cast into the Nile and tasted by the Lepidotus (or scaled fish), the Phagrus, and the Oxyrhynchus, which the Egyptians curse above all other fish; Isis, however, fashioned a <term>phallus</term> <note>A representation of the male generative organ used in religious ceremonies to symbolize fertility.</note> in imitation of it and consecrated it, which the Egyptians use in their sacred rites even today.

For this reason, the Priests, according to Plutarch, *abstain from all fish; and while on the ninth day of the ninth month all other Egyptians eat a fried fish before their doors, the priests do not taste it, but instead burn the fish before their gates.* <note>original: "πάντων τῶν ἰχθύων ἀπέχονται..."</note> The Priests abstain from all fish; but on the ninth day of the first month, when every one of the rest of the Egyptians eats a roasted fish before the doors of his house, the Priests do not taste it, but burn the fish before the entrance of the buildings. He offers two reasons for this: one is sacred and subtle, which we mentioned just before—namely, the devouring of the private parts of Osiris; the other is manifest and obvious, that fish is <margin>The Egyptian Priests abominated fish.</margin> not a necessary kind of food, but a superfluous one. For they live in the sea, which is excluded from the boundaries of the elements; they believe the sea is neither a part of the World nor an element, but a foreign, corrupt, and diseased excrement. Indeed, they abominate it to such an extent that they cannot even endure Sailors or other seafaring men, viewing them as people of a "Typhonian" nature; for they called the sea "Typhon's foam." And from this principle, the fish was also <margin>The fish as a symbol of hatred.</margin> adopted as a symbol of hatred, as Clement of Alexandria testifies in the 5th book of the *Stromata*. He says that in Sais, before the vestibule of the temple of Pallas <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian goddess Neith.</note>, symbols of this kind were engraved: an infant, an old man, a **Hawk**, a **fish**, and a **Hippopotamus**. The boy and the old man hinted at the condition of human nature, verging from childhood to old age and then returning to a state of second childhood; the **Hawk** signified God, and whatever is divine within us, and life itself; the **fish** signified hatred and death together, which they called ruin and destruction; and the **Hippopotamus** indicated impudent violence and the vehement discord of nature. These symbols, placed in order, were read as follows: *We are born, we grow old, we live, we die, by nature's discord.*

But to return to our purpose: the fish displayed on this Obelisk, together with the Hawk visible in its mysterious attire, signified symbolically the destructive force that intervened between Osiris and the "Typhonian brood" (of which kind the fish were) <margin>The meaning of the fish on the Obelisk.</margin> against Osirian fertility; and thus Osiris [does] nothing...

...signifies nothing other than a certain power over all evils, which obtains in this offspring born from the foam of Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, associated with chaos and the desert.</note>, a warding-off power. For Osiris is that penetrative force of the Universe, providing fertility to all things through motion and heat; this is indeed aptly suggested by the Serpent-bearing globe, and another orb enclosed by two Asp-snakes. And by the ship *Baris* <note>original: "Barym" — a type of flat-bottomed boat used on the Nile.</note>, carrying a Hawk-shaped statue, what else do they suggest but the transmission through all the paths of the World of that power mentioned shortly before, which dwells especially in moisture? Since the Typhonian powers, indicated by fish, were opposed to him, they thought Osiris should be placed as a most powerful <note>original: "ἰσχυρότατον" (ischurotaton) — most powerful</note> defense against them, like a most effective protective and prophylactic amulet <note>original: "Alexiterium" — a term for a remedy or preservative against contagion or poison.</note>. But these remarks on the Tiber Obelisk shall suffice.

### CHAPTER III.

->Fragment of the Roman College.<-

The question is therefore asked in this place, whether these three fragments belong to one obelisk, or to different ones? I respond that they are from different obelisks, because both the measurement of the fragments and the context of the hieroglyphs clearly demonstrate this. Indeed, the measurement matches none of these three fragments, nor can they be aptly joined together, as the fragments are sometimes narrower in the upper part and wider in the lower; this deformity of the parts and disproportion in the joining clearly teaches that they cannot possibly be fragments of a single obelisk. <margin>In the discussion of the Pamphilian Obelisk <note>The "Obelisco Pamphilio" is the one now standing atop Bernini’s Fountain of the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona.</note> we said the opposite, because it seemed so to us then; now, having explored more diligently, we find otherwise.</margin> In addition, there is the differing color of the fragments, which likewise indicates they cannot be parts of one obelisk. Secondly, it appears from the context of the hieroglyphs, which follows a disparate logic in each of the said fragments. From this, I conclude that these were fragments of three different obelisks. These obelisks, moreover, are of the number of those they call "minor," being equal to the *Mahutean* <note>The "Macuteo" obelisk, found near San Macuto and later moved to the Pantheon fountain.</note> and the *Medicean* <note>The obelisk formerly at the Villa Medici, now in the Boboli Gardens in Florence.</note> in terms of size; Publius Victor <note>An ancient cataloger of Roman regions and monuments.</note> testifies that forty-four such obelisks of varying sizes were brought to Rome from Egypt. As to where in the world such obelisks were erected, receive these few words.

<margin>44 minor obelisks were formerly erected in Rome.</margin>

It is established by the authors of Roman Topography that in that place where now stands the Church of the Blessed Virgin, which takes its name from Minerva <note>Santa Maria sopra Minerva, built over the ruins of an ancient temple.</note>, and the most celebrated monastery of the Order of Saint Dominic, the Temple of Isis once stood. In this temple, just as all Egyptian religions (more truly superstitions) were practiced with the greatest fervor, so it was adorned with every kind of apparatus of monstrous images in the Egyptian manner, such that in later times from no other place in the City of Rome has such a great abundance of Egyptian statues been unearthed as from this place; this is an open and clear testimony of the Egyptian <term>πολυμορφίας</term> <note>original: polymorphias — "multitude of forms" or "diversity of shapes."</note> which flourished in the said temple. <margin>The Temple of Isis formerly in Rome.</margin> In this Isiac shrine, undoubtedly among the other proofs of the Nilotic religion, obelisks were also erected, of which only these fragments remain, the rest being either buried in the earth or cast into the foundations of new buildings. Read what Pomponius Laetus, Boissard, and P. Alexander Donatus treat at length in their *Topography of the City of Rome* concerning this Temple of Isis and Serapis; they state that the entire space occupied by the Roman College and the monastery of the Order of St. Dominic all the way to the Pantheon was once taken up by the [Temple] of Isis and Serapis...

...they say it belonged to the region of <note>The text likely reads "Isidis" (of Isis) in the full version, referring to the Iseum Campense, a major Egyptian temple in ancient Rome.</note> Isis. This is clearly demonstrated by the huge abundance of Egyptian antiquities which, even as I write this, are being excavated from the ruins of that place. I display a significant portion of these for viewing in my own Museum.

In this same location, a fragment of a Nilotic vessel <note>A ritual bowl or "Nilometer" fragment used for measuring the Nile's flood or as a water-clock.</note> was unearthed, covered in hieroglyphic signs. From this, the nature and shape of these Nilotic vessels can be clearly understood. A line appears there, divided into twelve parts. Along the interior surface of the vessel, extending to the bottom, twelve equally spaced projecting markers are arranged in order. These markers were undoubtedly used either to measure the rise and fall of the river, or to indicate the hours in a water-clock <term>hydrologio: an ancient device that used the flow of water to measure time</term>. On the exterior surface of the vessel, near the outer rim, there is a circle divided into 365 stars, serving as an index for as many Guardian Spirits <term>Geniorum: protective spirits or minor deities</term> as there are days in the year. Next follow various Protective Deities <term>Apotropæa Numina: gods or symbols intended to ward off evil</term>. Since I have explained these elsewhere, I do not wish to be tedious in listing them here, but instead of a long discourse, I shall provide the illustration itself, as follows.

### CHAPTER III.

...over which they are also appointed as governors. We have already shown many times, following Horus <note>Kircher refers to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs</note> and other authors, that the mark of a star indicates a Genius <note>A presiding spirit or minor deity</note>. Below these stars, various images of divinities are seen, each of which we have marked with the letters G, D, C, E, F, H, M, N, and O; these represent the primary lesser gods commonly worshipped by the Egyptians, whom we have often mentioned. The statue marked **G**, distinguished by its canine head, the <term>Crux ansata</term> <note>Ankh: the "cross with a handle," representing life</note>, and a <term>Cucuphomorpho</term> <note>Was-scepter: a staff topped with the head of a hoopoe bird (cucupa), symbolizing power and dominion</note> scepter, represents **Anubis**. **C** represents **Isis**, notable for the globe and bovine horns she wears on her head, her feminine attire, and her scepter and Ankh-cross. Directly across from her, the image of an Isiac Genius, venerable in its basket-shaped tiara, offers two small vessels to Isis with both hands. This indicates that the Earth (which they called Isis) would not fulfill its duty unless it received the benefit of the "moisture of the Nilotic Osiris" <note>The floodwaters of the Nile</note>, by which it is made fertile. Through figure **D**, one might also understand a Priest who, having assumed the form of **Osiris**, entreats Isis through a sacred rite to obtain what he desires. Furthermore, figure **E** denotes **Horus**, as we have already frequently explained; the small sacrificer **F**, appearing in the form of a "Genius of the Hours," seems to offer a sacrifice to him by pleading through the mystical logic of the surrounding symbols. Following him is the image of another divinity, **H**, dressed in feminine clothing; this indicates **Nephthys**, the minister of Horus, equipped with the symbols appropriate to her. As for columns **I** and **K**, both of which feature the <term>Cucuphomorpho</term> staff at the top, their hieroglyphic inscriptions are identical and carry the same meaning, which I provide here:

> *May the Good Spirit <note>original: "Agathodaemon"</note>, the governor of universal Life, pour out the moisture of the great vessel—enriched with an immense variety of things over which the said Good Spirit presides—from the superior vessel into the inferior vessels, for the fertile propagation of life.*

The second figure displays another fragment which, however, does not seem to have fit with the first figure shown above, since it does not contain stars. It is likely that it was an intermediate fragment of the vessel. Here, the hawk-headed **Osiris** appears with his **Isis**, in exactly the same manner seen everywhere on the panels of Obelisks; therefore, I consider an explanation of these most famous images, which have been explained more than once elsewhere, to be superfluous. As for what the Hawk **P** sitting upon the square **S T** signifies, we have explained this in our study of the Ramessean Obelisk, where it appears with entirely the same figures. The hieroglyphic inscriptions **V** and **X**, being almost the same as inscriptions **I** and **K**, do not vary in meaning. For the inscriptions surrounding the borders, **P, Z, Q, R**, see the explanation of the Borghese Sphinx, which they match.

Therefore, all inscriptions of this kind were engraved upon the sacred vessel for the purpose we have often stated: because they were thought to possess great power for entreating the Divinities, owing to a hidden property most pleasing to the Gods. Figure **III** represents the head of **Horus**. Figure **IV** shows a **Lamp of Isis**, marked with her head; concerning this, see the *Treatise on Egyptian Lamps*. Let these few fragments out of countless others suffice.

-> END OF THE TWELFTH TREATISE. <-

# CHAPTER I.
### *On Metempsychosis.*

<margin>The Egyptian custom of embalming corpses</margin>
IT WAS the custom of the ancient Sacred Scribes <note>original: *Hierogrammatéon*; the priestly class responsible for sacred writing</note> of Egypt to embalm the bodies of those who had been most celebrated and conspicuous in this life—whether through religion and the worship of the Gods, or through beneficence and the contribution of other things leading to the benefit of the fatherland—treating them as if they were the bodies of certain earthly Gods. This was done with a specific and singular mixture of spices, discovered through great effort for this purpose, to ensure eternal duration against every stain of corruption and decay. Once embalmed, they wrapped them in fine linen <note>original: *carbasso*; often referring to high-quality flax or cotton</note> marked and painted with various hieroglyphic signs; and finally, once wrapped...

<summary>This page serves as the frontispiece and introduction to Kircher's study of mummies, dedicating the work to his scholarly correspondents and beginning an explanation of why the Egyptians sought to preserve the body eternally through embalming.</summary>

<keywords>mummies, embalming, Giovanni Nardi, Johannes Marcus Marci, metempsychosis, reincarnation, sacred scribes, funerary rites</keywords>

--- Page 391 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the ritual treatment of the dead in ancient Egypt. It moves from the general custom of embalming to the specific materials used (linens, wax, and glass beads) and the symbolic meaning behind the mummy's appearance. Kircher links the physical "swaddled" form of the mummy to the philosophical concept of Metempsychosis—the migration of the soul—and cites Diodorus Siculus and Homer to support his interpretation of Egyptian animal worship.</meta>

...and with Idols arranged here and there, as if keepers of the preserved bodies, they would bury them beneath the sacred structures of the pyramids. These matters require no other proof than an inspection of these present <term>schematisms<note>From the Greek *schematismos*, meaning the outward form or decorative arrangement of the mummy.</note></term> or Mummies. These bodies, which since time immemorial have been joined into a "Mummy" through various mixtures of ointments, are seen wrapped in a web of fine linen. A certain mixture of wax, pitch, and a chalky paste was applied to this cloth, both to protect the fabric against all corruption and to allow the hieroglyphic marks and characters to be imprinted onto the cloth more easily and firmly.

<margin>The forms of the Mummies.</margin>
<margin>The painting of the Mummies.</margin>
On the cloth prepared in this manner, the images of those whom it encloses are first seen, painted in a certain lasting color, shown with their hands carrying symbols of sacred religion along with the fruits usually offered to the Gods. On the rest of the cloth, one can see various ornaments everywhere, such as borders and strips made of tiny glass beads of diverse colors sewn together. There are also "Girdles" made of a material resembling gemstones, filled everywhere with dotted patterns, with which those fringed linens are girded at the top.

<margin>The hieroglyphics of the Mummies.</margin>
In the spaces between these borders, you may see the characters of sacred animals and other hieroglyphics inscribed. <note>Hieroglyphic description: Kircher lists the following figures present on mummy wrappings: the Sun and Moon, an Ibis surrounded by serpents, a golden Cercopithecus (baboon), Anubis with a canine neck, Lions as symbols of the Nile, the Scarab as the "World-Maker" (Orbis Opifex), and the Meleagrides (guinea fowl) as attendants of Isis.</note> Here shine the figures of the Sun and Moon; there, an Ibis gorged with serpents, and the golden likeness of a sacred Baboon. Here stands Anubis, lifting high his canine neck; there are Lions, symbols of the fertile Nile; nor is the muddy Scarab—that "Maker of the World"—missing, nor the Guinea-hens, the eternal handmaidens of Isis.

<margin>The Shape of the Mummies.</margin>
Finally, the shape of the whole Mummy—truncated and with indistinct feet—seems to vividly express the likeness of "Hermaic" statues <note>Statues consisting of a head or bust atop a plain rectangular column.</note> or, more clearly, the image of an infant bound in swaddling clothes. By this most mysterious representation of things, they indicated that hidden return of souls through <term>metempsychosis<note>original: *metempsychosin*; the migration of the soul into a new body.</note></term> to <term>palingenesis<note>original: *palingenesian*; rebirth or restoration to a former state.</note></term>, as will be explained later.

<margin>What is Metempsychosis.</margin>
Metempsychosis is nothing other than the revolution of souls, bound to bodies by a certain fatal necessity, until—once that "Great Year of the World" has turned—they are restored to their original bodies through palingenesis. For the Egyptians, imbued with this doctrine, believed that the souls of those who had excelled in holiness and wisdom in this life would, upon departing, enter into human bodies to perform the duties of sacred animals and the Gods acting as their deputies. In this way, they believed the deceased continued to heap great benefits upon Egypt, just as they did while living in human form. Far from considering this migration of souls into the bodies of brutes as something vile or unworthy, they believed nothing more worthy or honorable could happen to them. They asserted, as Diodorus witnesses, that these animals were common dwellings for the Gods; indeed, they believed the Gods even now travel the whole earth under the masks of said animals to inspect the virtues and vices of men.

<margin>The Egyptians believed in Metempsychosis. Diodorus.</margin>
The words of Diodorus are: > "They further relate that those five Gods travel through the whole world, sometimes clothed in the forms of sacred animals, sometimes converted into the likeness of men, exhibiting themselves to the eyes of mortals."

And this is not at all a fable, but is consistent with their power; for in truth, these are the ones who effect all generation. Homer also, having traveled to Egypt, accepted this from the Priests, and affirms in a certain place in his poetic work that it happens in this manner.

<summary>Kircher describes the physical construction and iconography of Egyptian mummies, interpreting their swaddled, "infant-like" appearance as a symbol of the soul's eventual rebirth. He explains the doctrine of metempsychosis, noting that Egyptians viewed animal reincarnation as a divine honor rather than a degradation.</summary>

Homer.

> ->And the Gods, like strangers come from afar,<-
> ->Enter cities in various images of form,<-
> ->So that they may see what wicked and what just things are done by men.<-
<note>This is a Latin translation of Homer’s *Odyssey*, Book 17, lines 485–487, reflecting the belief that deities walked the earth in disguise.</note>

Just as the aforementioned Divinities—on account of their outstanding virtues and the benefits bestowed upon Egypt during their lives—were believed (impiously) to have been taken up into heaven, having returned through the bodies of sacred animals by way of <term>metempsychosis<note>The Greek term *metempsychōtikōs* refers to the transmigration of the soul from one body to another.</note></term>; so they asserted that after death, all those who had emulated the virtues of the Heroes in life would reach similar honors through a similar passage. Hence Mercurius Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many esoteric and hermetic writings were attributed.</note> says in the *Pimander*: "Of human souls," he says, "there are many changes, partly for the better and more fortunate, and partly for the contrary. For some of the reptiles are changed into aquatic creatures; the souls of aquatic creatures migrate into land animals; those of land animals climb into birds; those of the air are turned into men; and then the immortal souls of men pass into Demons, and finally they fly happily into the Choir of the Gods." Thus says Trismegistus.

<margin>Trismegistus.</margin>
<margin>Herodotus.</margin>

All of which Herodotus confirms in Book 2: "These were the first who said that the soul is immortal, which from a dead body then migrates into another and yet another body as each is born, and when it has traveled through all things—terrestrial, marine, and winged—it enters into the body of a man being born; and they maintained that this circuit takes place within a period of 3000 years." From these things it is clear that the Egyptians felt that the souls of the holy descend into holy animals, but those of the reprobate into the reprobate and abominable—such as Crocodiles, Asses, Hippopotamuses, and fish, as they tell of Typhon <note>A monstrous deity in Greek/Egyptian mythology associated with chaos; here linked to the Egyptian Set.</note> and Ochus—according to the merit of each individual. And from here that prodigious <term>zoolatry<note>original: *zōolatria*; the worship of animals.</note></term> of the Egyptians found its origin, such as for Dogs, Hawks, and Cats (whom they admitted to a common table with themselves, nourished with the most exquisite foods, contrary to the custom of all other nations).

<margin>
The Egyptians believed the souls of the pious migrate into holy animals, those of the impious into reprobate ones.
**Zoolatry** of the Egyptians
</margin>

These superstitious dogmas, creeping gradually to the Hebrews and Greeks, finally filled the whole world with fanatical superstition. Indeed, the Hebrews—being more greedy for new dogmas than others—dragging these things into the Synagogue, were the first founders of that new heresy concerning the subterranean revolution of souls, which they call <term>the revolution of souls from the caves<note>original: *gilgul ha-neshamot me-mechiloth*; a Kabbalistic concept involving the "rolling" of souls through underground passages, especially to reach the Land of Israel for resurrection.</note></term>: concerning which Elias Levita <note>A 16th-century Jewish scholar and grammarian.</note> says thus in *Thisbi*.

<margin>Elias Levita.</margin>

<note>original Hebrew: ומה מה שאומרים בעלי הקבלה גלגול הנשמות ודעתם שכל נשמה ונשמה נבראת שלשה פעמים ר'ל שתהיא מתגלגלת בגופי שלשה בני אדם וכן אומרים שנשמתו של אדם הראשון נתגלגלה בגוף דוד המלך ומדוד התגלגלה בגופו של משיח ואדם ר'ת אדם דוד משיח וכן אמרו שהנשמות של בעלי עבירות יתגלגלו בגופי בעלי חיים כל אחד לפי עונו</note>
And this is what the masters of Kabbalah say concerning the **revolution of souls** <note>original: *Gilgul ha-Neshamot*</note>, and their opinion is that each and every soul is created three times; that is to say, it revolves through the bodies of three human beings. And so they say that the soul of Adam the First revolved into the body of King David, and from David it revolved into the body of the Messiah; and "ADaM" is an acronym for **A**dam, **D**avid, and **M**essiah. And they also said that the souls of the masters of sin would revolve into the bodies of animals, each according to his sin.

"From this it is," he says, "that the Kabbalistic authors differ concerning the revolution of souls, whose opinion is that each soul is created three times: as if they were saying that it rolls itself through the bodies of three sons of man; whence it is said that..."

### CHAPTER I. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS. 390

The Hebrew fiction concerning the transmigration of souls.
א Adam
