...that the soul of the first man [Adam] rolled itself into the body of *King David*, and from there it is destined to return into the body of the *Messiah*. They believe this is signified by the letters found in the word אדם *Adam* <note>original Hebrew: "Adam"</note>, each of which constitutes a complete name: *Adam*, *David*, and *Messias* <note>This is a Kabbalistic technique called Notarikon, where letters of a word form an acronym for other words</note>. They also said that the souls of men who have turned away from the truth migrate into the bodies of animals, each person's soul according to the nature of the sin committed. This is the opinion of the Kabbalists.

<margin>
Pythagoras drew metempsychosis from the Egyptians.
Iamblichus.
</margin>

Furthermore, the second author of this philosophy among the Greeks was Pythagoras. Iamblichus relates in his *Life of Pythagoras* that he was instructed by the Egyptian priest Canuphæus. Pythagoras held certain animals, such as roosters, peacocks, oxen, and magpies, in such singular honor that he even deigned to speak to them with familiar address. He had so deeply internalised this way of philosophizing that he was not ashamed to claim that his own soul had previously been in a peacock; from the peacock it moved into Euphorbus, a leader in the Trojan War; from Euphorbus into Homer; and finally from Homer into Pythagoras.

<margin>
The error of Julian the Apostate concerning metempsychosis.
The error of Plato concerning metempsychosis.
</margin>

Julian the Apostate <note>The Roman Emperor (r. 361–363 AD) who attempted to revive polytheism</note> used to assert that the soul of Alexander the Great had returned in his own person; and Simon Magus <note>A biblical figure often associated with occultism</note> used to claim that Helen, the cause of Troy's destruction, had returned in a certain woman of Tyre. Plato, himself a disciple of the Egyptian priests, dared to say that a soul migrating from a body ends up in that which it most resembled in life. From this he was accustomed to infer (as Olympiodorus testifies) that a person dedicated only to feeding themselves, who slumbers day and night, would become a tree; a kite <note>A type of bird of prey</note> would be one who lives by plunder through greed; a lion, one who serves excellently as a soldier; a dragon, one who rages cruelly against the human race; a man, one who lives civilly; a hero, one who searches into the secrets of nature; a "daemon" <note>Used here in the Greek sense of a 'daimon' or guiding spirit, rather than an evil entity</note>, one who studies mathematics; and an angel, one who studies divine things. For the mind becomes such as the habit it puts on.

<margin>
The opinion of Orpheus and Zoroaster concerning metempsychosis.
Zoroaster.
The Persians called the initiates Lions, hyenas, and crows.
</margin>

Hence Orpheus, in the hymn to the Terrestrial Mercury, says: "For it is necessary to circle the boundless path of eternity" <note>original Greek: "κυκλοῦν γὰρ ἀνάγκη ἀπειρέσιον οἶμον αἰῶνος"</note>. Dwelling in the irreversible house of necessity at the river Cocytus, he said the soul would attain its state after life according to what its works were during life. The words of Zoroaster harmonize with this in the book titled *The Magical Sayings of the Zoroastrian Magi*: "To thee, the beasts of the earth shall inhabit the vessel [the body]!" <note>original Greek: "Σοὶ δὲ ἀγγεῖον θῆρες χθονὸς οἰκήσουσι"</note>. Hence the Persians, in the Mithraic rites <note>Mysterious rituals dedicated to the god Mithras</note>, in order to indicate to others the kinship we have with animals, called all the initiates participating in the rites "Lions," the female initiates "Hyenas," and the ministers "Crows."

<margin>
The Egyptians sought to recognize Gods and Kings under the masks of animals.
Philostratus.
</margin>

Thus Porphyry says in Book 3 of *On Abstinence*: "They acknowledge metempsychosis in the mysteries of Mithras; hinting at our commonality with the animals, they are accustomed to initiate us through animal forms, so that they call the initiates participating in the same rites 'Lions'" <note>original Greek: "Τὴν μετεμψύχωσιν ἐν τοῖς τοῦ Μίθρου μυστηρίοις ὁμολογοῦσι· τὴν δὲ κοινότητα ἡμῶν τὴν πρὸς τὰ ζῶα αἰνιττόμενοι δι' ἐκ τῶν ζώων ἡμᾶς μυούων εἰώθασι, ὡς τῷ μὲν μετέχοντας τῶν αὐτῶν ὀργίων μύστας καλεῖν λέοντας"</note>. All these ideas flowed from nowhere else but the Egyptians, who studied to recognize their Gods and Kings in every way as they went about under the masks of animals; I thought I would not be doing a thankless task by bringing forward a few examples of this here.

<margin>
The fable of the King of Egypt wandering under the image of a Lion.
</margin>

Philostratus, the author of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, testifies in Book 2 that Apollonius possessed this kind of knowledge. For he relates in the following words that Amasis, a most powerful king of the Egyptians, was recognized by him in the form of a lion: "It is a wonderful thing," he says, "which happened to Apollonius while he was still in Egypt. A certain man was leading a tamed lion by a leash like a dog wherever he wanted; the lion was gentle not only to him but to all others who met him. In this way, the man seeking pay had already traveled through many cities, and even entered temples, because he was clean from slaughter and unpolluted: for he did not even lick the blood of sacrificial victims."

CH. II. 392 THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>
Various fables of the poets drew their origin from the Egyptian doctrine of <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>The transmigration of souls from one body to another.</note>.
Diodorus, Book I, Chapter 6.
</margin>
...hieroglyphic logic, where one will find this material handed down by profession. Furthermore, whatever the Poets invented concerning the <term>Elysian fields</term> <note>The paradise of the afterlife in Greek mythology.</note>, the <term>Styx</term> <note>The river forming the boundary between Earth and the Underworld.</note> and its rivers, and Mercury as the transporter of souls, Diodorus demonstrates that it all took its origin from the Egyptians with these words: *When these things were brought over to the Greeks by Orpheus, Homer imitated Orpheus, writing the same in his poem, saying that Cyllenian Mercury calls forth the souls of Heroes, holding a wand in his hands. And again: they were near the flow of the Ocean, and the Leucadian rock, and the gates of the Sun, the dreams of the people. There followed a green meadow, where the souls of the younger ones were, the images of the dead. Thus he calls the Nile "the Ocean," because the Nile is called Ocean by the Egyptians by its own name. He calls Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in Egypt.</note> "the Gates of the Sun." He considers the "Meadow" to be the fictional habitation of those who have been carried across the marsh called Acherusia. And near Memphis, and around it, are pleasant meadows and marshes full of reeds. He next continues that the dead inhabit these places, because the tombs of the Egyptians are indeed mostly placed in those locations. The bodies are carried across the river and the Acherusian marsh to the tomb and buried there; and many other things, which the Egyptians still observe today, give place to the fables that the Greeks invented about the underworld. For the ship that carries the bodies, called a Barys, is what the Greeks call an <term>embates</term> <note>original Greek: ἐμβάτης, meaning a passenger or ferry-traveler.</note>. He says a small coin is given to the ferryman, whose name was given by the inhabitants as Charon. They assert that around these places is the temple of shadowy Hecate, the gates of Cocytus, and the gates of oblivion distinguished by bronze bars. There are also other gates of Truth, near which sits a statue of Justice without a head. Many other fabulous things are reported about the Egyptians, which still persist in name and practice.*

# CHAPTER II.
### ->Why the Egyptians studied the preservation of corpses with such great zeal.<-

<margin>
The care of the Egyptians in burying the dead.
</margin>
I find that there has never been any nation in the world that studied to preserve the bodies of the dead with greater care and diligence, or to adorn them with greater preparation, than the Egyptians. The cause of this matter must be investigated; which we shall now provide, after first setting forth some necessary things to be known.

<margin>
The Egyptian dogma concerning the revolution of things.
</margin>
I suppose, therefore, first, that it was a specific dogma of the Egyptians that the state of the world would return to its original state after 36,000, or as others wish, after 40,000 years; from whom Plato, having been taught this, passed it on to posterity, although he defines the revolution of souls in a circle of 10,000 years: 

<margin>
Plato. Plato’s opinion on the revolution of souls.
</margin>
*In all these cases, he says in the <term>Phaedrus</term> <note>One of Plato's famous dialogues concerning the soul.</note>, whoever has led a just life afterward obtains a better lot; but he who has lived unjustly, a worse one; for the soul does not return to the same place from which it set out for a space of 10,000 years. For it does not recover its wings before this time, except for the soul of one who has philosophized without deceit, or who has loved beauty together with the study of wisdom; if these indeed choose this same life three times in a row, in the third circuit of a thousand years, they fly away with their wings thus recovered after three thousand years.*

...departing. And those things which follow. **Abenephi** <note>Also known as Ibn Wahshiyya, an Arabic author whose works Kircher believed contained genuine ancient Egyptian wisdom</note>, however, states that according to the true opinion of the Egyptians, souls revolve through various bodies every seven thousand years. At last, they are restored to their own body—but only if it has been preserved to the highest degree from all corruption and fortified by the assistance of the Divinities—until the completion of 49,000 years. This number is the square of seven, at which time the souls are finally restored to their own "Ideas" <note>In Platonic thought, the "Idea" is the perfect, eternal form of a thing</note> to be eternally blessed. In our work on the **Kabbalah**, we have shown that the Kabbalists also embraced this opinion, or rather this madness, alluding by a hidden analogy to the six days of Creation and the seven of rest.

<margin>The duration of the tutelary governance of Egypt</margin> I suppose secondly, from the same doctrine (as we taught in *Astrology*), that every seven thousand years, the reign of the seven tutelary princes of Egypt who rule the world comes to an end and revolves back to the first. This continues until 49,000 years, when a state of permanence of things is achieved, according to the mind of the Egyptians. Moreover, by the change of their governance, a change also occurs in the former state of the body; that is, a soul that has led a righteous life will, after an interval of 7,000 years and after various revolutions are completed, seek again its own body left in the tomb. However, it shall be promoted to a higher sphere until, having traversed all spheres, it is restored to its Idea, eternally blessed, and no longer subject to any law of **Adrastia** <note>A Greek name for Nemesis or Necessity; here referring to the inescapable cycle of fate or change</note> or mutation.

<margin>Plato. Plato's doctrine on the transmigration of souls.</margin> All of these things were undoubtedly received from the Egyptians and handed down to posterity by **Plato** in these words from the *Phaedrus*: *The rule of the Goddess Adrastia—that is, of the inevitable Divinity—is this: that whatever soul, having accompanied a God, has glimpsed any of the true realities, shall be unharmed until another cycle; and if it can always do this, it shall be forever unhurt. But if, being powerless to follow, it has not seen, and by some chance becoming filled with forgetfulness and vice, it is weighed down; and being weighed down, it breaks its wings and falls to the earth; then the law forbids this soul, in its first generation, to enter into any brutal nature. Instead, it commands that the soul which has seen the most should enter into the birth of a man who will be a Philosopher, or a seeker of beauty, or a Musician, or a Lover. The soul that holds the second place shall descend into a legitimate King, or a warlike man and Commander; the third into a governor of a Republic; the fourth into a hardworking Athlete or Physician; the fifth into a Prophet or an Initiate; the sixth into a Poet, and so on.* And in the *Phaedo*: *The souls of the wicked,* he says, *are compelled to wander around graves, paying the penalties for a wicked life passed. Thus they are driven about until, accompanied by the desire for a bodily nature, they put on a body again. Moreover, they put on such characters as are fitting to the habits they practiced in life.*

<margin>Trismegistus said souls migrate from sphere to sphere. Marsilio Ficino.</margin> That righteous souls are indeed promoted from sphere to sphere is proven from **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of Egyptian wisdom</note> by **Marsilio Ficino** in *Platonic Theology*, Book 17, Chapter 3. *Just as,* he says, *all the spheres of the world vary their forms through souls, yet at last repeat their own recurrences; so our souls, similar to the celestial spirits, put on various forms of bodies, and in certain circuits of time are involved in the same bodies as before.* This <term>palingenesia</term> <note>original: "palingenesiam"; Greek for "rebirth" or "regeneration"</note> is what **Zoroaster** calls "regeneration," about which **Hermes** disputes at length with his son **Tat**.

<margin>The goal of the Egyptians in embalming bodies.</margin> But let us return to the subject proposed to us for explanation. The Egyptians, therefore, being wonderfully anxious to establish a right and holy life, had this sole purpose in the mysterious exhibition of ceremonies regarding corpses...

...the preservation of bodies <note>original: "corporum conditura"</note> seemed to have been prescribed for themselves, so that their souls might find a dwelling worthy of their merits in the revolution after this life, most closely joined to God. And since they knew from tradition that souls who had lived wickedly linger around tombs, seeking some human body to enter, lest by the sentence of the Judge they be forced to undergo the bodies of beasts—a fate matching their beastly actions—and be compelled to lead an eternally miserable life; for this reason, they destined their bodies for eternity with such great ceremonies and burial places. 

Furthermore, they were persuaded that souls could by no means enter bodies that were subject to corruption, reduced to ashes, or mutilated in any way. Hence came their great care and concern for preserving the bodies of the dead free from any stain of corruption; hence they applied themselves with such diligence so that, in hidden places most fortified against all injuries of time, they might safely store them—previously purified with all the solemnity of ceremonies and protected with the greatest zeal by so many Divinities and tutelary Spirits against the power of adverse Deities. They relied on the firm hope that once the revolution of souls prescribed by the law of Adrastia <note>Adrastia is a Greek name for Nemesis, representing inescapable Fate or Divine Law</note> was completed, they would reclaim those bodies and, being promoted to higher spheres, finally—once the whole period of revolution was finished—they would be restored to their eternally blessed Idea <note>the perfect, eternal archetype of the soul</note>, no longer subject to any laws of change or circumvolution. 

For as the most excellent physician <margin>Ioannes Nardius.</margin> Ioannes Nardius <note>Giovanni Nardi, a 17th-century Italian physician and commentator on Lucretius</note> teaches from Lucretius: *The Egyptians, deeming it a sacrilege to expose to various dangers that body which, after three myriads <note>A "myriad" is 10,000; thus, 30,000 years</note> had passed, was to be the home of the returning soul, etc., therefore warded off the dreaded injuries with every skill. Since these injuries could arise from a double source—namely internal and external—they provided for both with great <margin>The Egyptians smeared the bodies of the dead with bitumen.</margin> caution. First, with a most powerful and deeply penetrating ointment, they blocked the rot whose final offspring are decay and worms, meeting them with that same coating and new fortifications.* 

Certainly, at all times the primal nature of the Egyptians was so prone to immortality and metempsychosis <note>the transmigration of the soul into a new body</note> that they not only firmly believed what was handed down to them by their predecessors but also entirely persuaded other nations of it—among others, <margin>Herodotus.</margin> Pythagoras, who (as has been said) first brought this doctrine to the Greeks, as Herodotus clearly teaches. *For the Egyptian race, most eager for eternity,* says Nardius, *since they considered it well-advised for the most excellent portion of man, through the change of lodging and transmigration, brought immense aid to the perishable part (as much as lay in their power); and after the funerals were performed with costly care and pomp, they warded off putrefaction from the corpse by every ingenious means. For, according to the testimony of Diodorus in Book 2: they think the time of the present life is of little value, but the glory of the future, which is obtained through virtue, is to be most highly esteemed. They call our houses 'inns,' as if they were to be inhabited by us only for a short time; but they call the sepulchers of the departed 'eternal homes.' Therefore, they disregard the care of building houses, but spend the greatest zeal and labor on the magnificence of their tombs, as the vast masses of the Pyramids and the unheard-of tombs of Simandius <note>Simandius is the name used by Diodorus for Ozymandias, or Ramses II</note> clearly show.* But that these things are so will become clearly evident from the interpretation of the following diagrams.

### On the preparation of mummies, that is, on the method of preserving corpses.

-> § I. <-

<margin>Herodotus. Diodorus. Nardi.</margin>The method of preserving <note>original: "condiendi"</note> and burying the bodies of the deceased used by the Egyptians is described at length by Herodotus in *Euterpe* (Book II), and by Diodorus Siculus in Book 1, Chapter 6; I also made ample mention of this in the first volume concerning the Politics of the Egyptians. The physician Giovanni Nardi <note>An Italian physician (c. 1585–1654) who wrote on Lucretius and ancient medicine</note> describes the same rite in detail in his commentaries on Lucretius toward the end. We shall weave in the words of Herodotus at this point. *The mourning rituals <margin>The Egyptian method of preserving and burying bodies.</margin> and burials of these same Egyptians are as follows: Whenever a person of some importance dies in a household, all the women of the family smear their heads and faces with mud. Then, leaving the corpse at home, they wander through the city wailing, with their clothes tucked up and breasts exposed, joined by all their female relatives. On the other side, the men beat themselves, their chests bared. Meanwhile, they do not wash, nor do they consume wine or any but the coarsest food, nor do they wear fine clothing. When these things are done, they finally bring the body for embalming. There are certain people appointed for this very task, who practice this craft professionally. When the corpse is brought to them, they show the bearers wooden models of the dead, painted to look like the real thing. And they say one of these is most accurately fashioned—a name I will not mention, out of reverence <note>Herodotus is referring to the god Osiris, whose name was often considered too sacred to speak in the context of death</note>. The second is inferior to it and cheaper. The third is the cheapest. There are three <margin>Three types of Egyptian tombs: sumptuous, moderate, and humble.</margin> types of burials: the sumptuous, the moderate, and the humble. For the first, they charge a talent of silver; for the second, twenty minas; for the last, they spend very little. Those who <margin>The sumptuous type of burial.</margin> handle the funerals of the dead, following the practice handed down by their ancestors, present a description of the funeral expenses to the relatives, asking at which level they wish the funeral to be celebrated. First of all, they draw out the brain through the nostrils with a curved iron tool, and as they remove each part, they fill the space with preservatives. Next, with a very sharp Ethiopian stone <note>Usually obsidian or flint, used for ritual surgery because it was "pure"</note>, they cut along the flank and pull out all the internal organs. Showing the disemboweled dead man to the Sun, they then cast the intestines into the river, but not without an incantation: "O Sun, Lord of all things, and you heavenly gods, who grant the use of light to mortals, receive me, and add me as a companion to the heavenly dwellers; for indeed, I have always piously and religiously worshipped the Divinities shown to me by my ancestors while I lived; I always honored the authors of my birth; I have killed no man, nor defrauded anyone of a trust, nor committed any other unspeakable act. If I have committed any fault by eating or drinking what I should not, all that was done not for my sake, but for the sake of these." At these words, he threw the chest <note>original: "arcam," likely referring to a canopic jar or container for the viscera</note> in which the stomach was hidden into the flowing water, preserving the rest of the body as pure and free from blemish. When they have cleansed the cavity and filled it with Phoenician wine <note>Palm wine was often used for its high alcohol content and antiseptic properties</note>, they stuff it again with mixed spices; then, filling the membranes with pure crushed myrrh, cassia, and other spices—except frankincense—they sew it up again. After they have done this, they pickle the body in a hidden place for seventy days. For lon-*

...cannot go further. After seventy days have passed, they wash the corpse and wrap it in fine linen <note>original: "sindone byssinâ"</note>, using cut strips of cloth smeared with gum, which the Egyptians often use in place of glue. After this is done, the relatives make a wooden effigy in the shape of a man, into which they soon insert the deceased; having thus enclosed the body, they "treasure" it—that is, they store it away.

<margin>The average type of burial.</margin> However, those who desire the average method, wishing to avoid excessive expense, prepare the body thus: they fill a syringe <note>original: "Clysterem"</note> with an ointment derived from the cedar tree. Then, without cutting open the belly of the deceased or removing the organs, they inject this into the abdomen through the lower passage; they then preserve the body in salt <note>likely natron</note> for the seventy days mentioned before. On the final day, they drain the cedar ointment they had previously injected; this substance is so powerful that it carries out the liquefied stomach and intestines along with it. The natron <note>original: "Nitrum"</note>, meanwhile, dissolves the flesh, so that only the skin and bones of the deceased remain. When <margin>The lowest type of burial.</margin> they have done this, they return the body and take no further trouble. The third method of preparation is for those of more modest means. They wash out the belly with a purge, dry it with salt for seventy days, and then return it to be taken away.

<margin>The burial rites of the Egyptians.</margin> Before the body is buried, the relatives announce the day of burial to the judges and the friends of the deceased. They bring the body, calling the deceased by name, to cross the lake. More than forty judges stand by, sitting in a prepared semicircle <note>original: "hemicyclo"</note> beyond the pool. A boat, constructed for this purpose, is then piloted by those assigned to the task, under the direction of a Master whom the Egyptians call in their own language **Charon** <note>Kircher links the Egyptian ferryman to the Greek mythological figure who carries souls across the River Styx</note>. From this, they claim that Orpheus (about whom more will be said shortly), having witnessed this custom among the Egyptians, later invented the Underworld, partly imitating what he had seen and partly devising his own additions. Once the boat has crossed the pool, before the corpse is placed in the tomb, the law permits anyone who wishes to accuse the deceased. If it is proven that he lived an evil life, the judges pass a sentence decreeing that the body be deprived of burial. However, anyone found to have brought an unjust accusation is punished with a great penalty. When there is no accuser, or if it is clear the accusation was slanderous, the relatives end their mourning and turn to praises of the dead. They do not recount his lineage, as the Greeks are accustomed to do (for all Egyptians consider themselves equally noble), but beginning from his childhood, they review his upbringing and education, descending to his adulthood and commemorating his piety toward God, his justice, his self-restraint, and his other virtues. Having invoked the gods of the Underworld, they pray that they might place him among the pious. To these words, the entire multitude responds, extolling the glory of the deceased as one who will dwell forever with the blessed in the Underworld. Afterward, each family buries their own; some in private tombs, while those who lack them keep the coffin of the body upright against a sturdy wall in their home. Those prohibited from burial due to a crime or debt are kept at home without a coffin. If their descendants later become wealthy and pay off the debts or atone for the crimes, they then bury them honorably. For the Egyptians boast greatly that their parents and ancestors were magnificently buried.

...although many physicians have copiously described their virtues, there have been none who have—I will not say handed down the account and method of preserving them—but who have even touched upon the subject. Most people believe that the corpses which they call Mummies are prepared by no specific embalming process, but rather reach this state of incorruption through the artifice of pure nature alone, in the following manner. There is in the region of Africa across the Nile a vast desert, stretching out into immense heaps of grit and sand; for this reason, it has rightly earned the name of the "Sandy Sea." <margin>The African wilderness called the Sandy Sea.</margin> Indeed, when these sands are stirred by the winds, they occasionally trigger such savage tempests that, with the sands piled into hills by the violence of the whirlwinds, they bury alive both beasts of burden and travelers together with their merchandise, leaving no hope of escape. Herodotus <margin>Herodotus.</margin> testifies to the cruelty of this Sandy Sea; Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, King of Persia, whose "lost army" was allegedly swallowed by a sandstorm in 524 BCE.</note> experienced it when almost his entire army was swallowed by the force of the boiling sand during an expedition made against the Ammonians. Pomponius Mela reports of a certain rock existing in this desert, consecrated to the South Wind <margin>Mela. A rock consecrated to the South Wind in the legendary African wilderness.</margin>, which, as soon as it is touched by a hand, provokes the South Wind to move the most savage storms, with the sand swelling so much that it appears to be a sea stirred by vortices of waves and tides. It is said that when the Sylli <note>An ancient Libyan tribe.</note> once approached this rock imprudently—whether by some hidden force of nature or by the deceptions of magical incantations—the wind soon rose and drove mountains of sand over them, and they were all killed to a man. There is also <margin>Sphinxes in the desert and sands of Africa, according to Strabo.</margin> in this desert the Oracle of Ammon, and the Serapeum <note>A temple dedicated to the Greco-Egyptian deity Serapis.</note>, and giant Sphinxes, some of which, as Strabo testifies, are seen buried up to the head, and others halfway in the sand. When Alexander the Great once intended to consult this most famous Oracle, he prepared himself for a journey full of risk; he did indeed reach it safely, but it is recorded that those soldiers of his army whom the whirlwinds of the sandy sea did not finish off, the heat and thirst did. 

But to return to the point from which I digressed: some say that in this sandy desert, Mummies are created by the industry of nature alone. They claim that the bodies of travelers killed by the desert storms are dried and "toasted" over a long time by the power of both the Sun and this most fervent, "fatter" <note>Meaning sand rich in minerals or salts.</note> sand, and thus degenerate into this state of <term>bituminization <note>Greek: ἀσφαλτώσεως (asphaltoseos); the process of becoming like asphalt or bitumen.</note></term>. However, even if such bodies dried out by the Sun are occasionally found in this Libyan desert, they are by no means to be called Mummies; for a Mummy is properly a corpse preserved by a singular art. Let us now reveal what kind of art that is. <margin>Mummies are not corpses dried by the heat of the sun in the Libyan desert.</margin>

Haly, the Arab physician <note>Haly Abbas, a 10th-century Persian physician.</note>, in his book on the medicinal virtue of the human body, mentions Mummies quite frequently <margin>Haly.</margin>, and asserts that they achieved the gift of incorruption through the benefit of asphalt, balsam <note>original: Opobalsami</note>, myrrh, and similar substances. This, however, should not be said of all, but only of the bodies of the wealthier classes. Certainly, that most diligent philosopher and physician, Giovanni Nardi <note>Ioannes Nardius, a 17th-century Italian physician and friend of Kircher.</note>, took an experiment in this matter above all others regarding Mummies—both those he keeps in his own home and those which the Grand Duke of Tuscany <margin>Nardius. Mummies were preserved with asphalt alone or gum.</margin> keeps in his most opulent laboratory <note>The Medici family's scientific collections.</note>. He unwrapped the bodies from their bandages and dissected them with the greatest care, but found them preserved with no other aromatic preparation except asphalt. ### CHAPTER III, 398 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS. HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER.

...I expected a fragrance from the embalmed corpse, stuffed with so many and such great spices <note>original: "aromatibus"</note>: But hope failed me, and only the heavy scent of gum <note>likely referring to resin or cedar oil</note> was encountered after the body was stripped; Although indeed it was not of a single sort, and even though much credit was given to its antiquity, yet there were only traces of gum; indeed, I observed globules of homogeneous gum in the recently dissected belly. Meanwhile, being curious, I examined the skull, and I found it smeared inside with the same gum: then indeed I freely confessed that I had wasted all my labor; while I examined each part of the corpse more attentively, and I saw the gum deeply absorbed. I broke it, I tore it apart, and I did not spare the bones; everywhere they smelled and tasted of gum. Too late, I finally condemned my own cruelty <note>Nardius expresses regret for the destructive nature of his "autopsy" on the ancient remains</note>, and I bid a long farewell to Egyptian tricks.

<margin>An abundance of salt added to preserved bodies does not make them incorruptible. **Baronius**. History of a body found in salt mines.</margin> In what way, then, corpses attained the gift of incorruption through asphalt or bitumen alone is a matter of doubt. Many think they were preserved by an abundance of added salt; but this cannot hold up, since salted bodies easily melt away, as is clear from the history which Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a famous church historian</note> also inserted into his *Ecclesiastical History* because of its noteworthy outcome: While in the mountains of Salzburg, which are pregnant with fossil salt, miners in the subterranean caverns happened upon a pit filled with salt water, and quite deep; as they were diverting the water for the use of boiling salt, it happened that during the emptying, they discovered a human body in it. It was entirely whole and incorrupt; the color of the skin shone with a snow-white brightness; the eyes were open and breathed life itself; the hair and fur in their places were immune to all corruption; otherwise, the whole body was rigid like a stone. The miners being stupefied at such an unusual prodigy of nature, the matter was reported to the Duke of Bavaria; who himself, astonished by the novelty of the thing and moved by the desire to see the portent, ordered it to be brought to him the next day. When this was done, and for three days this salt-figure had been exposed to the eyes of all, behold, finally, as if impatient of the air, within a few days it dissolved into water, and having been restored to its own element, it completely flowed away. From which history it is sufficiently clear that salted bodies, even if they resist corruption for a certain time, nevertheless flow away over a long period. Therefore, since—according to the testimony of the aforementioned Nardius—the whole body smells of asphalt or bitumen, its being preserved by that is a clear indication.

<margin>By what method bodies were preserved with asphalt or bitumen. **Nardius**.</margin> In what way, however, and by what art and industry this was performed, and how the bitumen, absorbed through the innermost substance of the body, degenerates into a hard and consistent essence, is indeed difficult to know, but not inscrutable. Nardius seems to have hit the mark. His words are: *Since asphalt is a liquefiable mixture, and softens when heat is present, especially if a similar substance is added as an aid, such as the fluid bitumen which they call Naphtha <note>A flammable oil or petroleum derivative</note>. Thus, when these were joined together in a suitable cauldron, with fire forcing them, they immersed the corpse in a bituminous bath, and soaked it so long until they judged the accompanying liquid had been deeply absorbed. Nor is it right to dispute whether, while these things were being done, the fire spared the fat and flesh of the corpse: for it is reasonable to believe that as these melted, they added a significant increase to the growing bitumen. It is not our place at present to settle the dispute over the powers of "Mummy" <note>In the 17th century, "Mummy" (Mumia) was a common medicinal substance believed to have healing properties</note>, or to which they should be attributed: whether to the asphalt or to the corpse: though I do not doubt the indicated mixture is fully strong enough to settle all troubles and put an end to controversies. Finally, having removed the corpse from there, they were forced to set aside the excess*

The things that lead me to adhere to the aforementioned artifice are the equal distribution of bitumen into each individual limb, the hair still compacted with bitumen, and the eyelashes and eyebrows sometimes sticking to small fragments of that same bitumen. And I believe this was the method of embalming and preserving bodies from corruption; which I remember having read also among the Arabs; and what I have often observed in the mummies of Pietro della Valle <note>original: "Petri à Valle"; an Italian traveler (1586–1652) who brought some of the first "mummy portraits" and intact remains to Europe.</note> agrees with this. ### CHAPTER IV.

->*Regarding the Crypts and subterranean places in which Mummies, or treated bodies, were usually stored.*<-

It was not enough for the Egyptians to adorn the corpses with the stated preparation of spices; rather, so that they might not be corroded in the future by the injuries of air, water, heat, and time, or by the predations of animals, they were replaced with the greatest caution—not in places exposed to the flooding of the Nile, nor in open fields accessible to robbery—but either in the eternally lasting pyramids or in subterranean crypts carved with the greatest labor into the living rock, having first been veiled and stuffed with various coverings and wraps of bandages with a supreme and scarcely imitable industry. But let us first explore the place destined for storing the bodies, and then <margin>Crypts in which the Mummies were stored.</margin> the individual ornaments. The place of the cemetery consisted of subterranean crypts, carved, as I said, from living Alabaster <note>Kircher uses "alabaster" to describe the fine-grained white limestone of the Memphite necropolis.</note>, divided by various vaulted chambers like huge halls, and entangled with such manifold twists of windings and paths that it could be seen as a labyrinth. A <term>Ichnographia<note>A technical term for a ground-plan or architectural floor-map.</note></term> of this was sent to me not long ago by the frequently praised Tito Livio Burattini <note>An Italian polymath and explorer who spent years in Egypt and provided Kircher with precise measurements and drawings.</note>, who, out of his commendable curiosity and at no small expense while investigating the antiquities of Egypt, also penetrated these crypts. He sketched everything with singular dedication and sent the drawings to me, according to his remarkable zeal for promoting the "Republic of Letters" <note>An international community of intellectuals and scholars in the 17th century.</note>. But before we display the figure, I have decided to place here first his letter written in the Italian language, and then the ground plan of the subterranean structure, from which all things will be more clearly revealed to the curious reader.

*Letter of Tito Livio Burattini to the Author of this Work, in which whatever he observed worthy of note regarding the subterranean crypts is exactly described, together with a ground plan of the same.*

<margin>Letter of Tito Livio Burattini regarding the crypts of the Mummies.</margin> Regarding Mummies, there are various opinions, among which the most common is that they are found among the sands in Desert Arabia, and that they are the bodies of those who are buried in them when the South Wind blows <note>Burattini is debunking the "natural mummy" theory, which claimed mummies were simply travelers dried out by desert winds.</note>. How much these people are mistaken does not need to be shown, their error being very well known to those who have been in Egypt; since Mummies are nothing other than the bodies embalmed by the ancient Egyptians, of which even today a great quantity is found in the caves, especially—

### CHAPTER IV.

...directly beneath; where the famous City of <term>Memphis</term> once stood, which was located between the pyramids of <term>Giza</term> and those of the mummies, of which I shall give as detailed and true an account as I am able. Anyone who takes pleasure in reading ancient histories will have seen that after the ancient Kings of Egypt, called <term>Pharaohs</term> in their language, had lived for a long time in the most famous city of <term>Thebes</term>, they later built the City of <term>Memphis</term> on the western side of the Nile—the former having been on the eastern side—where they then resided until the time of <term>Alexander the Great</term>. By him, the city near the Mediterranean Sea was later built, which was called <term>Alexandria</term> after his name, where <term>Ptolemy Lagus</term> <note>Ptolemy I Soter (c. 367–282 BCE), the founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt.</note>, his captain, lived with his successors. <term>Memphis</term>, therefore, was the last metropolis of the ancient Egyptians, and consequently, more vestiges of antiquity are seen near it than are seen in any other place, because the Greeks used different ceremonies in the burial of their dead than the Egyptians did.

<margin>Memphis retains many vestiges of antiquity. <note>original: "Memphis multa antiquitatis vestigia retinet."</note></margin>

Beneath and around where that city stood, a great quantity of caves are seen where they buried their dead, both of the order of the Priests and that of the Knights. They entered these through a square well, but only as wide as a man can stretch one foot from the other, placing their feet in holes made in the sides for this purpose, as can be seen from the drawing. 

<margin>Caves around and below Memphis. <note>original: "Cauernæ circa & infra Memphim."</note></margin>

The depth among them varies, depending on how much more or less they excavated; however, I have not seen any of a depth less than six men high. Note that all these caves are made in the stone, which is quite soft and white in color; in these deserts, by digging under the sand no more than a cubit <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.</note>, one immediately finds the stone in which, as I said above, they carved their sepulchers. Because of this, the entire City of <term>Memphis</term> remains hollowed out, with much space still around it. 

<margin>Variety and depth of the Memphite caves. <note>original: "Cauernarum Memphiticarum varietas & profunditas."</note></margin>

Having descended into the cave, one finds a square hole the size of the chamber one enters, but one must stoop because of its low height. Its length varies, being in some places ten feet long, in others fifteen, and in others more or less. At the end of this, one enters a square room with a vaulted ceiling, each side of which is around 15 to 20 feet. In the middle of each of these four sides, there is a hearth made of the same stone, about five feet long, two and a half wide, and one high, and they are opposite one another. 

<margin>The form of the Memphite caves. <note>original: "Cauarum Memphiticarum forma."</note></margin>

Upon these they placed their dead, some put in stone <term>cases</term> <note>sarcophagi</note> from the same mountain, and some in <term>cases</term> of sycamore wood <note>original: "legno di fico moro"; the Sycamore Fig (*Ficus sycomorus*) was prized in Egypt for its durability and resistance to rot and insects.</note>, which by its nature never decays. These <term>cases</term>, both of stone and of wood, are made in the likeness of the human figure with arms extended, as we bury our dead, all adorned with hieroglyphs and gilded. The embalmed bodies inside are also adorned, many of which have a small thin plate of gold under the tongue, at most the value of two or three Hungarian ducats <note>original: "Ongari"; gold coins used as a standard of value.</note>. Out of greed for this gold, the Arabs destroy all those bodies they can find intact—though in many they find nothing—and then they sell the remainder of the body for a very low price to Muslim merchants. A great quantity of these bodies are found in the City of Cairo, which are bought by Christian merchants to be brought to Italy. 

<margin>Mummy cases of stone or wood. <note>original: "Capsæ Mumiarum e saxo, aut ligno."</note></margin>

All the cases of these cadavers have an Idol at the head and a Bird at the feet, which they also worshipped. On the wall above the case, in some of these caves, there are hieroglyphs, which I believe were epitaphs written in praise of the deceased. In many of these rooms, besides the four principal cases placed upon the stones, there are others still placed on the ground...

<margin>

Decoration and hieroglyphs of the cases. <note>original: "Capsarum ornatus & hieroglyphica."</note>

What Burattini has narrated so far in his letter is displayed in this present diagram. <margin>Ground plan & Perspective view of the chambers in which the Mummies were stored. <note>original: "Ichnographia & Scenographia camerarum in quibus Mumiæ condebantur."</note></margin> The ground plan shows the structure of the crypts, together with the <term>abaci</term> <note>Kircher uses this term to refer to the stone slabs or pedestals used as resting places for the dead.</note> upon which the bodies, enclosed in their small cases, were placed. In this location, the ground plan shows nine chambers marked by empty spaces, of which "D" is one example; all of these are equal in size. Each one has marble slabs on its four sides of a size sufficient to receive the receptacle in which the Mummy was stored. These slabs, as well as the four walls of the individual caverns in the ground plan, are marked with the numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4; those marked with the letter "X" indicate the foundations of the walls upon which the partitions rise.

These details are seen more exactly in the perspective view, in which "S" and "T" are two chambers furnished with their own vaults. Within the four walls of chamber "S," you see four slabs—A, O, P, and K—each of which contains its own <term>medicated corpses</term> <note>A literal translation of "medicata funera," referring to embalmed mummies.</note>, that is, the Mummies, adorned with the apparatus we have described. For the most part, idols are seen placed near these; there are certain swaddled "boys"—statues of guardian Gods—at the head; at the feet, you will find a Hawk <note>Referring to the falcon-headed deity Horus or the sons of Horus.</note> (of which we will speak more extensively in the following pages). For they believed that by the assistance of these figures, the body would be immune from all violence.

The second chamber, "T," contains just as many slabs, which are marked with the letters L, M, N, and B, in which you see the embalmed bodies placed together with the Guardian Gods set near them. The letters "Q" and "R" show the remains of two other chambers and the location of slabs "G" and "H." "G" shows the access or entrance into various other chambers, the multitude of which was once related to me by Michael Schatta <margin>The vast number of caverns in which the Mummies were stored. <note>original: "Cauernarum, in quibus condebantur Mumiæ, numerus ingens."</note></margin>, a Coptic Egyptian and a diligent inspector of them. He stated that they extend for many miles and are much superior to the Roman catacombs in both number and magnificence; indeed, he added that more and more new ones are detected every day.

Because of this, some are of the opinion that these types of subterranean meanders extended to that most famous place, the Oracle of Ammon and the <term>Serapeum</term> <note>A temple or religious complex dedicated to the syncretic deity Serapis.</note>, providing a great convenience for the Priests traveling back and forth, as they were immune from the heat of the sun and the whirlwinds of the sands. This will not seem at all improbable to anyone who has more deeply contemplated the many other works of the Egyptians. Indeed, some Arabs (cited elsewhere) recount that Heliopolis was joined to Memphis by a hidden passage, constructed with stupendous workmanship even beneath the bed of the Nile.

But let us return to the crypts. The individual sides have hieroglyphic patterns carved in an oval figure, which are marked in the perspective view with the letters E, Y, Z, and F. These are nothing other than the schematics which we called "sacred tables" in our interpretation of the Obelisks; of which the first, "E," and the last, "F," are entirely the same as those which occur most frequently on Obelisks. This one we call <term>Osiriac</term>, and the other <term>Momphto-Mendesian</term> <note>Kircher's invented terms for specific types of hieroglyphic groupings relating to the gods Osiris and possibly a combination of Memphis (Momphta) and Mendes.</note>; and here...

### THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS
### Page 402

...and here are positioned diagrams that correspond to those taken from the aforementioned obelisks. The remaining two, marked Y and Z—the first being a staff with a goat’s head <note>original: "baculum Hircino capite"</note> with a cycloid and water-symbol, the other a Scarab with a globe—are likewise extracted from the obelisks and are found three times on the Heliopolitan Obelisk. Since their interpretations have been provided in the cited locations, the reader may consult them there. As for why these hieroglyphic Deities were carved into the wall in a tilted position rather than upright, they marked, by a kind of hidden symbol, the sympathetic inclination that the guardian Deities had toward the preservation of bodies. For these were certain sacred amulets, of great efficacy and power among them, as has been proven in the appropriate places; thus it is no wonder that they were applied to the dead as <term>phylactica</term> <note>From the Greek 'phylakterion,' meaning a protective charm or amulet intended to ward off evil or preserve the wearer.</note>, uniquely conducive to the preservation of the bodies.

All of this is confirmed by what the most Excellent Nardi <note>Giovanni Nardi (c. 1585–1654), an Italian physician and scholar who wrote a commentary on Lucretius.</note> presents in his *Lucretius*, where he mentions the recorded subterranean cemeteries of the Egyptians. You may contemplate their site and arrangement, which is quite clearly expressed in the following figure:

**A** Modern Memphis, which is Cairo;
**B** The ruins of ancient Memphis or Babylon;
**C** The Nile flowing past from the South to the North;
**D** A carved stone, the cover of the shaft;
**E** The entrance through which one descends into the vaulted chambers;
**F** A stone chest <note>A sarcophagus.</note> marked with hieroglyphs, the guardian of another wooden one, **G**, which is displayed to be seen along with a standing statue and guardian Deities.

Through the shaft **E**, a servant descends, carrying his master sitting on his shoulders after grabbing a rope; once he has set him down, a hole first appears in the bottom side of the shaft, through which they suddenly enter a magnificent vaulted chamber. In the middle of this was situated that marble chest, heavy with a magnificent corpse. From here, a complex entrance opens into various chambers, so that a traveler might repeatedly be in danger regarding his return, unless he uses a thread in the manner of Ariadne <note>A reference to the Greek myth of the Labyrinth, where Ariadne gave Theseus a ball of thread to find his way out.</note>. In this crypt or <term>hypogæum</term> <note>An underground chamber or tomb.</note>, the bodies were placed so securely that neither the flooding of the Nile nor the humidity (which is non-existent in that scorched soil) could do any harm. The ingenuity of the craft was aided by a great deal of sand piled on top, by which both the place and what was placed within were made unknown. All of these things the most Excellent Pietro della Valle <note>A famous Italian traveler (1586–1652) who brought back mummies and manuscripts from the East.</note> confirms in his *Travels* <note>original: "Itinerario"</note> on page 372, with these words:

> In the morning, I was not yet dressed when I had more than fifty peasants around me; some brought me small idols, some said they would lead me to one place, and others to another: I sent them all off and set out cheerfully. I had with me, besides these peasants, twenty-five or thirty men; because in addition to my own people and some soldiers I had brought for protection (as the places are not safe), I had many friends... <note>original Italian: "La mattina non era ancora vestito, che haueua più di cinquanta contadini attorno..."</note>

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>CH. IV.</margin> burials, not Pyramids, but there were made anciently as structures beneath the earth infinite very deep pits <term>pozzi</term> <note>Italian for "wells" or "shafts," referring to the vertical burial shafts common in Egyptian necropolises.</note>; in the bottom of which, all around in a vault, like in our cisterns, there are indeed built some tombs, or low little grottos; inside which they placed the bodies arranged as I will describe later, and buried, to preserve them better, in the same sand; with which they then filled the pit as well, and covered it so high even with the ground, that it could not be seen, nor known where it was. And in one of these pits were placed many, many bodies, which were perhaps all of one family or kindred; as we do, who have private burials for all our people. That it was so, <margin>Belon.</margin> I know both from the account of Belon <note>original: "Belonio." Referring to Pierre Belon (1517–1564), a French traveler and naturalist who visited Egypt.</note>, and from many of these pits, open and empty, which I saw in the countryside; the Mummies, or buried bodies of which, had been found and dug up at different times by the peasants who are constantly searching for them. I did not care to descend, as many do, and as I suspect <margin>Belon.</margin> Belon did, into any of those empty pits; because my principal desire was to see the bodies as they lie, to be able to speak from sight, and not from hearsay from those ignorant peasants. Therefore, leaving the empty pits aside, and having a quantity of practical workers with me, I wanted to have them dig in new places, to find one that was full and no longer touched, if it were possible. But because, not knowing where they are, one must search at random; I considered where the ground appeared to me less moved and less probed (for one knows the signs where the peasants probe many times and find nothing) and there, in various places that seemed to me most suitable, I divided my workers, spread over a large part of the countryside; and to give them more spirit, I pitched my tent <term>padiglione</term> <note>Literally a "pavilion," used here as a base of operations for the excavation.</note> there in the middle, with the determination and promise that I would not depart from that place until I had first found something. And because I alone could not be everywhere, I put each of my men on guard at one of those excavations that were being held, to secure myself against any fraud; and so that whoever first discovered a burial or a beautiful thing would call me immediately. While the work was being attended to with fervor, one of those peasants, who since evening had let it be known that he had I know not what thing to sell me, approached the ear of my Interpreter and told him very softly that he had a whole and very beautiful Mummy, and that if I wanted to buy it, he would show it to me, for it was nearby: but that he did not want any of the other peasants to know, because they would have wanted to share in the price as well, as they must do among themselves; therefore, if I wanted to see it, it was necessary that I go without them to where he would lead me. When these words were reported to me by the Interpreter, I was immediately pleased; and having left good orders with all those who were digging, I took with me Thomas and the Painter, and followed the peasant on foot, with whom came also two or three of his relatives. They made us walk more than a mile, and perhaps two; it seeming to me very far, while he, pointing with his finger, always said "here, here, here," quite close. Finally, we arrived at a place where, near a dug pit which he told me had been discovered by him three or four days earlier, from inside certain sand under which he kept it hidden, he pulled out a Mummy, or the entire body of a dead man, which for being very well preserved and most curiously adorned and composed, seemed to me a very beautiful and gallant thing. Whatsoever things are narrated in this place...

### COLLECTION XIII. ON MUMMIES. CHAPTER IV.

Pietro della Valle <note>original: "Petrus à Valle"</note> agrees with those things which Pierre Belon <note>original: "Bellonius"</note> discovered long ago and Tito Livio Burattini <note>original: "Burattinus"</note> has recently revealed. They further assert, based on the records of the Arabs, that the multitude of these winding passages is so great that, as we said above, they extend all the way to the very temple of the Oracle of Ammon <note>The Siwa Oasis, famous for the temple of Zeus-Ammon visited by Alexander the Great</note>; and thus this entire "sandy sea" is hollow underneath, marked by innumerable chambers for the bodies of the dead. Certainly, anyone who reads of the vastness of ancient Memphis and the density of its inhabitants in the works of the cited authors will easily be persuaded that it is not at all unlikely, as is confirmed by the testimonies of so many authors. But to the matter at hand. The author <note>Kircher is referring to Pietro della Valle's travel accounts</note> then proceeds to describe the discovered mummies in minute detail, the first of which is marked with the letter **A** in the present figure.

*The mummy thus discovered, then, was seen to be a person stretched out and naked: but tightly bandaged, and wrapped in a great quantity of linen cloths <note>original: "panni lini"</note>, embalmed with that bitumen <note>A natural asphalt used in ancient embalming</note>, which, once incorporated with the flesh, is called among us "Mummy."* <note>In Kircher's time, "mumia" referred both to the preserved body and the bituminous substance itself, which was often ground up and used in European medicine.</note>

### CHAPTER IV. THE THEATRE OF EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPHS

...[mum]my, and reliable as medicine <note>In the 17th century, "mumia" (powdered mummy) was a common, though gruesome, ingredient in European pharmacies.</note>. Those bandages and bindings immediately made me remember <margin>John</margin> the resurrected Lazarus, who likely was wrapped in this way. Furthermore, over the body all around, there was a covering of the same cloths, entirely painted and gilded, which was very well sewn and pitched <note>Coated with bitumen or resin for preservation.</note>, as I believe, on all sides, and sealed on every side with many lead seals: things that all gave the impression of a person of respect. 

But what matters is that on the upper part of the body, which because of the quantity of the wrappings came to be flat, almost like the lid of a small chest, there was painted an effigy of a man of youthful age, which without doubt is the portrait of the deceased; and it was adorned in a beautiful habit, and from head to foot, with so many trifles made of painting and gold, with so many hieroglyphs and characters and similar fancies, that Your Lordship can believe me, it is the most graceful thing in the world; besides that men curious about letters can derive a thousand arguments from them for the certainty of the antiquities of those times. 

The clothing of this man is seen to be long down to the ankle, and shows that it was made of linen cloths, of which we have [record] in <margin>Herodotus</margin> Herodotus, that the ancient Egyptians of his time used to dress: however, the habit of this man, over the white of the linen, is seen to be entirely scattered with small plates of gold, with various ornaments of jewels, and of signs, or unknown characters, impressed upon them. 

The head is also covered with an ornament of gold and gems, under which the hair is seen poking out, black and curly; and thus also black, curly, and thin is the beard: at which, as also at the color of the face and hands, which is quite brown, and exactly the color of earth, not unlike that of the clearest Ethiopians, it seems to me I can believe that this man was a native of the upper and more southern parts of Egypt, and not of those of the Delta, where men ordinarily do not happen to be so brown. 

It is clearly known that he was a person of greatness, as much by the ornaments of gold and jewels that I mentioned above, as by those lead seals that hang all around from the sides of the wrapping of his body, in which it seems that a more than ordinary care for his preservation is shown; and in their imprint, which is not well discerned, it seems there is an animal sculpted. 

And also an indication of the great quality of his person is a gold necklace that he wears on his neck in the manner of our <term>Golden Fleece</term> <note>original: "Tošoni"; a reference to the prestigious Order of the Golden Fleece, used here as a familiar European comparison for high-ranking insignia.</note>; in the middle of which, upon the breast, is attached, like a jewel, a large plate of gold representing the figure of a bird, and in the middle it is sculpted with various unknown signs. According to <margin>Diodorus</margin> Diodorus Siculus, the High Judges anciently in Egypt wore such necklaces with the image of <term>Truth</term> <note>Diodorus refers to the figurine of Maat, the goddess of truth and justice, worn by Egyptian magistrates.</note>: perhaps this man was one of those: and perhaps the depicted bird he wears on his chest signifies some such sign of <term>Truth</term>, or some other similar thing. 

In the right hand, he holds a gold cup full of a red liquid, which, <margin>Herodotus</margin> whether it be wine or blood (though I believe wine more likely, conforming to the sayings of Herodotus), I hold for certain denotes some libation of sacrifice. With the left hand (on two fingers of which, that is on the index and the little finger, he has a gold ring for each, on the last joints near the nails) he holds a certain other thing, oval in shape and dark in color, which, if I am not mistaken, seems to me to be one of those fruits that in good Tuscan are called <term>Petronciani</term>, but by the Lombards are called <term>Melanzane</term> <note>Eggplants</note>; and in Rome by the common folk <term>Marignani</term>; and, if I do not remember incorrectly, in the coarse Neapolitan language <term>Molegnane</term>: and his holding it in his hand must have some mystery. His legs and feet are bare, only with black sandals, which do not cover—

...nothing else than the sole of the foot; and by passing a thong of the same black color, which comes from beneath the sole between the big toe and the toe closest to it, it is fastened with two small loops that come from behind the heel, and creates an ornament over the foot with a graceful little strap. The Author now continues by describing the word ΕΥΤΥΧΕΙ <note>original Greek: ΕΥΤΥΧΕΙ (Eutychei)</note> described on the pectoral band; it is an Egyptian word and signifies the same as "may he prosper," as we have shown extensively elsewhere. From this it is clear that the Egyptians occasionally mixed certain words of their native language into their hieroglyphs; since many deny this, they can be clearly refuted by this very example. See what we have handed down on this subject in various places of this Work, as Pietro della Valle himself demonstrates in the following words:

> *The most curious thing there is, is a band, like a belt, where in black ink—in Egyptian letters, of which I shall speak later—this word is written:* ΕΥΤΥΧΕΙ <note>original Greek: ΕΥΤΥΧΕΙ</note>, *that is Eutyche, or Eutychios. As the Greek language teaches us, this signifies "Good Fortune," which I cannot believe to be anything other than his proper name. The fact that it is written with an "I" at the end, and not with "ES" as it should be in Greek, is perhaps an Egyptian corruption; just as the letter* $\dagger$ <note>a symbol resembling a cross or the Greek letter Tau; likely the Coptic letter "Ti" (Ϯ)</note>, <margin>Origen, St. Jerome. Exodus. Apocalypse. Ezekiel. Genebrardus.</margin> *which they now call "Dei," is also Egyptian, used here in place of the T. It is without doubt that famous "Tau" of the ancient Hebrews and of other nations, in the form of a Cross, according to Origen and Saint Jerome. This is the sign of the elect, mentioned in Exodus and the Apocalypse, but more clearly in Ezekiel. The figure of this sign has been maliciously changed among their characters into another form, in the manner they use it today, by more modern Hebrews out of hatred for the Cross, as the most learned Genebrardus well says. It could also be that the word* ΕΥΤΥΧΕΙ *was a verb in the imperative mood, in the second or third person—given that, for some reason of the Egyptian language (which differs from Greek in this regard), the ending of the final syllable did not prevent this—and that it meant: "May he be happy." This was perhaps a motto used to be said then to the dead as a final ceremony, much like our modern "May he have peace" or "Go in peace." This is exactly the way that Aeneas, when sending the body of Pallas to his Father and to the tomb, is induced by Virgil to say as a final farewell:*

### DISCOURSE XIII. CONCERNING MUMMIES. CHAPTER IV.

Fff 2

I had myself lowered down cheerfully; but in the descent, I found the way much easier than I had thought, so that, without any other help, I climbed down very well and very quickly by myself. Reaching the bottom, I found the tombs all around full of dead bodies; indeed, as the peasant had said, it was clear the well had only just then been discovered. The bodies lay without order, buried—as I have told <term>Your Lordship</term> <note>original: "V. S." (Vostra Signoria), a formal address to the recipient of the letter.</note>—in the sand, which, being extremely dry, maintains them and preserves them from corruption. They lay one on top of the other, wrapped in it, just like macaroni among cheese. They were all prepared in the same way, with the same bandages and bitumen; but there was this difference: besides the two we had already taken out, there was only one other decorated with gold and painting, and even that one was not so well preserved, because perhaps it had been damaged by the peasants when they found it. All the others, which were a great quantity, had only the wrapping of simple bandages and bitumen, without gold, without painting, and without any other ornament. 

This made me think that the gilded and painted ones belonged to people of quality and the masters, and the others belonged either to servants or to people of lower condition; according to the account of <margin>Herodotus. Diodorus.</margin> Herodotus, as also that of Diodorus Siculus, who exactly report this manner of "seasoning" the bodies of the Egyptians in various ways, with more or less expense according to the quality of the persons; <note>original Latin: "de quibus vide quoque Brasauolum" — concerning which see also Brasavolus.</note> <margin>Brasavolus on the examination of medicines.</margin> <note>The margin refers to Antonius Musa Brasavolus, a famous 16th-century physician who wrote on medicinal substances.</note> 

That one mummy which I found down there with painting and gold, besides the linen wrapping, was found by the peasants inside a wooden chest, carved on top with the likeness of a maiden. One could recognize her as such by the carriage of the head with that wide, even band around the face, which hangs down from two sides toward the chest, exactly like the carriage of the head of the Sphinx. This Sphinx—signifying the fertility of Egypt due to the floods of the Nile, which occur precisely when the Sun is found in Leo and in Virgo—is therefore fashioned with the figure of a Lion from the middle down, and a Virgin from the middle up. This time, as <margin>Julius Solinus</margin> Julius Solinus says, was estimated by the Egyptian priests to be the birthday of the World. Thus it becomes clear that the carriage of its head is the carriage of a Virgin; and this same carriage was seen in the figure carved upon the aforementioned chest. It was quite different from the carriage of the head of that other woman I found together with the man, which is why we must believe that she was married, the wife of him near whom she was buried. 

Of the Egyptian custom of preserving corpses inside wooden statues representing the likeness of the deceased, instead of chests, I remember that the same Herodotus, a most ancient author, makes mention. Now, this chest or statue of the maiden had been opened there in the same tomb; and as I looked at it, I found upon it many <note>Hieroglyphic inscription: The author mentions finding "molti hieroglifici intagliati" (many carved hieroglyphs) on the wooden statue/coffin, though they are not reproduced visually on this page.</note> carved hieroglyphs. Liking it very much, I desired it and had it pulled out. 

But as for the body of the maiden that was inside (who was recognized as such also by her small size), I did not care to take it out whole, as it was not, as I have said, well preserved. Instead, I had it broken apart in my presence: first, to see how the bandages, the bones, and the bitumen were arranged inside; and second, to obtain some of that material which is medicinal and highly valued, as <term>Your Lordship</term> knows. Here they say that the material from maidens and virgin bodies is the best. I also did this to see if, inside or around the bandages, I might find any curiosities such as small idols or similar things; for in Cairo they told me that these little idols, which are seen in great quantities (and I have various kinds of them), are found inside these mummies. When they preserved the bodies, they would place them either inside the chest or at the side, for protection as tutelary gods: in...

### CHAPTER IV. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Herodotus.</margin> ...and in this one, which was among the most ornate and rich, and perhaps the daughter of the two already taken out, it seemed likely that I would find something curious more than in any other. I broke it open, therefore, but found nothing inside; indeed, from the way I saw it was, it seems difficult to me that little idols <note>original: "idolietti"</note> can be found inside those bodies, especially of the size of a piece of jasper that had been shown to me in Cairo. This is all the more so since we have it from Herodotus that they did not always cut the bodies open, but sometimes cleaned them inside and made the entrails come out with <term>cedar oil</term> <note>original: "cedria"</note> enemas; and they pulled the brain out of the head with iron tools through the nose, seasoning them in this way without breaking the bodies in any part. However, regarding this detail of the little idols found either inside or wrapped within the bandages, I defer to those who have seen better than I. In undoing the body of the maiden, I found nothing other than a very great quantity of bandages and bitumen, which makes up the entire mass of the wrapping; because the bones and the flesh are so dry, burnt, and shrunken that they are reduced exactly to the state of sticks. From this, I understand that bitumen is very powerful. And so also inside the body—whether it was whole and filled via enemas, or whether it was cut open, which could not be determined—everything was full of bitumen, to such an extent that it formed a single mass pasted together; when broken, one could hardly distinguish what was bitumen and what were bones.

All of which exactly harmonize with those things which we related above from Nardi. One thing must not be kept silent: that material was so hard that, wishing to break it, it was necessary to strike it with stones and iron tools with very strong blows, and I broke it only with great effort. From these things, <term>Your Lordship</term> <note>original: "V. S." (Vostra Signoria), the formal address to the recipient of Valle's original letter.</note> can understand how much the poor Egyptians toiled to preserve the bodies, along with the souls if it had been possible, for eternity. From this broken mummy, I took for myself the entire head and a good piece of bitumen with one of those bandages; the rest, because it seemed to me I had plenty for the money I was spending, I left entirely to those poor peasants, who are accustomed to breaking them in that way and selling the material in Cairo to those who buy it, with great profit, as merchandise. <note>In the 17th century, mummified remains were ground into a powder called "mumia" and sold as a medicinal panacea.</note> Many other things full of curiosity he found in the same place, which even to this day are seen in the Museum of the said Pietro della Valle; but as the shortness of time did not permit them to be engraved <note>Kircher refers to the time-consuming process of creating copperplate illustrations for his book.</note>, I have thought they should be omitted on purpose. There are, however, among other things, a golden plate notable for a female head, entirely filled with hieroglyphs, with various idols, and the head of <term>Apis</term> <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, often associated with Osiris.</note>, and other things, which can be both read about and seen in the Author’s work; of these we shall also make mention in the following sections.

And these are the things which we thought should be presented before we undertake the interpretation of the hieroglyphic inscriptions found on the mummy bodies. # CHAPTER V.
## Interpretation of the Hieroglyphics on Mummies, which were taken partly from the Museum of the Grand Duke of Etruria, and partly from that of Joannes Nardius.

<margin>
Nardius. Joannes Nardius’s diagrams of Mummies.
</margin>
**In that golden** commentary on Lucretius, at the end, Joannes Nardius <note>Giovanni Nardi (c. 1585–1654), a Florentine physician and scholar.</note>—physician to the Grand Duke of Etruria <note>Tuscany</note> and a man second to none in learning and erudition among the foremost physicians of this time—appended several diagrams of mummies, or preserved remains. He included them, however, not so much to explain their meaning as to demonstrate the custom of the ancients in preparing bodies for burial. Therefore, I considered it my duty to provide a timely interpretation of these figures in this place. Furthermore, so that no unnecessary expense would be incurred in engraving them anew, out of his great kindness, he sent the impressions of the copperplates <note>original: "laminarum... ectypa"</note> with which he had already printed his own work, so that they might be printed again here alongside my interpretation for the new benefit of the Republic of Letters. The diagrams which they represent were taken from the original mummies preserved partly in the aforementioned Treasury <note>original: "Gazophylacio"</note> of the Grand Duke of Etruria, and partly in Nardius's own museum, as follows.

<margin>
Diagrams of Mummies taken from the Museum of the Duke of Etruria.
</margin>
Note here, Reader, that two things can be considered in the arrangement of mummies: first, the shells or cases <note>original: "thecas seu capsas"</note> in which the bodies, marked with various hieroglyphics, were placed; and second, the substance of the mummies themselves, clothed in a manifold wrapping of bandages. While the mummy itself is often stripped of all hieroglyphic apparatus, the interior decoration of both the cases and the mummies alone shines with hieroglyphics. In this way, you see in Plate II the first and second figures. The former represents the exterior decoration of a wrapped mummy that was enclosed in a wooden chest. The second figure shows the small case together with the wrapped body placed within it. For, as was proven above from <term>Diodorus</term> <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BCE historian who described Egyptian mummification.</note>, a case was prepared for each of the deceased according to the quality and condition of the person, whether of lesser or greater value. These cases always bore the image either of the Divinity to whose protection the body was committed, or of the person who was buried within, as is evident in the first and second figures of the present Illustration of Plate II. There you see the image of a woman, remarkable for her variegated veil <note>original: "velo polymito"</note> woven in a diverse order of stripes, like a <term>Phrygian work</term> <note>A style of intricate embroidery famous in antiquity.</note>. Her breast is to be seen with various circular borders, beneath which is a female figure with extended arms, each hand equipped with a feather. This is followed by a triple row of wings; the rest of the body, following a spiral path, tapers away into various zones of lattice-work with proportionate reduction. In the middle of this, a divide of columns descends, filled with hieroglyphic symbols; in the first three, the diagrams of six Divinities are placed. But let us explain what such a mystical apparatus signifies.
The figure of the woman represents Isis, together with the <term>apotropaic</term> <note>Protective or "evil-averting" deities.</note> Divinities, as her variegated robe <note>original: "peplum"</note>—without which she is never seen—demonstrates more than sufficiently.

<margin>
Mummy shells or cases decorated with hieroglyphics.
</margin>

<margin>
Hieroglyphics of Mummy Plate II by Nardius.
</margin>

### CHAPTER V. OF THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.
