### TREATISE XIII. ON MUMMIES. CHAPTER V.

The whole body is joined together by a net-like garment <note>original: "reticulato amictu"; referring to the beaded faience net often placed over mummies</note>, and by a spiraling path it tapers toward the lower parts; by this, it is indicated that nature is, as it were, entangled by hidden and subtle principles, and rendered complex and inaccessible. The figure placed below the borders signifies the **Iynx** <term>Iynx: In Neoplatonism, a mediating spirit or "power of transmission" between the divine and material worlds</term>, of whom **Isis** is the minister, or the "Paternal Depth" composed of three triads. This is indeed aptly signified by the arrangement of three wings—that is, the various choirs of Intelligences—as we have taught in the *Theology of the Egyptians*, by which she administers the entire World. With her arms extended, she expresses a **Cross** <margin>The Iynx, Isis, the second triad.</margin> with the rest of her body, by which the influx into all members of the World is signified. She holds a feather in each hand to show the swiftness of her operations; she is swollen with a breast because she is pregnant with generative principles; she sits because she has dominion over all things; she wears a circle on her head because it is the greatest of divine things. She sits upon the breast of Isis because, in the nature of things (which is Isis), she most clearly offers herself to be seen. 

Below this figure, within three Zones, are placed six **averruncating Deities** <note>original: "auerrunca Numina"; deities who avert or turn away evil</note>, to whose custody and protection the body is committed, as shown by the nooses they hold in their hands, with which they are said to bind the force of opposing powers. The first of these, in the form of a boy, signifies **Horus**; the second, in a canine form, **Anubis**; the third, kneeling, **Nephthys**; the fourth, a **Cynocephalus** <note>A dog-headed baboon</note>, or the **Lunar Iün** in the form of a long-tailed monkey; the fifth, in the form of a Hawk, signifies **Osiris**; the sixth, likewise kneeling, signifies **Arueris** <note>Haroeris, or Horus the Elder</note>. And these are the Deities who accomplish the passage of souls through the Zones, which is why they are seen depicted for that purpose on almost all mummies. For the Egyptians believed that by these symbols, the deities were rendered favorable to the deceased and were somewhat enticed to protect the bodies. The border, containing intermediate hieroglyphics, holds hymns or an adjuration, by which they believed they could compel the said Deities to protect the bodies. I would gladly explain these here symbolically if they had been faithfully drawn; but since we shall exhibit these more distinctly in the following pages, we refer the reader there.

The second figure of the plate shows another form of the lid, which is a wooden chest, empty of hieroglyphics except that it shows a female face with a veiled head. Inside this was placed the corpse, wrapped in bandages and preserved, as is clear in Figure II of the first Illustration placed above.

The second column has this meaning: *May he live the supernal life <note>A life in the higher, spiritual realms</note>, joined and united to the supreme Deity through contemplation; with all adversity driven away, and submerged in the intellectual bowl of **Hemphta** <term>Hemphta: In Kircher's Egyptian theology, this represents the supreme creative spirit or Divine Mind</term>, let him be joined to the chain of beneficial Deities; let him reign in the zones of blessedness, free from the cravings of lower things, moistened by the supermundane dew; may he acquire strong wings that never fall away, remaining perpetually vigilant.*

The third column expresses this sense: *Let him cling to the supreme providence through contemplation; let him return to his own celestial zone by the vehicle of supreme providence; let the generative appetite <note>The physical urge for rebirth into a body</note> be absent from him, let the desire for corruptible things be gone; let his wings be strengthened by the power of contemplating the superior World; and if after a long time, as determined by fate, he should be returned to the corruptible sphere <note>Meaning the physical world or the cycle of reincarnation</note>, let him find this his dwelling place.*

And this is the "Ideal" <note>Kircher uses "Ideal" to mean a symbolic or mystical interpretation rather than a literal one</note> interpretation of these three hieroglyphic arrangements. Just as these have been extracted partly from the **Bembine Tablet** <term>Bembine Tablet: Also known as the Mensa Isiaca, a famous Roman-era bronze tablet engraved with Egyptian motifs that Kircher used as a primary source</term> and partly from Obelisks, and inscribed upon this lid, I have also chosen not to be overly long in citing authorities to prove this, since these symbols have already been explained quite frequently in various places. Note, however, that just as these inscriptions suffered some corruption through the carelessness of the transcriber, they could not have been explained correctly unless they had regained their integrity from the Ludovisian statue of **Isis**, upon which these same symbols are seen exactly as they were engraved. But more on this at length later.

Within the first Zone on both sides occurs an **eyed phallus**, from which a human arm is stretched out as if about to set some hidden mechanism in motion, holding a feather in the hand and a circle placed upon it. What the "eyed phallus" indicates has already been sufficiently explained in countless places; <margin>What the human arm protruding from the phallus signifies.</margin> but let us see what the human arm, which emerges outside the phallus, indicates in this place. It is established from the preceding sections that **Osiris** is indicated everywhere by an eye and a phallus; by the eye, because he sees all things, foresees all things, and provides all things for everyone; by the phallus, however, which **Typhon** <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, the brother and enemy of Osiris</note> threw into the Nile after cutting it from his body, is indicated the generative fertility of things, which consists primarily in moisture. This is also why the Mythologists tell the story of **Saturn** being castrated by the Heavens and his genitals being cast into the sea, from which **Venus** was born. We have also shown in many places that Osiris is represented by an extended arm, a sign of beneficence and liberality; and thus this "eyed phallus" with the arm emerging secretly from it signifies nothing else than the beneficent providence of the divine Osiris, shining forth in fertile generation, by which he makes all things fruitful through a hidden and insensible operation. <margin>The eyed phallus was an amulet of the Egyptians.</margin> Among the Egyptians, it was a most powerful amulet, which was hung not only on brute animals but also on humans of both sexes, as was evident from the Bembine Tablet. For this same reason, it is placed here in the position of an amulet to scare away the machinations of opposing powers. Following this phallus in the second zone are four **Cynocephali** <term>Cynocephali: Dog-headed baboons, often associated in Egyptian art with the god Thoth or the spirits of the sun and moon</term>, or long-tailed monkeys, by which are indicated the **Lunar Geniuses** to whom the body is committed; concerning whose mystical significance, see the Obelisk...

In the fourth zone follow two Iynges <term>Iynges: In the mystical traditions Kircher followed, these are spiritual "wheels" or winged messengers that link the divine mind to the material world</term>, whose heads are human-shaped <note>original Greek: "$\alpha\iota\delta\epsilon\iota\mu\omicron\rho\phi\alpha$" (aideimorpha) — likely a variation of anthropomorphous, or "venerable-form"</note>, while the rest of the body shows they are birds; by these <margin>What the human-shaped Iynges signify.</margin> the Spirit of the World or the **all-shaped Soul of the World** <term>pantamorpha Mundi anima: A concept of a universal soul that contains the forms of all living things</term> is indicated, whose role is to assign to each its fitting receptacle in the world; therefore, they quite properly chose her here for the protection of the body, as the minute writing clearly shows. Thus, the body was handed over to be preserved by this fourfold choir of Deities, as the hieroglyphic inscription of the intermediate border teaches, which was extracted partly from the preceding text and partly from the Obelisks, as will be clear to anyone comparing the two. It is evident, then, that the Egyptians believed that by the power and efficacy of the hieroglyphic symbols, the protective Deities inscribed on the lids could be attracted to the preservation of the bodies.

Now follows Plate IV from the **Nardian tables** <term>Nardian tables: Engravings from the collection of Dr. Giovanni Nardi of Florence, depicting Egyptian antiquities</term>, whose figures I and II demonstrate the method of wrapping mummies in bandages, which is established with such skill that the entire industry of modern surgeons seems to fail in comparison to such a feat. Figure I shows the bandaged mummy with the external ornamental gear removed; Figure II, hidden beneath the former, presents the skillful windings of the linen bandages, as appears in the following illustration. On the left side, the first has a human face, followed by a companion visible with a Dog's face; both are semi-naked and, dressed in sacred cloaks, each carries nooses in their hands. By these are indicated nothing other than the images of the Deities explained above—**Osiris, Nephthys, Isis, and Anubis**—and the sentinels of the funeral, from which they are never absent; they were thought to be the transporters of wandering spirits into their fitting celestial zone. Figure IV is an Alabaster fragment and served as a lid, perhaps torn from the walls of the tombs themselves; it displays the rites and ceremonies by which they strove to appease the protective funeral Deities just recounted. On the right, three images show minor priests, the first of whom seems to petition the Deities with raised hands; the second, similar to the first, carries a pyramid and a noose in the left hand; the third carries a Nilotic vessel <note>A vessel for holy water from the Nile</note> in the right. By these they suggest the purification <note>original: "lustrationem"</note> of souls by fire and by supermundane water—a cleansing from every pollution they had contracted while in the flesh. The Deities are the **All-shaped Deity** and **Isis**, as is clear from the symbols, and these...

<margin>The smaller hieroglyphic characters are not common letters.</margin>
While considering these smaller characters, let no one suppose them to be the common letters of the Egyptians, as many people have persuaded themselves. For they are pure and simple hieroglyphs, drawn from the Obelisks and other monuments where they occur very frequently, and were inscribed upon these little idols by the labor of the primitive Priests. That this is the case requires no other authority for proof than a diligent comparison of these symbols with those we have presented in the preceding sections. Furthermore, in all the diagrams shown here, the inscriptions of the symbols remain the same; this would not happen if they denoted the common script of the Egyptians. You will also see that the symbols are variously rearranged, so that those placed on the right in the first instance are placed on the left in another, in reverse order; this is a specific characteristic of hieroglyphics, as we have demonstrated at length previously. I have chosen to include these observations here to correct the error of those who think that this kind of smaller hieroglyphic character is the commonly used script. For the Egyptians, besides this sacred 
<margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin>
hieroglyphic script, had another writing—namely the <term>Pharaonic script: Kircher’s term for what we now identify as Hieratic or Demotic, the scripts used for administrative and everyday purposes rather than monumental inscriptions.</term>—as Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150–215 AD), a Christian theologian who wrote about the different types of Egyptian writing.</note> testifies. In this script, they recorded political business, familiar letters, 
<margin>Diodorus. Herodotus.</margin>
histories, the deeds of Kings, and inscriptions displaying the praise and honors of Kings. We have presented some of these in this Work from the accounts of Diodorus and Herodotus; however, the greed of unmemorable ages has denied us the enjoyment of such books, as they were written on papyrus and perishable scrolls.

### § III.

->**On Hieroglyphic Bandages.**<-

<margin>Hieroglyphic bandages of Mummies.</margin>
Occasionally, certain bandages are found within Mummies, marked with innumerable hieroglyphics and twisted in the manner of scrolls, two of which the illustrious Nardi <note>Giovanni Nardi (c. 1585–1654), a Florentine physician and correspondent of Kircher.</note> sent to me. It is now time for me to explain what these signify. It has now been demonstrated time and again that the Egyptians believed hieroglyphs were not only symbols of secret mysteries, but also possessed great power to hasten the protection of the Gods for those upon whom they were inscribed.

### TREATISE XIII. ON MUMMIES. CHAPTER V.

...they believed; so it is no surprise that they were so intensely occupied with winning the favor of the Gods for the protection of the entombed remains. This is clearly seen from these papyrus scrolls <note>Original: *voluminibus*</note>, almost all of which you see decorated with the primary hieroglyphic diagrams. <margin>Diagrams of the mummy wrappings.</margin> You will find depicted in these the principal statues of the deities, which either the Obelisks or the Isiac Table <note>The Bembine Tablet, a famous bronze plate of pseudo-Egyptian imagery popular in the Renaissance, which Kircher studied extensively</note> represent, in precisely the same order as they used to carry those same idols in the more solemn festivals of the *Comasiae* <term>Comasia: From the Greek *komasia*, a ritual procession or "moving about" where sacred objects were displayed</term> in the manner of a procession, as we have taught throughout from Herodotus, Clement of Alexandria, and others. They placed a great mystery in the harmonious order of the gods following one another, believing that this religious act would infallibly draw the favor of the gods to themselves. For the same reason, I say, they placed such diagrams on funerals of this kind, namely so that the body might be kept safe from all the violence of opposing powers, and the soul might be well-off through the kindness of the gods when its cycle <note>Original: *revolutione*, referring to the soul's journey or reincarnation</note> was completed. <margin>A funeral procession printed on the mummy wrappings.</margin> The wrappings <note>Original: *fasciae*</note> here show nothing else but a funeral procession; which they performed as magnificently as possible, especially in the funerals of Kings, or Priests, and other men distinguished by the nobility of their lives. They carried the statues of almost all the gods placed on sacred biers to reconcile their favor toward the deceased, and they themselves were transformed into various forms <note>Likely a reference to priests wearing the masks of animal-headed deities during the rite</note>. Apuleius describes this procession quite elegantly in his own style in Book 11 of the *Metamorphoses*, which we shall cite shortly.

In the tenth series, the triumph continues, solemnized by various displays of statues.

Thus you see here a most complete form and logic of a funeral procession, in which the funeral itself is central, preceded and followed by various ghostly apparitions of the Deities, which [we interpret] as something mystical and full of mysteries...

<margin>A charming description of a funeral procession by Apuleius.</margin>

> Behold, the precursors of the great procession advance little by little, each beautifully adorned according to their own zeal. Here, one girt with a belt acted the soldier; another, tucked into a cloak with hunting knives and spears, played the hunter. Another, wearing gilded slippers, a silk dress, precious ornaments, and false hair attached to his head, mimicked a woman by his flowing gait. Furthermore, you would think another—distinguished by his greaves, shield, and blade—had come straight from a gladiatorial school. Nor was there lacking one to play the Magistrate with purple robes and fasces <note>Bundles of rods symbolizing Roman judicial power</note>; nor one to feign the Philosopher with a cloak, staff, sandals, and a goat-like beard. There were those with different reeds acting as a Fowler with birdlime, and another as a fisherman with a hook. I also saw a tame bear being carried in a lady's chair, and a monkey with a woven cap and Phrygian saffron-colored clothes in the likeness of a beautiful young shepherd, carrying a golden cup. There was even a donkey with wings glued on, walking next to a certain weak old man, so that you would call the one Bellerophon and the other Pegasus, though you would laugh at both. Then came the flute-players dedicated to the great Serapis, who, through an elongated reed held out to the right ear, repeated the familiar melody of the temple and the God. But then came the high officials of the sacred rites, those leaders who, girded in white linen, carried the notable relics of the most powerful Gods pressed tightly against their chests, reaching down to their very feet.

For the rest, see the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 433. Thus far Apuleius, who has indeed graphically described the "triumph" we proposed regarding these bandages; traces of this are also found in the Medici Garden on the Pincian Hill, on a certain round column across from the Obelisk, with the same display of symbols, which the figure placed shortly hereafter expresses.

<margin>The funeral procession of the Romans. Gutherius.</margin> Certainly, Gutherius skillfully demonstrates in his book *On the Law of the Manes* <note>original: "de iure Manium"; the Manes were the spirits of the dead in Roman religion</note> that the ancient Romans studiously imitated funeral displays of this kind. For first, the flute-players following the magnificence of the funeral would play at equal intervals through the crossroads and forums; after the trumpet-players, those who carried the gifts of relatives and friends would advance—scents, ointments, feasts, and clothes—which Tibullus recites in Book 2, Elegy 4, and Statius in Book 5 of the *Silvae*, poem 1.

### DISSERTATION XIII. ON MUMMIES. CHAPTER V.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: Two vertical columns of Egyptian symbols. 
**Column 1 (Left, labeled A-G):** Includes a bird (A), a throne atop ripples and triangles (B), an eye and wave-like symbols (C), a seated figure (D), geometric shapes (E), a hawk on a standard (F), and a lotus or ritual vessel (G).

Fragrances were carried in bundles, <margin>Polybius. Tacitus.</margin> ointment in small vessels, the feast of the <term>silicernium</term> <note>A traditional Roman funeral meal served at the grave to nourish the deceased.</note> on trays, and garments on frames. After these, images of the Gods were conveyed on chariots, or also carried on litters. At the front, an effigy was placed upon the couch to represent the face of the deceased: thus Polybius in book 6 and Tacitus in book 3 of the *Annals*. Amidst trumpets and horns, the Scribes and attendants were present for the Magistrates; whom the Senate and Knights accompanied, having set aside the insignia of their rank. This is clear to anyone who has rightly compared the words spoken thus far, as the authors cited a little earlier variously prove; since these things are commonplace and known to every learned person, I deliberately omit them.

->### Exposition of the Peiresc Bandage.<-

<margin>Exposition of the Peiresc Bandage.</margin> The man worthy of eternal memory, Nicolaus Peiresc <note>Nicolaus-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637) was a famed French scholar and collector who corresponded frequently with Kircher.</note>, once sent me this preceding hieroglyphic bandage, which he had found inside a mummy he had unstitched; since it was longer than could be inserted into the book, I thought it should be divided into two columns, as you see on the preceding leaf, which we will also appropriately explain in this place.

This bandage shows nothing other through its symbols than a certain prayer, by which the spirits of the deceased desired the refreshment of the vital fire implanted in the celestial waters, as the symbols placed in order indicate, and their ideal sense is that which follows. **A**: By the vital fire implanted in the celestial waters, may the spirit of this deceased person be refreshed by the providence of the beneficent fiery Deity; **B**: and by religious worship **C**: through the statue of the provident Deity itself, and through the statue **D** of Mophta <note>Kircher's term for a creative or craftsman deity, often associated with the Egyptian Ptah</note> adorned with religious **E** worship, let **F** all unlucky Typhonian <note>original: "typhonia" - referring to Typhon (Set), the god of chaos and destruction</note> influences be turned away from him; since in life he held works **G** conforming to God, by which he always took care to unite himself to the Gods through contemplation; may the beneficent Mercurial Deity **H I**, the lord of the years, pour over it **K** the water of the celestial Nile; may **L** Amon <note>Amun</note> saturate it with the bowls **M** of the triple world; may **N** the celestial Osiris cherish it with fiery heat **O**, through the effective power of the beneficent statue **P** of the same. Since the symbols are already known from the preceding pages, they require neither further explanation nor the citation of authorities to establish them, as they have already been extensively confirmed elsewhere;

The sense of these is as follows:

*By the sacred statue’s worship, let the Typhonian force be expelled from the sacred pit and the Nilotic water (the bestower of necessary things) by the virtue of the eight legal constitutions which he [the deceased] observed in life; let <term>Chenosiris</term> <note>A name Kircher derived from the Egyptian "Chen" (goose) and "Osiris."</note> the guardian put to flight the Typhonian Owl lying in wait for the Barys-boat; let the lord of times introduce him into the super-mundane pool, where he may enjoy the four-towered region and the Nilotic waters prepared by the providence of the triform Deity.*

The inscription of the second column, O, is composed partly from the preceding one and partly from the inscription on the left side, I, which is marked with the letter T; thus, it suffices to have explained one.

The third figure, I, exhibits the left side, whose column T V (as we said a little earlier) has exactly the same inscription as column P of the right side, as will be clear to anyone comparing one with the other; and the column S which follows is composed from column *d* of the first figure G on the front part, and from column O of the right side of figure H; so it is that almost the same symbols are always repeated.

The fourth figure, K, shows the back part of the Image, whose column Z A exhibits exactly the same inscription as those of figure I, columns T V. Moreover, columns S, T, V, and W contain exactly the same inscription as those mentioned; but since they are most corrupt, I would waste time if I persisted longer in reviewing them. I have no doubt the curious reader <margin>The same figures are often repeated on the same Mummy.</margin> will find that what I have said is true by comparing each one with the others; and thus they repeated the same epigraph so many times for no other reason than for the sake of ornament and for filling the empty borders of the Image. For this reason, they always depicted the same figures around the base of the statue: two <term>Cucuphomorphous</term> <note>original: "Gucuphomorpha"; staffs topped with the head of a hoopoe bird, representing life-giving power</note> sceptres which flank a <term>Crux Ansata</term> <note>The Ankh, the Egyptian symbol of life</note>. as well as in the Astral and Elemental worlds. But we have explained these things elsewhere. And to finally conclude, let the Reader know that these inscriptions by no means indicate the life and deeds of the deceased, as some have falsely persuaded themselves, but are rather entreaties and adjurations to the Gods expressed through effective symbols. They believed the Gods would be moved by these symbols to take up the protection of the corpse, as is clear from these same inscriptions being repeated over and over again; this would not happen if they contained the deeds or praises of the deceased. The reader will sufficiently perceive my meaning from these few words; therefore, let us proceed to other matters.

### Explanation of the figures marked with the letter <note>Greek letter Upsilon</note> Υ.

<margin>Explanation of the figure from the Van Werle plate.</margin>

**T**he second figure represents both a casket and a statue, showing a woman with a veiled face and head. With her hands crossed, she carries a flail in one and a <term>Hieralpha</term> <note>A symbolic "Sacred Alpha" composed of various geometric or divine attributes</note> in the other; these are symbols of the warding-off <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>original: "Agathodæmonis"; the 'Good Spirit' or protective deity</note>, as we have explained elsewhere. The hieroglyphic inscription which she displays on her front is as follows:

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: Kircher describes a linear sequence of symbols on the front of a statue or mummy case. 1. Two hooks. 2. The child Horus with an eye, a serpent, and a globe. 3. A globe on the back of a bird. 4. An egg containing Horus. 5. A knife with a hand. 6. A papyrus staff. 7. A bird with a water-vessel.</note>

Two hooks; Horus as a child with an eye, a Serpent, and a globe; by which is shown the providence of Horus, a Divinity drawn out from the Nile and restored to life. There follows afterwards a globe placed upon the back of a bird carrying a curved staff in its feet, which is followed by an egg with the boy Horus; and a knife with a contracted hand; then a papyrus staff with a triple inverted branch; finally, the procession is closed by a bird with a water-vessel. The meaning of these is as follows: *Intellectual power from the Ideal World-egg leads forth Horus—that is, the Universe—which effectively exerts its dominion in the period of a tripartite year, by the virtue and dominion of Osiris, ruler of the moist substance.* They wish to indicate by this that just as the World emerged from the egg of the divine archetypal providence, and even time emanating from here is the cause of all changes (chiefly by the power of the Sun), so all things led out from the "prison-house" of the body are reserved to be transformed according to their merits by the revolutions of time.

<margin>Front part</margin> 
**Front Inscription E** produces this meaning: *The vital dominion of the provident Divinity, through the worship of Mendes <note>Mendes was an Egyptian city associated with the ram-god, whom Kircher links here to fertility</note> during the three-fold season of the year, animates the material pools with a fertile influence; it blesses the sacred repository with a heavenly abundance of beneficial flows, lest they fail in their fruitfulness. The Mercurial Divinity, indicated by the Canine scepter <note>The Anubis-headed scepter, which Kircher associates here with Hermes/Mercury as a guide of souls</note>, protects and fortifies the house of the supramundane repository against adverse forces by its health-giving influence.* These symbols allude to the soul of the buried person; they believe that repositories have been prepared to refresh the soul if it lived well, and that, having been led there by Mercury (the vigilant guardian of those places), it is fortified against all adverse fates.

<margin>Back part</margin> 
**The Back Inscription** produces this meaning: *From which the beneficial gate is opened by the vehicle of celestial liquid, or the Boat <note>original: "Bary" (ⲃⲁⲣⲓ). In Coptic, this refers to a boat or bark, specifically the solar bark of the gods.</note>, through which the provident Divinity, after the operation of religious worship has been completed in life, presents the transported souls to the supreme Osiris; here, purified in the celestial repositories, he imbues them with supramundane life.* Nardi <note>Giovanni Nardi, a 17th-century physician and antiquarian</note> provided us with a wooden statue from the Museum of the Grand Duke of Tuscany that is entirely similar to this one, in which there is no difference at all, except that the one he provided represents a wooden statue, while this one represents a preserved corpse; otherwise, whether you look at the ornaments or the hieroglyphic inscriptions, they are equal.

### Regarding the Mummies brought from the Museum of Pietro della Valle.

**P**ietro della Valle <note>A famous Italian traveler (1586–1652) who brought back some of the first mummies seen in Europe</note> was a particularly singular friend while he lived, and I confess I am greatly indebted to him for his supreme merits toward this Work. While he had traveled through almost the entire Orient and had surveyed Egypt with the greatest zeal to understand all its antiquities, among other monuments of Egyptian magnificence, he penetrated the subterranean crypts with a most daring heat of mind. From these, he brought forth for us two mummies, or preserved bodies; the first, marked **A**, is seven and a half palms in length and represents a man; the second represents a woman, seven palms and two fingers in length. The first is covered throughout with various imitation gems and precious stones; on the chest, it bears an Ibis with outstretched wings, holding a bowl in the right hand and a fruit in the left. Below this, as if on a sort of diaphragm, the word <term>Boat</term> <note>original Coptic text: ⲃⲁⲣⲓ (Bari)</note> is seen inscribed in the common characters formerly used by the Egyptians <note>Kircher refers here to what we now call Demotic or Coptic script</note>. Then, across the entire surface divided into various squares, rhombs, and circles, various figures of Egyptian Divinities are interspersed everywhere. All of these can be better understood from the diagram itself placed a little further on, rather than through many winding paths of words.

The other Mummy, **B**, which represents a woman, is even more conspicuous for its greater variety of features, as is evident from its following image. Since there is nothing hieroglyphic in it that requires interpretation (for these are images of the tutelary Divinities that have already been explained quite often and were customarily imprinted on the dead, by whose assistance and protection they believed these remains would be immune from adverse fate), I have judged it superfluous to spend further labor in repeating them. For this reason, anyone who desires a more minute account of all these things...

<meta>This page concludes the thirteenth treatise (Syntagma) of Oedipus Aegyptiacus, continuing from the previous page's discussion on the dating of mummies found by Pietro della Valle. Kircher concludes his argument that the mummies must predate the Persian conquest of Egypt.</meta>

<header>OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS. HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER.</header>

<sig>SYN-</sig>

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>...that happened during the invasion of Egypt <note>This refers to the Persian conquest of Egypt by Cambyses II in 525 BCE.</note>, where all the rites and ceremonies of the ancient priests were abolished together. Likewise, the use of hieroglyphic literature perished, with the rites of the Persians introduced in place of ancestral customs. Thus, it is certain that after these times, all the aforementioned things gradually expired, with the priests partly killed and partly sent into exile. All hieroglyphic monuments were also damaged by fire and iron—a truly clear sign of the immense hatred with which the Persians pursued the Egyptians and their doctrine. These events occurred roughly at the same time when Numa Pompilius, the second King of the Romans, held power in the City <note>Kircher is synchronizing world history; Numa Pompilius (reigned c. 715–672 BCE) was the legendary successor to Romulus.</note>. Since, therefore, hieroglyphic literature ceased at that time, and yet almost all mummies are filled with hieroglyphic inscriptions, it follows that they were prepared before the said times and buried within the said places. They were certainly not prepared in later times, as the laws of the Persians and Greeks <note>The Ptolemaic period followed the Persian and preceded the Roman.</note> stood in the way of similar things being done, and the Egyptians were by then already imbued with the customs of foreign nations. This was true even though ancestral tradition fixed such deep roots in their minds that they never relinquished the worship of the gods passed down by the ancients even until the times of the Roman Caesars, as is evident from histories provided elsewhere. 

From this, another difficulty is resolved: namely, the fact that common Egyptian characters were occasionally inserted among the hieroglyphics <note>Kircher refers to the mixture of "vulgar" or Demotic/Coptic script with ancient hieroglyphs.</note>. This certainly could not have happened at any time other than the one we have mentioned—specifically, before the invasion of Cambyses. This is most clearly evident from the word ⲉⲛⲧⲱⲩⲥ <note>original Coptic: "ⲉⲛⲧⲱⲩⲥ", likely a transliteration of "entous," which Kircher relates to an Egyptian root.</note>, which is found on the chest of the mummy wrapping described above. For if it had been inscribed on the said body in later times, it would necessarily follow that the hieroglyphs, with which the said wrapping swarms, were also in use at that time. But since we have most extensively rejected this in various places in this work—as it is contrary to almost all historians—it is brilliantly clear that both this mummy and its inscription were buried and inscribed before the times of Cambyses.

He uses the presence of Coptic-style script (entous) on mummies to date them to a transitional period before the final loss of the ancient priestly traditions.</summary>

## ON HIEROGLYPHIC CANOPIC JARS

->TO THE MOST EMINENT AND REVEREND<-
->PRINCE<-
# FRANCESCO MARIA
->CARDINAL BRANCACCIO OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH,<-
->Bishop of Viterbo and Tuscania.<-

That singular knowledge of yours in all things divine and human, most Eminent Prince, claims by its own right a place in this Egyptian theater, in which the stage of hidden sacred things is revealed. And indeed, what more welcome spectator can this arena have than You, who are most highly learned in the knowledge of hidden antiquity and the Greek and Latin languages; you who are a most skilled judge of the art I practice, and likewise know how difficult and laborious it is to perform on this stage. We offer Egyptian <term>Canopic jars<note>In Egyptian archaeology, these are jars used to store the internal organs of the deceased, though Kircher here treats them more broadly as symbols of ancient theology and idolatry.</note></term>, that is, the primary likenesses of ancient learning, which Antiquity celebrated with such pride as the chief Divinities of the World—though more truly they are monsters and portents, to put it simply. But to know these things is of great importance for confirming the excellence and Truth of the Christian Religion. For while these ruins of ancient superstition are brought to light, it becomes clearly evident how great the <note>original: "Theologiæ Nox"</note> Night of Egyptian Theology was, and how much it owes to the Heaven of Rome, which, removed far beyond these shadows, was established as the interpreter of the true Divinity, the sincere Mistress of Theology, and the true seat of Oracles. Whatever this gift may be, however, I wish it to please You on this account: that it comes from a man who both singularly loves You and ought to love You. Certainly, because of the extraordinary kindness which you kindly showed to my humble self while I was exploring the nature of the Viterbo territory <note>Kircher conducted significant geological and natural history research in Viterbo, which he documented in his later work, Mundus Subterraneus.</note>, I feel so obligated to You that I thought I must testify to posterity by some perennial monument to Your Virtues, like trophies of a kind, and indeed your most ample merits toward me and my intellectual offspring. Farewell, most Eminent Cardinal, and as you have supported me with the full outpouring of your <term>Graces<note>original: "Charitum"; Kircher uses this to mean both divine grace and the classical Graces, suggesting the Cardinal's favor and kindness.</note></term>, do not cease to support me hereafter.

# TREATISE XIV.
## On Hieroglyphic Canopic Jars and Their Interpretation.
## CHAPTER I.
### ->What a Canopus Is.<-

<margin>What a Canopus is.</margin>CANOPUS, in Egyptian <term>kanobos<note>original: "κανωβος"</note></term>, was an image fashioned in the swollen shape of a vessel, presenting a likeness of the sacred Nile and of the presiding Deity of the waters. We have dealt with this subject specifically both in various places throughout this work and most especially in Volume I, Treatise III, folio 208; we refer the reader to that section, as in this place we intend only to explain the mystical significations of the Canopic Deities, an immense abundance of which is found everywhere. These types of images are found to have been displayed under various forms, as is evident in the following illustration, where we have presented all of them collected into one, as far as was possible, together with an interpretation of each; so that our Oedipus may not seem to have omitted any hidden matters.

### ->Explanation of Canopus Figure I, displayed in the Illustration.<-

<margin>Explanation of the Gualdi Canopus.</margin>In the extremely wealthy Pincian Treasury of Francesco Gualdi, Knight of St. Stephen, there is found a Canopus of the size expressed here, fashioned from a greenish or leek-colored stone. Although it presents the shape of a vessel, it is not at all hollow inside, but is instead carved from solid stone; a fragment similar to this also exists in my own Museum. It is entirely covered with hieroglyphic figures; so that these might be seen more distinctly, we have seen fit to divide the whole image into four parts—that is, into the front, back, right, and left portions—as is clearly evident from figures A, B, C, and D of the present illustration.

<margin>Front part of the Canopus.</margin>Thus, the image is seen to be composed of a wonderful metamorphosis of hieroglyphics. It bears a female head, adorned with I know not what mysterious veil; the breast is protected by a <term>handled cross<note>original: "Cruce ansatâ"; today commonly known as the Ankh, a symbol of life.</note></term> and other amulets. Flanking this on both sides are, first, two hawks, which they call <term>Thauts<note>original: "Thautos"; Kircher associates the hawk with the god Thoth.</note></term>; second, two <term>Harpocrates<note>The Greco-Egyptian god of silence, often depicted as a child with a finger to his lips.</note></term>; third, two dog-headed baboons sitting upon crocodiles, in the midst of whom is a globe, from which two swelling-breasted, striped asps rise up on either side. Below these appears a frog covered with the shell of a tortoise, notable for a certain ridiculous rowing of wings. The back part is then occupied by two dog-headed baboons <margin>Back part</margin> ending in the costume of Anubis; in their midst is an <term>ether-shaped<note>original: "αιθερομορφος" (aitheromorphos); implying a celestial or spiritual form.</note></term> image in similar dress, with symbols—

<margin>Water as the principle of all things according to the Ancients.</margin>
It is well established that the Ancients considered Water to be the principle of all things—indeed, the Mother of all the Gods—which they called either the "Ocean" or the "Nile." Thus Homer says:

<margin>Homer.</margin>
-> Ocean, the origin of the gods, and Tethys the mother. <note>original Greek: "Ὠκεανόν τε Θεῶν γένεσιν, καὶ μήτεα Τηθύν."</note> <-
-> *Namely, the origin of the Ocean of the Gods,* <-
-> *And Tethys the Mother of all those who are beneath the heavens.* <-

Homer followed Orpheus, the most ancient of his lineage, when he sings:

<margin>Orpheus.</margin>
-> Ocean, who brings forth the generation for all, <-
-> Ocean first undertook the fair-flowing marriage, <-
-> Who married Tethys, his sister born of the same mother, etc. <note>Kircher provides these verses in both Greek and Latin to show the lineage of the idea that water is the "first parent."</note> <-

But without any mystical veil, it is expressed differently as follows:

-> Water is the soul; death is a transformation for the waters; <-
-> From water comes earth, and from earth water again, <-
-> From which the soul changes the entire ether. <note>This passage explores the ancient idea of elemental cycling, where water is the primary medium of change.</note> <-

<margin>Trismegistus.</margin>
Orpheus undoubtedly learned this doctrine from Hermes [Trismegistus], who in the *Poimandres* <note>The *Poimandres* is a foundational text of Hermeticism, a philosophical system attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note> expressly teaches that Water was the first principle of all things when he says that **darkness was changed into a certain moist nature, unspeakably disturbed**, that is, darkness was transformed into an ineffably turbulent, humid state from which everything later emerged. For they saw that nothing could exist without water; experience taught them that water nourishes, fertilizes, animates, and transforms all the bodies of the World. Therefore, it is no wonder that Homer called the Ocean the father and mother of the Gods. Its earliest beginnings are in darkness—as has already been shown from Hermes—which is to say, **Prime Matter** <note>original: "materia prima," the formless state of the universe before creation.</note>. From this, the immediate element and first thing to emerge was water; from water, earth; from earth <margin>The Ancients called water the "Ocean."</margin> finally air, and then fire burst forth, as they believe and as is gathered from the context of Hermes. This [primordial water] the Ancients, taught by the Egyptians, called the "Ocean"; the Egyptians themselves originally referred to the Nile by no other name than "Ocean," as was stated in Volume I, Chapter 1. From this, Egypt also acquired the name of the **Oceanic Land**. Since they saw the Nile endowed with such wonderful properties, they considered it to be something more sublime than mere nature. <margin>The Egyptians worshipped the Nile.</margin> Consequently, they soon began to exalt it with divine honors, instituting sacred rites and erecting statues, of what-

...of the kind shown in the present diagrams: namely, vessels provided with bulging bellies, which they called "Canopi" after the pilot of Osiris; concerning these, see what we have handed down most extensively in the place cited above. But let us return to the matter at hand.

<margin>Hieroglyphics of the front part of the Gualdo Canopus.</margin> The figure of this first illustration was one of the Canopic statues, by which they secretly expressed the protection of the Canopic Divinity over the watery substance. Through the female head of the image, they indicated the passive physical principle of all things—truly that supra-mundane fertile Mind from which all things emanate, as if from a perennial spring. It is seen with a veiled crown because its nature is hidden and inaccessible to human minds. It is distended with a bulging belly because it is pregnant with a certain *panspermia* <note>original: "panspermiâ"; a Greek-derived term meaning a "universal mixture of seeds" or the potential for all life.</note> of things. Upon its neck, it has fixed the **handled cross** <note>The *Crux ansata* or Ankh symbol.</note>, which ends in two testicles, and an amulet within which two naked boys, carrying pyramids in their hands, are placed in a sitting posture. By these things, nothing else is indicated but the fertile influence through the "testiculated cross" into this **sensible world** <note>The physical world perceived by the senses.</note>, indicated by the **b** twin boys. 

In astrology, we have called the twin boys **Horus** and **Helitominus**, that is, the sons of Osiris. Indeed, Horus indicates the sensible world, while the other indicates the same world still subject to many imperfections (according to Plutarch), which the Canopic Mind restores to perfection. They carry pyramids as symbols of fire, because the sensible world is the receptacle of divine heat, which the Osirian Minds—that is, the **Solar Intelligences** indicated by the **a** two hawks—distribute to the world. These are followed on both sides by the Isiac Minds, which are indicated by the two female images placed behind the hawks. 

Symmetry and harmony are provided by the **c** Harpocratean Minds, which are marked by the two **Harpocrates** <note>The god of silence, usually depicted as a child with a finger to his lips.</note> on either side, urging silence with their fingers and carrying **gnomones** <note>Measuring rods or carpenter’s squares used to ensure straightness and proportion.</note> in their hands. This signifies that just as an unrefined body attains its perfection when a measuring rod or rule is applied, so through the wise arrangement of the Harpocratean Minds, the world (still subject to many imperfections) may attain its symmetry. This is achieved through a certain hidden and insensible motion, which is the mark of silence, signified by the finger moved to the mouth. 

Truly, since the Solar Intelligences are connected by a tight chain to the Lunar Intelligences—as nothing can be accomplished without their concord—for this reason they quite aptly placed two **dog-headed baboons** <note>original: "Cynocephalos"</note> sitting atop crocodiles, conspicuous with a crescent moon. By these, the **Luno-Solar Intelligences** are understood, as was said in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. They sit upon crocodiles because, as Eusebius testifies, the motion of the Sun and Moon occurs in moisture for the generation of things; and by the crocodile, they denote the fresh water which the Sun purifies with its heat. For this same reason, according to Eusebius, they used to place the image of the Sun in a ship that carried crocodiles. There follows a globe **d**, from which two **striped asps** emerge on either side with chests erect; by these is signified fertile life, or vital fertility, by which the world is made pregnant for the generation of all things (as has been said elsewhere), both through those already recounted and through the **Ophionic Agathodaemones** <note>Good serpent-spirits or "Good Daemons."</note>,

<margin>The Frog on the Gualdo Canopus.</margin> who are the ministers of the supreme Canopic Mind. There follows next a **frog**, remarkable for the rowing of its wings and covered by the shell of a tortoise—truly a ridiculous garment—surrounded...

# TREATISE XIV. CONCERNING THE CANOPI. CHAPTER I.

...surrounded; which, by a certain secret similarity, denotes sublunary matter <note>Matter in the realm below the moon, subject to change and decay</note>, insofar as it is joined to the power of Osiris—indicated by the shell of the Turtle—and is imbued with the offspring of innumerable forms, signified by the wings extended in a manifold order of feathers, from which the World was then called *Aeon* <note>original Greek: αἰὼν; meaning an age, eternity, or a divine power</note>. You see how the Frog, a symbol of matter, acquires all its nourishment by sucking it from the celestial life, that is, the serpent-bearing globe; since we have treated this extensively in the *Isiac Tablet* <note>The *Mensa Isiaca*, a famous bronze plaque studied by Kircher as a key to Egyptian wisdom</note>, we refer the reader there.

->You also see how matter, which is indicated by the Frog, is primarily<- <margin>First matter, signified by the Frog.</margin> the subject of celestial influences. For since the Divine Mind and Canopic providence are adorned with the forms of all things and are especially fertile, through a great inclination of beneficent nature, they cause the shadows of their perfection to be imparted to other bodies. This could certainly not happen without some common subject that would be submitted to the efficient cause and receive the shadows of the Ideas. Therefore, they fittingly placed a Frog covered with the shell of a Beetle beneath the celestial globe filled with vital influences—that is, sublunary matter pregnant with celestial influences, from which the beauty of all forms subsequently exists.

You see, finally, how this pot-bellied little god <note>original: "Deaster"; a term for a minor or idolized deity</note> is divided into a fourfold World. Indeed, the veiled head indicates the Archetypal World; the Hawks, Harpocrates, Horus, and Helitominus represent the Genial <note>The "Genial World" refers to the realm of generating spirits or intelligences</note> World; the globe with two Serpents represents the Sidereal <note>Starry</note> World; and finally, the winged Frog indicates the Material or Hylic <note>from the Greek "hyle," meaning matter</note> World. Thus, both extremes—the mind in the act of creating and matter in the act of receiving—possess a certain quality of infinity.

Since, however, there are those noted for malice—the *opponents* <note>original Greek: ἀντίστοιχοι; those standing in opposite rank or counter-elements</note>—who set themselves against the beneficent forms impressed upon the waters by the Canopic Mind; <margin>The back part of the Canopus is explained.</margin> for this reason, they engraved the Anubic triad upon the back of the vessel, not without cause. These are the three statues f, g, and h, carved on the back part of the figure marked D. The middle one, g, indicates the Father of the Anubic triad; f indicates the Mind, and h <note>The original text repeats "g" here, likely a printer's error for "h"</note> indicates the Power of the same. They are dressed in garments with a conical surface pointing downwards, by which the influence from the higher to the lower regions is noted. In one hand they hold a gnomon <note>A rod used for measuring or the pin of a sundial</note>, and in the other a sickle; by the gnomon, the preservation of symmetry in the World-body is noted, while by the sickle, the cutting away of unharmonious things is signified. They are depicted with dog-heads because they are most keen-sighted and are the presiding spirits of human invention. They are also *apotropaic* <note>Protective figures intended to ward off evil</note>, watching over the preservation of the things committed to their faith with the greatest zeal, as the two canine images demonstrate. Apuleius makes mention of this Canopus, or Urn, in Book 11 of the *Metamorphoses*, which they used to carry in the Isiac procession, in these words:

> But behold, toward that World [was carried] a little Urn fashioned with gleaming gold, most skillfully hollowed out, with a rounded bottom, and decorated on the outside with wondrous images; upon its twisted knot sat an Asp, raised high with the scaly swelling of its neck;

which Asps are indeed clearly seen delineated on the vessel. But let these few words suffice concerning this Canopus.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the symbolic meaning of Canopic jars. Following the analysis of the Gualdo Canopus, Kircher now turns to figures documented by Georgius Herwart von Hohenburg, specifically examining the hieroglyphic inscriptions arranged in columns on the body of the vessels. # CHAPTER II.

->Interpretation of the Canopus marked as Figure II.<-

<margin>Canopus from Herwart's *Hieroglyphic Theater*.</margin> This Canopus was taken from the *Hieroglyphic Theater* of Georgius Herwart <note>Georgius Herwart von Hohenburg (1553–1622), a Bavarian statesman and scholar whose work on Egyptian "hieroglyphs" Kircher often referenced</note>. That Canopus which is seen to this very day in the palace of the Ambassador of the Order of the Knights of Malta is entirely similar to it, both in form and in the inscription of the hieroglyphs. It is indicated by Figure VI, divided into a front and back part. Both, however, are fashioned in the manner of a vessel with a conspicuous belly-like swelling, upon which is placed the head of a woman visible with a veil. Through the hollow of the vessel, two hands with crossed arms are stretched outward, one of which holds an ibis feather in its hand. On the front part, the hieroglyphic descriptions are placed in eight columns, which signify the powers, effects, and influences of the <term>ibimorphous</term> <note>Having the form of an ibis, the sacred bird associated with Thoth or Hermes</note> spirits. Lest we cause boredom to the reader with their exposition, we shall omit the authorities already cited more than once in the preceding sections and set down only the ideal or symbolic sense according to the same number of columns. However, because the hieroglyphic columns in Figure II of the Canopus were drawn from the archetype by an unreliable hand, we shall first interpret here the hieroglyphic inscriptions shown in Figure VI of the Canopus; these, if you except a few details, are almost the same as the former, as will be evident to anyone comparing one with the other.

# CHAPTER III.

->Interpretation of the Canopus shown in Figure VI.<-

<margin>Canopus of the palace of the Ambassador of Malta.</margin> Column I has this meaning: *Let the ibis-shaped <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>The "Good Spirit," a protective deity in Hellenistic-Egyptian thought, often depicted as a serpent or a bird</note>, servant of <term>Momphta</term> <note>In Kircher's Egyptian theology, Momphta is a supreme creative intelligence or "craftsman mind"</note>, direct the sacred pool with his intellect, and let him support the Nilotic canals by his beneficial dominion through three parts of the year; let him promote the life-giving dominion of Osiris in the <term>dodecapyrgon</term> <note>Literally "twelve-towered," a symbolic structure Kircher relates to the twelve signs of the Zodiac or the twelve months, governing the cycles of life</note> into the life and fertility of things.*

Column II. *Let him govern the moisture of the sacred pool, drive it forth from the opposing sacred pit, and adapt its influence to the ratios of the archetype; let him sprinkle vegetables with the hidden motion of a moist nature; let the ibis-shaped one fill the Nilotic vial with vital moisture, the executors of which are the Intelligence of Momphta and Mercury, the presiding lord of the vital moisture.*

Column III. *The foresight of the moisture of the sacred pool shall flow waters from the dodecapyrgon, if the Priests call forth the vital powers into them through sympathetic rites and ceremonies, and if they drive away opposing forces through the statues of the three triads: Father, Power, and Mind.*

Column IV. *Hence, the hidden agitation of the sacred pool disposes matter toward the conception of forms in the variety of things by a hidden motion; alternately, the Sun diffuses its sympathetic Virtue into the fourfold region of the World, which, according to the command of Momphta or the Canopic Mind, is bound to grant life to the World through the beneficial force of moisture, which the dodecapyrgon pours forth.*

<meta>This page continues the symbolic analysis of Canopic jars from Athanasius Kircher’s *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, Volume III. Specifically, it concludes the column-by-column interpretation of the inscriptions found on these vessels, which Kircher believes describe the divine management of the Nile and the protection of the Egyptian "water economy."</meta>

### COLLECTION XIV. ON CANOPIC JARS. CHAPTER III.

**Column V.** Through the benefit of the <term>favissa</term> <note>original: *favissæ*; historically these were underground temple cellars or pits for sacred objects. Here, Kircher uses the term to describe subterranean reservoirs or hidden spiritual sources</note>, the Divine Power will repel Typhon <note>The Egyptian god Set, whom Kircher views as a symbol of chaos and destructive heat</note>; from this, Osiris, the master of vital moisture, shall fill all things with the support of life; the <term>Nilometrium</term> <note>original: *Nilometrium*; a device or temple structure used to measure the rising level of the Nile</note>, having summoned the rites of the Gods, will display a beneficial abundance of things.

**Column VI.** The fields shall be irrigated by the increases of the Nile through the secret mastery of water; the chain of Divinities shall be drawn down by the hymns and prayers of the Priests; for the purpose of doing good, the all-shaping Spirit <note>original: *pantamorphus Dæmon*; from the Greek *daimon*, referring to a guiding spirit or celestial force capable of taking any form</note>, by his influence and powerful dominion, will fertilize all the lower receptacles of the waters.

**Column VII.** Through the providence of Thaustus <note>Kircher’s name for Thoth or Hermes Trismegistus</note> or Osiris, he will fill the <term>favissa</term> with an abundance of necessary things by the virtue of the sacred Nilotic vessel; and once the Baboonish Owl <note>original: *Noctuâ Bebonia*; a peculiar term Kircher uses for a specific hieroglyph, likely combining the owl (associated with night) and the baboon (associated with Thoth)</note> has been put to flight, the four-fold World shall be harvested; life shall be granted with an abundance of increase; the moist substance of the twelve-towered World <note>original: *dodecapyrgi*; a reference to the twelve signs of the Zodiac or the twelve gates of the celestial spheres</note> and of the great <term>favissa</term> shall hold dominion over the four-fold World.

**Column VIII.** Through the fiery power of the all-shaping Spirit, through the gates of the twelve-towered world, through the sledge of Osiris, through the influence of Ammon into the <term>favissas</term> and Nilotic channels, through the arm of Thaustus, through the Nilotic vessels, and through the sacred <term>Barys</term> <note>original: *Baryn*; a type of Egyptian river boat mentioned by Herodotus, here treated as a ritual vessel</note> of Hermanubis <note>A hybrid deity combining Hermes and Anubis, often associated with the transition between worlds</note>.

<margin>The Ibis feather in the hand of the Canopic Idol.</margin> Let us now reveal what the Ibis feather in the hand of the Idol truly signifies. It has already been shown frequently from the works of Horus <note>Horapollo, an author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphs</note> that the feather of the Ibis can stun a crocodile by its touch alone. Since the crocodile signifies Typhon—the origin of all evils—this sign was placed in the hand of the **Canubic Mind** to signify that it dissipates all the snares of adverse powers and repels them from the management of the watery substance committed to its trust. It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that the feather of the Ibis is a symbol of the "warding off" <note>original: *averruncatricem*; a term for a protective or evil-averting power</note> nature of the Canopic Deity who presides over the waters.

And this is the symbolic sense of the inscriptions contained in the eight columns shown on the Canopus of Figure VI. Since the symbols of these columns have been explained here and there in the preceding pages and established by their respective authorities, I have judged it to be superfluous to repeat them here again with useless labor.

Note, however, Reader, that the inscriptions of the Canopus shown in Figure II are, as far as their substance, the number of columns, and the meaning of the symbols are concerned, exactly the same. The symbols are also entirely identical to those we have already explained, except that they have been extracted from the Archetype in a poorly transformed state, and several things are placed there which are never found among hieroglyphics. From this, I suspect that the transcriber, not understanding certain symbols that were almost worn away on the Canopus, fashioned whatever his imagination could suggest. And although I have searched diligently for the original prototype to explore the truth of the figures, I have not been able to achieve this by any amount of care. Nevertheless, the Canopus of the sixth figure was first compared by me with its prototype with the greatest study, which is why I undertook to interpret it first. We also compared this with another Canopus contained in the Pincian Museum of **Francesco Gualdi**, and they displayed exactly the same symbols. Furthermore, since anyone can explain the inscriptions written in a series of four columns on the back of this Canopus from what has already been said, I have left them to be explained by the studious Reader as an exercise.

# CHAPTER IV.

## *Interpretation of Figure III, which exhibits the Canopic Oracle.*

<margin>The Canopic Oracle of Gerard Reinst.</margin>
**T**he schematic of the third figure displays the Canopic Oracle, extracted and sent from the museum of the most illustrious man, Master Gerard Reinst, Senator and Magistrate of Amsterdam, through the patronage of that most learned man and singular friend, Master Bertholdus Nihusius. The stone is a parallelogram four fingers thick, showing the architecture of Egyptian temples. In its center, positioned like an altar, is an image of the <term>Canubic Mind</term> <note>original: *Canubicæ Mentis*; referring to the divine intellect or spirit associated with the city of Canopus</note>, fanning a flame of fire with its hand; directly opposite is a statue fashioned in the manner of a consultant. The base upon which the Canubic Genius stands is square, with two triangles inserted into each other to form a hexagon <note>a six-pointed star or hexagram</note> engraved on each side, with a lamp placed nearby. On the <term>abacus</term> <note>the flat top or crowning slab of the stone</note> of the stone, thirty characters are placed, which are the indicators of the thirty Divinities of the entire land of Egypt, distributed into thirty <term>Nomes</term> <note>original: *Nomos*; the administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note>. Let us now reveal what each and every one of these things signifies.

<margin>The Oracle in the City of Canopus in Egypt. Plutarch.</margin>
->Pausanias reports that there was a most celebrated Oracle in the City of Canopus,<-
as does Suidas, to which Egyptians flocked from all sides to consult about future events. Plutarch also writes of this: *And Heraclitus Ponticus says that there is an oracle of Pluto <note>original symbol: $\odot$; Kircher often uses this solar symbol to represent the "Intellectual Sun" or Pluto/Serapis as a hidden source of light</note> in Canopus.* That the Pluto of the Greeks is everywhere confused with the Serapis of the
<margin>Serapis and Canopus are the same.</margin>
Egyptians has already been stated in many places. Furthermore, that Serapis and Canobus are the same is evident from the fact that he whom the Egyptians commonly call Serapis, the Priests and Initiates call by the secret name "Canobus," as if you were to say, the "subterranean Deity of the waters." And since water cannot obtain its fertilizing power if the fiery spirits are excluded, they followed the said Deity with a fiery cult, as is clear enough from the statue. It wears a cap fitted in the shape of a gourd, a sign of the abundance of moisture over which it presides; moreover, it is clothed in a simple garment without any folds or wrinkles, by which the nature of the simple element <note>water</note> is expressed. With its right hand, it is seen to fan a flame, by which is noted the fiery portion that is inserted into the waters by the benefit of the Deity—for without this, no generation of things could achieve its effect. The lamp placed nearby notes that a fiery worship must be exhibited to the same. Moreover, the hexagonal figure impressed on the sides of the abacus abundantly teaches that it persuades all things toward the granting of life by its <term>hot-moist</term> <note>original: *calido-humida*; in Aristotelian physics, the quality associated with air and fertility</note> virtue; we have shown in our *Arithmetica* that this is a symbol of the Elementary Universe. This is confirmed by what the Oracle of Serapis says of itself, according to Opsopœus on page 69 of his book on Oracles:

<margin>Opsopœus.</margin>
> The sphere and the dwelling are illuminated by the light of the God,
> For he came, and the great God transformed them; he beheld my
> Invincible power, a splendor ruling the flames,
> Youthful hair from his head over his joyful brow,
> While the priests of this lineage are cheered by his locks.
> <note>original Greek: Σφαιρὴ μὲν καὶ δῶμα Θεῶ καταλάμπετ’ αὐγὴ... Kircher quotes this to show the solar and fiery nature of the Oracle</note>

<margin>The Canopic Divinity is the greatest of all.</margin>
According to Suidas <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note>, the Canopic Divinity was held to be the greatest of all gods, for the reason that whatever deities existed in the rest of Egypt were represented in this one alone. This is how the god speaks of himself through the Oracle, according to Opsopoeus <note>Johannes Opsopoeus, a 16th-century scholar of Oracles</note> in *Oracles of the Ancients*, page 7:

> *I am the Sun, Horus, Osiris, King, Bacchus, Apollo,* <note>original: "Ἥλιος, Ὧρος, Ὄσιρις, Ἄναξ, Διόνυσος, Ἀπόλλων"</note>
> *Steward of the seasons and times, of the winds and rains,*
> *Guiding the reins of the Dawn and the many-starred night,*
> *King of the fiercely blazing stars, and immortal fire.*

> *A liquid of water filled with seeds of every kind, and penetrating the bosom of the earth,*
> *Born of himself, taught by no one, without a mother, unshakable,*
> *A name not even to be grasped by a word, dwelling in fire.*
> *This is God; and we Angels are but a small portion of God.*

It is clear, therefore, that in the Canopic Divinity, all the aforementioned deities are included as various effects within their primary cause. All this is evident from the thirty characters engraved on the stone base, each of which signifies a specific Divinity. These are the same characters that we explained in *Hieroglyphic Magic*, page 484 and following; namely, certain mystical signs of the Gods, composed of Hermetic characters of the Planets, as we have taught in *Astrology*. Hence, they expressed the twelve Presiders of the <term>twelve-towered zodiac</term> <gloss>original: δωδεκαπύργος (dodekapyrgos); the twelve divisions of the sky</gloss> and the seven Presiders of the Planets by as many hieroglyphic characters. Most of these emerged from a single Hermetic character or <term>Tautic seal</term> <note>a symbol based on the 'Tau' or cross of the god Thoth/Hermes</note>. See the figures of these engraved on the "averting" statue <note>a statue intended to ward off evil</note> in the previously cited section of *Hieroglyphic Magic*. But now let us explain the individual characters.

CONSTITUTION XIV. CONCERNING CANOPI. CHAPTER V.

Since these matters have been described extensively in other places, we did not wish to be more long-winded here; Reader, from these few points you will easily perceive the mindset of the Ancients.

Therefore, in this present Canopic Oracle, these symbols were engraved because while they invoke the Canopic deity, all other Deities subjected to its protection were thought to be implicitly invoked. The Canopic Oracle itself beautifully teaches this, as found among the other Oracles collected by Opsopæus <note>Johannes Opsopæus (1556–1596), a scholar known for his collection of Sibylline and Oracular texts</note> on page 55, where the Oracle commands the invocation of the Deities at opportune times, and with other ceremonies, as follows:

->Invoke Hermes and the Sun likewise<-
->On the day of the Sun; and then the Moon when her<-
->Day has come; and Saturn, and thereafter foreign Venus,<-
->With silent invocations, which the best of the Magi found,<-
->The King of the seven-sounding instrument, whom all know.<-
<note>original Greek: "Κλήιζειν Ἑρμῆν ἠδ’ ἥλιον... Τῆς ἑπταφθόγγου Βασιλεύς, ὃν πάντες ἴασιν." This poem describes the planetary associations for magical or oracular invocation.</note>

->*Invoke Mercury and the Sun in the same manner*<-
->*On the day of the Sun; and the Moon, when her*<-
->*Day is present; and Saturn, and consequently Venus,*<-
->*With silent invocations, which the best of the Magi found,*<-
->*The King of the seven-sounding instrument, whom all know.*<-

# CHAPTER V.

### Figure IV. The Canopic Apotropaic Genius, and its interpretation.

<margin>Canopic Apotropaic Genius.</margin>
**F**igure IV in the Illustration of Canopi displays a Canopic <term>Apotropaic Genius</term><note>A protective spirit or deity intended to "turn away" (Greek: *apotrepein*) evil or bad luck</note>, which a certain anonymous Architect and distinguished Mathematician sent to me not long ago from Frankfurt am Main. It is carved from black stone, in which first a winged globe occurs: then an image, on whose head a <term>cydaris</term><note>A type of royal Persian headdress or tiara, often tall and stiff</note> fashioned in the shape of a Nilotic vessel is seen, formidable with a hook and a whip. The edges of the stone contain hieroglyphic inscriptions, as is evident in the engraving.

<margin>Hieroglyphics.</margin>
Through the winged globe, **Hemphra** <note>In Kircher’s system, Hemphra represents the supreme, benevolent creator-god of the Egyptians</note> or the supreme triform Deity is indicated, as has already been declared often; the image, a servant of Hemphra, indicates the Canopic guardian Genius. It has a cydaris fitted to the shape of a vessel or a Nilotic gourd placed upon its head, because it has power over watery substance. It holds a hook in its right hand, because this is said to draw out Osiris—who was cast into the Nile by the Titans—and it leads the Nile (which they everywhere confuse with Osiris) over the parched, dry, and waterless land through its inundation for the necessary sustenance of life. All Typhonian <note>Referring to Typhon or Set, the Egyptian god of chaos and enemy of Osiris</note> powers are put to flight, which the whip indicates; and the hieroglyphic inscriptions G, H, and I demonstrate this more than enough. For they knew how much—

# OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

...to such an extent that the <term>demons of rival art</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντίτεχνοι (antitechnoi); refers to spirits that mimic or oppose divine works through deceptive crafts</note> are terrified by scourges fashioned by a certain secret method and placed in the hands of the Gods; for they cannot endure that which is fortified by the seal of a higher power, which is so contrary to them. Thus, when the Egyptians consulted the Oracle on how they might be safe from ill-omened powers, the Oracle responded:

-> The demons who wander about the earth and the sea, <-
-> Tireless, are subdued under the scourge of GOD. <-
<note>original Greek: Δαίμονες οἳ φοιτῶσι περὶ χθόνα καὶ περὶ πόντον, Ἀκάματοι δάμνονθ᾽ ὑπαὶ μάστιγι Θεοῖο.</note>

-> *The demons who walk about the land and about the sea* <-
-> *Untiring, are tamed under the scourge of GOD.* <-
<note>Kircher's Latin translation of the Greek above: "Dæmones qui ambulant circa terram, & circa pontum Indefessi, domantur sub flagello DEI."</note>

But let us return to the subject. Therefore, in this first arrangement under letter G, there occurs a pyramid with a papyrus scepter, the yoke of a balance, and a square containing an egg and an eye. These are followed by Nilotic flasks, a sacred Alpha, an extended arm, a sacred pool with a footprint, and two Nilotic vessels. Next follow the head of a Hawk, with a crescent Moon resting upon a pyramid; after these, an extended arm, an egg, a papyrus scepter, a sphere, an eye, a pyramid, and an altar. On side H, exactly the same symbols occur, if you except three of them. Let us explain all of these.

<margin>Interpretation</margin> Rightly, therefore, the pyramid is placed in the first position with the papyrus scepter, because the <term>Canubic Mind</term> <note>Kircher's term for the divine intelligence governing the element of water and the Nile</note>, as the overseer of the watery substance, cannot produce an abundance of necessary things without a portion of fire, nor can it temper the Elemental World according to the laws of justice. This is beautifully indicated by the yoke of the balance and the square with the egg: the former indicates the exact measure of justice, while the latter two indicate the <gloss>material world</gloss> <note>original: "Mundum hylæum"; from the Greek 'hyle' for matter</note>. Thus, the providence of the Canubic Mind, indicated by the eye, is necessary; and through sacred worship, which the following Altar denotes, it grants what is necessary while it mixes itself with the Nilotic vessels through a hidden motion. These are aptly indicated by the extended arm, the footprint, and the Nilotic vessels placed on both sides. For the Sun, joined with the influence of the Moon obtained through the prayers of the Priests—which are indicated by the Hawk’s head, the crescent moon attached to the pyramid, and the two arms stretched upward—bestows an abundance of all necessary things through its provident benevolence, granted by the mixing of sacred fire with the watery substance. And this is the ideal meaning of the hieroglyphs placed on side G. This inscription is the same as the one shown above in the *Depiction of Mummies*, Figure G, column d.

Furthermore, these same symbols were placed on both sides because they were believed to possess great efficacy for attracting the <term>Apotropaic</term> <note>Warding off evil; from the Greek 'apotropein' to turn away</note> Canubic Genius, and for obtaining what they desired, as we have taught extensively in our work on *Magic*. From these characters, the Priests moreover composed a prayer formula, by which they believed they could bind, compel, and bring the adjured Canubic Divinity under their own power; it was roughly of this sort: *"By <term>Hemphta</term> <note>A Kircherian name for a supreme creative spirit or 'Good Spirit'</note>, the triform Divinity, by the sacred fire, by the scepter of the <term>Pantomorpheus</term> <note>The 'All-Formed' one, a deity encompassing all shapes of nature</note>, by the balance of <term>Omphta</term> <note>Another divine name used by Kircher, likely signifying a benevolent or life-giving power</note>, by the eye of all-seeing <term>Osiris</term>, by the sacred..."*

SYNTAGMA XIV. ON CANOPI. CHAPTER VI.

Lll

...[souls] and the vials of the sacred Nile, etc., we adore and beseech you, that you might grant us that which we intend.

<margin>Hieroglyphics on the abacus of the Apotropaic Genius.</margin>
Furthermore, on the <term>abacus</term> <note>The flat slab forming the top of a pedestal or monument.</note> of this monument, another series of hieroglyphics occurs. In the first place, there is a balance with a <term>gnomon</term> <note>The pin or pointer of a sun-dial, used here to indicate precise measurement or judgment.</note>, a flying serpent, two feathers, a bird with a transverse staff, a circle with a square, an eye with the figure of an altar, and a square with an extended arm, which is followed by a papyrus reed, and finally a Nilotic canal. By the balance, the law of justice is indicated; by the flying serpent, the efficacy of the fiery power is shown, which penetrates all lower things (indicated by the three globes). But because this power cannot have its effect unless an aerial Intelligence acts as a patron, he joined the two feathers with the bird and the scepter, which are placed to form a <term>decussis</term> <note>An X-shape.</note>. This was done to show that this power pervades the members of the entire Universe by its motion, using the influx of heat and moisture as a kind of vehicle. For these things, when rightly cultivated, provide for all—as the altar with the eye placed above it indicates—and by this beneficence, it confers an abundance of all necessary things upon the <term>hylaeic world</term> <note>The material or physical world, from the Greek word "hyle" (matter).</note> through the Nilotic canals, which the square, the extended arm, the papyrus thyrsus, and the Nilotic canal aptly designate. And this is the interpretation of the monument proposed to us. Since the truth of all these things has been demonstrated everywhere in the preceding pages through various authorities, we have deemed it superfluous to repeat them here.
