# CHAPTER VI.

-> Interpretation of the Canopic vase in Figure V. <-

<margin>Canopic Vase.</margin>
**F**igure V shows two faces of a Nilotic vessel, the front and the back, which are connected by a binding. This vessel, among others cited throughout this Work, was sent to me by the most refined man Berthold Nihusius, having been drawn from the Museum of Gerard Reinssius, a Senator of Amsterdam. It is a portable Canubic vessel, as the handles E, F, and A, B clearly demonstrate, in which they used to carry the sacred water of the Nile into the Shrines and Inner Sanctuaries.

<margin>The front face of the vase is explained.</margin>
On the front face of this vessel, figure B is shown as a small child—that is, Horus—with this mystical apparatus, as we have taught elsewhere. He has two marks, C and D, placed on either side. The first, C, fashioned in the shape of an arrow, indicates that the care of this <term>Genius</term> <note>A guardian spirit or divine power.</note> is to destroy, by his own tempering virtue, the excessive dryness sent by the power of <term>Typhon</term> <note>The Egyptian god Set, often associated by Kircher with destructive dryness, chaos, and heat.</note>. The other, formed in the shape of a hook, indicates that Osiris-Horus extracts the "suffocated in water"—that is, the excessive moisture by which the World is sometimes overwhelmed—and restores it to a temperate state. For Horus, according to Plutarch, is nothing other in this context than a certain spirit nourishing and preserving all things by its power; he is the very temperateness of the air, adjusted by the heating power of the Sun. For this reason, the Egyptians mythologize that he was raised in the marshes around Buto. And indeed it is so: for marshy earth, overflowing with water, nourishes the vapors that destroy aridities and droughts.

CHAPTER VII. 448 THEATRE OF EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPHICS FROM OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS

<margin>The rear part of the vessel is explained.</margin> The other side, marked with the letters A, B, C, and D, contains hieroglyphic characters of every promiscuous kind, which we previously set forth in the Canopic Oracle, Figure III. Although these have been very poorly distorted <note>Kircher is likely complaining about the quality of the engraving or the preservation of the original artifact</note>, they are nevertheless easily recognized from other inscriptions. The first character is an inverted branch, the meaning of which we explained in an entire chapter above regarding the Flaminian Obelisk, and in the Pamphilian Obelisk under the *Hierogrammatismo* or Sacred Writing of plants. Following this are two thyrsi <note>A ritual staff or wand, often associated with Bacchic or Egyptian festivals</note> leaning toward each other, which occur everywhere in the Bembine Tablet; then two characters, though exceedingly corrupted, are—judging from the Flaminian Obelisk where they occur quite often—nothing other than a Serpent, a goat-headed scepter, and two squares. Finally, in the last place, there is the figure of an arrow, a Serpent inserting its tail into a globe <note>The Ouroboros, or snake eating its own tail, symbolizing eternity or cyclical nature</note>, and a noose, under which are placed an Owl with a <term>hydroschema</term> <note>A specific symbolic representation of water or a water-vessel</note>. The sense of all these is this: *Ceremonies of the Thyrsian Genii [spirits of the ritual staff], performed according to the three seasons of the year, entice the Nilotic Deity Mophta to grant a life fertile in all things within the material worlds, once the Typhonian drought has been driven away by the waters.* These were placed on the vessel as a kind of prophylactic, to bring about that which they signify.

---

# C A P V T VII.

## *Interpretation of Figure VII.*

<margin>The Nilotic vessel and its interpretation.</margin> **F**igure VII is taken from the Museum of Pietro della Valle <note>A famous 17th-century Italian traveler and collector</note>, and it indicates nothing other than Canopus, as the bellied vessel and the hieroglyphics inscribed upon it expressly show. For instance: **a** is a <term>hydroschema</term> figure, under the figure <note>Hieroglyphic: A lowercase omega with a line or dot above, representing water</note>; **b** is under the figure <note>Hieroglyphic: A square or rectangle</note>; **c** is under the figure <note>Hieroglyphic: A vertical line crossing a circle, similar to the Greek letter phi Φ</note>. These three characters are Coptic, as we taught in the Hieroglyphic Alphabet, and they signify the same as "Mu," the watery Deity; for <note>original: "ω"</note> [omega] signifies water, while <note>original: "μ"</note> [mu] indicates the sphere of love, by which all things are shown to be connected through the power of Mophta. Furthermore, the <term>hieralpha</term> <note>A "sacred alpha," a term Kircher uses for a specific primary symbol</note> **A** <note>Hieroglyphic: A large capital 'A' printed in the right column of the text</note> indicates the Agathodæmon <note>The "Good Spirit," often depicted as a protective serpent</note>; the curved staff indicates governance and influence-bearing power; **C**, a <term>hydroschema</term>, indicates water; finally, **f**, the figure of a vessel, indicates the Nilotic water, as we have already taught in countless places. Thus, this entire inscription conveys this sense: *Mophta Agathodæmon, with supreme power, presides over the Nilotic watery substance* <note>original symbol: A circle with a horizontal bar</note>.

### TREATISE XIV. CONCERNING THE CANOPIC JARS.
### CHAPTER VIII.

XII. The breast-shaped Canopus <term>mastoiedēs</term> <note>original: <term>μαστοειδὴς</term>; meaning shaped like a breast or mammiform</note> was extracted from the same source. All these figures present that history which we read in Suidas, and it goes as follows: *Once, as the story goes, the Chaldeans, extolling their God—which is fire—with magnificent words, carried him about everywhere so that he might be compared with the Gods of all the Provinces, and so that he who conquered the others might be judged God by everyone.* Because the Gods of the other Provinces and nations were made of bronze, silver, wood, stone, or other such materials, and were placed in temples and sacred sites, and such materials were easily consumed by fire, it was inevitable that fire would always conquer everywhere. Hearing this, the Priest of Canopus devised a certain clever plan of this sort: in various parts of Egypt, earthenware water-jars were usually made with tiny, continuous holes pierced throughout, so that the turbid water, filtered through those holes, might be rendered pure and clear. When the Priest of Canopus had taken one of these and stopped up those holes with wax, and had painted it with various colors— <margin>The history and origin of Canopus.</margin> in the Greek it is, <term>and having painted it with various colors</term> <note>original: <term>καὶ διαφόροις ζωγραφήσας χρώμασι</term></note>, that is, with various hieroglyphic figures of animals and colors being drawn—and filled it with water, he set it up as a God. After he had cut off the head of an ancient statue, which was said to have belonged to a certain pilot named Menelaus, he placed it upon his new statue, fitting it accurately. Afterward, the Chaldeans arrived: the fire was lit, and the wax with which those holes had been stopped began to melt. As the jar "sweated" and ejected water through the holes, the fire was extinguished. Thus, by this cleverness and cunning, Canopus was declared the victor over the Chaldeans, and from that time he has been worshipped as a God.

And indeed, the figures VIII, IX, XI, and XII of the coins proposed a little earlier accurately relate this history. But let us explain above all the mysterious one marked with number VIII. The figure placed upon the vessel indicates the Canopic Mind bestowing a wealth of moisture upon all things, which the breast-shaped Canopus <term>mastoiedēs</term> <note>original: <term>μαστοειδὴς</term></note> in fig. XII also denotes, as we have explained elsewhere. The Egyptians later, rushing headlong into every kind of superstition in their usual manner, fashioned this in a certain material according to the sequence of the related history and placed it among the sacred symbols. That they afterwards used these as a phylactery <note>A protective charm or amulet</note> against the violence of fire and flames is abundantly shown by the <term>protective charm</term> <note>original: <term>φυλάκλα</term>, likely for <term>phylakteria</term></note> or <term>protective writing</term> <note>original: <term>φυλάγραμμα</term></note> joined to its side. For it is well known from the history of Antiochus Soter—who, about to fight against the Galatians, is said to have achieved a signal victory with the help of this symbol placed on his banners, which he had been warned to make in a dream—that because this Greek word <term>HEALTH</term> <note>original: <term>ΥΓΕΙΑ</term>, Hygeia</note>, which signifies health or safety, is represented in various positions, it was a symbol of prosperity among the Egyptians.

On the other side, the square shows nothing other than a <term>monogram</term> of the name Kanub, that is, of Canopus <margin>Monogram of Canopus.</margin>; the letters <term>kanub</term> <note>original Coptic: <term>ⲕⲁⲛⲩⲃ</term></note> are all contained within the said monogram. And the method of writing was peculiar to the Egyptians, as will be said elsewhere. With these two symbols, they signified <term>hieroglyphically</term> <note>original: <term>ἱερογλυφικῶς</term></note> that a prophylactic image of the Divine Power of Canopus should be employed against the harms of fire and flames. As for the Coptic letters placed on the individual channels of the vessels, I do not think any other authority is needed to prove it, except for a certain parallel comparison of the said characters made with one another, which I leave to the Reader to judge from this table.

Regarding the ten letters surrounding the vessel: although in my <term>Coptic Prodromus</term> <note>Kircher's 1643 work, *Prodromus Coptus sive Aegyptiacus*, which was an early attempt to explain the Coptic language</note> I confessed they were unknowable, nevertheless, having been practiced in the hieroglyphic discipline through the labor of many years, I am so far from judging them unknowable that, on the contrary, nothing has been easier for me to explain. For they indicate the ten degrees of being, which I discussed in the <term>Hieroglyphic Arithmetic</term> <note>A section of Kircher's work where he assigns metaphysical and numerical values to symbols</note>, upon which the <term>Canopic Mind</term> <note>original: <term>Canopica Mens</term>; referring to a divine intellect or presiding spirit associated with the Egyptian deity Canopus</note> pours out the abundance of its goodness.

*   <note>A variant of the Coptic letter Mu</note> The first letter indicates Minerals.
*   <note>A variant of the Coptic letter Pi</note> Flowers and juices that ordain the generation of metals, as we taught in the <term>Pamphilian Obelisk</term> <note>Kircher's 1650 study of the obelisk now in Rome's Piazza Navona</note>.
*   <note>A variant of the Coptic letter Epsilon</note> The sea, lakes, rivers, etc.
*   <note>A variant of the Coptic letter Beta</note> Vegetable nature.
*   <note>A variant of the Coptic letter Omicron</note> The powers and the feminine principle <note>original: <term>fœmina</term></note> instilled in each individual thing.
*   <note>A variant of the Coptic letter Alpha</note> Sensitive nature.
*   <note>A cursive variant of the Coptic letter Alpha</note> The nature of insects and reptiles.
*   <note>A variant of the Coptic letter Lambda, appearing as a double slash</note> The nature of aquatic creatures.
*   <note>A variant of the Coptic letter Kappa</note> The nature of birds.
*   <note>A variant of the Coptic letter Zeta</note> The nature of quadrupeds.

And upon these ten degrees of being, the <term>Canopic Mind</term> scatters the abundance of its fertile moisture and preserves them in their existence. Moreover, that these letters indicate the said degrees of being is demonstrated by the fact that these are the capital letters of the words representing those degrees, as shown in the preceding table.

<note>Decorative initial letter N, intricately carved with vine and floral patterns.</note>**W**isdom has no more noble heroes, Most Eminent Prince, than the learned men of the Purple <note>original: <term>Purpuratos</term>; a reference to Cardinals, named for the distinctive red/purple color of their robes</note>, whose learning shines like the Sun in the heavens of the Church; from which the world draws its light, and the greatness of all mankind receives the radiance of instruction. Nor is it a wonder; for he who does not possess what he values is unable to truly estimate its worth. And even from this beginning, people may rightly look up to and admire the vivid energy of Your nature, moving gracefully and magnificently at once through every kind of prudence and wisdom, through all the mysteries of the secret arts, and through nearly all the duties of the State. Although, to confess frankly, another reason moved me no less, so that I, having long been in your debt, might dare to present this part of my Work to You: namely, that singular kindness of Yours with which you have always received me; by embracing my works, you made me believe that what was approved by You would not be unwelcome to others. Indeed, in this you have surpassed my Sphinx, while you showed that my humble trifles <note>original: <term>myricas</term>, literally "tamarisks." This is a classical literary allusion used by poets like Virgil to describe modest or lowly works</note> were not unwelcome to Your Wisdom, by which only the highest things are usually approved. Farewell, Most Eminent Prince, praised for all Wisdom, and look with favor upon my endeavors.

# TREATISE XV.

## ->On the Nilotic Sphinxes and their True Meaning.<-

---

<margin>What the Nilotic Sphinx signifies.</margin> THE Nilotic Sphinx is a hieroglyphic of a composite nature, as has been indicated throughout this entire Work; we say its anagogical <note>interpretive or spiritual meaning</note> or mystical significance is nothing other than a symbol of secret Wisdom. For as Plutarch says: <note>original Greek: "Περὶ τῶν ἱερῶν ἐπικινῶς ἴσαντες, ὡς αἰνιγματώδη σοφίαν & Θεολογίας αὐτῶν ἐχούσης" — "They place [them] before the temples as a warning, as their theology contains an enigmatic wisdom."</note> *By placing Sphinxes for the most part before their temples, they signify that their doctrine of sacred things consists of a perpetual Wisdom, hidden under veils.* <note>original Greek: "Οὐδὲν γὰρ ἄλογον, οὐδὲ μυθῶδες, οὐδὲ ὑπὸ δεισιδαιμονίας, ὥσπερ ἔνιοι νομίζουσιν, ἐγκατεστοιχειοῦτο ἱερουργίαις, ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν ἠθικὰς ἔχοντα καὶ χρειώδεις αἰτίας, τὰ δὲ οὐκ ἀμοιρὰ κομψότητος ἱστορικῆς, ἢ φυσικῆς ἐστιν." — Plutarch, *Isis and Osiris*, Ch. 8.</note> *For nothing irrational, nor fabulous, nor subject to superstition (as some suppose) was established in their sacred rites; but some parts have ethical and necessary causes, while others are not without a historical or physical elegance.* Therefore, the Sphinx was a symbol of secret Wisdom and of virtues abstracted from matter. In this way, they placed it everywhere in the temples so that people might be reminded that nothing can be more effective for obtaining <term>Theomorphosis</term> <note>original: <term>Θεομόρφωσιν</term>; the process of being transformed into a divine likeness or union with the divine</note> than to prepare the soul for the companionship of divinity through hidden symbols of this kind. 

However, when considered from a physical perspective, it indicates nothing other than the rising of the Nile. It is represented by the Egyptians in two ways: for they express it either under the figure of a Lion reclining upon a pedestal, or under a figure that exhibits the body of a Lion and the face of a Virgin. In the first manner, it indicates <term>Momphta</term> <note>a name Kircher uses for a specific protective spirit or aspect of the Nile's power</note>, the <term>Agathodaemon</term> <note>a "Good Spirit" or protective deity</note> presiding over the Nilotic increase; whose powers, effects, and duties we have described more fully both in preceding sections and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on page 282, to which we refer the reader. In the second manner, it indicates the actual rising of the Nile, which lasts primarily while the Sun is passing through the constellations of Leo <note>the Lion</note> and Virgo <note>the Virgin</note>; about which we shall speak more fully in the following sections. But so that the matter may be demonstrated "from the egg" <note>from the very beginning</note>, we shall treat first of the Nile, then of the <term>Niloscopes</term> <note>devices used to measure the height of the Nile flood, often called Nilometers</note>, and finally of the significance of the Sphinxes, as far as the powers of our mind permit.

# CHAPTER I.

### ->On the Nile, and its worship practiced by the Egyptians; as well as on Niloscopes and their use.<-

REGARDING the Nile, its origin, and its greatest prerogatives among other rivers, we have spoken expressly in the first Volume on page 48. Therefore, in this place we must only deal with its worship, and why the Egyptians held it in such...

# TREATISE XV. ON SPHINXES. CHAPTER I.

...that they honored it with worship at all times, may be revealed to the curious reader; and so the structure of the hieroglyphs, which for the most part rests upon this, may be more clearly demonstrated. Not only the Egyptians, but also the later Greek philosophers, believed that the Nile had fallen from heaven from Jupiter; <margin>The Nile was thought to be a gift of the Gods.</margin> whence some called it a gift of Jupiter, others a tear of the Gods, others a vein of Paradise, the seed of the Gods, the fishpond of Proteus, or the husband of Isis, and honored it with other epithets, as was shown in the cited passage. Indeed, they did not only venerate the Nile <margin>Divine worship was shown to the Nile.</margin> as something divine and granted by the singular favor of God, but they also worshiped it as Osiris himself, following it with divine cult, according to the testimony of Plutarch. In his book *On Isis and Osiris*, he says: <margin>Plutarch.</margin> *The wiser of the priests do not only accept the Nile by the name of Osiris, and the sea by the name of Typhon; but they consider Osiris universally as all principles endowed with the power of moistening, as the cause of birth and the substance of seed. Typhon, however, they consider as everything dry, fiery, and whatever finally has the power of drying and is opposed to moisture.* <note>Plutarch, *De Iside et Osiride*, Ch. 33. Kircher uses this to explain the Egyptian dualism between life-giving water and destructive heat.</note> Hence <margin>Hecatombs were made to the Nile.</margin> the frequency of hecatombs <note>original: *hecatombæ*; a massive sacrifice, literally of one hundred oxen</note> around the beginning of the inundation, which the Egyptians performed in honor of the fertile Numina <note>divine powers</note> of the Nile. Proteus revealed the principal cause of this increase when he said that hecatombs must be performed to Jupiter, according to that verse:

-> *Until you reach the waters of the Jovian river of Egypt,* <-
-> *And there again you shall perform those sacred hecatombs to the Gods.* <-
<note>A Latin translation of Homer’s *Odyssey*, Book 4, referring to the Nile as the "river fallen from Zeus."</note>

And he called the river <term>Diapetes</term> <note>original: <term>Διιπετής</term> (diipetēs); "fallen from Zeus" or "fallen from the sky"</note>, that is, fallen from Heaven. For if hecatombs are to be offered to any of the Gods, they are surely to be offered most of all to him to whom the increase of the river was chiefly credited. Since he is that Jupiter or Osiris so often celebrated by us, who does not see it clearly denoted that the increase flowed from Jupiter? For what waters come from Jupiter, if not those which come from the heavens in rains? Therefore, although it does not rain in Egypt, the Nile is nonetheless not incongruously called *Diapetes*, because it grows from rains <note>Kircher correctly identifies that the Nile's flood is caused by rains elsewhere, even if not in Egypt itself</note>. Thus, they thought hecatombs should be made to Jupiter because he presides over the rains falling from Heaven, by which the Nile is increased.

Moreover, according to the testimony of Eusebius, Plutarch, Diodorus, and Herodotus (cited in various places in Volume I), it was the custom of the Egyptians to worship those things from which they perceived some remarkable utility or benefit for sustaining life, doing so with a certain headlong zeal and the insane and foolish religion of superstition. Hence, driven by a frenzy, they extended this most vain religion not only to Ibises, Crocodiles, Hawks, Dogs, Beetles, and other unclean godlings <note>original: *Deastros*; minor or false gods</note> which Egypt, the mother of monsters, produced, but even to those foolish and <margin>2<br/>1<br/>CL<br/>CA<br/>CT<br/>COS<br/>...</margin> ridiculous deities of the gardens: onions, garlic, and melons; against which the Satirist Juvenal not undeservedly inveighs:

> -> *O holy nations, for whom such deities grow in their gardens!* <-

# CHAPTER I.

They honored and venerated the river with a certain singular devotion; especially since they claimed the first of men were created in their own land. Between the goodness of the soil and the prosperity of the Nile—which generates so much and, by its very nature, easily nourishes what it has brought forth with a fertile spirit—they perceived that all their happiness hung upon it as if from a perennial fountain. They saw that this river fertilized a land otherwise sterile, sandy, and fruitlessly bare with an overflow of fertile silt, as if by an alluvium of all good things. They recognized it as the sole cause of the copious yields of herbs, fruits, plants, grains, and animals on both land and sea. Beyond these stated benefits, they knew its water was not only pleasing to the taste, but also most healthy for healing bodies; indeed, they knew it profited the fertility not only of beasts, but of humans as well. Thus, they did not wrongly call it "fruit-bearing"; <margin>The Nile as the cause of fertility.</margin> so much so that they dared to ascribe the extraordinary multiplication of humans (in which Pliny asserts women were accustomed to give birth to four offspring at a time, a fact other authors confirm) to no other thing than the fertility of the Nile’s water. Consequently, all sacrifices were assigned to it; all rites and solemnities of festivals were performed for it, as if for the parent of all Gods and superstitious spirits, as we shall see shortly. Thus, the <term>Phallophoria</term> <note>A festival involving the carrying of symbols of generation, usually associated with Osiris/Dionysus.</note>, the <term>Pammelia</term> <note>An Egyptian festival celebrated as the "Voice of the Good Spirit," often linked to the birth of Osiris.</note>, and other execrable solemnities drew their origin from nowhere else but here. For this reason, Apuleius swears by the "increments of the Nile," as if by the reverence of a divine power. The Egyptians therefore worshiped the Nile as a kind of Deity, or rather as Osiris himself, whom they also called <term>Momphta</term> <note>A name Kircher uses for the Egyptian demiurge or generative intellect.</note>, as Plutarch testifies in the words cited above.

Just as the origin of the Gods is unknown to mortals, and God is difficult to find, so too Herodotus testifies that the origin of the Nile was never perceived by anyone. <margin>Herodotus; comparison of the Nile to divine virtues. Praises and benefits of the Nile.</margin> Just as God provides the greatest pleasure to mortal minds and bodies by his flowing presence, so they confessed the Nile, having fallen from heaven, to be the cause of all their happiness. Again, just as the Gods, having glided into lower things, enrich them by their arrival, so does the river. Whence, as Elias of Crete writes, just as every race of Gods descends from that celestial Isis-Moon—the mother of humans and Gods (to speak with Apuleius)—so the Nile is said to have descended from the Mountains of the Moon. Just as the celestial Osiris, or that celestial Jupiter, namely the Sun, causes the production of all things in the sublunary world by running to and fro in the space of 365 days; so the Nile, by gradually increasing and decreasing according to the pattern of the Sun, blesses the entire region of Egypt with a fertile overflow of silt. This it also seems to show by the numbers hidden in its own name: for the number collected from the name <term>NEILOS</term> <note>original Greek: "ΝΕΙΛΟΣ"</note> constitutes exactly 365, as many as there are days in the year.

Furthermore, just as the Moon, when viewed by the <margin>The increases and decreases of the Nile.</margin> Sun, provides certain increases or decreases of its power to terrestrial things—since it is now horned, now full, and now descending through the same degrees until it vanishes entirely—so too the Nile, according to Plutarch, demonstrates a periodic motion near the city of Elephantine of twenty-eight cubits. This reflects the movement of the Moon, or the <term>syzygy</term> <note>The alignment of the Sun, Moon, and Earth.</note> of the Moon and Sun. Reaching these degrees, it then vanishes entirely in the fullness of the river. According to the <term>Nilometric</term> <note>The "Nilometer," a device for measuring the river's height.</note> record near Mendes and Xois, it increases to fourteen cubits...

# VOLUME XV. ON SPHINXES. CHAPTER I.

...it exactly shows us the full Moon, for then the middle of the <term>Nilometer</term> <note>A device used by ancient Egyptians to measure the height of the Nile's floodwaters.</note> instrument stood half below and half above the waters. <margin>The Nile emulates the phases of the Moon and its effects.</margin> Near Memphis, however, where the water rose to seven cubits, it most closely reflected the horned crescent Moon. Furthermore, just as they believed these phases of the Moon were the cause of wonderful effects in sublunary things, and divined from them—as if from certain infallible signs—the state of the seasons and the fertility or sterility of things, so they did regarding the rise and fall of the Nile. For just as the horned and imperfect Moon is considered among the malignant "aspects" <note>An astrological term describing the positions of planets relative to one another.</note> according to <term>Ptolemy</term>; so too an increase of only seven cubits threatened sterility. And just as the full Moon is considered favorable and fertile for a moderate configuration, so too is an increase of fourteen cubits. Finally, just as the Moon of 28 days, when joined to the Sun, produces the greatest effects and acts most efficiently; so too the Nile, exceeding an increase of 28 cubits, is "joined" to the earth—that is, to <term>Isis</term>—to fecundate her with vegetable principles. All of which <term>Plutarch</term> beautifully indicates in his book *On Osiris and Isis*. <margin>Plutarch: The image of the Sphinx from the Museum of Reynst.</margin>

### TREATISE XV. CONCERNING SPHINXES. CHAPTER I.

->[The figure is] conspicuous with a feathered crown, positioned with a scepter of a goat’s head, to which <margin>See figure A B.</margin> is joined a frame, and beneath this the figure of a Nilometer <note>original: "Niloscopij"; an instrument for measuring the height of the Nile's flood.</note>. For what else is that feathered crown of the lion-shaped Osiris but the impenetrable power of the nature of Momphta <note>Kircher identifies Momphta as a supreme Egyptian deity associated with divine intelligence.</note>, most remote from human understanding? What else is that mysterious symbol of the <term>Ankh</term> <note>original: "ansatæ Crucis"; the looped cross representing life.</note> but the preservation of all created things by its fertile influence? Indeed, the goat’s head seems to signify nothing other than the fertile influence of the said Deity and a certain fiery power, which truly penetrates all things through a diffusion of rays, which are like horns. Immediately <margin>What the symbol of the Nile signifies.</margin> beneath the head is placed the symbol of the Nile, indicating that from that fiery virtue of the Sun and heat mixed with the water or moisture, the generation of all things results; since the entire power of generation consists only in the moist and the warm; that is, all things are brought to perfection by the Momphto-Mendesian virtue <note>Mendes was the Egyptian god of fertility, often represented as a goat.</note>. Certainly, they did not incongruously place the symbol of the Nile immediately below the channel of the goat’s head, so that they might show the generation of all things resulting from the fiery virtue (or heat) and the vegetal moisture—that is, from the Sun and the Nile. Just as, however, in order for that fertile power of the Sun and Nile to have an effect, it necessarily requires a subject that corresponds to the celestial Sun and is receptive to its power—I mean the Moon, or the celestial Isis, in whom it sows the vegetal principles—so too it seemed to require an earthly subject that corresponds to the earthly Osiris: that is, the earth or the earthly Isis, which it would fertilize. Thus, from the meeting and coupling of water and earth—that is, of Osiris and Isis—the internal generation of the lower world would come forth, which occurs most especially during the inundation of the Nile. Hence, Isis was not poorly described by Plutarch as that part of nature which, as if feminine, receives all births into herself, like a certain nurse and the common receptacle of all things, called <term>pandoches</term> <note>original: "πανδοχὴς"; meaning "all-receiver" or "all-welcoming."</note> by Plato, and by many <term>myrionymos</term> <note>original: "μυριώνυμος"; meaning "with ten thousand names."</note>, that is, endowed with innumerable names, because she turns herself into all forms and species of things to be generated. But as for the Nilometer <margin>Nilometer</margin> placed below the goat’s head, it is that same instrument which Aben Vaschia and Abenephius <note>Arabic authors cited frequently by Kircher as sources for Egyptian wisdom.</note> call the measure of the Nile. See his Arabic words cited above in the section on the Flaminian Obelisk; their interpretation follows: *To show the fertile nature of the Nile, they place that structure by which the increases of the Nile are measured under the form of a Lion. Its traces are still seen in some places. It appears to have been in the likeness of a tailed and reclining animal.* Strabo describes the <term>Nilometrium</term> <note>original: "Νειλομέτριον"; a Nilometer.</note> in these words: <term>Syene is an island a stadium in size, and in it is a city having a temple of Cnuphis, and a Nilometer constructed of a single stone on the bank of the Nile, which marks the greatest, the least, and the middle increases [of the river].</term> <note>original Greek: "Συήνη νησὸς ἐστὶ μὲν σταδιαῖα... τὰς μέσας."</note> This is: *Another Island half a Stadium in size is placed in the Nile before Syene, in which is that City which has the temple of Cnuphis and a Nilometer; this, however, is a certain pit constructed on the bank of the Nile out of a single stone, in which the maximum, minimum, and average increases of the Nile are denoted.* Following Herodotus, Diodorus, Apuleius, and Plutarch, <margin>Joannes Leo Africanus, book 8.</margin> Joannes Leo Africanus also mentions this kind of instrument; he says he was an eyewitness to this structure, for he speaks thus: *From the region of the Old City in the middle of the Nile, the Michios <note>The Nilometer on Rhoda Island in Cairo.</note>, that is, the measure, is seen—an Island from which, according to the proportion of the Nile's inundation, [the harvest] of that year is predicted...*

# ### CHAPTER IV

<margin>Diodorus Siculus, Book 1.</margin> ...they collect the yield throughout all of Egypt by a most certain method employed by the ancient Egyptians. Diodorus Siculus mentions the Nilometer <note>An instrument used to measure the height of the Nile's annual flood.</note> in these very words: *For since, he says, the inundation of the Nile weighed upon the inhabitants with care and distress, an observation for measuring the increase was devised at Memphis by the ancient Kings. For those to whom this task was assigned signify to the Cities and villages by letter how many cubits or how many fingers <note>A "digit" or finger-breadth was a standard unit of measurement in antiquity.</note> the flow has increased; and at the same time, at what moment it begins to decrease. In this way, the people are freed from anxiety, and from the magnitude of the increase or the mark of the decrease, they immediately know the future abundance based on the manner of the inundation, by noting previous times.* The Nubian Geography <note>A reference to the work of the 12th-century Arab geographer al-Idrisi.</note> describes this even more exactly in Book 2, which we cite in Volume I, folio 33, together with a figure of the Nilometer.

-><-

But I shall not dwell on the science of measuring the Nile <note>original: "Niloscopia"</note>, as it is a matter well known everywhere. One thing in the Arabic text of Auen Vaschia <note>Ibn Wahshiyya, a 9th/10th-century author often cited by Kircher for Egyptian lore.</note> concerning the culture of the Egyptians kept me in great suspense and utterly perplexed, nor was I able to understand what he meant by the image of a "lying and tailed animal"; until, by consulting various antiquities, finally smelling out what it was, I investigated the hidden context of the words. For Auen Vaschia intends to say nothing else by these words except that it was in the likeness of a Sphinx, which is found among authors as a symbol of the inundation of the Nile. Now, Sphinxes were (as is apparent from those which were brought to Rome from Egypt and are seen here and there throughout the City) biform statues, the front of which <margin>What kind of figures Sphinxes are and why they were fashioned thus.</margin> showed a human face, while the rest represented a Lion, as we have more than sufficiently taught a little earlier. Moreover, these figures were expressed by the Egyptians not because they believed such animals were found anywhere, but to denote more recondite meanings of the mind. Thus, Sphinxes expressed in this way denoted the station of the Nile inundating Egypt. For since the rising of the Nile lasted through the whole of July and August, and the Sun during said months for the most part traversed Leo and Virgo; it was easy for a people otherwise very prone to portentous and many-formed compositions of things to form monsters from the Virgin and the Lion, which they called Sphinxes. These were properly <term>statues</term> <note>original: "stuatuæ", likely a printer's error for "statuæ"</note> consecrated to the Nile, lying on their bellies, by which they represented the station of the inundating Nile. Sphinxes of this kind are seen even to this day <margin>Various statues of Sphinxes in Rome.</margin> at the Baths of Diocletian at the Aqua Felice, vomiting waves from their great gaping jaws; likewise in the Quirinal garden, at the fountain of the Capitoline, and in the Villa Borghese, as well as in the garden of Prince Giustiniani before the Flaminian Gate, most famous for its all-encompassing collection of antiquities, the interpretation of which we are working on in this Treatise. And a great number of these Sphinxes, <margin>Pliny, Book 36, chapter 13.</margin> according to Pliny, were in Egypt; some of which, of immense mass, were placed in the more famous locations of Egypt, especially around the places where <margin>Sphinxes in diverse locations of Egypt.</margin> the Nile is accustomed to inundate, such as at Heliopolis, and Sais, and in the Memphite desert; in which, among others, is one of prodigious magnitude, 143 feet long and 62 feet wide. Moreover, they seem to have had the function of designating the increases of the Nile, as appears from the words of Aben Vaschia. Indeed, I shall say something more. Certainly the very figure of the Nilometer, which the Egyptians placed here as a symbol of the fertility of the Nile, in its rough form insinuates nothing else...

...seems to continue. Pierius <note>Pierio Valeriano (1477–1558), a famous Renaissance scholar who wrote a massive treatise on hieroglyphics.</note> confirms our opinion, saying that the Egyptians used the hieroglyphic of a reclining Lion to represent the rising of the Nile—which in the Egyptian language means **Nun** <note>original: "Nun"; this refers to the Coptic or ancient Egyptian concept of the primordial waters or the river itself</note>—because when the Sun enters the back of the Herculean Lion <note>The constellation Leo</note>, it triggers the Nile’s flood. Often, while the Sun remains in that sign, the volume of fresh water overflows twofold. This force of water, widely diffused across the vast Egyptian plains, renders the soil pregnant with such fertility that the inhabitants not only gather food for themselves but also relieve a great part of the world from hunger. All of these things are most fittingly displayed on a certain gem belonging to Petrus Stephanus, a Roman citizen, which it seemed appropriate to present here.

In this gem, you see a winged Sphinx with swollen breasts standing over two Lions, who appear to be tearing a bull apart with violent force. Certainly, by the Sphinx, nothing else is designated but the presiding Spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> of the Nile’s inundation. By the Lions is meant that star <note>meaning the constellation Leo</note> which the Sun enters when the Nile’s rise begins. By the Bull, the Earth or the labors of agriculture are suggested, which are, as it were, swallowed up by the flood of waters from the <term>Momphtaean</term> <note>Kircher's term for a specific Egyptian creative principle, often associated with Ptah or the city of Memphis</note> Lion. But since these interpretations savor more of a Greek than an Egyptian character, let us leave them aside.

Because of that overflow of water, which they experience annually through the benefit of the Lion, it has become an established custom now accepted by all nations that channels, pipes, and siphons that spout water are usually sculpted in the form of Lion’s heads at appropriate places. The water is channeled through bored holes so that it appears to be spewed from the Lions' gaping mouths. Not a few examples testify to this fact, such as the Lions seen to this day in Rome: as I have mentioned, at the foot of the Capitoline hill, and at the fountain near the Church of the Blessed Virgin of Victory <note>Santa Maria della Vittoria, famous for the Fontana dell'Acqua Felice</note>, which vomit water with full mouths. <margin>
Astronomical Characters ♌ & <note>Aquarius symbol: ♒</note>
</margin>
They indicated that it was more advisable to represent it through that same character by which the Egyptian Astrologers prefigured the shape of the Lion—that is, through ♌, the tail of the Lion. For it was shown above that the Astronomical characters of the signs and planets were first devised by the Egyptians, as <term>Deeus</term> <note>John Dee (1527–1608/9), the famous English mathematician and occultist.</note> proves extensively in his *Hieroglyphic Monad*; we also treat these matters specifically in our *Egyptian Astronomy*. But the sign placed below ♒ also demonstrates this clearly; for it has been shown very extensively elsewhere that this is a symbol for water, derived from the resemblance to the shape of wavy water. For the same reason, it was adopted as the symbol for waters by the Egyptians and by the common consensus and approval of Astrologers. Accordingly, wherever it occurs in hieroglyphics, it refers to the moist element and indicates either water or some kind of humor <note>In ancient science, a "humor" refers to any fluid or moisture.</note>. But more on these things in their proper places.

<margin>
Why the Egyptians placed the sign of Aquarius next to Leo.
</margin>
But someone might object here: what has Aquarius to do with Leo? To this I respond: when the Egyptians wished to demonstrate the excellence of something, they did so primarily through the juxtaposition of opposites. For they saw that the Nile was enriched with certain wondrous gifts of nature beyond all other rivers in the world, insofar as it not only shows evidence of the greatest fertility throughout the whole course of the year, but especially at that very time when the Sun, inflamed by the heat of Leo <note>The sign of Leo corresponds to the height of summer, usually July and August.</note>, scorches everything. While all other rivers fail due to a lack of moisture, the Nile seems to fill everything with its own fullness. Conversely, it reaches its greatest state of depletion when the Sun is in Aquarius, while other rivers are prone to floods only in Aquarius (the sign opposite to Leo). Therefore, to express this preeminence of the Nile symbolically, they seem to have wanted to place the opposite sign, Aquarius, beneath the sign of Leo.

Therefore, whether this symbol refers to a <term>Nilometer</term> <note>A structure, often a pillar or well, used by ancient Egyptians to measure the clarity and vertical level of the Nile during the annual flood season.</note>, or a Sphinx, or a Lion, it is all the same; the Reader cannot go wrong, whichever they choose. For we demonstrated just before that the Nilometer, the Sphinx, and the Lion were each hieroglyphics of the inundation. It may even be that they constructed those structures which, representing both the Sphinx and the Lion, performed the duty of a Nilometer. Indeed, that it was something similar is suggested not only by the Author's words, but also by Strabo (Book 17), Herodotus, and other Ancients—indeed, by as many statues of the Nile as are found today. But we leave all these things to the Keen Reader for further investigation.

Before I explain their meaning, it must be noted that this Lion mystically signifies nothing other than <term>Momphta</term> <note>A name Kircher uses for a divine force or deity he associates with the creation and the Nile's inundation.</note>, the guardian of the Nile's rising, as was shown above. All the mystical meanings of these signs allude to his power, efficacy, and effects. For they imagined that if he should ever show himself to be less benevolent or propitious, he could be appeased by the secret power of these signs and enticed toward granting what they desired: the fortunate rising of the Nile. <margin>Various amulets for attracting Momphta. <note>original: "Amuleta varia ad Momphtam attrahendum."</note></margin> Thus, one can see many sacred tablets or amulets suitable for attracting <term>Momphta</term> placed upon the plinth. The theme of the entire inscription is nothing other than that the aforementioned Momphta is propitiated by the power of these sacred symbols to grant the fertile rising of the Nile river—upon which the salvation of all Egypt rightly depended—and is drawn by sacred rites and ceremonies to favor their prayers.

# § I.

### Interpretation of the hieroglyphics which are seen inscribed on the plinth of the first Lion.

<margin>Hieroglyphics inscribed on the plinth of Lion A.</margin>
In the **first** place is the **handled cross** <note>The Ankh symbol.</note> marked with the letter *a*; then the sacred table *b*; then two reversed segments *c*, with three boundaries; which are followed by the **Goose** *d*; <note>The goose was associated by Kircher with "Chenosiris," a protective aspect of Osiris.</note> then the sacred table *e*; and finally, these are followed by the symbols *f, g, h, i, k* in sequential order. <margin>Hieroglyphics on the right side of the plinth.</margin> Since, therefore, nothing in this world can prosper without the influx of the Divinities, they fittingly place in the first position the **handled cross**, a <term>periapton</term> <note>A protective charm or amulet worn to ward off evil.</note> of great power, which indicates the divine influx into the universal World, as we have shown extensively elsewhere. This is followed by the sacred table with the **Hawk**, an extended arm with a segment of a circle; by which it is indicated that the aforementioned influx into the Nile is not obtained except from **Osiris**, the supreme giver of all good things; these are aptly indicated through the **Hawk**, the arm, and the segment. For from this source, all lower things acquire an increase of goods through the threefold portion of the year, which is beautifully indicated by the two segments and three boundaries. But because these things cannot endure—due to the resistance and violence of adverse powers—unless they are guarded by continuous protection, there follows the **sacred Goose**, or **Chenosiris**, who is thought to be bound to perpetual guardianship through the following amulet. Furthermore, the sacred table *e* contains two upright arms of an amulet, with a **Scarab** and a globe: through the upright arms, the ceremonies to be performed by the Priests occupied in pouring out prayers to the Divinity are indicated; through the **Scarab** and the globe, the labors of **Osiris** in the economy of the terrestrial World are shown, while by his spermatic influx he animates and preserves all things. The **All-formed Good Spirit** <note>original: "Pantamorphus Agathodæmon"</note> indicated by *f* and *g*, distributes all lower things into forms of matter suitable to the nature of each, in order to produce an abundance and variety of necessary things. But since the adverse powers mostly resist his operations as well, it is commanded at *h* to supplicate the providence of the three effective powers: for by their virtue the **bowl of Osiris**, that is, the receptacle of moist nature <note>The Nile river or its valley.</note>, is defended from all enemy powers, namely by the virtue of the triple dominion of the three already reviewed Divinities, **Osiris**, **Chenosiris**, and the **All-formed Good Spirit**; and these are skillfully signified by the three **Lotus-bearing** sceptres, which, just as the **Lotus** is continually turned toward the Sun, so by a certain sympathetic force these three Divinities are turned toward protecting the things committed to their faith, according to the ideas prescribed by the triform supreme Divinity.

<margin>Hieroglyphics on the front of the plinth.</margin>
Now follows another <term>synthema</term> <note>A symbolic composition or "arrangement" of signs.</note> of great power displayed on the front of the Lion, which they call **Thausticum** after the Hawk; and these are the **Asp** with its head raised, with a **Hawk** with its neck contracted as if about to sleep, which are followed by *m*, an extended arm, a sacred channel with the figure of a pool, and finally the **Hawk** closes the line with *n*, the handled crosses by means of a bundle of cords. Indeed, these same symbols in retrograde order and in the same order to the Cross...

# CHAPTER II.

...are terminated and indicate that the Typhonian machinations <note>In Kircher’s system, Typhon represents the forces of chaos and drought that threaten the Nile's flow.</note>, so that they might not harm the sacred channels, are checked by the influx of the sacred Osiris, bound in a certain way, and stopped, being intercepted and packed tight by the seal of the Thautic Cross. <note>original: "Thauticæ Crucis"; referring to the Ankh, which Kircher associates with Thoth (Thaut).</note> It should be noted, however, that <margin>Hieroglyphs were carved in order.</margin> the Egyptians attributed much power to hieroglyphic symbols not only because of a certain secret composition of them, but also because of their order and arrangement. For they had long known that the order of things is most pleasing to the Gods. Hence, they took the greatest care so that symbols would not be carved onto Obelisks or other monuments at random or in a tumultuous heap, but in a certain order well-pleasing and very acceptable to the Gods; which they seem to have observed most especially in this place. For you see that the symbols *l, m, n* recur in a retrograde <note>Reverse or mirrored order.</note> sequence as *q, p, o*; so that two <term>Hawks</term> <note>original: "Accipitres"</note> hold the <term>handled cross</term> <note>The Ankh (Crux ansata), symbolizing life and divine breath.</note>, the most mysterious symbol of all, as if in the center. All other things are turned toward it as if toward a symbol of the influx of the supreme Divinity, seeing as it is the source from which all remaining series of linked minds draw their power. 

From this, it is not incongruously called an <term>amulet</term> of great power and "Thautic" by the Thautic Solar Intelligence; for the influx of the supreme Divinity, which (as has been indicated quite often now) is diffused through this Cross into the mind of the Solar Intelligence, fills the sacred pools and sacred channels from every side with bounty, which is aptly indicated through the figures marked *m*. By these means, the <term>Serpentine Divinity</term> <note>original: "Ophionium Numen"</note> and the Hawklike divinity—indicated by the Asp with an upright chest and the hawk about to sleep—provide life and motion to those things. Note, however, that in this place the Hawk is not properly displayed due to the local sculptor's drowsiness, but rather resembles a Quail; but this is an error. Indeed, on all Obelisks it resembles now a guinea-fowl, now a Hawk, as is clear from the Pamphilian Obelisk <note>The obelisk currently in the Piazza Navona, Rome.</note> on page 514, where you will find the true meaning of this symbol extensively explained.

Furthermore, this hieroglyphic synthesis is placed on the front of the lion's pedestal; this is not without mystery. For the ideal influx of the supreme Divinity <term>Momphta</term> <note>In Kircher's idiosyncratic theology, Momphta is a name for the creative, demiurgic intellect of God.</note> has its origin from the supra-mundane intellect, from which—as if from a certain perennial spring—it is diffused into all parts of the World, and from there into <margin>Hieroglyphs of the left side of the pedestal.</margin> all regions of the World and the bodies subject to them, filling all things with its goodness, life, and motion.

The hieroglyphic inscription *EF* on the left side follows now. But when it is considered in retrograde order, it becomes exactly the same as that which is placed in direct order on the right side of the Lion, the explanation of which is already known; therefore, I have judged it superfluous to repeat the exposition of the same. We indicated a little while ago the reason why they repeated the same symbols so many times. Therefore, let us apply ourselves to describing the hieroglyphic epigraph of the other Lion, marked *B*.

COMPILATION XVI. ON SPHYNGES. CHAPTER II.

## § II.

### ->The Image of the left Lion B, standing upon the pedestal, and its significance<-

<margin>Hieroglyphs of Lion B carved into the pedestal.</margin>
On the pedestal of the left Lion B, which is shaped into an oval figure and twisted into the form of a sacred tablet, a hieroglyphic inscription marked with the letters E and F is seen. This inscription is indeed entirely similar to the previous one; in fact, it is the same, as will be evident to anyone comparing one with the other. Thus, it is certain that it contains the same meaning. Therefore, he who has rightly understood the interpretation of the previous inscription cannot remain ignorant of the meaning of this one.

### ->Notes on the completed interpretation.<-

<margin>Why the pedestal of the Lion is oval-shaped.</margin>
**I**t is asked first: why is the pedestal of the Lions twisted into the oval figure of a sacred tablet? I respond that this was done by the Priests for the sake of mystery: for they believed that the more mysterious the structure of any hieroglyphic monument was, the greater power it obtained for attracting that Deity, <term>Momphta</term> <note>Kircher identifies Momphta as a creative, governing spirit of nature, often associated with the humidity of the Nile and the fertility of the world.</note>, to whom it was dedicated. Since, therefore, the following sacred or amulet-like tablets are placed in this inscription, they even thought it necessary to adapt the very base of the Lion upon which it rested into the oval figure of a sacred tablet, so that no part of the mysteries would be lacking. Thus, the <term>Momphtaean</term> Lion resting upon the sacred tablet would reflect that same tablet which we find everywhere among hieroglyphs in this shape—that is, the shape of the World impregnated with a fertile offspring.

<margin>Why the same hieroglyphs are repeated on both pedestals.</margin>
**Y**ou will ask secondly: why, in the two pedestals displayed here, is almost every single thing repeated? I respond that this was done partly for the sake of mystery—so that just as the oval figure represents the World, so the Deities who preside over the World might be attracted from every side by the hidden property of these marks—and partly so that the very harmonious arrangement of the characters, in which the Deities delight, might more easily allure them, as we hinted a little earlier. This was done especially to attract <term>Momphta</term>, the presiding governor of the entire moist substance, which the water of the Nile represents.

It must be noted, however, that this hieroglyphic <term>passage</term> <note>original: "periochen"; refers to a specific section or summary of text.</note> signifies not only the benefit of the Nilotic liquid, but also that supramundane liquid lying hidden in the Ideal essence of the supreme Deity, from which, as if from a most redundant spring, an abundance of all good things overflows. This liquid is first shared by the Genii <note>In this context, Genii are intermediary spirits or divine ministers who carry out the will of the supreme deity.</note> who serve the supreme Deity, and is then channeled into all worldly bodies. From these things, the true sense and reason of this hieroglyphic inscription will be easily apparent to the Reader. Therefore, let us now proceed to the interpretation of the <term>Sphinges</term> <note>The plural of Sphinx.</note>.

# CHAPTER III.

->*Interpretation of the Sphinxes which are seen in the Villa Borghese.*<-

<margin>The Sphinxes of the Villa Borghese.</margin>
**T**hese two Sphinxes are viewed in the Villa Borghese behind the Palace, on the left side of the courtyard, notable for their hieroglyphs; two others correspond to them on the right side, but these are marked by no hieroglyphs. Therefore, leaving those aside, let us turn to explaining the Sphinxes proposed to us in the first place.

<margin>These Sphinxes denote the rising of the Nile.</margin>
It should be noted, indeed, that these Sphinxes properly represent the rising of the Nile <note>original: "Nili incrementum"</note>; for they are composed of a Leonine body and a Virginal face, reclining upon their pedestals <note>Kircher uses the term "abacis," referring to the flat slabs or bases supporting the statues.</note> which are fashioned into the oval shape of a sacred tablet and elegantly carved with visible hieroglyphs.

<margin>Interpretation of the left Sphinx.</margin>
The left Sphinx has the following series of hieroglyphs inscribed on its right side, marked by the terminal letters V and X; the front contains those which the letters X and T encompass; the inscription on the left side is comprised by the letters S and R, which indeed, in reverse order, is the same as the first inscription encompassed by the letters V and X, if you except a few symbols. Therefore, to explain the meaning of this side, it will suffice to have explained the former. Finally, the marks contained by the letters R and P occupy the rear part of the pedestal. But with these things having been premised, let us now begin the interpretation.

<margin>Difference between Sphinxes and Momphaean Lions.</margin>
Furthermore, it should be noticed that a certain difference exists between the <term>Momphaean Lion</term> <note>Momphaean refers to Momphta, an Egyptian deity Kircher identifies as the spirit of creative humidity and the Nile's power.</note> and the Sphinx. For the Momphaean Lion signifies nothing else but Osiris, insofar as he presides over the Nilotic moisture. He is depicted under the figure of a Lion because, when the Sun enters Leo, he exhibits the greatest strength of his power, as we have already taught in various places. The Sphinx, however, is an image of a composite nature, transformed from a Lion and a Virgin; in this place, it signifies nothing other than the meeting of the Momphaean or Nilotic Osiris with Isis, as has been shown in countless places elsewhere.

<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
For as Plutarch rightly says: <note>original quote from Plutarch's "De Iside et Osiride": "τῶν δὲ ἄστρων τὴν μὲν Ἴσιδα νομίζουσι, ὑδραγωγὸν οὖσαν, καὶ τὸν Λέοντα τιμῶσι...". Kircher inserts solar symbols (☉) into the Greek text to highlight celestial connections.</note> "Of the stars, they consider Isis ☉ to be the bringer of water, and they honor the Lion, and decorate the doorways of temples with lion-like gapes, because the Nile overflows when the Sun first encounters Leo; but as the Nile is the outflow of Osiris ☉, so they hold the body of Isis ☉ to be the Earth, and they consider not all of it, but that which the Nile, stepping upon, manifests and mingles with ☉. From this intercourse they bring forth Horus; and that Horus is the preservation of all things, and the nourishment of the surrounding ☉ air, or the health of the air." <note>Kircher inserts the solar symbol ☉ into the Greek text, likely as a marker for divine or celestial names.</note> And concerning the stars, they ascribe the sacred [attribute] to Isis, inasmuch as she brings the water; but they venerate the Lion, and adorn the gates of temples with the gaping mouths of Lions, because the Nile overflows when the chariot of the Titan <note>A poetic reference to the Sun.</note> first touches Leo. Moreover, just as they think the Nile is the outflow of Osiris, so they think the body of Isis is the earth—not the whole earth, but that which the Nile, splashing into waves, renders fertile; from this union, they say Horus is born. Now, Horus is the season and the temperance of the surrounding air, preserving and nourishing all things: for when the Sun enters Leo and Virgo, Osiris is said to lie with Isis, that is, the Nile with the earth, from which union the fertile and all-nourishing Deity, Horus, is rightly born. For from the Nile fertilizing the Egyptian land and impregnating it with its moisture, [comes] the happiness of all Egy— <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

### SECTION XV. ON SPHINXES. CHAPTER III.

The Egyptian origin shines through; so that no one may wonder that the Nile was worshiped at all times with so many diverse ceremonies and rites, and that with such great care this health-giving union <note>original: "concubitum"</note> of Osiris and Isis was expressed. This was transfigured through the Sphinx, by a secret and mystical reason, from the female face of Isis and the leonine form of Osiris. This union shines forth most clearly in the hieroglyphic diagram displayed by the Bembine Tablet <note>Also known as the Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet depicting Egyptian mysteries, once owned by Cardinal Bembo.</note>, which follows. There you see the Nilotic Lion, or Osiris <term>Momphtæus</term> <note>Kircher's name for a specific manifestation of the Egyptian creator god, associated with the humid power of the Nile.</note>, arranged in the form of a bed; its foreparts represent the feet of a Lion; within, however, Isis—wrapped in a latticed cover and joined with Osiris—brings forth Horus. But see the interpretation provided in the cited place, where you will find the matters pertaining to this location explained more clearly. But now, to the interpretation.

# CHAPTER III.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription R: A rectangular panel containing various symbols: a semi-circle above horizontal bars (abacus), a hawk-headed figure, a human eye, a Djed-like pillar or mummy figure, a hawk (Accipiter), a triangle (pyramis), and an Ankh (Crux ansata). <margin>Hieroglyphs engraved on the right side of the Sphinx’s base. The consecration of the Nile canals.</margin>
In the inscription on the right side of the left-hand Sphinx, there occurs in the first place a segment with a panel <note>original: "abaco"</note> of the Nile canals; by which symbol nothing else is indicated but the consecration of the Nile canals, which was considered one of the more famous festivals in Egypt. Indeed, in the last month, **Mesori** <note>The final month of the Egyptian calendar, roughly equivalent to August, coinciding with the rising of the Nile.</note>, and preceding the future inundation, the Priests <margin>Herodotus.</margin> would assemble (as Herodotus testifies in **Clio** <note>Book I of Herodotus's *Histories*.</note>) in the inner sanctuaries, and having placed figures upon the panel of the canals, they would consecrate them with the customary rites and ceremonies. For as Horus <note>Horapollo, the purported author of the *Hieroglyphica*, a text Kircher used as a primary key for translation.</note> testifies in Book I, chapter 21: *Those who preside over sacred works are accustomed to fashion the tubes and canals of the sacred springs in the form of a Lion; for which reason, even to this day, those who pour themselves out in prayer for a mighty inundation are accustomed to use the sign of the Lion.* They did this by imploring a divine influx, which they hoped to obtain when they had appeased the sacred Divinities by carrying around the sacred amulets in the order of **a b c d e f g h**. 

Amulet **a**, first distinguished by a Hawk’s head and with a circular handle below suitable for carrying, signifies the celestial power of Osiris. The second, **b**, is the palm, a symbol of Solar fertility; it denoted the greatest benefits which the Solar Divinity conferred upon Egypt through this kind of increase in the waters, of which Plutarch teaches that the palm bestows 365, as many as there are days in the year. Next follows **c**, the handled cross <note>original: "Crux ansata," the Ankh symbol.</note> soliciting the influx of the supreme Divinity; then the pyramid, **d**, indicating the fiery force and quality, without which moisture is destitute and brings forth nothing, remaining sluggish and sterile; there follow, **e**, the two feathers of the Hawk, the perpetual ornament of the Divinities and the symbol of the sublime Intelligence of the <term>Agathodæmon</term> <note>A "good spirit" or protective deity, often depicted as a serpent or a winged disk.</note>, which the Sphinx represents. These are followed by **g**, the handled cross placed between two lotus-bearing scepters, a symbol of the sympathetic <margin>Amulets used by the Egyptians to obtain the Nilotic increase.</margin> dominion of the supreme Divinity over inferior things, from which the life of inferior beings results, as the Serpent with the segment, **h**, notes. 

And the Priests used these amulets in duly performing the sacred ceremonies to obtain a happy Nilotic increase and an abundance of all necessary things, as the <term>Nilometrium</term> <note>A device or pillar used to measure the height of the Nile's flood.</note>, **i**, and the papyrus thyrsus <note>A ritual staff or wand.</note> joined to it—a symbol of the things mentioned—sufficiently teaches: for by these, the chain of Divinities, **k**, having been moved, bestows life upon the lower material world <note>original: "hylæo Mundo," referring to the world of matter as opposed to the spirit.</note> through the influx of the divine Power—that is, by the virtue of the handled cross and through the powerful efficacy of the following sacred table; in which first appears a Serpent with a water-scheme <note>original: "hydroschemate," a symbolic representation of water distribution.</note>, then another Serpent transformed into the shape of a Nile vessel with a scepter, a Hawk, and three boundaries to which a young goat is applied. Through the Serpent and the water-scheme, the vital liquid is implied; through the Nile vessel which the Serpent fashions, it is signified—

<summary>Kircher interprets the hieroglyphic panels on a Sphinx's base as a sequence of amulets and symbols used by Egyptian priests to ensure the annual flooding of the Nile. He identifies specific icons like the Ankh and the Hawk-headed figure as tools for channeling divine influence into the material world's irrigation systems.</summary>

### DISCOURSE XV. ON SPHINXES. CHAPTER III.

...life <note>The text continues from the previous page, describing the "life-giving" nature of the Nile.</note>, the moisture of the Nile penetrating everywhere through the virtue and dominion of Osiris, who is the overseer of the three stations of the year for vegetation. In these lower regions, the dominion of the **polymorphic Demon** <note>A 'daemon' or guiding spirit capable of taking many forms</note> also contributes to the attraction of an abundance of necessary things, once every opposing power has been cut away.

<margin>Hieroglyphs engraved on the front of the Sphinx's base.</margin> Furthermore, on the front, another amulet is contained, which is comprised of the letters **X** and **T**; these are a staff in the shape of a letter, a goat-shaped scepter, and a **Hawk** (or **Thaustus** <note>Kircher's name for a Thoth-like figure</note>) with a <term>handled cross</term> <note>original: "Cruce ansata," the Ankh symbol</note>. These symbols are explained in backward order, as you see; by which nothing else is indicated except that the life of this World is poured into all bodies of the World by the power of the <term>amulet</term> <note>original: "periapti"</note>.

# TREATISE XV: ON SPHINXES.

...it pertains; by which it is indicated that for the successful rising of the Nile, a statue of a <term>Hawk</term> <note>original: *Accipitris*</note> with a feather and the sacred vessel of the Nile must be placed, so that <term>Momphta</term> <note>A name Kircher used for a supreme Egyptian deity or world-soul responsible for the generative powers of the Nile</note> may be entreated to grant this. The mystical reasons for the <term>Nilometer</term> <note>original: *Niloscopij*, an ancient instrument used to measure the height of the Nile's flood</note> have been fully described, as have the others; see the preceding sections.

From these matters, therefore, which have been drawn out more lengthily than perhaps is necessary, it is clearly evident that these hieroglyphic <term>Sphinxes</term> <note>original: *Sphynges*</note> were placed for this purpose: so that through the hidden connection of symbols with the supreme divinity, the Divine Powers who preside over lower things might either be appeased if angry, or, if favorable, be drawn to comply with their prayers as if by certain sympathetic attractions, in order to grant an abundance of all necessary things through the successful rising of the Nile. Hence the frequent repetition of the same symbols; hence the mysterious arrangement of each inscription into an <term>oval</term> <note>original: *ouatam*, referring to the oval frames or 'cartouches' containing the signs</note> shape. I leave all these things to be considered further by the wise Reader, who is now better instructed from the preceding pages.

**Y**our merits, Most Illustrious Men, bestowed upon the **Republic of Letters** <note>The international community of scholars and intellectuals in the 17th century</note> at all times, are so great that among learned men there is no one who would not admit—such is your singular humanity, courtesy, and benevolence—that he has obtained from you signal assistance for the promotion of literature. # CHAPTER I.
### On Household Gods, Hearth-Gods, and Serapes in general.

<margin>What the <term>Penates</term>, <term>Lares</term>, and <term>Serapes</term> were among the Egyptians.</margin>
The **Egyptians** at all times held in the highest veneration certain statues, which they called **Serapes**, and the Latins called **Penates** or **Lares**. And first indeed, we shall explain what the Penates and Lares were among the Latins, and then what the Serapes were among the Egyptians. Some report that the **Penates** are nothing other than those **Genii** <note>Guardian spirits</note> or <term>Lesser Gods</term> <note>original: *Deastros*</note> through whom <gloss>spi-</gloss> <note>Likely the beginning of "spiritus" (spirit) or "spirat" (breathes), continued on the next page</note>

<meta>This page continues Chapter I of Treatise XVI. It transitions from a general definition of the Roman Penates (household gods) to an investigation of their Egyptian counterparts, the Serapes, and their Hebrew equivalent, the Theraphim.</meta>

...we breathe, through whom we perceive, through whom we see, through whom we behold the Sun: namely, Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, and Vesta. For they said that Jupiter is the middle ether, Juno the lowest, Minerva the highest part of the ether—which is the power of divine Intelligence—and Vesta is the earth. These they named and believed to be both the Gods of the Fathers, and Birth-gods, and protectors of cities, and guardians of private homes. Dionysius of Halicarnassus <note>A Greek historian and teacher of rhetoric who lived in Rome during the reign of Augustus.</note> states: <margin>Dionysius of Halicarnassus</margin>
> These gods the Romans call Penates; but those translating the name into the Greek language, some declare them ancestral gods <note>original: *πατρίους* (patrious)</note>, others birth-gods <note>original: *γενεθλίους* (genethlious)</note>, some gods of property <note>original: *κτήσιους* (ktesious)</note>, others gods of the courtyard <note>original: *ἑρκίους* (herkeious)</note>, and others gods of the inner chambers <note>original: *μυχίους* (mychious)</note>.

Now, the Romans call these gods Penates, and some, translating into the Greek language, have interpreted them as *genethlios* or "gods of the lineage"; others call them domestic and familiar gods, others protectors of possessions, others Secret Gods. But why are they called Birth-gods <note>original: *Genethlij*</note>? Because <margin>What are the Birth-gods;</margin> they were thought to be assigned to the guardianship of men as soon as they were born; or because by their vigilance all things are generated, whence they are also called *Genii*, the presiding spirits over things to be generated. Why Ancestral <note>original: *Patrij*</note>? Because they were believed to preside only over those things which are common to a Kingdom or Province; in which they administered with the greatest diligence not only individual Cities, but also individual houses, and even individual men, plants, and animals, according to the care committed to them; hence they are also called tutelary gods. The Penates differ from the **Lares** <note>Guardian deities of the Roman household and hearth</note> not in duty, but in origin, for the duties of both are common in the care of private affairs. But concerning these, consult more extensively the first Volume, Treatise III. <margin>What are the Serapes of the Egyptians</margin>

The **Serapes** <note>Kircher is likely referring to *shabti* or *ptah-sokar-osiris* figures—small, mummy-form funerary figurines—rather than the major Greco-Egyptian god Serapis</note> of the Egyptians, however, were nothing other than images without any protrusion of limbs, as if wrapped in certain bandages <note>Referring to the shroud-like appearance of mummy-form statues</note>, a great abundance of which, and of varying size, is brought out of Egypt; they are fashioned partly from appropriate stone, partly from metal, wood, or earthenware. Some of these were placed in public locations as tutelaries for their guardianship; others truly were destined for the guardianship of these [private] things, and were stationary tutelaries; certain others were portable, which they carried with them wherever they might go; some they even wore in the manner of amulets around the neck, on belts, and on their hands. Furthermore, they were expressed with various facial features. For some were shown with a female face and a veiled crown; some under the form of a boy bound with fillets <note>original: *victati*; ceremonial ribbons or headbands</note>; others in other ways, as will be seen later. They also differed in their instruments; some, which they called **Averruncos** <note>Deities who "avert" or ward off calamity</note> or **Apotropaeos** <note>Greek term for "turning away" evil</note>, were depicted with various instruments, such as shields, whips, and nets hanging from their shoulders. Nevertheless, all such idols were adorned on the front and back face with various carvings of hieroglyphs, as will later be clear in the explanation of the same. <margin>The Theraphim of the Hebrews</margin>

And these are the idols which the Hebrews call **Theraphim** <note>Commonly spelled Teraphim; small household idols mentioned in the Old Testament</note>, which the sacred text of Genesis chapter 31 testifies that Rachel stole from her father Laban; concerning which we have dealt in an entire tract in Volume One, Treatise IV, folio 254; and we have taught that they were carried from Egypt by the servants of Abraham into Palestine and propagated there. They called them *Theraphim* because, since they could not pronounce 'S', they changed the 'S' into 'T' in the custom usual for the Chaldeans, and changed the final 'S' into 'im' [the Hebrew plural]; thus they called those idols *Theraphim* which the Egyptians called *Serapes*.

Furthermore, the **Penates** of the Egyptians were the same as Osiris, Isis, Nephthys, and Horus.

<summary>Kircher identifies the Roman household gods (Penates) with the Egyptian Serapes (mummy-form figurines) and the Hebrew Theraphim, arguing they all share a common protective function and origin. He uses linguistic shifts—specifically the Chaldean substitution of 'T' for 'S'—to link the names "Serapes" and "Theraphim."</summary>

-> CHAPTER I. 476 THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS <-

<margin>Who were the Penates of the Egyptians?</margin> Horus, Harpocrates <note>The god of silence, often depicted as a child with a finger to his lips.</note>, Arueris <note>A form of Horus the Elder.</note>, Apopis <note>Usually a serpent-demon, here categorized among minor deities.</note>, and countless minor deities <note>original: "Deastri"</note> of this sort; who, although they were held to be universal Spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note> of all nature and the same in their essence, differed only in their effects. Insofar as they were assigned to the guardianship of private affairs, they obtained the name of "Tutelary" gods and were worshipped as private Divinities. However, since we have spoken very amply about these in Synthesis III and IV of the first Volume <note>Referring to earlier sections of Kircher's massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*.</note>, we refer the Reader there.

<margin>Why the Egyptian Penates are formless.</margin> At this point, someone might rightly wonder why all the statues of the Egyptians are constructed so that no limb of the body stands out, but all are so carved into the body that they seem to make one single trunk? I answer that the Egyptians took the greatest care for the integrity of their statues. For they superstitiously believed that the statues of the immortal Gods, consecrated with such great ritual and ceremonies, would possess their power and efficacy only as long as they preserved their proper wholeness; if they should suffer an injury, harm, or fracture of some limb, they believed that at that very same moment all the assistance and influence of the Gods would cease. For this reason, they not only fashioned their statues from the hardest and almost incorruptible stone, but also adapted the limbs to the body so that it would be impossible for any limb to be broken without the destruction of the entire statue.

<margin>The Egyptians fashioned statues of the Gods almost formless, while the Greeks did the opposite.</margin> This also resolves a question often asked by sculptors: why the Egyptians alone made statues without protruding limbs, while the Greeks did the opposite. The Greeks, seeking to display their artistic skill, established images of the Gods with that majesty and decorum they thought fitting, looking to the living example of nature; the Egyptians, however, being more superstitious and excessively anxious about the indignation or offense of the Gods should they ever be mutilated, constructed them in such a way that they were immune to all breakage or mutilation. By this integrity, they sought to continually preserve the assistance and influence of the Gods who had been "attracted" to the statues through sacrifices; they believed this would by no means happen if even the smallest limb were spoiled, whether by human negligence or malice. Furthermore, since they carried these protective <term>prophylactic<gloss>intended to ward off evil or provide protection</gloss></term> images with them wherever they went, if they had protruding limbs, it could easily happen that an arm, hand, finger, foot, or some other attribute they usually held in their hands would be broken by continuous use and transport. Foreseeing such inconveniences, they made them with that specific sculptural style, as is clearly shown by the "types" of images of which a huge multitude has been brought from Egypt at all times. These, being enclosed in bags or chests without any danger of breaking a limb, easily withstood even significant violence. From this, it is also clear that the idols of Laban—which Holy Scripture says Rachel stole from her father—were idols of this sort brought from Egypt or constructed in imitation of them in Chaldea. These were likely cubit-sized statues lacking protruding limbs, which could easily be transferred from place to place and hidden without danger even among hay, straw, wood, or stones. Having premised these things, let us now at last pursue the matter proposed to us.
