### On the hieroglyphic significance of the Penates, or Tutelary Deities of the Egyptians.

<margin>Two statues of the Egyptian Penates, and their explanation.</margin>
Certain types of protective statues are hidden within the pyramids, which the ancients intended for the guarding of bodies and the transferring of souls into their proper celestial spheres. The following two statues are of this kind; hear briefly how they came to me.
In the year 1632, while I was staying in Marseille on business, a merchant of that city had recently brought with him two massive statues from Egypt. Since they seemed highly worthy of being included in the *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher’s monumental work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempted to "solve" the riddle of the Egyptian language and religion.</note>, I took care to have their likeness reproduced with as much diligence as possible. > First, let Your Reverence know that the black statue is carved from Pharian stone <note>original: "phario lapide." While this usually refers to white marble from the island of Paros, Kircher uses it here to describe a dark Egyptian stone, likely basalt or granodiorite.</note>, and the other from common marble; the former shows a female face, the latter a male one.
> **II.** The aforementioned idols were found in the Province of Sa'id <note>Upper Egypt.</note>, in a place not far from the Red Sea, inside a certain large pyramid. Through the passage of time, one side had suffered decay, opening an entrance through which the Turks entered and found said idols. They believed these were what the Pharaoh of this province once worshipped, and had commanded to be worshipped by all his subjects; they also built this pyramid for him after his death, within which he is said to be buried together with these two idols. And the wise men of this province say that this Pharaoh, trusting in the diligent worship of these, believed he would be carried into Paradise by the power <note>original: "opera"</note> of the animals depicted hieroglyphically upon these statues. And this was the custom of this ancient people, to bury their dead along with small idols, the kind of which are still found today inside mummies.
> **III.** These idols were brought from Sa'id to Cairo with the greatest labor, both because of the distance of a sixty-day journey and because of the danger of Turkish bandits who commonly wander through the deserts of this province.
> **IV.** The weight of each idol was found to be eight hundred pounds; having been placed on a ship, they fortunately first reached Genoa, where Prince Doria, admiring the rarity of the idols, offered a large sum of money if the merchant had been willing to sell them to him.

### Interpretation of the First Figure, A.

<margin>Explanation of the first figure or statue of Serapis.</margin> The first figure is made of Parian stone <note>A high-quality white marble from the Greek island of Paros, prized by ancient sculptors.</note>, with a veiled head and a feminine face. The rest of the body is in a turbinated <note>original: "turbinato" – cone-shaped or whirling, like a top. Kircher likely refers to the tapering, mummiform shape of an Egyptian statue.</note> garment ending in a base. On the front part, hieroglyphic images are inscribed in this order:

In the first position, a figure appears with widely spread wings, a hawk-like head, and lotus-bearing scepters inserted into each foot; each wing terminates in two outer hieroglyphic columns, A and B. In the center, descending in a straight line, seven figures follow that are similar to the first, each of which has hieroglyphic symbols attached. I shall reveal what this mysterious arrangement of hieroglyphs signifies with as much brevity as I can.

<margin>The Chains or *Seiras* of the Egyptians.</margin> We have stated in the *Theology and Medicine of the Egyptians* that the Egyptians established certain chains of the Gods, which they called <term>seiras</term> <note>original: "σειρὰς" – Greek for "chains" or "cords." In Neoplatonic philosophy, these represent the continuous flow of divine power from the highest source down to the material world.</note>. They believed the care and administration of the entire world was entrusted to these chains through a continuous influence of one upon another. These chains took their beginning from the first Mind of all things, and being derived through the spheres of the world, each had its own leader and minister similar to the first Mind. They believed these chains possessed such efficacy and power that as soon as their mystical characters were inscribed on an image according to the prescriptions of sacred laws, the image would acquire wonderful virtue against all the machinations of adverse powers. And the present hieroglyphic inscription displays just such a chain, which they called the Iyngean chain.

<margin>The Iyngean chain. What the *Iynx* was among the Egyptians.</margin> Among the sacred interpreters <note>original: "Hieromantas"</note>, the <term>Iynx</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the Iynx was a bird used in love magic, but in the "Chaldean Oracles" and Kircher's Hermeticism, it refers to a "mediator" or "transmitter" of divine thought.</note> was nothing other than the first Mind, comprehensible by intellect alone, hidden in the innermost retreat of the Deity. They indicated the ineffable darkness of its incomprehensible nature quite fittingly through the black marble, the veiled top of the image, and the cone-like garment, as if it were far removed from every stain of bodily and material contagion. The hieroglyphic character marked by the letter A expresses its nature and property through hidden symbols quite clearly—

# SYNTAGMA XVI. CONCERNING THE PENATES, LARES, AND SERAPES. CHAPTER I.

...we breathe, through whom we know, through whom we see, through whom we gaze upon the Sun—namely Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, and Vesta. For they said that Jupiter was the middle ether, Juno the lower, and Minerva the highest part of the ether (which is the power of the divine Intelligence), while Vesta was the earth. They named and believed these to be the Ancestral Gods, the Gods of Birth, the presiding deities of cities, and the guardians of private homes. <margin>Dionysius of Halicarnassus</margin> Dionysius of Halicarnassus wrote: <note>original Greek: "Τὺς δὲ Θεὸς τέτες Ῥωμαῖοι μὲν Πενάτας καλᾶσιν..."</note> *These gods the Romans call Penates, but those translating the name into the Greek tongue declare them, some as ancestral gods, some as gods of birth, some as gods of possessions, others as gods of the courtyard, and others as gods of the inner chamber.* But why are they called **Genethlii**? Because they were thought to be assigned to the protection of men as soon as they were born; <margin>What are the **Genethlii**?</margin> or because all things are generated through their vigilance, which is why they are also called **Genii**, the presiding spirits over things to be generated. Why are they called **Ancestral**? Because they were believed to preside only over those things common to a Kingdom or a Province; in which they administered with the greatest diligence not only individual cities, but also individual houses, and even individual men, plants, and animals, according to the care committed to them; hence they were also called **Tutelary** deities. The **Penates** differ from the **Lares** not in their duty, but in their origin; for the duties of both are common in the care of private affairs. But concerning these, consult more extensively the first volume in Syntagma III. <margin>What the **Serapes** of the Egyptians were</margin>

The **Serapes** <note>These are distinct from the god Serapis; Kircher uses the term here to refer to small, mummiform household idols or amulets.</note> of the Egyptians, however, were nothing other than images without any protrusion of limbs, as if wrapped in certain bandages, a great abundance of which are brought out of Egypt in various sizes, made partly of appropriate stone, partly of metal, wood, or clay. Some of these were placed in public locations as tutelary guardians of the same; others were destined for the protection of homes and were tutelary statues; some others were portable, which they carried with them wherever they went; some they even wore around the neck, on belts, or on their hands in the place of amulets. Furthermore, they were expressed with various facial features. For some had a female face and a veiled crown; some were shown in the form of a boy bound with fillets; others were displayed in other ways, as will be seen later. They also differed in their instruments; some, which they called <term>Averruncos</term> <note>Deities who avert or "run off" calamity.</note> or <term>Apotropaeos</term> <note>Protective symbols meant to turn away evil influences.</note>, were figured with various instruments such as whips, scourges, and nets hanging from their shoulders. All such idols, however, were adorned on both the front and back faces with various carvings of hieroglyphs, as will become clear later in the explanation of them. <margin>The **Teraphim** of the Hebrews</margin>

And these are the idols which the Hebrews call <term>Teraphim</term> <note>Kircher identifies the "Serapes" of Egypt with the household idols stolen by Rachel from her father Laban in Genesis 31.</note>, which the sacred text of Genesis, chapter 31, testifies Rachel stole from her father Laban; concerning which we have dealt in an entire treatise in Volume One, Syntagma IV, page 254, and we have shown that they were carried out of Egypt into Palestine by the servants of Abraham and propagated there. They called them **Teraphim** because, as they were unable to pronounce the letter 'S', they changed the 'S' into 'T' (following the usual custom of the Chaldeans), and by changing the final 'S' into 'im', they called those idols **Teraphim** which the Egyptians called **Serapes**.

Moreover, the **Penates** of the Egyptians were the same as Osiris, Isis, Nephte, Ho...

### CHAPTER I. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>
Who the household gods of the Egyptians were
</margin>
Horus, Harpocrates, Arueris, Apopis, and countless minor deities <note>original: "Deastri," literally "star-godlings" or "little gods"</note> of this sort; although they were considered universal Spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note> of all nature—being the same in substance and differing only in their effects—insofar as they were assigned to the protection of private affairs, they obtained the name of **Tutelary** deities and were worshipped as private Divinities. However, since we have spoken most extensively about these in the third and fourth Treatises <note>original: "Syntagmate"</note> of the first Volume, we refer the reader there.

<margin>
Why the household gods of the Egyptians are unformed
</margin>
In this place, someone might rightly wonder: why are all the statues of the Egyptians constructed in such a way that no member of the body stands out, but all parts are carved into the body so that they seem to form a single trunk? I respond that the Egyptians took the greatest care regarding the **integrity** of their statues. For they believed that the statues of the immortal Gods, consecrated with such great ritual and ceremony, would possess their power and efficacy only as long as they preserved their required wholeness. If they suffered any injury, harm, or fracture to any limb, the Egyptians superstitiously believed that at that very same moment, all the assistance and influence of the Gods would cease. For this reason, they not only fashioned their statues out of the hardest and almost incorruptible stone, but they also fitted the limbs to the body in such a way that it was impossible for any limb to be broken without the destruction of the entire statue. This also resolves the doubt of sculptors as to why the Egyptians alone fashioned statues without protruding limbs, while the Greeks did the opposite. The Greeks, seeking skill in their art, established images of the Gods with that majesty and grace they thought fitting, looking upon nature as a living model. The Egyptians, however, being more superstitious and excessively worried about the indignation or offense of the Gods should they ever be mutilated, constructed them in such a way and reason that they would be immune from any rupture or mutilation. Thus, through their wholeness, they would continually preserve the assistance and influence of the Gods drawn to them through sacrifices; they believed this would by no means happen if even the smallest limb were spoiled, whether by the carelessness or the malice of men. Furthermore, since they carried these <term>prophylactic</term> <note>From the Greek word for "protective" or "warding off evil"; here referring to amulets or portable idols.</note> images with them wherever they went, if they had protruding limbs, it could easily happen that an arm, hand, finger, foot, or some other instrument (which they mostly carried in their hands) would be broken by continuous use and transport. Therefore, foreseeing such inconveniences, they made them with that style of sculpture; the models of images, of which a huge multitude has been brought out of Egypt at all times, clearly show this. These, enclosed in bags and chests without any danger of breaking a limb, easily withstood even considerable violence. From this, it is also evident that Laban’s idols—which Holy Scripture says Rachel stole from her father—were idols of this sort brought from Egypt, or constructed in Chaldea in imitation of them. These were certainly cubit-sized statues, destitute of any prominence of limbs, which could easily be moved from place to place and even hidden among hay, straw, wood, or stones without danger. These things having been established, let us now at last pursue the subject matter proposed to us.

<margin>
The Egyptians fashioned statues of the Gods almost unformed; the Greeks, by contrast, sculpted them otherwise.
</margin>

<sig>CA-</sig>

<summary>Kircher explains that Egyptian statues were carved as solid blocks without protruding limbs to ensure their "integrity," believing that any break would cause the indwelling deity to flee. He links this "blocky" style to the portability of Egyptian amulets and identifies them with the biblical Teraphim stolen by Rachel.</summary>

### CHAPTER II.

# On the Hieroglyphic Meaning of the Household Gods, or the Tutelary Deities of the Egyptians.

**T**here used to be hidden in the pyramids a certain type of tutelary <note>protective</note> statues, which they intended for guarding bodies and for transferring souls into their respective spheres. Of this kind are the following two statues; hear briefly how they came to me.

<margin>Two statues of the Egyptian household gods, and their explanation.</margin> In the year 1632, while I was staying in Marseilles for business, a merchant of that city brought back with him from Egypt two massive statues. Since they seemed highly worthy of being included in the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher's massive work on Egyptology, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>, I took care to have their likeness expressed with as much diligence as possible. Later, Father Louis Brusset, a priest of our Society <note>The Society of Jesus, or Jesuits</note>, sent the drawings to me at Avignon along with a historical account. I have thought it necessary to include his words here, translated from French into Latin <note>now translated into English</note>, for the authentication of the whole matter.

---

->**Reverend Father in Christ.**<-

**B**ehold, I finally send the likeness of the two statues which Your Reverence desired, together with an exact drawing of the hieroglyphs contained on them.

I. First, let Your Reverence know that the black statue is carved from Pharian stone <note>original: "phario lapide"; likely referring to a high-quality dark stone or basalt, though named after the marble of Paros</note>, and the other from common marble; the former has a female face, while the latter represents a male face.
II. The mentioned idols were found in the Province of Saïd <note>Upper Egypt</note>, in a place not far from the Red Sea, inside a certain large pyramid. Through the passage of time, one side had suffered decay, opening an entrance through which the Turks <note>In this period, "Turk" was often used as a general term for people of the Ottoman Empire</note> entered and found said idols. They believed them to be those which the Pharaoh of this province once worshipped and commanded all his subjects to worship. It is said that after his death, they built this pyramid for him, within which he is reported to be buried together with these two idols. The wise men of this province say that this Pharaoh, trusting in the diligent worship of these figures, believed he would be carried into Paradise by the aid of the animals seen expressed hieroglyphically on the said statues. And this was the custom of this ancient nation: to bury their dead along with small idols, of the kind still found today within mummies.
III. These idols were brought from Saïd to Cairo with the greatest labor, both because of the distance of the journey—a length of sixty days—and because of the dangers of plundering Turks, who are accustomed to wander everywhere in the deserts of this province.
IV. The weight of each idol was found to be eight hundred pounds. Having been placed on a ship, they fortunately first arrived at Genoa, where Prince Doria, admiring the rarity of the idols, offered a large sum of money if the merchant had been willing to sell them.

### Interpretation of the first figure, A.

<margin>Explanation of the first figure or statue of Serapis.</margin> The first figure is made of Parian stone <note>A fine white marble from the island of Paros, highly valued in antiquity.</note>, with a veiled head, a feminine face, and the rest of the body in a tapered, cone-like shape <note>original: "turbinato habitu," describing a figure that narrows toward the base, similar to a spinning top or a funerary shabti.</note> ending in a base. Hieroglyphic icons are inscribed on its front in the following order.

First, a figure appears with widely spread wings, a hawk’s head, and lotus-bearing scepters tucked into each foot. Each wing terminates in two outer hieroglyphic columns, A and B. In the center, descending in a straight line, seven figures follow that are similar to the first, each having joined hieroglyphic patterns. I shall explain as briefly as I can what this mysterious arrangement of hieroglyphs signifies.

<margin>The Chain or <term>Seira</term> of the Egyptians.</margin> As we have stated in *The Theology and Medicine of the Egyptians* <note>Kircher is referring to his own earlier scholarly theories.</note>, the Egyptians established certain "chains of the gods," which they called <term>seirae</term> <note>original: σειρὰς. In Neoplatonic philosophy, a "seira" or "chain" represents the vertical link through which divine power flows from the highest god down to the material world.</note>. To these chains, the care and administration of the whole world was committed through a continuous flow of influence from one to the other. These chains took their beginning from the First Mind of all things, and being derived through the spheres of the world, each had its own leader and servant resembling that First Mind. They believed these chains to be of such efficacy and power that as soon as their mystical characters had been engraved on a statue according to the prescriptions of the sacred laws, the statue would acquire wonderful power against all the machinations of opposing forces. The present hieroglyphic inscription displays just such a chain, which they called the Iyngean chain.

<margin>The Iyngean chain. What the Iynx was among the Egyptians.</margin> Among the sacred diviners <note>original: "Hieromantas," those who interpret holy mysteries.</note>, the <term>Iynx</term> <note>In ancient Greek magic, an *Iynx* was a bird (the wryneck) used in charms; however, in the "Chaldean Oracles" followed by Kircher, the *Iynges* were divine mediators or "thoughts" of the Creator that transmit divine will.</note> was nothing other than the First Mind, graspable by the intellect alone, hidden in the innermost recess of the Deity. They very aptly indicated the ineffable darkness of its incomprehensible nature through the black color of the marble, the veiled top of the statue, and the tapered garment—representing that which is far removed from every stain of bodily and material contagion. The hieroglyphic character marked by the letter A expresses its nature and property through hidden symbols very clearly—

### CHAPTER II. THE HIEROGLIPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...it expresses: It carries a globe placed upon its head to express its divinity. It is fashioned with a hawk's head to indicate the force and power of a fiery intellect. It has outstretched wings to show that there is nothing that is not nurtured and preserved by its virtue. Beneath the wings, a certain triangular shape shines forth, from whose two angles—in the place of feet—two channels extend, ending in a circle. From this circle, two scepters rise, marked with the blossom of a lotus. Finally, beneath the triangle, the tail of a bird, together with the ends of the feet, forms a <term>handled cross</term> <note>original: "Crucem quandam ansatam," referring to the Ankh symbol</note>. All of these things, teeming with mysteries in their arrangement, we interpret in this way.

The triangle denotes that this <term>Iynx</term> <note>In Neoplatonism and the Chaldaean Oracles, "Iynges" (singular: Iynx) are mediating spiritual entities or "wheels" that transmit divine ideas into the material world</note> receives all its force and power from the archetypal triangle. And first, the World—which the circles signify—flowed out together with it from those same most abundant channels; thus, all things that are in the World were produced according to this model. The symbol of this is the lotus flower: for just as the lotus turns toward the Sun, so all the substances of the Worlds are turned toward their archetype, reflected back into the same. From this, it is sufficiently apparent why the Egyptians displayed the bird with a mysterious apparatus of channels arranged into the Worlds in place of feet. For while the feet hieroglyphically denote the manifest and sensible "footprints" of the Gods in the Worlds (which consist of a wonderful analogy of things to divine virtues), the highest powers and effects of the <term>Iynx</term> are only reached by the "flower of the mind." Hence, it is no wonder they wished to display the image of the <term>Iynx</term> only through hidden symbols, accessible only through deep contemplation of the mind.

<margin>
Seven Iynges linked to one another.
</margin>

->Since indeed in the "Iyngic chain" all things possess a virtue participated from the mind of the first <term>Iynx</term>, hence the seven <term>Iynges</term>—which are said to preside over the seven spheres of the World—are seen linked to one another in order and adorned with entirely similar patterns of symbols. Their duty is to conform themselves in the administration of the World to the ideas of the first <term>Iynx</term> in all things, and to lead the flow from the highest <term>Iynx</term> of all, through the middle ones, into the lowest sphere of the World by a certain linked propagation for the good of all members contained within the circuit of the World. For as Zoroaster rightly says:<-

<margin>
Zoroaster.
</margin>

> For the paternal mind sowed symbols throughout the world; he who perceives the intelligible things, and beautifies the inexpressible things, is the divider, both dividing and undivided. <note>original Greek: Σύμβολα γὰρ πατρικὸς νόος ἔσπειρεν κατὰ κόσμον... This is a fragment from the Chaldaean Oracles, traditionally attributed to Zoroaster.</note>

<margin>
What are the seeds of the Paternal Mind?
</margin>

*For the paternal mind sowed symbols throughout the world; it understands the intelligible things, and the whole partition—both divisible and indivisible—adorns the ineffable things.* What are the seeds of the paternal mind according to Zoroaster and the ancient <term>Hieromants</term> <note>Priests or interpreters of sacred mysteries</note>, if not the "Second Intellect," the immediate work of God? And what are those seeds scattered into the starry and material worlds, if not the paternal influx of virtues emanating from intellectual minds into the economy of the spheres committed to them? What are those intelligible and ineffable things that the paternal mind both understands and adorns, if not the ideas of all possible things existing in the divine mind—indivisible in their eternal archetype, but divisible when their virtues are diffused outwardly? And these are those Zoroastrian seeds of the divine mind, diffused through the universal series of the Worlds by means of the <term>Iynges</term>. For as we have taught in the *Oracles of Zoroaster*:

<margin>
Zoroaster.
</margin>

> For many Iynges leap into the shining worlds, jumping into them, in which there are three summits; beneath them lies a ruling [Iynx], and others lie beneath which, having perceived the works of the Father, [bring] the intelligible, immaterial [works] into the sensible works, for... <note>original Greek: Ἴϋγγες γὰρ πολλαὶ ἐπεμβαίνουσι φαεινοῖς... This quote describes the descent of divine mediators from the immaterial realm into the sensory world.</note>

### SYNTAGMA XVI. ON THE PENATES, LARES, AND SERAPIS. CHAPTER II.

...and they will call out to bodies. <note>The Greek text begins mid-sentence: "καὶ σώμασιν ἐνακλήσειν" (and they will call out to bodies).</note> For many <term>Iynges</term> <note>singular: Iynx; in Neoplatonism, these are spiritual mediators or "wheels" that transmit divine ideas into the material world</note> shall ascend, leaping into the shining Worlds; and in those where there are three summits, a prince is placed over them, and others beneath him. These, understanding the works of the father, have revealed the things of the intellect to the works of the senses and to bodies. What else is signified by these, if not the depth of the paternal triple summit which the Egyptians adored? The immediate executor of the concepts lying hidden within that summit is the <term>Iyngic</term> choir, subject to it, which—while they understand these Empyrean Worlds of the paternal depth of the triple triads through contemplation—reveal them to the works of the senses and to bodies. That is, according to the prescriptions of divine laws, they insert them into the members of the World through certain ineffable virtues. And as <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>Kircher attributes the "Chaldean Oracles" to the Persian sage Zoroaster</note> says: <gloss>Standing as messengers between the Father and Matter, and working the manifest imitations of the unmanifest.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Διαπορθμίοι ἐστῶτες φαῦαι τῷ πατρὶ, καὶ τῇ ὕλῃ, καὶ τὰ ἐμφανῆ μιμήματα τῶν ἀφανῶν ἐργαζόμενοι.</note> They are the "transporters" standing to speak to the father and to matter, performing the manifest imitations of hidden things, and inscribing hidden things into the manifest <term>Cosmopœia</term> <note>the making or creation of the world</note>.

<margin>The first of the seven Iynges is greater than the rest.</margin> Indeed, the hieroglyphs clearly teach that this is the case. You see in Figure A that the Iynx is first in order and also larger than the others; indeed, it is as if it were the <term>choragus</term> <note>the leader or conductor of a choir</note> of the Iyngic hierarchy. You see in its belly a triangle, from whose angles channels are led down into a globe, and from there they are reflected back into a lotus-bearing scepter. By this, nothing else is indicated except that the Iynx—the immediate work of the triadic paternal depth—draws the works of the father and his depth from the archetypal triangle through certain occult and ineffable channels into the Worlds, and from here they are reflected back into the father himself by a certain perennial contemplation and affection of love. For the supreme Mind, as <term>Hermes</term> <margin>Hermes.</margin> says, being most full of the fecundity of both sexes, reflects its love back upon itself. Thus the fecund paternal Mind, not only toward the inside but toward the outside, generated the World from its archetypal triangle; as <term>Plato</term> <margin>Plato.</margin> bears witness, flowing into it also by a perennial emanation of its virtues, it preserves it through the administration of the <term>Iyngic</term> choir. All these things are skillfully signified by the <term>Tautic Cross</term> <note>The "Crux Tautica" refers to the Ankh or Tau cross, which Kircher views as a symbol of the "Life" or "Nurturing force" of the universe</note> emerging beneath the triangle. Furthermore, the first Iynx, impregnated by fire from the first Mind, fills all the members of the Worlds with heat; whence, not without cause, it is seen expressed under the figure of a <term>Hawk</term> <note>original: Accipitris</note> with extended wings, as if nurturing all things. For as <term>Zoroaster</term> rightly says: <gloss>For the intelligible is food for the intelligence.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Ἔστι δὲ τοῦ νοητοῦ ὁ νοῦς.</note> <gloss>Learn the intelligible, for it exists outside the Mind, and of the Mind which leads forth my fiery world; for the Mind of the Mind is the architect of the world's fire.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Μανθάνετε τὸ νοητὸν ἐκ τοῦ ἔξω ὑπάρχειν...</note> And then he teaches that the fiery force of love is diffused into all members of the World with the following words: <gloss>It flashes with intellectual divisions; and all things were filled with love, shaping the formless, and they are carried like swarms, breaking through the bodies of the world.</gloss> <note>original Greek: Νοεραῖς ἀστράπτει τομαῖς...</note> Truly the supreme Iynx, the <term>choraga</term> of its order, as it emanated immediately from the paternal depth, having attained an intellect most similar to the paternal Mind, so it acts upon the following <margin>The supreme Iynx flows into the others.</margin> seven Iynges, the presidents of the seven spheres, by a similar influx of the fiery Mind. Thus indeed, the supreme Iynx itself, fixing its seat in the starry heaven—in the Intelligible World filled with ideas of every kind—acts upon the eighth heaven with a fiery vigor of influx according to a certain analogy; and then from here into

THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

# CHAPTER II.

...in order, the following Choir of <term>Iynges</term> <note>singular: Iynx; in the Neoplatonic system Kircher follows, these are "wheels" or spiritual agents that transmit divine thoughts into the material world</note>, here into the sphere of Saturn; and in this way, the Iynges expand their influence in order into the corresponding spheres of the Starry World, all the way
<margin>Zoroaster.</margin>
to the Moon. For as <term>Zoroaster</term> <note>Kircher attributes the "Chaldean Oracles" to the Persian sage Zoroaster, though modern scholars date them to the 2nd century AD</note> aptly says: <note>original Greek: "Νῷ μὲν κατέχει Iυξᾶ τὰ πάντα, ἀρρήτοις δ' ἐπάγει κόσμοις..."</note> *With the Mind indeed, the Iynx contains all intelligible things, but it leads sense-perception into the Worlds; with the Mind it contains the intelligibles, but it leads the soul into the Worlds.* For as we taught in the [volume on] Theology, all things emanate from the Paternal Mind filled with <term>Pantamorphic</term> <note>from the Greek "pantamorphos," meaning all-forming or possessing every shape</note> ideas; they are arranged by the mental fire, and they bestow life and motion through the seven diverging channels of the World. Zoroaster described all of this so clearly that his own words can serve as an interpretation; I cite his words here: <note>original Greek: "Νοῦς πατρικὸς ἐρρίπιζε νοήσας ἀκμάδι βουλῇ παμμόρφους ἰδέας..."</note> *The Paternal Mind, conceiving with vigorous counsel, fanned the all-forming ideas, and from a single source they leaped forth, springing out. For from the Father were both the counsel and the end; these ideas, being joined to the Father, were divided by the mental fire into other mental entities, through various lives from shared channels. For the multiform King set before the World an incorruptible mental pattern, following whose form the World appeared, graced with all kinds of ideas. Of these, there is one source, from which other divided streams hiss forth, being scattered around the bodies and recesses of the World.* These things are
<margin>Hieroglyphics carved on columns B and C of the statue of Serapis.</margin>
also sufficiently indicated by the hieroglyphic inscriptions on columns B and C; for they signify nothing else than the effects and operations which they perform in the Starry World, and then in the Elementary World. In column C, in the first place, <note>Hieroglyphic inscription: Kircher describes a serpent with hawk wings (Serpens cum pennis Accipitrinis) followed by eight hawks (octo Accipitres), representing the Iynx influencing the Sun and the eight celestial spheres.</note> a Serpent occurs with Hawk wings, followed by eight Hawks. By this, it is indicated that the <term>Iynx</term> first flows into the Sun, through which it then diffuses Solar virtue to the remaining eight spheres (indicated by the same number of eight Hawks). These spheres, being impregnated with the Solar-Iyngic virtue, likewise imbue the lower World with their own virtue for the good of the World. I deliberately omit the significance of the smaller hieroglyphs, partly so as not to confuse the Reader with most intricate characters, and partly because they contain nothing other than what I have already said, and can easily be understood by a curious Reader who compares these inscriptions with others occurring throughout this work.

<margin>Why so many hieroglyphics were carved on the statue of Serapis.</margin>
At this point, one might only ask why they carved such sublime Philosophy into this Idol? I respond that this was done because, as we demonstrated above, the Iynges were the immediate executors of the divine or paternal will. Furthermore, it was believed that after souls had shed the coverings of the body, they were each to be restored to their respective spheres from which they had first flowed—and the Iynges are the "minds" or governors of these spheres. Hence, they carved the Iynges, the handmaidens of the Paternal Mind, onto the Idol (which represented the Supreme Mind) and placed them in tombs. This was done with the intent that by the adornment of sacred symbols containing such excellent mysteries, the assaults of opposing powers <note>meaning demons or malevolent spiritual forces</note> might be shattered, and so that through this religious cult, the soul, whose body [rested] in the tomb...

<margin>The Iynx is the Intelligence closest to God.</margin>

<margin>Psellus.</margin>
**A certain bond between the father and the soul** <note>original Greek: δεσμός τίς ἐστι μεταξὺ τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τῆς ψυχῆς</note>. 

<margin>Why eight Iynges are attached to the idol of Serapis.</margin>
Indeed, eight Iynges are placed here, the first of which is the leader of the other seven. This was done so that the eight spheres might be indicated, into which souls—according to the fitness of their merits—would be inserted by the individual Iynges assigned to their care, moving now to this sphere, now to that.

### CHAPTER II. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...by impregnating them with the ideas of these influxes. For this reason, the <term>Iynx</term> <note>A term from the "Chaldean Oracles" referring to spiritual agents or "wheels" that transmit divine will</note> is aptly joined to the Divinity, acting as the executor of the affairs committed to it. It derives these ideal influxes from the "fontal craters" <note>source-vessels of divine energy</note>, which are impressed by the Iynx, into the individual spheres. Just as the highest chain of the Iynges is produced by the Supreme Iynx, so from this is derived the <term>Zonary</term> chain <note>associated with the "zones" or planetary spheres</note> of the spirits assisting those spheres. The former looks toward the Intelligible World, while the latter looks toward the Sidereal (Starry) World, so that the presiding spirits of the Starry World are parallel to those of the Super-intelligible World—the lower being subject to the higher—as we have deduced at length in our *Egyptian Theology*. For this reason, the former was represented by black stone, due to the depth of its inaccessible darkness which is unsearchable to the intellect; the latter was represented by white stone, due to the brilliance of the Starry World.

<margin>Hieroglyphics on the second Isiac statue.</margin>
But let us now reveal these truths from the structure of the hieroglyphics themselves. In this statue, there are three series of hieroglyphics, marked by the letters **M, N, and O.** In the first column of the series (**M**), one sees an arm with a chain and a circle, a bier, another arm, a serpent with a <term>water-pattern</term> <note>original: "hydroschemate," a zigzag symbol representing water or fluid flow</note>, and a vessel, followed by four water-patterns. What the arm, the bier, the serpent with the water-pattern, and the rest signify has already been explained very frequently; therefore, omitting a long description, let us assign only the meaning, which in the first column **M** is as follows: *The beneficent chain of the spirits presiding over the Starry World derives vital moisture into the fontal vessels; as the Solar Genius and the Falcon-headed statue denote, it commits these to the beneficent Isis, just as the following statue teaches; it instills the moist substance into the vessel of the lower sylvan worlds by the help of the chain of the Solar Genius, by whose providence the gate is opened to the Mendesian Genius (indicated by the Goat), and all lower things are animated.*

<margin>Column M.</margin>

<margin>Column N.</margin>
In the second column (**N**), there appears the statue of another Genius, whose office and dominion is to lead the supernal flows into the three-fold parts of the year, assigning to each its proper proportion. The chain of the Solar Divinity, moved from that point, fills the fontal vessels of the lower world with moisture.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription described in Column N: A deity holding a lotus, a dove (representing the seasons), and a cornucopia. This represents the seasonal distribution of divine abundance.</note>

<margin>In what the love of things consists.</margin>
The "love of things" consists in that conformation by which all things seek their own archetype, as the three Lotus flowers aptly teach; for these, from Sunrise, Midday, and Sunset, moved by a constant motion toward the Sun—as if stirred by the love of the Star—follow it

# TREATISE XVII.
## On Idols of Great Efficacy, or on the Averting Gods of the First Rank.

# CHAPTER I.
->**What are called the Averting Gods.**<-

<margin>What are called the Averting Gods.</margin>
Among the various Egyptian statues, many are found representing those gods whom the Greeks call *apotropaious* <note>original: "ἀποτροπαίους"; literally "those who turn away" evil.</note>, the Latins call *Averrunci* <note>Derived from the Latin *averruncare*, meaning to avert or ward off a calamity.</note>, and others call *Curetes*. They were called *Averrunci* because they were believed to turn away all occurrences of impending evils; hence they are called by the Greeks *apotropaious*, from the verb *apotrepein*, which is "to turn away." Indeed, these types of images are divided into various classes. We shall aptly provide the interpretation of all of them in this place.

<margin>An Averting Statue of great efficacy.</margin>
In the first place, those occur which are said to be of "great efficacy," because by their position, gesture, and their power to ward off the unwanted <note>original: "ἀπευκταίαις" (*apeuktaiais*); referring to powers used to repel or avert abominable things.</note>, they seem to strike terror. Such is the present statue, drawn from the Museum of Hippolytus Vitteleschi <note>Hippolytus (Ippolito) Vitteleschi was a 17th-century Roman nobleman and collector of antiquities.</note>, threatening in its expression and hands. Statues of this kind were typically placed before the doors of shrines to block the assault of opposing powers. In this figure, the veiled crown of the head is a sign of hidden divinity; it presents a threatening face, and with arms hanging down and hands tightly clenched, it is intent on striking terror with the goads <note>original: "stimulis"; the rod-like objects or symbols of authority held in the statue's hands.</note> it carries. With feet also positioned for a forceful resistance, it fiercely exhibits an air of threats and indignation. Two statues of this kind, of giant size, are seen to this day at Tibur <note>Modern-day Tivoli, Italy.</note>, before the entrance of the Cathedral church; they are called "Goei." <note>These are the famous colossal "Egyptianizing" statues, or Telamones, discovered at Hadrian's Villa and moved to the Tivoli Cathedral in the Middle Ages.</note> You may see these shown in the genuine drawing in the illustration of the Barberini Obelisk; they are of exactly the same form and dress as the one you see here, except that they are *Canophorae* <note>original: "Canophorae"; basket-bearers, usually referring to statues that support a weight on their heads.</note>.

->Concerning<-

<summary>Kircher defines the "Averting Gods" (Averrunci) as protective deities designed to turn away evil and describes a specific threatening statue used to guard temple entrances.</summary>
<keywords>Averrunci, apotropaic, Hippolytus Vitteleschi, Tivoli, Goei, Canophorae, protective magic, Egyptian statuary</keywords>

### On the Speaking Statue.

We have shown in various parts of this work that demons spoke not only from various statues, as if they were certain Oracles, but also that the priests themselves, in order to hold the people in greater worship and veneration toward the gods, imposed upon the simple commoners by their own clever art. Indeed, the use of such speaking statues was so frequent in Egypt that there was scarcely a <term>Nome<note>A "Nome" (from the Greek *nomos*) was an administrative district or province in ancient Egypt.</note></term> that lacked them. It seems the principal goal of the priests was this: to draw demons—through magical adjurations and various incantations—into statues that had first been consecrated with the proper rites in the inner sanctums <note>original: "adytis"</note>, and once they were drawn in, to consult them on various inquiries. And because the demons did not always give answers consistent with the truth, but instead completely maddened those who consulted them by mocking them in various ways, it happened that the priests took over the role of the demon. Turning to fraud, they adorned the statues with such craftsmanship that, by leading hidden passages and tubes <note>original: "syphonibus"</note> through to the head of the statue, they could murmur through them whatever they wished to impose upon the superstitious commoners, as if they were the voices and pronouncements of the gods. We have discussed this at length regarding the Memphite Sphinx in our work on *Mechanics*, and regarding the nature of Oracles and the construction of speaking statues in our work on *Magic*.

<margin>
From the Museum of Francesco Serra.
</margin>

And such was this present statue, which is exhibited for viewing in the Museum of the most Illustrious Knight Francesco Serra, a Roman—a man distinguished both by his nobility and his cultivation of all the fine arts. It is so similar to the preceding one that no difference at all can be discerned between them, except that the former was fashioned from black stone, while this one is of a brown color. Furthermore, this one has a wide mouth that is perforated through to the back of the head <note>original: "occiput"</note>, and from the back of the head to the middle of the back it has a passage. Through this, without a doubt, a tube inserted into this passage from the mouth of the <term>godling<note>original: "deaster"; a term used dismissively by Kircher to refer to a minor or false deity.</note></term> was led through the wall into a certain hidden chamber. In that chamber, the priests gave answers to those consulting them on various matters by murmuring brief spoken utterances through the tube. In this way, it happened that those who hung upon the response given—as if it were pronounced from the mouth of the Divinity—became not only more superstitious and obstinate in the worship of that Divinity (or rather, that Demon), but, deceived by this impious trickery of the priests, they were more and more encouraged to bring offerings and gifts. These were owed to the gods, as they themselves thought, but were in truth to be offered to the deceitful <term>initiates<note>original: "Mystis"; referring to the priests of the mystery religions.</note></term>; something of great significance...

Various protective instruments of the Averting Gods.

# CHAPTER I. 490 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER.

...was believed by all of Egypt; which, according to the testimony of Plutarch <note>Plutarch was a Greek historian whose work *On Isis and Osiris* is a primary source for Egyptian myth in the Renaissance</note>, is remembered to have caught the corpse of Osiris—thrown into the Nile by Typhon—with a hook and a net outside the currents of the Nile. And this is what is quite aptly expressed in this place by the hook and the net hanging from the shoulders. Isis is the Spirit of the Nile, warding off opposing powers from it by the sound of the sistrum <note>a sacred rattle used in Egyptian ritual</note>, as testified by the cited Plutarch; therefore the sistrum is the proper symbol of Isis. 

<margin>
Hieroglyphic statues as Warders of Evil.
</margin>

And lest the Typhonic powers <note>the chaotic and destructive forces associated with the god Typhon or Set</note> again plot something against the body of Osiris—that is, the Nile (for it has already been often said that Osiris was taken to represent the Nile)—either by immoderate drought or suffocating humidity, to the detriment of all Egypt; they had established this statue, terrifying with its hooks and grappling irons, as well as its net, as a <term>warder of evil <note>Greek: ἀπότροπον (apotropon), an object or deity used to turn away "evil eye" or bad luck</note></term>; so that by symbols contrary to their power, the evil forces might cease from harming and hurting. These symbols were of great efficacy (as they call it) for restraining them; and the hieroglyphs carved on the front part of the statue clearly teach this. 

First, a statue of a figure sitting in a specific manner is displayed with extended hands, containing below itself a <term>sacred pit <note>original: fauissa, an underground cellar or storage area in a temple for sacred objects</note></term> with a Nilotic channel and a Hawk. Another statue follows soon after, though poorly formed, with three boundary stones and the figure of a hook. This hook is not separate as it is here, but worn away by the "greed of time," and so is nothing other than a statue carrying a hook in its hand; the truth of this is shown everywhere by similar statues among the hieroglyphs that are equipped with hooks.

*Isis, the protective statue warding off evils from the sacred pit and its channels, as well as the guardian of the bowl of Osiris; Isis, the warder of evils from the three material Worlds; providence adapts all things to the archetype, restrains the Typhonic powers with a fourfold influence upon the lower World, and directs the bowl of Osiris into the fourfold World; she turns away noxious and destructive things, a providence of moist substance to be venerated with all honor; Isis, the one who extracts Osiris from the Nile, the mistress and administrator of Lunar humidity.*

-># TREATISE XVII. ON THE AVERTING GODS. CHAPTER I. #<-

...the symbols of averting <note>original Latin: "averruncationis." The term "Averruncus" refers to a Roman deity who warded off calamity; Kircher uses it here to describe Egyptian protective deities.</note> [evil] testify abundantly. What the veiled head and the symbols mean has already been stated above; let us now reveal what the hieroglyphs signify.

<margin>The hieroglyphic figure thus [presented].</margin>

**The first row** contains a **Serpent** with four small lines, though what they represent could not be discerned; this is followed by a sacred vessel <note>original: "ampulla sacra"</note> with semicircles and an extended arm (for it ought to show such a thing, even if the illustrator did not achieve it exactly). There follow two <term>Ibises</term> <note>The Ibis was sacred to the god Thoth (Mercury), the patron of wisdom and writing</note> separated by a square, then a triple inverted branch; after this follows a figure which, as is evident from other hieroglyphic schemes, refers to nothing other than a seated statue; this is a pyramid standing upon a sacred pool, which is followed again by an **Ibis** with an ax and an Altar, an eye, a Serpent, and a knotted staff; a thyrsus <note>A staff tipped with a pine cone, associated with Dionysus but here interpreted as a general sacred wand</note> closes the procession. The meaning of these is as follows: *The vital moisture of the lower world, through the benevolence of the Mercurial Spirits presiding over the material <note>original Greek/Latin: "hylæo," referring to the physical world of matter</note> world, is communicated during the three-fold division of the year through the statue which flows into the sacred pool; by this, the Mercurial Power is attracted and, through its providence, bestows life upon those committed to its care.*

**The second row** produces this meaning: *The Mercurial Power influences the three-fold division of the year; and when a propitiatory statue is placed for it, it opens the channels and repels adversities. The Mercurial Power, worshipped with due honor, imbues the air and the substance of the lower world with the offspring of things, through the statues appropriated to it and religiously worshipped.*

**The third**, as is evident from the symbols, produces this meaning: *The Typhonian <note>Referring to Typhon or Set, the principle of chaos and evil in Egyptian myth</note> powers are routed by the Ibis-like intelligences, which propagate the influence of the supreme Divinity into lower things through the religious worship of the Priests; from this, a great Stability is born for the material world.*

**The fourth.** Through this series of symbols, this meaning is produced: *The higher and lower worlds are preserved by the dominating chain of the Ibis-like—that is, Mercurial—Powers, once evils have been expelled.*

**The fifth.** *Life is given to the Vessel <note>original: "Crateri." In Hermetic philosophy, the 'Crater' or Mixing-Bowl is the receptacle of divine intellect sent down to humanity</note> of the great Osiris through the mystic and Memphite <note>original: "Momphiticas"</note> statues surrounding it and nourishing it with beneficial force.*

**The sixth.** *The celestial Vessel, by the aid of the Intelligences, acquires great power for conferring abundance upon lower things.*

I do not explain the remaining three series, both because they are known from the figures themselves, and also so that some exercise may be left for the curious investigator: for they contain symbols that are well-known and have already been explained very many times.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: The illustration on the left depicts a mummiform statue with a nemes-like wig and arms crossed on the chest holding a crook and flail. The body of the figure is divided into ten horizontal registers containing various symbols. Register 1 includes a serpent and two ibises. Register 2 contains seated figures and eyes. Register 3 shows various animals and geometric shapes. Kircher interprets these as a progression of spiritual influences from the "Mercurial" realm to the material world.</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the general study of mummiform inscriptions to a specific discussion of small, portable Egyptian idols. It establishes a link between these artifacts and the concept of protective or "averting" deities found in Greek and Hebrew traditions, specifically the Theraphim.</meta>

### CHAPTER II.
### *On the portable idols of the Egyptians.*

<margin>Portable idols of the Egyptians.</margin> Nothing is more common than these idols; there is hardly a Museum in which they are not found, and a great multitude of them is brought from Egypt every year. They are usually the length of a single finger, though some reach a cubit <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> in height, and they are adorned in almost the same manner as the larger statues. The question is asked: what do "little gods" <note>original Latin: "Deastri," a somewhat dismissive term for minor or false deities</note> of this kind signify? I respond that they belong to the class of those we have called the *Averrunci* or *Apotropaei* <note>From Greek, "averters of evil." Protective figures meant to turn away bad luck or malevolent spirits.</note>, and those whom the Hebrews called <term>Theraphim</term> <note>Hebrew: "Teraphim," household idols or images mentioned in the Old Testament, often used for protection or divination.</note>. That this is so is clearly taught by the symbols with which they are adorned; for they are for the most part equipped with <term>hieralphas</term> <note>A-shaped symbols Kircher believed represented a "sacred Alpha" or primordial principle.</note>, hooks, grappling-irons, flails, whips, and similar symbols of "averting" power. They are fashioned partly from clay, partly from wood, and occasionally from metal. Three of these idols may be seen in my Museum; the first, made of terracotta, was donated by the most distinguished and highly learned man **Nicolaus Heinsius** <note>A famous Dutch scholar and poet (1620–1681).</note> for his services to the Republic of Letters; the second, made of metal and exactly similar to the first, was given by the Most Illustrious Inquisitor of Spain; the third, made of cedar wood, was recovered in Egypt from within the wrappings of a Mummy by Father Marcus of the Order of St. Francis, a missionary of the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith in Egypt. Out of his truly singular kindness toward me, he had it transported from Egypt and placed it in my Museum. Each figure bears weapons in crossed hands to drive away evils. Since the hieroglyphic inscription is the same on each, it will suffice to explain one here.

# TREATISE XVII. ON THE AVERTING GODS. CHAPTER IV.

Many [statues] of this kind are seen in the Gualdi Museum, the Angeloni, the Barberini, and other private houses. In Malta, the most distinguished Giovanni Francesco Abela, Vice-Chancellor of the Order <note>The Order of the Knights of Saint John, or Knights of Malta.</note>, possesses three statues of this kind, two palms high, which I would gladly present here; but since they are exactly the same as those I described a little earlier, I have deliberately omitted them to avoid wasting time.

And indeed these statues are nothing other than the **Teraphim** of the Hebrews <margin>Hebrew Teraphim?</margin>, which the Holy Scriptures testify Rachel stole from her father and hid; regarding which we have dealt most extensively in the first volume in the *Pantheon of the Hebrews*, in the chapter on the Teraphim, and we refer the reader there.

To this class are also recalled those statues which are found sewn into the wrappings of mummies; about which we shall deal at length later in Treatise XVIII; the reader may consult that.

### C H A P T E R III.

->*On the Averting statues of another form, which they call <term>mediators</term>.*<-

There occur several statues of Egyptian minor deities <note>original Latin: "Deastrorum," a term Kircher uses for false or minor gods.</note> which they call <term>mediators</term> <margin>Averting statues called mediators.</margin> <note>original Greek: μεσίτας (mesitas).</note>, that is, mediating figures; and they are so called because the deities of a higher order were presented as needing to be solicited by deities of a lower order from the Supreme Mind in order to obtain what they sought. **Chrysippus** mentions these in his book *On the Cave of Mithras* <margin>Chrysippus.</margin>: <note>original Greek: "Τὰ τάχα τῷ σπηλαίῳ πάντα ποικίλοις ἄνθεσι κοσμηθῆναι, καὶ τὰ τῷ Θεῷ μεσίτας καλοῦσι, ἀγάλματα ἀπεισάμεθα."</note> *The walls of the cave were adorned with images of every kind, and the statues of the gods, whom they call mediators, stood around.* And these are again divided into various classes: some are kneeling, some standing, others sitting, exhibiting the images of the mediating gods placed before them; all the obelisks are filled with these figures, as was clear in its proper place; and these, carved separately on appropriate stones, were placed in shrines, sanctuaries, and private homes for the sake of averting evils, and were thought to have the greatest power and efficacy for obtaining heavenly gifts <note>original: "charismata," used here in the sense of spiritual or divine favors.</note>.

There is seen to this day in Rome, in the **Farnese Palace**, a kneeling image in female form, which carries before itself another image of a deity dressed in a conical garment; it holds a scepter in its hand, and on its head is a miter <note>A tall, formal headdress.</note> adapted into the shape of a gourd, upon which a globe sits, visible as appears in the following figure. The female form indicates **Isis**, that is, the earth; the idol which she holds before her expresses a **Canopic deity**, whose property it is to bless the earth with fertile moisture; the gourd-shaped tiara which it carries on its head is a symbol, which two horns also surround with a globe in between, by which they indicated that moisture could by no means be had except by the power of the celestial rays. But see what we have spoken of more extensively concerning this idol in the Treatise on the Canopi, in the exposition of figure VI of the Canopic Illustrations, where we presented one not unlike this. <note>Hieroglyphic inscription: Four columns of symbols extracted from the back of the Farnese Statue.
Column 1 (A-I): Includes two triangles (A), a hawk/Horus bird (B), a Was-scepter (C), an eye or solar disc (D), a figure with raised arms (E), an owl (F), a knotted rope or chain (G), a hetep-table or altar (H), and walking legs (I).
Column 2 (K-N): Includes a fish (K), a hes-jar (L), a tall obelisk or djed-pillar form (M), and a plover or ibis bird (N).
Column 3 (O-V): Includes a solar disc/eye (O), a sacred barque (P), a kneeling figure holding a tablet (Q), a jar pouring water (R), a pylon or gateway (S), a papyrus plant (T), and a scepter (V).
Column 4 (X-c): Includes a fish (X), a square pool or basin (Y), a bird/hawk (Z), a small jar (a), a scepter (b), and an owl (c).</note>

The meaning of the second column is this: **O** The fourfold faces of the Worlds are filled with celestial and elementary liquid, **P** by the benefit of the <term>Isiac statue</term> <note>A statue dedicated to Isis.</note>, **Q** by whose worship the <term>Polymorphous Demon</term> <note>original: "Polymorphus Dæmon." A term for a deity or spirit that takes many forms, possibly referring to the mediating power of the divinity.</note> **R** unloads the celestial womb into the pools of the lower World; under this power, to which all things are subject, he opens the gates of the lower Worlds **S**, the gates **T** of moist nature to Vegetable nature with supreme **V** dominion and wisdom; whence, **T** once the religion has been duly performed for him by the Priests, **V** with evils dispelled and the **X** <term>Typhonic offspring</term> <note>The descendants or manifestations of chaos and evil.</note> cast out, **Y** the face of the fourfold lower World is filled with the light of **X** Osiris, and the celestial womb is unloaded into the lower regions; **Z** the chain of <term>Solar Genii</term> and <term>Agathodaemons</term> <note>original: "Agathodæmonum," meaning "good spirits" or "good geniuses."</note>, conformed to his idea, **a** fills the three beneficent and fertile stations of the year with **b** moisture according to the requirement of each, **c** once the owl [of darkness] has been put to flight.

TREATISE XVII. ON THE DEITIES WHO WARD OFF EVIL. 497 CHAPTER III.

Rrr 2

### ->*Concerning the Messitic <note>Kircher uses the term "Messitic" (from the Hebrew 'Mizraim') to refer specifically to Egyptian artifacts.</note> Statue of Orignano, which is displayed for viewing in the Town of Orignano.*<-

**T**he town of Orignano is situated at the foot of Mount Soracte, twenty-four miles distant from Rome. In its cemetery, which lies before the church of the said town, a statue can be seen made of <term>Pharian stone</term> <note>White marble, traditionally from the island of Paros.</note>. It is in a kneeling posture, entirely and in every respect similar to the preceding one, except that it is much larger. Indeed, I do not recall seeing a larger Egyptian statue, unless one counts those placed at the <term>Basilica of Tivoli</term> <note>Likely referring to the Hadrianic Egyptianizing statues found at Villa Adriana.</note>. For, kneeling according to the proportions of the human body, it stands seven <term>palms</term> <note>A "palm" was a traditional unit of measurement; seven palms would be approximately five feet (1.5 meters) tall.</note> high. Due to the ravages of time, it has been mutilated at the head and somewhat at the chest. In front of itself, it holds another statue placed upon a rectangle, exactly the same as that which the Farnese statue (mentioned above) holds, containing two other idols and serpents. On its back, it displays a vast collection of hieroglyphs arranged in three columns; these were indeed transcribed by me, but due to the shortness of time and constraints, it was not possible to have them engraved. Regarding this statue, Fabio Chigi—who formerly served as Apostolic Nuncio in Germany and is now a most Eminent and worthy Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church—wrote the following in a letter after he had passed through that area and, having been informed of the statue, had examined it:

### CHAPTER III. OF THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

->To the Very Reverend Father Athanasius Kircher of the Society of Jesus, Fabio,<-
->Bishop of Nardo, sends many greetings.<-

I departed from Rome on the 16th and arrived at nightfall at the Town of Rignano, which is under the jurisdiction of the Excellent Prince Borghese (now Duke of Muti), at the 22nd milestone from the City. I found there a very ancient statue, though not complete, of a seated man, made of black stone, if I am not mistaken, supporting two small figures, and marked all around with secret signs, such as you, most learned man, search for and observe on each of the Pyramids. I judge the work to be Egyptian, and full of great erudition: therefore, I wanted to point it out to you, so that you might visit the place sometime, and have a rich supply from there to adorn the most learned volumes which you are preparing, etc. Cluenti, June 19, 1639. <note>Fabio Chigi, the author of this letter, would later become Pope Alexander VII. He was a long-time patron and friend of Kircher.</note>

->Another item from the Museum of the Most Excellent Man Joannes Rhodius,<-
->Physician of Padua.<-

<margin>Statues of the deity who wards off evil sent by Rhodius.</margin> 
We show you four faces of this statue: the front, the back, the left, and the right. The front shows you a woman conspicuous with a veiled head, in the Egyptian manner, who displays before herself another idol standing without a head, and with crossed arms carrying two clubs. The female figure is Isis, representing the female sex, yet endowed with a certain masculine power, as was demonstrated in the exposition of the <term>Bembine Table</term> <note>Also known as the Mensa Isiaca, this was a famous bronze tablet found in Rome that Kircher used as a primary source for his "decipherment" of hieroglyphs.</note>.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: The engraving shows four views of a single statue. 1. Left profile: Isis holding the headless Horus. 2. As shown in that explanation, the figure it represents is the statue of <term>Horus</term>, the son of Isis; it is without a head because Isis raised him to immortality after <term>Typhon</term> <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, whom Kircher identifies here as the antagonist of Osiris and Horus.</note>, desiring his divinity abolished, had killed him: for as <term>Plutarch</term> <note>A Greek philosopher whose work "On Isis and Osiris" was the primary source for early modern scholars of Egyptian myth.</note> rightly says, Isis is that female force and the receiver of all generation.

# TREATISE XVII. ON THE AVERTING GODS. CHAPTER III.

...generation, and not without reason was she called the <term>nurse</term> <note>original Greek: τιθήνη (tithēnē)</note> and the <term>all-receiver</term> <note>original Greek: πανδεχής (pandechēs)</note>; for she possesses an innate love toward that which is first and highest among all things, namely the Good itself. Toward this she is drawn, this she desires, and this she follows; but that which is evil, she flees and opposes. Hence, it is not without purpose that they represented the soul of Osiris as incorruptible and eternal, but his body as torn apart by Typhon <note>Typhon is the Greek name for the Egyptian god Set, the antagonist of Osiris.</note>, and Isis seeking it out and restoring it into its limbs. For that which is perpetual is much more excellent than that which is fleeting and changeable; and the impressions which she takes from the changeable image neither endure nor remain always the same, but like seals in wax, the impressions and traces are deleted. When she admits and borrows these things beyond reason, she is then said to join hands against Horus, and Typhon destroys him—Horus, whom Isis brought forth as a sensible image of the intelligible World. Traces of this are held in the Gualdo Museum on the Pincian Hill, where two statues are seen of Isis sitting with the boy Horus received upon her knees and nursing him, all of which allude to what has been said. But what of the nature of Horus, born of Isis and Osiris? What of the body of Horus, mutilated without eyes or head, if not the first and still imperfect generation made, as they thought, before the visible constitution of the World, or a certain raw and imperfect image of the nascent World, to speak with Plutarch? This the statue of Horus, which Isis displays as naked and <term>headless</term> <note>original Greek: ἀκέφαλον (akephalon)</note>, demonstrates more than sufficiently. Isis, therefore, displays Horus as a <term>mediator</term> <note>original Greek: μεσίτην (mesitēn)</note> to Osiris the Father, so that, the efforts of Typhon having been scattered, he might protect, restore, and perfect the sensible image of the World, which Isis, as the nature of things and the passive principle, produced from her womb. Hence the Priests believed that a statue of this kind, adorned with these mystical reasons, obtained great power for eliminating Typhonian powers.

However, what I have said confirms that this is the case.

# CHAPTER IV.

### On Polymorphous and Averting Statues of every kind.

<margin>What polymorphous statues are.</margin>
**P**olymorphous statues are so called because they are seen transformed from human shape into the various countenances of sacred animals. A great multitude of these are found, reflecting the variety of the deities to be expressed, since there is scarcely any Obelisk or Egyptian monument in which you will not find them carved. Thus, it is clear even from this chapter that Obelisks were nothing other than a certain [collection] of idols described with hieroglyphs...

COLLECTION XVII. ON THE PROTECTING DEITIES. CHAPTER IV.

...a heap of images, from which, as if from certain archetypes, the Priests and Sacred Scribes would separately extract and form statues for both public and private use. Among their number are the following statues, notable for their various transformations, some in standing and others in sitting positions. The following statue is preserved today in the Museum of the Barberini Palace; it was excavated from the ruins of the Church of the Dominican Fathers, commonly called the Minerva. Just as this site once stood as a temple of Isis, so no other <margin>A statue unearthed from the temple of Minerva.</margin> place in the City has supplied us with a greater abundance of Egyptian monuments. 

<note>Hieroglyphic illustration: A standing male figure with the head of a hawk (hawk-formed), wearing a striped nemes headdress and a short Egyptian kilt (schenti). The figure is barefoot and holds a crux ansata (ankh) in its left hand, which hangs by its side. The style is a Roman-Egyptian hybrid.</note>

The statue is <term>hieraxomorphon</term> <note>original: "ἱεραξόμορφον," meaning hawk-faced or hawk-formed</note>, that is, consisting of a hawk’s face, with a veiled crown, in an upright posture, with hanging hands, one of which carries a <term>Crux ansata</term> <note>The "handled cross" or ankh, the Egyptian symbol of life.</note>. The body is nude, if you except the veil with which the private parts are covered. This statue represents <term>Osiris Averruncus</term> <note>Osiris as a protector or "averter" of evil.</note>; his symbol is the hawk's face and the "handled cross," which is attached to nearly every idol consecrated to him. Since the mysteries of this symbol have been explained in countless places throughout this *Oedipus*, I shall not linger here in repeating them. A statue similar to this one may be seen in the Barberini Gardens attached to the Quirinal Hill; it is ten palms in height and is remarkable for its "handled cross."

## On the Statue of the Polymorphic Demon.

<margin>Statue of the Polymorphic Demon</margin>
Not long ago, the Most Serene Prince, the Grand Duke of Tuscany, out of his supreme benevolence and incredible affection for enriching the Republic of Letters in every way, sent me an <term>ectypon</term> <note>A cast or molded copy of an original work.</note> of an Egyptian statue, adorned on all sides with innumerable hieroglyphs. The letter A signifies the front part, and B the back. I had already discovered some things similar to this here in Rome: the first of these, taken from the Barberini workshop, we have displayed on the Pamphilj Obelisk; another was held in the Museum of Francesco Angeloni, and upon his death and the auctioning of the workshop, it was acquired by Captain Torquato de Alexandro. A third, entirely similar, is contained in the Royal Museum of Francesco Gualdo on the Pincian Hill. However, since I have found none more complete than this present Medici specimen, I have decided to explain it here in detail.

<margin>The front part of the statue.</margin>
The front portion of the statue shows a female form, entirely nude in body, with swelling breasts, standing upon two crocodiles, and exhibiting an <term>androgynous</term> <note>Having both male and female characteristics.</note> sex. A curl of hair on the head is twisted into a ram’s horn, while upon the head—

### CHAPTER IV. 504 THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...of the world, celestial and elementary, life: through the Lion, <term>Momphta</term> <note>In Kircher’s system, Momphta is a formative, creative power often associated with the Nile and moisture.</note>, the overseer of moist nature, is represented; through <term>Anubis</term>, the watchful guardian of the world's mixing bowls <note>original: "craterum mundialium." These 'bowls' likely refer to the celestial spheres or the reservoirs of elementary forces that mix the ingredients of life.</note>, is signified, which is why he has his right foot placed upon a bowl. It displays an androgynous nature, because in relation to the lower things committed to its trust, it acts as an active principle; but insofar as it depends on supra-mundane influences, it acts as a passive principle. He stands upon two crocodiles and seems as if to trample them; for indeed this Divinity subdues and exterminates all <term>Typhonian</term> <note>Refers to Typhon/Set, the Egyptian god of chaos, storms, and destruction.</note> force by its own power. He holds two scepters placed on either side, ending in a lotus flower; on the right one, an <term>Androsphinx</term> <note>A sphinx with a human head, representing human intelligence joined with divine power.</note> is seen positioned, expressing the supra-mundane Mind, according to whose influx of ideal reasons he directs and governs his formed operations. The other scepter has a plant placed upon it, which the Ancients called <term>moly</term> <note>original: "μῶλυ" (moly). A mythical herb mentioned in Homer’s Odyssey, said to protect against sorcery and death.</note>, because <margin><term>moly</term> herb</margin> it frees one from death; you may see its virtues described in the chapter on Egyptian Herbs. It was a symbol of an antidote, which they used against the pestilential and contagious oppositions of Typhonian powers. In the upper part, you see various types of divine attendants, which denote the tutelary <term>Genii</term> <note>Guardian spirits or lesser deities.</note> of things and the ministers of the <term>pantheomorphic</term> <note>A deity that possesses "all forms" or can manifest in any shape.</note> Divinity; see the extensive explanation of these in my work *The Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 464. The remaining hieroglyphs scattered in the intervening space are placed there not so much for meaning, as to frighten away hostile Spirits by the hidden allusion of the mysteries they express. For with these and similar signs they used to mark not only the Inner Sanctuaries, but also Obelisks, statues, and other monuments, as has been more than sufficiently shown in the context of this Work.

### SECTION XVII. ON THE DIVINITIES WHO DIVERT EVIL. 505 CHAP. IV.

The serpent in whose coils he is entwined, and the globe upon which he stands, clearly show that through vital heat, <term>Momphta</term> <note>Kircher identifies Momphta as a creative, life-giving power, often linked to the Nile or a "fecundating" spirit.</note> nourishes and sustains all things that are in the World. And indeed, in this form, the Egyptians were accustomed to represent that Momphta of theirs. But now let us take up again the thread we let go. 

Now follow 16 rows of hieroglyphic inscriptions, by which they signify nothing else than the effects and operations which each of the said spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note> performs in the World. I would gladly present their meaning in this place; however, since the figures are very poorly drawn and can scarcely be distinguished except by anxious conjectures, I did not wish to dwell longer on explaining them, especially since from those figures that are known, the meaning of the rest became easily known to me. Thus, they are nothing other than the effects and operations of the followers of the <term>All-Forming Mind</term> <note>original: "Pantamorphæ Mentis"</note>, as I said, and are entirely the same as those we assigned to the <term>All-Forming Nature</term> <note>original: "Pantamorphæ naturæ"</note> and its ministers in the exposition of the <term>Isiac Table</term> <note>The Bembine Tablet of Isis, a Roman-era bronze plate with Egyptian-style motifs that Kircher studied extensively.</note>; therefore, let the reader go to that cited place. 

Other multi-formed statues are also observed under the masks of the Hawk, Ibis, Dog, Wolf, Lion, and <term>Long-tailed Monkey</term> <note>original: "Cercopitheci"; referring to the baboons or monkeys often seen in Egyptian art.</note>; but since we have explained all of these partly in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher's 1650 work on the obelisk in Rome's Piazza Navona.</note> and partly in various places in this third volume, we refer the reader there.

# TREATISE XVIII.
## Concerning Polycharacteristic Egyptian Statues—that is, those distinguished by a fabric of hieroglyphs over the entire body.

->TO THE MOST EMINENT PRINCE<-

# ADALBERT, CARDINAL PRIEST OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH
### Of the Title of Saint Praxedes, von Harrach, Archbishop of Prague, and Primate of Bohemia.

To you alone, Most Eminent Cardinal, a Prince truly <note>original: "αὐτοδιδάκτῳ" (autodidaktō)</note> self-taught, was this argument of mine concerning the polycharacteristic <note>A term coined by Kircher meaning "having many characters/symbols."</note> images of the Egyptians owed. Indeed, among the few, I have observed you at all times to be the greatest, who are accustomed not only to discern and value the dignity of literary business with equity, but also, when opportunity is given, to zealously strive to promote the labors of learned men. You possess not only a mind fit for carrying out any arduous task due to your knowledge of political discipline, but also a genius wonderfully capable in penetrating the inner sanctuaries of nature and in the science of things divine and human; meanwhile, I shall remain silent regarding your most ardent zeal for propagating divine glory, your solicitude in the care of the pastoral office committed to you, and your vigilance in restraining the wolves from the Lord's sheepfold. By these gifts granted to you from heaven, you raise the branches of your virtues so much more sublimely than others, as you yourself tower higher. Receive, therefore, this as a kind of perennial symbol of my affection toward you. If anything in the course of this work should respond less than perfectly to the most refined judgment of your genius, I trust I shall easily obtain pardon from your kindness on this account: if you understand that the cause of the work performed was not the insignificance of my own person, but the command of the Great Emperor <note>Refers to Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand III, Kircher's patron.</note>.

### CHAPTER I.
#### Concerning Polycharacteristic Egyptian statues—that is, those distinguished by a fabric of hieroglyphs over the entire body.

<margin>
Polycharacteristic
<note>original: "πολυχαρακτηρισικαὶ" (polycharaktēristikai)</note>
Statues.
</margin>

There are found in the most ancient ruins of the City of Rome several fragments of statues, woven over the entire body with a marvelous decoration of hieroglyphs, which for that reason we call <term>polycharacteristic</term> <note>From the Greek for "many-signed" or "many-lettered."</note>; two of this kind are found in my Museum, donated by friends of antiquity. What these may have indicated, let us disclose in a few words.
