# SYNTAGMA XVIII. ON MANY-CHARACTERED STATUES. CHAPTER I.

It must be noted, therefore, that there existed among the Egyptians certain images which represented the deities of the first rank <margin>Deities of the first rank of the Egyptians</margin>—those who were placed immediately beneath the supreme tri-form Deity—acting as the leaders of the choir <note>original: "Archichoragos," a Greek-derived term for a chief leader or conductor</note> for all other spirits. Just as these deities were allotted the universal care not only of the intellectual world but also of the sensible world, so too were they adorned with a peculiar devotion of sacred carvings. In this way, the secret symbols of both the gods and of worldly things might more aptly fit the universal intellect of said deities. Hence, various symbols of mysteries, drawn both from obelisks and from other monuments, were engraved upon the images of these deities with such ingenuity that almost no space in these images appeared empty. This can be seen in the present fragment of a statue <margin>The torso of a statue without a head.</margin> where you first see the torso of a statue without a head, entirely adorned with hieroglyphics. Indeed, the amulet **F** hanging from the breast by a cord is entirely the same as that which we described in the preceding pages. Furthermore, the figure

- **C**: A central circular pectoral scene containing a seated bird-headed deity (ibis or hawk), a solar disk containing a character resembling a digit '7' or a Hebrew letter, and other smaller figures.
- **D & E**: Flanking groups of three human-like figures with arms raised in a gesture of adoration or prayer.
- **F**: A small mummy-shaped amulet (likely Osiris or a Ptah-Sokar-Osiris figure) suspended from the neck of the statue by a cord.</note>

engraved upon the breast and marked with the letter **C** is an averting statue <note>original: "statua averrunca," a deity intended to ward off evil</note>, distinguished by a many-formed headdress <note>original: "tutulo polymorpho"</note>, kneeling, and of female form. Two hawks <margin>Explanation of the hieroglyphics of said statue.</margin> crowd her on either side, while toward the shoulders, eight solar spirits <term>hawk-shaped <note>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφοι (hierakomorphoi)</note></term> are placed in order. These are the ministers of "All-Formed Nature" <note>original: "Pantamorphae naturae"</note>, to whom they also seem to pray with outstretched arms. The explanation of these things is as follows: The image was of All-Formed Nature, whose principal minister is the figure engraved on the breast; kneeling, she is the leader of the choir of the immediately inferior rank of spirits, just as the headdress is marked with a <term>serpent-shaped <note>original Greek: ὀφιμόρφῳ (ophimorphos)</note></term> globe and three gourds—that is, with the seal of the tri-form Deity and the paternal source, which is the seal of All-Formed Nature.

# CHAPTER I. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

->Two<-

<note>original: "culo conspicuo significat"</note> ...signifies by a conspicuous circle. The hawks and the sitting <term>Solar Intelligences</term> <note>Kircher believed Egyptian gods were "Intelligences" or spiritual forces governing the planets</note> denote the administrators of the same. It is placed upon a circle because it exercises its dominion over the Universe; to which also eight <term>Solar Genii</term> <note>Minor spirits or protective entities</note> transformed with hawk-like heads, with hands extended, seem as if to supplicate it, and to await its commands and the execution of the <term>influences</term> <note>The celestial "flow" of power from stars to earth</note> of the things committed to their faith. 

The remaining hieroglyphics—partly because they are well-known (for they show nothing other than the effects and operations of the aforementioned things), and partly because they are too small to be discerned due to the great corruption <note>damage or erosion of the stone</note> which they have suffered (as happens in almost all smaller characters of this kind)—I have decided should be omitted. Therefore, let us gird ourselves to explain only those larger hieroglyphics whose figures remain certain in their form.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A large, irregularly shaped fragment of a stone monument. The central vertical column is divided into five registers labeled A through E:
- Register A: A winged sphinx or creature with a solar disk on its head, below what appear to be the legs of a larger figure.
- Register B: Two horizontal sub-panels; the upper contains a crocodile or lizard; the lower shows a seated deity with a complex headdress (horns and disk).
- Register C: An Ibis bird on a standard (Thoth), a central squatting figure (possibly Heh or a creator deity) holding palm ribs, and a standing figure on the right.
- Register D: A group of deities, including one standing with a disk and horns, and several smaller seated and standing figures.
- Register E: Three figures, including a jackal-headed deity (Anubis) and others in ritual poses.
The left and right sides of the stone are covered in vertical columns of varied hieroglyphs, including birds, eyes, vessels, and geometric signs.</note>

# SYNTAGMA XVIII. ON POLYCHARACTERIC STATUES. CHAPTER I.

<margin>
Hieroglyphics carved on the back of the aforementioned statue.
</margin>

The back of the statue is likewise adorned with innumerable hieroglyphics; among these, the middle space contains figures divided into various Classes. However, since the statue is broken, the first and last hieroglyphic schemes are missing; but we have marked the middle Classes of the schemes with the letters **A B C D E**. In space **A** is placed the figure of a winged Bull with a human face, from whose head flames shoot forth, with a globe hanging over it, and it stands upon a wavy Serpent.

<margin>
A Bull with a human face emitting flames from its head.
</margin>

The Bull with a human face emitting flames from its head with a globe placed above indicates the Mind of <term>Apis</term> <note>The sacred bull of Memphis, seen here by Kircher as a symbol of cosmic life</note>, the presiding spirit of vital motion propagated through the four stations of the World. Its symbol is the Serpent, upon whose four coils it stands with its four feet. The globe signifies divinity, the flames signify fiery power, and the wings signify the speed with which it pervades all the paths of the World. This is followed shortly after in space **B** by its principal minister, the Dog-headed Deity <note>The Cynocephalus, or baboon-headed god, often associated with Thoth</note>, having a Scarab between globes on its head as a headdress, holding two Serpents in its hands, and likewise containing a wavy Serpent beneath its feet. By these symbols, the "Luni-solar" life is indicated, which it distributes into the portions of the lower World. Opposite this is a Crocodile enclosed in a receptacle with an eyed phallus, followed by a globe teeming with a Serpent along with another Crocodile; by this is indicated the Typhonian force <note>Referring to Typhon/Set, the god of chaos and destruction</note>, the destroyer of vital and fruitful propagation, which the Dog-headed deity, by its opposing skill, dissipates and eliminates. Furthermore, in level **C** follows a frog-shaped Scarab conspicuous for its Hawk’s head, holding in its front feet a headdress composed of three Nilotic vials, and standing with its hind feet upon an altar. By this is signified the Solar force ruling over material power (which consists in the moist substance of the Nile), which is indicated by the frog-shaped Scarab and the three vials; this is promoted by the Mercurial Ibis, or the Lunar <term>Agathodæmon</term> <note>A "Good Spirit" or protective deity, often depicted as a serpent or bird</note>, with a staff transformed into a <term>hieralpha</term> <note>A sacred letter or symbol, often resembling the letter A, used in Kircher's mystical interpretations</note>. Indeed, a human figure wearing a feather on its head and holding two vessels in its hands seems to supplicate it, so that the moist substance may be imbued with its virtue.

<margin>
Note: the painter has not expressed the Lion heads well according to the original.
</margin>

In level **D** follow the Memphite Deities transformed with Lion heads, the first of which carries a Cross <note>The Ankh, or "handled cross"</note>, and with the other hand seems to protect another kneeling statue, with a hand placed upon its head; all of which are symbols of the <term>Memphite Power</term>, the Presider over the lower water, and are signs of command and dominion.

<margin>
Symbol of the Memphite Power.
</margin>

The kneeling figure which immediately follows, wearing a basket on its head teeming with a Serpent, indicates the averting <note>Protective or evil-shunning</note> minister of the Memphite Deity, who was placed there to repress those adverse powers that lie in wait for the abundance of life and the goods resulting therefrom. Finally, what is contained in the last level **E** are the effigies of three Deities: the ministers of the many-formed God, <term>Agathodæmon</term>, Anubis, and Osiris; since these have been explained very often elsewhere, I shall not dwell on them.

As for the four Deities placed on each side, all equipped with handled Crosses <note>Ankhs</note> and transformed in wondrous ways, they are the ministers of the Deities mentioned so far, who, wandering through all the bodies of the World, execute those things which are for the good of the Universe, having routed all adverse Powers. But since these figures are explained at length in the <term>Bembine Tablet</term> <note>A famous bronze tablet with Egyptianizing motifs, also called the Mensa Isiaca</note>, as well as on other Obelisks, I would waste time if I lingered on them any longer.

->Conclusion.<-

<margin>An image of the supreme Master of Ceremonies of the Creative World.</margin>
From these things, therefore, it is clear that this present image, inscribed entirely with composed hieroglyphics from all orders of nature, expressed nothing other than the supreme <term>Master of Ceremonies</term> <note>original: "choragum"</note> of the Creative World. The other listed Divinities are called his administrators, the leaders or rulers of the World, because they stand beneath the said Chief Master and are moved by his command. All these things are indeed beautifully described by <term>Psellus</term> <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar</note> in his exposition of the <term>Oracles of the Zoroastrians</term> <note>The Chaldean Oracles, a collection of mystical texts</note> in these words: <note>original Greek: Δυνάμεις ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ οἱ Χαλδαῖοι τιθέασι...</note> *The Chaldeans placed Powers in the World, which they named Leaders and Rulers of the World, because they govern the World with movements of providential care; the Oracles call these Powers "Sustainers," because they support the entire Universe; these are subjected to the command of the supreme Leader, whom they call the <term>Pantarch</term> <note>The "All-Ruler" or supreme governor</note>.* They stand, because as Psellus says, <note>original Greek: Τῷ μὲν ἀκαμπτῷ...</note> by their unbending and steady posture, their firm and stable power is declared. By their "psychic providence," they provide support through the care of guardianship and preservation. <note>original Greek: Ταύτας δὲ τὰς δυνάμεις...</note> *They designate these Powers solely through the causes and immobility of the Worlds.* For just as all lower <term>Demons</term> <note>In this context, "daimones" refers to intermediary spirits or lesser deities, not necessarily evil beings</note> are subject to these, so they seem to supplicate them, requesting the kind execution of their commands from them, as the final figures behind the four "world-leaders" on either side clearly demonstrate with bowed knees. For as Psellus rightly says in his booklet *On Demons*, just as a Prince in his kingdom relates to his officials, so do the greater Divinities relate to the Demons subject to them. Thus, by setting up this image and worshiping it correctly, the Egyptians promised themselves all happiness on account of the power and efficacy of these unspeakable symbols. I do not explain the smaller hieroglyphics since, as I said, they can hardly be discerned, and they contain nothing other than the effects and operations of the said Divinities. Therefore, let these few remarks on <term>Polymorphic statues</term> <note>Statues having many forms or shapes combined</note> suffice, and the curious Reader will easily judge from the exposition of this one what should be determined regarding similar statues.
<margin>Psellus.</margin>
<margin>The Powers, Leaders, and Rulers of the World according to the Chaldeans.</margin>
<margin>Psellus.</margin>

<margin>The Greeks adorned the images of the Gods with letters.</margin>
Following the Egyptians, the Greeks were likewise accustomed to adorn their own images with a similar context of letters, just as was said in *Hieroglyphic Magic* regarding <term>Diana of Ephesus</term>; they used to adorn her with letters which, for that reason, were called "Ephesian letters." Indeed, <term>Bulinger</term> <note>Jean-César Bulenger, a Jesuit scholar of Roman antiquities</note> teaches in his book *On Circuses* that statues placed everywhere in the Circuses were adorned with this kind of <term>polygrammatism</term> <note>The practice of writing many letters or symbols on an object</note>; his words are: *The Circus was not only adorned with statues and columns, but those statues were for the most part engraved with letters that signified something, placed there by Magi and Philosophers, in which words fate was contained.* Following the Greeks, the Arabs—since they were not permitted by the prescription of their law to fashion statues—customarily adorned their utensils, such as urns, cups, and bowls, with innumerable letters everywhere, using sentences drawn from the <term>Alcoran</term> <note>The Quran</note> and admitting Magical characters which they took from the <term>Cabala</term>. This custom was so powerful that it extended its branches even into the farthest parts of the earth, such as China and Lapland, where...
<margin>Bulinger.</margin>
<margin>The Arabs engraved letters on their utensils.</margin>

> *For no mortal head is joined to limbs,*
> *Indeed, two branches do not shoot forth from the shoulders,*
> *No feet, no swift knees, nor shaggy private parts,*
> *But it is a sacred mind, and immense alone,*
> *Moving through the whole World with swift skin.*

<margin>Prophylactic statues.</margin>

...the latter part: *May they be imbued with celestial life through the worship of the supreme Deity, the ruler of time, by whose providence they may obtain the place due to them according to the decree of the Gods.* They allude to the mystical operations of asphalt <note>original: "asphalti"; likely referring to bitumen used in mummification</note> which preserves against corruption, as if they were saying: Just as asphalt makes bodies immune to decay, so may the providence of the Anubic or Mercurial Deity—which the lid marked with a **Dog's head** indicates—preserve this dwelling-place of the soul uncorrupted for immortality.

<margin>Sacred vessels sent by Nihusius</margin> The most distinguished Nihusius <note>Holstenius's friend and a frequent correspondent of Kircher</note> sent me similar items extracted from the Museums of the Dutch; the first of these has a lid that is <term>dog-headed</term> <note>original Greek: "κυνοκέφαλον" (kynokephalon)</note>, like the preceding one; however, we show the hieroglyphic carving, expressed in slightly larger characters, separately in the figure placed just before this. **A I.** *May the Celestial Intelligence, ruler and guardian of the lower realms, turn away the adverse force of Bebon <note>A Typhonian or chaotic deity in Kircher's system</note> from this deposit.*

**B II.** *May the Celestial Intelligence from the material worlds <note>original: "hyleis Mundis"</note> and their contagion transfer [the soul] through the Mercurial Deity to the shining Zone of Osiris, the ruler of time.*

**C III.** *Through the worship of the Deity enclosed in the precinct, through the influence of Osiris, through the scepters of the great Powers, through the Ibis-shaped Deity presiding over water, through the feather of Arueris <note>Horus the Elder</note>, through the Momphtaic Deity, subjecting all things to himself by a threefold dominion and providence.*

**D IV.** *Through the life flowing into the pool, through Thauštus the averter of Typhonian evils, through the Ibis and the Hawk, the averters of evils from the sacred pool.*

And this is the ideal reading of the inscription placed on the vessel, as is evident from the symbols already explained many times, and it holds no difficulty at all.

...unwilling to be marked with signs on the left side. Adjacent to this Mummy, on the left side, lies a small clay figurine of Isis <note>original: "fictilis Icuncula Isidis"</note>, packed into the spice preservative and largely submerged in it; this was a solemn custom of the Egyptians in every such adornment of corpses. On the outside of the urn is carved the history of a miserable misfortune, written by the Priests in the most ancient hieroglyphic characters. This urn is the top of a column, for it clearly appears below that it has been cut away from the solid rock. The most excellent man, Mr. David de Willem, unearthed this from subterranean vaulted hiding places four miles from Cairo, across the Nile in the vicinity of the Pyramids, in the year 1619, and placed it there as an ornament for the Anatomical Theater. Mr. Otto Heurnius, Professor of Medicine, Anatomy, and Surgery <note>Heurnius was a Dutch physician and philosopher who collected Egyptian antiquities</note>.

Therefore, this most learned man says that the statue represents a Canopus <note>A term used by early scholars for these jars, named after the city of Canopus</note>, inscribed with the ancient literature of the Priests; which is true. He says, furthermore, that Egypt was illuminated by the light of the Christian religion in the year 300 after Christ under Constantine the Great; about which I have doubts, since from the very origin of the primitive Church—that is, from St. Mark the Evangelist—until the invasion of the Saracens, the Egyptian Church flourished in a wonderful manner at all times, as is abundantly clear from so many Holy Fathers, Anchorites, and Monasteries flourishing in Egypt. This was at a time when Egyptian literature had already long since faded, or rather, had utterly perished. I do not deny that the corpse of some sort of miscarriage <note>Kircher likely refers to a fetal or small remains found within</note> was preserved in the small urn, but that a "misfortune" was described in it with hieroglyphics—that I can in no way approve, by the good leave of that learned man. Therefore, so that the truth of these sayings may be clear, I shall here begin the exposition of the writing; which will best be done if I first set forth certain things to more deeply clarify the truth.

<margin>Egypt received the faith immediately after the passion of Christ.</margin>

<margin>Hieroglyphic literature perished in the times of Cambyses.</margin>

We have shown in innumerable places of this *Oedipus* <note>Referring to Kircher's massive work, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note> that Egyptian literature was not in use during the times of the Roman Caesars, or immediately before the coming of Christ in the flesh, much less in the time of Constantine the Great, but had already then been destroyed and lost by the impiety and drunkenness of Cambyses <note>Cambyses II, the Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE</note> when he invaded the Egyptian Empire. That this is true, we have taught from innumerable authors everywhere, both in the section on the Obelisk and in the context of the present work, as we have said. We say, therefore, that this little urn was buried in subterranean crypts in ancient times—when hieroglyphic literature, as well as the preparation of bodies which they call Mummies, were still in use according to Priestly laws—with that apparatus of hieroglyphics which it displays. The corpse of the human fetus preserved in it was the son of either a King or of the Nobles of the Kingdom. For we have said above in the treatise on Mummies that all the medicated corpses of the Egyptians, preserved with such great zeal, clothed in so many wrappings of bandages, and finally adorned with such an ingenious context of hieroglyphics, were not of common people, but of either Kings, or Nobles, or men conspicuous for the praise of Wisdom, for whom...

# CHAPTER III. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

We have shown from Herodotus, Diodorus, and other historians that there was hope for those who were the only ones at the helm of the Kingdom. However, as for the claim that the <term>Mumiacum</term><note>A term used by Kircher to refer to the mummified remains or the substance found within a funerary urn.</note> preserved in the small urn was an aborted fetus—a conclusion drawn from the tiny size of the body—that proves nothing. Long-standing experience has now made it known that through the constricting power of <term>asphalt</term><note>Bitumen or pitch used in the mummification process.</note>, which penetrates even the bones themselves, the bodies of mummies contract so much over the course of time, and are so far removed from their natural <margin>Asphalt contracts corpses.</margin> state, that those who in life represented a man of proper stature now seem to represent children. This became known to me through experimentation on many parts of mummies—namely hands, feet, and heads, of which there is a great abundance in the Roman apothecaries—which I measured with the greatest zeal and compared with the proportions of a living body. Therefore, what that learned man considers an embryo, I assert was a boy, whether the son of a King or of some other Noble.

<margin>The Egyptians cast out abortions; they did not bury them.</margin> Added to this is the fact that if it had been an aborted fetus, it would never have been honored by the Egyptians with this usual apparatus of ceremonies. For since they execrated every abortion as the work of a malignant Demon, they either burned it or threw it into the Nile, as something subject to the curse of the good Spirit, as has been demonstrated by me elsewhere. Therefore, that it is the body of a child—contracted into such a state of smallness by the length of time and the quality of the asphalt exerting greater force upon a very tender little body—is more than sufficiently shown by the <term>imaguncula</term><note>A small image or figurine, likely an ushabti or a protective amulet.</note> which expresses the guardian Spirit of the little body (which is seen placed with almost all mummies); and indeed by the hieroglyphic inscription, the true <margin>Hieroglyphic interpretation of the aforementioned vessel.</margin> and genuine interpretation of which is that which follows. The lid displays the head not of an Owl, but of a Hawk. For since the Owl is a symbol of the perverse and deadly nature of the <term>Typhonian</term><note>Related to Typhon (Set), the Egyptian god of chaos and storms.</note> Powers, they by no means employed it for the use of sacred images: for you will not find among all the hieroglyphics <margin>Statues of Egyptian sacred rites were adorned only with the faces of animals.</margin> a sacred statue distinguished by the head of an Owl, or a Quail, or a Crocodile; for this would be contrary to the intended end at which they aimed. All statues, therefore, were fashioned transformed with the faces of only sacred animals, in order to strike terror into their <term>adversaries</term><note>original: "ἀντιτέχνοις" (antitechnois) - rivals or opposing spiritual forces.</note>. Of such a kind is this vessel, the lid of which is marked with a Hawk’s head; and by the Hawk they indicated the Solar Deity <note>The god Horus.</note>, as is evident from innumerable places in this Work, to whose protection the little body placed in the vessel was committed. The hieroglyphic inscription carved on the vessel has four columns, which are marked with the letters N, O, P, Q, of which the first two, N and O, have exactly the same symbols, while the remaining two, P and Q, differ.

In the first column, therefore, in the first place, a vessel occurs from which a Serpent emerges; beneath which is placed the head of Horus with a feather; there follows a cycloid <note>A circular or curved shape.</note> with the figure of an eye; then a <term>gnomon</term><note>An L-shaped tool or the pointer of a sundial, used here to describe a specific hieroglyphic shape.</note> with the figure of an Altar; which is followed by an eye, with

Columns P and Q contain various birds (hawks/vultures), water ripples, and other symbols including eyes and limbs.</note>

In column P, first a Goose occurs, with a Serpent, a Scepter, and a Water-scheme <note>a symbol representing water or fluid</note>, and two angled points; which is followed by the same statue as the one that is last in the second column, conspicuous with a Hawk-like head; below which is placed a Water-scheme, with two Rhomboids, and a semicircle; then follows an Ibis with a curved staff; finally an Ibis-morphed statue with the figure of an enclosure; the sense of which is this: *Chenosiris the guardian may bless the spirit of the deceased with divine liquid through celestial influence, and may refresh it with the celestial liquid of Solar intelligence, and may Hermanubis <note>a fusion of Hermes/Thoth and Anubis</note> by his ruling influence introduce it into the enclosure of Osiris.*

In column Q, the first place is held by a Serpent with a semicircle, and an extended arm; an averting statue <note>a protective figure meant to ward off evil</note>, with an altar; a twisted cord, with three Lotus flowers; a crested bird attempting flight resting upon two scepters; there follows a sacred underground cellar <note>original: "fauissa sacra"</note>, a scepter, a circular shape, an eye, a bird attempting flight, and a curved staff with a human foot. The sense of these is: *May the tutelary Deity grant life to this person, attracted by sacrifices and appropriate and sympathetic rites; may he carry the Spirit of this body into the celestial spheres, blessed by the hidden fellowship of the Deities.*

And this is the sense of this inscription. That this is true is shown by another inscription entirely similar to this one, which we exhibited separately engraved on the back of Figure II in the Illustration of Mummies, from which we also corrected this one, which was not so well formed; so that henceforth it should by no means be thought that the fate of this boy is contained in this inscription, but rather that true and genuine sense which we have expressed. But as to why they placed the same inscription in the first two columns, <margin>Why the same hieroglyphic inscription is sometimes repeated in the same place.</margin> that was done for the sake of efficacy, since almost nothing occurs more frequently than the repetition of inscriptions and symbols of this kind on one and the same subject, as has been demonstrated at length in the preceding sections.

## On Amulets, and Charms, and other portable Little Images, which the Egyptians used.

<note>Decorative initial 'U' depicting a classical or biblical scene with several figures in a landscape.</note>In order that a grateful posterity may recognize the magnitude of your merits toward this present Work, I have decided that the subject of this Treatise should be dedicated to your honor. In a word, you have fulfilled all the parts of a sincere friend. Let this be, therefore, whatever it may be, a symbol of my gratitude toward you—unequal indeed to your merits, but drawn from the heart.

# TREATISE XIX. ON AMULETS, PERIAPTS, ETC. CHAPTER II.

they exhibited the logic of a mixed or composite nature; there are even those that exhibit insects, such as the Beetle <note>original: *Scarabæum*</note>, of which there is again a huge variety. Parts of the human body were also adopted for use as Amulets, and indeed instruments of every kind employed in sacred rites; so much so, that there is almost nothing so small on all the Obelisks that has not passed into use as an Amulet. Thus it has become clearly known to me that the sacred literature of hieroglyphics indicated nothing other than a certain System <note>original: *Syntagma*</note> of the Amuletic art, arranged with the greatest diligence and no less industriousness of wit. From these, as if from certain prototypes, Amulets—or <term>hierogrammatisms</term> <note>sacred symbolic inscriptions or drawings believed to possess magical power</note> of great virtue—were gathered for peculiar and private use. ### CHAPTER II.

->**Concerning Amulets which reflect the form of the Gods and sacred animals.**<-

<margin>Amulets reflecting the form of the Gods and sacred animals.</margin> Among the Amulets which were bound to the neck, arms, belts, thighs, and any part of the body, were first the Beetles <note>Scarab beetles</note> expressed in the form of sacred animals; such as Ibises, Hawks, Rams, Cats, Oxen, Dogs, Dog-headed men, and many others, the images of which we place here. All of these were certainly <term>periapts</term> <note>from the Greek *periapton*, an object tied around a person for protection; a charm</note> intended for certain ends by the Egyptians, who, just as they were divided into different <term>Nomes</term> <note>administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note>, so too did they worship the Divinities of the Nomes with diverse cults.

<margin>Amulets for the obtaining of good things.</margin> The Ibis, a Periapt of the Mercurial Divinity <note>Thoth, whom Kircher identifies with the Roman Mercury</note>, was worn to obtain gifts proper to Mercury from the same, such as the gift of intellect and constant aid in obtaining knowledge of natural things.

<note>Hieroglyphic illustration: An Ibis standing on a small platform.</note>

The Hawk, a symbol of the Sun <note>Horus</note>, was worn both to obtain perfect health and vital vigor of the heart, and to dispel contrary infirmities of the heart.

<note>Hieroglyphic illustration: A Hawk or Falcon (Accipiter), representative of the Sun/Horus, standing on a platform.</note>

The Ram and the Goat were employed as Amulets to obtain fertility, as they were consecrated to Ammon and Mendes.

<note>Hieroglyphic illustration: A Ram (Aries) standing on a platform.</note>

<note>Hieroglyphic illustration: A Goat (Hircus) or Ibex standing on a platform.</note>

They persuaded themselves that the figure of the Ox served to obtain the influence of Apis; but when the same figure was placed in public, it was to promote the good of agriculture.

<note>Hieroglyphic illustration: An Ox (Bos), likely the Apis bull, adorned with a saddle-cloth, standing on a platform.</note>

The Amulet of the Dog, or the <term>dog-headed man</term> <note>original Greek: *κυνικέφαλος* (kynikephalos)</note>, was worn everywhere by the Priests in honor of Anubis to obtain sagacity in the sciences and a vigilant guardianship of things.

<note>Hieroglyphic illustration: An anthropomorphic figure with a dog or jackal head (Anubis/Cynocephalus), standing upright.</note>

# THEATER OF EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPHICS

<margin>Amulets for the repelling of evils.</margin> Indeed, for the repelling of evils, the following were carried as most effective <term>Periapta</term> <note>from the Greek 'periapton,' meaning an object tied around the body; a charm or amulet</note>: the Crocodile, the Fish, and the Wolf. For as we have stated in our work on Magic, just as various honors were shown to the benevolent Divinities so that they might assist with their various favors, so too were sacrifices performed with the greatest fervor to the malignant Demons so that they might not cause harm. Moreover, they considered the sacred arrangements of letters to be of such great importance that they believed themselves unable to be immune from any unlucky encounters without them. Hence, an Oracle is said to have responded to one consulting on this matter:

->Hear me, though I am unwilling, for you have bound me by necessity.<-
->Call upon this powerful name of necessity, even though it be heavy;<-
->Come quickly with these words<-
->Which I bring forth from my heart through these sacred symbols.<-
<note>original Greek: "Κλυθὶ μὲν οὐκ ἐθέλοντος... ἱεροῖσι τύποισι." Kircher provides a Latin translation which is here rendered into English. The "sacred symbols" refer to the hieroglyphs themselves as conduits of power.</note>

<margin>Other various amulets.</margin> There follow now the Amulets of the Hawklike Jupiter, of Horus, Pan, Canopus, Isis, and Harpocrates; by the wearing of these, they hoped that various favors would come to them according to the specific property of the Divinity. Whoever desires more on these matters should consult the <term>Pamphilian Obelisk</term> <note>Kircher’s 1650 work on the Roman obelisk commissioned by Pope Innocent X</note>, where in the third book concerning <term>Hierogrammatism</term> <note>The study of sacred writing or the science of priestly symbols</note> he will find everything most amply explained.

### CHAPTER III.

->Concerning Amulets of a mixed and monstrous nature.<-

<margin>Mixed and monstrous amulets.</margin> **Nardi**, whom I have frequently praised, presented at the end of his work on **Lucretius** a peculiar plate from his own Museum showing clay amulets of various colors covered in glass <note>likely referring to faience or glazed ceramics</note>; we have deemed it appropriate to place the explanation of these here. Contemplate the plate on the following page.

<margin>The origin of the word Phylactery.</margin> The said plate exhibits amulets of a mixed and monstrous nature; I have decided to explain in a few words what they signify according to the mind of the Egyptians. It must be noted, therefore, that "phylacteries" are named from the Greek <term>phylattein</term> <note>original: φυλάττειν</note>, that is, "to guard," because those who wore them were believed to be immune to the snares of opposing powers. And because they knew that the Good Spirits <note>original: Agathodæmones</note> perpetually engage in terrible struggles with the "anti-skilled" demons <note>original: antitechnis Dæmonibus; these are "crafty" or opposing spirits who mimic divine works to deceive</note>, they decided that this terror could be expressed by no better means than through fearsome appearances. Indeed, they thought that the very images of the good Spirits, constructed with a certain terrible and monstrous architecture, would strike fear into the said opposing Spirits. For this reason, they consecrated these in the inner shrines with set words and adjurations full of horror from the threats of "barbarous" voices <note>referring to the "voces magicae" or unintelligible magical names often found in papyri</note>, as we have deduced at length in the *Hieroglyphic Magic*.

<margin>Statues intending threats.</margin> Hence, statues 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, and 9, with joined hands and horrendous faces, transformed into both humans and animals, intend I know not what threats; for which reason they were called "terrors" <note>original: ἐμπληξίαι</note> by the Greeks, and by the Copts <term>mitolexia</term> <note>original: ⲙⲓⲧⲟⲗⲉⲝⲓⲁ</note> from their audacity. The first and ninth, terrible with a Leonine <note>lion-like</note> countenance, refer to the **Mophtaean** Spirits; the second and eighth, equipped with a Canine face, refer to the **Anubic**; the third and seventh, with monstrous heads and beards, to the **Isiac**; the fourth and sixth, to the **Nephtaean**; finally, the fifth indicates **Horus** as a boy with a monstrous head. The twelfth and 14th, as well as the 21st and 25th, signify the same **Mophtaean** Spirits as the first and ninth. The eleventh and 15th are the same as the 4th and 6th. The sixteenth, with a terrifying face carrying a huge stone on its shoulders, as well as 11, 23, and 19, intend threats against the opposing spirits, which **Demophilus** describes <margin>Threats intended against the opposing Gods. Demophilus</margin> in his book *On Sacrifice and the Exorcisms of Priests*: <note>The following is a translation of the Greek/Latin magical formula</note> *"Unless you yield, I shall wrap you in mountains, I shall bury you by casting down cliffs, I shall stop the Baris <note>the sacred Egyptian boat</note>, I shall break the bolts of Osiris,"* etc. For as **Psellus** says in his book *On Demons*, the malignant Demons are struck by no threats of words <margin>Psellus: Demons abominate threats.</margin> so much as those of imprisonment and extermination; not because they can be exterminated or shut in prisons, but because these things are contrary to the order prescribed for them by the author of nature, such as perpetual condemnation to a single place: for they are so terrified by threats of this kind, that...

[they themselves...]

And these are the charms proper to the Egyptians; and that they were portable is clearly shown by the small loops with which each one is seen to be equipped.

# CHAPTER IV.

-> **Concerning Prophylactic Scarabs.** <-

<margin>Prophylactic Scarabs</margin> I find no charms more frequent in the whole range of hieroglyphics than those marked with the figures of <term>Scarabs</term> <note>Dung beetles, which the Egyptians associated with the sun god Khepri and the idea of rebirth.</note>, so that their frequency itself teaches more than enough that they were held in great esteem among the Egyptians. There are those who have woven entire crowns from a multitude of them. These amulets are met with in every Museum, and are of various sizes: there are very small ones, medium ones, and very large ones. They also differ in antiquity, since some are the offspring of the Gnostics and others truly of the Egyptians, as the variety of hieroglyphics with which they are marked sufficiently teaches; we shall begin an exposition of these in this place, as far as our ingenuity permits. The first four are extracted from the <margin>Scarabs from the Reinstian Museum.</margin> **Reinstian Museum** <note>The collection of Gerrit van Rheinst, a 17th-century Dutch merchant and collector of antiquities.</note>, as follows. The one marked with the letter A is of the size which you see.

### CHAPTER VI.

->Concerning the parts of the human body adopted by the Egyptians for the use of <term>Amulets</term> <note>original: "Periaptorum" — objects worn for protection or luck.</note>.<-

<margin>Amulets which represent parts of the human body. The Phallus formed in various ways by the Egyptians.</margin> Among the other hieroglyphics with which the Obelisks teem, the <term>Phallus</term> is the most celebrated and frequent. The phallus is an image fashioned in the likeness of the human male organ. And among the phalluses, the "eyed phallus" holds the chief place, being encountered everywhere; concerning which, see what we have treated most extensively in the first Volume, in the <term>Pantheon of the Hebrews</term> regarding <term>Peor</term> <note>original: "Phegore" — the Moabite god Baal-Peor, often associated by early modern scholars with Priapus.</note> or <term>Priapus</term>, where we also handed down the origin of the entire superstition. Consult also the Indices of the three Volumes of this Work, where you will find it discussed in innumerable places. It was, moreover, adapted with a manifold variety of decorative forms: sometimes in a simple form, as can be seen in the illustration of the <term>Canopic jars</term> in figure VI; sometimes <term>eye-shaped</term> <note>original: "ὀφθαλμοειδὴς" (ophthalmoeides)</note>, that is, in an ocular figure, just as figure 13 in the preceding Nardian illustration shows; and in this manner it occurs in countless places among the hieroglyphic monuments of the Egyptians. There were those who fashioned it in the form of a winged Serpent, conspicuous with a triple feather on the tail, the head, and the natural place; a specimen of which was not long ago shared with me by that most distinguished and learned man, Lord <term>Francesco Serra</term>, a Roman Knight and a most ardent zealot for promoting the Republic of Letters; however, shame and modesty have inhibited me from including its image. Others inserted the same into a human arm. In this manner it is seen in <term>Lorenzo Pignoria's</term> exposition on the <term>Isiac Tablet</term> <note>original: "Mensa Isiaca" — a famous bronze tablet of Egyptian-style imagery that fascinated Renaissance scholars.</note>. A trace of this also appears in the third Nardian illustration or plate, where we have given the reasoning for the mysterious arrangement. Time would fail me if the ridiculous delusions and false insanities of the Ancients regarding the worship of such a shameful idol had to be described. Let it suffice for the Reader that these types of amulets were worn and employed for no other reason than to ward off <term>the evil eye</term> <note>original: "fascinum"</note> and to obtain fertility. But concerning these, as I have said, see the cited places, where you will find everything accurately described.

# TREATISE XX.
## On the Lamps of the ancient Egyptians.

### CHAPTER I.
#### *On the origin of Lamps.*

<margin>Fire as a symbol of the subterranean Osiris.</margin>
<margin>The worship of fire among the Ancient Egyptians.</margin>
We have elsewhere copiously taught that fire was a symbol of the subterranean Osiris—whom the Greeks call Pluto, and others Vulcan <note>Kircher identifies the Egyptian Osiris with the Greek god of the underworld and the Roman god of fire to show a universal "pagan" theology.</note>. For just as they placed an Osiris over each of the Worlds—the Archetype in the Intelligible world, the All-Formed in the Intellectual, and the Solar in the Sidereal—so, according to a certain analogy of fire, they placed a presiding deity of the material sun in the Material World. These were indeed so arranged among themselves that the supernal influence would terminate in the lowest world through those in between. And as nothing in the lower nature of things is more excellent or more necessary than the fiery color (being analogous to the Sun), so too they pursued it with the greatest zeal, strained forces, and wondrous worship and ceremonies, lest it should ever fail, or the Deity be found wanting in his duty of preservation.

<margin>The festival of Lamps among the Egyptians.</margin>
From this, that most celebrated festival and solemnity of Lamps found its origin, by which on certain days of the year all Egypt was illuminated by the glow of lamps; of which Herodotus makes ample mention in the second book, which he inscribed *Euterpe*.

<margin>Herodotus.</margin>
> When they have gathered at the city of Sais for the sacrifices, during the night they all kindle many lights in the open air around their houses in a circle. The lamps are small vessels filled with salt and oil, with a wick floating on the surface, and this burns all night long. The name given to the festival is the Burning of Lamps <note>original Greek: λυχνοκαΐη</note>. Those of the Egyptians who do not come to this assembly, observing the night of the sacrifice, also kindle lamps themselves, all of them; and thus they are burned not only in Sais, but throughout all Egypt. But as to why this night obtained such light and honor, a certain sacred story is told concerning it.

*That is: But when they have assembled at the City of Sais to sacrifice, they all kindle numerous lamps by night under the open sky around their houses, soaked with salt and full of oil, with a large wick which burns the whole night; to which festival the name "the lighting of lamps" <term>Lychnokaia: from the Greek lychnos (lamp) and kaiein (to burn)</term> is given. Whosoever of the Egyptians does not go to this assembly, observing the night of the sacrifice, they too all kindle lamps, and thus the lamps are lit not only in Sais, but through the whole of Egypt. Truly, for what grace this night was allotted such light and honor, a certain sacred reason is commemorated.*

<margin>Why the festival of Lamps was instituted.</margin>
Thus says Herodotus. But as to what the sacred reason was for which such a great festival was instituted, Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian from the 3rd century BCE.</note> (as cited in Syncellus) teaches that when Osiris was slain, Typhon <note>The Greek name for Set, the god of chaos and brother/murderer of Osiris.</note> covered all Egypt with darkness and thick gloom. Terrified by this portent, the Egyptian Priests consulted the Oracle, which responded that the gloom spread over the land would not cease unless they appeased Osiris, who had been slain by Typhon, with the frequent glow of lamps. When this was done, the darkness was soon dispersed, the longed-for light returned, and thus the festival of the lighting of lamps was instituted and celebrated with the greatest fervor thereafter. There are some, however, who wish that the origin of the lighting of lamps alone...

# CHAPTER I. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

...derived its origin from the ten plagues of Egypt, with which Moses struck Egypt by divine power, among which the "darkness that could be felt" <note>Exodus 10:21</note> was one. I do not disagree with this, especially since we have shown throughout this entire work that the Egyptians borrowed many things from the Hebrews and made them their own, even if they were corrupted by various fables and inventions, as is clear from what has been said. However, it seems more likely that the Priests of the Sacred Rites <term>Hieromantas: those who interpret sacred mysteries</term> <margin>Why fire was held in such high honor by the Egyptians.</margin> established this practice, wrapped in mystical reasons, primarily for Osiris, the ruler of the celestial lights and stars. For at all times and in every place, as we have taught throughout, Osiris was held in the highest veneration as a certain Solar Deity. Since nothing in the lower world is more similar to the Sun—which they called the "celestial fire"—than fire itself, they judged that he should be worshipped by no better means than the frequent use of lamps. <margin>Seneca. Suidas. Beroaldus. Plutarch.</margin> Indeed, to such an extent that the lamp, according to Seneca in *On the Happy Life* ch. 27 and Suidas, became a hieroglyphic of religion; Beroaldus explains this skillfully in his commentary on Chapter 11 of Apuleius's *The Golden Ass*. Furthermore, on the authority of Plutarch in *Table Talk* Book 7, Chapter 14, they considered it a matter of the highest religious scruple to extinguish a lamp by any violent means. Therefore, having supplied the oil, they would leave the lamp unextinguished until the fire had consumed all the oil, and the lamp would fail of its own accord as the nourishment ran out. When this was done, they would provide new nourishment, and they performed this out of reverence for the sacred fire, as Cosenus reports in Plutarch; or as Lucius says in the same place, lest they seem to bring death to an element that is in some way "animated"; or as Florus thought in that same passage, lest by extinguishing the lamp they should seem to grudge the light to others.

But indeed, <margin>Why the lighting of lamps was instituted.</margin> let us return to where we digressed. Regarding the feast or solemnity of the lighting of lamps, different authors hold different views. Some believe the Egyptians were accustomed to lighting lamps to search for Osiris with Isis. Just as this search by Isis is said to have happened with a great outpouring of tears, so too the Isiac mourning, lamentations, and wailing were never absent from a solemnity of this kind. Indeed, according to Plutarch, during the full moon under the open sky amidst the darkness, as if to accompany the Moon (that is, Isis), they sought Osiris with lit lamps and great mourning, promising themselves a great abundance of things from the vain observation of this cult. But let us hear Pausanias: <margin>Pausanias.</margin> "The Egyptians are accustomed to celebrate a feast for Isis when they say they are mourning Osiris." And in those days the rising of the Nile begins—an argument that the flooding of the river and the fields is procured only by the tears of Isis, according to that line of Statius <margin>Statius.</margin> in Book 1 of the *Thebaid*:

->- - - better for you that Mareotic<-
->Coptos smokes, and the mourning rivers of the parched Nile.<-
<note>original: "melius vobis mareotica fumat / Coptos, & erisoni lugentia flumina Nili."</note>

Whatever the case may be, that "never sufficiently sought Osiris," to speak with Lucan, indicated nothing other than the Sun. When they thought the Sun, as the author of life, had been snatched from them by the gloom of the "palpable darkness" sent by God, and the death of the firstborn of Egypt had followed that darkness, a great cry soon arose in Egypt, as the Sacred Text <note>The Bible</note> testifies; for there was no house in which there was not someone dead. # SYNTAGMA XX. ON THE LAMPS OF THE EGYPTIANS. CHAPTER II.

Through a memorable and unheard-of event, the solemnity of Lamps—instituted to appease Osiris—flourished among posterity throughout all of Egypt; for <margin>Apuleius.</margin> Apuleius, in the passage cited shortly before, clearly shows this with these words: *Furthermore, a great number of both sexes, with lamps, torches, and other kinds of light, were seeking the favor of the celestial stars with an offering of light.* <note>original: "stipem propitiantes" - referring to a ritual donation or offering to win favor.</note> Truly, he who desires more concerning the superstitious cult of Lamps should read Clement of Alexandria, Book 1 of the *Stromata*; Eusebius, Book 10 of *On the Preparation*; and Lactantius, Book 6 of the *Divine Institutes*. Regarding the cult of fire exhibited to any of the stars, based on a certain analogy of fiery splendor to the light of the celestial fires, see if you please Volume I, Syntagma 3, *On the Sacrifices and Rites of the Egyptians*. But before all else, one should consult that rare and most learned work, filled with every kind of erudition, which the most excellent <margin>Fortunio Liceto.</margin> Fortunio Liceto <note>A famous 17th-century physician and philosopher who wrote a massive treatise on ancient lamps.</note> recently published for the great benefit of the Republic of Letters, *On the Lamps of the Ancients* <note>original: "De Lucernis Veterum"</note>; lest we put our sickle into his most fertile harvest, we shall pursue in this Syntagma only those things which properly pertain to the argument of our undertaking—that is, Egyptian Lamps either omitted there or only superficially explained.

# CHAPTER II.

->*Concerning the place, shape, and other properties of Egyptian lamp-stands and lamps in general.*<-

<margin>Places in which Lamps were placed among the Egyptians.</margin> The places in which Lamps were accustomed to be placed were Shrines, Inner Sanctums <term>Adyta: the most sacred, restricted inner areas of a temple</term>, and Crypts or subterranean cemeteries, about each of which we shall speak in order. In the Shrines, they were accustomed to place a Lamp according to the quality of the Deity to whom they were sacrificing. Thus, in the Temple of Anubis, they placed a Lamp conspicuous either for a Dog’s head <margin>Various shapes of Lamps among the Egyptians.</margin> or for the complete figure of a Dog, as we shall show later. In the Shrine of Osiris, it was usually visible with a Hawk’s face, or even in the habit of the entire bird. In the Temple of Isis, they fashioned Isis herself, venerable with a Lunar semicircle and flames rising from her crown. In the Temple of Canopus, they sketched the likeness of the Canopic Deity, "pot-bellied" <note>original: "ventripotentis" - referring to the jar-like shape of the deity Canopus.</note> and protruding like a jar. Not otherwise in the other Temples of the Gods, they adorned the Lamps with that decoration by which they fashioned the very idols of the Deities usually worshiped in them. That all these things are true is testified by the Lamps surviving to this day, brought out of Egypt, which we shall introduce later. The Greeks and Romans—who at all times were like certain apes of the Egyptian religion (or more truly, superstition)—imitated this custom, as is evident from the inscriptions of the Lamps brought forward by the famous Fortunio Liceto, which clearly teach that they were consecrated now to Jupiter, now to Diana, or Minerva, and the other Deities.

In the more secret Inner Sanctums of the priestly assemblies, I find that besides <margin>What kinds of fires were in the Egyptian inner sanctums.</margin> Lamps, they also employed fires prepared with marvelous industry; for they did not designate fires from just any material for nourishment, but from that appropriated to the Gods and sacrifices. Thus, the fire of Haro <note>Likely referring to Horus/Haroeris.</note> was from the wood of the persea tree, that of Osiris from the laurel,

# CHAPTER II 534 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

<margin>
Lamps in Crypts and Sepulchers.
</margin>
Some used lamps made of rushes, others of different types of wood; this is clearly evident from the smoke and soot which, according to the testimony of Burattini <note>Tito Livio Burattini (1617–1681), an Italian scholar and traveler who explored Egypt.</note>, still clings to the vaults of such sanctuaries to this day. Finally, in the crypts designated for the deposition of the dead, lamps adorned with a diverse array of hieroglyphic apparatus are found in great quantities to this day, as witnessed by Valle <note>Pietro della Valle (1586–1652), a famous Italian traveler who brought back mummies and manuscripts from the East.</note> and Burattini; this is an open sign that there was a specific place in those locations appointed for the placement of lamps, which it now seems appropriate to discuss at somewhat greater length.

<margin>
The Egyptians worshiped the celestial Gods with fires.
</margin>
It has been stated elsewhere that just as the Egyptians worshiped the earthly Gods with flowers and fruits, so they worshiped the celestial Gods with fires. For fire was the symbol of the divine nature—immortal, incorruptible, and indivisible; and for that reason, they most frequently placed it upon the heads of the Gods, as the images of the **Isiac Table** <note>A famous bronze tablet (Mensa Isiaca) depicting Egyptian deities and rites, much studied in the Renaissance.</note> show, mystically indicating the fiery power and efficacy within the divine Mind. From this they constructed pyramids, likewise a symbol of fire <note>The author derives "pyramid" from the Greek *pyr* (fire), suggesting their shape mimics a flame.</note>, of such solidity that they could easily overcome all the injuries of time, and demonstrate the immortality of minds by their very shape. But since we have discussed these matters copiously in our *Hieroglyphic Geometry*, we refer the reader there.

Indeed, this custom of worshiping fire gained such admiration in the hearts of foreign nations that there was no nation which, having been taught this **fire-worship** <note>original: <term>πυρελατρείαν</term> (pyrelatreia)</note> by the Egyptians, did not receive and propagate it in every way. For what else are the sacrifices of Mithras than the worship of that celestial fire—I mean the Sun—which took on its greatest increase especially among the Persians? For as George the Monk <note>A 9th-century Byzantine chronicler.</note> rightly says of Perseus: *He taught them the foul rites of the mysteries, and the magic called that of Medea; because of which fire also came down from heaven in Persia, from which he lit another fire, and building a temple, he placed it within, calling it the temple of the immortal fire; and appointing prudent men to serve and guard the fire, he commanded them to be called Magi, whom the Persians, holding in great honor until now, practice fire-worship.* <note>original Greek: Ἐδίδαξε δὲ αὐτοὺς καὶ τὰ μυσαρὰ τελετῶν... πυρελατρεύουσι.</note>

<margin>
Cedrenus.
</margin>
But that fire was worshiped long before Perseus, and introduced by Zoroaster, Cedrenus <note>Georgius Cedrenus, an 11th-century Byzantine historian.</note> notes in these words: *From the lineage of Belus came also Zoroaster, the renowned astronomer among the Persians, who prayed to be struck by lightning from the aerial fire and consumed, charging the Persians to gather his bones after the burning, and to keep and honor them.* <note>original Greek: Ἐκ τοῦ γένους τοῦ Βήλου... καὶ τιμᾷν.</note> He traced his origin from Belus himself, and was a most famous astronomer among the Persians; since he knew and desired to be touched by fire from heaven, he instructed the Persians to collect, preserve, and worship his bones after his cremation. That this Zoroaster—the son of Misraim <note>In biblical genealogy, Misraim is the progenitor of the Egyptians.</note> from the line of Ham or Belus—was none other than Mithras (who it is established was also called Osiris), we have deduced at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. For he was the first who taught the worship of fire to the Egyptians and Chaldeans; so that whatever we have said there concerning Osiris, Mithras, and Zoroaster exactly agrees with what we hand down here. For just as the Egyptians did in their sanctuaries, so the Persians in their caves taught the worship of fire with a great apparatus of ceremonies, in these words, as...

<margin>
Zoroaster taught the Persians the worship of fire.
</margin>

### SYNTAGMA XX. ON THE LAMPS OF THE EGYPTIANS. 535 CHAPTER II.

As Firmicus Maternus <margin>Firmicus Maternus.</margin> testifies in Book 5, <gloss>they introduced the initiates of fire by means of a stolen composition</gloss>, <note>original: "Μυστάς πυρὸς ἀπὸ κλοπῆς συνθέτην παρεισήγαγον"</note> and they were so maddened by the insanity of this <term>fire-worship</term> <note>Greek: πυρολατρεία (pyrolatreia)</note> that they pursued with sacred cult not only fire itself, but everything that bore the appearance of fire, as Dionysius testifies in *On the Situation of the World*: <gloss>everything fire-bright is divine</gloss>; <note>original: "πᾶσα πυριφλεγὲς ἔνθεον"</note> hence they also held the <term>pyropo</term> <note>A "fire-faced" gemstone, likely a carbuncle or garnet.</note> <margin>Dionysius the Geographer. Strabo.</margin> in honor as if it were emitting flames, according to Strabo in Book 15, which they would no more bring near a corpse than fire itself. From this, that superstition also seems to have been born, that nothing was denied to those who had carried fire into a river; and unless they were stopped in person, they would threaten to drown the fire in the water, as Plutarch asserts. Fire was primarily worshiped among the first things in Persia, not only by the common people, but especially by the Kings in houses <margin>Theodoret.</margin> sacredly prepared for that purpose, according to Theodoret in Book 1 of his *Ecclesiastical History*; hence those houses were called <gloss>fire-temples</gloss>, <note>Greek: πυρεῖα (pyreia)</note> and the fire indeed was called <gloss>unquenchable fire</gloss>. <note>Greek: πῦρ ἄσβεστον (pyr asbeston)</note> In the Pyreum <note>A fire-altar or temple.</note> they preserved the fire for divinations, holding it in the same place as the Romans held Vesta, says Procopius in Book 2 and Strabo in Book 15. <gloss>Indeed, the one performing the sacrifices prayed before the fire starting from them.</gloss> <note>original: "Ὁ μὲν δὴ τὰς θυσίας ποιῶν ἀπ᾽ αὐτῶν πρὸ τῷ πυρὶ εὔχετο"</note> To whichever God they might sacrifice, they first addressed their vows to the fire, <margin>Procopius. Strabo.</margin> <gloss>allotting honors to all, and so that they cover the lips of each in the middle with a veil, so that he sacrifices as if in silence, hanging down tiaras of thick wool from both sides</gloss>, <note>Kircher notes that the Greek text here includes a transliterated Latin phrase: "ex lana densa utrinque demissis" (from thick wool let down on both sides).</note> so that they cover the lips and cheeks, <gloss>and sacrificing to the fire they call upon it, saying much to the fire while sacrificing and praying.</gloss> Those about to sacrifice to the fire and offering it fuel would say, <term>Lord Fire, eat</term>. All of these things, propagated from the Egyptians to the Persians, and from there to the Greeks and Romans, always received the greatest increase.

->But to return to our proposed narrative concerning the Lamps of the Ancients,<-

It must be noted that lamps were of entirely various shapes, whether you <margin>The Lamps of the Ancients were of various shapes.</margin> look at the wicks or the shape of the lamps themselves. # CHAPTER II. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

We have already taught extensively in the Treatise on Mummies that these were not placed there until before the founding of Rome. I call the wick <note>original: "ellychnium"</note> a lamp-wick, a flaxen or papyrus tow <note>coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp</note> usually placed in oil as a kind of fuel for the fire, <margin>Prudentius</margin> which Prudentius describes quite skillfully in his hymns:

> The lively flame thrives, whether a hollow tube
> Supplies the juice to the drunken little linen cloth,
> Or the pine tree bears its pitchy nourishment,
> Or the warm tow drinks the smooth wax.

The Egyptians, therefore, used not only lamps equipped with wicks made of tow, papyrus, or rushes, but also wax tapers, torches, or links made of bark, which <margin>Naphtha</margin> Athenaeus calls "Naphtha" (Alexis calls it a "wooden lamp-holder" <note>original Greek: ξυλολυχνοῦς</note>; to Cicero it is a "little wooden lamp-stand" or a "spit-lamp," when wood burns on a small spike in place of a lamp); they also used rush-stalks, which Aristophanes calls "lamp-wicks" <note>original Greek: λύχνου θρυαλλίδας</note> in *The Wasps*; and lotus-stalks coated in wax and resin—to say nothing for now of the various piles of wood in the Inner Sanctuaries. <margin>Aristophanes. Herodotus. Virgil.</margin> Aristophanes calls the lighting itself "lamp-lighting" <note>original Greek: λυχνυκαΐα</note> or "lamp-viewing" <note>original Greek: λυχνωψία</note>, and "light-bringers" <note>original Greek: φωσφόρους</note>; Herodian in Book 4 calls them "all-night vigils." But even in all these things, a great difference intervened. Some lamps were hanging, others were stationary; regarding the former, Virgil says in Book 1 of the *Aeneid*:

> Burning lamps hang from the golden paneled ceilings,
> And the waxen torches conquer the night.

->**Paulinus of Nola, Nativity 9.**<-

> And from the roof above,
> The hanging lamps are held by bronze coils,
> And in the empty space the wandering lights sway on loose
> Ropes; a light breeze tires the waving flames.

**Regarding these same things, Paulinus says in Nativity 3:**

> The bright altars are crowned with crowded lamps.
> Scented lights are burned with waxed papyrus,
> They shimmer by night and day.

From these citations, unless I am mistaken, the system of Egyptian lamps is clearly evident; wherefore let us now approach a little more closely to a detailed description of the same.

## CHAPTER III.

-> **Concerning Egyptian Lamps in particular.** <-

### § I.

<margin>Lamps placed by King Mycerinus for his daughter.</margin>
**H**erodotus describes at length how King Mycerinus <note>The Greek name for the Pharaoh Menkaure, builder of the third pyramid at Giza.</note> placed skillfully crafted lamps both for himself and for his daughter before a Cow, inside of which he had enclosed his daughter's corpse; but since the history is worthy of being understood from the Author himself, I shall set down his words here:

<margin>Herodotus.</margin>
> They said that after this Chephren, Mycerinus, the son of Cheops, reigned in Egypt. He, loathing his father's deeds, reopened the temples and gave the people—who had been afflicted to the ultimate point of misery—the power to attend to their own affairs and to perform sacrifices. Indeed, he exercised justice above all other Kings. For this reason, the Egyptians praised him most of all the Kings, both for other matters which he judged well, and truly because if anyone complained about his decision, he would give to them from his own property to satisfy the man's indignation. But while Mycerinus was so merciful and so devoted toward the citizens, the beginning of his misfortunes happened to be the death of his daughter, who was his only offspring at home. While he grieved beyond measure at this disaster, and wished for his daughter to be buried in some more excellent manner than others, he had a hollow wooden Cow made; and when he had gilded it with gold, he buried his deceased daughter within it. This Cow was not hidden in the ground, but even to my own memory it was in plain sight in the city of Sais <note>An ancient Egyptian city in the Western Nile Delta.</note> at the royal palace, placed in a certain decorated chamber, into which all kinds of incense are brought every day: and by night, a burning Lamp stands perpetually beside it. In another adjoining chamber stand the images of the Concubines of Mycerinus, as the Priests in the city of Sais used to say. For there stand Colossi—that is, great statues—about twenty in number, fashioned from wood, most of them naked: as to which women they represent, I cannot say, except for what is told. There are those who relate these things concerning this Cow and the Colossi: that Mycerinus, seized by love for his daughter, offered violence to her; then, when she had hanged herself out of grief, the father buried her in this Cow; and the mother cut off the hands of the maidservants who had betrayed the daughter to the father: and now these are the statues of them, representing the evil they suffered while alive. These things (as I think) are told by triflers, as are other things, including the story about the hands of the Colossi: for we ourselves saw that they had fallen off through the length of time, and they were seen lying at their feet even until my age. The Cow also, while the rest of the body is covered with a purple cloak, has its neck and head covered with very thick gold: between its horns is attached a circle, made to resemble the Sun. The Cow is not standing, but kneeling on its knees, in size as large as a great living Cow. It is carried out of the chamber every year; and after the Egyptians have beaten a certain God <note>Likely a reference to Osiris, whose mysteries involved ritual mourning.</note>, whom I do not think I should name in such a matter, then they also bring the Cow out into the light. For they say that she begged her father Mycerinus that, once dead, she might look upon the Sun once a year. To this King, after the disaster of his daughter, this second thing happened: an Oracle came from the city of Buto, stating that he would live only six years in total, and would die in the seventh. He, taking this poorly, sent back to the Oracle insulting complaints: that, whereas his father and uncle, who were unmindful of the Gods and closed the temples—

# § II.

### Concerning the Lamps of the Egyptians transformed into sacred animals.

<margin>Lamps sent by the Duke of Tuscany.</margin>
Out of his affection for the Republic of Letters, the most wise Prince, the Grand Duke of Tuscany <note>A member of the Medici family, likely Ferdinando II de' Medici, who supported Kircher's research.</note>, has long since sent from his museums—which are most richly furnished with every kind of antiquity—several lamps of the ancient Egyptians, which I have thought appropriate to introduce in this place.

<note>Hieroglyphic illustration: A bronze or terracotta lamp fashioned in the shape of a reclining bull (Apis). On its back sits a small human figure (a boy or genius) leaning against a large leaf, identified in the text as a fig leaf. This symbolic object represents the vital heat and vegetative life protected by the bull-god Apis.</note>

<margin>A lamp in the shape of a Bull in the Temple of Apis.</margin>
The first of these represents the figure of a reclining Bull, with a boy leaning on its back, and fig leaves, as the present figure shows. We have taught throughout this work that the Bull expressed the figure of Apis, and that Apis was the <term>Genius</term> <note>A guardian spirit or presiding deity of a place or concept.</note> presiding over agriculture. Therefore, in the Temple of Apis, they would place a lamp adorned in honor of this Divinity; and indeed, by the lamp they signified a pious and religious affection toward the Divinity, while by the fire they denoted the "vital heat." They believed that if this heat were absent from agriculture, all things would fall into ultimate destruction. Thus, they silently petitioned the Divinity through this symbol to grant this heat of life to the fields and plains. The lamps were lit in honor of the deities who were customarily carried about in the <term>Comasiae<note>Processions of the gods, from the Greek 'komasia'.</note></term>; and they indicated the propitiation of those gods who presided over the four seasons of the year. For as we have said above, the Egyptians equipped their lamps with as many wicks as the number of units consecrated to a particular Deity contained.

### § IV.
-> **Concerning the Canubic or Canine Lamp, or the <term>Dog-faced lamp<note>original: "Κυνοπρόσωπος" (Kynoprosopos)</note></term>.** <-

<margin>The Canubic Lamp.</margin> **N**othing was more frequent among the Egyptians than to fashion their lamps in the shape of a Dog: for Anubis was chief among their tutelary <note>guardian</note> gods. Of this sort of lamp, the Most Serene Duke of Tuscany sent one, along with others, expressed in the complete figure of a reclining Dog. Other lamps are also found featuring a Dog’s head in place of the wick-holder; all of these indeed allude to the vigilance of the guardian Deity, by which he was thought to guard the bodies deposited in the subterranean crypts. Hence, for this same reason, the figure of a Dog is seen impressed upon almost all the wrappings of mummies. But since all these things have been most amply explained in the treatise on Mummies, we shall not linger here. While I treat of these matters, there occurs to me a diagram drawn from a gemstone in the excellent work of Fortunio Liceti *On the Lamps of the Ancients*, page 1178, in which, if anywhere, the genius of the Egyptians truly shines forth most greatly. Three figures are seen in it, the first of which is naked, <margin>An Egyptian lamp in Liceti.</margin> <term>three-legged and three-headed<note>original: "τρίποδος, καὶ τρικέφαλος" (tripodos, kai trikephalos)</note></term>, that is, of three thighs with three heads, each of which is attached to a single trunk of a body and marked with a Lotus flower; it carries lamps in both hands, with ribbons fluttering here and there, and it denotes Hermes Trismegistus. The second, half-naked and covered with a small cloak, carries a <term>modius<note>A grain-measure used as a crown, symbolizing fertility.</note></term> on its head, in whose right hand is a reed, or as Liceti thinks, a lily-topped <term>thyrsus<note>A ritual staff.</note></term>, with a Dog standing by and fawning upon him; and this signifies Serapis; see the similar figure presented by us in the first Volume, page 198. The third exhibits Isis, visible with a <term>sistrum<note>A sacred rattle.</note></term>, a pipe, and a Lotus flower on her head; concerning her, see the similar dress explained in Volume I, page 189. But since the most learned Liceti has illustrated each detail with a beautiful exposition most suited to the mind of the Egyptians in the book and page cited, I would deservedly waste my effort if I attempted to unroll the secret meaning of the same with further interpretation.

## § VI.
->Of Phallic Lamps.<-

<margin>Phallic lamps.</margin>
**W**ith how much honor the Egyptians at all times pursued the shameful cult of the phallus has been shown in innumerable places in this Work. For they not only carried this in the first place of the procession during the <term>Phallophoria</term> <note>A festival where phallic symbols were carried</note> or <term>Pammylia</term> <note>A festival dedicated to the birth of Osiris</note> festivals dedicated to Osiris, but men and women of both sexes were also accustomed to wear it tied to the neck, thigh, or arms as a protection against the evil eye and the reproach of sterility. Furthermore, we see it attached everywhere to sacred animals and the images of the Gods; what wonder is it, then, if they impressed this upon lamps as well? For as we have often said, lamps were shaped according to the nature of the Deity to whom they were sacrificing: for Anubis they established a <term>Cynomorphic</term> <note>Dog-shaped; original: "Cynomorpham"</note> lamp; for the Solar Osiris, one transformed with a Hawk-like face; and so for the Nilotic Osiris, the deity of fertility, they established a <term>phallomorphic</term> <note>original Greek: "φαλλόμορφον", meaning shaped like a phallus</note> lamp. Let the same judgment hold for the other Deities, namely, that the lamp be congruent to the effects and operations of each one. Licetus <note>Fortunio Liceti, a 17th-century scholar of ancient lamps</note> explained several of these on page 910 and page 1142.

---

## § VII.
->Of the Typhonian Lamp.<-

<margin>Typhonian lamps.</margin>
**T**he Egyptians established lamps not only for the beneficent Gods, but also for the malevolent ones—for the former so that they might be helpful, and for the latter so that they might not be harmful. One of this kind, formerly brought from Egypt, was sent from the Medici Museum by the renowned Nardius; it is a ridiculous lamp with an Ass’s head, which Silenus holds, as follows. We have taught everywhere that the Ass was the symbol of Typhon <note>The Egyptian god Set, associated with chaos and storms</note>; and Plutarch reports that Typhon had a voice very closely resembling the braying of an Ass, which is why they could not endure the clangor of a trumpet, as it was similar to the braying and the voice of Typhon. Indeed, they say that in the Month of Payni, asses paid the penalty for the sake of the accursed Typhon, whom they say the Ass resembled both in its sluggishness and stupidity, as well as in its color. "And when making cakes," these are the words of Plutarch, "they stamp them with the figure of a bound ass" <note>original Greek: "Καὶ τὰ πόπανα ποιοῦντες ἐπιπλάττουσι δέσμιον ὄνον"</note>. Let us explain why they decorated a lamp with this symbol of the Typhonian Ass.

<margin>Why lamps were decorated with the figure of an Ass.</margin>
It is established from what has been said everywhere that Typhon was considered by the Egyptians to be every evil thing that brought about sterility, contagion, scorching heat, and a certain force for cor—

## § VIII.

### ->Concerning the multi-wicked lamps which are found everywhere in the subterranean crypts of Egypt.<-

<margin>Lamps found in the Crypts of Egypt.</margin> **L**amps constructed with multiple rows of wicks are frequently found in the cemeteries of Egypt; concerning which an eyewitness, **Tito Livio Burattini** <note>An Italian inventor and traveler (1617–1681) who explored Egypt</note>, whom I have cited very often in the preceding pages, writes to me in a letter as follows: *“In these caves there are also found a great quantity of baked clay vessels, made in the manner of lamps, but some capable of holding four, and others six, eight, and twelve wicks; which the Arabs say were perpetual lights, but I believe they were ordinary lights, since all the caves have soot on their ceilings. The Arabs claim, however, to often find these perpetual lights when new tombs are opened; but having never seen one myself, I cannot affirm anything.”* These things certainly prove what we said above regarding the multi-wicked lamps of the Egyptians, and **Michaël Schatta** <note>A scholar and correspondent of Kircher</note>, mentioned above, clearly teaches in his Arabic letters sent to me, with these words:

->And you know, O our Father, that I found in the caves of ancient Memphis many lamps,<-
->and among them were three, and others four and eight fire-lamps, and their form was in the likeness of the dog and the human<-
->and the bull and the hawk and the serpent and others like them, as you see in the image I sent to you. ❂<-

> *“Know also, Father, that in the subterranean crypts of ancient Memphis many lamps were found, some of which had three, others four, eight, or twelve wicks, shaped into the likeness of a Dog, a Man, a Bull, a Hawk, and a Serpent, and other things similar to these, as you see from the figure I sent to you.” And that lamp, which due to the shortness of time could not be engraved here, is a <term>dodekalychnos</term> <note>original Greek: δωδεκάλυχνος; a lamp with twelve wicks</note>, undoubtedly consecrated to the honor of the twelve Principal Deities of Egypt.* No small difficulty occurs to us in this place concerning the lamps which Burattini says, according to the mind of the Arabs, shine with perpetual light in the subterranean crypts; which, in order to be resolved, thus—
