# SECTION IX.

->*Whether the Egyptians truly placed lamps burning with a perpetual light in their underground crypts; and what their craftsmanship consisted of.*<-

<margin>Lamps thought to be perpetual</margin>
Although Licetus <note>Fortunio Liceti (1577–1657), an Italian physician and philosopher who wrote extensively on "ever-burning" lamps.</note> treats this matter extensively and learnedly in his work *On Lamps*, we have decided to set forth our own opinion on the subject here, lest we seem to have overlooked an argument of such illustrious merit. Many people up to this point—based on certain lamps they found in underground crypts by the evidence of some appearing light—have firmly persuaded themselves that the Ancients mastered this great secret of perpetual light. They demonstrate this through various examples, two of which they bring forward as having been discovered within the memory of our ancestors. <margin>Two examples of the said lamps.</margin> The first is the Lamp of Pallas, which was found during the time of Emperor Henry III in the year 1401 by a certain farmer not far from the City [Rome] near the Tiber, together with the prodigious and giant-sized body of Pallas. It had been burning with a perpetual fire for more than two thousand years, and could not be extinguished by a gust of wind, nor by the pouring on of water or any other liquid. However, as soon as it was punctured at the bottom and broken by meddlesome <term>haters</term> <note>original: "osoribus" – those who despise or are hostile to such wonders</note> of that marvelous light, the liquid poured out and the flame immediately vanished. Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei (1451–1522), a humanist scholar known as Volaterranus.</note> reports that this was the body of Pallas the Arcadian, son of Evander, who was once killed by Turnus, <margin>Volaterranus</margin> bearing this inscription:

->*Pallas, son of Evander, whom the spear of the soldier*<-
->*Turnus slew, lies here in his great mass.*<-

---

The second lamp is said to have been found on the Appian Way during the time of Pope Paul III, in the tomb of Tulliola, the daughter of Cicero, as the inscription on the tomb shows:

->**TO MY DAUGHTER TULLIOLA.**<-

This lamp, I say, having been found, is said to have been kindled with a perpetual fire for nearly one thousand seven hundred years, and it lasted until the memory of our fathers; but upon the entry of the incoming air, the flame had scarcely appeared before it vanished. Thus Guido Panciroli <note>An Italian jurist and historian (1523–1599) who wrote about "lost" ancient inventions.</note> relates in his book *On Memorable Things Lost*, and Licetus examines the whole business more extensively. <margin>Panciroli.</margin>

Certainly, we are approaching a slippery argument regarding perpetual light, and one scarcely explained sufficiently by anyone. If you deny it, you will find that the authorities cited here are of such great weight that to not grant them credit would be the same as rejecting the sincerity of such great authors with a silent dissent. Therefore, we shall explain what should be thought of this business, and what method the Egyptians used in maintaining lamps with perpetual light, after we have first posited a few things to more clearly demonstrate the argument we have undertaken.

# CHAPTER III. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>Perpetual lamps so-called, constructed in various ways. Namely, first, miraculously.</margin> I suppose, therefore, first of all, that among the lamps of the Ancients—which authors report to have shone with a perpetual light, and of which Fortunius Licetus <note>A 17th-century physician and philosopher who wrote a famous treatise on ancient lamps</note>, a truly most fortunate writer, brings forth a huge number extracted from all antiquity—they were constructed by various means and methods. There were those which are asserted to have shone perpetually by a preternatural and miraculous light, such as was the Lamp of Antioch, which is said to have preserved its light in an open and public 
<margin>Cedrenus.</margin> place above the gate of the Church for five hundred years, as the author Cedrenus <note>An 11th-century Byzantine historian</note> records in the work of François Citesius, a physician of Poitiers, titled *Consolatory Abstinence*. Truly, for Him who animates the stars with perpetual light, it is likewise not at all difficult to preserve the material fire of lamps by His almighty right hand, not merely for five hundred years, but for perpetual eternities; so that, accordingly, our discourse is not at all concerning lamps of this kind.

<margin>Secondly, by the fraud of a Demon.</margin> I suppose, secondly, that not a few of those lamps which were found burning with a perpetual light were represented through the works of Demons, in order to kindle in the minds of idle men either curiosity, or avarice, or the worship of false Gods, through a thousand frauds of which the Devil is the 
<margin>St. Augustine.</margin> craftsman. So says St. Augustine in Book 21, chapters 5 and 6 of *The City of God*. For whoever reads how many prodigies and false doctrines occurred in the consultation of the ancient Oracles by the help of Demons, will openly confess that this power of preserving lamps shining with a deceptive perpetual fire has by no means been denied to them. For it is characteristic of <term>Cacodemons</term> <note>Evil spirits or demons</note> to first draw men by the object of prodigious things, as if by some lure, and having drawn them, to pave the way to superstition and the false worship of Gods, and thus finally to bring them under their own law. Thus, for men exploring the sepulchers of the Gods, nothing was easier than to be drawn—by the appearance of those things which savored of something divine, such as lamps hidden from time immemorial with a living flame—first into admiration, and then even into the cult and veneration of that Deity by whose favor the lamp had been established with perpetual fire. Therefore, at the first entrance of some crypt, a Demon could present to the eyes of men a flame, or some other appearance of a shining thing, which, while they deemed it something higher than the forces of nature, they would ascribe solely to the power of that <term>Deaster</term> <note>A petty or false god</note> to whom the lamp had been consecrated; which indeed is the first step toward idolatry. And 
<margin>Deceptive perpetual lamps, established by a Demon.</margin> such, I think, were all those lamps which authors report were placed in the sepulchers of the Heathens for the worship of some certain Deity, and then found by chance burning with perpetual fire; not because they burned with perpetual fire, but because the Demon, at the first entry, as has been said, offered such an appearance, which would be to them like a stumbling block toward the impious worship of the Gods. He is accustomed to perform the same thing in Chemical operations, with the intention that he might bind incautious men to himself as perpetual slaves of avarice and <term>chrysolatreia</term> <note>original: "χρυσολατρείας" — the worship of gold or obsession with making gold through alchemy</note>, whose characteristic it is, while they are unable to reach the hidden Sacrament of the art by vain effort, to "stir Acheron" <note>A classical idiom meaning to stir up the underworld or seek help from hell</note>, to provoke Demons who might teach the secret of the art, and finally to devote themselves to the same with the eternal destruction of their souls. These things having been supposed, it must now be discussed—

# TREATISE XX. ON THE LAMPS OF THE EGYPTIANS. CHAPTER III.

It remains for us to investigate whether such a wondrous mechanism of perpetual light can be constructed by some natural power.

<margin>Whether a lamp of perpetual light can be naturally constructed. Argument for the negative opinion.</margin> I find a great controversy among authors regarding this subject. There are those who openly deny that it can be done naturally, and they argue as follows: Everything that is eventually consumed by being resolved into the vapor of smoke cannot be perennial; but any fatty fuel of fire, while it is ignited, is soon resolved into vapor and consumed; therefore, the fuel of fire cannot be perennial.

<margin>Argument for the affirmative opinion.</margin> On the other hand, the followers of the opposite opinion deny the minor premise in this case, and they say that there are given in the nature of things certain specific substances which resist fire equally and are never entirely overcome by it. They press their argument with empirical evidence of Asbestos, Amiantus <note>A type of flexible, fibrous mineral often confused with asbestos in antiquity</note>, and some sort of "potable gold"; they claim that by such means the previously cited lamps were radiant with perpetual light. But it is a wonder that among so many and such curious searchers of things, these types of Asbestine wicks, with which the said lamps were supposedly equipped, have never been found. I myself confess that if any thing in the nature of things could provide a <term>device</term> <note>original Greek: τέχνασμα (technasma)</note> for perpetual light, Asbestos and Amiantus ought to provide it; for just as a wick made of their fibers is incombustible, so no one who has deeply inspected the nature of both can deny that an oil extracted from them would be irresolvable. <margin>An incombustible wick can be provided.</margin> Indeed, a wick made from Amiantus (which I have now seen burning in my own lamp for two years, and I find it has not failed in the slightest, nor do I think it will cease) clearly proves the signs of being <term>unquenchable</term> <note>original Greek: ἀσβέστας (asbestas)</note>. The difficulty lies only in the irresolvable oil; if someone were to extract it for me from Asbestos, there is no doubt that he would provide me with the fuel for a perpetual fire. But who is this man? We shall praise him! <margin>An incombustible oil cannot be provided.</margin> Certainly, I have long since dealt with the greatest masters of the chemical art and distinguished distillers regarding the undertaking of this business; nor were there lacking those who "moved every stone" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to try every possible means</note> to extract it. But it was in vain; for the oil extracted from it either did not catch fire, being more similar to an aqueous substance than an oily one, or it turned out so dreggy that it was utterly unfit and unsuitable for catching fire. <margin>A perpetual lamp cannot be provided.</margin> Thus, having despaired of the business, I have come to the opinion that the mystery of extracting this kind of oil is, if not <term>impossible</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατον (adynaton)</note>, at least more difficult than the industry of human labor can reach. Therefore, just as the <term>squaring of the circle</term> <note>original Greek: τετραγωνισμός (tetragonismos)</note>, perpetual motion, the Philosopher's Stone, and similar subjects of hitherto inaccessible matter, so also the artifice of perpetual fire must be considered among the hopeless causes.

<margin>Objection.</margin> But you will say: that which once was and has been done, can also be and be done now; and the irreproachable authorities cited above clearly show that the method of preparing such lamps was known to the ancients; therefore, it is not <term>impossible</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατον (adynaton)</note> for it to be investigated by sagacious minds in modern times. <margin>Response. Sudden flames occasionally burst forth from opened crypts.</margin> I respond that it can be proved by no reasoning that the lamps cited above were equipped with perpetual light, since that sudden light could have presented itself to the eyes of the workers in various ways, either from the deceptions of Demons, or even from a natural cause. For when air, through a long period of time, is shut up—

# CHAPTER III. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

...trapped [within a tomb], and having become saturated with the fattiness of exhaling bodies, nothing could be easier than for it to be ignited—perhaps even at the first approach of entering fresh air—through <term>antiperistasin</term> <note>A philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite, such as heat being compressed and ignited by sudden cold air.</note>. Daily experience in cemeteries teaches us this, where flames of this sort are frequently seen. Indeed, mine workers, with whom I have often discussed this matter on purpose, have admitted that they almost never open new caverns without such flames bursting forth. It must be added that when such prodigious lights are first discovered, a powerful imagination is capable of imagining anything other than what actually was. In this way, what the aforementioned diggers thought was the effect of a **perpetual lamp**, I assert was a sudden effect of meteorological pressure. They think they have seen smoke, but it was nothing other than the breath of their own mouths, which they are accustomed to spreading out quite thickly in the denser air. But since we shall discuss this matter in an entire book and by profession in the **Subterranean World** <note>Kircher refers to his famous work *Mundus Subterraneus*, published later in 1665.</note>, God willing, I will not dwell on it longer here. Therefore, something remains to be said regarding the perpetual light used by the Egyptians and how they prepared it.

<margin>How the Egyptians constructed lamps shining with perpetual light.</margin>
It is established—both from the authority of Burrattini <note>Tito Livio Burattini, an Italian Egyptologist and inventor who provided Kircher with many reports.</note> and from Arabic writers, as will be seen later—that the Egyptian priests possessed lamps shining with perpetual light hidden in their inner sanctuaries and sepulchral crypts. These were not, however, fashioned from asbestos, but were adorned by another truly supreme effort of ingenuity. But so that everyone may see what method they maintained in the adaptation of said lamps, I shall attempt to demonstrate the matter from the very beginning.

Just as the ancient Sages were equipped with the highest sharpness of wit and no less skill in natural matters, so too they undertook nothing unless it was deep, arduous, unusual, and close to divine works. Among other contrivances, since they recognized the state of souls to be beyond all limits of death and immune from all contagion, they established certain lamps for the bodies of the deceased. They attempted to animate these with perpetual fire so that, as much as possible, they might correspond to the nature of souls. But since nothing could be found in the nature of things that could provide this effect, they thought it could be accomplished by the perennial operations of nature and her helping hand, in the manner that follows.

<margin>Bituminous places of Egypt.</margin>
There are many places in Egypt filled with an inexhaustible multitude of bitumen and petroleum, as all explorers of Egyptian affairs—Belon, Radziwiłł, della Valle, and Burrattini—testify, established there by the hidden counsel of nature. Therefore, the Egyptians, penetrating the secret workings of nature, diverted hidden channels from such wells into the very subterranean crypts destined for the tombs of bodies. There they would fit a lamp which, by a channel inserted as a vehicle for the "fatness" <note>Meaning the oily fuel.</note>, was continually nourished by the suction of the liquid brought from elsewhere. With this liquid, the asbestos and incombustible <term>wick</term> <note>original: "lychnus" or "myxus"</note> placed in the lamp was saturated. Since the flow of the oily liquid was perennial, and the <term>asbestos flax</term> <note>original: "stupa Asbestina"</note> was incombustible, it was a necessary consequence that a perpetual light would endure. And that this is so, the Arab Schiangia <note>Likely a reference to an Arabic geographical or historical source used by Kircher.</note> testifies in his history of the memorable things of Egypt in these words:

<note>original Arabic: وكان (And it was...)</note>

<summary>Kircher argues that "perpetual lamps" found in Egyptian tombs are often optical illusions caused by gases or, more significantly, clever engineering that piped natural petroleum into tombs to feed asbestos wicks. He cites European travelers and Arabic historians to support this geological explanation.</summary>

# TREATISE XX. ON THE LAMPS OF THE EGYPTIANS. CHAPTER III.

There were in Egypt regions filled with pitch and naphtha, and the philosophers knew this power of nature and extended channels from it even to their caves. In these were lamps connected to the aforementioned channels, and in the lamps was a thread of wick that could not be consumed by fire. Thus, the lamp would shine forever because of the naphtha which flows forever, and because of the wick which is not burned by fire. <note>original Arabic: "وكان في مصر بقاع مملوة بقار ونفط..." This passage provides an Arabic translation of the Latin text below, likely sourced by Kircher from Eastern manuscripts to bolster his argument for the physical reality of these lamps.</note>

<margin>Schiangia <note>Likely a reference to a specific geographical location or an Arabic source name.</note></margin>

*There was, moreover, in Egypt a field whose trenches were full of pitch and liquid bitumen; from which the Philosophers, recognizing the force of nature, established certain channels from such places all the way to the subterranean vaults. In these they placed a Lamp, which was joined with the aforementioned channels; the Lamp truly had a thread made of flax <note>asbestos or "mountain flax"</note> which cannot be consumed by fire. In this manner, the Lamp, once lit, burned perpetually on account of the perpetual flow of bitumen and the incombustible thread of flax.*

And this, in my own opinion, is the truest method for constructing a perpetual light. Since it is purely natural, it presents no great difficulty—especially in places abounding in petroleum—to construct similar Lamps. Consequently, the Arabs do not reason without foundation concerning the perpetual light of the burning Lamps arranged among the Vaults. <margin>Why the Egyptians placed perpetually burning Lamps in the Vaults.</margin> Finally, the purpose and end for which they fashioned Lamps of this kind was none other than to show that, just as the nature of fire is most similar to the operations of the Gods, so too the Divinities assigned to the guardianship of the body were thought to assist these [lamps]. They were attracted to them as if by a sensible symbol of divinity, partly for the protection of the deceased and a perennial presence, and partly for the perpetual illumination of the soul, owing to a certain hidden sympathy and agreement which they maintain toward the same. And let these remarks suffice concerning the Lamps of the Ancient Egyptians.

# A RECAPITULATION
<note>original: "Anacephalaeosis"</note>
## OF THE ENTIRE WORK,

->In which it is demonstrated, through various and irrefutable arguments and reasons, that the exposition and interpretation of hidden and most abstruse matters has been performed by the Author truly according to the mind of the Ancient Egyptians; and that the Egyptians understood nothing else through their celebrated hieroglyphic marks than what has been stated.<-

### P R E F A C E.

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral motifs and scrolling foliage.</note>BEFORE we draw in our sails and commit ourselves to the harbor from the immense ocean and utterly inexhaustible sea of this Work, it seemed fitting to show in this place that we have performed the duty of a true and genuine <term>Oedipus</term><note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx; Kircher uses this as a metaphor for deciphering the "riddles" of Egypt.</note>, free from all deceit. We have adapted our interpretation to the mind of the Ancient Priests in such a way that it exhibits nothing diverse or colored by the feigned imposture of wit beyond what they themselves intended. Rather, we show that this doctrine which we have interpreted is the true teaching of the ancient ages—first discovered by the Egyptians, then propagated by others, and finally (such is the inevitable inconstancy and vicissitude of time) lost and abolished, now restored by us through the singular favor of God. This we shall endeavor to demonstrate shortly against certain <term>Zoiluses</term><note>A "Zoilus" is a harsh, nitpicking critic, named after the ancient Greek grammarian known for criticizing Homer.</note> and Slanderers.

I ask the benevolent Reader above all else to consult those things which we have delivered most abundantly on this subject in the <margin>The hortatory Letter of the Pamphylian Obelisk should be read.</margin> "Hortatory Letter" which we prefixed to the *Pamphylian Obelisk* <note>Kircher's 1650 work on the obelisk in the Piazza Navona, Rome.</note>. There the Reader will find the occasion by which we first arrived at the construction of this Work; he will also marvel at the method we observed in clearing away the ruins and unfolding the most abstruse parts of all disciplines. He will contemplate the Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Chaldean, Arabic, Armenian, Coptic, and Persian authors, and those writers most celebrated for the monuments of innumerable Oriental languages, from whose use and reading we have profited, all cited in order. He will also find the most famous <term>Cabinets of Antiquities</term><note>original: "Cimeliarchia," referring to the "cabinets of curiosities" or early museums of Europe.</note> in all of Europe whose scrutiny we employed. Finally, he will see the objections of certain Philologists and the ignorant censures of <term>know-it-alls</term><note>original: "Nasutulorum," literally "those with little noses," a Latin idiom for overly critical or "stuck-up" people.</note> refuted. Therefore, I judge that this hortatory letter should be approached before anyone, driven by a dog-like tooth and a perverse heat of envy, attacks us; so that at last, he may weigh the labor I have provided in this Work with a more equitable scale of judgment. Lest we be forced to repeat the same things to the nausea of the Reader, and having referred the Reader to the cited exhortation, we shall here demonstrate—God willing—that the doctrine set forth by us is the same <margin>What the Egyptian Oedipus must know.</margin> as that which was once intended by the Priests, based on the condition of the things explained and the context and property of the hieroglyphic literature.

# ## ### CHAPTER I.
### Concerning the doctrine and wisdom of the ancient Egyptians.

<margin>The doctrine of the Ancient Egyptians is restored in this work.</margin>
Throughout this entire work, we have done nothing other than hunt for this wisdom—memorable from every age—from the monuments of ancient authors. Traveling in a chariot far more sublime than the one we read that Triptolemus <note>A figure in Greek myth who traveled the world in a winged chariot to spread the knowledge of agriculture</note> rode, we have searched through the <term>Hieromantic</term> <note>original: "Hieromanticas"; referring to sacred divination or the interpretation of sacred mysteries</note> sanctuaries of all arts and sciences. Indeed, by this intense study, persistent speculation, and truly Herculean labor, we seem to have achieved this: that this doctrine—which was as if abolished by the antiquity of time, or inserted only scatteringly into the monuments of ancient authors, and torn as if into a thousand pieces—we have studiously collected and restored to its integrity. Therefore, I think it superfluous to repeat it in this place.

Almost all the <term>Syntagmata</term> <note>original: "Syntagmata"; here referring to the organized treatises or "lessons" in Volume I</note> in the first volume hand down the cradle of this wisdom. In the second volume, through the <term>Sphinx Mystagoga</term> <note>original: "Sphingem Mystagogam"; the "Sphinx who leads into the mysteries"</note>, we have defined this wisdom through the hidden sayings of the Ancients, and we have extracted it like marrow lurking under the various husks of the sciences. Finally, in this last volume, we have set it forth in its entirety, expressed by hieroglyphic symbols; and we have explained the aim and end by which the ancient Priests <note>original: "Mystæ"; initiates or priests of the mysteries</note> were driven to veil it with such hidden marks. Consequently, nothing else now remains but for us to demonstrate that we have approached the sanctuaries—closed and inaccessible for two thousand years—by the right path and by the <term>thread of Ariadne</term> <note>A metaphor for a guiding logic used to navigate a labyrinth</note> (which is the mind and reason of the Sages of Egypt); that we have unbolted the gates; and that we have brought to light the hidden treasure, stored away for so long, not faked or in the least bit adulterated, but sealed with the true and genuine seals of ancient Wisdom.

<margin>The surviving Obelisks contain the doctrine of the Ancient Egyptians.</margin>
If the Obelisks or other hieroglyphic monuments had not survived, it is certain that every effort in restoring the hieroglyphic doctrine would have been in vain. But since we see that they have endured for two thousand years and more unto this day, both in Egypt and here in Rome, certainly no one who studiously turns the pages of this work of ours will deny that whatever hieroglyphics were produced by the Ancients are contained within them. If, therefore, the doctrine pointed out a moment ago—dissipated here and there among authors—is rightly compared and combined with these monuments by a constant weighing of the mind, there should be no doubt that by the scrutiny of a sagacious mind, Oedipus shall penetrate to their true meaning; just as we, of the whole...

# RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK. CHAPTER I.

<note>original: "Anacephalæosis Totivs Operis"</note>

The summary of this work teaches what we have accomplished through divine grace. For just as in <term>mental diagrams</term> <note>original: "phrenoschematis"; likely referring to emblems or memory aids</note> or printed emblems, a sentence cannot be understood without its accompanying symbolic figure, nor can symbolic figures be understood without the words of the attached sentence—but rather, to penetrate the force of the hidden wit, the positioning of both is required—so it is exactly with hieroglyphics. Until now, the uncorrupted doctrine or wisdom was passed down to us as if through certain fragments and pieces scattered here and there, but without the symbols. The symbols also existed, carved only on Obelisks and other monuments, but until now there was no one who could combine the symbols with the doctrine, and by combining them, examine them. <margin>The Author’s study in unearthing the doctrine of the Egyptians from hieroglyphic monuments.</margin> Therefore, it is no wonder that for such a long time, the true meaning of hieroglyphics has remained hidden. From my early youth, driven by I know not what instinct, I finally undertook this work. Over a space of twenty years, exhausted by the continuous scrutiny of the mind, I combined the symbols with the doctrine; I compared them by skillfully adapting each to each according to the rules of the <term>combinatorial art</term> <note>A method of logic and categorization popularized by Ramon Llull</note>; and finally, with the inner sanctuaries unlocked and the husks broken, I found the kernel—that is, I attained the true and infallible truth of hieroglyphic meaning, which I have resolved to consecrate to posterity in this massive work. But so that unskilled critics may see the irrefragable reasons for these matters, I shall first propose several arguments by which the truth of my statements may be more clearly revealed.

# ARGUMENT I.

->*That the multitude of Hieroglyphic Symbols is not innumerable, as some critics object.*<-

<margin>Hieroglyphics are not innumerable.</margin> There have been some who came to the opinion that the doctrine of hieroglyphics is <term>impossible</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀδύνατον" (adynaton)</note> due to the innumerable multitude of symbols; I have deemed it necessary to contend against them here. However, since this entire demonstration depends on the exhibition of figures, and the exhibition consists of a singular and specific enumeration of all things, it is impossible to satisfy the proposed goal unless I properly fulfill all the parts of an <term>Anatomist</term> <note>Kircher uses "Anatomy" here as a metaphor for a detailed, structural breakdown of a subject</note>; and so I shall fulfill them.

<margin>The triple order of Hieroglyphics.</margin> The entire context of the sacred carvings is completed and constituted primarily from a triple order. In the first order are placed various animals, drawn from the Republic of men, quadrupeds, birds, serpents, and insects, and adopted into the fabric of symbols. These indeed perform the task of signifying things in various and diverse ways: for they signify either as whole figures placed by themselves, or through their parts being placed, or through the adoption of a portion of another different living creature, with which they constitute a single multiform entity. Such are the carvings that are <term>hawk-shaped</term> <note>original Greek: "γερακίμορφοι" (gerakimorphoi)</note>, <term>dog-headed men</term> <note>original Greek: "κυνανθρωποι" (kynanthropoi)</note>, <term>hawk-headed men</term> <note>original Greek: "ιερακάνθρωποι" (hierakanthropoi)</note>, and six hundred other monsters which we have displayed everywhere on our Obelisks.

In the second order are contained things of a different kind, such as herbs,

# CHAPTER I. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

...herbs, flowers, vessels, staffs, scepters, crosses, altars, seats, tools of craftsmen, various garments, head ornaments, mitres, baskets, hair-knots <note>original: "tutuli," a high priestly hairstyle or cap</note>, musical instruments, and geometric figures; in a word, they adopted as sacred symbols for signifying meanings all those things which they commonly used in the festivals and solemnities of the Gods, or which they believed **Osiris**, or **Isis**, or the offspring of the rest of the Gods had once employed.

In the third order are contained those things which are called *hieroglyphics* <note>original Greek: ιερογλυφικά</note> by **Clement of Alexandria**, that is, those which possess a certain likeness to the things they denote, such as the figure of the Sun and Moon, of harbors, walls, crowns, boundaries, flames, fire, water, bowls, and pools, and many similar things; these signified nothing other than the very thing they represented; you may see all these explained throughout this book. Having set forth this "anatomy," let us now see what is that infinite multitude of animals and wild beasts occurring on the hieroglyphic Obelisks, which some might imprudently thrust upon us as "impossible to know" <note>original Greek: ἀδύνατα (adynata)</note>. 

And first, it must be assumed that the Egyptians rarely, or perhaps never, were accustomed to leave their native soil for the sake of philosophizing; <margin>Strabo says the Egyptians did not leave their native soil for the sake of philosophizing.</margin> for, as **Strabo** and **Herodotus** testify, they regarded the rest of the nations as barbarians, ignorant, and in need of their own wisdom; they believed that arts and disciplines, and the true method of philosophizing, were to be sought nowhere but in Egypt, which, as it was the first of lands, was also the first producer of all things. 

From this it must be assumed, secondly, that the Egyptians had no singular knowledge of animals living outside the boundaries of Egypt, <margin>Only Egyptian quadrupeds were adopted by the Egyptians for signifying meanings.</margin> but only of those which their fertile Mother Egypt produced for them. This appears clearly from the fact that, since the Egyptians were entirely devoted to scrutinizing the virtues, properties, <margin>Plutarch.</margin> character, nature, and the sympathetic and antipathetic affections of animals, as well as other gifts of nature, they observed every nod and gesture—as **Plutarch** testifies—and even the smallest actions to the point of superstition; indeed, they placed the greatest part of their secret Philosophy in knowing these things. Certainly, the observation of these virtues and properties could not have occurred except in the most obvious and familiar living creatures. 

If this is so, it is evident from what has been said that no other animals besides Egyptian ones, whose virtues and properties were known from daily inspection, were adopted for the structure of symbols or <term>hierograms</term> <note>sacred drawings or inscriptions</note>. <margin>Ammianus Marcellinus.</margin> Wherefore I cannot wonder enough what came into the mind of **Ammianus Marcellinus** (Book 17, on Constantine and Julian), when he dares to say that on the Obelisks, besides innumerable marks of forms, the Egyptians also engraved many kinds of birds and beasts of *another world*. Certainly, I have never been able to detect animals of this "other world" on our Roman Obelisks; unless perhaps Ammianus is describing for us some Utopia, and its Obelisks and animals as well; let him see to that himself. For what would unknown animals—such as the Northern **Wolverine** <note>original: "Gulo Septentrionalis"</note> or the American **Gray Fox** <note>original: "Americus Vulpilupus," likely referring to a New World canine</note>, whose nature and character they had not perceived even by rumor—be doing among these symbols? Truly, the **Scarab** <note>Dung beetle</note> would be placed as a symbol for the Sun in vain, unless its actions were known to be conformable to the likeness of the works of the Sun...

...they might recognize. For example, the Ibis or the Ape would be assumed as a symbol of the Moon to no purpose, unless they had experienced the "Lunar" qualities of Apes in all their actions. <note>Kircher refers to the ancient belief that certain animals naturally "sympathize" with celestial bodies; here, the ape's behavior was thought to change with the phases of the moon.</note> Indeed, the fact that one may never and nowhere observe Elephants, Giraffes, Rhinoceroses, Lynxes, Stags, Bisons, Elks, Bears, Ostriches, Birds of Paradise, Parrots, or images of similar animals possessing the greatest virtues in the sacred carvings; there can certainly be no other <margin>Fish were not adopted by the Egyptians as Hieroglyphics.</margin> reason than that they had no intimate knowledge of such animals. For the same reason, they rejected species of fish as if they were unknown; and those whose virtues were difficult to investigate, they rejected as unsuitable for hieroglyphic symbols—except for the *Oxyrynchus* <note>A sharp-nosed fish of the Nile, often associated with the goddess Hathor or Isis.</note> and the *Phagrus* <note>Likely a sea-bream or eel-like fish.</note>, a certain kind of fish that is encountered everywhere in all hieroglyphic monuments. For since the Sages chiefly sought out "Solar" and "Lunar" things, or those which by their natural endowments reflected the properties of their Gods, they feared that if they admitted unknown animals, they might—instead of the things of *Oromasdes* <note>The principle of Light/Good (Ahura Mazda).</note> and *Osiris*—select *Arimanian* <note>The principle of Darkness/Evil (Ahriman).</note> or *Typhonian* <note>Related to Typhon/Set, the Egyptian god of chaos.</note> things, attracting what they ought to flee. Therefore, they used great caution in establishing symbols through animals. Hence they also seem to have neglected the domestic Rooster in hieroglyphics, for no other reason than that it was <margin>Why the domestic Rooster is not found among the hieroglyphics.</margin> contrary and hostile to the Lion (which is surely a Solar animal), being full of a Typhonian spirit. But if, in many ancient fragments, the figures of the animals indicated above—such as Stags, Elephants, Roosters, Bears, and the like—are found incised, they are by no means to be judged as Egyptian, but as the fictions of the Greeks. We therefore encompass that entire infinite multitude of quadrupeds used in sacred symbols, which was presented to us above, in this single verse:

->*The Ape, the Ox, and the Ram, the Goat, the Lion, and the Dog,*<-
->*The Cat, and the Hare.*<-

To which are added from the amphibians the Crocodile and the Hippopotamus. Among the genus of Apes, we also place the *Cynocephalus* <note>The dog-headed baboon, sacred to Thoth.</note>. And besides these, let anyone search as much as they wish and examine all the columns; they will find no others in the entire scope of hieroglyphics, whether whole or mixed from others.

But someone will perhaps ask, what was the cause of such a rarity of quadrupeds <margin>The cause of the rarity of quadrupeds in Egypt.</margin> in Egypt? I can truly give no other reason for this than that they found no stable habitation there, whether because of the frequent flooding of the Nile, or because of the great inconveniences they suffer from flies, gnats, serpents, and other harmful beasts left behind by the stagnant Nile. Hence, on this account, *Horus* <note>Referring to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphics which Kircher often critiques.</note> is rendered quite suspect to me, as one who records those species of <margin>Why Horus counts animals not found in Egypt among the hieroglyphics.</margin> animals everywhere in the register of hieroglyphics which nevertheless never occur in any priestly diagrams; and which are found to be known—I will not say to Egypt—but not even to other nations, such as the Hyena, the Phoenix, and similar things; unless perhaps Horus himself is said to have graced them with this <term>arrogant</term> <note>original: ὑπερηφάνῳ (hyperephano) - meaning magnificent, overbearing, or distinguished.</note> honor by his own authority, which is likely. I will not deny, however, that many animals were introduced into Egypt from elsewhere...

Flamingos, Crows, Owls, Quails, Sparrows, and from the family of insects the Scarab beetle, the Fly, and the Butterfly; you will have embraced the entire knowledge of hieroglyphic birds. Furthermore, the second class of symbols is also not so great, nor so difficult that their meaning cannot be obtained from ancient authors. For symbols of this kind are such that to have merely seen them is to have explained them.

And from all these points established, I conclude first: the multitude of sacred marks is not so great as ignorant critics everywhere claim, who thrust such ideas forward to deter noble minds from such an excellent endeavor. Wherefore, the same thing seems to happen to them in their judgment as happens to the unrefined common people, who, gazing upon the starry face of Heaven, accuse Astronomers of some sort of rashness because they dare to bring the innumerable multitude of stars back to a calculation. Yet it is so far from the case that they are innumerable to the sight, that even as many stars as have been able to be seen by the sharp-sightedness of the naked human eye were reduced by Astronomers to only 1022 (excepting those which in these most recent times have been noted in the Galaxy and in the New World by the aid of the telescope). By a similar reasoning, many people—when they behold the pyramids distinguished by such a variety of written elements—falsely persuade themselves that these hieroglyphics run on into infinity. However, when I reduced the matter to a calculation, having scraped together sacred carvings from here and there in Asia and Africa, and from the more famous antiquarians of Germany, France, Italy, and the City of Rome, and having instituted a comparison with singular industry and applied a certain method of the combinatory art, 
<margin>Hieroglyphics do not exceed 300.</margin>
I was not able to detect more than three hundred distinct hieroglyphics; which indeed might seem a <term>paradox</term> <note>original: παράδοξον; an unexpected or marvelous thing</note>.

# RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK. CHAPTER I.

<margin>Many hieroglyphs are amulets.</margin> It has been established that these were instituted to indicate mysteries concerning the Spirits of the World, demons, the stars, and the elements. Furthermore, the greater part of the hieroglyphs are nothing other than certain amulets or phylacteries <note>protective charms worn to ward off evil</note>, placed to keep the incursions of evil away from Egypt, as we have shown throughout this theater of work.

<margin>Hieroglyphs do not contain the deeds of Kings.</margin> Therefore, those are greatly deceived who fabricate the idea that the deeds, riches, travels, victories, and annual revenues of Sesostris, Psammetichus, Ramesses, and other Kings of Egypt are contained beneath the hieroglyphic inscriptions. Those also err significantly who think that the Egyptians had no other writing besides the hieroglyphic in the earliest times, and therefore expressed the deeds of Kings with it. Truly, these opinions will seem ridiculous to those who have tasted even a little of the more recondite <note>hidden or deep</note> literature of the Egyptians, as they rest on no foundation. For if they had decided to leave these as fixed testimonies of excellence for posterity to achieve the glory of an eternal name, what need was there to obscure the glory of their deeds—which by its very nature seeks the light—with such dark and hidden coverings of enigmas as the hieroglyphs were? For it would be foolish, not to say stupid, to wish to explain the excellently performed deeds of any King or Emperor with a genus of characters unknown to everyone. But if the deeds and admirable efforts of the most powerful Kings were recorded in them, why were they communicated to none of the common people? Why was the populace barred from reading them—the very people to whom they ought to have been read to incite admiration and reverence toward the Kings? You see, therefore, that histories were not written here, nor the lives of Princes, nor the famous deeds of Kings, but mysteries communicated to no one except those who held power in Egypt and who knew how to apply them.

<margin>The error of Herodotus.</margin> Furthermore, as for what Herodotus says—that nothing else is contained on the pyramids except the expenses incurred in their erection, and that six hundred talents spent on garlic, onions, and other foodstuffs for the laborers were written in hieroglyphic letters—this surpasses all fables. It appears clearly that this Herodotus was of a simple mind and too easy to believe even the slightest little story, seizing upon whatever was said by anyone in any place as true and most certain; just as it appears elsewhere regarding that ridiculous origin of the Nile springing from the two mountains <term>Crophi</term> and <term>Mophi</term> <note>mythical mountains mentioned by Herodotus as the source of the Nile</note>, which was jokingly told to him by a sacred Scribe and believed. Finally, that the hieroglyphic interpretation of <term>Hermapion</term> <note>an ancient translator of obelisks cited by Roman historians</note> found in <term>Ammianus Marcellinus</term> is for the most part fabricated is evident from the fact that he places many things in it entirely foreign to the logic of hieroglyphs, such that the truth cannot even be conceived from the sacred marks of the Obelisk. But because we have shown all these things at length in the interpretation of the <term>Pamphilian Obelisk</term> <note>The obelisk now in the Piazza Navona, Rome</note>, let us for now refrain from saying more about them.

-> Concerning <-

<summary>Kircher argues that hieroglyphs are mystical symbols and protective amulets rather than historical records of Egyptian kings. He dismisses the literal historical accounts of Herodotus and Hermapion as misunderstandings of the true, hidden nature of the script.</summary>

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Chapter I of the "Theatrum Hieroglyphicum" (Hieroglyphic Theater). Kircher establishes the rigorous intellectual requirements for any scholar attempting to decode Egyptian symbols, arguing that Egypt is the source of all ancient mystical wisdom.</meta>

# On the requirements for the interpretation of Hieroglyphics.

<margin>Requirements for the interpretation of hieroglyphics.</margin>
Since hieroglyphic symbols do not always signify the same thing, but rather assume a different meaning according to the diversity of their position, their parts, and other marks joined to them (for example, a Hawk represents one thing while sitting, another while flying, another by its head alone, its feather, or its headdress, and yet another in a different posture, as has been seen in this hieroglyphic theater), an "Oedipus" <note>Kircher refers to himself as Oedipus, the mythical solver of the Sphinx's riddle.</note> will undoubtedly roll the stone of Sisyphus <note>original: "Sisyphi saxum"; a metaphor for a never-ending, futile task</note> in this business, unless he is properly equipped with two things most conducive to expediting the work. And first, indeed, he must not only have a most excellent understanding of the virtues and properties of the sacred animals, as well as the plants or herbs produced by Egypt and consecrated to the Gods, and the qualities and accidents of the instruments encountered therein; but he must also know how to apply them skillfully, aptly, and congruously according to the intended analogy <note>original Greek: "ἀναλογίας"</note> of the more secret Philosophy and Theosophy <note>term: Theosophy (divine wisdom regarding the nature of God and the world)</note>, which consists in the similarity and concatenation of the three Worlds. To perform this with the necessary sagacity, a second thing is immediately required: namely, an all-encompassing knowledge of the aforementioned Philosophy and Theosophy, so that he understands in what its reasoning and its so-called essence chiefly consist; what its use is in human affairs, in sacrifices, in the divinatory arts, in the conjuring of Demons, in the enticing of the Spirits of the World, and in similar hidden actions. These things can by no means be obtained except from the hidden inner chambers of all Philology, and from a comparison of various ancient Poets, Mythologists, and Historians made with the highest genius and persistent study; indeed, they must be deduced from the monuments left by the Hebrews (whose rivals, as we said above, the Egyptians were), as well as the Arabs, Ethiopians, Persians, and Greeks, who seem to have succeeded to that inheritance before all other nations. Therefore, unless someone is imbued with at least a moderate knowledge of the Oriental languages—Hebrew, Greek, Arabic, and Chaldaic—which must be sought from their very sources; unless he is consulted in all Antiquity; and unless he is endowed with an extraordinary knowledge of the more recondite Philosophy, he will be least able to bring the Work to the required perfection, as is sufficiently clear from the present volume. For whatever is secret and hidden in the Masorah <note>original: "Masura"; the tradition of Hebrew biblical text preservation</note> of the Hebrews, the Kabbalah of the Chaldeans, the Magic of the Persians, the Astrology of the Phoenicians, the Philosophy of the Greeks, the Mathematics of Pythagoras, the Chemistry <note>original: "Chimia"; here referring to Alchemy</note> of the Arabs, and finally the Theology of Plato, the sacred and symbolic Wisdom of the Egyptians seems to claim uniquely for itself. You see, therefore, how great an apparatus is necessary, and how many foreign monuments must be visited. From these things, unless I am mistaken, it is clearly evident that "Oedipus," equipped only with the furniture of the aforementioned hidden arts, has exhibited the true intended meaning of the hieroglyphic doctrine; since all these things, as we have most abundantly shown, proceeded from nothing other than the School <note>original: "Gymnasio"</note> of the Egyptians.

# SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE WORK. 559 CH. I.

## ARGUMENT II.

->*That Hieroglyphics do not consist of syllables, words, and sentences, as other languages do, but are the knowledge of ideal things.*<-

---

<margin>Hieroglyphs are not letters.</margin> Many have wrongly believed that the Egyptians—just as occurs in other languages—constructed their hieroglyphs by some alphabetic method which renders words, distinguishes sentences, and places a kind of speech before the eyes of readers. That this is false has been demonstrated throughout this entire Work, and is sufficiently clear from the propositions placed at the beginning of this Volume. Indeed, from the inscriptions on the Obelisks, it is entirely evident that hieroglyphic symbols, much like <note>original: "Chinensium literaturam"</note> Chinese writing, always preserve their full meaning regardless of how they are placed. This was clear from the various inscriptions of both the Obelisks and other monuments cited in this Volume; as these are exactly the same, they maintain no difference in position, since they are displayed sometimes in a perpendicular order, now upward, now downward, now in a sloping position, now to the right, and a little later to the left. This would by no means happen if they had been woven from alphabetic elements; in which, nevertheless, a reading from the left teaches nothing other than what is shown from the right; for hieroglyphs, however the reading is established, always obtain a full and perfect sense.

<margin>Hieroglyphic literature is symbolic.</margin> Furthermore, that this literature is by no means composed of any Alphabet, but is purely symbolic, is evident from the fact that almost all Obelisks display nearly the same inscription of figures in their upper part.

<note>Hieroglyphic inscription: A rectangular diagram containing three horizontal rows of symbols. 
Top row: Two seated figures facing right with arms raised in a gesture of adoration or offering. 
Middle row: Three hawk-headed birds (accipitres) standing and facing right. 
Bottom row: Three crouching quadruped animals (likely rams) facing right. 
Kircher uses this figure to demonstrate that if these were phonetic letters, their constant repetition on obelisks would result in nonsensical, repetitive words (e.g., a "five-syllable word" repeated twelve times).</note>

For first, one always observes this inscription wonderfully transformed with symbols adorned in a symbolic manner; that these are letters, one neither should nor can say by any reasoning. For either the whole figure—for example, a <term>Hawk-headed man</term> <note>original: "Accipitrinus homo"</note> armed with a scepter and a Cross—indicates one word, or many together which then render a word: neither can be said. For if individual figures represent the same letter (I speak always of elements or Alphabetic letters) and on each side of the Obelisk the first five patterns, as is clear in the attached figure, are almost the same; a five-syllable word would necessarily emerge, which, being placed three times on each side, would be exactly the same, repeated twelve times to no benefit. Thus this word, for example, <term>Soul</term> <note>original: "Anima"</note>, repeated twelve times, would form no concept at all in the mind of the reader, nor would it determine anything, but would be idle, without any determined meaning; as this would be a ridiculous and foolish fiction, so it is far removed from the design of the <term>Priests of ancient Wisdom</term> <note>original: "Sapientiæ Mystarum"; refers to the keepers of Egyptian esoteric knowledge</note>, as only he who has not thoroughly weighed what we have handed down in this Work could fail to know. Nor should you say that the sense is deter—

# CHAPTER I. THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...be terminated by a sequence of following letters: for even on the very largest column, a single vertical inscription never contains more than a hundred letters; it is impossible that so many and such great mysteries, which the Egyptians displayed in inscriptions of this kind, could be contained in such a small number of letters. Therefore, they can in no way be called alphabetic letters. Nor can it be said that figures of this kind are adorned with a mass of several letters, such that a human or animal body constitutes one letter, a headband or a scepter another, or an <term>Ankh Cross</term> <note>original: "Crux anfata"; the looped cross or 'handled cross' of ancient Egypt, symbolizing life</note> another, and a seat yet another. For if a <term>hierogrammatism</term> <note>a sacred or symbolic writing/composition</note> were composed of several such letters, one might then ask what place the first, second, or third (and so on) would hold to form any particular word; since no letter stands in a fixed order, as is evident from the <term>columns</term> <note>original: "selidibus"; referring to the vertical registers or panels of text on an obelisk</note> of the columns themselves, where they are displayed now in a straight and now in an inverted order. Thus, it is in no way possible that these visual schemes are constructed from other letters as words composed of syllables.

<margin>The oval tablets of the Obelisks are not letters.</margin> Furthermore, the sacred tablets or amulets, which are seen enclosed in oval figures <note>cartouches</note> on all obelisks, can in no way constitute an alphabetic sense; for they would be repeated so many times in vain on a single obelisk. Rather, they must be judged as great symbols of power, attractors of the Divine Powers, expressed through ideal principles, by which the Powers might present themselves as if to hidden and appropriate symbols, and favor the prayers of the suppliants. Hence, these were inscribed not only on obelisks, but also on other statues and sphinxes, and even on the wrappings of mummies for the same reason. It is, therefore, a symbolic and mystical kind of writing, in which, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the Egyptian mysteries</note> rightly teaches, *dismiss the voices, and receive the meaning*.

<margin>Hieroglyphs are similar to Mental Schemas.</margin> For just as we have said before, and as we have taught abundantly in Volume Two concerning the institution of <term>mental schemas</term> <note>original: "phrenoschematon"; a term Kircher uses for symbolic emblems or "thought-figures"</note> or Emblems on page 8, two things are contained in any Emblem: the symbol and the sentiment <note>the motto or "soul" of the emblem</note>, by the conjunction of which we finally arrive at the hidden significance of that which the symbol displays. For example, in this present <term>Mental Schema</term>, you see a Magnet from which a concatenated series of rings is drawn; you have seen the symbol, now consider the motto, which is: *By secret knots* <note>original: "Arcanis nodis"</note>. Unless these words had been applied, nothing certain would be known in the symbol; but with the motto added to the symbol, the Virgin Congregation of the Roman College of the Society of Jesus, to whom it is inscribed, is taught by this hidden prompting of the inner soul that the growth of the said Congregation is perfected only by a certain hidden pull of divine inspiration. In this, while each person—by the attraction of good example, holy conversation, and mutual edification—draws those nearest to them, it happens that all, bound by the chains of brotherly love and concord, report a most fertile harvest with joined forces in that state to which divine goodness has appointed them, and are finally associated with the blessed minds as eternally happy. Behold how great a wealth of meanings and contemplations lies hidden under even a single mental schema. In exactly the same pa-

## ->The Nature of Hieroglyphic Doctrine<-

In this manner, I say, it happens in the hieroglyphic doctrine, wherein through abstract concepts, or even in a single symbol, the material and argument of an entire Philosophical speculation appears. This is seen in the following figure; where you see a statue seated upon a variegated throne, transformed with a **Hawk-like countenance**, remarkable for the **basket-shaped tiara** <note>original: "cidari calathoide"</note>, the gourd, and the vine-tendril inserted into it. In his right hand he carries a **thyrsus** <note>A staff associated with Bacchus/Dionysus, whom Kircher identifies with Osiris</note> before him, and with his left he imperiously commands something. Indeed, by this mysterious display of symbols, the operations of the **supreme intellect** are secretly hinted at—not through some arranged manner of discursive words, but through a certain ideal concept signifying the virtues lying hidden in the Supreme Mind, represented by the power of the contemplative intellect as if in a mirror. 

Thus, one skilled in hieroglyphic literature, while gazing upon this present schematic, soon recognizes the Deity: the operations of the divine mind; his empire over the economy of the Worlds; the abundance of light, life, and heat by which he produces, animates, and preserves all things, flashing with infinite majesty and power. Here appears the offspring of ideal concepts; here is the power of life, light, and heat diffused into all the paths of the World; here is the variety of things in the sensible and elemental World, and the highest harmonic mixture of "consonant-dissonants" <note>The Pythagorean idea of harmony arising from opposing forces</note> resulting from the immense unity of the divine intellect, and countless other things which, since we have explained them elsewhere, we refer the Reader to those places.

The Sages sing, therefore, of how God differs from others: that the World and time exist beneath Him; furthermore, that God is the author of causes, and that He created each thing according to its own specific nature. In these things, He illuminates the Intelligences <note>The highest angelic or spiritual beings</note>, and through them the middle intellect; through the intellect, He illuminates the middle universal soul and the celestial soul; and through that middle soul, He illuminates the nature of things that are born and pass away. Who does not see that these concepts fit this present illustration <note>original: "Iconismo"</note> most aptly? Here, the globe <note>The winged disk at the top</note> provides a symbol of the divine mind and the tri-form Deity. Clearly, the Archetypal and Supramundane Osiris <note>The divine source beyond the world</note> continues the communication of divine influences through a wonderful analogy: into the All-Formed Osiris <note>original: "Osirin Pantamorphum"</note>, the leader of the Intellectual World; and from here into the Solar Osiris, the soul of the Sidereal World; and finally into the Material Osiris, the governor of the Elemental World.

From these points, unless I am mistaken, it is most clearly evident that nothing else can or should be implied by this interpretation than what I have stated. Even Plato himself, and Aristotle, and their followers, not only asserted these things but embraced them as sacred dogma. # SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE WORK. CHAPTER L.

...it is clearly evident from these things that this doctrine was none other than a mystical and secret interpreter of the Supreme and Archetypal Mind <note>The "Archetypal Mind" refers to the divine intellect or the world of ideas in Neoplatonic thought</note>. If anyone should dare to deny this, let him know that with the same audacity he would be openly disparaging the authority of the greatest geniuses of the human race who assert it—nay, I shall say more, he would disparage the Sacred Scriptures themselves. In those Holy Books, frequent mention is made of Egyptian Wisdom, and it is clearly taught that Moses was instructed in it. Moreover, it is known to all the halls of the higher schools that Wisdom can be no other science than the investigator of the highest things lying hidden in the secret recess of divinity, just as the first definition cited on page 2 of this Work teaches. Therefore, one would search in vain beneath these symbols for the histories of the deeds performed by the Kings of Egypt. For just as Wisdom is the queen of all arts and sciences, so she holds all others subject to her; hence, as the necessity of order demanded, Medicine, Magic, and Mathematical sciences also crept into the hieroglyphic doctrine as a consequence, alongside Theology, like streams flowing from the fountain from which all things spring. But now let us demonstrate all these things more clearly.

## ARGUMENT III.

->*That Hieroglyphics, according to the mind of the Egyptians, were not only significant symbols of the highest things, but also, due to a certain hidden connection with supramundane causes, were attractive of Divine Powers and preservative against adversities.*<-

<margin>
Hieroglyphics were thought to have the power to attract Divine Powers.
</margin>
**J**ust as hieroglyphic symbols were assumed from all classes of worldly things, it has been amply demonstrated from every kind of learning in this Work that they were also of great virtue and efficacy, owing to a wondrous and hidden connection with supramundane <note>beyond the physical world</note> causes. For no one should persuade himself that the first founders of this literature rashly or by chance applied the images of any obvious things to the purpose of sacred sculpture. Rather, they chose those which they knew—through long study and experience of the hidden seals of natural characteristics—to have a great similarity, property, and analogy to the worldly chains of Spirits <note>Geniorum</note>. Indeed, these symbols were thought to be all the more efficacious the more they expressed a greater similarity to the presiding Deity <note>Numen choragum</note> of some worldly chain. From this, the chains of the Divine Powers, which they call *Seiras* <note>original Greek: Σειρὰς, meaning "chains" or "links," a Neoplatonic concept of divine radiation</note>, drew their origin. To these chains they would assign all those things—whether in the Starry or Material World, among quadrupeds, birds, plants, or minerals—which seemed to display a certain analogy in their virtues to the Deity presiding over a specific chain, as if committed to the protection of that chain's Deity. # CHAPTER I. 564 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

...certain classes of things were taken from the orders of the different Worlds, in which individual things, however disparate they might be, expressed the virtues and properties of some presiding Divinity's "chain" <note>original: *catenae*. Kircher uses this term to describe a vertical link of sympathy connecting a high deity down through various animals, plants, and stones.</note>. And just as they thought that said things flowed from the Leader of the Choir <note>original: *Archichorago*. A Greek-derived term for the primary source or "conductor" of a spiritual influence.</note> of such a chain, so they also believed those things held a sympathy with that Divinity. They believed that when such an object was positioned, the Divinity would be affected and drawn to it infallibly and necessarily, as if to a thing vehemently symbolic of itself and most appropriate to its nature. <margin>The origin of Magic.</margin> From this, Magic was born, through which they believed they could produce miraculous effects by the magical application of lower things to heavenly Beings—much like applying passive elements to active ones. From this source also flowed the architecture of <margin>Of Oracles</margin> Oracles, by which, through said magical skill, they confined Demons into statues and extorted answers to proposed questions through their barbarous and portentous words; from this, the divinatory art found its birth. Finally, from this heading, the <margin>The origin of the art of Amulets.</margin> art of Amulets was discovered, by which sacred symbols—adapted in the aforementioned manner to the worldly chains—were carried in the place of charms <note>original: *periaptorum*. From the Greek *periapton*, something tied around the body, like a pendant.</note> to attain the good they sought, or to avert the evil they fled. Indeed, they first engraved these symbols of great efficacy, with the highest connection to the principles contained in the "Idea of Ideas," into the hardest stones of the Obelisks as prototypes intended to last forever; from these, anyone might then draw out for private use either charms to attract good or protective amulets to ward off evil. The Priests also, according to the ideal principles which the manifold apparatus of symbols in the images displayed, performed their sacrifices in the Inner Sanctuaries in order to obtain <term>Theomorphosis</term> <note>original: *θεομόρφωσιν*. The process of being transformed into the likeness of a god.</note>. These things being established:

<margin>What Hieroglyphic literature is.</margin> I say first, that the Hieroglyphic literature displayed on the Obelisks was nothing other than the theoretical and practical science of God and the divine orders of the Governors of the Worlds, by whose concatenated influence everything in the economy of the Worlds is administered. Theory pursued this knowledge; Practice, however, supplied the method for either propitiating the Divinities or bringing them under one's own influence, as demonstrated by Theory. But that this is so, I show as follows.

If the Obelisks contained anything other than this Theosophy <note>Divine wisdom or the science of God.</note>—such as histories, prophecies, the praises of Kings, and similar things—it is certain that just as individual Obelisks displayed different things, so they would have been marked with different symbols and a different context of the same. However, this can in no way be said, and the matter is obvious to the eye; for there is scarcely an Obelisk that does not contain nearly the same things. In each one, not only are the same symbols seen, but even entire compositions of figures are seen transferred from one to another, as we have demonstrated in the actual interpretation. <margin>The minor Obelisks are similar to one another.</margin> And to approach the matter a little more closely: the Minor Obelisks, which we have named the Monti-cœlium, the Mahutæum, and the Mediceum, are so similar that you could call them the same without error. The larger Obelisks also, although they are marked with a more extensive context according to the nature of the argument, nevertheless tend toward the same goal and exactly the same end as the smaller ones. Again, the Flaminian and Sallustian Obelisks, as has been shown...

# RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK. 565 CHAP. I.

was in its proper places, they are entirely the same. This is also evident from the inscriptions of almost all Obelisks, which indicate the influence of the Supreme Mind diffused, as if from a certain center, into all the Classes of the Worlds subjected to it. And thus the same thing seems to have happened to the Egyptians which we see performed in modern times in the presentation of the mysteries of our Christian religion; in which, although you may see the mysteries of the divinity—such as the **Most Holy Trinity** <note>original: "SS. Therefore, just as the Egyptians exhibited the supreme Cause of causes according to the variety of powers flowing from it, together with the Paternal Foundation and its Word, in entirely different ways and structures of symbols; so today the mysteries of the **Most Holy Trinity** and of Christ performed on earth are expressed everywhere in various and different paintings according to each person's conception; yet in such a way that there is almost no one who, while inspecting such paintings (however different they may be) more deeply, does not immediately understand what they aim at. The same must be felt regarding the variety of the images <note>term: "ectypon" - a molded copy or image</note> of the Spirits and Secondary Powers, which Orthodox doctrine calls Angels. Thus, it is clear from what has been said that the Obelisks represent nothing other than what I have stated.

<margin>Hieroglyphs were thought to be effective for attracting Divinities.</margin> I have said above that the Obelisks did not merely express the greatest sacraments of Divine Wisdom <note>term: "Theosophia" - here referring to ancient sacred knowledge</note> through their symbols, but were furthermore, in the estimation of the Egyptians, seals of great power, established by the Priests not only for appeasing the Divinities, but also for attracting them and bringing them under their influence. This is so true that, to demonstrate it, nothing else seems required except that you examine by diligent comparison what we have handed down above in the proper Treatises concerning Mummies, Canopic jars, Sphinxes, and other averting <note>term: "averruncis" - deities or objects intended to ward off evil</note> images. For by that very fact, you will find that almost no form of an image or any representation of a symbol exists separately that is not also seen on the Obelisks themselves. This is surely an irrefragable argument that all symbols among them were not only *signifying* but also *effective*; that is, they were Seals of great efficacy, which are commonly called Amulets, Charms <note>original: "Periapta"</note>, Phylacteries, or Protective Wards <note>original: "Alexiteria"</note> by Authors. Since, however, Amulets of this kind are directed only toward propitiating the supernal powers, it is certain that, besides this, they were symbols of the highest things and divine virtues, which spoke of a wondrous order and proportion with supramundane causes. Thus, they believed that the Leaders <note>term: "Choragos" - leaders of a choir or group</note> of the said orders, whom they expressed, were wonderfully moved to obtain what they intended by a property of reciprocal and hidden action known only to the Priests. We do this both for a perpetual memory of the benefits conferred upon us, and to attest to the honor, reverence, and worship due to God, Christ, the Blessed Virgin, and the Saints, and finally to obtain help in adversity through living faith by a most praise-worthy custom; for these are effective seals of the confidence conceived toward God and the Saints

The Obelisks, therefore, contained not only symbols signifying divine matters, but also symbols effective in attracting Divine Powers. Indeed, each individual Obelisk, whether in temples or public places, presented itself as a kind of prototype or universal Amulet <term>Amuletum: a protective charm or talisman</term> composed of innumerable particular parts, remarkable for the mysterious shape of the pyramid. They persuaded themselves that as long as these endured, the Egyptian land would remain immune from every assault of enemies and the sinister outcomes of wars, by the gift of the immortal Gods whom they represented, as we have taught elsewhere throughout our work.

<margin>The intention of the Egyptians in erecting Obelisks.</margin> Since, therefore, the Obelisks are of such a nature, it is certainly concluded from this that the ancient Priests had no other intention in both erecting the Obelisks and distinguishing them with such a great apparatus of figures, except that which we have demonstrated both just before and throughout the laborious preparations of this *Oedipus*. It remains, therefore, that our interpretation is truly and genuinely established according to the mind of the Ancients.

But perhaps someone will object at this point with these words: "I do not at all deny that this was the wisdom of the ancient Initiates <note>original: "Myſtarum"</note>, and that it consisted in this; but since these things have only been demonstrated under certain universal concepts, I do not see how you have descended to particulars, or by what aids you have done so, or how you have truly described individual things according to the mind of the Ancients." I confess, however, that the types of some symbols seemed so unknown to me at first glance that I was not far from calling them "unknowable," as Apuleius did. Yet, because a constant and untiring spirit conquers all things, it happened that by combining everything with everything, and individual things with individual things, that which at first was incomprehensible—as one wave pushes another—seemed to me not, shall I say, <margin>By what aids the Author acquired knowledge of Hieroglyphs.</margin> impossible <note>original: "ἀδύνατον" (adynaton)</note>, but easy by the grace of the Divine Power. And indeed, the first difficulty was truly the greatest, occurring both in the instruments, vessels, scepters, and similar things, and in discerning the genuine species of animals, all of which are seen carved into the stones with only a rough skill <note>original: "rudi tantùm Minerua," an idiom for unrefined craftsmanship</note>. # RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK. CHAPTER I.

...and so, the authority of the Copts <note>The Coptic Christians of Egypt, whom Kircher believed preserved the ancient Egyptian language</note> was such that the matters mentioned were confirmed. It was sufficient to have cited their words or to have explained the entire mystery, just as you see demonstrated throughout this whole Work. Therefore, once the fountains of universal principles were uncovered, nothing was easier than to discover the streams flowing out in every direction—that is, the particulars. For these depend upon the principles as an effect depends on its cause, as an object depends on its idea, or as a mark depends on a seal. Thus, it could not have happened that, by leaping from one to another with a diligent mental investigation, we would not eventually arrive at a knowledge of the particulars. You see then, benevolent Reader, by what aids and by what art I have gradually arrived at a universal knowledge of hieroglyphs; and thus I can truly infer that this exposition of hieroglyphs which we have brought forth in this Volume is not feigned or imaginary, but is the true and genuine meaning intended by the Ancients. This I show as follows:

<margin>What Hieroglyphic Wisdom is.</margin>
The Hieroglyphic Wisdom of the Egyptians, according to the testimony of all the monuments of Ancient Writers, was nothing other than the science of God and divine virtues, the science of the order of the Universe, and the science of the Intelligences <note>Angelic or celestial beings believed to govern the planets and elements</note> presiding over the World. This is the science which Pythagoras and Plato, according to Plutarch, learned from the columns of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij columnis"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>—that is, from the Obelisks.
<margin>The true Hieroglyphic doctrine explained in this Work.</margin>
But we have not only treated this science throughout this entire Work; we have also explained that which was contained within the hidden envelopes of the hieroglyphs on the said columns. Therefore: if the writing contained any science other than the aforementioned Theosophic <note>Divine or mystical wisdom</note> science, it would have to be either Mathematical, Historical, Physical, or Moral. But it has already been demonstrated in the preceding pages that none of these are contained in the Obelisks, nor indeed could they be. Therefore, we have explained no other wisdom than that which we have called the true and genuine wisdom of the Egyptians, consisting of the knowledge of God, of divine virtues, and of His diffusion through the universal series of the Worlds. For the Egyptians recorded the remaining sciences—Mathematics, Physics, Morals, and Divination, which they were accustomed to teach in public schools—not in hieroglyphs, but in a language known to all and idiomatic, which we call Pharaonic and Coptic.
<margin>Hieroglyphic doctrine was handed down to Priests alone.</margin>
And just as Hieroglyphic Wisdom contained the sacraments of the greatest and most secret things, so too was it handed down only to those who had hope for the throne of the Kingdom—men of the Priestly order—under a strict and rigorous silence in the Inner Sanctuaries <note>original: "Adytis"; the most sacred, restricted parts of a temple</note>, as has been proven. For since the hope and safety of the entire Kingdom seemed to be placed solely in the protection of the Deities, and the Deities were believed to be moved in a wondrous way toward the preservation of the Kingdom by the worship and religion of hieroglyphic wisdom, certainly no one was bound by a greater right to learn it than the men of the Priestly order. From their number the King was first chosen; he believed that through sacrifices instituted according to hieroglyphic laws, he might be blessed by the company of the Gods, or even command the Deities themselves, turn away evils threatening the Kingdom, and thus render the Kingdom safe and secure from every hostile assault by the sole protection of hieroglyphic Amulets. But see what we have treated copiously on these matters in the *Egyptian Politics* and elsewhere. But if anyone of a more shrewd disposition should bring forward another explanation better than this one we have handed down, and more in agreement with the genius and mind of the Egyptians,
