->ARGUMENT IV.<-

->*The consensus of all Philosophers and Poets regarding the Theology of the Egyptians is demonstrated.*<-

<margin>Trismegistus, the founder of hieroglyphics.</margin>Hermes Trismegistus, the Egyptian, just as he was the first founder of Hieroglyphics, is also rightly considered the Prince and Parent of all Egyptian Theology and Philosophy. He was the first and most ancient among the Egyptians who perceived divine matters correctly; he carved his opinions on these things into stones intended to last forever and into massive blocks of rock, as has been proven extensively elsewhere. Not only the pagan commentators of ancient philosophy, but also the orthodox records of the Holy Fathers demonstrate more than sufficiently that whatever Orpheus, Musaeus, Linus, Pythagoras, Plato, Eudoxus, Parmenides, Melissus, Homer, Euripides, and others uttered that was worthy of praise concerning God and divine matters proceeded from him. And first, indeed, Trismegistus in the *Pimander* and *Asclepius* <note>These are foundational texts of the "Hermetica," attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, which blended Greek and Egyptian philosophy.</note> asserts that God is essentially one and good, whom the remaining philosophers then followed. But so that all these things may be made clear, we shall explain each point in as many paragraphs.

->§ I.<-

->*Concerning the unity and goodness of God, as the cause of all things and the productive principle of things.*<-

<margin>Trismegistus knew the Unity of God.</margin>Trismegistus was the first among the Pagans to describe the divine Unity. For he had learned primarily from the Patriarchs <note>Kircher suggests here that Hermes learned monotheism from Biblical figures like Abraham or Joseph.</note> that there is one God, the supreme Founder of heaven and earth; for this reason, in the first discourse of the second part of the *Pimander*, the Divine Mind speaks thus to Mercury: <margin>Trismegistus</margin>*"But as for the fact that all these things were created, my sweetest Mercury, there is no need for you to learn it through my disputation; for they are bodies, they possess a soul, and they are moved. However, it is impossible for these to come together into one without the power of a gatherer. It is necessary, therefore, that there be someone of such a kind, and who is utterly one. For since there are many and various motions, and dissimilar bodies, yet one order of velocity in them all, it is impossible for there to be two or more makers: for a single order would not be preserved among many. Furthermore, whoever among them was the weaker would greatly envy the more powerful, from which a certain discord would arise. And so, if one of them had stood forth as the Author of changeable living beings, he would also desire to beget immortal ones, just as the progenitor of immortals would strive for mortals. Moreover, since there is one soul and one matter, to which of them would the fabrication chiefly belong? But if to both, to which would the greater Province belong? etc."* And a little further down: *"It is therefore conspicuous that there is one Author of all these things above the rest: for there is one soul, one life, and one matter."*

...Who is that? Who else besides the one God? Does it belong to anyone else but God alone to procreate living things? Therefore, the one God has confessed that the World is one, the Sun is one, the Moon is unique, and the divinity is also unique; but how many do you wish God himself to be? Therefore, the One performs individual acts in many things. <margin>God is one according to Trismegistus.</margin> So it is said there. Moreover, he adds this, as if giving a reason for these things: Do you think it is something arduous and laborious for God to effect life, an immortal soul, and change? For while you can do so many and such great things—you see, hear, smell, taste, touch, speak, walk, breathe, and understand—it is not one person in you who sees and another who hears, nor does one speak while another walks, or this one smell while that one tastes, or this one breathe while that one understands; rather, one person performs all these things. Nor is it even possible for those things to happen without the divine power of God. For just as he who ceases from these functions is no longer a living creature, so he who would cease from the construction of those things would be least of all God; but to suspect such a thing is wicked. But if it is granted that nothing exists in the nature of things which does not possess a certain natural vigor for acting, and at the same time the execution of a certain work: how much more must it be asserted that God does not lack the power and effect over all things? For whatever is idle is imperfect; and to call God imperfect is a sin. Therefore, one God makes all things. Thus he spoke.

<margin>The Ancient Philosophers learned the Unity of God from Trismegistus.</margin> This Theology of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij," referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> is most high and profound, since it proves the divine unity with living reasons; indeed, however many others have disputed concerning the unity of God, they have used these same reasons, such as Xenophanes of Colophon, Zeno the Citiean, and Aristotle the Stagirite. From here Parmenides, and from here Melissus, took everything regarding the unity of God. From him Empedocles learned that all things proceeded from the one: visible, invisible, present, past, and future—whatever is born of the sea and the earth, wild beasts, birds, fish, and finally the Gods themselves; understand this to mean the Angels. Therefore, the first Sacrament of this most ancient <margin>Pythagoras.</margin> philosophy was the unity of God, which Pythagoras, having admired and imitated it upon his return from Egypt, published under the enigmatic significance of numbers, saying: *Unity is the root of all things, the fount and origin, <margin>Unity according to Pythagoras is God.</margin> calling Unity "God"*, which Syrianus, the teacher of Simplicius, wrote most clearly in his *Metaphysics*. Eudoxus also, reporting the decrees of ancient Theology, especially of the Pythagoreans, says (according to the author Simplicius in the first book of *Physics*): *And according to another mode, they called Unity itself the principle of all things, because all things were born from it, even primary matter.* Damascius the Platonist, speaking to the ears of Pythagoras concerning Unity, <margin>Damascius. Aristotle rashly attacks him in the first book of the *Physics*, condemning him because he confused all things. For Parmenides did not deal with the material principles of things in that place where he is criticized (which it is established he explained elsewhere), but with the principle of all principles, God, who is indeed one and alone, and in whom all things are one. For in him are all things, and in all things he alone is.

Therefore, Parmenides understood God through "that which is," and he asserted that it was unbegotten and foreign to destruction, without beginning, without end, and likewise whole and only-begotten, or total and one. # RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK. 571 CH. I.

...it is customary for that which is "infinite" to be described as frustrated or lacking. For this reason, later theologians usually speak of the infinite in a *privative* sense <note>meaning defined by what it lacks</note>, because it is deprived of a fitting end; in this way, many have called "prime matter" infinite—that is, lacking its proper form and boundary by its very nature. However, concerning God, whose power and authority have no boundary, no limit, and no end, they have called Him infinite in a *negative* sense <note>meaning He is not limited by anything</note>. Therefore, regarding that first definition of the infinite, where "infinite" is taken as a lack of perfection, Parmenides did not want that First Being to be considered infinite, but rather finite and perfect; hence he sang:
<margin>Parmenides.</margin>

->**It remains firm, for a mighty force / Constrains it within the bond of a limit.**<-

As if nothing could be added to His perfection, since He lacks nothing. For if <margin>Simplicius.</margin> God (as Simplicius says in his commentary on the first book of *Physics*) is that which He is, He lacks <margin>In what sense God is called "Finite."</margin> nothing and is perfect; moreover, that which is perfect has a limit <note>original: "finis," meaning a completion or goal</note> and is not without a limit; and that which has a limit is "finite." He is therefore finite—that is, complete—in the perfection of His essence, even though He is infinite in His power. And in this way, He is called sometimes finite and sometimes infinite by Parmenides and Melissus. This was also observed by Bessarion in his first book against Trapezuntius, though he explains it best in the cited passage of Simplicius, where he reconciles the opinion of Xenophanes and Parmenides (who say the Principle is one and finite) with Melissus (who asserts that the One is infinite). For the former called it "finite" meaning "perfect," because it is the cause of the end and boundary for all things, just as it is the beginning of all things; but the latter pronounced it "infinite" because he considered the power within it to be infinite both in vigor and duration. He also wished it to be <margin>Trismegistus.</margin> indivisible and a whole similar to itself in every part; this he took from Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage</note>, who in the first discourse of the second part of the *Pymander* says: *"For nothing is like Him, who is dissimilar [to all else], and is alone and one."*

But see how far the knowledge of Parmenides reached, that he said "that which is" remains the same, and exists through itself, not wanting, not needy? For the Lord does not need our goods, and he contended that God's "act of understanding" is the same as the Intellect and the thing perceived by the intelligence. <margin>God is a Circle, according to the opinion of Parmenides and others.</margin> He also calls Him complete from every side and equal within all His boundaries, like a circle, which has a circumference equal in all its lines. For this reason, perhaps, he asserted it was very similar to the mass of a well-rounded sphere, to show His perfection and absolute equality in all things: for just as a circle is equal on all sides, so also God is uniform from every direction. Simplicius thinks this was said poetically by him, just as he thinks it was said by Orpheus.

But others also designated God as either a circle or similar to a circle. For the first of all, Trismegistus said that God is an **Intellectual Sphere**. Democritus also demonstrated that God is contained in a fiery circle, according to Galen’s book on *Philosophical History*. The Egyptians also understood God through the hieroglyphic of the circle, just as the Persians called Jove <note>Jupiter/the supreme deity</note> the "Circle of Heaven." But Parmenides had this from Xenophanes...

### CHAPTER I.

From his teacher, who asserted that the substance of God is round and spherical, having nothing in common with men (according to Laërtius in the *Life of Xenophanes*); all these ideas stem from Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage</note>, who always expressed God and divine matters hieroglyphically through the circle.

<margin>The Theology of Parmenides is similar to our own.</margin> This, therefore, is that most sublime Theology of Parmenides, which is indeed very similar to our own <note>Kircher refers here to Christian theology</note>, which believes that God is from Himself, out of Himself, and through Himself; that He is unbegotten, without beginning, without end, immaterial, indivisible, perfect, eternal; that He is in all things and is all things; the very same, established by Himself, independent, invariable, unmixed, incomprehensible, and inestimable—which can neither be sustained, nor carried, nor tracked down. For whence, and whither, and where, or how, or of what kind He may be, is unknown, as Hermes (besides our own writers) also left written in the *Asclepius*. From these points it is clear that Parmenides should be numbered not among the Natural Philosophers, but among the Theologians; for his dogmas require a "deep swimmer" <note>A metaphor for a profound thinker capable of navigating deep waters</note>, as even Plato testifies in the *Parmenides*. <margin>Aristotle wrongly rebukes Parmenides.</margin> Moreover, Theophrastus (according to Simplicius) calls him and his teacher Xenophanes "Theologians," as do Nicolaus of Damascus and Alexander of Aphrodisias. Thus, Aristotle is surely to be blamed for translating Parmenides' writings—concerning the one, unbegotten, incorruptible, eternal, invariable, and infinite God—into the language of natural principles, and for rebuking him because he said the principle of all things is one and immobile.

<margin>Melissus’s opinion concerning God.</margin> Melissus, therefore, following in the footsteps of his teacher Parmenides, brought forth the very same ideas concerning God, whom he likewise called "That Which Is" <note>original: "id quod est" — a translation of the Greek 'To On' or Being</note>. He added only this: that he judged nothing should be defined concerning God, for he said (according to Laërtius) that we possess no certain knowledge of Him. However, he investigated the first Being of all—which he asserted to be one, true, unbegotten, incorruptible, infinite, and independent—by this method of reasoning. <margin>Melissus.</margin> For he began his work thus, as Simplicius records in his commentary on the first book of the *Physics* (comm. 18):

> *If indeed nothing exists, how can anything be said of it as if it were something? But if it is something, it is either begotten or it always is. But if it is begotten, it is either begotten from that which is, or from that which is not. But it can neither happen that something is made from that which is not, nor indeed can anything else which is, much less that which is absolutely. Nor can it come from that which is; for in that case, it would already be that which it is, and would not be "becoming" or being begotten. Therefore, "That Which Is" is not begotten; therefore, "That Which Is" always is. Nor shall "That Which Is" perish; for it cannot happen that "That Which Is" changes into that which is not, nor into that which is; for in the latter case it would remain, and not perish. Therefore, "That Which Is" was not begotten, nor shall it perish; therefore it always was, and shall be. But since that which is begotten has a beginning, that which is not begotten has no beginning. Therefore, "That Which Is," being unbegotten, had no beginning. Furthermore, that which perishes has an end; but if there is something that cannot perish, it has no end. That which has neither beginning nor end is infinite. Therefore, "That Which Is" is infinite; and if it is infinite, it is One; for if there were two, it would be impossible for them to be infinite, but they would have boundaries between one another. But "That Which Is" is infinite. Therefore, there are not many things that exist. Therefore, "That Which Is" is One. And if it is one, it is immobile. For "That Which Is" is always similar to itself; and that which is similar can neither perish, nor become greater, nor be converted into another*
-> *arrangement,* <-

<summary>Kircher argues that the Pre-Socratic philosophers Parmenides and Melissus were actually theologians whose concept of the "One" mirrors both Christian doctrine and Egyptian Hermetic wisdom. He defends them against Aristotle's physical interpretations, emphasizing God as an infinite, eternal, and immobile Being.</summary>

# SUMMARY OF THE ENTIRE WORK. 573 CHAPTER I.

[The One Being] will not suffer, nor will it be affected by any pain or distress. For if any of these things were to fall upon it, it would by no means be one. For that which is moved by any motion is changed from something and into something else. But there was nothing else besides that which is, therefore it will not be moved, especially since there is no vacuum <note>original: "vacuum," referring to empty space or non-existence</note> in that which is: therefore, that which is does not move, for it cannot withdraw, since there is nowhere that is empty. And a vacuum is nothing, etc.

<margin>The Theology of Melissus is similar to ours. Trismegistus.</margin> Truly, one may recognize the entire Theology of the Hebrews and Christians in these words. For Melissus calls God—just as his teacher Parmenides did—"that which is" <note>original: "id quod est," a Latin rendering of the Greek philosophical concept of Being, echoing the divine name revealed to Moses</note>, following not only Moses in the third chapter of Exodus, but also Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage</note> in the *Asclepius* when he said: *God alone is, and deservedly he alone is in himself, and from himself, and around himself, whole, full, and perfect. And he is established in his own form, nor can he be moved by the impulse of anyone, nor by place, since all things are in him, and he alone is in all things.* Thus he spoke. For this reason, Melissus asserted that "that which is" lacks a beginning and an end, because it is unbegotten and exists from itself. But if it is unbegotten and never to perish, it is deservedly called infinite; if infinite, then one; for two or more things could not be infinite, since they would have boundaries between them. And if it is infinite, it is immobile and always similar to itself, not divided, not flowing, not distinct, but the whole at once, always the same, always full, always perfect; therefore it is not moved, because it does not change from one thing into another, nor does it pass from place to place, since it fills all things, contains all things, extending itself to all things: for as Trismegistus used to say: <margin>Trismegistus</margin> *Outside of God, nothing; outside of nothing, God.*

This is that most profound Theology of Melissus concerning God, which Aristotle criticized, dragging it down to the level of Physics. This is that <term>One Being</term> <note>original: "Ens unum," the fundamental philosophical concept of a single, unified reality</note> which Plato also handed down in the *Parmenides*, celebrating its excellence. This is also that "one" which Aristotle—being somewhat inconsistent with himself—so celebrated in the work called the *Metaphysics*, exclaiming: <margin>Aristotle wrongly criticizes Melissus.</margin> *There cannot be many Gods, and it is necessary that there be one God. The rule of many, he says, is not good; for Beings do not wish to be poorly disposed. Therefore, let there be one Prince, let there be one King.* This is the same One Being whose Act of Understanding and Intellect are the same as the thing perceived by the intelligence, as Parmenides said, and from whom Aristotle borrowed that very idea in the third book of *On the Soul*, text 19. This is that One Being of Parmenides: unchangeable, simple, pure, sincere, and needing nothing; borrowing from this, Aristotle wrote in the first book of *On the Heavens*, text 100: *It is necessary that the Divine itself be unchangeable, being the first and most supreme; for it possesses no depravity, nor is it in need of any of its own goods.*

<margin>Plato's opinion concerning God.</margin> But Plato also, in the *Parmenides*, confirmed these same things drawn from the fountains of these Theologians, so that even from these you may recognize that these men spoke most profoundly concerning the Deity. For in that Dialogue in which Plato discourses on the "One," he teaches things truly similar to what Parmenides and Melissus established concerning the Deity. These points, scattered here and there through that Dialogue, sound thus when collected into one from Champier <note>Symphorien Champier (1471–1539), a French physician and philosopher</note>, book three of *Platonic Philosophy*, chapter one: *The One itself (says Plato) is not many, nor does it have a part, nor a whole, nor a beginning, nor an end, nor a middle; it is infinite and formless, and is circumscribed by no place.*

<summary>This page argues that ancient philosophers like Melissus, Parmenides, and Plato shared a unified theological vision of God as the "One Being," aligning their teachings with those of Moses and Hermes Trismegistus. Kircher defends these early thinkers against Aristotle's criticisms, asserting they understood God as an infinite, unchangeable, and all-encompassing reality.</summary>

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

### CHAPTER I.

*...it will be [limited], it remains nowhere, it is moved by no motion of place or alteration, nor is it made in any way; it is neither the same as itself nor different from another, nor like nor unlike, nor equal nor unequal, nor old nor new, nor in any time, but entirely without time. For this reason, it was neither generated, nor is it being generated, nor was it ever, nor has it just now been made, nor is it being made, nor is it, nor will it be hereafter, nor will it be generated, nor will it exist, nor is it a participant in or the Prince of substance. For these words—was, was becoming, was generated—signify past time; while will be, will become, and will be generated signify the future; but is, is being generated, and is being made signify the present. However, that which is subject to no time, neither was, nor is, nor will be. From which it follows that no name has been bestowed upon it, no definition is given, no knowledge exists; it is neither spoken of, nor thought of, nor known, nor perceived by any being. These are the words of Plato in the Parmenides, though collected as a few points out of many.* <note>original: "ista enim verba...". Kircher is paraphrasing the famous "negative theology" of Plato's Parmenides, which argues that the absolute "One" cannot be described by any human categories.</note>

<margin>Plotinus's opinion on God.</margin> But Plotinus also, in the sixth book of the fifth Ennead, confirmed this very point with many arguments, proving that the One Being, existing as one and the same, is simultaneously whole everywhere. These ideas, surely drawn from Parmenides and Melissus, Plato was the first to receive, and he himself later published them as if drawn from the very fountains of Theology. He proves there through many points that all things are one, as Parmenides and Melissus used to say—not indeed by a unity of individual essence (for no one would have said that), but because all things are in the One as if in an Idea, and flow from the One as if from a beginning, and are led back and flow together toward the One as if toward an end by a certain natural inclination of desire. You will find more there concerning these matters, which are in harmony with this most sublime Theology that Parmenides and Melissus handed down.

<margin>The inscription of the Delphic temple.</margin> The Delphic temple, according to the testimony of Plutarch, displayed this inscription: *EI* <note>Greek: εἶ</note>; that is, *Thou Art*. Those entering used to salute God by saying *EI*, that is, *Thou art*; as if they were saying: "You alone are One, in whom there is nothing prior, nothing posterior, nothing future, nothing past, nothing older, nothing more recent; but since you are One and True Being, you fill an everlasting duration in a single 'Now,' and by reason of this, that which is said 'to be,' you truly are—not future, not past, neither having a beginning nor destined to end." With all of which Orthodox writers agree.

It was not without cause, therefore, that the Egyptians, when they wished to express the incomprehensible nature of God, depicted Sigalion <note>Kircher refers to Sigalion (Harpocrates), the god of silence, depicted as a youth with a finger to his lips, a common motif in Kircher's interpretation of Egyptian "silent" theology.</note> as a boy urging silence with his finger. By this it was hinted that the incomprehensible God is to be worshipped and adored not so much by curious investigation as by sacred silence. Truly, he who desires to know all these things more clearly should approach the <term>Sphinx Mystagoga</term> <note>Literally "The Sphinx who leads into the mysteries." This refers to Kircher's own method or perhaps a specific section of his work where he explains the hidden meanings of symbols.</note>, Arithmetic, and Geometry, as well as Music and Hieroglyphic Theology. There he will find everything concerning God, His goodness, His providence, and how all things come from one fire, and how He flows into His creatures, most amply described in the hieroglyphic manner according to the mind of the Ancients. For whatever the aforementioned authors handed down at length concerning the divine nature, only he who has not penetrated the interpretations provided in this Work could fail to know that all those things proceeded from the Pillars of Hermes <note>original: "columnis Mercurij". These are the legendary pillars on which the god Hermes/Thoth was said to have inscribed all ancient wisdom and scientific knowledge.</note>.

<summary>Kircher uses the philosophy of Plato and Plotinus alongside the Delphic "Thou Art" to argue that God is a timeless, incomprehensible unity. He concludes that the Egyptian figure of Harpocrates (silence) represents the only proper way to approach this divine mystery.</summary>

# RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK. 575 CH. I.

-> ### Corollary. <-

<margin>A compendium of Egyptian Theology</margin>
**F**rom what has been said, the following inferences are clear. If God is the good, the one, the beginning and the first, then before the first there is nothing; after the first are all things; from the beginning all things; from the good all things; from the supreme triune Divinity <note>original: "triuno Numine"</note> all things: from the one comes primeval unity; from unity first come all unities; from unities come essences; from essences, lives; from lives, minds; from minds, souls; from souls, natures; from natures, qualities; from qualities, forms; from forms, bodies. All these are contained in this worldly house of the universe; through all of which a descent is prepared from the first to the last, and from the last an ascent and return is prepared back to the first, to God. Behold the compendium of all Egyptian Philosophy.

## § II.

### Concerning the Egyptian doctrine of the triune principle.

<margin>The Egyptians knew the Triune God.</margin>
**W**e have shown throughout from the works of Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> that the Egyptians believed in a triune principle of all things, which they also call the triform Divinity; this they expressed hieroglyphically by a winged globe teeming with a Serpent.

<note>Hieroglyphic emblem: A winged disk or egg, flanked by two outspread wings, with two serpents (uraei) emerging from the central body. This represents Kircher's "Agathodaemon" or the triune generative principle.</note>

Almost all followers of the Pythagorean and Platonic Schools embraced this dogma. I shall now reveal how they recognized the triune within the one.

From the Hermetic fragments <note>Texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth.</note> it is gathered that from the beginning, from the one, from God, all things were made; for without a beginning nothing was made. Moreover, the beginning comes from nothing except itself; but the beginning, as has been demonstrated, is the "one" itself. "One" and the <term>Monad</term> <note>The number one, representing the indivisible source of all things.</note> are the same according to the same Hermes: <gloss>for the Monad is the beginning of all things, and the root, existing in all things.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ἡ γὰρ μονὰς πάντων ἔζα ἀρχὴ, καὶ ῥίζα, ἐν πᾶσιν ἐστὶ."</note> Therefore, since the Monad is the beginning, it contains every number while being contained by none; it generates every number while being generated by no other number.

<margin>How the Monad is the beginning and root of all.</margin>
Hence, not without reason, it is called by Hermes the <gloss>paternal Monad</gloss> <note>original Greek: "μονὰς πατρικὴ"</note>; if it is paternal, it therefore generates. But what? Surely that which is second in nature after the first itself: namely, the number two. Therefore, the Monad generates two before all things.

<margin>The Monad generates the Dyad.</margin>
<gloss>For to every thing the Monad has extended, which generates two,</gloss> <note>original Greek: "Παντὶ γὰρ μονὰς, ἡ δύο γεννᾷ"</note> says Zoroaster <note>The ancient Persian prophet, to whom many mystical "Chaldean Oracles" were attributed in the Renaissance.</note>; which he also names the <term>Dyad</term> <note>The number two, representing duality or the first step away from unity.</note> sitting beside the Father: <gloss>for the Dyad sits beside him</gloss> <note>original Greek: "δύας γὰρ παρὰ τῷ κάθηται"</note>. Thus the Monad, joined to the Dyad, constitutes the <term>Triad</term> <note>The number three, or Trinity.</note>, which he teaches shines everywhere: <gloss>For in the whole World the Triad shines, of which the Monad is the Prince.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "παντὶ γὰρ ἐν κόσμῳ λάμπει τριὰς, ἧς μονὰς ἀρχὴ"</note>

<margin>Zoroaster. Zoroaster's opinion on the Trinity.</margin>
According to them, this entire Monad results in three principles (because these three are one principle): which rule the World so that all things serve them: <gloss>for by certain principles, you may understand, all things serve these three.</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ἀρχαῖς γὰρ τισὶ τῇ δὲ λάβας δουλ’ειν ἅπαντα"</note> Hence he often calls that Monad the father and the first principle, but the second he calls the <gloss>paternal self-generated mind</gloss> <note>original Greek: "πατρικὸν νόον αὐτογένεθλον"</note>...

It argues that ancient Egyptians recognized a triune Godhead symbolized by the winged disk.</summary>

# CHAPTER I.

He names the power of the Father with these words: <term>for the Mind, having enclosed its own fire within its power</term> <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ νοῦς ἐν ἑᾷ δυνάμει κλείσας ἴδιον πῦρ</note>. Nor did he enclose his own fire within his power alone. Indeed, he calls the third principle the "Second Mind"; <term>the Father commanded these things, and the Mind delivered them to the second</term> <note>original Greek: ταῦτα δὲ ἐπέταξε πατήρ, καὶ νοῦς παρεδίδου δευτέρῳ</note>. The Father perfected all things and delivered them to the Second Mind. He calls it the "Second Mind" because that <term>self-begotten</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτογένεθλος; meaning born of itself</note> one was the first generated by and from itself, and is the boundary of the paternal depth, yet in such a way that it remains within the paternal depth, <term>neither going forth, but standing firm in the paternal abyss</term> <note>original Greek: μήτε προελθών, ἀλλ’ ἑδραῖος ἐν τῷ πατρικῷ βυθῷ</note>. Furthermore, he calls this <term>self-working and the fiery architect of the world, having perceived by fire</term> <note>original Greek: αὐτοργὸν καὶ τῇ πυρίᾳ τεχνίτην κόσμου, καὶ τῷ πῦρ νοήσας</note>—operating from itself, the craftsman of the World—the "Mind of Mind." <margin>Trismegistus’s opinion on the Trinity.</margin> Trismegistus indeed calls him <term>the Lord of all, and God, and Source, and Life, and Power, and Light, and Mind, and Spirit</term> <note>original Greek: πάντων τὸν κύριον, καὶ Θεόν, καὶ πηγήν, καὶ ζωὴν, καὶ δύναμιν, καὶ φῶς, καὶ νοῦν, καὶ πνεῦμα</note>, and asserts the three-in-one in these words: *There was one sole intellectual light before the intellectual light, and there was always the shining Mind of Mind: and the union of this was nothing other than the spirit connecting all things, always existing in itself, <term>always containing all things in its own mind, light, and spirit</term> <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ ἐν ἑαυτῷ νῷ, καὶ φωτὶ, καὶ πνεύματι πάντα περιέχων</note>.* Always containing all things by its own Mind, light, and spirit. Where, surely, by mind, light, and spirit, he seems to hint at nothing other than the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And that he feels this way is expressly taught in the cited passage. *From the first mind*, he says, *the shining Word, the Son of God, is the same as the Father, <term>and their union is from one another; for the union of these is life</term> <note>original Greek: ἡ δὲ ἕνωσις αὐτῶν ἀπ’ ἀλλήλων· ἕνωσις γὰρ τούτων ἡ ζωή</note>.* For they are not distant from one another, but their union is life; and elsewhere he also called it <term>consubstantial with the Creator</term> <note>original Greek: τῷ δημιουργῷ ὁμοούσιον</note>, that is, *consubstantial with the Father*. <margin>Trismegistus’s opinion on the creation of the World.</margin> He says that the Mind, with the Word, established seven Governors, who contain the sensible World within circles. <term>But his Word, being entirely perfect and fertile, falling into fertile nature and fertile water, made the water pregnant</term> <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ λόγος αὐτοῦ περιφθῶν παντελῶς, ὢν καὶ γόνιμος, τῷ δημιουργὸς ἐν γονίμῳ φύσει πεσών, τῇ γονίμῳ ὕδατι, ἔγκυον τὸ ὕδωρ ἐποίησε</note>. *For the Word proceeding from him, being most perfect and falling into fertile nature, made the generative water pregnant. <term>The Father-Creator made the whole world, not with hands, but by the Word</term> <note>original Greek: Τὸν πάντα κόσμον ἐποίησεν ὁ δημιουργὸς ὁ πατὴρ, οὐ χερσὶν, ἀλλà λόγῳ</note>.* The Father-Creator made the entire World, not with hands, but by the Word. And these are the most ancient dogmas of all sacred Theology, proclaimed to the primeval world by Zoroaster and Hermes (whom we have, however, conflated in the Pamphilian Obelisk); so that consequently <margin>Proclus.</margin> Proclus asserts this doctrine to be <term>divinely handed down and God-given</term> <note>original Greek: Θεοπαράδοτον, καὶ θεόδοτον</note>. The Holy Fathers have at all times admired this as if uttered by men inspired by the divine spirit. Orpheus, then, illustrated by the splendor of this doctrine, <margin>The opinion of Orpheus and Plato on the Trinity.</margin> also recognized this triad, which he asserts as Phanes, Uranus, and Cronus—one Deity distinguished by three names; Plato indeed called them the "Three Kings," and Egyptian Theology, delivered by word of mouth by Plato and <margin>Aristotle.</margin> proclaimed by Aristotle, confirms it in these words: *Therefore we assert that God created the first Intellect, and established it as the Procreator of other things; but he created it by means of the Word; how? for no other medium intervenes between God and the Intellect except the Word, which was also the coagulant of the Intellect.* And from these authors, most of the Platonists took the occasion for the following opinions <margin>The opinion of the Platonists on the Trinity.</margin> in their treatises on the three principles; such as Porphyry, Plotinus, Iamblichus, Proclus, Syrianus, and Damascius; in which, although they disagreed among themselves regarding these three principles, they all nevertheless seem to have agreed in this: that they made these three the principles of all things and of the entire World, or the three founding substances.

# RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK.

But how those first <term>Theosophists</term> <note>Literally "God-wise" men; those who possess divine wisdom.</note> were advanced to such great enlightenment of the mind might deservedly seem a wonder to anyone. However, he who has read our teachings scattered throughout this work will easily be freed from the doubt he has conceived. For since we have demonstrated everywhere that Hermes was of the lineage of Canaan and a <term>contemporary</term> <note>original Greek: σύγχρονον (synchronon)</note> of Abraham, it could not have happened otherwise than that his curious and all-knowing mind fished out many things from them concerning true and right Theology. This theology they held as having proceeded by word of mouth from the first-created man <note>Adam</note> and derived in a continuous succession down to Noah. Among these secrets of divine revelation, the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity was not the least; which he then handed down to posterity clothed in various coverings of symbols. All the ancient Philosophers, following the Egyptians, called this Triune Deity of the Most Holy Trinity an insuperable, incomprehensible, eternal, and infinite power and mind, existing always and everywhere. It is an insuperable power because it prevails by infinite virtue, and therefore it cannot be grasped. It exists everywhere and always, filling all things with its infinite existence. Hence Orpheus says, *You who contain all parts of the World, devoid of generation*; and Virgil, *All things are full of Jove*. Since, therefore, He fills all things by His power and is within all things, providing life and motion to the individual bodies of the World; hence, not without reason, <margin>What the Triune Deity of the Holy Trinity is according to the Egyptians.</margin> Dionysius <margin>Dionysius the Areopagite.</margin> calls the same <term>mundane, circum-mundane, supra-mundane, super-celestial, and super-substantial</term> <note>original Greek: κόσμιον, περικόσμιον, ὑπερκόσμιον, ὑπερουράνιον, καὶ ὑπερούσιον</note>. He also calls Him Star, Sun, Fire, Water, Spirit, Dew, Cloud, Stone, all existing things, and nothing of existing things; and thus filling all things, He makes all things resound. The Egyptians felt the same way.

How truly God, the Best and Greatest, is unfolded through a concatenation of Divinities into the triple World—the Angelic, the Sidereal <note>The world of the stars and planets.</note>, and the <term>Hylic</term> <note>The material or physical world; from the Greek 'hyle' for matter.</note>; how the same, and by what ceremonies the individual Divinities of the World-chains are to be attracted; by what rites and sacrifices they are to be appeased if they should ever be angry; has been declared everywhere in this whole work from the all-encompassing erudition of Oriental Theologians, Philosophers, and Poets alike.

Since, therefore, the instructors of hieroglyphic doctrine had no other aim or intention than to bring it about—through this hidden context of sacred symbols analogous to the supreme Deity and the <term>world-chains of Intelligences</term> <note>The hierarchical series of spiritual beings connecting God to the material world.</note>—that they might derive the influence of the divinity and the Genii connected to it through very similar rites and sacrifices, not only for the public but also for the private good; and as this was the sum of all Egyptian Wisdom (that is, the hieroglyphic doctrine) by the consensus of all, and we have set it forth in this work as is evident from innumerable authorities; it is certain that this interpretation of ours is true and genuine, and not different from the intention of the <term>Hieromants</term> <note>Priests or interpreters of sacred mysteries.</note>.

# I.

->*The Purification of Minds among the Egyptians, necessary for the reception of divine influences.*<-

<margin>The care for purifying the soul among the Egyptians.</margin>
Since they truly knew that the proposed goal—which was <term>theomorphosis</term> <note>original: "θεομόρφωσις"; becoming like God or deification</note> or <term>sacrifice</term> <note>original: "ϑυσία"; here used in the sense of a sacred offering of the self</note>, by which they believed themselves to be thoroughly conformed to God and blessed with the happiness of all good things and sciences—could by no means be attained without chaste and religious actions and the exercise of good works; hence they applied themselves to these with such zeal as we read no other nation has done. But let us prove all these things from various learning, in the order in which <margin>Pansa.</margin> Pansa <note>Mutio Pansa, an author who wrote on the libraries of the ancient world</note>, a not ignoble author, recorded them.

Furthermore, all the ancient Sages warn that the soul must be purged of vices so that one may be made similar to God. For in this way, the knowledge of divine things will become known to us. There exists an epistle of Lysis the Pythagorean to Hipparchus concerning the purification necessary before Philosophy, in which he teaches that all vices must be expelled from souls so that one may obtain true knowledge of human and divine matters. Plato certainly thought that a successive and continuous purification of the soul was necessary before being admitted to the highest mysteries of philosophy: which he taught at the beginning of the Seventh book of the *Republic*, when he wished to lead men nourished in a dark cave out to behold the most splendid radiance of the Sun. He declared and distinguished this entire purification more clearly in the *Sophist*, where he demonstrated that this purification is nothing other than casting out what is depraved from the soul and preserving the rest; and he discusses in the same place how there are two species of depravity in the soul, namely Wickedness and Ignorance, by which minds are hindered from ascending to the knowledge of the highest things. But first of all, <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of Egyptian wisdom</note> asserted this, when in the first discourse of the <term>Poimandres</term> <note>The first treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum</note>, having been asked in what way one might ascend to life, he replied that it could happen when a man, being a partaker of the Mind, perceives himself: for the Mind is not in all men, but only in those who are pious, good, pure, religious, and holy, and who yield the body to its death, loathing the allurements of the senses, deeming the enticements of the senses to be lethal, closing the entrance to foul flatteries, and extinguishing the fuel of lusts; but on the contrary, the Mind is absent from the ignorant, the envious, the wicked, the idle, the unjust, murderers, and the impious, and dwells very far from them.

<margin>Purification of the soul is necessary before the illumination of God.</margin>
From which words we have most clearly that, before the illumination of God, a certain purification of the soul is necessary, which is accustomed to take its beginning from an affection directed toward God. Indeed, in Plato’s fifth book of the *Republic*, Philosophy meditates on nothing other than God himself; for Philosophy ought not to be occupied in other things than in the knowledge of the Good and the True itself, since it is itself the gift of God, as Plato says in the *Timaeus*.

<summary>Kircher argues that the ancient Egyptians required spiritual purification and moral virtue as prerequisites for attaining divine wisdom, a tradition he links to Hermes Trismegistus, Pythagoras, and Plato. He emphasizes that true philosophy is a gift from God accessible only to the pure of heart.</summary>

# II.

->*Necessary Silence.*<-

<margin>In what the purification of the soul consists.</margin>
**T**his purification of souls consists not only in the expulsion of vices from the mind, but also in a fitting silence regarding the mysteries. For the secrets of Philosophy are not to be divulged to everyone. Indeed, the eyes of common souls are unable to endure the rays of divinity, as Melissus <note>Melissus of Samos, a Pre-Socratic philosopher</note> used to say. For this reason, Pythagoras considered those who shared the gifts of Wisdom with people whose minds had not been cleansed and purified—not even in their dreams—to be equally impious and unjust as those who exposed the mysteries of the Eleusinian Goddess <note>Demeter; a reference to the Eleusinian Mysteries of ancient Greece</note> to the profane. <margin>Divine mysteries must be hidden.</margin> For it is not right to offer to just anyone those things which are preserved and acquired through such great labors. This is also what Christ the Lord taught when he said that the Holy thing must not be given to Dogs, nor Pearls cast before Swine, in Matthew 7. For this cause, they say that Hipparchus the Pythagorean was accused and expelled from the School, and that a pillar was erected for him as if for a dead man, because he had openly written down the decrees of Pythagoras which the master himself had always kept hidden; as <margin>Clement. Nazianzen. Cantherus. Plato.</margin> Clement <note>Clement of Alexandria</note> testifies in the 5th book of the *Stromata*, and Nazianzen <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note> in his letter to Nyssen, as well as Cantherus in the first book of *Various Readings*, chapter 12. Furthermore, Plato asserted the same in his second letter to Dionysius, in which place he eloquently discourses on not publishing Wisdom to everyone and on maintaining the purification of the soul. For he says that *an investigation of divine matters not rightly performed—that is, not equipped with the required steps of both purification and discipline—is the cause of all evils; namely, that those who investigate God in such a way eventually reach a point where they either deny that God exists, or affirm things about God which do not belong to God.* Thus he spoke. For this reason Pythagoras, whom Plato venerates in all things, began the sacred mysteries of his teachings with a most exacting expiation of the mind; and Plato similarly commands that secrets not be brought out to the common people, lest the common people, having received them perversely, either despise them or fall into errors. He judges in that same place that the secrets of the Deity are more safely committed to words than to letters, for letters make things common to anyone. In these words, Plato seems to have followed the ancient custom of the Jews, who assert that the mystical sense of the Law was handed down from God himself through Moses, not so much in letters as entrusted to the soul. The Pythagoreans certainly observed this, and Pythagoras himself publicly forbade philosophizing <note>original: "philosophari"; here meaning to discuss philosophy openly</note>, as Lysias is the author in his letter to Hipparchus. Moreover, when he set forth his records to his daughter Dama, he forbade her to hand them over to anyone outside the family. She, although she could have sold such books for much money, refused; she judged poverty and her parent's command to be more precious and more ancient than gold. They say that she, when about to die, gave this same command to her daughter Bistalia, and all this was done lest the mysteries of the Deity become common to everyone.

# III.

## ->The method and reasoning to be observed in purification.<-

<margin>How the soul is to be purified. Trismegistus.</margin>But now let us discuss how the soul must be purified, so that the knowledge of divine things may become known to us. In this, we must first listen to Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus.</note> in the 7th Discourse of the *Pimander*, where he speaks in this manner: *First, however, it is necessary (he says) to strip off the garment you carry about, which is the clothing of ignorance, the foundation of wickedness, the bond of corruption, the dark veil, a living death, a sensing corpse, a walking tomb, and finally, a domestic thief; who, while he flatters, hates; and while he hates, envies. Such is the enemy shadow that you carry about. It drags you downward toward itself, lest perhaps by beholding the beauty of Truth and the nearby good, you might hate its wickedness, and lest you might eventually perceive the snares which it constantly plots against you. This dulls and blunts the edge of the inner senses, suffocating them with thick matter; it intoxicates them with abominable and loathsome pleasure, so that you may never hear, nor perceive those things which by right ought to be heard, and especially to be looked upon.* Thus he spoke: Therefore, it is necessary to strip off the "old man" <note>A reference to the Pauline concept of the "old self" (vetus homo) in Romans 6:6.</note> and lay aside the sensuality of the body, so that one purified in soul may be able to contemplate divine things. But even these things are not enough; the soul must be raised up into God, and, so to speak, "deified," so that one may be able to understand God. Because of this, Trismegistus again exclaims in the second part of the *Pimander*, Discourse 1: <margin>Trismegistus.</margin> *Unless (he says) you make yourself equal to God, you will never understand God. For like is always known by its like.* Thus he spoke. But what is it to make oneself equal to God, if not to cling to God and become one with God? *He who adheres to God,* says Paul, *becomes one spirit with God.* 1 Corinthians 6. <margin>The soul is purified by the pursuit of mortification.</margin> Moreover, we adhere to God most of all through the rectitude of the soul—not as the Stoics wished, and especially Chrysippus, who in his book *On Nature* claimed that no Wise Man is surpassed by Jove <note>Jupiter/Zeus</note>, and for that reason considered the rectitude by which a good man acts to be an equality with God—but rather so that, joined to God through grace, one may do those things which God commands, or which He judges and desires to be done. Pythagoras, however, extended this "equalization" to a transformation into God, when he sang thus in his *Golden Verses*:

<margin>Pythagoras.</margin>
> *When, however, having left the body, you go free to the upper air,*
> *You shall be an immortal God, incorruptible, and no longer mortal.*

Furthermore, he took this from Trismegistus, who left it written in the first Discourse of the *Pimander*: *And (he says) that is the supreme good of those to whom the lot of knowing falls: namely, to become God.* Therefore, the soul must be stripped from the body—not by a true separation <note>i.e., physical death</note>, but by the mortification of sensible pleasures—so that one may be able to understand divine things. And so that one may be transformed into God, the soul must be deified; that is, it must be rendered as similar to God as possible. Whence also Zoroaster said in an Oracle: *Man, in a certain way, draws God into himself when, retaining nothing mortal, he is entirely intoxicated by divine draughts.*

# RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK. CHAPTER I.

Man, therefore, passes into God through separation from the allurements of the flesh; he also passes through faith, according to the Theology of John: *He gave them power to become the sons of God, to those who believe in his name, John 1.* Whence these are also called the sons of God through adoption, according to that passage in Romans 8: *In which we cry out, Abba, Father.* <note>The author is linking the mystical "becoming God" with the biblical concept of adoption into God's family.</note> Moreover, Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> explains this beautifully in the second part of the *Pymander*, Chapter 1, where, speaking of this equalization with God, he says: *Extend yourself into magnitude without limit; emerge from the body; transcend all time; become eternity. Thus, finally, you shall know God.* In this passage, he suggests not only the purification of the soul but also a real separation of the soul from the body, which the Greeks call *ecstasy* <note>original: "extasin"</note> and the Hebrews call the <term>kiss of death<note>Hebrew: "Neshika." A mystical term for a death experienced in a state of divine contemplation, where the soul leaves the body out of love for God.</note></term>. This second purification follows the first. But regarding the casting off of vices and the lifting of the soul to the highest heights, hear how Hermes expressed it in the tenth Discourse of the *Pymander*. <margin>Trismegistus.</margin> *It is impossible, O son,* he says, *for the soul of man lying in the filth of the body to assume the divine form; nor is it permitted to gaze upon the beauty of God, unless one has been reformed into God from that state.* See how he asserts one must rise from the filth of the body and commands man to be reformed into God, so that he may be able to understand divine things. <margin>Zoroaster.</margin> Zoroaster, in the *Oracles*, wished for "expellers of the soul" to be summoned so that one might assume the divine form; for he wrote thus: *Summon the expellers of the soul.* <margin>Two expellers of the soul are required to purify it.</margin> This was said because, since there are two primary diseases of the soul—namely ignorance and malice (or wickedness), as Plato taught in the *Sophist*—two expellers or constant Physicians are likewise required: namely, doctrine and purity of life. Yet not just any doctrine, but celestial and divine doctrine, by which the knowledge of GOD descends into us and ignorance is driven out. This consists chiefly in Faith, for unless divine things are believed, they are not understood.

And lest anyone think he is dreaming in this exposition, one must also listen to <margin>Proclus.</margin> Proclus, who confirms these things as follows: *For those who desire to reach the highest good, there is no need for science or the exercise of the intellect, but for firmness of soul, quiet, and tranquility, which is indeed divine Faith; it is this which draws and joins us to the highest good and all divine things by an ineffable reason. Truly, we ought not to seek the highest good or aspire to it through science or any action of the intellect, but rather offer and commend ourselves to the divine light, and with the senses closed, rest in that known and hidden Unity of Beings. For this kind of faith is more ancient than all doctrine.* Proclus wrote these most profound things regarding the faith necessary to know God, such that many believe he was instructed by St. Paul, being his contemporary <note>original: "synchronū"</note>; however, he more truly received this from Trismegistus, who in the ninth Discourse of the *Pymander* teaches that Faith is necessary for one wishing to understand God—not unlike Paul, who wished the intellect to be held captive in faith. <margin>Trismegistus's opinion on believing.</margin> For Hermes holds it thus: *To understand God is to believe; and not to believe is, without doubt, to be ignorant.* And a little further down: *For those things said of divine matters are believed when understood, and denied when not understood.* Certainly <margin>Plato.</margin> Plato, in the *Theaetetus*, taught that one must flee from the World into Heaven, so that one may become most like God; for he says: *Indeed, we must try to flee from here to there as <margin>What "flight from the world" means according to Plato.</margin> quickly as possible,* and declaring what he understands by "flight," he adds...

This is the flight itself: the likeness of God, as much as is possible within us. This likeness consists in our being holy and just, combined with prudence. This is the highest Theology of Plato regarding the preparation for understanding God and the things that belong to God; it is necessary, namely, that we be just and holy. In the sixth book of the *Republic*, he said, *Man is rendered like unto God when he imitates divine things.* Hence, in his book on *Laws*, he called the temperate man like unto God, but the intemperate man unlike Him. From this it followed that Theodoret, in the eleventh book of *Cures for Greek Affections* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD) was a Christian theologian who wrote this work to compare Greek philosophy with Christian truth.</note>, said that Plato established the goal of all good things to be that we should acquire the likeness of God as much as is in our power, for in this way we shall be able to understand God.

## IV.

->The Vessel <note>original: *Crater*</note> is necessary for purification.<-

<margin>A passage of Trismegistus is explained.</margin>
Since we have happened upon this subject, we must explain a passage of Hermes <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> in the fourth discourse of the *Pymander* <note>The *Poimandres*, the first and most famous book of the *Corpus Hermeticum*.</note>, which Plato followed in the *Timaeus*. For Hermes writes there that *God indeed imparted Speech <note>original: *Sermo* / Greek: *Logos*</note> to all men, but Mind <note>original: *Mens* / Greek: *Nous*</note> by no means so; not because He was envious—for all spite is absent from Him—but because He wished to set it in the midst as a prize and reward for souls. Therefore, filling a wide Vessel with Mind, He sent a herald, commanding him to announce such things to the souls of men: Let whichever soul is able dip itself into this bowl, namely that soul which believes the Vessel will lead it back to the One who sent it down; and which knows the purpose for which it was born. Therefore, whoever heard the proclamation and immersed themselves in Mind, they were made partakers of knowledge <note>original: *cognitio* / Greek: *Gnosis*</note>, and receiving Mind, they turned into perfect men. But those who neglected the proclamation, they remained partakers of Speech indeed, but devoid of Mind, ignorant of both the purpose for which they were generated and by whom.* So he says. This Theology of Hermes is sublime and most worthy of all contemplation. For he calls "Mind" that divine ray by which men are illuminated beyond the rational discourse from which speech proceeds; concerning which John says in Chapter 1: *It was the true light which illuminates every man.* Aristotle, in the third book *On the Soul*, calls it the <term>Active Intellect</term> <note>The part of the mind that makes thinking possible by "lighting up" concepts, often compared to light.</note>. Plotinus calls it <term>Intellect simply</term>, and before these, David called it "light" when he said in Psalm 35: *In your light we shall see light.* Pythagoras likewise called it by the same name of light. Augustine, however, calls it the "superior portion." The Hebrews call it <term>Neshamah</term> <note>The highest level of the soul in Jewish thought, representing the divine breath or intellect.</note>, or the "breath of lives." This Mind, therefore—this ray or light—is not given to all, although as Hermes explains in the fourth discourse of the *Pymander*, it dwells together with the souls of men who lack Mind; for even if it is within all, it is not perceived by all, as Plotinus testifies in Chapter 9 *On Beauty*, where he calls it an eye, saying: *Which eye all indeed possess, but few truly use.* This is what John had said before in the first chapter: *And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.* It is also called by Christ the "Kingdom of God," which is nothing other than the dwelling of divinity within us, revealed to us through the light and love of God. Which light, indeed, since Christ brought it to us, he not undeservedly said of himself—

## CHAPTER I.

He himself speaking said in John 17: *The Kingdom of God is within you.* <note>The author attributes the quote "The Kingdom of God is within you" to John 17, though it is famously found in Luke 17:21.</note> The same teacher warned that this Kingdom must be sought before all things, saying in Matthew 6: *Seek first the Kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added unto you.* Now, this Light is called the Kingdom because that divine element which dwells within us comes from a place which, among the more secret Theologians, is called in Hebrew <margin>What **Malchut** is</margin> **Malchut**, which signifies "Kingdom." For by the power of the Deity dwelling within us, we are Kings, and we are able to dominate and command all things, according to that passage in Luke 9: *Behold, I have given you (namely, through the communication of divinity) the power to tread upon Serpents and Scorpions, and over every power of the enemy.* It is also called *eternal life*, according to the saying: *This is eternal life, that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, John 17.* Therefore, the **Knowledge** of the Deity is the Mind, or the divine light—the light, I say, by which all men are illuminated; whence David says: *The light of your countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us.* 

With this **Mind or Light, God filled a wide Cup**, says Mercurius <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the "Hermetica" texts.</note>, and sent a herald to announce to souls that they should immerse themselves in it, so that they might thereby obtain both Mind and Wisdom. This **wide Cup** is the flowing and superabundant knowledge of things divine and human, which the Father established in the Word, in whom (as Paul says) *are all the treasures of the science and wisdom of God.* Moreover, that crying herald is the appetite and desire for knowing innate within us, of which it was said by Aristotle in the 1st book of the Metaphysics: *All men by nature desire to know*; or it is **Truth** itself, which alone is the food of the soul, filled with a certain incredible delight; or it is the <term>synderesis</term> <note>The innate spark of moral consciousness or the capacity to distinguish good from evil.</note> urging and impelling us toward the good. Whoever, therefore, has immersed themselves in the Cup, having attained the Mind, has known God. In this Cup, then, the soul must be immersed and washed, so that it may prevail in reaching divine things. And to speak plainly and with the veil removed, the full **Cup of the Mind** is the knowledge of the Son, through whom alone we ascend to the Father; *For no one knows the Father except the Son, and he to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him;* and again: *No one comes to the Father, except through me, John 14.* Mercurius advises that we must first know Him and first apply the soul to Him, so that we may be able to understand the other things that pertain to God. For this Word of God, the Messenger and Interpreter of God, came into the World for no other reason than to manifest the name of the Father to men. He can lead the soul back to where it came from, as Mercurius explains.

It is established that the **World consists of two Cups**, as the ancient Sages <margin>The World consists of two Cups: the superior, in which all things are pure; the inferior, in which all things are impure.</margin> advise. One of these is superior, in which all things are pure; this is that intelligible and exemplary World, according to whose likeness Plato testifies in the *Timaeus* that this sensible World was made. Of this, Christ said in John 8: *My Kingdom is not of this World*, affirming His Kingdom to be of that superior World, which elsewhere He calls the Kingdom prepared for His friends. The **other Cup** is the inferior one, most full of the knowledge of sensible things; those who drink more of this thirst more, and in it all things are impure, as if the good were mixed with the evil. Therefore, he who drinks from the first Cup, to which Mercurius <margin>Mercurius.</margin> invites us, there shall be in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. But he who drinks from the second shall thirst again. However, no one can drink in the first Cup unless first his own—

# CHAPTER I. 584 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER

...he should hate and trample upon the body, as Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the invention of writing and magic</note> suggests in the same passage, saying: *Unless you first hate your body, O son, you cannot love yourself; but as soon as you have loved yourself, you shall immediately attain the Mind.* This is to be understood such that one cannot love the true man—which according to Plato is the rational soul—unless he holds in hatred his opposite, namely the animal man. Christ himself taught this same principle in John 12: *He who loves his soul shall lose it; and he who hates his soul in this world, keeps it unto life eternal.* The reason for this is adduced by Mercury in that same place: that it is impossible for mortals to attend to both the mortal and the divine at once; whence Christ himself said in Matthew 6: *You cannot serve God and Mammon.* Therefore, the mind must be immersed in this <term>Crater</term> <note>The "Crater" or Mixing Bowl is a central concept in the Hermetica, representing a vessel filled with Mind (Nous) sent down by God for those seeking spiritual baptism</note> of divinity.

From this practice of washing in the Vessel which Mercury established, the Gymnosophists <note>literally "naked philosophers," a term used by Greeks to describe Indian ascetics</note> derived their custom of ablution. Among them, it was a sacred duty to wash with cold water three times by day and twice by night before they could enter the venerable inner sanctums of the sacred rites. They likewise wore a linen garment, freshly washed every day, for they considered wool to be a profane clothing, seeing it as the excrement of beastly filth shorn from livestock. The wisest men of India, whom they call Brahmans, observed the same. For it was their custom to wash in a certain fountain with their clothes removed, having first anointed the head with amber drops and scents suited for that purpose. Then, after they deemed themselves sufficiently clean according to the ritual, they went out as quickly as possible around midday to the sacred rites, dressed there in the manner of a Choir in white linen and a white miter, wearing rings on their fingers and carrying staffs in their hands. This cleanliness of body and dress, and other similar things, were believed to assist the purity of the soul in no small measure. Hence Hesiod sang in the book titled *Works and Days*:

<margin>Hesiod</margin>

> ->In the morning, beware of pouring a libation to Jove and the other gods above<-
> ->With unwashed hands. The Gods refuse filthy sacrifices.<-

<margin>Homer</margin>

Homer observed this custom most diligently in his work; for when he describes Telemachus about to pray to Pallas <note>Athena</note>, he first brings him to wash his hands in the sea; and when he brings forward Thetis, the mother of Achilles, to entreat Jove, he makes her emerge from the waves of the sea. Also in the 6th book of the *Iliad*, he sang thus:

> ->It is not fitting to pour out sparkling wine to Jove the supreme<-
> ->With unwashed hands; shame forbids doing this; for a man<-
> ->Defiled by blood and slaughter to pour out prayers to the Gods.<-

<margin>Maro</margin>

But also our Maro <note>Virgil, whose full name was Publius Vergilius Maro</note>, the "Ape of Homer" <note>A common Renaissance epithet for Virgil, acknowledging his skillful imitation and refinement of Homeric style</note>, observed this very thing in various places of his work, especially in the 2nd book of the *Aeneid*, where he sang:

> ->You, father, take the sacred objects and our ancestral gods in your hand;<-
> ->For me, having come from such great war and recent slaughter,<-
> ->It is a sin to touch them, until I have washed myself<-
> ->In a living stream.<-

# RECAPITULATION OF THE WHOLE WORK.

<margin>Ablution of the body is a symbol of the ablution in the mind.</margin>The ablutions of the body among the nations were, therefore, a symbol of the ablution in the mind, as can be gathered from what we have written. For the Ancients believed that the purification of the soul and the body were the same, so that when someone had washed his hands or body in a river, he was immediately made pure. Concerning this matter, <margin>Anticlides.</margin>Anticlides <note>A Greek historian who wrote on Alexander the Great and various regional histories.</note> writes thus in the 74th book of *Returns*: *It was,* he says, *the custom of the Ancients, which is even now preserved, that those who had committed the slaughter of men or other animals should wash their hands in perennial water for the purification of the crime committed.* Not only was it forbidden for the polluted to approach the altars, but they could not even pray to the Gods, who turned all their anger or indignation toward those praying in an impure state. <margin>Tymarchides.</margin>Tymarchides <note>A Greek poet and mythographer.</note> is a witness to this fact in his book *On Crowns*, who sang that Asterius was struck by a lightning bolt because he had touched the altar of Jupiter with impure hands. It goes as follows:

->With unwashed hands, pouring a libation, he touched the altar of Jove,<-
->Wherefore the Father burned him with the fire of a flaming bolt;<-
->It is right for only the exceptionally pure to touch sacred things.<-

---

But indeed, all these rites of the Nations were drawn from the monuments of the Hebrews, to whom it was said, *Wash yourselves, be clean, and be purified from all your defilements*, <margin>Isaiah. 2 Kings 6.</margin> in Isaiah 1. Moreover, because Uzzah <note>original: "Ozam"</note> dared to touch the Ark of the Lord, sacred History testifies in 2 Kings 6 that he fell dead before it.

God, therefore, offers himself to be known by pure and purified souls. <margin>Pythagoras.</margin> Moreover, the soul must be purified from vices and the senses; hence Pythagoras commanded that one must sacrifice to God with bare feet—that is, that passions must be laid aside when we wish to obtain something from God. For our passions, denoted by the feet, must be "unshod" while we sacrifice to God. Thus the Lord commanded <margin>Exodus 3.</margin> Moses to take off his shoes when He spoke to him in the bush in Exodus 3. Furthermore, Plato taught in the *Phaedo* that wings must be taken up and fastened to our souls, so that, having in a sense stripped off the body, we may ascend to higher things. According to Plato’s mind, these wings are contemplative and moral knowledge—namely, speculation and action; but according to Christian Theology, they are Faith and Charity, or the love of God and neighbor. Therefore, what Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> judges should be done through ablution in the Mixing-Bowl <note>The "Crater," a reference to the Hermetic *Corpus Hermeticum* IV, where souls dip into a bowl of Mind.</note>, Plato contends can be done through the fastening of wings to our souls. This was certainly first a dogma of Zoroaster, whom certain Chaldeans asserted was accustomed to say: that the soul is winged, but when the wings are broken it is carried headlong into the Elements, then as they grow back it flies back to the heavens. This dogma was certainly followed by <margin>Pythagoras. Plato. Plotinus.</margin> Pythagoras and Plato as well, and was confirmed by the great Plotinus in book 8 of the 4th *Ennead*, concerning the descent of souls into bodies. <margin>Rhodiginus.</margin>Rhodiginus <note>Ludovico Ricchieri, an Italian philologist.</note> is the author in book 9 of *Ancient Readings*, chapter 39, who states that the twin wings signify a twin instinct inborn in the mind toward heavenly things: in the intellect, an instinct toward divine Truth; in the will, an instinct turning toward the divine Good with all its strength. When these are relaxed, the Pythagoreans believe the soul falls from heaven.

But we must now listen to Plotinus in his book *On Beauty*, who most elegantly <margin>Plotinus.</margin> indicated this necessity of a pure mind. *Let it be done, therefore,* says Plotinus—

<summary>Kircher argues that ancient physical rituals of washing were symbols for mental and spiritual purification, a concept he traces from Hebrew scripture through Greek philosophy. He specifically links the "wings of the soul" in Plato and Zoroaster to the Christian virtues of Faith and Charity.</summary>

# CHAPTER I. 586 THE HIEROGLYPHIC THEATER OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>Purity of Mind is necessary; an Example regarding the purity of Mind.</margin> Plotinus <note>A major Greek-speaking philosopher of late antiquity, founder of Neoplatonism</note> says that whoever is to behold God and beauty must be divine, beautiful, and **God-like**. And a little earlier he writes: *If you do not yet recognize yourself as pure and beautiful, imitate the sculptor; for when he desires a beautiful statue, he cuts away part, straightens another, and scrapes to polish, smooths and wipes away, until he brings out a lovely face in the statue. So you too: remove what is superfluous, straighten the crooked, illuminate the dark by purging it, and do not cease working on your statue until the divine brilliance of Virtue shines upon you. If you achieve this, and dwell purely within yourself, having no impediment, and no longer needing a leader or judge; then, having become solitary, you will be able to behold that immense beauty. For it is necessary that the one who is to see becomes kindred and similar to the thing seen.* Thus far Plotinus.

<margin>Orpheus.</margin> But let us also hear Orpheus, who in the Songs he wrote concerning virtue—because he intended to relate hidden things about God—invites only those who, being purified in mind, cultivate virtue, but drives the profane as far away as possible. For thus he sang:

->*You who cultivate virtue, to my words alone*<-
->*Give ear, and direct your minds.*<-
->*But you who despise the holy laws, flee*<-
->*From here, and go far from here, you wretches, far off, you profane.*<-

<margin>Maro <note>Virgil</note>.</margin> Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil</note> sang similar things in the 6th book <note>of the Aeneid</note>, where he introduces the Sibyl, about to deliver her Oracles, crying out:

->***Far, O far away be ye, O profane ones,***<-
->***The Prophetess proclaims aloud.***<-

For this reason, to touch upon something of the secret wisdom of Zoroaster, he asserted that a certain vehicle must be boarded so that the soul may return to the place from whence it came. This vehicle is nothing other than the elevation of the mind toward God, which is perfected by prayer; as if you were to say, it is the joining of good work with prayer, as Gemistus <note>Plethon, a Byzantine scholar</note> prefers. <margin>Plato.</margin> Plato certainly established in the *Phaedrus* a certain chariot drawn by neighing horses, by which every soul is carried, but he says it must be ruled and moderated by a charioteer, lest it be carried headlong into a precipice. <margin>Philo.</margin> We have Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria</note> as an expositor of this saying in his book *On Agriculture*. *The horses,* he says, *are fury and concupiscence <note>intense desire</note>; the former male, the latter female. Therefore, the former, like a male, exults with a high neck, seeking liberty; but the latter, more feminine and cunning, grazes upon and devours the house like a woman. The rider and charioteer, however, is one: namely, the intellect. But he is a charioteer when he ascends with prudence; <margin>Plutarch.</margin> however, when he does so with imprudence, he is merely a rider.* Plutarch, in the 8th of his *Platonic Questions*, similarly interprets these horses as the concupiscible and irascible powers: calling the concupiscible <note>desiring</note> horse altogether stubborn, refractory, shaggy, deaf in the ears, and one who hardly obeys the whip or the spur. <margin>Philoponus.</margin> But the irascible <note>spirited/angry</note> horse is easily obedient to reason and is its helper. I know that Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a Christian commentator on Aristotle</note> explained both horses differently in his 1st book *On the Soul*, for he believed...
