# RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK. CHAPTER I.

...said that these are the faculty leading to higher and lower things. Therefore, this vehicle by which we are always carried and led is perhaps what **Zoroaster** <note>The legendary Persian prophet, often cited in Renaissance magic</note> advised us to cast off; explaining him, **Plato** in the *Phaedrus* added a Charioteer and a Ruler so that it might be rightly governed. Therefore, the Mixing Bowl or Vessel of **Mercury** <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, the wings of **Plato**, the vehicle of **Zoroaster**, the Pythagorean shedding of the body, and the Gymnosophist <note>Ancient Indian "naked philosophers"</note> purification all seem to mean the same thing, and indicate the mystery that the passions of the body must be subdued so that one may be able to understand divine things. We have deduced these things at length so that the <term>hieroglyphic doctrine</term> <note>The symbolic wisdom of the ancients</note> may be consistent with itself through the consensus of all writers, both sacred and profane.

But so that what has been said thus far may be confirmed by the opinion of the Hebrews, I shall subjoin here the discourse of **Rabbi Schabthe** <note>Shabbethai Donnolo, a 10th-century Jewish physician and mystic</note>, <margin>Rabbi Schabthe.</margin> in which he describes the **Holy Trinity** and its influence and emanation into the worldly orders quite appropriately: for he speaks thus. <margin>Description of the Holy Trinity and its influence and emanations into the worldly orders.</margin>

> *And behold, that which we explained in the earlier chapters is clear to us: namely the mystery that the Sages of the <term>Kabbalah</term> <note>Jewish mystical tradition</note> or Theology have said—that the three primary <term>Numerations</term> <note>The Sefirot, or divine attributes/emanations</note>, which are the **Supreme Crown** <note>Keter</note>, **Wisdom** <note>Hokhmah</note>, and **Intelligence** <note>Binah</note>, are in equal dignity as if they were most highly one single thing. It must also be noticed why they said they are in equal dignity as if they were most highly One thing, and did not say they were "one" properly and simply (even though all the Numerations are Unity), for this reason: For although the three primary ones—Supreme Crown, Wisdom, and Intelligence, which are three Minds—are nothing but the opening and diffusion of the center, which is contained by three shrines in the mystery of the primordial light, the most splendid light, and the light most splendid of all the most splendid, which are united to the center itself in the mystery of the radical and essential name, just as we explained in Chapter 1. This is because that center is simply and absolutely one in all its parts, and all things are contained in it, namely in its unity. Yet the three Minds which are diffused from it are nothing but the opening of the center, which reveals the hidden, the stored away, and the occult that is within its own selfhood; and there is no difference between them, except that the center consists of three shrines which are contained in the hiddenness, namely in the unity of the center. But in the three Minds they are diffused and revealed, because each of them is a Mind by itself, and because of this they are in equal dignity, as if they were most highly one thing. Yet they are not "one" properly and simply as they are in the center itself; because in the center itself no shrine is discerned, but only the unity of the center. However, these three shrines have already come forth and are now distinct into three shrines, which are the Supreme Crown, Wisdom, and Intelligence—three distinct shrines, I say. Nor should it be objected: "If so, they will not be in equal dignity as if most highly one thing, but will be in equal dignity as three." This is no objection. Because these three (Minds, I say) are nothing but the manifestation of the Unity of the center, and they unite themselves to their root in such a way that they are nothing other than the Unity of the center; and nothing is manifest except that which lay hidden in secret. Because of this, they are in equal dignity as if most highly one thing; as if he were to say they are equal in dignity just like the Unity of the center, because they came forth from one center, and the center is revealed in them. And from this is also perceived the Unity of all the Numerations, since although these three Minds are close to their emanator (namely, Him who caused them to emanate), behold, because of...*

<meta>This page concludes the discussion of the ten Sephirot (divine emanations) from the previous section and transitions into the formal Epilogue of the entire work. The author, Athanasius Kircher, uses the language of Christian Neoplatonism to explain Jewish mystical concepts before reflecting on his twenty-year labor completing the "Oedipus Aegyptiacus."</meta>

*...because of their proximity, their light is exceedingly great; so much so that it is impossible for created beings to enjoy their light. For this reason, it was necessary for it to extend and diffuse itself into branches—into the Head, the Middle, and the End—which are the seven Numerations <note>original: "Numerationes," referring to the Sefirot</note>: Magnificence or Mercy <note>Chesed</note>, Strength or Severity <note>Gevurah</note>, Beauty <note>Tiferet</note>, Victory <note>Netzach</note>, Triumph or Eternity <note>Hod</note>, Glory <note>Yesod</note>, and Foundation; and the Kingdom <note>Malkuth</note> to manifest their Sanctuaries to created beings, so that they might enjoy them, insofar as there are three degrees or orders:*
*The first Order is the mystery of the center; the second Order is the mystery of the three Minds <note>The higher triad of Keter, Chokmah, and Binah</note>; the third Order is the mystery of the diffusion of the Minds into the seven Numerations (that is, the attributes common to the three Minds) which all together make up the ten Numerations; and they are one, three, and seven. And behold, in this respect all are at once a perfect Unity, because the center manifested its sanctuaries in the three Minds, and the three Minds were manifested in the seven Numerations; and whatever is found in the seven Numerations is also found in the three Minds, and whatever is found in the three Minds is also found in the unity of the center, and is found also in the Infinity <note>Ein Sof</note>; blessed be He. And there is no difference between them—between the Numerations, I say—except that in the seven Numerations they are in the manifest, while in the three Minds, because of the magnificence of their light, they lie hidden in the concealed. And even in the three Minds, with respect to the center and because of the magnificence of its light, they (the Minds, that is) are in the manifest, while in the center itself they lie hidden in the concealed. And so also the center with respect to the Infinity, blessed be He; because for the Infinity, with respect to His most magnificent light, there is no end nor limit: those others are indeed in the manifest. But in the Infinity, blessed be He, they lie hidden in the concealed even unto the every "non-end" of infinity and "non-limit." All are one power of His highest, most perfect, and most absolute unity, which without end or limit encompasses the whole number of ten in the mystery of the unity of the Infinity, blessed be He, and reveals the power of His unity in the mystery of the Withdrawal <note>Tzimtzum</note> through the mystery of the ten; and nothing is in the manifest except that which also lies hidden in the concealed; and just as in the concealed that power is one, so also in the manifest it is one power. And let these things suffice for suggesting our intention to the Reader.*

## EPILOGUE.

At last, through the immense windings of an inexhaustible Ocean, through the rapid whirlpools of the vast deep; through rocks and inaccessible precipices, through the pathless and unknown recesses of the widest sea—having tamed the fierce portents of monsters by the assistance of divine grace, and having slain the monstrous Sphinx—we draw in our sails and enter the long-desired harbor, sought with the restlessness of an anxious mind, and finally found by the singular protection of the Divine Power. Having endured the tide of twenty years, I say, we enter the harbor: the unique fulfillment of our will. How many labors, how many perplexities, how many sweats, how many dangers, and what crises of affairs we have exhausted in our desire for this, a grateful posterity (unless I am mistaken) will recognize from the present specimen of a Work attempted until now by no one else, as far as I know. Prudent men of exquisite judgment...

# RECAPITULATION OF THE ENTIRE WORK. EPILOGUE <note>original: "ANACEPHALÆOSIS TOTIUS OPERIS. EPILOG"</note>

Powerful men, whose industry has at times toiled in unearthing similar unknown things, will—as if taught by their own experience—candidly confess how difficult and full of risk a task it is to attempt unknown paths and to commit oneself without a guide to solitudes filled with every kind of monster; and thus, if they do not extol everything, they will at least praise the effort in unearthing all things.

And these are the things which I thought should be said concerning the Wisdom of the Egyptians <note>original: "Ægyptiorum Sapientia"</note>, veiled in hieroglyphic symbols, as far as the weak powers of my intellect permitted. Furthermore, nothing remains except that, with eyes and hands removed from the table of interpretations and lifted up to heaven, I should establish for Thee, Triune God, giver of all good things and most beneficent Father, for so great a benefit, not a hecatomb <note>A great public sacrifice, literally of a hundred oxen</note>, nor burnt offerings of bulls or calves, but a sacrifice of a pure mind instituted by divine love, with the humble obedience of the heart. For Thou alone art He who makes the tongues of infants eloquent; Thou alone instillest into the human mind little sparks emanating from the vein of Thy light and the spring of life, by which it is inflamed to search into the incomprehensible magnitude of Thy works. Inflamed by these, I have completed this work, undertaken by the help of Thy kindness; Thou didst inspire me when I was not yet willing, so that I might will it; Thou didst assist the efforts of a good will, so that I might act, Thou who workest both the willing and the perfecting in Thy people. 

Therefore, let the Work return to Thee, which flowed from Thee. If there is anything good in it, it is Thine; if anything evil, it is mine. Whatever it may finally be, I, Thy humble and dejected creature, ash and cinder and nothingness, as I acknowledge receiving it from Thy supreme, unending, and incomprehensible goodness, so also I demand with all the prayers of my soul that it may yield solely to the honor and glory of Thy most excellent Majesty. My mind has always been ready to philosophize as correctly as possible; if, therefore, anything unworthy of Thy counsels has been brought forth by me, mayest Thou deign to inspire me to amend it, according to Thy infinite goodness. If, having followed the sacred mysteries of Ethnic Theology <note>The study of pagan or non-Christian religions</note>, I have fallen into rashness in searching the incomprehensible abyss of Thy judgments, or if I have sought my own praise in a Work destined for Thy glory, I earnestly pray that Thou wouldst forgive me according to that clemency which is infinite. If, finally, I have ignorantly brought forward anything not everywhere consistent with the Orthodox Faith and the Most Holy Roman Church, Thy Spouse, I wish all of that to be erased, rejected, and revoked. It remains now that, as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of Egyptian wisdom</note> once did, I should likewise establish for Thee a Thrice-Holy hymn <note>original: "Trisagion"</note> as an everlasting trophy of my love toward Thee.

# THE AUTHOR
## TO THE READER.

I attach no catalog of typographical errors here, because none occur in this third volume that might offend you, or which, if they should offend, you could not easily correct yourself. Indeed, you may credit this to the diligence of our already oft-praised <term>typesetter</term><note>original: "Typothetae"</note>, Zacharias Dominicus Acsamitek of Kronenfeld, a German-Bohemian from Prague. Farewell.
